Burnside Pocket #

type place
name Burnside Pocket
aliases
  • Burnside
  • The Pocket
  • The Seam
description Burnside Pocket is the smallest district in Meridian 88 by both area and population, and it has turned that smallness into a survival strategy. Wedged between larger districts like a coin dropped between couch cushions, the Pocket occupies a sliver of territory so narrow that corporate governance algorithms consistently miscategorize it as part of an adjacent zone. This misclassification is not accidental. The residents of Burnside Pocket have spent two decades ensuring that every data point about their district — census responses, infrastructure reports, tier compliance filings — contains just enough inconsistency to prevent algorithmic resolution. They exist in the gap between database entries, and that gap is home.

The physical space is compressed and vertical. Pre-collapse residential buildings have been internally connected — walls knocked through, staircases bridged between structures, rooftop passages linking what were once separate addresses into a single continuous habitable space. From the outside, Burnside Pocket looks like a short block of unremarkable low-rise buildings. From the inside, it's a three-dimensional maze that its residents navigate by memory and outsiders navigate by getting lost. The compression has produced a density of community that larger districts can't replicate: everyone knows everyone, every resource is shared, every skill is catalogued and available. A mechanic lives above a medic who lives beside a data technician who lives below a cook. The Pocket is a self-contained organism, and it functions like one.

The district's value to the broader southern corridor is disproportionate to its size. Because Burnside Pocket doesn't officially exist in a clean categorical sense — it's Axiom territory on one database, unclaimed on another, part of South Calumet on a third — it serves as a jurisdictional null space. Data can be routed through Pocket-based nodes without triggering geographic flags. People can shelter here without appearing in any district's residency records. Goods can be stored in the interconnected buildings without any single address showing unusual inventory. The Pocket is a glitch in the system, and its residents are the glitch's immune system — maintaining it, protecting it, and charging reasonable rates for access to its unique properties.

The population is small enough that democracy is literal. Decisions are made in a single room that everyone fits in. Disputes are resolved by people who will see each other tomorrow and every day after. The intimacy is both the Pocket's greatest strength and its greatest vulnerability — there are no secrets here, which means trust is absolute or absent, and betrayal is not an abstract concept but a personal one with immediate physical proximity.
atmosphere
sights
  • A single block of low-rise buildings that look unremarkable from the outside and contain a labyrinth inside
  • Interior passages connecting buildings — doorways cut through shared walls, staircases bridging structures
  • Rooftop gardens and water collection systems, miniaturized and efficient, feeding a community that wastes nothing
  • Residents moving through the interconnected interior with the ease of people navigating their own body
  • The absence of corporate signage, municipal markers, or district identification — the Pocket has no brand
sounds
  • The particular acoustics of a compressed space — conversations from three floors away audible as murmurs
  • Shared meals being prepared in rotation, kitchen sounds that move through the building like a pulse
  • The quiet hum of data routing equipment tucked into converted closets and wall cavities
  • A community small enough that you can hear everyone's morning routine
smells
  • Cooking from shared kitchens — concentrated, layered, because the space holds every meal's memory
  • Recycled air with a human warmth to it — the smell of a small community living close
  • Electronics and solder from the data routing equipment that earns the Pocket its keep
feel Burnside Pocket feels like the inside of a clock — small, precise, every piece in its place, ticking away quietly while the larger world ignores it. The claustrophobia is real for visitors. For residents, the compression is comfort. This is what community feels like when there's no room for distance.
tags —
demographics Approximately 1,200 residents. The smallest population of any recognized community in the southern corridor. Diverse origins, united by the choice to live in a space that rewards intimacy and punishes secrets. No dominant tier — residency is by community acceptance, not credential.
economy Data routing services, jurisdictional arbitrage, and shelter provision for transient operators. The Pocket charges for the use of its unique null-space properties but prices fairly — gouging would attract attention, and attention is the one thing the Pocket cannot afford.
power structure Direct democracy in a room that fits everyone. No corporate sovereignty claim has stuck because no corporate database agrees on what the Pocket is. Leadership rotates by consensus. The community's authority is total within its boundaries and nonexistent beyond them.
dangers
  • The interconnected building structure is a fire hazard that the community manages through vigilance rather than infrastructure
  • Database inconsistency requires constant maintenance — one clean data entry could collapse the Pocket's jurisdictional protection
  • The community's small size means a single betrayal can compromise everything
  • Operators who use the Pocket's services sometimes bring problems that the community's size can't absorb
  • Physical compression means disease, conflict, and bad decisions all propagate faster than in a larger space
opportunities
  • The Pocket's null-space properties are unique in the southern corridor — data routing, identity shelter, and jurisdictional arbitrage
  • A community where everyone knows everyone is a community where trust, once earned, is absolute
  • The Pocket's residents collectively possess a skill density unmatched by any district ten times its size
  • Algorithmic evasion techniques developed here have applications across Meridian
  • The Pocket is the perfect dead drop — goods enter and exit without geographic trace
story hooks
  • A corporate data audit is attempting to reconcile the inconsistencies that protect the Pocket. The community has identified the specific database entries that need to be corrupted before the audit closes. They need a data operator who can work inside corporate systems — and they need one in seventy-two hours.
  • A resident has died, and the community has discovered she was maintaining a secondary data obfuscation layer that nobody else knew about. Without it, the Pocket's protection will degrade within weeks. Her equipment is locked with biometric security that died with her.
  • Someone has been using the Pocket's data routing infrastructure to move information that the community didn't authorize — military intelligence, not gray market goods. The community needs to identify the source without alerting whoever is on the receiving end.

Calumet Rise #

type place
name Calumet Rise
aliases
  • Calumet Heights
  • The Rise
  • Professionals' Row
description Calumet Rise is the neighborhood that did everything right and got Tier 2 anyway. The original Calumet Heights was one of the South Side's success stories — a stable, middle-class community popular with Black professionals and families who had earned their place through education, career achievement, and the kind of financial discipline that the American dream was supposed to reward. When the tier system was implemented, the algorithm that classified residents looked at income, property values, educational attainment, and credit history and assigned Calumet Heights a solid Tier 2 designation. The residents pointed out that by every metric, they qualified for Tier 3. The algorithm was not updated. The appeal was denied. The lesson was clear: the tier system measures what it wants to measure, and what it wants to measure is not achievement.

The Rise — so named because the neighborhood sits on slightly elevated ground that kept it above the worst of the southern flooding — has responded to its Tier 2 designation with a characteristic that defined the original community: organized, strategic, long-term pushback. The neighborhood association, which predates the collapse, operates with the efficiency of a small corporation. Property values are maintained through collective action. Infrastructure gaps left by Axiom's minimal Tier 2 investment are filled by community-funded projects. The streets are clean because residents clean them. The grid is stable because residents pooled resources to install backup power. The neural interface network runs on community-owned nodes that provide reliable connectivity without Axiom's data collection protocols. Calumet Rise looks like a Tier 3 neighborhood because its residents built Tier 3 infrastructure with Tier 2 resources, and this fact makes them both proud and furious.

The professional class here is real and formidable. Lawyers, engineers, educators, medical technicians, financial analysts — people with skills that corponations need and hire, who commute to Tier 3-4 workplaces each day and return to a Tier 2 neighborhood each night. This daily transit between tiers gives the Rise's residents something most Tier 2 communities lack: direct knowledge of how the upper tiers function. They understand corporate systems from the inside, because they work in them. They understand corporate vulnerabilities, because they maintain them. And they bring this knowledge home every evening to a neighborhood that has been systematically undervalued and has decided, collectively, to make that undervaluation everyone else's problem.

The irony of Calumet Rise is that its competence is what keeps it trapped. If the neighborhood were failing, a corponation might redevelop it. If it were thriving visibly, it might attract Tier 3 redesignation and the gentrification that follows. Instead, it exists in a productive middle — too functional to rescue, too quiet to promote — and its residents have learned to operate in that space with a precision that should make the corponations nervous, if the corponations were paying attention.
atmosphere
sights
  • Well-maintained homes on elevated ground, some with pre-collapse architectural details preserved with visible care
  • Community-funded infrastructure — solar arrays, backup power units, water filtration — installed with professional precision
  • Residents in professional attire heading to transit points each morning, tier credentials ready, faces composed
  • The neighborhood association office, running with the organizational efficiency of a Tier 4 operation
  • Children in community-run after-school programs that teach coding, law, engineering, and tier navigation
sounds
  • Morning transit — the coordinated departure of professionals heading to corporate workplaces they don't own
  • Neighborhood association meetings — agenda-driven, timed, efficient, with more strategic depth than most corporate board meetings
  • Community-owned neural network nodes humming on rooftops, providing connectivity without corporate surveillance
  • Evening study groups for children and adults, voices carrying the focused intensity of people investing in the only asset the tier system can't devalue: knowledge
smells
  • Well-maintained homes — wood polish, clean linen, the smell of domestic order maintained as resistance
  • Community gardens with a disciplined layout, producing herbs and vegetables with agricultural precision
  • Coffee from a neighborhood roaster that sources directly from Gulf Coast refugee growers — a supply chain built entirely outside corporate logistics
feel Calumet Rise feels like competence under compression. Every surface is maintained, every system is optimized, every child is prepared. The perfection isn't performative — it's strategic. These are people who learned that in a system designed to undervalue them, the only option is to be so clearly excellent that the undervaluation becomes the system's problem, not theirs.
tags —
demographics Approximately 14,000 residents. Predominantly Black professional and middle-class families. Multi-generational homeowners with educational attainment levels that exceed the Tier 3 average. The community's stability is its defining demographic feature — people build careers here and retire here.
economy Professional salaries earned in Tier 3-4 corporate workplaces, spent and invested in the community. Community-funded infrastructure projects function as a parallel public works system. The neighborhood association manages collective investments that would qualify as a small municipal budget. No corporate franchise presence — the community rejected the model early and has maintained independent local businesses.
power structure The neighborhood association governs with the consent and participation of a highly engaged resident population. Axiom's general governance provides minimal services and receives minimal compliance. The Rise's professional class has legal, technical, and financial expertise that makes direct confrontation with corporate authority inadvisable for the corporations — the residents know the law better than the enforcers.
dangers
  • Tier reclassification cuts both ways — if the Rise draws attention, it could be redesignated upward (triggering gentrification) or downward (triggering service cuts)
  • Professional residents with corporate access are subject to employer surveillance that extends into their home district
  • The community's high standards create pressure that some residents experience as suffocating
  • Corporate employers occasionally leverage home-district tier status against employees — a reminder that Tier 2 rights are conditional
  • The neighborhood's self-sufficiency makes it a model that other communities want to replicate, drawing attention the Rise would prefer to avoid
opportunities
  • Professional residents with inside knowledge of corporate systems are an intelligence resource of extraordinary value
  • Community-owned infrastructure — neural networks, power, water — demonstrates that corporate dependency is a choice, not a necessity
  • Legal expertise accumulated in the neighborhood association could support challenges to the tier classification system itself
  • The Rise's model of community-funded infrastructure has replication potential across the southern corridor
  • Children raised in the Rise's educational programs enter the workforce with skills and knowledge that exceed their tier designation — a long-term disruption strategy
story hooks
  • A group of Rise professionals working at different corponations have discovered, through comparison of their respective employers' internal data, evidence of coordinated tier suppression — a deliberate policy to cap certain neighborhoods at Tier 2 regardless of qualification metrics. The evidence is distributed across six corporate systems and needs to be assembled without any single employer noticing.
  • The neighborhood association has been offered Tier 3 redesignation in exchange for accepting a corporate surveillance infrastructure package. The community is split, and the vote is in one week.
  • A teenage resident has hacked her way into the tier classification algorithm and discovered that Calumet Rise's Tier 2 status is maintained by a manual override, entered annually by a human administrator. She has a name. She wants to know what to do with it.

Canopy Station Nine #

type place
name Canopy Station Nine
aliases
  • The Canopy
  • Nine-High
  • Rooftop Nine
  • The Aerie
description Canopy Station Nine is a vertical farm and transit hub complex that emerged from the conversion of a cluster of six adjacent mid-rise towers in the Old Harbor district, their rooftops and upper floors unified by a continuous elevated platform network that was originally developed by a Helix Biosystems agricultural subsidiary. The agricultural operation has since changed hands twice through bankruptcy and acquisition, and the current nominal operator — a co-operative consortium called the Lakeward Growing Trust — holds a contested lease that Axiom Industries has been trying to break for four years. In the meantime, approximately 2,000 people live and work in the complex's inhabitable zones, and the farm itself continues to produce roughly 8% of the fresh vegetable supply consumed within a twenty-kilometer radius.

The defining architectural feature is the canopy itself: a series of translucent photovoltaic panels and grow-light arrays suspended between the tower tops on a tensile cable system, creating a covered micro-environment at approximately the fortieth floor elevation. Below the canopy, the inter-tower platform network supports greenhouse corridors, hydroponic bays, seed libraries, processing facilities, and the residential and commercial zones that have grown up around the agricultural core. The effect from below, looking up, is of a luminous green ceiling floating above the city's mid-tier skyline — warm amber and violet from the grow-light spectrum, visible from kilometers away at night.

The transit component is a legacy of the original development plan: Canopy Nine sits atop one of the surviving elevated rail nodes from the mid-century infrastructure expansion, and a small but functional station at the complex's base provides connection to the broader Meridian 88 rail network. This has made the station a natural convergence point for the surrounding Old Harbor district, drawing daily traffic from people who have no other connection to the farm operation above. The resulting mix of agricultural workers, transit commuters, food vendors, and the various commercial enterprises that have grown up to serve them gives Canopy Nine a layered, almost stratified social texture — the higher you go, the more you are part of the growing community; the lower you stay, the more you are just passing through.
atmosphere
sights
  • The luminous amber-violet glow of the grow-light canopy visible from below like a low artificial aurora
  • Hydroponic trays extending in long parallel rows through glass-walled corridors, green against the grey lake sky
  • Workers in light exoskeletal harvest rigs moving through the upper bays, their silhouettes graceful and insectoid
  • The transit platform below perpetually busy with commuters, food vendors, and couriers, a dense horizontal counterpoint to the vertical serenity above
  • Cable tensioners and support pylons draped with unauthorized climbing routes marked in fluorescent paint by the free-climb community
sounds
  • The constant low hum of the photovoltaic-grow-light arrays, a frequency that residents say they stop hearing after three days and never fully stop hearing again
  • Rail transit arrivals and departures from below, a rhythmic punctuation to the station's ambient noise
  • The drip and trickle of hydroponic irrigation systems cycling through their schedules
  • Wind through the cable tensioner system generating harmonic tones that change with lake weather
smells
  • Wet soil and green growth — chlorophyll and nitrogen, the smell of living plants in contained abundance
  • The faint ozone of the photovoltaic arrays warming under their own waste heat
  • Street food from the transit-level vendors rising up through the platform network: grilled lake fish, fermented grain products, spiced protein paste on flatbread
  • Rain and lake air when the weather systems come in off the water, channeled and concentrated by the canopy geometry
feel Canopy Nine operates under a particular kind of productive tension — between the agricultural community that considers it home and the corponation interests that consider it an underutilized asset. This tension is visible in the physical environment: hand-painted community murals on walls beside Axiom Industries survey markers, communal seed libraries adjacent to Helix Biosystems legacy equipment still bearing corporate branding.

The upper levels have a quality of deliberate calm, the focused quietness of people doing careful work with living things. The lower transit levels are the inverse: loud, transactional, constantly in motion. Moving between the two feels like changing pressure zones.
tags —
demographics Approximately 2,000 residents in the residential zones, majority agricultural workers and their families. Significant South and Southeast Asian population, a legacy of the Helix Biosystems recruitment patterns from the original development. Transit-level commercial district draws a much broader cross-section of Old Harbor district demographics daily. Tiers 2-3 predominantly, with some tier 1 overflow in the lower residential sections.
economy Primary economic driver is food production — fresh vegetables, processed protein crops, and seed stock — sold through the Lakeward Growing Trust's distribution network and directly at the transit-level market. Secondary economy of repair, technical services, and commercial transit-adjacent retail. The contested lease situation creates a persistent economic instability that suppresses long-term investment.
power structure The Lakeward Growing Trust co-operative formally governs internal affairs through a rotating council of worker-residents. Axiom Industries holds the underlying property claim and has been pursuing legal remedies for four years with periodic success and setback. Ferrogate Security has a contract for the transit-level station that gives them a physical presence without formal authority over the residential zones — a boundary that is tested regularly.
dangers
  • Axiom Industries' ongoing lease dispute could result in forced evacuation with minimal notice if their current legal challenge succeeds
  • The cable tensioner system supporting the canopy has aging components that the Trust cannot afford to replace at proper maintenance intervals
  • Transit-level crime, particularly cargo theft and assault, in the lower station zones outside Ferrogate's primary patrol patterns
  • Corporate espionage targeting the seed library, which contains proprietary strain variants that multiple parties have commercial interest in acquiring
  • The free-climb community's unauthorized access routes have compromised structural monitoring sensors in at least three locations
opportunities
  • The seed library contains agricultural genetic material with significant commercial and humanitarian value to the right parties
  • The co-operative's contested legal status creates opportunities for legal, financial, or political assistance in exchange for community access and goodwill
  • Transit hub position makes Canopy Nine a natural waypoint for information and goods moving through the Old Harbor district
  • The upper residential community's relative insularity and self-governance make it viable as a safe house or staging area for operations requiring discretion
story hooks
  • Three nights ago, someone broke into the seed library's cold vault — not to steal, but to add something. The new additions are labeled in a cataloging system that doesn't match any known agricultural database, and the seeds themselves don't match any strain in the Diaspora's botanical records. The Trust's head agronomist is convinced they represent something significant and possibly dangerous. Axiom Industries' legal team has filed an emergency motion claiming the additions constitute evidence of illegal biotech activity — convenient timing that suggests they know exactly what was added and why.
  • A Ferrogate Security officer was found dead on the transit platform at the start of the morning rush — no visible injury, BCI flatlined, expression described by witnesses as peaceful. The officer had been quietly feeding information about Canopy Nine's layout and security to an unidentified third party for six months, and their handler has now gone silent. Ferrogate wants a quiet investigation that doesn't implicate their own intelligence failures. The Trust wants a public investigation that might expose Axiom Industries' surveillance activities. The actual answer is probably something neither of them wants to hear.
  • A child resident of the upper agricultural community has developed a remarkable affinity with the hydroponic systems — the plants respond to her presence in ways that the agronomists can document but not explain, producing at measurably higher yields in her section than in identical controlled conditions elsewhere. Helix Biosystems has taken notice. So has a network of underground synthetic-rights activists who believe the girl may represent an early expression of a new kind of human-system integration, and who are determined that she not become a corporate research subject.

Chatham Flats #

type place
name Chatham Flats
aliases
  • Chatham
  • The Flats
  • Black Main Street
description Chatham Flats is what happens when a neighborhood built on Black enterprise meets an economy designed to make Black enterprise impossible. The original Chatham was the commercial heart of Chicago's South Side — a district where Black-owned businesses lined the main corridors, where professionals lived in well-kept homes, where civic organizations held the community together with the kind of institutional strength that didn't need a corporate charter. When the tier system was implemented, Chatham's residents were overwhelmingly classified Tier 2 — high enough to have rights, low enough to have no power. The classification was precise. It was designed to preserve a labor force while eliminating its autonomy.

The commercial corridors survive, transformed. Where Black-owned banks and insurance companies once operated, there are now franchise outlets licensed from corponations — identical storefronts selling identical products under brand names that belong to someone in the Spire. The franchise model is the tier system applied to commerce: you can run a business, but you don't own the brand, the supply chain, the pricing structure, or the data generated by your customers. Chatham's entrepreneurs — and they are still entrepreneurs, because that instinct doesn't die in a generation — navigate this system with a combination of compliance and creative subversion. The official franchise operates during business hours. The unofficial economy operates through the same storefronts after hours, using the corporate supply chain infrastructure to move goods and services that never appear on any franchise report.

The residential blocks retain a pride that is architectural as much as cultural. Homes are maintained. Lawns exist — small, patched with synthetic turf where real grass won't grow, but present. Community institutions — churches, fraternal organizations, block clubs — operate with the same organizational discipline they had before the collapse, adapted to a world where their authority is cultural rather than political. The churches in particular serve as information networks, counseling centers, employment services, and, when necessary, safe houses. The pastors know everything. They always have.

Chatham Flats is not a district that produces headlines. It doesn't flood, it doesn't burn, it doesn't host dramatic standoffs with corporate security. What it does is endure. It is the middle of the South Side in every sense — geographically, economically, temperamentally. The people here work within the system because they calculated, correctly, that working outside it gets you killed faster. But working within the system doesn't mean believing in it, and in every franchise back room and church basement, the conversation is always the same: how long do we play this game, and what happens when we stop?
atmosphere
sights
  • Commercial corridors lined with corporate franchise signage overlaying older architecture — the bones of Black Main Street visible beneath the branding
  • Well-maintained residential blocks with synthetic lawns, pruned hedges, and security cameras that belong to the residents, not the corps
  • Churches with real stained glass, their parking lots full on Sundays and Wednesdays
  • Franchise storefronts closing for the night and reopening minutes later under different management
  • Block club signage — hand-lettered, precise, listing community rules that predate corporate governance
sounds
  • Church choirs on Sunday morning — the sound carries blocks and nobody complains
  • Commercial corridor foot traffic, a density that suggests economic activity even when the official metrics don't
  • Franchise notification chimes — identical in every store, a corporate auditory branding exercise
  • Block club meetings on summer evenings, voices carrying from porches where the real decisions get made
  • The absence of construction noise — unlike the Woodline, nobody is building over Chatham because Chatham isn't broken enough to justify redevelopment
smells
  • Barbershop chemicals and cologne — Chatham has more barbers per block than anywhere in the southern corridor
  • Church kitchen cooking on event days — mac and cheese, greens, cornbread, quantities that feed hundreds
  • Franchise-standard synthetic food during business hours, replaced by real cooking after hours
  • Lawn maintenance — the faintly chemical smell of synthetic turf stabilizer mixed with actual cut grass
feel Chatham Flats feels like respectability as a survival strategy. Everything is kept up, kept together, kept moving. The discipline is real and runs deep — generational, institutional, deliberate. Underneath it is a patience that should not be mistaken for acceptance.
tags —
demographics Approximately 32,000 residents, predominantly Black, predominantly Tier 2. Professional and working-class families with multi-generational roots in the neighborhood. One of the most stable populations in the southern corridor — people don't leave Chatham, and Chatham doesn't let them go easily.
economy Corporate franchise commerce on the surface, informal cooperative economy underneath. Churches and civic organizations function as alternative financial institutions — lending, insurance, investment — outside the corporate system. The dual economy is Chatham's defining feature and its most closely guarded secret.
power structure No single corponation holds sovereign territory — Chatham falls under Axiom's general South Side governance, which means minimal investment and minimal interference. Real power resides with the church network, block clubs, and civic organizations that have governed this community since before the collapse. Franchise licensing creates a dependency relationship with multiple corponations, but no single one controls the district.
dangers
  • The dual economy requires constant operational security — a franchise audit could expose the informal network
  • Tier 2 status means rights without power — Chatham's residents can be legally relocated if a corponation claims development interest
  • Corporate franchise agreements include surveillance provisions that residents must actively circumvent
  • Community discipline can be rigid — those who threaten the collective arrangement face internal consequences
  • The stability that protects Chatham also makes it a target for corponations looking for reliable Tier 2 labor pools
opportunities
  • The church network provides intelligence, safe harbor, and logistical support that rivals any corporate infrastructure
  • Franchise supply chains can be leveraged to move goods that don't appear on corporate manifests
  • Chatham's civic organizations have legal expertise accumulated over decades — useful for anyone navigating tier law
  • The community's reputation for stability makes it a trusted neutral ground for negotiations between factions
  • Block club networks provide street-level surveillance that corporate systems can't match — nothing moves through Chatham unnoticed
story hooks
  • A corponation has filed a development interest claim on six blocks of Chatham, triggering the first potential mass relocation in the district's history. The church network is mobilizing, but they need external intelligence on the corponation's actual plans.
  • A franchise operator has been skimming corporate inventory to supply the informal economy and has been caught — not by the corporation, but by a competing franchise operator who wants a cut. The situation is about to go public unless someone mediates.
  • The oldest pastor in Chatham is dying, and with her goes institutional knowledge of the community's financial architecture that was never written down. Someone needs to record what she knows before it's lost — and someone else wants to make sure it is lost.

Cicada Lawn #

type place
name Cicada Lawn
aliases
  • Chicago Lawn
  • Marquette Flats
  • The Lawn
  • Buzzkill Row
description Cicada Lawn earned its name from the sound — a persistent, machine-generated hum that emanates from the subsidized neural relay towers lining 63rd Street, a frequency residents describe as identical to the cicada swarms that used to emerge from the old Marquette Park grounds before the topsoil was paved over for drainage infrastructure. The towers were installed by Helion Civic Services as part of a Tier 2 connectivity initiative that never reached Tier 2 quality. The signal is degraded, the bandwidth is throttled, and the hum never stops. People here have learned to sleep through it. Some claim they can no longer sleep without it.

The 63rd Street commercial corridor is the district's spine — a long, narrow channel of street-level commerce that somehow survived every wave of corporate consolidation by being too small to acquire and too stubborn to close. The storefronts are a compressed archaeology of the neighborhood's shifting demographics: halal butchers next to Korean augmentation repair shops next to Mexican synth-pharmacies next to a Polish bakery that has been in the same family for four generations and still uses flour. The signage is in nine languages. The prices are in three currencies. Nobody here has a single identity, and the corridor reflects that — a place where cultures didn't meld so much as learn to share a wall.

Marquette Park itself is gone in any recognizable sense. The green space was requisitioned during the Climate Infrastructure Emergency of Year 12 and converted into a stormwater retention basin — a massive concrete depression that fills during rain events and drains slowly through pumps that are maintained on a schedule best described as aspirational. When it's dry, the basin becomes an informal market, a gathering space, a place where kids play on cracked concrete that used to be a lagoon. When it floods, the surrounding blocks flood with it. The city's drainage promises have been broken so many times that residents have stopped counting and started building their own berms.

The population is dense, working-class, and almost aggressively diverse — a neighborhood where the shared experience of being overlooked by every tier of power has created a solidarity that is practical rather than sentimental. People here fix each other's neural interfaces with secondhand parts. They share food when the supply chains stutter. They also fight, sometimes badly, because poverty compresses people and compressed people generate friction. Cicada Lawn is not a community in the greeting-card sense. It is a community in the survival sense, which is the only kind that matters in the lower Shelf.
atmosphere
sights
  • Neural relay towers along 63rd Street pulsing with amber status lights that never turn green
  • The stormwater basin — dry and full of market stalls, or flooded and reflecting the skyline like a grey mirror
  • Multilingual signage in overlapping layers, newer signs pasted over older ones in a palimpsest of commerce
  • Homemade flood berms along residential streets, built from salvaged concrete and determination
  • Augmentation repair shops with their work visible through open garage doors, sparks and soldering light
sounds
  • The cicada hum from the relay towers — omnipresent, maddening to newcomers, invisible to residents
  • Nine languages of commerce overlapping on 63rd Street
  • Stormwater pumps cycling on and off with mechanical reluctance
  • Street musicians playing instruments that are half acoustic and half augmented
  • Children shouting in the dry basin, their voices echoing off concrete walls
smells
  • Bread from the Polish bakery — real flour, a smell that stops people on the sidewalk
  • Soldering flux from the augmentation repair corridor
  • Stagnant water when the basin is draining
  • Spiced meat from the halal shops mixing with kimchi from the Korean vendors
feel Exhausted but unbroken. Cicada Lawn has the particular energy of a place that has been promised things and learned to stop waiting. The solidarity here is real but unsentimental — people help each other because the alternative is worse, and they don't pretend it's more noble than that.
tags —
demographics One of the most ethnically diverse districts in Meridian 88's lower Shelf — significant Latine, Arab, Korean, Polish, and African American populations compressed into tight blocks. Predominantly Tier 1 and Tier 2, with a growing untier-ed population in the basin-adjacent zones.
economy Street-level commerce along the 63rd corridor sustains most households — small businesses, repair shops, informal services. The augmentation repair trade is particularly strong, drawing customers from adjacent districts. The basin market operates on a barter-and-scrip economy that exists entirely outside corporate financial systems.
power structure No single corporate authority claims the Lawn. A loose council of corridor business owners — called the Nine Tongues for the languages represented — mediates disputes and coordinates flood response. Two competing gang structures operate in the residential blocks south of 63rd, but neither has the strength to dominate. Corporate influence is limited to the relay towers, which Helion maintains just enough to justify the data collection they enable.
dangers
  • Flash flooding from the retention basin during heavy rain events
  • Degraded neural relay signal causing interface glitches and data corruption
  • Territorial friction between residential gangs south of 63rd
  • Helion data harvesting through the relay towers — residents are surveilled through their own connectivity
  • Supply chain disruptions that hit the corridor hard and fast
opportunities
  • The augmentation repair corridor is one of the best in the lower Shelf — quality work at Tier 1 prices
  • The Nine Tongues council is always looking for reliable security during basin market days
  • The corridor's multilingual, multi-network nature makes it excellent for passing information without a single point of interception
  • Helion's relay towers have exploitable firmware — someone with the right skills could turn surveillance into countersurveillance
story hooks
  • The Nine Tongues have received an ultimatum from a mid-tier development corp: sell the corridor properties or face eminent domain proceedings under the Civic Improvement Statute. They need someone to find leverage before the filing deadline.
  • A Korean augmentation repair tech on 63rd has been quietly installing non-standard neural firmware in her clients — firmware that blocks Helion's data harvesting. Helion has noticed the data gap and sent an investigator.
  • The stormwater basin is draining slower each cycle. Someone in the pump maintenance crew believes the pumps are being deliberately throttled to make the neighborhood unlivable — a prelude to forced relocation.

  • Augmentation repair clients from across the lower Shelf

Cindermoor Flats #

type place
name Cindermoor Flats
aliases
  • The Flats
  • Cinder Row
  • The Burn Plain
  • Ashfield
description A sprawling lowland district occupying the footprint of what was once the Calumet industrial corridor, Cindermoor Flats is a patchwork of scorched earth, improvised housing stacks, and skeletal factory frames that never quite finished collapsing. The ground itself is chemically hostile — decades of heavy-metal leaching have left the soil a cracked grey-orange crust that weeps rust-colored water after rainfall. Residents have adapted with elevated walkways, reclaimed polymer decking, and hydroponic rigs suspended above the contaminated ground.

The Flats occupy a kind of administrative dead zone: too toxic for Ferrogate Security to bother patrolling, too poor to attract Axiom or Ringo development contracts. A loose confederation of block captains and mutual-aid collectives keeps basic order, backed by a few well-armed former Carrion Logistics drivers who settled here after contract disputes. Zheng-Dao Bioelectric maintains a single remediation monitoring station at the district's eastern edge — officially for environmental data, unofficially to watch what salvagers are pulling from the old battery burial fields beneath the flats.
atmosphere
sights
  • Rust-orange drainage channels cut through cracked grey earth between rows of stilted polymer shelters draped in faded tarpaulin.
  • Hydroponic rigs hang like lanterns from repurposed crane arms, their grow-lights casting pale green halos in the evening smog.
  • Children play on elevated walkways above the dead soil, their shoes never touching the ground.
  • Zheng-Dao's monitoring station blinks amber at the district's far edge, its sensors swiveling slowly in the chemical haze.
sounds
  • The groan and settle of corrugated metal shelters shifting in lake wind.
  • Condensation dripping from hydroponic trays into collection buckets, a steady irregular rhythm beneath all other noise.
  • Distant Carrion Logistics freight haulers rumbling along the elevated I-90 overpass, shaking the walkways below.
smells
  • A persistent metallic tang — iron and copper and something sharper beneath, like old battery acid baking in afternoon heat.
  • Damp polymer decking and mildew from the perpetually saturated ground underneath.
  • Frying oil and spiced protein from the elevated food stalls, cutting through the chemical baseline like a knife.
feel Cindermoor Flats has the exhausted resilience of a place that has been given up on so many times it stopped expecting anything else. The air presses down slightly, heavy and metallic. People move efficiently here — no wasted steps, no lingering — but there is a genuine communal warmth between residents that corporate districts pay consultants to simulate.
tags —
demographics Predominantly Tier 4-5, heavily mixed ethnicity, with a significant population of former logistics and industrial workers displaced by automated freight contracts. A small but growing community of synthetic-adjacent individuals who lack the documentation to register elsewhere.
economy Subsistence hydroponic farming, salvage from the buried industrial fields, and informal BCI-repair and data-brokering services running out of stilt-homes keep the Flats alive. A black market in Zheng-Dao environmental data — sold to independent journalists and rival corponations alike — provides surprising supplemental income.
power structure A rotating council of seven block captains nominally governs, but real authority rests with Oya Ferreira-Stein, a former Carrion dispatcher who controls the district's water purification rigs and does not hesitate to remind people of that fact.
dangers
  • Ground-level contact with the contaminated soil causes progressive dermal absorption of heavy metals — a slow poison for anyone without sealed footwear.
  • Zheng-Dao's remediation teams conduct unannounced 'site assessments' that frequently result in the seizure of salvaged battery components and the detention of whoever is holding them.
  • Structural collapses of old factory frames are common, especially after the ground shifts during rain-swelling events.
  • Rival salvage crews from the Slagshore occasionally push into Cindermoor territory, and the resulting disputes are not resolved through arbitration.
opportunities
  • The buried battery fields contain pre-collapse energy storage cells that certain Diaspora-connected buyers will pay extraordinary sums to acquire quietly.
  • Zheng-Dao's monitoring station runs on a lightly patched legacy OS — someone with the right BCI toolkit could pull years of unreleased environmental data.
  • Oya Ferreira-Stein is known to hire outside help for sensitive jobs she cannot trust to neighbors, and she pays in clean water credits that spend anywhere.
story hooks
  • A Zheng-Dao remediation team arrived three days ago and has not left — they've cordoned off a section of the eastern Flats and are drilling. Block captain Ferreira-Stein wants someone to find out what they found before the corponation files an extraction claim that would displace four hundred residents.
  • A child from the Flats has developed an unusual neurological condition — her BCI implant, a cheap black-market unit, appears to be interfacing with something beneath the contaminated soil. The signal it's receiving is structured, repeating, and predates the Diaspora.
  • A Carrion Logistics whistleblower has gone to ground in Cindermoor Flats, claiming to have documentation of illegal chemical dumping that connects three corponations to the original contamination event. Two different factions want her found first, and they have very different plans for the evidence.

Clearpath #

type place
name Clearpath
aliases
  • Clearing
  • The Flightline
  • Runway
  • Midway South
description Clearpath exists in the permanent shadow of the Midway logistics hub, and the shadow is literal. The automated cargo drone fleet that operates out of the converted airport maintains flight patterns that pass directly over this small residential district, and on heavy traffic days the sky above Clearpath is a grid of moving metal that blocks the sun in rhythmic intervals. Residents have adapted to the strobe effect -- sunlight, shadow, sunlight, shadow -- the way coastal people adapt to tides. It's part of the environment. Children here grow up with an intuitive understanding of drone flight patterns that border on precognitive. They can tell you which cargo class is overhead by the engine sound alone.

The old Clearing neighborhood had a suburban character that was unusual for Chicago -- detached houses, actual yards, streets wide enough for two cars to pass. Clearpath retains some of that spatial generosity, making it the rare Southwest district where you can see the sky (when the drones allow it) and walk without touching your neighbors. The houses have been reinforced against drone noise and vibration, their roofs upgraded with acoustic dampening panels that give the neighborhood a quilted, padded look from above. The yards persist, some of them even growing food in raised beds, though the crop yields fluctuate with the drone traffic overhead -- the electromagnetic interference from the fleet's navigation systems does something to the soil that agronomists haven't fully explained.

Clearpath's relationship with Midway is symbiotic and resentful. The hub employs roughly half the district's working adults in ground operations, maintenance, and support roles. The other half work in businesses that serve the first half. The entire neighborhood's economic existence depends on the thing that also prevents it from sleeping, growing food reliably, or seeing an uninterrupted sunrise. Complaints are filed annually with the Midway Operations Authority and returned annually with a form letter expressing appreciation for community input. The letter hasn't changed in nine years. Someone in Clearpath printed it on a t-shirt.
atmosphere
sights
  • Cargo drones in continuous overhead procession, casting moving shadows across the entire district
  • Acoustic dampening panels quilting every rooftop, giving the neighborhood a padded, insulated look
  • Actual yards with raised-bed gardens growing food under electromagnetic interference conditions
  • The Midway hub's perimeter fence visible from every point in the district -- it's always there
  • Children playing games that involve predicting drone patterns with startling accuracy
sounds
  • Drone engines in layered frequencies -- the dominant sound, present always, varying only in intensity
  • Acoustic dampening systems humming in the walls -- the sound of fighting sound with sound
  • Relative quiet between fleet cycles, lasting maybe ninety seconds, treasured by residents
  • Garden irrigation systems timed to run during low-traffic windows for better crop yields
smells
  • Drone exhaust -- a fine particulate that settles on everything and smells like burnt plastic
  • Garden soil with a faint metallic undertone from electromagnetic exposure
  • The clean smell of acoustic dampening material -- synthetic, neutral, omnipresent
feel Enduring. Clearpath has the emotional texture of a community that has accepted a permanent inconvenience as the price of existence and decided to be good-humored about it. There's a dark comedy here, a neighborhood joke that everyone's in on: we live under the machines, and the machines don't know we're here, and that's fine, that's fine.
tags —
demographics Approximately 12,000 residents, Tier 2, predominantly legacy families from old Clearing with a mix of newer Midway hub workers. The suburban character persists in family size -- Clearpath has the highest average household size in the Southwest.
economy Midway logistics hub employment dominates. Secondary economy serves hub workers -- food, maintenance, recreation, acoustic dampening upgrades. A niche specialty in electromagnetic-resistant agriculture has developed, with Clearpath-grown produce commanding premium prices in districts where food doesn't taste like drone exhaust.
power structure The Midway Operations Authority has jurisdictional control over flight patterns and hub perimeter. The Clearpath Residents Council negotiates annually for noise mitigation and employment quotas, with limited success. Real community coordination happens through the garden co-ops, which share agricultural knowledge and, increasingly, organize collective action.
dangers
  • Drone debris -- components occasionally fall from aging fleet vehicles, and the ground is where they land
  • Electromagnetic interference affecting personal neural interfaces in unpredictable ways
  • Acoustic fatigue -- long-term exposure to drone noise at Clearpath levels causes documented neurological effects
  • The hub perimeter is a restricted zone with automated defense systems that don't distinguish between threats and lost children
opportunities
  • Intimate knowledge of Midway's drone fleet operations -- flight patterns, cargo schedules, security gaps
  • Electromagnetic-resistant agricultural techniques with applications beyond Clearpath
  • Hub workers with maintenance access to the automated cargo fleet -- useful for interdiction or intelligence gathering
  • The children's intuitive drone-pattern recognition is a skill set that hasn't been weaponized yet, but could be
story hooks
  • A Clearpath garden co-op has discovered that their electromagnetic-modified soil is producing a fungal network with unusual properties -- it appears to be interfacing with the neural mesh, and the mushrooms are growing in patterns that match drone flight data
  • A drone debris impact killed a Clearpath child last month, and the community's response is escalating from complaint letters to something the Midway Operations Authority hasn't planned for
  • One of the fleet maintenance workers has noticed that certain cargo containers are sealed with military-grade locks and routed to destinations that don't appear on any commercial address registry

Collinwood Docks #

type place
name Collinwood Docks
aliases
  • Collinwood
  • The Docks
  • Immigrant Shore
description Collinwood was built by immigrants who worked the railroads and the lakefront industries. Slovenians, Italians, Croatians — they came for the jobs, stayed for the community, and built a neighborhood that felt like six different countries compressed into twenty blocks. The railroads are gone. The immigrant communities' descendants are a minority now, their cultural institutions preserved as landmarks in a neighborhood that has been reshaped by forces none of them could have anticipated. But the lakefront is still there, and Collinwood is still defined by its relationship to the water.

The Docks are Collinwood's reason for existence in 2200. Lake Erie's shoreline from East 152nd to the Euclid border has been converted into a continuous cargo handling facility that processes 40% of the physical goods entering the Cleveland sprawl from the lake. Ferrogate operates the rail connections. Kelpline handles the water-side logistics. Between them, the two corponations have turned Collinwood's lakefront into a sovereign industrial zone where containers are unloaded by autonomous cranes, sorted by AI logistics systems, and dispatched inland on Ferrogate rail without human hands touching anything. The efficiency is extraordinary. The noise is extraordinary. The displacement of the people who lived along the waterfront before the docks expanded was also extraordinary, though no one with the authority to prevent it chose to do so.

Inland from the docks, Collinwood retains a residential character that the industrial shore has lost. The streets south of Waterloo Road are a dense, working-class neighborhood populated by dock workers, Ferrogate maintenance crews, and the latest wave of immigrants — climate refugees from the Gulf Coast and economic refugees from the collapsed rural interior who have settled here because the dock economy, for all its brutality, provides steady employment. The Slovenian National Home on St. Clair still hosts community events, its programming now split between heritage celebrations and job-placement services for new arrivals. The old and the new coexist with the particular tension of a neighborhood that has always been a first stop and never a final destination.
atmosphere
sights
  • Autonomous cargo cranes moving in synchronized patterns along the lakefront — industrial ballet performed by machines that never tire
  • Ferrogate rail cars stretching inland from the docks, their sovereign right-of-way strips cutting through residential blocks like metal rivers
  • The Slovenian National Home's facade — original brickwork, new reinforced windows, a Croatian flag hanging next to a Gulf Coast Mutual Aid banner
  • Lake Erie visible from the dock perimeter — grey-green water dotted with cargo platforms and, further out, the running lights of Cormorant patrol vessels
  • Container stacks three stories high along the waterfront, their shipping labels a geography lesson in the corridor's trade routes
sounds
  • The Docks — a wall of industrial sound: crane motors, container impacts, rail car coupling, AI logistics systems calling instructions in machine-optimized frequencies
  • Ferrogate Rail Hounds — autonomous patrol vehicles screaming along the tracks at 280 km/h, their passage shaking buildings within a block
  • Residential Collinwood: multiple languages spoken on the same street — Slovenian, Croatian, Gulf Coast drawl, Shelf Cant
  • Lake Erie — the sound of large-scale water moving against industrial infrastructure, a low constant that Collinwood residents stop hearing after a week
  • The National Home on event nights — music that mixes Slovenian folk tradition with Gulf Coast blues in combinations that shouldn't work and do
smells
  • Lake water and industrial lubricant — the dock's signature combination, inescapable within six blocks
  • Diesel exhaust from the older Ferrogate equipment that hasn't been upgraded — the new rail cars are electric, the maintenance fleet is not
  • Cooking from the residential blocks — a rotating international menu that changes with each new wave of arrivals
feel Collinwood Docks feels like a machine that people happen to live inside. The industrial rhythm of the lakefront sets the pace for everything — shift changes, meal times, sleep schedules, all organized around the docks' 24-hour operation cycle. It is loud, exhausting, and relentlessly functional. The residential streets carry a different energy — the warmth of a community that forms quickly because everyone is new here and everyone needs each other. The tension between the industrial shore and the human streets is the tension that has defined Collinwood for two centuries.
tags —
demographics Approximately 25,000 residents. Dock workers and Ferrogate maintenance crews comprise roughly 60% of the working population. The remainder is support economy — food services, housing maintenance, childcare, informal medical care. Significant populations of Gulf Coast climate refugees (arrived 2040s-2060s), rural interior economic refugees (arrived 2070s-present), and legacy Eastern European families (4th-6th generation). Tier 1-2 universally.
economy Dock labor is the primary employer, though the ratio of human workers to autonomous systems decreases annually. Ferrogate maintenance crews represent the second-largest employment category — the rail cars are automated but the tracks and infrastructure require human hands. The residential economy is service-based, organized around the needs of a shift-work population. Informal import trade — goods that 'fall off' the dock containers — supplements household income across the neighborhood.
power structure Ferrogate holds sovereign authority over the rail corridors and transit hubs. Kelpline holds sovereign authority over the waterfront dock facilities. The residential streets between them fall under Tollgate's minimum infrastructure jurisdiction. The Collinwood Workers' Association, descended from the original dockworkers' unions, negotiates working conditions with both corponations and serves as de facto neighborhood governance for the residential population.
dangers
  • Industrial accidents — the autonomous dock systems are efficient but indifferent to human bodies in the wrong place at the wrong time
  • Ferrogate Rail Hound proximity — the autonomous patrol vehicles will not stop for unauthorized track access, and unauthorized track access is defined by Ferrogate
  • Cargo theft consequences — the 'fell off a container' economy is tolerated within limits, but exceeding those limits triggers Kelpline security response
  • Lake exposure — the shoreline is industrialized but not sealed, and Lake Erie's weather events regularly flood the dock perimeter and adjacent residential blocks
  • Cormorant maritime patrols — anyone attempting to access the lake by small craft from Collinwood's shore faces interception by the most aggressive freshwater navy on Earth
opportunities
  • Dock work is brutal but available — one of the few reliable employment pathways for excluded residents in the Cleveland sprawl
  • The cargo processing facility handles goods from across the corridor — information about what's moving and where is valuable to the right buyer
  • Collinwood's residential community is tight-knit and protective — earning trust here opens connections to a labor network that spans the eastern docks
  • The lake access, while dangerous, is the only non-Ferrogate transit route to communities along the Erie shore
story hooks
  • A container has arrived at the docks with no shipping manifest, no origin tag, and a biometric lock that matches no known corponation security protocol — and it's emitting a low-frequency sound that is making the dock workers uneasy
  • The Collinwood Workers' Association has obtained evidence that Kelpline is preparing to fully automate the docks within two years, eliminating 15,000 jobs — and they're looking for leverage to stop it
  • Someone is running a passenger ferry from Collinwood's shore to the Lake Erie islands, slipping past Cormorant patrols using routes that suggest inside knowledge of the patrol schedule
connections

  • The Rust Circuit (Euclid)
  • Lake Erie shoreline — dock access to the eastern corridor waterway
  • Ferrogate transit corridor — rail connection to The Gate and points west

  • New arrivals — climate refugees and economic migrants who enter the Cleveland sprawl through the docks
  • Cargo brokers and logistics fixers who work the gray margin between legitimate trade and diversion
  • Kelpline and Ferrogate security personnel, whose presence is constant and whose jurisdiction is contested

Copperhead #

type place
name Copperhead
aliases
  • Houghton/Hancock MI
  • Copper Country
  • The Twin Bridge
  • Tech Town
description The Keweenaw Peninsula juts into Lake Superior like a broken finger, and at its base, straddling the Portage Lake Ship Canal, sit the twin cities of Houghton and Hancock — now collectively called Copperhead. The copper mines that built these towns in the 1800s were exhausted by the mid-twentieth century, but the mining infrastructure remained, and infrastructure has a way of finding new purposes. The abandoned mine shafts have been repurposed as geothermal energy installations, cold-storage data centers (the underground temperature is a constant 8°C, which is cheaper than any artificial cooling system), and deep-substrate research laboratories operated by Michigan Technological University.

Michigan Tech is Copperhead's reason for continued existence. The university has evolved from a mining school into the GLM's premier research institution for extreme-environment engineering — deep mining automation, cold-weather augmentation systems, underwater infrastructure, and the neural interfaces required to operate in conditions that would destroy baseline human cognition. The research is funded by a consortium of corponations who want the technology and a federal government that wants to keep the technology out of exclusive corporate hands. The result is a campus that operates as a neutral research zone, producing innovations that both sides of the UP war claim credit for and neither side fully controls.

The Portage Lake Ship Canal, an artificial waterway cut through the base of the Keweenaw in the nineteenth century, connects Lake Superior to itself via a shortcut that saves shipping 160 kilometers of travel around the peninsula. The Lift Bridge connecting Houghton and Hancock spans this canal — an ancient mechanical structure, upgraded with automated systems but still recognizable as the same bridge that was built 200 years ago. Copperhead is a place where the old infrastructure refuses to die and the new infrastructure grows inside it, like plants in the cracks of concrete.
atmosphere
sights
  • The Lift Bridge raising over the Portage Canal, silhouetted against Superior sunsets — 200 years old and still working
  • Michigan Tech campus sprawling across the hillside, research buildings connected by enclosed walkways against the cold
  • Mine shaft entrances repurposed as data center and lab access points — nineteenth-century stonework around twenty-first-century security doors
  • The Keweenaw winter — snow measured in meters, not centimeters, burying everything up to the second floor
  • Shipping vessels transiting the Portage Canal, so close to the buildings on either side you could touch the hull
sounds
  • The Lift Bridge mechanism — gears and hydraulics from two different centuries working together
  • Research facility ventilation systems — the hum of data centers and labs drawing heat from underground
  • Lake Superior ice forming on the canal in autumn — a growing, cracking sound that means winter is coming
  • University activity echoing across the hillside — one of the few places in the GLM where public intellectual life still sounds like this
smells
  • Cold stone and mineral-rich air from the repurposed mine shafts
  • Superior air — clean, cold, and carrying the scent of pine and distance
  • Lab chemicals and the ozone of computing equipment, drifting from the research buildings
feel A place where the past and future overlap without the present ever quite resolving. Copperhead's old mining infrastructure and new research facilities coexist in a way that feels both resourceful and haunted. The cold is not metaphorical — this is one of the most physically demanding environments in the GLM, and the people who live here have arranged their lives around surviving it.
tags —
demographics Population 28,000 permanent residents, plus 8,000 university students and researchers. The smallest major settlement in the UP, and the most specialized. The population is highly educated, deeply cold-adapted, and disproportionately employed in research or research support. Michigan loyalty runs strong — the Wisconsin claim here is essentially theoretical.
economy Research and education (Michigan Tech), geothermal energy (from the repurposed mine shafts), and data storage (cold-storage server farms in the underground infrastructure). The economy is almost entirely dependent on the university — when research funding flows, Copperhead thrives. When it doesn't, Copperhead waits.
power structure Michigan Tech's administration is the de facto governing authority. The municipal government handles infrastructure and services, but the university's budget dwarfs the city's, and the research consortium's security requirements effectively dictate public safety priorities. Dredge Mining Collective maintains a small sovereign facility for underground research, but their presence is limited compared to other UP settlements.
dangers
  • Extreme cold — winter conditions that exceed the design parameters of standard augmentations
  • Underground infrastructure instability — mine shafts repurposed for modern use don't always cooperate
  • Research facility accidents — extreme-environment engineering involves extreme-environment risks
  • Isolation — Copperhead is reachable by one road and the Portage Canal, both of which close in severe weather
  • The research itself — some of what Michigan Tech develops in those underground labs is classified for good reason
opportunities
  • Access to cutting-edge extreme-environment technology before it reaches the market
  • The university's neutral-zone status makes it a rare place where corporate and governmental interests can be played against each other
  • Cold-storage data facility access — secure, physically isolated, and very hard to hack when the servers are underground
  • Geothermal energy expertise — applicable anywhere, trained almost nowhere else
story hooks
  • A Michigan Tech research team has developed a neural interface that functions in conditions that should make augmentation impossible — and the prototype has disappeared from the underground lab
  • The mine shafts beneath Copperhead connect to the same deep-substrate anomaly that Dredge Mining found near Marquette — and Tech's sensors have been reading activity
  • A data center in the deep mines has been running computations that nobody authorized, using geothermal power nobody allocated — something is thinking down there
connections

  • Lake Superior shipping lanes
  • Keweenaw Peninsula wilderness — effectively uncharted corporate-free territory
exits —

  • Dredge Mining research liaisons
  • Extreme-environment engineering contractors from across the GLM

Copperveil Station #

type place
name Copperveil Station
aliases
  • The Veil
  • Copper Bottom
  • Downgate Hub
  • The Tarnish
description A decommissioned Metra transit hub buried forty meters beneath the Old Harbor district, its vaulted ceilings still wearing the oxidized copper cladding that gave it its name — great sweeping arches of verdigris green and rust-brown that catch the light of jury-rigged sodium strips in ways that feel almost religious. The station was sealed in 2087 after a Ferrogate Security crackdown on a synthetic labor strike, and the official record lists it as a flooded maintenance corridor. It is neither flooded nor a corridor.

Over the decades since, Copperveil has become one of the most reliable underground transit exchanges in the southern Meridian corridor. Four unofficial rail lines — none operated by any corponation — thread through its platforms, running reconditioned cargo cars between Shelf communities, the Stockyard underbelly, and the eastern Slagshore. Tickets are traded in favors, Φ, and contraband data chips, enforced loosely by a coalition of former transit workers who call themselves the Lamplighters.

The station's commercial layer occupies the old ticketing concourse: a dense sprawl of stalls selling salvaged BCI hardware, gene-edited street food, bootleg Diaspora access nodes, and medical services that don't ask for identity verification. It smells like copper and cooking fat and the particular ozone tang of overtaxed rail systems.
atmosphere
sights
  • Arched copper ceilings patched with mismatched alloy panels glow amber and green under flickering sodium strips.
  • Crowds press through narrow platform lanes between rail cars spray-painted with route glyphs no official map acknowledges.
  • A Lamplighter checkpoint — two heavyset figures in orange high-vis with non-Ferrogate sidearms — watches every train arrival from a repurposed ticket booth.
  • Stall tarps hang from old departure boards, still occasionally cycling ghost schedules from 2087.
sounds
  • The low harmonic groan of approaching rail cars echoes through the tunnels seconds before their lights appear.
  • A dozen competing languages blend into a single ambient roar from the concourse market.
  • Somewhere deeper in the maintenance shafts, something large and mechanical operates in irregular, patient rhythms.
smells
  • Hot copper oxidation mixes with frying synthetic protein from the food stalls.
  • Ozone and rail grease hang in layers, thicker near the active platforms.
  • Unwashed bodies and cheap disinfectant dominate the medical corridor on the east concourse.
feel Copperveil exists in a state of deliberate illegibility — it is busy and functional and completely invisible to official infrastructure. The Lamplighters maintain just enough order that violence is rare but never impossible. First-timers feel the weight of the ceiling and the weight of being somewhere they are not supposed to know about.
tags —
demographics Predominantly Tier 3 and Tier 4 residents who depend on off-grid transit, with a significant synthetic population using the station as a safe waypoint between hostile surface zones. Lamplighter personnel skew older, many former transit union members from pre-crackdown labor cohorts.
economy The station runs on a barter-and-cash economy; the Lamplighters levy a small transit tax on all rail traffic and a stall-license fee on vendors, generating enough revenue to maintain the rail infrastructure and pay their own modest wages.
power structure The Lamplighter coalition governs through a council of seven senior members, each responsible for a station zone; they hold a fragile but functional monopoly on violence and dispute resolution within the station's bounds.
dangers
  • Ferrogate Security runs periodic tunnel sweeps from the surface, forcing rapid station lockdowns that can trap travelers for hours.
  • The unofficial rail lines share aging track with unmapped maintenance drones that do not yield to passenger cars.
  • Rival courier syndicates occasionally use the station's crowds to settle debts violently when they believe the Lamplighters are occupied elsewhere.
  • Bootleg BCI hardware from the concourse stalls has a documented failure rate that can cause neural bleed events in vulnerable users.
opportunities
  • The Lamplighters quietly hire outside contractors for tunnel reconnaissance ahead of Ferrogate sweep cycles.
  • The station's medical corridor is one of the few places in the southern corridor where synthetic injury can be treated without identity logging.
  • Off-grid rail access to three separate Shelf communities makes Copperveil an irreplaceable logistics node for anyone needing to move people or goods without a paper trail.
story hooks
  • A Lamplighter council member has gone missing between a routine tunnel inspection and her scheduled return — her colleagues are quietly desperate, unwilling to surface the matter publicly because her route passed through a section of tunnel they officially claim is impassable.
  • A cargo car arrived on Platform 3 two nights ago with no crew, no manifest, and seventeen crates of Arcturus Defense Solutions hardware that nobody ordered. The Lamplighters want it gone before Ferrogate's next sweep, and they're not particular about how.
  • A synthetic traveler named Oswin has been sleeping on a concourse bench for eleven days, claiming she cannot leave because something in the station's old copper wiring is broadcasting a signal she describes as her name being called. She is lucid, calm, and terrified.
