Dearborn Forge #

type place
name Dearborn Forge
aliases
  • Dearborn
  • The Forge
  • Ford Country
  • Little Beirut
description Dearborn Forge is two cities occupying the same geography and pretending the other doesn't exist. The northern half is Ford Meridian's global headquarters — the Forge proper, a sprawling corporate campus that evolved from the original Ford World Headquarters into a sovereign manufacturing, R&D, and administrative complex covering twelve square miles. The southern half is the largest Arab-American community in North America — 120,000 people whose families have lived in Dearborn since the 1920s, when Henry Ford's factories needed labor and didn't care where it came from. The two populations share a city. They do not share a reality.

Ford Meridian's campus is the autonomous vehicle industry's cathedral. The company that once defined the automobile has redefined the autonomous vehicle, and Dearborn Forge is where the redefinition happens. The testing facilities, the design studios, the AI training labs, the military platform development centers — all of it operates behind a sovereign perimeter that Ford Meridian maintains with the same precision it applies to its vehicles. The campus employs 85,000 people, most of whom live in corporate housing within the perimeter and commute to nothing because everything they need is provided. Ford Meridian didn't build a company town. It built a company country — sovereign territory with its own laws, its own currency (Ford Credits, pegged to the Φ at a favorable rate), and its own social contract that starts with 'you work for Ford' and ends with 'everything else is handled.'

South Dearborn — the Arab-American community — watches the Forge the way a village watches a castle. The community is old, established, and deeply rooted: mosques, community centers, Arabic-language schools, and a commercial strip along Michigan Avenue that has been selling halal meat and serving Arabic coffee for over a century. The community survived Ford's decline, Detroit's collapse, and the Corporate Sovereignty Acts by doing what immigrant communities have always done — taking care of their own. The current tension is Ford Meridian's expansion. The campus perimeter has moved south three times in twenty years, each time consuming blocks that the community considers non-negotiable. The most recent expansion displaced the Al-Huda Islamic Center, which had served the community for sixty years. Ford Meridian relocated it to a new building. The building is nicer. Nobody thinks that's the point.
atmosphere
sights
  • Ford Meridian's campus — glass and steel and autonomous vehicles moving in test patterns visible from outside the perimeter
  • Michigan Avenue's Arabic commercial strip — neon in Arabic and English, storefront displays unchanged in fundamental character for a century
  • The perimeter wall — Ford Meridian calls it a 'campus boundary,' the community calls it what it is
  • The new Al-Huda Islamic Center — architecturally stunning, spiritually displaced, its orientation toward Mecca slightly different from the old building because the geometry changed
  • Community protest art on buildings facing the perimeter — not vandalism, not permitted, just present
sounds
  • Arabic conversation on Michigan Avenue — three generations of the same families, still here
  • Ford Meridian's testing range — autonomous vehicle acceleration tests produce a distinctive whine that carries over the perimeter
  • Call to prayer from three mosques, their timing coordinated by community agreement
  • The perimeter's security system — a low-frequency deterrent hum designed to be subconsciously uncomfortable for loiterers
  • Community radio in Arabic — news, music, and commentary that Ford Meridian's PR department monitors but cannot control
smells
  • Arabic cuisine along Michigan Avenue — shawarma, falafel, cardamom coffee, fresh-baked flatbread
  • Ford Meridian's campus — the sterile, conditioned air that leaks through the perimeter carries no smell at all, which is its own olfactory statement
  • Hookah smoke from the cafes — a social tradition that has survived every public health regulation and corporate objection
  • Machine oil from the small repair shops that service what Ford Meridian's autonomous systems can't
feel Divided. Dearborn Forge feels like two tectonic plates grinding against each other — one corporate and expanding, the other communal and resisting. The Forge side is clean, quiet, and purposeful. The community side is loud, dense, and determined. The boundary between them is a line of constant, low-grade friction that everyone navigates daily and nobody has resolved.
tags —
demographics Ford Meridian campus: 85,000 employees and dependents, predominantly Tier 3-4, ethnically diverse but culturally homogeneous (corporate). South Dearborn: 120,000 residents, predominantly Arab-American (65%), with significant Tier 1-2 population. The demographic split across the perimeter is the starkest in the Detroit metro.
economy Ford Meridian's campus generates Φ1.2 trillion annually — the largest single-site economic output in the GLM outside Meridian 88. South Dearborn's economy is community-scaled: small businesses, service industries, and a significant informal economy built on community trust networks. Average household income south of the perimeter: Φ28,000. North of the perimeter: Φ290,000.
power structure North: Ford Meridian, sovereign and absolute. South: The Dearborn Community Council, an elected body representing the Arab-American community and its allies, currently chaired by Hassan Bazzi, a third-generation Dearborn resident and civil rights attorney. The DCC has no legal authority over Ford Meridian's expansion but has successfully used media pressure, community organizing, and strategic litigation to slow the campus perimeter's advance. The relationship between the DCC and Ford Meridian is adversarial, respectful, and exhausting for both sides.
dangers
  • Perimeter expansion — Ford Meridian's campus grows, and the community shrinks, and the legal mechanisms favor the corponation
  • Economic pressure — Ford Meridian is the region's largest employer, and community members who work there face loyalty conflicts
  • Surveillance spillover — the campus perimeter's security systems monitor well beyond the boundary line
  • Cultural erasure — each displaced block removes a physical anchor of community identity that no relocation can replace
  • Community radicalization — the younger generation's patience with Hassan Bazzi's measured approach is wearing thin
opportunities
  • Ford Meridian intelligence — community members who work inside the campus have dual loyalties and dual access
  • The DCC's legal strategies reveal corporate vulnerabilities — their litigation discovery process has uncovered information Ford Meridian wanted buried
  • Michigan Avenue is an intelligence corridor — information flows through the community's trust networks faster than through corporate channels
  • The community's international connections — Arab-American family networks span the globe and provide logistical capabilities that no corponation can easily replicate
story hooks
  • Ford Meridian's next expansion plan targets a four-block area containing the community's oldest mosque, a school, and 400 households. Hassan Bazzi has evidence that the expansion isn't needed — the campus has unused capacity. But the evidence was obtained through means that would compromise a source inside Ford Meridian.
  • A young community organizer is building a coalition with Mexicantown Libre and the HPAZ to create a unified resistance network. Ford Meridian's intelligence division has identified her and is debating whether to co-opt, discredit, or ignore her.
  • A Ford Meridian engineer of Arab descent discovers that the autonomous vehicle routing system deprioritizes pedestrian safety calculations in South Dearborn. The bias is statistical, not coded — an artifact of training data. Proving it is a technical challenge. Living with it is a daily one.

Deepwell Station #

type place
name Deepwell Station
aliases
  • The Fortress
  • Superior Free City
  • Iron Reef
  • The Cold Republic
description Deepwell Station is what happens when you build a seacrete city on the most unforgiving freshwater body on Earth. Lake Superior is deep, cold, and violent — it doesn't give up its dead, as the saying goes, and it doesn't make life easy for the living. The people who founded Deepwell in 2167 knew this. They were miners, mostly — iron range workers from Minnesota's Mesabi Range who'd been automated out of existence, plus a contingent of Canadian resource engineers from Thunder Bay who'd watched their industry collapse when the corponations consolidated mineral extraction. They had no future on shore. So they took their engineering expertise, their tolerance for misery, and their complete lack of alternatives, and they dropped wire-mesh frameworks into Superior's mineral-saturated waters and started growing a city.

Superior's water chemistry is different from the lower lakes — colder, deeper, with a mineral profile heavy in iron, silica, and dissolved carbonates that produces seacrete with a distinctive reddish-black coloration and exceptional compressive strength. Deepwell's structures look like they were carved from volcanic rock — dark, dense, angular. The city sits lower in the water than Freestone, its upper surfaces barely cresting the wave line during storms, most of its mass submerged. This wasn't an aesthetic choice; it was survival engineering. Superior's storms would shred a surface-dominant structure. Deepwell hunkers, absorbs, and endures. The residents call this design philosophy 'The Crouch.'

The city's economy is built on what Superior provides: mineral extraction from the lakebed, processed through Deepwell's own refining platforms. The iron-rich sediment of Superior's floor yields high-grade ore that the city processes and trades to shore-based manufacturers. Deepwell also harvests rare earth elements from deep-water thermal vents — a resource that the corponations would kill for and have, in fact, tried to take by force twice. Both attempts were repelled by Deepwell's defense force, the Keel Guard, whose submersible fleet operates in water too deep and too cold for Cormorant Naval Systems' Lake Erie-optimized vessels to follow. Superior is Deepwell's moat, and the city has learned to use the lake's hostility as a weapon.

Governance is a workers' council system — practical, blunt, and merciless toward inefficiency. The founding miners brought their union culture with them, and Deepwell runs like a mine that votes: shift schedules, resource allocation, and defense priorities are decided by council, with foremen (elected, not appointed) managing execution. There is no pretension of utopian politics here. Deepwell is hard, cold, and functional. It works because the alternative is the lake, and the lake is worse. Population: 120,000, every one of them earning their oxygen.
atmosphere
sights
  • Dark reddish-black seacrete structures barely cresting the waterline — the city looks like a volcanic island that hasn't finished rising
  • Mining platforms with crane arrays extending into the lake, hauling sediment from the deep floor
  • The Keel Guard's submersible pens — armored docks built into the city's submerged lower levels
  • Ice — in winter, Deepwell's surfaces accumulate ice formations that the residents carve into functional windbreaks rather than remove
  • The aurora borealis reflected in Superior's black water on clear nights — the one beautiful thing the lake gives freely
sounds
  • Wind — Superior's wind is constant, aggressive, and personal. It finds every gap in every structure.
  • The grind of mining equipment hauling ore from the lakebed
  • The deep, resonant hum of the accretion current running through iron-heavy seacrete — lower-pitched than Freestone's, almost subsonic
  • Council debates echoing through the commons halls — Deepwell argues loudly about everything
smells
  • Iron — the seacrete, the ore, the water itself all carry the metallic bite of ferrous mineral
  • Cold air off the lake — clean, sharp, and hostile
  • Machine oil from the mining rigs and refinery platforms
  • The mineral-rich steam from the thermal vent processing stations
feel Hard. Deepwell feels earned in a way that no place in Meridian does. Every surface was grown from hostile water by people who had nothing else. The cold gets into your bones. The wind never stops. The food is functional, the housing is tight, and the people look at you like they're deciding whether you're worth the oxygen. But there's a solidity here — physical and social — that the tier system can't replicate. These people chose the hardest lake on the continent and made it home. They're proud of that, in the quiet, stubborn way of people who don't need you to be impressed.
tags —
demographics 120,000 permanent residents, predominantly descended from displaced iron range miners and Canadian resource workers. Ethnically mixed but culturally cohesive — Deepwell has developed its own identity built on labor solidarity and Superior endurance. Children are educated in both technical trades and democratic governance from age six.
economy Primary exports: refined iron ore, rare earth elements from deep-water thermal vents, high-density seacrete prefabrication components. Imports: electronics, medical supplies, agricultural products (Superior's cold limits food production). Internal economy runs on work-shares — a labor-hour currency tied to actual productive output. External trade volume: approximately Φ6.8 billion annually, heavily weighted toward mineral exports.
power structure Workers' council system. The Shift Council — twenty elected foremen representing each major work sector — governs by majority vote. A General Assembly of all residents convenes quarterly for major decisions. The Keel Guard operates under Shift Council authority but maintains operational independence during active defense. No corporate entities permitted; the founding charter is explicit.
dangers
  • Lake Superior itself — storms, cold, depth. The lake has killed people on Deepwell's outer platforms and will do so again.
  • Corponation mineral-rights challenges — Dredge Mining Collective and Arcturus Defense Solutions both want Deepwell's thermal vent resources
  • Isolation — Deepwell is far from shore and far from the other lake cities. Supply disruption is an existential threat.
  • Infrastructure age — the oldest seacrete sections are forty years old and require constant maintenance against Superior's erosive chemistry
  • The Keel Guard's independence — a military force with operational autonomy in a democracy is a structural tension that hasn't broken yet
opportunities
  • Rare earth elements — Deepwell controls resources that every corponation needs and cannot easily replicate
  • Submersible expertise — the Keel Guard operates in conditions no other naval force can match
  • A labor economy that actually values work — radical concept in a world of corporate extraction
  • Strategic alliance potential — Deepwell's resources make it a valuable partner for anyone opposing corponation mineral monopolies
story hooks
  • Dredge Mining Collective hires a mercenary flotilla to 'survey' Superior's thermal vents. Deepwell's Keel Guard intercepts. The resulting standoff needs someone on shore to negotiate — or sabotage — before it becomes a shooting war.
  • A structural failure in Deepwell's oldest seacrete section threatens to flood the lower residential warrens. The repair requires materials only available from shore-based corponation suppliers, who see an opportunity to extract concessions.
  • A Deepwell miner discovers something in the lakebed sediment that isn't mineral — it's artificial, it's old, and it shouldn't be there.

  • The Vagrant (mobile platform — seasonal trade partner)

Dunning Preserve #

type place
name Dunning Preserve
aliases
  • Dunning
  • The Asylum Grounds
  • The Preserve
  • The Warded Forest
description Before the incorporation, Dunning was known for two things: being far from everything, and the former state mental hospital that had been converted into a forest preserve. The hospital closed in 1970. The ghosts didn't. When the corps carved up the city, Dunning's remote northwest location and its unsettling history made it unattractive for development. Axiom Environmental Services acquired the forest preserve land for carbon credit accounting purposes — trees on paper, value on balance sheets — and the residential blocks around it were left ungoverned. What happened next was either a miracle or a horror, depending on your relationship with the natural world.

The forest grew back. Not the manicured, corporate-approved green space of the Core. Real forest. Unmanaged, unfiltered, fed by decades of Chicago's buried topsoil and whatever the old hospital had put into the ground. The trees in Dunning Preserve are wrong in ways that botanists from the Core's research divisions have tried and failed to categorize. They grow too fast. Their root systems interface with buried infrastructure in ways that suggest intentionality. In Year 22, a survey team found fungal networks connecting the preserve's trees to decommissioned fiber optic cables, creating what one researcher described as 'a biological internet running on mycelium and dead copper' before her report was classified and she was reassigned to atmospheric monitoring on the lakefront.

The people who live in and around the Preserve have adapted. The old residential blocks on the perimeter house a community of roughly 12,000 who have developed a symbiotic relationship with the forest that corporate science does not have a framework to explain. They call themselves the Wardens, and their knowledge of the Preserve's ecology is practical, generational, and deliberately undigitized — nothing written down, nothing stored on any network, everything taught person to person. They harvest the forest's pharmaceutical products — compounds that no lab has synthesized, painkillers and nootropics that grow on bark and in root systems — and trade them through the Souk and the Circuit. The Preserve is Dunning's economy, its pharmacy, its religion, and its weapon.

The old hospital's foundations are still down there, under the roots. The Wardens say the forest grew from it. They say this without metaphor.
atmosphere
sights
  • Canopy so dense it blocks the Meridian haze — actual sky visible in gaps between branches
  • Trees growing through and around pre-collapse structures, absorbing brick and steel into living wood
  • Bioluminescent fungi along forest paths that pulse in patterns the Wardens can read like signage
  • The hospital foundations visible in places — concrete and tile emerging from root systems like bones from skin
  • Warden settlements built into the canopy and forest edge, structures that look grown rather than constructed
sounds
  • Wind through real leaves — a sound so rare in Meridian 88 that visitors sometimes cry
  • Bird and insect life that exists nowhere else in the Corridor — an ecosystem in a bottle
  • The forest's own sounds — creaking, settling, the deep subsonic hum of root systems moving
  • Silence that is actually silence, not the corporate simulation of it
  • Warden communication — subtle percussive signals against tree trunks that carry through the root network
smells
  • Earth. Real, living soil — the single rarest smell in Meridian 88
  • The pharmaceutical compounds — sweet, resinous, faintly metallic, growing on bark and fungus
  • Decay and growth simultaneously — the forest recycling itself in real time
  • Rain captured by canopy, released slowly — petrichor that lasts for hours
feel Sacred. Whether you believe in anything or not, the Preserve triggers something primal — the recognition that this is older than the city, older than the corps, older than the tier system. It feels like standing in the one place that the incorporation couldn't reach. The Wardens say the forest is watching. Spending any time under the canopy, you start to believe them.
tags —

Untier-ed by choice — the community rejected the tier system in Year 6 and has maintained autonomy through the Preserve's pharmaceutical value and its genuine inaccessibility. Ethnically diverse but culturally unified around the Warden tradition.

Edgewater Prism #

type place
name Edgewater Prism
aliases
  • Edgewater
  • The Prism
  • Andersonville Strip
  • Lightside
description Edgewater Prism is what happens when a neighborhood's progressive identity survives the apocalypse and has to figure out what it means on the other side. The original Edgewater was the North Side's most welcoming community — diverse, lakefront, anchored by the Andersonville commercial district's legacy of LGBTQ+ culture and immigrant enterprise, and characterized by the kind of deliberate inclusivity that takes constant effort and looks effortless from the outside. When the Consolidation came, Edgewater did not resist — it adapted, absorbing waves of displaced residents from adjacent neighborhoods with the practiced flexibility of a community that had been taking in outsiders for generations. The result is a district that is simultaneously one of Meridian 88's most functional and most fragile — held together not by infrastructure or corporate backing but by a social contract that requires active, daily renewal.

The lakefront is Edgewater Prism's defining geography. Unlike the flooded districts to the south, Edgewater's shoreline was elevated and reinforced during the Climate Infrastructure Emergency — a rare instance of proactive investment that residents attribute to the district's vocal advocacy rather than any corporate priority. The lake is visible from most of the district, and its presence shapes everything: the light, which refracts off the water and gives the streets a prismatic quality that inspired the neighborhood's new name; the air, which is cleaner here than in inland districts; and the psychological landscape, which is oriented toward openness in a way that the interior Shelf's compressed blocks cannot replicate.

The Andersonville Strip is the district's commercial and cultural spine — a multi-block corridor of shops, cafes, clinics, cultural spaces, and community organizations that has evolved from a Swedish immigrant neighborhood through an LGBTQ+ cultural hub into something harder to categorize but easier to feel. The Strip operates on an ethic of radical inclusion that is encoded in its commercial practices: sliding-scale pricing, identity-blind service policies, and a merchant collective that enforces anti-discrimination standards more rigorously than any corporate code. The collective — called the Prism Council — is equal parts business association and social movement, and it governs the Strip with a combination of democratic process and moral authority that makes it one of the most effective grassroots governance models in Meridian 88.

The fragility is real, though, and the Prism Council knows it. Edgewater Prism's inclusivity makes it a magnet for every displaced population in the northern Shelf — climate refugees, corporate escapees, untier-ed people seeking a community that will not check their papers, and a growing number of neural-interface refugees who have rejected or been rejected by the augmented economy and need a place where analog existence is not treated as disability. The demand on the district's resources exceeds its capacity, and every year the gap widens. The Prism Council debates the impossible calculus of inclusion versus sustainability at every meeting, and the answers get harder each time. Edgewater Prism's identity is built on never turning people away. Its survival may eventually require exactly that, and nobody here is ready for what that compromise would mean.
atmosphere
sights
  • Lake Michigan visible from most streets — open water, open sky, a visual relief from the Shelf's compression
  • The Andersonville Strip's dense, colorful commercial corridor — murals, banners, and signage in dozens of languages
  • Prismatic light refracting off the lake surface, casting rainbow patterns on east-facing walls in the morning
  • Diverse populations moving through shared space with practiced ease — the visual texture of genuine multiculturalism
  • Community gardens and public art installations maintained by the Prism Council
  • Neural-interface refugees with visible implant scars, analog in a digital world, accepted here
sounds
  • Multilingual conversation on the Strip — a denser language mix than even Cicada Lawn's corridor
  • Live music from cafe doorways — acoustic, electronic, hybrid, reflecting the population's diversity
  • Lake sounds — waves, gulls, the particular audio signature of a shoreline that has not been industrialized
  • The Prism Council's public deliberations, broadcast on speakers along the Strip
  • Laughter — genuine, frequent, the sound of a community that still has enough social trust to find things funny
smells
  • Lake air — salt, moisture, the clean smell of open water
  • The Strip's food diversity — Swedish bakeries alongside Ethiopian kitchens alongside Vietnamese pho shops
  • Community garden herbs and flowers — lavender, basil, marigold, planted for beauty and medicine
  • Coffee — real coffee, Edgewater Prism has three cafes that source beans through a fair-trade network the Prism Council negotiated
feel Hopeful and strained. Edgewater Prism feels like a place that is trying to prove something — that inclusion can work, that community can survive, that progressive values are not a luxury of comfortable times but a necessity of desperate ones. The effort is visible and sometimes exhausting, but the alternative — becoming like everywhere else — is more exhausting, and the people here know it.
tags —
demographics The most diverse district in Meridian 88 by virtually every metric — ethnicity, gender identity, national origin, tier status, augmentation status. Significant LGBTQ+ population, climate refugee population, and neural-interface refugee population. Tier 1 and Tier 2, with a growing untier-ed population the Prism Council is working to support. Population approximately 20,000-28,000 and growing.
economy The Andersonville Strip's commercial corridor drives the local economy — small businesses, cafes, clinics, cultural spaces, and service organizations. The Prism Council's sliding-scale pricing model keeps commerce accessible but compresses margins. A growing care economy — healthcare, mental health, social services — has emerged to serve the refugee populations. External income comes from residents with employment in the Meridian Core and a small tech sector specializing in analog alternatives to corporate neural-interface systems.
power structure The Prism Council governs the Andersonville Strip and, by extension, much of the district. Council membership is open to any resident or Strip business operator, with decisions made by consensus process. The Council's authority is cultural rather than coercive — compliance is maintained through social contract rather than enforcement. A volunteer community safety team called the Watch handles security without weapons, using de-escalation and community mediation protocols.
dangers
  • Resource strain from ongoing refugee absorption — the district is approaching carrying capacity
  • The inclusivity ethic makes the district vulnerable to exploitation by bad actors who use the community's openness as cover
  • Corporate interest in the lakefront property — the reinforced shoreline has significant development value
  • Internal tension between the demand for unlimited inclusion and the reality of finite resources
  • The Watch's non-violent security model is tested by increasingly desperate populations and increasingly aggressive external actors
  • Neural-interface refugee medical needs exceeding the district's clinic capacity
opportunities
  • The Prism Council's governance model is a genuine innovation — democratic, inclusive, and functional enough to study
  • The lakefront provides strategic advantages — clean air, water access, and line-of-sight communication
  • The analog tech sector produces interface alternatives that have market value across Meridian 88
  • Edgewater Prism's diverse population includes people with knowledge, skills, and connections from across the world
  • The community's reputation for inclusion makes it a trusted meeting ground for parties who do not trust each other
story hooks
  • The Prism Council has received a lakefront development proposal from a corporate entity offering to build a medical facility for neural-interface refugees in exchange for a long-term land lease on the shoreline. The proposal would address the district's most critical resource shortage, but the land lease would give a corporation a permanent foothold in the community. The Council is deadlocked.
  • A neural-interface refugee has arrived in Edgewater Prism claiming that their disconnected implant is still receiving transmissions — data packets that contain what appears to be internal corporate communications from a corponation that does not officially operate in the district. If the transmissions are genuine, someone is using deactivated implants as a covert communication network.
  • The Watch has identified a pattern: every month, several residents disappear from the district for exactly 72 hours and return without explanation. The disappearances correlate with no known employment, medical, or personal pattern. The returning residents show no signs of distress but refuse to discuss where they were. The Prism Council wants to investigate without violating the community's privacy ethic — a contradiction that may not have a resolution.

Edison Grid #

type place
name Edison Grid
aliases
  • Edison Park
  • The Grid
  • Blue Line's End
  • Coptown
description Edison Grid is the neighborhood that polices itself and doesn't apologize for it. The far northwest corner of Meridian 88, Edison Park was always Chicago's most suburban enclave — tidy bungalows, neat lawns, families where both parents worked for the city. Police officers, firefighters, paramedics, public works employees. When the corporations privatized everything, Edison Park's residents found themselves in a unique position: they were the people who'd kept the old city running, and the new city needed their skills even if it didn't want their independence. Axiom Security Solutions absorbed the police force. Corporate emergency services absorbed the fire department. The old public servants became corporate contractors with better salaries and fewer rights. But they kept living in Edison Park, kept raising their families on the same blocks, and kept the one thing the corps couldn't privatize: the institutional knowledge of how a city actually works, passed down through families like a genetic trait.

The Grid earned its name from the power infrastructure. When Meridian 88's energy grid was being built, Edison Park's residents — many of them electrical workers and engineers by trade — negotiated a deal that no other neighborhood managed: a dedicated power substation feeding the district directly, bypassing the corporate metering system. It was supposed to be temporary. That was thirty years ago. The Grid still has the most reliable electricity in Meridian's outlying districts, and the substation has been quietly expanded, modified, and hardened by residents who understand power systems the way other people understand cooking. The electricity is technically corporate property. The Grid's position is that they built the system, they maintain the system, and anyone who wants to renegotiate can discuss it with the electricians' union, which is also the neighborhood militia.

The culture of Edison Grid is cop culture — for better and worse. The streets are orderly. Crime is low. Community standards are enforced by social pressure and, when necessary, by retired Axiom Security contractors who still have their training and most of their augments. There's a code: you look out for your neighbors, you maintain your property, you don't bring trouble home. It's effective and stifling in equal measure. The Grid's children grow up safe and grow up to leave, because safety and predictability are not the same as freedom. The ones who stay become cops or electricians or both, and the cycle continues.

The Grid's relationship with Axiom Security is the district's defining tension. Many residents work for the corporation. Many residents distrust the corporation. These are often the same people. An Edison Grid Axiom Security officer follows corporate orders during shift and comes home to a neighborhood that views corporate authority with the skeptical eye of people who remember when authority was public and accountable. This cognitive dissonance produces a population that is simultaneously Axiom's most competent workforce and its most quietly resistant. The Grid doesn't rebel. It doesn't protest. It maintains its power substation, trains its children in skills the corporation needs, and waits — with the patience of people who understand infrastructure — for the system to need them more than they need it.
atmosphere
sights
  • Neat residential blocks — bungalows maintained to standards that would have been normal in the old city and are remarkable now
  • The power substation at the district's center, expanded and reinforced over decades, humming with dedicated electricity
  • Retired security contractors walking patrol routes out of habit, augmented eyes scanning without urgency
  • Family gardens in every yard — practical vegetables, not decorative landscaping
  • The Blue Line terminal at the district's edge — the last stop, literally and figuratively, before the suburban wastelands begin
  • Memorial plaques on homes — names of officers and firefighters who died in service, maintained by families who remember
sounds
  • The hum of the power substation — louder than you'd expect, a low throb that residents stop hearing after a week
  • Children playing in actual yards — one of the few districts where outdoor play space exists
  • Scanner chatter from homes where off-duty security personnel keep a radio on — old habit, professional compulsion
  • The Blue Line train arriving and departing — a schedule so reliable it functions as a neighborhood clock
  • Quiet — but a different quiet than the Palisade. This is the quiet of a place where trouble knows better than to make noise.
smells
  • Grilled food from backyard cookouts — the Grid maintains a cookout culture that is part social tradition and part defiant normalcy
  • Ozone from the power substation, strongest in humid weather
  • Cut grass — real grass, maintained by hand, a point of pride
  • Coffee from kitchens in the morning — the Grid wakes up early because shift work starts early
feel Controlled. Edison Grid feels like a place where everything works because someone made it work and continues to make it work through daily effort and communal will. It's reassuring and claustrophobic — the safety is real, the order is real, and the social pressure to conform is equally real. The Grid is what a neighborhood looks like when the people who run the city's systems build a place for themselves. It's functional. It's dependable. It's not a place that welcomes questions about whether there might be a better way.
tags —
demographics Approximately 10,000 residents, predominantly Tier 2 and Tier 3. Multigenerational families with backgrounds in public safety, infrastructure maintenance, and emergency services. Racially and ethnically mixed but culturally uniform — the shared identity is occupational, not ethnic. The most stable population in Meridian's northwest.
economy Skilled labor export — Edison Grid's residents work throughout Meridian's infrastructure and security sectors. The power substation generates surplus electricity that's traded to neighboring districts. Small-scale commercial services support the residential population. The economy is wages, not entrepreneurship.
power structure The Grid Council — elected from resident families, heavily weighted toward senior infrastructure and security workers. The electricians' union holds veto power over energy-related decisions. Axiom has no direct governance role but exercises influence through the employment relationship with most working-age residents.
dangers
  • Social conformity enforcement — deviance from community standards is punished by isolation and ostracism
  • The Axiom loyalty question — residents who are seen as too corporate or too resistant to corporate authority face suspicion from both sides
  • Power substation dependency — the Grid's independence is built on infrastructure that could be targeted
  • Insularity — outsiders are tolerated but not trusted, and the Grid's closed culture limits information exchange
  • The militia's competence — Edison Grid's residents are trained, equipped, and organized enough to be dangerous if the wrong situation triggers a response
opportunities
  • Reliable power — the Grid's electricity supply is a strategic resource in a city of rolling blackouts
  • Skilled labor connections — the Grid's workers have access to every level of Meridian's infrastructure
  • Institutional knowledge — these families know how the city works in ways that blueprints don't capture
  • Security expertise — retired Axiom personnel with training and augments, available for contract work if the cause is right
  • The Blue Line terminal — the last transit connection to the northwestern suburbs, a smuggling route that the Grid quietly tolerates
story hooks
  • An Edison Grid Axiom Security officer discovers that the corporation is planning to bypass the neighborhood's power substation — routing the Grid into the metered system. The Grid Council prepares for a confrontation that could turn the district's quiet resistance into open conflict.
  • Kyle needs information that only an active Axiom Security officer can access. The officer is Edison Grid — loyal to the community first, the corporation second. The price of the information is a favor that puts Kyle on the wrong side of people he'd rather not cross.
  • A Grid family's child returns from a stint in the Shelf with augments, ideas, and associations that violate everything the community stands for. The family is torn between protecting their own and maintaining the social contract that keeps the Grid functioning.

  • Off-duty Axiom Security personnel living among the community they serve and question
  • Electricians and infrastructure workers maintaining the power substation and trading surplus energy
  • Blue Line commuters — the terminal is a transit point for anyone moving between Meridian and the northwest
  • The occasional outsider buying surplus power or hiring skilled labor, tolerated but watched

Engelheim #

type place
name Engelheim
aliases
  • Englewood
  • The Helm
  • Engelheim Transit Nexus
  • The Crossing
description Engelheim is the place where things pass through. The old 63rd and Halsted transit hub — once the commercial heart of Englewood — has been rebuilt, expanded, and rebuilt again into a multi-level transit interchange that connects the southern Shelf districts to the Meridian Core's lower tiers. Four maglev lines converge here, plus a surface-level bus grid and an informal network of unlicensed transit vehicles that fill the gaps the official system refuses to serve. The interchange is the district's heart, its economy, and its curse: everything flows through Engelheim, but very little stays.

The transit nexus dominates the landscape. Its upper levels are corporate-managed space — Helion Transit Authority signage, functioning surveillance, automated fare enforcement, and the particular sterility of infrastructure maintained for throughput rather than habitation. Below the fare gates, the station's lower concourses have become a permanent market and gathering space — the kind of informal settlement that grows in transit infrastructure the way moss grows on stone. Vendors sell food, repairs, information, and temporary shelter in the corridors beneath the platforms. The transit police nominally patrol these lower levels but have reached an unspoken accommodation with the market operators: commerce continues as long as the trains run on time and nothing happens that generates a report.

Around the nexus, the district radiates outward in concentric rings of decreasing investment. The blocks immediately adjacent benefit from foot traffic and transit access — small businesses, flophouses, clinics, the services that travelers need. Two blocks out, the investment drops sharply. Three blocks out, Engelheim begins to resemble West Engelheim — vacancy, improvised shelter, the architecture of disinvestment. The targeted reinvestment that characterized pre-Consolidation Englewood has been replaced by targeted extraction: the transit hub generates revenue that flows upward through Helion's balance sheets while the surrounding neighborhood receives exactly enough maintenance to prevent the kind of collapse that would interrupt service.

Engelheim has a reputation as a dangerous district, and it is — but the danger is specific rather than general. The transit nexus itself is relatively safe, because too many corporate interests depend on its function. The danger lives in the rings beyond the nexus, where the jurisdiction is muddled and the population is transient enough that disappearances go unrecorded. Fixers, runners, and street operators use Engelheim as a waypoint precisely because of this transience — it is easy to arrive, conduct business, and leave without establishing a pattern. Kyle has passed through Engelheim more times than he can count. Everyone has. That is its nature: a place defined by passage, not by presence.
atmosphere
sights
  • The transit nexus rising like a concrete cathedral — platforms stacked four levels high, maglev lines threading through like steel arteries
  • The lower concourse market — dense, improvised, lit by vendor lights and the glow of information screens
  • Fare enforcement drones hovering at gate lines, scanning for valid transit credentials
  • The rings of decreasing investment visible from the upper platforms — a gradient from commerce to vacancy in three blocks
  • Transient populations moving through with purpose — nobody lingers in Engelheim longer than necessary
sounds
  • Maglev arrivals and departures — the doppler whine that means the southern Shelf is still connected to the city
  • Market vendors calling in the lower concourse, their voices competing with transit announcements
  • Fare gates cycling — the click-beep of authorized passage, the harsh buzz of rejection
  • The particular acoustic signature of a space designed for movement, not habitation — echoes that never settle
  • Unlicensed transit vehicles honking at surface level, a chaotic counterpoint to the maglev's precision
smells
  • Transit infrastructure — ozone, lubricant, the metallic smell of maglev braking systems
  • Lower concourse food vendors — grilled protein, synthetic spices, nutrient paste reheated into something almost appetizing
  • Crowd density — the compressed human smell of a transit hub that processes thousands daily
  • Rain coming in through the nexus's incomplete upper roof, mixing with concrete dust
feel Impermanent. Engelheim feels like a place that exists in motion — remove the people passing through and there would be nothing here but infrastructure and vacancy. There is energy in the transit flow, but it is borrowed energy, and when the last train runs each night, the district exhales into something quieter and more honest and significantly more dangerous.
tags —
demographics Transient population makes accurate demographics impossible. Residential population in the outer rings is predominantly African American, Tier 1 and untier-ed, continuous with the demographics of adjacent districts. The transit nexus itself sees the full spectrum of the lower Shelf passing through daily.
economy Transit-dependent. The nexus generates significant revenue for Helion Transit Authority, none of which is reinvested locally. The lower concourse market operates on an informal economy. Adjacent blocks subsist on traveler services — food, repair, temporary shelter, information brokerage. Beyond the second ring, the economy is indistinguishable from West Engelheim's salvage-and-barter system.
power structure Helion Transit Authority controls the nexus and its immediate perimeter. Beyond that, authority fragments. The lower concourse market is managed by a broker collective called the Platform, which allocates vendor space and mediates disputes. In the outer rings, authority defaults to whoever can hold it — block-level strongmen, gang affiliates, or in some cases, no one at all.
dangers
  • Transient-on-transient crime in the outer rings — people who won't be missed targeting people who won't be missed
  • Fare enforcement drones that scan more than fare status — Helion collects biometric data on every transit user
  • The jurisdiction gap between Helion's nexus perimeter and the ungoverned outer rings — a no-man's-land where accountability vanishes
  • Unlicensed transit vehicles that serve as fronts for trafficking operations
  • Structural decay in the outer-ring buildings, accelerated by transit vibration from the maglev lines
  • The Platform's enforcement arm, which maintains market order through methods that do not appear in any handbook
opportunities
  • The transit nexus is the best-connected point in the southern Shelf — four maglev lines means four directions of escape
  • The lower concourse market is an excellent place to buy, sell, or trade information without establishing a traceable pattern
  • Helion's biometric data collection creates a valuable intelligence resource for anyone who can access the transit authority's databases
  • The Platform is always hiring security for high-value vendor operations during peak transit hours
  • The outer rings offer cheap, anonymous shelter for those who need to disappear temporarily
story hooks
  • A maglev line running through Engelheim has been experiencing brief, unexplained signal blackouts — thirty-second windows where the train's surveillance and tracking systems go dark. Someone is creating these windows deliberately, and someone else is using them to move cargo that cannot be scanned.
  • A Platform broker has been murdered in the lower concourse — the first killing inside the market in two years, which violates the unspoken peace that keeps commerce flowing. The Platform needs the killer found before the incident escalates into a market shutdown that would cost every vendor their livelihood.
  • Helion Transit Authority is planning a nexus expansion that would demolish three blocks of residential housing in the second ring. The residents have no legal standing to resist. Someone with leverage over Helion, or the ability to create it, could change the equation.

Escanaba Gateway #

type place
name Escanaba Gateway
aliases
  • Escanaba MI
  • The Gate
  • South Port
  • UP's Back Door
description Escanaba occupies the UP's southern shore, facing Lake Michigan across Little Bay de Noc, and its function is exactly what the name suggests: it is the gateway. The port handles the ore, timber, and manufactured goods that flow south from the UP's interior to the markets and mills of the lower Great Lakes. Kelpline Logistics operates the port facilities under a sovereignty charter, and the automated cargo handling systems move tonnage 24 hours a day through a facility that was built for ten times the human workforce it currently employs. The port is efficient, profitable, and nearly empty of people — the automation revolution hit Escanaba harder than anywhere else in the UP, replacing dock workers with systems that don't take breaks, don't form unions, and don't spend money in local bars.

The result is a city that processes enormous wealth and retains almost none of it. The ore comes down from Marquette and Iron Mountain. The timber comes down from the northern forests. The finished materials come from Copperhead's fabrication facilities. All of it passes through Escanaba's port, loaded onto lake barges bound for Meridian 88, The Lattice, and points south. The city takes its cut — port fees, maintenance contracts, fuel sales — but the cut is thin and getting thinner as automation reduces the human infrastructure required to move cargo. The residential population has been declining for two decades, and the downtown district has the particular emptiness of a place that was built for more people than currently inhabit it.

Escanaba's strategic value in the UP war lies in its position. Control the southern port and you control the UP's economic output. Michigan holds it. Wisconsin wants it. The Mackinac Bridge — 150 kilometers east — is the only other route south from the UP, and it's a chokepoint, not a port. Whoever holds Escanaba can starve the UP or feed it, which makes the city's small population disproportionately important and disproportionately nervous.
atmosphere
sights
  • Automated cargo cranes operating on the port — massive, precise, and eerily unmanned
  • Empty storefronts on Ludington Street — the downtown built for a population that left
  • Lake Michigan visible from everywhere — blue-grey and busy with cargo barge traffic
  • Kelpline Logistics sovereign territory markers along the waterfront — corporate authority over public shore
  • The ore trains arriving from the interior, loaded cars stretching to the horizon
sounds
  • Automated port operations — the whir and clank of machines handling cargo without human direction
  • Wind off Lake Michigan — steady, cold, and carrying the sound of barge traffic
  • The absence of crowds — Escanaba's streets are quiet in a way that feels like a warning
  • Ore trains arriving and departing — the rhythm of extraction moving through the city like a pulse
smells
  • Lake Michigan air — cleaner than Superior, warmer, carrying a different mineral profile
  • Iron ore dust from the transit operations — the UP's export made visible and breathable
  • Diesel and electric motor exhaust from the cargo handling systems
feel A city that serves a function and wonders if the function will continue to need a city. Escanaba works, but it works the way a machine works — efficiently, impersonally, and without any particular attachment to the people who live alongside it. The emptiness is not desolate. It is procedural.
tags —
demographics Population 18,000, down from 35,000 two decades ago. The decline tracks automation adoption almost exactly. The remaining population is predominantly port support workers, Kelpline employees, and the businesses that serve them. Median age is rising. Young people leave for Iron Crown or the lower peninsula. The ones who stay have reasons.
economy Port operations (Kelpline Logistics) and cargo transit. Escanaba is a throughput economy — value passes through without accumulating. The city's GDP per capita is technically high; the city's livability is technically declining. The automation dividend goes to Kelpline shareholders, not to Escanaba residents.
power structure Kelpline Logistics holds port sovereignty. Michigan municipal government holds residential jurisdiction. The practical power balance is determined by employment — Kelpline employs 40% of the remaining workforce directly, and another 30% indirectly. The mayor governs at Kelpline's convenience.
dangers
  • Economic obsolescence — automation is reducing the human workforce required, and the trend has no floor
  • Strategic vulnerability — the port is a high-value target in the UP war, and the population is too small to defend it
  • Kelpline workforce reductions — each round of automation eliminates jobs that don't come back
  • Wisconsin-aligned sabotage of port operations — disrupting southern shipping to weaken Michigan's economic position
  • The psychological toll of living in a shrinking city — Escanaba's mental health infrastructure is as understaffed as everything else
opportunities
  • Port access — Escanaba is the gateway to southern markets, and access has value
  • Automation systems expertise — the port's technology is state-of-the-art, and technicians who maintain it are employable everywhere
  • Strategic intelligence — shipping manifests from Escanaba reveal the UP's economic activity in real time
  • Real estate — the depopulation has made property cheap, which attracts certain kinds of operations that prefer low visibility
story hooks
  • Kelpline Logistics is negotiating a 'security partnership' with Wisconsin that would effectively surrender the port without Michigan's consent
  • Automated cargo containers are being loaded with unmanifested materials at night — the port's own systems are being used to smuggle something south
  • A Wisconsin military force is staging 80 kilometers west, and the only thing between them and Escanaba is forest and a population too small to matter

  • Ironvein (Iron Mountain, northwest along the border zone)
  • The Mackinac Bridge (east, connecting to the lower peninsula)
  • Meridian 88 (south across Lake Michigan, via cargo barge routes)

  • Cargo barge crews transiting to southern markets
  • Michigan military observers monitoring the Wisconsin border
  • The shrinking community of permanent residents who haven't left yet

Fenwick Float #

type place
name Fenwick Float
aliases
  • The Float
  • Fenwick's
  • The Raft Quarter
  • Lake Fenwick
description Fenwick Float is a semi-permanent flotilla of linked barges, decommissioned ferry hulls, and modular platform sections anchored roughly two kilometers off the Chicago Lakeshore, accessible by water-taxi, private skiff, or the one functional mag-cable gondola that runs from a crumbling pier near the old Adler site. The Float began as an emergency housing overflow measure during the 2161 Shelf flooding crisis and was never formally dissolved — it simply accumulated residents, commerce, and eventually its own internal logic, drifting slightly with seasonal anchor adjustments but always remaining within the same rough coordinates.

Because the Float sits in jurisdictionally ambiguous water — technically under Meridian 88 municipal charter but practically unreachable by standard Ferrogate ground patrols — it has become a preferred location for operations that require distance from civic scrutiny. Legitimate floating restaurants and water-purification co-ops share deck space with unlicensed medical clinics, data brokerage nodes, and at least two competing smuggling operations that have achieved a workable truce. The lake wind is constant and the horizon is always visible, which residents cite with surprising frequency as reasons they stay.
atmosphere
sights
  • The Float's connected platforms undulate gently in a slow, breathing rhythm, making every structure on it appear subtly, perpetually in motion.
  • String lights and bioluminescent algae panels illuminate the inter-platform walkways at night, reflecting in broken columns across the black lake surface.
  • Laundry, solar collection film, and signal-mesh antennae all compete for vertical space on every mast and railing, giving the Float a festive, cluttered skyline.
  • The mag-cable gondola arrives every forty minutes, its single cabin lit warm amber against the dark water, trailing a thin wake of spray.
sounds
  • The constant low percussion of lake swells against hull metal creates a rhythm that residents stop consciously hearing within days of arrival.
  • Competing music from the floating restaurant barges bleeds together across the walkways into a layered, accidental ambience.
  • The gondola cable hums a descending note as it approaches the Float's main dock, serving as the closest thing to a public clock the community has.
smells
  • Lake air dominates — clean and cold with an algal mineral edge that sharpens in the morning and softens at dusk.
  • Cooking smells from a dozen different culinary traditions drift and combine across the platform walkways, strongest near the central barge cluster.
  • Below the waterline access hatches, a persistent smell of treated bilge water and hull sealant rises whenever they are opened.
feel There is a looseness to Fenwick Float that the city proper cannot replicate — the sense that the rules apply differently here, or not at all, or only the ones that residents have agreed to among themselves. The constant motion underfoot is disorienting for newcomers and becomes, for long-timers, a physical reassurance. The lake horizon provides a psychological expanse that the corridor's vertical density forecloses entirely.
tags —
demographics A genuinely mixed population ranging from Tier 1 laborers who could not secure Shelf housing to deliberate off-grid professionals (data brokers, unlicensed medics, gray-market logistics coordinators) to a small number of Tier 3 residents who maintain secondary residences here for privacy reasons.
economy Tourism and food service from the restaurant barges, water purification co-op revenues, and a substantial gray-market economy centered on data brokerage, unlicensed medical services, and logistics coordination for contraband moving in and out of the Lakeshore Corridor.
power structure The Float has no formal governance; a rotating Harbor Committee handles platform maintenance and inter-operator disputes, but real authority is exercised by the two dominant smuggling operations — Carrion Logistics' unofficial lake division and an independent crew known as the Meridian Drift — who maintain their truce through mutual dependency.
dangers
  • Platform connection joints fail periodically, separating sections of the Float during storm conditions and stranding residents until emergency lashing can be rigged.
  • The jurisdictional ambiguity that protects the Float also means emergency services response times from the shore average forty-seven minutes — effectively nonexistent.
  • The Meridian Drift crew is volatile; their truce with Carrion Logistics has collapsed twice in six years, and both incidents produced casualties among uninvolved Float residents.
  • Arcturus Defense Solutions operates an intermittent aerial surveillance drone pattern over the lake, and the Float is logged in their tracking database as a 'person of interest aggregation site.'
opportunities
  • The Float's unlicensed medical clinic operates with equipment and pharmaceutical access that rivals some legitimate Tier 3 facilities, at a fraction of the cost and with no identity verification.
  • The data brokerage nodes on the Float maintain Diaspora connections routed through lake-bed relay buoys that are effectively invisible to standard municipal traffic monitoring.
  • Carrion Logistics' lake division offers reliable, quiet transport of persons and cargo to points along the entire Great Lakes coastline, no manifest required.
story hooks
  • A Palladian Group corporate attorney arrived on the Float three weeks ago and has not left — she is not using her credentials, not contacting her firm, and the one Float resident who tried to speak with her says she seemed genuinely terrified. Someone from the Spire is now offering Φ15,000 for her safe return, and someone else is offering Φ20,000 for confirmation that she never makes it back.
  • The mag-cable gondola broke down mid-crossing yesterday with six passengers aboard, and when the maintenance crew finally reached it, four of the six were dead from apparent BCI-induced cardiac arrest — the other two have no memory of the crossing at all.
  • The water purification co-op has quietly discovered that the lake-bed relay buoys routing the Float's Diaspora connections are also carrying an encrypted secondary signal of unknown origin — one of the co-op's engineers believes it is an E.L.F. using the Float's infrastructure as a refuge node.

Forest Hollow #

type place
name Forest Hollow
aliases
  • Forest Glen
  • The Hollow
  • The Blind Spot
  • Ghost Grid
description Forest Hollow is the district that Meridian forgot, and that's exactly how its residents like it. The old Forest Glen was always Chicago's least densely populated community area — winding streets, large lots, a suburban feel that made no sense inside city limits. When the Corporate Reconstruction mapped Meridian 88's zones, Forest Glen's low population density, minimal commercial value, and confusing street layout caused it to fall through the cracks of multiple corporate planning algorithms. It was assigned to no sovereign territory. It appeared on no development plan. It was, in the language of corporate logistics, a null zone — a place that existed in geographic space but not in administrative space. By the time anyone noticed the oversight, the residents had adapted to their invisible status and had no intention of being noticed.

The Hollow's winding streets — originally a product of the neighborhood following the contours of the North Branch river and the forest preserves — now serve as a natural labyrinth. Drone navigation struggles with the irregular grid. Surveillance coverage is patchy because the camera placement algorithms were designed for Meridian's standard block structure, not Forest Glen's organic curves. The tree canopy — maintained by residents who understand that overhead cover defeats satellite imaging — creates a green ceiling that makes the Hollow invisible from above. The forest preserve land, never developed and never formally acquired by any corporation, has grown wild, its paths known only to the Hollow's residents and the animals that have moved in as Meridian's development pushed wildlife to the margins.

What Forest Hollow does with its invisibility is a matter of some speculation among the few outsiders who know it exists. The truth is less dramatic than the rumors suggest: the Hollow is a community of roughly 3,000 people who live off the grid in the most literal sense. Power comes from solar panels hidden under tree cover. Water comes from wells tapping the old aquifer. Communication uses mesh networks that don't route through Axiom's infrastructure. The residents grow food, maintain their homes, educate their children, and ignore Meridian with the comprehensive commitment of people who've decided that the city's problems are not their problems. It's not paradise — the medical resources are primitive, the winters are brutal without corporate climate control, and the isolation can eat at you. But it's free, in a way that nowhere else in Meridian can claim to be.

The Hollow's relationship with the outside world is managed through a single controlled point of contact: a resident designated as the Interface, who handles all necessary interactions with neighboring districts and ensures that nothing about Forest Hollow enters any database, manifest, or conversation that corporate systems might parse. The current Interface is a woman in her fifties who worked for Axiom's surveillance division before she disappeared — officially dead, actually living in a bungalow surrounded by oak trees, making sure that the community that took her in stays invisible. She is very good at her job.
atmosphere
sights
  • Winding streets under a full tree canopy — green overhead, dappled light, the visual signature of a place that hides
  • Solar panels concealed beneath leaf cover, visible only from the right angle
  • Wild forest preserve land — overgrown paths, animal tracks, the unmanaged beauty of nature left alone
  • Homes that blend into the landscape — maintained but not conspicuous, designed to not be seen from any distance
  • The absence of corporate signage, surveillance cameras, or any evidence that Meridian 88 exists here
  • Deer. Actual deer, standing in yards, unbothered by human presence.
sounds
  • Forest sounds — rustling leaves, birdsong, animal movement in the underbrush. Sounds Meridian has forgotten.
  • Wind through the tree canopy — a continuous, layered sound that masks other noise naturally
  • The absence of electronic ambient noise — no drone hum, no maglev whine, no corporate audio. Profound silence by Meridian standards.
  • Children's voices from somewhere in the trees — the Hollow's kids play in the forest like children from another century
  • Well pumps and hand tools — the analog sounds of a community that maintains itself manually
smells
  • Forest floor — decomposing leaves, damp earth, mushrooms, the rich biological smell of land that hasn't been paved
  • Woodsmoke from heating fires in winter — the Hollow doesn't have corporate climate control
  • Growing things — vegetable gardens, fruit trees, herbs. The smell of food being produced, not manufactured.
  • Clean air — genuinely clean, not filtered or processed, just air that's been through a forest and nothing else
feel Hidden. Forest Hollow feels like stepping through a door in a wall you didn't know had a door. The transition from Meridian's constant electronic presence to the Hollow's analog silence is physically disorienting — your neural interface gets quieter, your augments find fewer signals to process, and your senses recalibrate to an environment that hasn't been optimized for human comfort but hasn't been stripped of natural comfort either. It feels like trespassing in a place that chose to leave the world, which is exactly what it is.
tags —
demographics Approximately 3,000 residents, officially zero. No tier assignments — the Hollow doesn't exist in Axiom's population databases. A mix of original Forest Glen families, corporate defectors, off-grid idealists, and people who needed to stop existing on paper. All ages, but skewing toward adults who made a deliberate choice to disappear.
economy Subsistence — the Hollow grows its own food, generates its own power, and maintains its own infrastructure. Trade with the outside world is minimal and conducted through the Interface. The Hollow's only export is invisibility, offered selectively to people who need it.
power structure Consensus governance among household heads. The Interface holds unique authority over external relations. No formal hierarchy — the community is small enough for direct negotiation. Disagreements are resolved face-to-face because there's nowhere to hide from your neighbors in a community of 3,000.
dangers
  • Discovery — if Axiom's planning systems correct the null-zone oversight, the Hollow's independence ends
  • Medical emergencies — the Hollow's healthcare is pre-corporate level, and serious injuries or illnesses require breaking cover to access outside facilities
  • Internal conflict — in a community this small and isolated, personal disputes can become existential threats
  • Winter — without corporate climate control, the Great Lakes winter is a survival challenge that claims lives in bad years
  • The forest itself — the wild preserve contains animals, terrain, and weather that an urbanized population isn't always prepared for
opportunities
  • Total invisibility — Forest Hollow is the only place in Meridian that genuinely doesn't exist in any database
  • The Interface — a former Axiom surveillance specialist whose knowledge of corporate monitoring systems is invaluable
  • Off-grid infrastructure knowledge — the Hollow's residents know how to build and maintain systems without corporate supply chains
  • Forest preserve resources — medicinal plants, clean water, building materials, and wildlife that the rest of Meridian has lost access to
  • Perspective — time in the Hollow reminds you what human life looked like before the optimization
story hooks
  • The Interface intercepts a corporate survey drone that's been programmed with Forest Hollow's coordinates — someone inside Axiom has noticed the null zone, and the Hollow has weeks, maybe days, before a planning team arrives to fill the gap on the map
  • A critically injured person is brought to the Hollow's border by someone who shouldn't know the community exists. The injury requires medical resources the Hollow doesn't have. Saving this person means exposing the community to outside contact. Not saving them means letting someone die.
  • Kyle discovers that Forest Hollow exists during a job that takes him through the northwest. The community's existence — proof that opting out of Meridian is possible — changes his understanding of what his life could be. The Interface offers him a choice he's not ready to make.

  • Wildlife — deer, foxes, coyotes, and birds that have been pushed out of every other part of Meridian
  • The Interface — moving between the Hollow and the outside world, the only person who regularly crosses the boundary

Fort Anchor #

type place
name Fort Anchor
aliases
  • North Chicago
  • The Processing Center
  • Anchor
  • The Funnel
description Fort Anchor is the name the GLM Metropolitan Authority gave the former Great Lakes Naval Station when they converted it — or more accurately, when Ringo Defense Solutions converted it on a no-bid contract and the Metropolitan Authority signed the paperwork. The original naval training facility, which had processed American sailors for a century and a half, now processes a different kind of human traffic: climate refugees, economic migrants, and the steady flow of undocumented people moving north through the Corridor seeking entry into the upper GLM's marginally less catastrophic labor markets.

The processing center occupies the eastern half of the old base, a grid of repurposed barracks and administrative buildings where new arrivals are biometrically registered, neurally scanned, and assigned a provisional tier status that will determine every aspect of their life in the Corridor. Provisional Tier 1 — which is what most arrivals receive — grants the right to exist within M88 jurisdiction without being arrested for it. It does not grant employment authorization, medical access, or housing assistance. It grants existence. The distinction between Provisional Tier 1 and 'excluded' is technical, legal, and in practical terms, largely meaningless.

The western half of Fort Anchor is a Ringo garrison — the ground-force complement to the air and logistics operations at the Waukegan compound. Approximately 8,000 Ringo security personnel are stationed here, and their presence gives the processing center its particular character: a place where the humanitarian language of refugee assistance coexists with razor wire, automated sentry turrets, and the constant reminder that the people being 'processed' are being processed by the same company that sells weapons systems. Ringo's contract with the Metropolitan Authority specifies 'humane and orderly processing.' The contract does not define humane. The contract does not define orderly. Ringo defined both, and their definitions prioritize throughput.

The town of North Chicago — the civilian community surrounding the base — has been economically dependent on military and quasi-military installation spending since the 1940s. Nothing about that has changed except the uniform. Local businesses serve Ringo personnel. Local housing absorbs people who completed processing and couldn't afford to go anywhere else. The result is a community where the processors and the processed live side by side, eat at the same restaurants, and send their children to the same underfunded schools. The awkwardness of this is lost on no one.
atmosphere
sights
  • The processing center's intake queue — visible from the main road, a line of people that fluctuates between hundreds and thousands depending on the season
  • Ringo garrison vehicles moving in convoy along the base perimeter road, armored and unhurried
  • Biometric scanning stations at the processing center entrance, their blue lights visible at night from a kilometer away
  • Civilian neighborhoods pressed against the base fence line, close enough to hear the PA system announcements
  • Children playing in vacant lots while their parents wait in processing queues that can last days
sounds
  • The processing center PA system — automated announcements in twelve languages, cycling continuously
  • Garrison activity — vehicle engines, equipment loading, the organized noise of a military installation
  • The processing queue — thousands of people waiting, talking, arguing, praying, and trying to keep children calm
  • Local traffic along the commercial strip — the ordinary sounds of a town that exists because a base exists
  • The occasional sonic crack of a Ringo aerospace vehicle launching from the garrison's vertical pad
smells
  • Institutional food from the processing center's mass feeding operation — nutritionally adequate, culinarily punitive
  • Vehicle exhaust from the garrison — Ringo runs hydrogen fuel cells but the support fleet still burns synth-diesel
  • The particular smell of too many people in too small a space, drifting from the intake barracks on warm days
feel A place where bureaucracy and human desperation have reached a stable equilibrium. Fort Anchor processes people with the efficiency of a logistics operation, because that is what it is. The humanitarian framing is not entirely false — people are fed, scanned, documented, and released into a system that will largely ignore them. The alternative is not being processed at all, which means not existing in any system, which means the ungoverned corridors. Fort Anchor is better than the alternative. This is the most damning thing about it.
tags —
demographics Permanent population approximately 45,000. Transient processing population fluctuates between 5,000-20,000 at any given time. Permanent residents are predominantly Tier 1-2, split between Ringo personnel families and settled former refugees. The processed population is drawn from every displacement crisis of the last thirty years: Gulf Coast, Central American climate corridor, Pacific Island submersion, and the ongoing internal displacement from the Dust Belt.
economy Ringo garrison spending drives the local economy. Processing center support contracts. Small-business service economy catering to base personnel. The informal economy among the processed population is survival-based: barter, labor exchange, and the careful hoarding of whatever resources arrive.
power structure Ringo holds effective authority over the entire district through its garrison command and processing center contract. The GLM Metropolitan Authority maintains a liaison office that rubber-stamps Ringo's operational decisions. Local civilian government exists but operates within parameters Ringo defines. The processed population has no political representation of any kind.
dangers
  • Ringo automated security — the perimeter systems do not distinguish between threats and confused civilians
  • Processing delays — being stuck in the intake system for weeks or months, with no legal recourse and diminishing resources
  • Exploitation of the processed — labor trafficking, organ harvesting, and neural interface theft targeting people with no documentation and no advocates
  • Garrison personnel off-duty behavior — not all Ringo employees handle the moral weight of their work gracefully
  • Data vulnerability — biometric and neural scan data from processing is stored on Ringo servers with Ringo's definition of privacy
opportunities
  • Intelligence on Ringo operations — the processing center is Ringo's most visible and least secure operation
  • Humanitarian contacts — the NGO workers and aid organizations operating at Fort Anchor are connected to networks throughout the GLM
  • Identity documentation — the processing system creates identities, and any system that creates identities can be exploited
  • Recruitment — the processed population includes skilled people from every profession, available for any work that offers a path forward
story hooks
  • A batch of processing records has been altered — someone inside Ringo is creating false identities for people who were never processed, and the question is whether this is corruption or mercy
  • A former Ringo processing officer has gone public with testimony about 'expedited disposition' protocols for arrivals flagged by NeoCortex's pattern recognition systems
  • Someone Kyle knew before — from before the story starts — appears in the processing queue
