Freestone #

type place
name Freestone
aliases
  • The First Reef
  • Freestone Republic
  • The Raft
  • Michigan Free City
description Freestone is the first and largest of the Great Lakes seacrete cities — a sovereign free nation grown from the body of Lake Michigan itself. It began in 2161, when a coalition of climate refugees, displaced academics, anarchist engineers, and people who had simply run out of continent built a wire-mesh framework twelve nautical miles off the Wisconsin shore, dropped it into the lake, and ran electrical current through it. The principle is electrodeposition: pass low-voltage direct current through a submerged conductive framework in mineral-rich water, and dissolved calcium and magnesium carbonates precipitate onto the mesh, building up layer by layer into a material harder than concrete. The pioneers called the process seacrete — mineral accretion, the same chemistry that builds coral reefs, accelerated by human engineering. Marshall T. Savage described it in 'The Millennial Project' as a way to colonize the oceans. The Freestone founders used it to escape the corponations.

The city grew the way coral grows: slowly, organically, and in every direction. The original framework was a flat platform roughly the size of a city block. Within five years, it had accreted into a multi-level structure with subsurface foundations reaching thirty meters down to the lakebed. New frameworks were attached to the edges and submerged; the current was extended; the reef expanded. Solar arrays and wave-energy converters powered the electrodeposition continuously. By 2180, Freestone was a floating reef-city of 340,000 people, roughly two kilometers in diameter, with docking platforms, desalination systems, hydroponic farms, workshop districts, and residential warrens grown directly from the lake's own minerals. The structures are rough-textured, organic, vaguely biological — walls that curve like bone, archways that look grown rather than built, surfaces encrusted with the mineral patterns of their own creation. It looks like someone taught a coral reef to be a city.

Freestone's sovereignty is a legal accident that became a political fact. The original platform was anchored in water deep enough to be outside any state or corponation's territorial claim — the Great Lakes sovereignty framework, written by corporate lawyers for corporate purposes, never anticipated that anyone would build a nation in the middle of the lake. By the time M88's legal apparatus noticed Freestone, it had 50,000 residents, its own desalination infrastructure, a functional economy, and enough defensive capability to make forced removal expensive. The Corridor Council issued seventeen non-recognition declarations between 2168 and 2175. Freestone ignored all of them. The corponations tried economic blockade; Freestone traded with the other lake cities instead. They tried diplomatic pressure; Freestone's elected council responded with a one-sentence communique: 'We grew this from water. Come take it.' Nobody did.

Governance is direct democracy mediated by rotating councils. There are no corporations on Freestone — the founding charter prohibits sovereign corporate entities within its waters. The economy runs on a labor-credit system internally and trades in Q externally, primarily exporting seacrete construction expertise, desalinated water, aquaculture products, and a fierce independence that the shore-based population finds either inspiring or irritating depending on their tier. Freestone is not utopia. The housing is cramped, the infrastructure is perpetually strained, the mineral-accretion walls sometimes grow in directions nobody planned, and the democratic process is exactly as slow and frustrating as democracy always is. But nobody here answers to a board of directors, and that fact is worth more than comfort.
atmosphere
sights
  • Mineral-accretion architecture — walls and archways grown from the lake itself, rough-textured, organic, faintly luminescent where phosphorescent algae has colonized the surfaces
  • Solar arrays and wave-energy converters ringing the city's outer platforms like a mechanical reef
  • Hydroponic farms in transparent-roofed growing halls, green against the grey lake water
  • Fishing boats and trade vessels docked along the organic harbor formations — coral-like piers that grew into their current shape
  • The Anchor Stone — the original wire-mesh framework, now encrusted in decades of mineral growth, preserved as a monument at the city's center
sounds
  • Water — everywhere, always. The lap of waves against accreted walls, the rush through channel passages, the drip in lower-level corridors
  • The low electrical hum of the accretion current — the sound of the city growing
  • Market noise from the harbor platforms — trade in four languages plus the lakeside pidgin
  • Wind through the upper-level structures, which are more porous than planned and sing in storms
smells
  • Clean lake water — Freestone sits far enough from shore that the toxicity is manageable
  • Mineral deposits — a faintly chalky, calcium-rich scent that clings to everything
  • Hydroponic growth medium and fresh produce — the smell of food that wasn't synthesized
  • Salt-free brine from the desalination returns
feel Alive. Freestone feels alive in a way that Meridian's steel-and-glass corridors do not. The walls are textured, irregular, warm to the touch where the accretion current runs. The city shifts subtly with the lake's movement. Nothing is straight, nothing is polished, nothing was designed in a boardroom. It feels handmade — because it was, molecule by molecule, pulled from the water by people who decided to build something that belonged to them. It also feels precarious. The lake is not gentle, and Freestone is a human settlement balanced on a reef that humans tricked into existence. The precariousness is part of the identity.
tags —
demographics Approximately 340,000 permanent residents. Ethnically and nationally diverse — the founding population was climate refugees, academics, and political dissidents from across the Great Lakes region and beyond. No tier system — Freestone rejected M88's citizenship framework entirely. Literacy rate: 97%. Average age skews young; people come to Freestone to build something.
economy Internal: labor-credit system where contribution to city infrastructure, food production, or public services earns credits exchangeable for housing, goods, and leisure. External: Freestone trades seacrete engineering expertise, desalinated water, aquaculture products (lake perch, engineered kelp, freshwater crustaceans), and artisanal goods. Imports include electronics, medical equipment, and raw metal stock for new accretion frameworks. Annual external trade volume estimated at Φ8.2 billion.
power structure Direct democracy with rotating councils. The Reef Council — twelve members, term-limited to two years, selected by sortition — handles day-to-day governance. Major decisions go to general assembly vote. No corporate entities permitted. The military defense cooperative, the Breakwater, operates under civilian oversight and cannot initiate offensive action without assembly approval.
dangers
  • Storm damage — Lake Michigan storms can be brutal, and seacrete structures, while strong, are not invulnerable
  • Cormorant Naval Systems patrols — Freestone exists in a legal grey zone and Cormorant occasionally tests boundaries
  • Infrastructure strain — 340,000 people on a structure that grows slowly; capacity is always being chased
  • Political tension with M88 — the Corridor Council has never formally recognized Freestone's sovereignty
  • Internal democratic gridlock — direct democracy means every major decision is a fight
opportunities
  • Seacrete construction expertise — Freestone's engineers are the best in the world at mineral accretion building
  • A genuine alternative to corporate life — Freestone proves it's possible to live outside the tier system
  • Trade connections with all seven lake cities and several shore communities
  • The Breakwater's intelligence network — they know what moves on the lake
story hooks
  • Freestone's Reef Council offers Kyle asylum — a life outside the tier system, if he can get there and if he's willing to leave everything on shore behind
  • A Cormorant Naval Systems operation targets Freestone's water supply infrastructure. The city needs someone shore-side to disrupt the operation before it launches.
  • Freestone's founding charter is being challenged from within — a faction argues that prohibiting corporate entities is holding the city back. The debate threatens to split the republic.

  • Independent traders running goods between shore and lake
  • Political refugees from M88's tier system
  • Researchers studying seacrete construction and alternative governance

Gage Circuit #

type place
name Gage Circuit
aliases
  • Gage Park
  • The Strip
  • Fifty-Five
  • La Franja
description Gage Circuit runs on 55th Street the way an engine runs on a crankshaft -- everything turns around it. The old Gage Park commercial strip was already one of the densest retail corridors on Chicago's Southwest Side before Meridian 88 formalized the district boundaries, and the transition to megacity economics only compressed what was already tight. The strip stretches for two and a half kilometers of uninterrupted commercial activity: stalls, shops, service counters, and popup vendors occupying every available square meter of ground-floor space, with residential blocks stacked above in four-to-six story layers that house the same families who run the businesses below. Living above your shop isn't a lifestyle choice here. It's thermal efficiency -- body heat rises, inventory stays cool, and the commute is one flight of stairs.

The commercial ecosystem on 55th is a closed loop that's almost entirely divorced from Meridian's formal economy. Transactions happen in a local scrip system that the vendor association manages through a decentralized ledger running on a neural mesh network that the vendors built, maintain, and control. Corporate currency is accepted but not preferred. Axiom's economic monitoring systems can see the scrip transactions but can't parse them -- the ledger's encryption was designed by a retired Circuit hacker who moved to Gage Park for the food and stayed for the community, and her work is, by any professional standard, elegant. The strip pays its Meridian taxes in corporate currency, calculated from revenue figures that bear a creative relationship to reality. Everyone involved, including the tax assessor who lives on 56th Street, understands this arrangement.

The density is the story. Gage Circuit packs 60,000 people into a footprint that was designed for 20,000, and the pressure creates its own physics. Disputes are resolved fast because there isn't room for them to linger. Businesses adapt or are replaced within weeks. Information travels the strip faster than neural mesh can carry it because the density of human contact is higher than the density of data connections. You can learn anything that's happening in the Southwest by standing on 55th Street for an hour and keeping your ears open. The challenge isn't getting information. The challenge is drinking from the firehose.
atmosphere
sights
  • The 55th Street corridor in full commercial frenzy -- a canyon of vendors, signage, and bodies
  • Scrip transaction holograms flickering between buyers and sellers in the vendor association's custom interface
  • Residential laundry and signal equipment crowding rooflines above the shops
  • Hand-lettered and holographic signage competing for attention in Spanish, Polish, Arabic, and Shelf Cant
  • The vendor association's communication nodes -- repurposed neural mesh relays bolted to lampposts
  • Foot traffic so dense the street functions as a single slow-moving organism
sounds
  • The roar of commerce -- haggling, hawking, laughing, arguing, all at full Southwest Side volume
  • Scrip ledger confirmation tones -- a custom two-note chime that means money has changed hands
  • Music from competing storefronts creating a block-by-block soundtrack that changes every fifty meters
  • The creak and groan of buildings bearing more weight than their architects intended
smells
  • Street food from every tradition represented on the strip -- grilling, frying, baking, and fermenting simultaneously
  • Fabric from the textile stalls -- new synthetics and recycled natural fibers packed in bolts
  • The human density itself -- 60,000 people in close quarters have an aggregate scent that's earthy and alive
  • Fresh paint and adhesive from storefronts being renovated on the fly, between customers
feel Overwhelming and alive. Gage Circuit feels like standing inside a living economy -- not the abstracted graphs and metrics of the Meridian Core, but the physical reality of people exchanging labor for goods at a scale that makes institutional economics irrelevant. It's exhausting, exhilarating, and completely authentic in a way that nothing above Tier 2 ever manages to be.
tags —
demographics Approximately 60,000 residents, predominantly Latino with significant Eastern European, Arab, and South Asian minorities. Overwhelmingly Tier 1 and Tier 2. The population density exceeds Meridian residential standards by 300%, a statistic the district has successfully kept out of official reporting.
economy The 55th Street commercial strip operates on a local scrip system with encrypted decentralized ledger. Revenue is substantial, uncounted by Meridian economic metrics, and recycled almost entirely within the community. The vendor association functions as a de facto central bank.
power structure The Gage Circuit Vendor Association controls the scrip system, the commercial strip's physical space, and the neural mesh network that supports both. Their authority is economic and therefore absolute within the strip. Outside the strip, standard Meridian governance applies, loosely.
dangers
  • Overcrowding -- structural and fire risks in buildings loaded beyond design capacity
  • The scrip system's opacity attracts occasional interest from Axiom Economic Compliance, whose audits are resisted collectively
  • Commercial disputes that escalate faster than mediation can contain them in the compressed environment
  • Pickpockets and petty theft in the crowd density -- an occupational hazard of 55th Street
  • Getting lost -- the strip's navigation is intuitive to residents and bewildering to everyone else
opportunities
  • Access to goods and services that don't exist in the formal economy, at prices the formal economy can't match
  • The vendor association's intelligence network covers every commercial transaction in the Southwest

Garfield Rack #

type place
name Garfield Rack
aliases
  • Garfield Ridge
  • The Rack
  • Badgetown
  • Midway Adjacent
description Garfield Rack is cop country. Always was, even before Meridian 88 absorbed Chicago's Southwest Side and reorganized everything into tiers and jurisdictions. Old Garfield Ridge was where the city's police officers, firefighters, and municipal workers bought homes, raised families, and built a community defined by the particular solidarity of people who carry badges. When the megacity transition came, that identity didn't dissolve -- it calcified. Garfield Rack became the residential stronghold for Meridian's enforcement class: Axiom Security operatives, corporate jurisdiction officers, fire suppression contractors, and the various private police forces that keep the tier system running. They live here, in neat rows of reinforced bungalows with security-grade neural mesh and perimeter monitoring that makes the neighborhood effectively self-surveilling.

Midway, the old airport, is the district's geographic anchor and its economic engine. The runways were converted decades ago into a logistics hub -- automated cargo drones launch and land in continuous rotation, distributing goods across Meridian's commercial network. The hub employs thousands, most of them Rack residents, in operations, security, and maintenance roles. The drone traffic is constant overhead, a mechanical migration pattern that residents have learned to sleep through. The noise complaints stopped years ago, not because the noise stopped, but because complaining would mean admitting that the thing that employs you is also the thing that's ruining your hearing.

The Rack's relationship with the rest of Meridian is complicated by the fact that its residents are the enforcement mechanism for a system they didn't design and don't fully benefit from. Tier 3 is the ceiling here -- comfortable enough, with corporate health coverage and retirement accounts, but forever below the Tier 4 and 5 executives whose orders they carry out. It creates a specific psychology: loyalty to the system paired with resentment of the system, expressed as a ferocious insularity. Rack residents take care of Rack residents. They don't trust the Spire, they don't sympathize with the Shelf, and they don't talk about what happens on shift. The bungalows are well-maintained. The lawns are trimmed. The silence about certain things is absolute.
atmosphere
sights
  • Rows of reinforced bungalows with security-grade perimeter arrays -- suburbia with teeth
  • Midway logistics hub visible from everywhere -- automated cargo drones in constant flight patterns
  • Off-duty enforcement personnel in civilian clothes that don't quite hide the augment profiles
  • Block watch holographics rotating at intersections -- community surveillance branded as community pride
  • Memorial walls listing Rack residents killed in enforcement operations across the city
sounds
  • Cargo drone engines -- a constant industrial buzz that defines the district's acoustic baseline
  • The click and hum of perimeter security systems cycling through detection modes
  • Police scanner frequencies bleeding from open windows -- off-duty but never fully off
  • Quiet conversations on front porches, voices kept low from professional habit
  • Shift change sirens from the Midway hub, marking time for the entire neighborhood
smells
  • Drone fuel exhaust from the Midway hub -- kerosene-adjacent, omnipresent on south wind days
  • Fresh-cut synthetic turf from fastidiously maintained yards
  • Gun oil and augment lubricant -- the smell of people who maintain their tools
  • Bar food from the enforcement-class taverns along the main drag
feel Controlled. Not the corporate control of the Meridian Core, but the self-imposed control of people who spend their working lives managing other people's chaos and need their home to be the opposite. There is warmth here, but it's conditional -- extended to those who belong and withheld from those who don't. The Rack feels like a fist that's learned to relax at home but never quite unclenches.
tags —
demographics Approximately 40,000 residents, overwhelmingly Tier 3 enforcement-class families. Historically Irish, Polish, and Latino -- old Garfield Ridge demographics persisting through the megacity transition. A closed community in the sociological sense: intermarriage within the enforcement class is common, outsider settlement is rare.
economy Midway logistics hub employment and enforcement-class salaries form the economic base. A secondary economy of enforcement equipment suppliers, augment maintenance shops catering to security-grade hardware, and service businesses that cater to shift workers.
power structure The Rack is informally governed by the Enforcement Veterans Association, an organization that functions as neighborhood council, mutual aid society, and lobby group. Axiom Security has a district liaison office but treads carefully -- the Rack's residents are Axiom's workforce, and they know their leverage.
dangers
  • Outsiders are noticed immediately and tracked through overlapping residential surveillance
  • Off-duty enforcement personnel who respond to perceived threats with professional-grade reflexes
  • The institutional silence about enforcement abuses -- asking the wrong questions gets you flagged
  • Midway drone traffic -- the flight paths are mapped but the drones don't stop for pedestrians
  • Getting caught between the Rack's loyalty to its residents and its loyalty to the system
opportunities
  • Enforcement-class contacts who know how Axiom Security operates from the inside
  • Midway logistics hub access -- cargo manifests, shipping routes, and the occasional misdirected package
  • The Enforcement Veterans Association has institutional memory about every major security operation in Meridian's history
  • Off-duty officers who are willing to trade information when they're angry enough at the system they serve
story hooks
  • An Axiom Security internal affairs investigation is targeting Rack residents -- and the Enforcement Veterans Association is closing ranks in ways that suggest what's being protected is bigger than any individual
  • A Midway logistics hub worker has discovered that certain cargo drone flights don't appear on any manifest -- they launch at 0300, carry no corporate markings, and their flight paths end in the Indiana Exclusion Zone
  • Kyle needs information that only someone inside the enforcement class would have, and the only person willing to talk lives in the Rack and is running out of time

Geartown #

type place
name Geartown
aliases
  • Corktown
  • The Proving Ground
  • Ford Zero
description Geartown is what Corktown became when Ford Motor Company — or rather, the entity that emerged from Ford's 2144 merger with three autonomous vehicle startups and a military robotics firm — chose the neighborhood as its global autonomous vehicle testing campus. The name stuck because the locals refused to call it the Ford Autonomous Mobility Innovation District, which is what the brass plaque at Michigan Avenue and Trumbull says. Geartown. Where the gears turn. Where they turned you out of your house to make room for a parking algorithm.

The old neighborhood — Detroit's oldest, settled by Irish immigrants in the 1830s — is unrecognizable. The historic homes were bought, preserved as facades, and hollowed out to serve as sensor calibration labs, AV routing substations, and the kind of office space that looks like a living room but costs Φ40,000 per month. Michigan Central Station, the grand ruin that became a symbol of Detroit's decline and then its rebirth, now serves as Ford Meridian's primary AV command center — a gorgeous, vaulted space filled with holographic traffic models showing every autonomous vehicle in the Great Lakes Metropolitan Area as a point of light. Eighteen million points of light, moving in patterns no human mind can track without augmentation.

The testing ground extends six blocks in every direction from the station. Public access is restricted. Autonomous vehicles of every configuration run continuous test loops — freight haulers, passenger pods, military platforms, emergency response units, and experimental configurations that don't have names yet, just serial numbers. The vehicles are silent. The neighborhood is silent. The loudest sound in Geartown is the whisper of tires on smart-surface roads and the occasional distant clang from the maintenance bays where human technicians still do the work that robots can't. The irony of a neighborhood full of autonomous vehicles that still needs human hands to fix them is not lost on the technicians. It's the only job security they have.
atmosphere
sights
  • Michigan Central Station's restored Beaux-Arts facade, its windows now displaying real-time AV fleet data
  • Autonomous vehicles running silent test loops through empty streets — an entire neighborhood that moves without people
  • Historic Corktown facades preserved but hollow — beautiful shells housing sensor arrays and routing hardware
  • The Proving Ground perimeter fence, tastefully designed to not look like a fence and failing
  • Maintenance bay doors opening to reveal vehicles that don't exist in any public catalog
sounds
  • Tire whisper on smart-surface roads — the sound of a neighborhood running on software
  • The low hum of charging stations embedded in every curb
  • Maintenance bay impacts — human tools on machine bodies, the oldest sound in Detroit
  • Security drone patrol patterns overhead, their rotors tuned to a frequency designed to be ignorable
  • Nothing else. Geartown is the quietest neighborhood in Detroit, and the silence is engineered.
smells
  • Ozone from vehicle charging infrastructure
  • Smart-surface road material — a chemical cleanliness that smells like nothing, which is itself a smell
  • Machine lubricant drifting from the maintenance bays — the one honest industrial smell left
  • The ghost of hops from the old Corktown breweries, which is probably imaginary but everyone claims to smell it
feel Eerie. Geartown feels like a city that asked humans to leave and most of them did. The streets are immaculate. The vehicles are perfect. The buildings are preserved. And the entire neighborhood feels like a museum exhibit about what happens when machines inherit a place that used to be alive.
tags —
demographics Approximately 8,000 residents — almost entirely Ford Meridian employees, security personnel, and the maintenance technicians who keep the fleet running. Pre-corporate displacement population was 12,000. The displaced residents received relocation packages averaging Φ180,000, which bought them approximately eighteen months of housing in adjacent districts.
economy Ford Meridian's AV testing campus generates Φ320 billion annually in patent development, fleet licensing, and military autonomous platform contracts. The neighborhood itself has no informal economy. You cannot sell anything in Geartown that Ford Meridian does not authorize.
power structure Ford Meridian holds sovereign authority over the entire Proving Ground. The company's Detroit Regional Director, currently Kenji Okafor, reports to the Ford Meridian board in Dearborn. Local governance does not exist. Geartown is a company town in the most literal sense.
dangers
  • Autonomous vehicle test incidents — the vehicles are good but not perfect, and experimental platforms are unpredictable
  • Restricted zone violations — entering the Proving Ground without authorization triggers an immediate security response
  • Surveillance — every surface in Geartown is a sensor, because that's what autonomous vehicles need to navigate
  • The military platforms — some of the vehicles running test loops are armed, and the perimeter between civilian and military testing is a painted line on the road
  • Displacement creep — Ford Meridian acquires adjacent properties annually, and the perimeter keeps growing
opportunities
  • AV technology theft — Ford Meridian's experimental platforms are worth billions on the gray market
  • The maintenance technicians know things the engineers don't — hands-on knowledge of systems that only exist in prototype
  • Michigan Central Station's AV command center sees every autonomous vehicle in the GLM — access to that data is access to the region's circulatory system
story hooks
  • A military autonomous platform disappears from the Proving Ground. Ford Meridian claims it was scrapped. The platform's maintenance technician says the bay was empty when he arrived for the scheduled teardown.
  • The AV command center's fleet data shows vehicles routing through areas that don't appear on any map — someone is using the autonomous fleet to access locations that officially don't exist
  • A group of former Corktown residents are suing Ford Meridian for displacement damages. Their lawyer keeps dying in autonomous vehicle accidents.

Ghostbridge Island #

type place
name Ghostbridge Island
aliases
  • Mackinac Island MI
  • The Island
  • No-Motor Zone
  • The Anomaly
description Mackinac Island banned automobiles in 1898. In 2200, it has banned everything else. The island sits in the Straits of Mackinac, 5 kilometers from the bridge that connects Michigan's two peninsulas, and it has leveraged its historical no-motor ordinance into something unprecedented in the GLM: a technology restriction zone. No motorized vehicles. No neural interface connectivity. No augmentation uplinks. No corporate sovereign territory. No surveillance infrastructure. The island operates under a municipal charter that predates corporate sovereignty law, and the charter's technology restrictions have been upheld by every court that's reviewed them — not because the courts agree with the principle, but because the precedent of overturning a 200-year-old municipal ordinance terrifies the legal establishment.

The result is an island of 600 permanent residents and up to 5,000 visitors at any time, living in conditions that most GLM inhabitants would consider medieval. Horse-drawn transport. Paper documents. Face-to-face communication. No data trail. No surveillance record. No jurisdictional tracking. The implications have not been lost on anyone. Ghostbridge Island is the GLM's premiere dead-drop location, negotiation venue, and disappearance destination. If you need to have a conversation that no system can record, you have it here. If you need to meet someone without creating a data point, you meet here. If you need to vanish, the island's analog infrastructure means you were never digitally here in the first place.

The Grand Hotel — a Victorian-era structure maintained in deliberately anachronistic condition — serves as the island's primary venue for the negotiations, deals, and betrayals that require total surveillance absence. The hotel's guest list is not recorded digitally. The rooms are not monitored. The staff are hired for discretion, paid in physical currency, and trained in the art of not seeing things. Ghostbridge Island is a loophole in the GLM's total information architecture — a place where the panopticon blinks — and every powerful interest in the Great Lakes knows it, uses it, and fears what happens when someone else uses it.
atmosphere
sights
  • Horse-drawn carriages on streets with no power lines, no signal towers, no surveillance cameras
  • The Grand Hotel's 200-meter porch, overlooking the Straits, populated by people whose faces you are not supposed to remember
  • The Mackinac Bridge visible from the east shore — the hypermodern world, close enough to see, far enough to deny
  • Victorian architecture maintained with deliberate precision — not nostalgia, but infrastructure for anonymity
  • Visitors unconsciously reaching for neural interfaces that don't connect — the phantom limb of a disconnected world
sounds
  • Horse hooves on pavement — the island's primary transportation sound
  • Human conversation without the overlay of augmented reality — raw, unfiltered, and strangely intimate
  • Lake water on the shoreline — the sound of a place where nature is louder than technology
  • The absence of electronic noise — no hums, no pings, no background data traffic — a silence most visitors have never experienced
smells
  • Horse, hay, and leather — the organic infrastructure of pre-motor transportation
  • Mackinac Island fudge — still produced, still sold, still the island's most innocent tradition
  • Lake Huron air, unprocessed and unfiltered — what air smelled like before the cities
feel Uncanny. Ghostbridge Island feels like a glitch in the timeline — a place where 2200 forgot to arrive. The sensation of disconnection is physical for augmented visitors. Neural interfaces go silent. Uplinks drop. You are alone with your unaugmented senses, and for most GLM residents, that is the most disorienting experience available. It is also, for some, the most honest.
tags —
demographics 600 permanent residents. Self-selected for analog life, multi-generational island families mixed with people who chose disconnection deliberately. Up to 5,000 transient visitors — a rotating population of fixers, negotiators, fugitives, diplomats, and tourists who want to know what silence feels like.
economy Hospitality, dead-drop services, and the anonymity premium. The island charges for what the rest of the GLM cannot provide: unrecorded space. The Grand Hotel's rates are astronomical. The smaller inns and boarding houses serve the same function at lower price points. The economy is entirely analog — physical currency, paper ledgers, handshake agreements. GDP is unmeasurable by design.
power structure Municipal charter authority, enforced by the island's own constabulary and the legal precedent that protects the technology restriction zone. No corporate sovereign territory. No state jurisdiction beyond what the charter permits. The island's governance is the closest thing to genuine self-determination in the GLM, sustained not by power but by legal precedent and the useful fiction that the island is too small to matter.
dangers
  • The lack of surveillance means the lack of emergency response infrastructure — violence here is private and unreported
  • Dead-drop operations gone wrong — the island's anonymity attracts people with things to hide, and some of those things are dangerous
  • The legal precedent protecting the technology restriction zone is always one court challenge away from collapse
  • Being recognized in a place designed for anonymity — some visitors take the unrecorded status very seriously
  • The ferry crossing — the 5-kilometer strait is the only access, and it can be watched even if the island cannot
opportunities
  • Unrecorded meetings — the island's primary commodity is surveillance absence
  • Dead-drop facilitation — serving as intermediary for information exchanges that cannot happen on the grid
  • Disappearance infrastructure — the island's analog systems can absorb identities that need to stop existing
  • The Grand Hotel's network of contacts — the staff know everyone who matters and remember nothing officially
story hooks
  • A negotiation at the Grand Hotel between two corporate sovereigns has gone wrong, and both parties are trapped on an island with no communications and no way to call for backup
  • The technology restriction zone's legal challenge has reached a court that might actually rule against it — and the island's permanent residents are preparing for a siege
  • Someone has been leaving analog messages at dead-drop sites across the island — written in a code that predates digital encryption — and the messages describe events that haven't happened yet
connections

Glenville Sound #

type place
name Glenville Sound
aliases
  • Glenville
  • The Sound
  • Frequency Row
description Glenville was Cleveland's cultural engine for Black art, music, and intellectual life for most of the 20th century. The neighborhood produced musicians, writers, activists, and community leaders at a rate that defied every metric of its poverty. That cultural infrastructure did not disappear when the corridor arrived. It evolved. Glenville Sound — named for the neighborhood's reinvention as the corridor's preeminent audio culture district — is where music, spoken word, neural-audio composition, and sound design converge in a neighborhood that has figured out how to make culture pay without selling its soul entirely.

The transformation began in the 2050s when a collective of Black audio engineers and musicians, priced out of the corporate studio complexes in the Meridian Core, established independent recording facilities in Glenville's abandoned commercial buildings. They brought two innovations that the corporate music industry couldn't replicate: neural-direct audio recording, which captures the composer's intended sound at the cognitive level rather than through physical instruments, and community licensing models that allow artists to retain ownership of their work while distributing through the excluded economy's networks. The corporate studios produce polished, algorithm-optimized content for Tier 3 and above. Glenville Sound produces art. The distinction matters to the people who live here, and increasingly to audiences across the corridor who are tired of music that sounds like it was designed by a committee.

The neighborhood's commercial strip along East 105th Street has become Frequency Row — a dense corridor of recording studios, listening rooms, instrument makers, and neural-audio calibration shops. The listening rooms are the draw. Unlike corporate venues that deliver audio through neural interface, Glenville's listening rooms use physical acoustics — tuned spaces that push sound through air and into bodies. The experience is different from neural-direct playback in ways that augmented listeners find disorienting and then addictive. You hear with your whole body. The corporate explanation is that analog acoustics activate vestibular and proprioceptive responses that neural-direct delivery doesn't reach. The Glenville explanation is simpler: this is what music is supposed to feel like.
atmosphere
sights
  • Frequency Row's studio facades — each one architecturally distinct, decorated by the artists who work inside
  • Sound-dampening panels on residential buildings, giving the neighborhood a quilted texture
  • Listening room entrances marked by bass frequencies you can feel through the sidewalk before you reach the door
  • Street-level instrument fabrication shops with custom-built devices in the windows — part instrument, part sculpture
  • Community murals depicting Glenville's musical history from the 1950s to the present, updated annually
sounds
  • Bass — always bass — a low-frequency presence that varies block to block as different studios bleed sound through imperfect insulation
  • Live performances spilling from open studio doors — neural-direct composition sessions that produce haunting, impossible harmonics
  • The rhythmic tap of instrument fabrication — someone always building something
  • Conversation conducted at the particular volume of a neighborhood where everyone has opinions about sound
  • Silence, in the listening rooms — the engineered, active silence that precedes a performance, so complete it has weight
smells
  • Resonance coating — a proprietary material used on listening room walls that emits a faint resinous scent
  • Food from the neighborhood's restaurants — soul food tradition adapted with synthetic protein, still recognizable, still good
  • The hot-metal smell of instrument fabrication shops working with custom alloys
feel Glenville Sound vibrates. Not metaphorically — the bass frequencies from the studios create a physical sensation in the streets that residents have learned to read like weather. Heavy bass means a major session is underway. Silence means someone important is listening. The neighborhood carries its history in its bones and its future in its speakers, and the tension between preservation and innovation is the creative engine that makes the whole thing work.
tags —
demographics Approximately 12,000 residents, predominantly Black families and artists, many with multi-generational roots in Glenville. A growing population of audio engineers, sound designers, and neural-audio specialists drawn by the district's reputation. Tier 1-2 predominantly, with a small Tier 3 creative class. Strong cultural connections to Hough Reclamation.
economy Audio production and performance are the primary industries. Community licensing revenue from neural-audio compositions distributed through the excluded economy generates Φ180 million annually — modest by corporate standards, significant by neighborhood standards. Instrument fabrication has become a secondary export industry. The listening rooms draw paying audiences from across the corridor, including Tier 3-4 visitors who spend liberally.
power structure The Glenville Sound Collective — an evolution of the original audio engineer cooperative — serves as the primary governance body, managing studio allocation, licensing disputes, and neighborhood security. Strong alliance with Hough Reclamation's block councils. Saltmarsh has attempted to bring Glenville's audio frequencies under its spectrum sovereignty three times; each attempt has been defeated by a coalition of legal challenges and community resistance that made the enforcement cost prohibitive.
dangers
  • Saltmarsh spectrum claims — the corponation has not abandoned its position that Glenville's audio frequencies fall under its sovereign authority
  • Neural-audio exposure — prolonged immersion in certain experimental frequencies has been linked to cognitive side effects that the Collective downplays
  • Gentrification pressure — the listening rooms' popularity is driving property values that threaten to displace the artists who created the district
  • Corporate poaching — the big studios offer Glenville artists contracts that strip their community licensing rights
  • Sound weaponization — the same acoustic engineering that makes the listening rooms extraordinary could be repurposed for less artistic purposes, and not everyone in Glenville has purely artistic intentions
opportunities
  • Neural-audio composition is a growing field with applications in therapy, military operations, and corporate training — Glenville's expertise is valuable
  • The community licensing model is being adopted by artists across the corridor, positioning Glenville as the center of an alternative creative economy
  • The listening rooms attract high-tier visitors who can be cultivated as contacts, clients, or sources of information
  • Alliance with Hough Reclamation creates a combined population base of 26,000 with shared infrastructure and mutual defense commitments
story hooks
  • A neural-audio composition being developed in one of Glenville's studios has an unintended effect — it triggers suppressed memories in augmented listeners, and someone wants it destroyed before it triggers the wrong memory in the wrong person
  • Saltmarsh has offered the Glenville Sound Collective a revenue-sharing deal that would legitimize their frequency use but place their communications under Saltmarsh monitoring — the Collective is divided
  • An instrument fabricator on Frequency Row has built something that isn't an instrument — it's a signal device that can penetrate Saltmarsh encryption, and he doesn't fully understand what he's made

Grainfort #

type place
name Grainfort
aliases
  • Thunder Bay ON
  • The Fort
  • Lakehead
  • North Post
description Thunder Bay is the end of the line, and it knows it. Situated on the northwest shore of Lake Superior, 1,400 kilometers from Toronto and 700 kilometers from the nearest population center that anyone would call a city, Grainfort exists because geography demands it. The port — one of the largest grain-handling facilities in the western hemisphere — connects the prairie agricultural zones to the Great Lakes shipping network. Grain goes in, everything else goes out, and the city survives on the margin between the two. Ironclad Agrisystems and Sulfur Crown Agriculture maintain competing sovereign terminals on the waterfront, their grain elevators rising like concrete cathedrals above a city that has never had the population to justify the infrastructure.

The isolation is the defining feature. The Trans-Canada Corridor connects Grainfort to Sault Ste. Marie and eventually Toronto, but the distance is real — 14 hours by ground transport, 3 hours by high-speed maglev if the weather cooperates, which it frequently doesn't. Winter temperatures drop to -40°C, and the lake effect weather systems produce storms that shut down transportation infrastructure for days at a time. During these lockdowns, Grainfort becomes an island — 150,000 people sealed inside a city that was designed for supply chain throughput, not human habitation. The residents have adapted with the particular resourcefulness of people who understand that help is not coming.

The mining operations north of the city — gold, platinum, rare earth minerals essential for augmentation manufacturing — provide the secondary economic base. Dredge Mining Collective maintains extraction facilities in the Canadian Shield bedrock, and the miners who work them are the hardest people in the GLM. The indigenous communities in the surrounding territory — Anishinaabe, Ojibwe, Métis — maintain treaty-based sovereignty that predates corporate charters, and their relationship with the mining operations is adversarial, litigious, and occasionally violent. Grainfort is where the GLM's supply chain meets the reality of geography, climate, and the people who were here first.
atmosphere
sights
  • Grain elevators towering above the waterfront — concrete monoliths visible from every point in the city
  • Lake Superior stretching to the horizon, grey and cold and indifferent to human scheduling
  • The Sleeping Giant — a peninsula formation visible from the shore, unchanged by anything the city has done
  • Mining transport convoys heading north into the Shield, carrying equipment and bringing back what the earth gives up
  • Winter lockdown conditions — everything sealed, everything white, everything waiting
sounds
  • Grain handling equipment — the rumble and hiss of millions of tons moving through automated systems
  • Lake Superior weather — wind that sounds personal, like the lake has opinions about your presence
  • Mining transport vehicles on the northern highway, diesel and electric in competing frequencies
  • The silence during lockdowns — 150,000 people being very quiet and very patient
smells
  • Grain dust — sweet, organic, and omnipresent during loading operations
  • Lake Superior air — cold, clean, and carrying more oxygen than any city-dweller is used to
  • Diesel exhaust from the mining transports, the last fossil-fuel vehicles in the northern corridor
feel Remote. Not romantically remote — not frontier mythology or wilderness adventure — but practically remote, in the sense that if something breaks, you fix it yourself or you wait. Grainfort's people have a patience born of latitude and a practicality born of distance. They don't complain about the cold. They complain about people who complain about the cold.
tags —
demographics Population 150,000 registered. Indigenous communities in the surrounding territory add an estimated 40,000, though those populations move between urban and traditional territories seasonally. The workforce divides cleanly between port operations and mining, with a small professional class serving both. Tier distribution is flat — mostly Tier 2, with limited Tier 3 corporate management. Nobody comes to Grainfort to be rich.
economy Grain transshipment and mineral extraction. Ironclad Agrisystems and Sulfur Crown Agriculture control the port. Dredge Mining Collective controls the northern extraction facilities. The local economy exists to feed, house, and supply the workers who run both. There is no service economy to speak of. There are bars.
power structure Three corporate sovereigns — Ironclad, Sulfur Crown, and Dredge — with competing interests and overlapping security jurisdictions. Canadian federal authority maintains a military installation (CFB Thunder Bay) for Arctic sovereignty purposes, which gives the federal government more presence here than in most GLM cities. Indigenous treaty councils hold legal authority over surrounding territories and maintain an uneasy détente with the mining operations.
dangers
  • Winter lockdowns — supply chain interruption when the corridor closes, sometimes for weeks
  • Mining operations in unstable Shield bedrock — collapses happen, rescue is slow
  • Indigenous-corporate land disputes that escalate past litigation into direct action
  • Isolation psychology — the distance affects people, especially in winter, especially in the dark
  • Lake Superior weather — the lake kills ships, and it doesn't distinguish between cargo barges and pleasure craft
opportunities
  • Rare earth mineral access — the mining operations produce augmentation components that the entire GLM needs
  • Treaty negotiation expertise — mediating between indigenous councils and corporate sovereigns is specialized and well-compensated work
  • The isolation creates information asymmetry — what happens in Grainfort stays in Grainfort until someone carries it out
  • Supply chain chokepoint leverage — control the port and you influence grain prices across the GLM
story hooks
  • A Dredge Mining operation has broken through the Shield bedrock into something — not a natural formation, not a geological feature, something built — and they've sealed the site
  • The grain elevators are being used to store something other than grain, and the manifests have been falsified for months
  • An indigenous treaty council has filed a sovereignty claim that would encompass the entire Grainfort port facility — and they have the legal precedent to win

  • Northern Shield mining territories
  • Prairie agricultural zones (west, via rail and road)

Grand Corridor #

type place
name Grand Corridor
aliases
  • Grand Boulevard
  • Bronzeville North
  • The Corridor of Sound
  • The Grand
description Grand Boulevard was the beating heart of Bronzeville — the street where the Regal Theater stood, where the chess players gathered at the checkerboard, where Muddy Waters and Mahalia Jackson and a thousand other voices defined what American music would become. It was not just a neighborhood. It was a frequency. And when corporate sovereignty arrived, that frequency did not die. It went underground.

The surface of Grand Corridor is a Cinderblock AI residential district, an extension of the Bronzeline development — clean towers, tiered housing, compliance monitoring. Cinderblock acquired the old Bronzeville landmarks and preserved them as cultural assets: the former Regal Theater building is now a Waxwing Neuromedia immersive-experience venue where audiences can neural-share the memories of jazz performances from a century ago. The experience is extraordinary. It is also theft — the memories were harvested from elderly Bronzeville residents through a Waxwing program that offered free neural-interface installation in exchange for memory-access licensing. The residents did not understand what they were signing. Waxwing understood perfectly.

Beneath the corporate surface, the Grand Corridor's basements and sub-levels house the most important underground music scene in Meridian 88. The clubs operate in spaces that predate the sovereignty era — former speakeasies, storage basements, utility vaults — connected by passages that mirror the surface streets one level down. The music is live, unaugmented, played on instruments that do not require power and voices that do not require amplification. Neural-interface enhancement is prohibited in the underground clubs by unanimous consensus. The performers and audiences want the imperfect, human version of the sound. They want the crackle. They want the breath. They want the thing that Waxwing's memory-harvested immersive experiences cannot replicate because it was never a memory — it was a moment.

The cultural war between the surface and the underground defines Grand Corridor's daily life. Cinderblock and Waxwing profit from Bronzeville's heritage by packaging it as content. The underground preserves that heritage by practicing it, live, in the dark, for audiences that pay in cash and keep their mouths shut. The two economies coexist in the same district, separated by a floor. The corporate tenants upstairs attend Waxwing memory-share events and feel connected to history. The musicians downstairs play until their fingers bleed and feel connected to the future. Both are right. Neither will acknowledge the other.

King Drive still runs through the center of Grand Corridor, the Walk of Fame plaques continuing north from Bronzeline. But here, someone has been adding plaques — unauthorized bronze markers appearing overnight, commemorating people the official history left out. The janitors. The dishwashers. The women who cleaned the Regal Theater and hummed the songs while they swept. Cinderblock security removes them. They reappear. It has been happening for three years. Nobody knows who is making them.
atmosphere
sights
  • Corporate residential towers above, their lobbies decorated with Bronzeville memorabilia as corporate art
  • The Waxwing Neuromedia venue in the former Regal Theater building — historic facade, holographic marquee
  • Unauthorized Walk of Fame plaques appearing on King Drive, commemorating unnamed community members
  • Basement club entrances hidden behind service doors, marked with symbols only the initiated recognize
  • The contrast: curated heritage above, living culture below, separated by a single floor
sounds
  • Surface: Waxwing memory-share audio bleeding from the venue — ghosts of performances, technically perfect
  • Underground: live jazz, blues, and gospel from basement clubs — imperfect, breathing, human
  • The low rumble of the Cinderblock server farms that underlie the residential blocks
  • Foot traffic on King Drive — tourists by day, musicians by night, the sidewalk serving both
  • The sound of a saxophone through a basement ventilation grate — the underground leaking upward
smells
  • Underground club atmosphere: sweat, whiskey, the brass-and-reed smell of live instruments
  • Surface level: corporate-standard filtered air with Waxwing's branded scent overlay
  • The old smell of the underground passages — century-old brick, coal dust, the city's memory
  • Food from underground kitchen operations: cornbread, greens, catfish — soul food prepared in speakeasy conditions
feel A district at war with itself over who owns its own history. Grand Corridor feels like standing between two speakers playing the same song in different keys — one pristine and recorded, one raw and live. The dissonance is the most honest sound in Meridian 88.
tags —
demographics Surface: Tier 2-3 corporate residents, predominantly Cinderblock-affiliated. Underground: displaced Bronzeville community members, musicians, cultural preservationists. The underground population is uncounted — estimated at 3,000-5,000 operating in basement-level spaces throughout the district.
economy Waxwing Neuromedia's memory-share venue generates the district's primary corporate revenue. Cinderblock's residential management provides supplementary income. The underground club economy operates on cash, barter, and the social currency of cultural authenticity. Soul food from underground kitchens commands premium prices from those who know where to find it.
power structure Cinderblock AI and Waxwing Neuromedia share corporate jurisdiction. The underground music scene is governed by a loose confederation of club operators and elder musicians whose authority derives from cultural respect, not force. The two power structures coexist by mutual ignorance — the corporations know the underground exists but find it easier to pretend otherwise.
dangers
  • Waxwing's memory-harvesting program continues to target elderly residents with exploitative licensing agreements
  • Underground clubs risk corporate raids — discovery would end the scene and displace the community again
  • Cinderblock surveillance in the residential blocks makes surface-to-underground movement risky
  • The unauthorized Walk of Fame plaques have become a political flashpoint — Cinderblock security is escalating enforcement
  • Cultural erasure: the corporate version of Bronzeville's history is slowly replacing the real one in public memory
opportunities
  • The underground club network is an information exchange disguised as entertainment
  • Waxwing's memory-harvesting technology, if stolen, has applications that would interest every faction in M88
  • The unauthorized plaque-maker is a folk hero — finding and protecting them would earn significant community loyalty
  • Underground soul food operations need supply chain support from districts like Little Furnace
  • The cultural war generates demand for intermediaries who can move between surface and underground
story hooks
  • Waxwing Neuromedia has discovered that its memory-share recordings contain something unexpected — the harvested memories include experiences that the donors could not have had, as if the memories themselves have been growing, adding scenes that never happened, and the Regal Theater venue is showing audiences visions of events that have not occurred yet
  • The unauthorized plaque-maker has been identified — she is a Cinderblock employee working in the residential management office, and she has been using corporate fabrication equipment to make the plaques on her night shift, and she has just made one with Kyle's name on it
  • An underground club has received a challenge: a Waxwing-sponsored performer wants to play a live set in the basement venue, unaugmented, to prove that the corporate version of the music can match the underground. The club scene is divided — some see an opportunity for exposure, others see the beginning of co-optation

Grand Crossing Gate #

type place
name Grand Crossing Gate
aliases
  • Greater Grand Crossing
  • The Gate
  • Crossing Gate
  • The Threshold
description Grand Crossing Gate sits at the boundary between the southern Shelf and what was once one of Chicago's most significant corridors of African American civic life. The name is a remnant and a reclamation — the original Greater Grand Crossing was a place where railroad lines crossed, and the neighborhood grew around that intersection. Now the rails are gone, replaced by maglev corridors that pass overhead without stopping, but the sense of crossroads persists. This is still a place where paths intersect, where people meet at the boundaries of different jurisdictions, different loyalties, different versions of what survival looks like.

The historic housing stock is Grand Crossing Gate's most visible inheritance — blocks of greystones and brick two-flats that were built to last a century and have, despite everything. The buildings are battered, patched, reinforced with whatever materials were available, but they are standing. Their persistence is not accidental. The civic organizations that characterized pre-Consolidation Greater Grand Crossing — the block clubs, the mutual aid societies, the church networks — did not disappear when the corporations drew their lines. They went underground, literally in some cases, and they have spent decades maintaining the neighborhood's physical infrastructure with a combination of salvaged materials, pooled labor, and a categorical refusal to let the buildings fall.

The Threshold Assembly is what these organizations became — a coalition of civic groups, church congregations, and block-level mutual aid networks that functions as Grand Crossing Gate's de facto government. The Assembly operates out of a converted greystone on what was once Cottage Grove Avenue, now called the Threshold — the street that marks the boundary between Assembly-governed territory and the ungoverned blocks to the west. The Assembly's authority is moral rather than military; they govern through reputation, mediation, and the accumulated weight of having been here longer than anyone else. Their legitimacy comes from history, and in a city where history is routinely demolished to make room for the next development cycle, that is a rare and powerful thing.

The district's danger is not internal — the Assembly keeps its territory as safe as any lower-Shelf neighborhood can be. The danger comes from the edges, where Assembly authority fades and the ungoverned blocks begin. It comes from above, where corporate interests periodically rediscover that Grand Crossing Gate's greystone housing stock sits on land that is technically unencumbered by any sovereignty claim and therefore available for acquisition. And it comes from the slow erosion of the Assembly's membership, as younger residents leave for districts with better infrastructure and the elders who remember what this place was — and what it cost to keep it — grow fewer each year.
atmosphere
sights
  • Rows of century-old greystones, patched and reinforced but still standing with stubborn dignity
  • The Threshold Assembly hall — a converted greystone with the only well-maintained facade on the block
  • Maglev lines passing overhead without stopping — a daily reminder of connection denied
  • Church steeples still rising above the roofline, some still active, all still tended
  • Block club gardens in narrow side lots, tended by residents who remember when the soil was clean
  • Young people leaving on morning transit, elders watching from greystone porches
sounds
  • Church bells — real ones, mechanical, rung by hand on Sunday mornings
  • The overhead passage of maglev trains that do not stop here
  • Assembly meetings — formal, procedural, conducted with a dignity that feels anachronistic and necessary
  • Block club patrols checking in with residents, the call-and-response of community surveillance
  • Gospel music from the churches, drifting through open windows on warm evenings
smells
  • Old building interiors — wood, plaster, the particular scent of spaces that have been lived in for generations
  • Church incense on Sunday mornings, mixing with cookfire smoke from block kitchens
  • Garden soil — carefully maintained, partially remediated, smelling of effort
  • The metallic ozone of maglev lines overhead, a smell that belongs to the trains that ignore this place
feel Dignified and burdened. Grand Crossing Gate carries its history like a weight that is also a weapon — the memory of what this community built, and what was done to it, and what it refused to surrender. There is grief here, but it is the kind of grief that has been composted into determination. The Assembly's formality is not stiffness; it is the insistence that these people and this place deserve the respect of proper process.
tags —
demographics Predominantly African American, reflecting deep historical roots in the community. Aging population as younger residents migrate to districts with better employment access. Tier 1 with some Tier 2 Assembly-affiliated households. Estimated population 12,000-16,000.
economy Limited formal economy. The Assembly coordinates a mutual aid network that functions as an internal redistribution system — labor, food, materials, and services exchanged on a ledger system that predates digital currency. Some residents commute to employment in adjacent districts via the Engelheim transit nexus. Church networks provide supplemental support. The greystone housing stock itself is the district's greatest economic asset, though its value is primarily defensive — maintaining the buildings prevents the vacancy that would invite corporate acquisition.
power structure The Threshold Assembly governs through moral authority and historical legitimacy. Assembly leadership rotates among a council of elders representing the district's churches, block clubs, and civic organizations. Decisions are made by consensus, which is slow but produces outcomes the community respects. The Assembly maintains a small security volunteer corps but relies primarily on social cohesion rather than force for internal order.
dangers
  • Corporate land acquisition scouts probing the district's legal vulnerabilities
  • Aging infrastructure — the greystones are standing, but plumbing, electrical, and structural systems need constant maintenance
  • The demographic drain as younger residents leave, weakening the Assembly's labor base
  • Incursions from ungoverned blocks to the west, where Assembly authority is not recognized
  • Medical emergencies with no nearby facilities — the closest clinic is in Engelheim, a transit ride away
opportunities
  • The Assembly's reputation makes Grand Crossing Gate one of the most trustworthy places in the southern Shelf for neutral meetings and negotiations
  • The greystone housing stock offers solid, defensible shelter — rare in the lower Shelf
  • The Assembly's ledger system is a functioning alternative economy that could be expanded or replicated
  • Church networks extend beyond the district, providing intelligence and connection channels that corporate surveillance cannot easily map
  • Historical records maintained by the Assembly contain information about pre-Consolidation land ownership that could complicate corporate acquisition attempts
story hooks
  • The Assembly has discovered that a shell corporation has been quietly purchasing tax liens on greystone properties throughout the district. The pattern suggests a coordinated acquisition strategy, but the shell company's ownership is buried behind layers of corporate structure. Someone needs to trace the money to its source before the liens are called in.
  • An Assembly elder has died, and with her, the location of a pre-Consolidation archive she maintained — physical records of original property deeds, community agreements, and corporate promises that were never honored. Her family believes the archive is hidden somewhere in her greystone, but someone else has already been inside looking.
  • A group of younger residents wants to petition a corponation for infrastructure investment — running water, grid power, medical access. The Assembly is divided: half see it as necessary pragmatism, half see it as the first step toward losing everything they have maintained independently for decades.

  • Block club patrol volunteers
  • Church congregations from across the southern Shelf

  • Historians and archivists interested in pre-Consolidation records

Gravesend Basin #

type place
name Gravesend Basin
aliases
  • The Basin
  • Sinktown
  • The Drowned Quarter
  • Gravesend
description A sunken district occupying what was once a lakefront industrial zone, Gravesend Basin sits three to eight meters below the surrounding city grade, the result of decades of subsidence, failed remediation efforts, and a catastrophic drainage collapse in 2161 that the city never fully addressed. Rainwater, runoff, and leaked coolant from upper-level infrastructure pools in the Basin's lower streets, creating a permanent shallow flood in the deepest sections that residents navigate by elevated walkways, repurposed boats, and improvised bridges between buildings. Despite — or because of — its abandonment by city services, Gravesend has developed a fierce internal community.
atmosphere
sights
  • Street-level floors permanently submerged, windows dark beneath murky water
  • Elevated wooden and metal walkways connecting building second floors
  • Bioluminescent algae colonies casting blue-green light on water surfaces
  • Laundry lines strung between buildings at third-floor height
  • Improvised boats — kayaks, flat-bottomed skiffs, repurposed cargo pallets with motors
  • Children fishing from walkway edges into the flooded streets
  • Rust and waterline stains marking every structure to twice human height
sounds
  • Water moving — lapping, dripping, the distant gurgle of drainage
  • Outboard motors on small craft navigating the deeper channels
  • Frogs and insects that have colonized the Basin's ecosystem
  • Sounds carrying strangely across water in the enclosed space
  • Distant city noise made muffled and dreamlike by the basin's below-grade acoustics
  • Generator hum from the self-managed power grid
smells
  • Stagnant water with an iron and algae undertone
  • Cooking fires on elevated platforms
  • Mildew and damp concrete
  • Surprisingly clean air in upper levels — the water filters particulates
  • Chemical traces from legacy industrial contamination
  • Woodsmoke from heating in the dry upper floors
feel Unexpectedly peaceful for a disaster zone — the Basin has found its own rhythm. The constant presence of water creates a meditative baseline that residents either embrace or slowly go mad from. Outsiders feel watched and slightly off-balance on the narrow walkways. There is a beauty here that city planners would never have designed.
tags —
demographics Predominantly residents who have nowhere else to go or who actively chose to disappear from civic records. Large populations of undocumented workers, people with warrants, those in debt to corporate creditors, and a surprising number of deliberate off-gridders — artists, ideologues, and people who simply do not want to be found. Multi-generational families exist alongside recent arrivals.
economy Subsistence and informal. Aquaculture in the flooded streets — fish, shellfish, and engineered algae — provides both food and a small export trade. Repair and fabrication workshops operate in upper floors. The Basin's off-grid status makes it attractive for services requiring anonymity, and a modest information-economy has developed around people who know how to disappear and how to find those who have.
power structure The Basin Compact — a council of building stewards, one per occupied structure, that meets weekly on a rotating central platform. The Compact manages the water pumping schedule, walkway maintenance, power grid allocation, and conflict resolution. It has no enforcement mechanism beyond collective social pressure and, in extremis, the threat of platform revocation. Remarkably effective. Two figures hold outsized influence: Maret Osei, who controls the algae cultivation network and therefore food security, and a person known only as the Cartographer, who maintains the only accurate map of which structures are safe.
dangers
  • Structural collapse — waterlogged buildings fail without warning
  • Contaminated water causing illness, particularly in flood season
  • Bounty hunters and debt collectors operating outside their legal jurisdiction
  • The deeper channels at night, where visibility is zero and accidents happen
  • City authorities occasionally threatening clearance operations that never quite materialize
  • Legacy industrial contamination in the soil and deep water
  • Territorial disputes over the most valuable elevated real estate
opportunities
  • True anonymity — no cameras, no grid connection, no official presence
  • Aquaculture products unavailable through licensed supply chains
  • A community that protects its own and asks few questions
  • Access to people who have successfully erased their official existence
  • The Basin's unique ecology has produced biological samples of interest to researchers
  • Salvage in the permanently flooded lower floors — the original industrial zone left a great deal behind
story hooks
  • The Cartographer has gone missing, and with them the only complete map of the Basin's structural hazards — without it, the Compact cannot safely route foot traffic, and three buildings they've been avoiding are now dangerously overcrowded
  • Something in the deep water of the Basin's lowest channel has been interfering with boat motors and electronic equipment — the Basin's children are calling it the Quiet, and two adults have drowned in circumstances that don't match simple accident
  • A corporate remediation company has filed a legitimate claim on the Basin's land and has been given a 90-day clearance order — the Compact has 90 days to either fight it legally, which requires resources they don't have, or make the project too costly to pursue
  • A person living quietly in the Basin for seven years is actually a disappeared corporate whistleblower whose testimony could reopen a closed case — multiple parties have just learned they're here
connections
adjacent to
  • Old Harbor
  • The Brine Warrens
  • Harrowgate Industrial Plateau
exits —
tags —
frequented by
  • Residents of the Basin community
  • Debt fugitives and warrant-holders seeking temporary refuge
  • Independent researchers studying the Basin's accidental ecosystem
  • Fixers with clients who need to vanish for a while
  • Salvage divers working the submerged lower floors
  • City officials doing the minimum required inspection visits
  • Artists drawn to the aesthetic of managed decay
notable locations
name The Float
description A 40-meter platform assembled from salvaged construction materials and permanently moored at the Basin's geographic center, The Float serves as the Compact's meeting hall, the Basin's largest communal space, and the closest thing Gravesend has to a public square. Markets are held here twice weekly. The structure is surprisingly solid — it has been continuously maintained and improved for over fifteen years.
tags —
name The Lung
description A former industrial air-handling unit whose interior has been converted into a network of dry, warm living spaces by an extended family of engineers. The Lung is the most technologically sophisticated structure in the Basin, running its own filtered air system and a small but reliable power generation setup. The family rents space to those who can pay and has been known to offer shelter to people in acute danger, for reasons they decline to explain.
tags —
name Channel Six
description The deepest navigable waterway through the Basin's flooded streets, wide enough for two boats to pass and dark enough that even augmented eyes struggle below the surface. Channel Six is the Basin's main artery and also its most dangerous passage after dark. The walls of buildings along its length are covered in marker paint indicating depths, hazards, and the names of those who drowned in the water below.

Grindstone Shore #

type place
name Grindstone Shore
aliases
  • Alpena MI
  • Limestone Coast
  • The Quarry
  • North Shore
description Alpena sits on the Lake Huron coast where the Thunder Bay River meets the lake, and its economy has been built on the same thing for two centuries: limestone. The quarries surrounding the city produce construction-grade limestone, aggregate, and chemical-grade calcium carbonate for the GLM's construction and manufacturing sectors. Palladian Construction holds sovereign extraction rights over the primary quarry complex — a 30-square-kilometer open pit that has been expanding since the twentieth century and that is now visible from orbit as a pale scar in the Michigan forest.

The city is small, remote, and thoroughly dependent on the quarry. Palladian employs 60% of the working population directly, and the remainder services Palladian's workers. The arrangement has the stability and the suffocation of any company town — employment is steady, wages are adequate, and the company's interests are the city's interests because no alternative exists. The municipal government administers residential services. Palladian administers everything that matters. Attempts to diversify the economy — tourism, forestry, aquaculture — have repeatedly failed because Palladian's extraction operations contaminate the waterfront, clear the forests, and alter the lake chemistry in ways that make alternative industries unviable. This is not an accident.

Lake Huron's coast north of Alpena is the most sparsely populated shoreline in the lower Great Lakes — forest, limestone bluffs, and automated Palladian extraction monitoring stations. The Thunder Bay National Marine Sanctuary, designated to protect the hundreds of shipwrecks on the lake bottom, technically still exists as a federal protection zone, but Palladian's discharge into the lake has made the water turbid enough to render the wrecks invisible from the surface. The sanctuary persists as a legal entity and an ecological ghost. Grindstone Shore is a place where one industry has consumed everything else, not through malice but through the simple mathematics of extraction: the quarry is profitable, and profitability eliminates competition.
atmosphere
sights
  • The quarry complex — a pale wound in the green forest, terraced walls descending into limestone depths
  • Palladian extraction vehicles moving along the quarry rim — enormous, automated, and perpetual
  • Lake Huron's turbid shoreline — water that was once clear enough to see shipwrecks, now opaque with limestone particulate
  • The city clustered between the quarry and the lake — nowhere to expand, nowhere to go
  • Northern Michigan forest stretching in every direction except the quarry — a reminder of what was here before
sounds
  • Quarry operations — blasting, crushing, and transport, a rhythmic cycle that the city's schedule is built around
  • Lake Huron surf on limestone gravel beaches — gentler than Superior, warmer, and carrying particulate
  • Palladian transport convoys moving extracted material to the port — heavy, constant, the city's heartbeat
  • Forest birds in the buffer zone between the city and the quarry — wildlife adapting to extraction
smells
  • Limestone dust — chalky, dry, and in everything: clothes, food, lungs
  • Lake Huron — a mineral tang enhanced by quarry discharge
  • Pine forest on west winds — the scent of everything the quarry hasn't reached yet
feel A company town that knows it's a company town and has made peace with it, the way you make peace with weather. Grindstone Shore is stable, predictable, and defined entirely by a hole in the ground. The quarry provides. The quarry constrains. The quarry will eventually consume the ground the city sits on, and everyone knows the timeline.
tags —
demographics Population 14,000. The smallest and most homogeneous settlement on the Lake Huron coast. Multi-generational quarry families, Palladian corporate employees, and a small service population. Tier 2 across the board. Nobody is rich. Nobody is destitute. Everybody breathes limestone.
economy Limestone extraction and processing (Palladian Construction). Monoculture in the purest sense — one industry, one employer, one economic dependency. The port handles limestone export to the construction markets of the southern GLM. Local commerce exists at the subsistence level required to keep the workforce functional.
power structure Palladian Construction. The municipal government exists because someone has to maintain the roads between the quarry and the port. The mayor is a Palladian retiree. The city council includes three current Palladian employees. The distinction between corporate governance and municipal governance is academic.
dangers
  • Quarry expansion — the extraction zone is growing, and the city's footprint is not
  • Limestone dust exposure — respiratory illness rates are the highest on the Lake Huron coast
  • Economic monoculture collapse — if Palladian leaves or the quarry is exhausted, nothing replaces it
  • Lake contamination from quarry discharge — drinking water comes from the lake and tastes like it
  • Isolation — Alpena is 150 kilometers from the nearest significant settlement, and the road infrastructure reflects Palladian's priorities, not the residents'
opportunities
  • Quarry access — limestone and calcium carbonate have construction and chemical applications across the GLM
  • The marine sanctuary's shipwrecks — legally protected, physically obscured, and containing historical artifacts that certain collectors would pay for
  • Palladian's operational data — extraction rates, reserves estimates, expansion plans — is valuable competitive intelligence
