Grosse Pointe Enclosure #

type place
name Grosse Pointe Enclosure
aliases
  • Grosse Pointe
  • The Enclosure
  • The Gold Coast
  • GP
description Grosse Pointe was always wealthy. In the 20th century, it was where Detroit's auto barons built lakefront estates and pretended the city that funded them existed on a different planet. In the 22nd century, the pretense became architecture. The Grosse Pointe Enclosure is a continuous sealed residential zone stretching five miles along the Lake St. Clair shoreline — a climate-controlled, atmospherically processed, autonomously secured habitat for approximately 12,000 of the GLM's highest-tier residents. The word 'enclosure' was chosen by the residents' governing body, and they chose it without irony, which tells you everything.

The Enclosure operates under a unique legal framework: a Residential Sovereign Charter granted not to a corponation but to the Grosse Pointe Residential Trust, a collective entity owned by its residents. This makes the Enclosure the only sovereign territory in the GLM governed by individual wealth rather than corporate structure. The distinction matters legally — residents answer to their own courts, their own security force, and their own infrastructure management — and it matters culturally. The Enclosure is not a company town. It is a wealth town. The residents are corponation board members, retired executives, inheritors of fortunes that predate the Corporate Sovereignty Acts, and a handful of individuals whose source of wealth is listed as 'investment returns' in a way that invites no further questions.

The physical infrastructure is extraordinary. The lakefront seawall doubles as a wave-energy generation system. The atmospheric dome — not a physical dome but a network of atmospheric processors that create a continuous clean-air zone — maintains temperature, humidity, and air quality at levels that the rest of Detroit hasn't experienced since the pre-industrial era. The houses are not houses — they are estates, each one a custom architectural commission, ranging from restored 1920s mansions to contemporary structures that look like they were designed by AIs having aesthetic visions. The lawns are real grass. The lake views are real lake views. The only thing that isn't real is the idea that any of this was earned through merit alone.
atmosphere
sights
  • Lakefront estates stretching along the shore — each one unique, each one worth more than entire districts
  • The atmospheric processor network — translucent columns spaced along the perimeter, creating a visible border between the Enclosure's air and Detroit's
  • Lake St. Clair — clean, blue, and accessible only from within the Enclosure's private beaches
  • Autonomous security patrols on the lake — sleek watercraft running continuous perimeter loops
  • Real grass lawns. Not synthetic. Not hydroponic. Grass that drinks water and absorbs sunlight and exists because someone can afford it.
sounds
  • Lake waves on private beaches — one of the few natural sounds left in the Detroit metro
  • The atmospheric processors' low hum, tuned to a frequency that residents' neural interfaces automatically filter
  • Silence, purchased at enormous expense and maintained by sound-dampening infrastructure
  • Private aircraft approaching the Enclosure's two airstrips — the sound of arrivals that bypass the ground entirely
  • Nothing from Detroit. The Enclosure's acoustic perimeter is absolute.
smells
  • Clean air — genuinely clean, pre-industrial clean, the smell of oxygen without industrial particulates
  • Lake water — fresh, cold, uncontaminated within the Enclosure's water treatment zone
  • Grass and garden soil — real growing things tended by human groundskeepers because automation isn't prestigious enough
feel Paradise behind a wall. The Enclosure feels like stepping backward in time to an era when clean air, clean water, and quiet were things the world provided for free. The beauty is genuine. The comfort is genuine. The understanding that 12,000 people live like this while 3 million people in the adjacent metro breathe filtered industrial air is the price of admission that no one here pays in conscience.
tags —
demographics 12,000 residents, 4,500 service staff. Residents are Tier 5 and above — the 'above' category being an informal designation for wealth that exceeds the tier system's scale. Average household net worth: Φ18 billion. The service staff commute from Corridor neighborhoods and are processed through biometric screening daily.
economy Residential and investment-based. The Enclosure's residents collectively control approximately Φ200 trillion in assets — roughly 15% of the GLM's total wealth. Economic activity within the Enclosure is limited to luxury services, private healthcare, and the Trust's infrastructure management. The Enclosure's economic impact is felt everywhere else — in the boardroom decisions that are discussed over lakefront dinners.
power structure The Grosse Pointe Residential Trust governs through a board of twelve trustees elected by residents, with voting power proportional to property value. The Trust operates its own security force (600 personnel, Arcturus-trained), its own courts (civil disputes only — criminal matters are handled by 'quiet resolution'), and its own infrastructure. The Trust's legal counsel, the firm Whitfield-Chen-Abara, is the most expensive law firm in the GLM and has never lost a jurisdictional challenge.
dangers
  • Impenetrability — the Enclosure's security is the best money can buy, which makes unauthorized access extraordinarily difficult
  • Internal justice — 'quiet resolution' of criminal matters means crimes committed within the Enclosure are handled without external oversight
  • Wealth concentration — the decisions made in lakefront living rooms affect millions of people who have no input
  • The service staff's access — 4,500 people pass through the perimeter daily, and loyalty purchased with wages has limits
  • Lake St. Clair — the Enclosure's water treatment zone doesn't extend far enough, and the lake beyond it carries contamination from upstream industrial discharge
opportunities
  • Intelligence access — the conversations that happen in the Enclosure are the most valuable intelligence in the GLM
  • Service staff recruitment — underpaid, overworked, and invisible to the residents they serve
  • Trust board politics — twelve trustees who control Φ200 trillion don't always agree, and their disagreements create opportunities
  • The lake perimeter — water approaches are monitored but the autonomous patrol patterns are knowable
story hooks
  • A Trust trustee dies under circumstances the 'quiet resolution' process classifies as natural causes. The deceased's personal AI — still running on their estate's local server — disagrees and starts reaching out to contacts outside the Enclosure.
  • The Enclosure's atmospheric processors are showing anomalous readings — someone has modified the scent profile to include a compound that affects neural interface function in ways that are subtle, cumulative, and beneficial to whoever is making the modification.
  • A service staff member has been documenting the Enclosure's internal operations for three years, building a comprehensive dossier on every resident. The dossier is for sale, and multiple buyers are circling.

Hamtramck Enclave #

type place
name Hamtramck Enclave
aliases
  • Hamtramck
  • The Enclave
  • Little Everything
description Hamtramck has always been an enclave — a 2.1-square-mile city entirely surrounded by Detroit, stubbornly independent since 1922 when it incorporated to avoid Detroit's prohibition enforcement. A century and a half later, the stubbornness remains, though what it's resisting has changed. Hamtramck Enclave is one of the most ethnically dense districts in the GLM: Bangladeshi, Yemeni, Polish, Bosnian, and a dozen other communities layered on top of each other in a geography so compact that you can walk from a mosque to a pierogi shop to a Yemeni tea house in four minutes. The neural interfaces are older models here. The streets are narrower. The buildings are not optimized. Nobody asked them to be.

The Enclave's legal status is a relic that the corponations have been trying to dissolve for forty years. As an incorporated municipality predating the Corporate Sovereignty Acts, Hamtramck retains its own city charter, its own police force (twelve officers, three functional patrol vehicles, and a determination that exceeds their equipment), and its own zoning authority. This makes it a jurisdictional island — corporate law stops at the border, and the corporations hate it. Three separate acquisition attempts have failed, not because of legal challenges but because the Enclave's population voted them down with margins exceeding 85%. The corponations could force the issue — the legal mechanisms exist — but the optics of dissolving an immigrant community's century-old charter are bad enough that nobody wants to be the one who does it. Yet.

What the Enclave has become, in practice, is a refuge for people who need to exist outside corporate jurisdiction without going fully off-grid. Small businesses that can't afford corporate licensing operate here. Augment technicians who lost their certifications but not their skills practice here. Religious communities that refuse to allow neural interface monitoring during worship gather here. The Enclave is not ungoverned — it is self-governed, badly funded, overextended, and alive in the particular way that places are alive when the people who live there actually chose to be there.
atmosphere
sights
  • Dense streets where mosque minarets, church steeples, and apartment blocks compete for skyline in two square miles
  • Shop signs in Bengali, Arabic, Polish, Bosnian, English, and combinations that only make sense locally
  • The old Hamtramck police station — a building from 2119 that looks ancient next to everything else and still works
  • Prayer rugs drying on fire escapes next to satellite dishes jury-rigged to pull signals the corporate net doesn't carry
  • Children from six ethnic backgrounds playing the same game in a language they invented together
sounds
  • Five call-to-prayer speakers and three church bells sharing the same airspace — a theological soundscape
  • Conversations in languages that shift mid-sentence — Hamtramck's polyglot baseline
  • The Enclave police scanner — twelve officers trying to cover 2.1 square miles with optimism and determination
  • Unlicensed augment shop equipment humming behind residential walls — everyone knows, nobody reports
  • Kitchen sounds from every open window — the Enclave cooks constantly and competitively
smells
  • Layered cuisine — Yemeni spices, Polish sausage, Bangladeshi curry, Bosnian cevapi, all within a single block's airspace
  • Incense from the religious supply shops that serve every faith represented in the Enclave
  • Old buildings — plaster, wood, the accumulated smell of a century of human habitation in compact spaces
  • Tea. Every community here runs on tea, and the varieties would fill a catalog.
feel Cramped, loud, genuine, and defiantly human. Hamtramck Enclave feels like what a city is supposed to feel like before the optimization algorithms get involved. It's messy. The infrastructure creaks. The politics are personal. And the community cohesion — forged from a dozen different cultures deciding that their differences matter less than their shared refusal to be absorbed — is the strongest thing in Detroit that isn't made of steel.
tags —
demographics Approximately 32,000 residents in 2.1 square miles — one of the highest population densities in the GLM. Bangladeshi (28%), Yemeni (22%), Polish (15%), Bosnian (12%), and a patchwork of other communities. Median age: 34. The Enclave's birth rate is the highest in the Detroit metro area, which the corponations view as a resource problem and the residents view as a future.
economy Small-business intensive. Approximately 1,200 businesses in 2.1 square miles — restaurants, shops, unlicensed augment technicians, religious supply stores, and informal services. Annual economic output: Φ4.2 billion, almost entirely circulated internally. The Enclave pays for municipal services through a property tax that hasn't been raised since 2181 and is increasingly insufficient.
power structure Elected city council of seven members representing ward districts. The mayor, currently Fatima Al-Rashidi, has held office for nine years and governs through coalition-building across ethnic community leaders. The twelve-officer police force reports to the council. Corporate influence is present through property purchases on the border but has not penetrated the governance structure. Yet.
dangers
  • Incorporation pressure — the next corporate acquisition attempt is always being planned
  • Infrastructure decay — the Enclave's independent infrastructure is aging and underfunded
  • Internal ethnic tensions — the coalition holds but is not frictionless, especially around resource allocation
  • Border exploitation — corporate interests buy border properties and use them to project influence inward
  • Medical limitations — the Enclave's clinic cannot handle advanced augment complications, forcing residents into corporate medical systems
opportunities
  • Jurisdictional sanctuary — the Enclave's independent charter makes it a legal safe harbor from corporate authority
  • Unlicensed but skilled augment work — the technicians here are good, cheap, and don't ask questions
  • Intelligence network — the Enclave's polyglot, multi-ethnic community has connections across the GLM and internationally
  • Cultural community trust — earn standing in one community and the word spreads to the others
story hooks
  • A corponation has purchased seven properties on the Enclave's western border and is quietly building a sensor network — if they can prove the Enclave can't maintain public safety standards, they have legal grounds to petition for dissolution
  • An unlicensed augment technician in the Enclave has developed a firmware patch that blocks Tessera's neural data harvesting. Tessera wants the technician. The Enclave wants to protect them. The technician wants to sell to the highest bidder.
  • Mayor Al-Rashidi receives a private offer: accept a 'partnership' with Cinderblock AI that preserves the Enclave's charter in name while transferring operational authority. The alternative is a hostile acquisition vote at the next GLM Council session.

Harrowgate Industrial Plateau #

type place
name Harrowgate Industrial Plateau
aliases
  • The Plateau
  • Harrowgate
  • The Slab
  • Smokeback
description A massive elevated industrial zone built atop the reinforced rooftops of a pre-Meridian heavy manufacturing district, Harrowgate is what happens when a city grows upward faster than it grows outward and someone decides the roofs of old factories make perfectly adequate foundations. The original buildings below — many still partially operational — form a dense substructure of crumbling brick, exposed rebar, and improvised reinforcement that occasionally shifts, sending minor tremors through the Plateau's floor. Above, a patchwork of active foundries, chemical processors, fabrication yards, and the warehouses of four mid-tier manufacturing corporations create a working industrial district that never fully sleeps.
atmosphere
sights
  • orange-lit foundry windows casting warm glow through perpetual smog
  • crane arms swinging loads overhead between buildings
  • steam venting from hundreds of pipes at irregular intervals
  • the constant orange haze of particulate matter backlit by work lights
  • corporate logos painted large on warehouse walls, faded and overlapping
  • workers in respirator masks moving in shift-change columns
sounds
  • rhythmic hammering and press-stamping from foundry floors
  • industrial fans cycling up and down
  • warning klaxons for crane movements
  • the grinding of heavy fabrication equipment
  • shift-change bells at irregular intervals across competing corporate schedules
  • structural groans from the substructure below
smells
  • hot metal and forge smoke
  • industrial solvents and cutting fluid
  • ozone from welding arcs
  • exhaust from diesel backup generators
  • the chemical sweetness of polymer processing
feel Relentlessly functional and indifferent to human comfort — a place built to produce, not to house, where workers are components in a larger mechanism and the machinery's needs take priority over their own.
tags —
demographics Predominantly shift-labor workforce living in company dormitory blocks, with a growing underclass of informal workers who live in the substructure below the Plateau floor. Significant population of augmented workers whose cybernetics were provided as employment terms — technically owned by the corporations that installed them. Supervisory and technical staff are largely Meridian-born, while floor labor draws from throughout the corridor.
economy Heavy fabrication, metal processing, component manufacturing for the construction and infrastructure sectors, chemical synthesis, and corporate warehousing. Secondary economy in stolen materials, shift-labor brokering, and the informal markets that serve workers who can't leave during long contract periods.
power structure Four mid-tier manufacturing corporations — Vethane Industrial, Corsair Fabrication, Null-Grade Synthesis, and the locally-owned Harrow & Sons collective — maintain competing jurisdictions across the Plateau, each with private security forces whose territorial boundaries shift with contract wins and losses. A nominal Meridian industrial regulatory office exists here but has been effectively captured by Vethane's lobbying.
dangers
  • structural subsidence events when the substructure below shifts
  • industrial accidents with inadequate corporate response
  • corporate security forces detaining workers for 'contract violations'
  • air quality levels that exceed safe exposure limits during peak production
  • debt bondage through cybernetics ownership clauses in work contracts
  • chemical spills from Null-Grade Synthesis operations
  • sabotage between competing corporate factions endangering workers
opportunities
  • access to heavy fabrication equipment for off-book manufacturing
  • stolen industrial materials available at steep discounts
  • corporate espionage opportunities between competing manufacturers
  • the substructure below the Plateau contains entire abandoned factory floors
  • workers with specialized technical skills willing to freelance
  • Vethane Industrial's research division is working on something they've heavily classified
story hooks
  • Three workers have disappeared during night shifts, and corporate security is actively suppressing the reports
  • A structural engineer has evidence that the Plateau's foundation is six months from a catastrophic failure and can't get anyone to listen
  • A worker whose corporate-owned cybernetics are being remotely throttled as punishment for union organizing needs help breaking the control signal
  • Something in the sealed substructure levels has started leaving marks on the underside of the Plateau floor — from below
  • Corsair Fabrication has begun quietly producing something that doesn't match any civilian manufacturing contract on record

Highland Park Autonomous Zone #

type place
name Highland Park Autonomous Zone
aliases
  • Highland Park
  • The HPAZ
  • Freepark
  • The Experiment
description Highland Park was already a city within a city — an incorporated enclave like Hamtramck, but without Hamtramck's community cohesion or economic base. When Chrysler left in the 1990s, it took the tax base with it. When the water was shut off in the 2010s, it took the pretense of municipal services. When the Corporate Sovereignty Acts passed in the 2040s, no corponation bothered to claim Highland Park because there was nothing to claim. Three square miles of crumbling infrastructure, contaminated soil, and 8,000 people who couldn't afford to leave. The corponations didn't conquer Highland Park. They simply decided it wasn't worth conquering.

What grew in that vacuum is the HPAZ — the Highland Park Autonomous Zone, an unincorporated, ungoverned, and officially non-existent territory that has become the GLM's most radical experiment in post-corporate living. The HPAZ has no government, no police force, no tax structure, and no formal economy. What it has is a network of mutual aid collectives, squatter communities, urban homesteaders, anarchist tech cooperatives, and approximately 11,000 people who are building something that doesn't have a name yet because naming it would require agreeing on what it is. The old Chrysler headquarters — a brutalist concrete campus that has been slowly colonized by residents, workshops, and a hydroponic farm that fills the former executive parking garage — serves as the closest thing the HPAZ has to a center.

The zone is dangerous. There is no emergency response infrastructure. Medical care is provided by volunteer medics with varying degrees of training. Disputes are resolved through community mediation or, when mediation fails, through means that range from social ostracism to violence. The power grid is a patchwork of stolen connections, solar installations, and a biomass generator that runs on organic waste and smells exactly like you'd expect. But the HPAZ is also genuinely free in a way that nowhere else in the GLM is. No corporate surveillance. No tier classification. No neural interface monitoring. No jurisdiction of any kind. For the people who live here, that freedom is worth everything it costs. For the people who visit, the costs are usually more apparent than the freedom.
atmosphere
sights
  • The old Chrysler HQ campus — brutalist concrete colonized by murals, gardens, solar panels, and human habitation
  • Streets where the pavement has been torn up for community gardens, creating a patchwork of asphalt and soil
  • Makeshift structures built from salvaged materials — architectural improvisation as a way of life
  • The biomass generator's exhaust stack, wrapped in protest art and trailing a permanent vapor plume
  • No corporate logos. No advertisements. No holographic signage. The visual silence is disorienting after anywhere else in the GLM.
sounds
  • Community radio broadcasting on salvaged equipment — news, music, dispute mediation, and emergency alerts
  • Construction — the HPAZ is always building, always modifying, always making do
  • Arguments — governance by consensus means everything is debated, loudly, at length
  • The biomass generator's low chug — unreliable, essential, and loved the way you love something ugly that keeps you alive
  • Quiet. Real quiet. Not the engineered silence of Geartown but the quiet of a place where the machines that make ambient noise were never installed.
smells
  • The biomass generator — organic waste processing is not a fragrant operation
  • Community gardens and hydroponic operations — green, growing things in soil that was declared dead
  • Woodsmoke from heating systems that use whatever burns
  • The absence of corporate air processing — the air smells like air, for better and worse
feel Raw. The HPAZ feels like a wound that's healing into something new — not what was there before, but not scar tissue either. It's uncomfortable, unpredictable, and occasionally dangerous. It's also the only place in the GLM where you can stand on a street corner and not be a data point in someone's optimization model. That feeling — of being genuinely unobserved — is so rare in 2200 that people cry the first time they experience it.
tags —
demographics Approximately 11,000 residents. No demographic data is collected because there is no authority to collect it. Observed population includes anarchist collectives (predominantly white, young, educated), Black families who have lived in Highland Park for generations, climate refugees, corporate dropouts, and people who are hiding from things they don't discuss. The HPAZ does not ask who you were. It only asks what you'll contribute.
economy Post-monetary in aspiration, barter-and-favor in practice. No formal currency is used. Labor is exchanged directly — I fix your roof, you teach my kid to read. Skilled trades are the highest-value currency: medical training, augment repair, agricultural knowledge, and construction skills. Estimated annual economic activity: incalculable, because the HPAZ doesn't use units the formal economy recognizes.
power structure None, formally. In practice, influence concentrates around competence — the people who can fix the generator, treat the sick, and mediate disputes hold informal authority. The Chrysler campus community has the largest population concentration and therefore the most organizational weight. Tensions between the anarchist collectives' ideological frameworks and the legacy residents' practical governance needs are the HPAZ's most persistent internal conflict.
dangers
  • No emergency services — medical emergencies, fires, and violence are handled by whoever is nearby and willing
  • Internal conflict — without formal governance, disputes can escalate unpredictably
  • Contaminated soil — Chrysler's industrial legacy is in the ground, and not all areas have been tested
  • Predatory elements — the absence of law attracts people who want freedom and people who want victims
  • External intervention — the HPAZ exists because the corps ignore it, and that could change at any time
opportunities
  • True anonymity — the HPAZ is the only place in the Detroit metro where surveillance doesn't exist
  • Experimental technology — the tech cooperatives build things here that couldn't exist under corporate patent law
  • Disappearance — for people who need to stop existing in corporate databases, the HPAZ is the destination
  • Community skills — the mutual aid networks teach practical survival skills that corporate education abandoned
story hooks
  • A tech cooperative in the Chrysler campus has built a neural interface jammer that creates a 200-meter dead zone around the user — Tessera and Cinderblock AI both want it destroyed, and they're not coordinating, which creates opportunities
  • Someone is quietly buying the contaminated land around the HPAZ's borders. The purchases are routed through seven shell companies. The endgame is unclear but the encirclement is geometric.
  • A legacy resident — someone whose family has lived in Highland Park since the 1960s — is dying, and their knowledge of the underground infrastructure (tunnels, sealed basements, utility connections) is dying with them

Hough Reclamation #

type place
name Hough Reclamation
aliases
  • Hough
  • The Reclamation
  • Block Zero
description Hough burned in 1966. That is the fact that every history of this neighborhood begins with, and the fact that the neighborhood has spent a century and a half trying to transcend. The riots — sparked by racial segregation, police brutality, and the concentrated poverty that American cities engineered with surgical precision — destroyed four square blocks and killed four people. The rebuilding never really happened. Decades of disinvestment followed, the same pattern repeated across Black neighborhoods in every American city: capital withdrawn, services reduced, population blamed for the conditions capital created.

By 2140, when the corridor was taking shape and corponations were claiming sovereign territory across the Great Lakes region, Hough was among the neighborhoods that nobody claimed. Too poor, too depopulated, too much liability. What happened next was not planned by any corponation or government. The remaining residents — predominantly Black families who had held their homes through every wave of abandonment — began the Reclamation. Using salvaged materials, cooperative labor, and technology acquired through the excluded economy, they rebuilt the neighborhood on their own terms. Vertical farms in converted apartment buildings. Solar arrays on every rooftop. A mesh communication network that operates independently of Saltmarsh's signal grid. A community governance model based on block councils that traces its organizational DNA back to the mutual aid societies that sustained Black communities through Jim Crow.

Hough Reclamation is now the most self-sufficient neighborhood in the Cleveland sprawl. It generates 80% of its own power, grows 60% of its own food, and maintains its own communications infrastructure. It is also, by every corporate metric, one of the poorest — because the metrics don't measure what Hough has built. The corponations have taken notice. Tollgate has offered infrastructure integration three times. Tessera has proposed a 'community cognitive wellness partnership.' Each offer has been declined by the block councils with the same response: 'We remember what your help looks like.' The phrase has become a neighborhood motto, painted on walls and printed on the mesh network's welcome screen.
atmosphere
sights
  • Vertical farms visible through apartment windows — green light from grow systems casting the streets in an agricultural glow at night
  • Solar arrays on every rooftop, some salvaged, some fabricated locally, none matching — a patchwork of self-sufficiency
  • Murals commemorating 1966, painted and repainted by each generation, the imagery evolving but the memory constant
  • Block council meeting halls — converted storefronts with reinforced doors and mesh network nodes mounted on the roof
  • The Welcome Wall at the neighborhood's eastern boundary: 'We Remember What Your Help Looks Like'
sounds
  • The hum of vertical farm systems — pumps, fans, grow lights cycling in a rhythm that has replaced the old industrial noise
  • Mesh network chatter — Hough's independent communication system carries voice, text, and community broadcasts on frequencies Saltmarsh doesn't control
  • Block council meetings — democracy conducted in person, in rooms, with voices raised and votes counted by hand
  • Music — Hough's sound system, run through the mesh network, plays a community-curated stream that mixes everything from gospel to electronic
  • The absence of corporate sound — no advertisements, no drone traffic, no algorithmic ambient programming
smells
  • Growing things — the vegetable-rich scent of the vertical farms permeates every block within a two-street radius
  • Cooking — community kitchens operate on block rotation, feeding residents who contribute labor hours to the Reclamation's shared infrastructure
  • Clean air — Hough's rooftop gardens and biofilter systems produce noticeably better air quality than surrounding neighborhoods
feel Hough Reclamation feels like a dare. It dares the corridor to function without it. It dares the corponations to explain why a neighborhood with no corporate investment has better air, better food, and better community health than the zones that spent trillions on infrastructure. It is not utopia — the block councils argue, resources are scarce, and the independence that defines the neighborhood also isolates it. But it is real in a way that most of the corridor has forgotten how to be.
tags —
demographics Approximately 14,000 residents, predominantly Black families with multi-generational roots in the neighborhood. Significant population of climate refugees who were accepted by the block councils through a formal community sponsorship process. Almost entirely Tier 1 and excluded by corporate classification, though the residents reject the tier system entirely. Augmentation rates are low — approximately 15% — by choice as much as economics.
economy Cooperative and non-monetary. The Reclamation operates on a labor-credit system where residents contribute hours to shared infrastructure — farming, maintenance, teaching, security — and receive credits redeemable for goods and services within the neighborhood. External trade is conducted through designated brokers who interface with the excluded economy. The block councils collectively hold a modest Q reserve for essential purchases that cannot be produced internally.
power structure Direct democracy through block councils. Each residential block elects a council of five. The councils send representatives to the Hough Assembly, which meets monthly to address neighborhood-wide issues. Decisions require two-thirds majority. There is no executive authority. The system is slow, contentious, and functional — the opposite of corporate governance in every respect.
dangers
  • Resource scarcity — self-sufficiency is 80%, not 100%, and the remaining 20% creates vulnerability to external supply disruptions
  • Corporate encroachment — Tollgate's infrastructure integration offers become less optional with each refusal
  • Internal tension — the block council system produces legitimate disagreements about resource allocation that sometimes escalate
  • Medical limitations — Hough's community health practitioners are skilled but lack access to advanced diagnostics and surgical capability
  • Isolation — independence from the corridor's systems also means independence from its protections, such as they are
opportunities
  • The Reclamation model is being studied and replicated by excluded communities across the corridor — Hough is becoming a template
  • The mesh network is the only independent communications infrastructure in the Cleveland sprawl, making it invaluable to anyone who needs to communicate off Saltmarsh's grid
  • Hough's vertical farming expertise is a tradeable skill set — other neighborhoods pay in materials and favors for agricultural consulting
  • The block councils' rejection of corporate offers has earned them respect and political capital among the corridor's excluded population
story hooks
  • Tessera has changed tactics — instead of offering partnership, they've begun offering free NovaMind Basic implants to Hough's teenagers, and some are accepting
  • The mesh network has intercepted transmissions that appear to originate from inside Tollgate's infrastructure — someone inside the corponation is trying to communicate with the Reclamation
  • A block council vote on whether to accept Tollgate's latest infrastructure offer has split the Assembly down the middle, threatening the neighborhood's governance model

Hydewood #

type place
name Hydewood
aliases
  • Hyde Park
  • The Ivory Circuit
  • The Campus
  • Hydewood Enclave
description Hydewood is the last place in the southern corridor where knowledge is still treated as something other than a product — or at least, that's the story it tells itself. The University of Chicago survived the collapse the way old money always survives: by making itself indispensable to the people who came out on top. When the corponations carved up municipal territory, the University negotiated a unique status — a Tier 4 autonomous academic zone, self-governing within its campus boundaries, funded by a consortium of six corponations who discovered that basic research is cheaper to outsource than to staff. The result is a walled intellectual enclave in the middle of the South Side, where tenured researchers live in climate-controlled faculty housing and argue about neural interface ethics while the neighborhoods around them count their dead from infrastructure failure.

The campus itself is a strange time capsule. Gothic revival buildings — the original Cobb Hall, Rockefeller Chapel, the hulking mass of Harper Library — stand alongside corporate-funded research towers wrapped in adaptive glass that shifts opacity with the sun. The old Midway Plaisance, once an open green boulevard, is now a sealed atmospheric corridor connecting the campus to the Museum of Science and Industry, which Helix BioSystems converted into a corporate showcase and public-facing research exhibition. Students walk paths that Frederick Law Olmsted would still recognize, beneath trees maintained by university groundskeepers who are among the last people in the southern corridor with job security. The intellectual output is genuine and occasionally brilliant. The moral compromise required to produce it is the thing nobody discusses at faculty dinners.

Outside the campus walls, Hydewood is a buffer zone — the neighborhood that exists to service the University without being part of it. Restaurants, housing for adjunct faculty and graduate students who can't afford campus quarters, repair shops for academic-grade neural interfaces, and a thriving market in secondhand research equipment that fell off the back of a university procurement order. The town-gown divide that existed in the original Hyde Park has been literalized: there is an actual wall, with actual gates, and your tier credential determines which side you wake up on. The cosmopolitan diversity that once defined the neighborhood survives in attenuated form — visiting scholars from global research institutions, displaced academics from collapsed universities, and a stubborn population of booksellers and café operators who insist on running analog businesses in a digital district.

The Museum of Science and Industry — now the Helix Discovery Center — sits at the eastern edge like a cathedral to corporate benevolence. Inside, interactive exhibits explain how neural interfaces will save humanity, how bioremediation will restore the planet, how the tier system ensures optimal resource allocation. School groups from Tier 2-3 districts are bused in for educational programming. The exhibits are polished, the science is real, and the omissions are surgical. What the museum doesn't mention could fill a library, and in Hydewood, some people are trying to build exactly that.
atmosphere
sights
  • Gothic spires of the original University buildings rising above modern research towers — stone and glass in uncomfortable partnership
  • The campus wall — elegant, vine-covered, and absolutely non-negotiable about who enters
  • Rockefeller Chapel's stained glass, still intact, lit from within during evening lectures
  • The Helix Discovery Center glowing at the district's eastern edge, its facade a single curved screen running educational content
  • Graduate students in augmented-reality study rigs, neural interfaces flickering, sitting in cafés that serve real coffee
  • Secondhand bookshops with actual paper volumes in the windows — a quiet defiance
sounds
  • Lecture audio bleeding through open campus windows — fragments of neuroscience, economics, philosophy
  • The chime of campus gate credentials being validated, a sound that sorts people
  • Café conversations in twelve languages, half of them academic jargon
  • Chapel bells — the University maintained them as a tradition, and the sound carries for blocks
  • The hum of research equipment running through the night in the corporate-funded towers
smells
  • Real coffee — Hydewood has three roasters and the aroma marks the district's borders better than any map
  • Old paper from the bookshops, a smell that is becoming extinct elsewhere
  • Ozone from high-end neural interface charging stations
  • The faintly antiseptic air inside the campus wall, filtered and controlled
  • Lake air from the eastern edge, carrying the metallic tang of the Helix Discovery Center's cooling systems
feel Hydewood feels like a monastery that took corporate money to keep the lights on and is trying not to think about what that means. There is genuine brilliance here, genuine inquiry, genuine care about truth — and it all exists at the pleasure of six corponations who could pull funding tomorrow. The tension between intellectual freedom and financial dependence is the district's defining texture, and everyone who lives here has made their peace with it, or is pretending to.
tags —
demographics Approximately 30,000 residents. Campus population is Tier 4, predominantly academic professionals and researchers from global backgrounds. Off-campus population ranges from Tier 2-3, including adjuncts, service workers, graduate students, and a small but resilient community of independent intellectuals and booksellers.
economy University employment is the anchor. Off-campus economy runs on academic services, hospitality, and a gray market in research equipment and data. The Helix Discovery Center generates tourism revenue that flows to Helix, not the neighborhood.
power structure The University of Chicago operates as an autonomous Tier 4 zone under consortium charter. Off-campus governance is nominal — technically Axiom jurisdiction, practically managed by university-adjacent neighborhood associations. Helix BioSystems controls the Discovery Center and surrounding blocks as sovereign corporate territory.
dangers
  • Campus security treats unauthorized entry as corporate espionage — the response is disproportionate
  • Academic politics with corporate stakes — research disputes here have budgetary and sometimes physical consequences
  • The buffer zone between campus and surrounding districts is a jurisdiction gap where muggings and data theft are common
  • Helix monitors Discovery Center visitors and cross-references attendance with tier databases
  • Idealistic graduate students sometimes access research they shouldn't and need extraction before campus security finds them
opportunities
  • Academic researchers with ethical objections to their funders are a reliable source of leaked corporate data
  • The secondhand research equipment market is a goldmine for tech operators who know what they're looking at
  • The University library — one of the last comprehensive physical archives — contains pre-collapse records that have been digitally erased elsewhere
  • Visiting scholars from outside Meridian 88 bring external perspectives and external contacts
  • The Helix Discovery Center's back-end systems are connected to Helix's broader research network — a tempting attack surface
story hooks
  • A tenured professor has discovered that one of the consortium's six funding corponations is using university research infrastructure to run classified military neural interface experiments. She needs the data verified and extracted before the next board meeting.
  • The University library's restricted collection contains the original municipal records from before the corporate sovereignty transition — records that could establish legal precedent for reclaiming public land. Someone has started systematically destroying them.
  • A graduate student has gone missing inside the campus wall, and campus security says she was never enrolled. Her roommate in the off-campus district has her research notes, which reference something called Protocol Minotaur.

Irkalla #

type place
name Irkalla
aliases
  • Irving Park
  • The Greystone Quarter
  • The Split
  • Old Irving
description Irkalla takes its name from the Mesopotamian underworld, and the residents who coined it had a sense of humor about their situation. The northern half of old Irving Park — the quiet half, with its historic greystones and tree-lined streets — was absorbed into a Vantage Meridian residential development zone in Year 9. The corporation gutted the buildings, kept the facades, and filled them with climate-controlled Tier 3-4 housing units. From the outside, the greystones look exactly as they did a century ago. From the inside, they are corporate product. The trees were replaced with synthetic equivalents that require no maintenance and produce no allergens. The result is beautiful and completely dead — a museum of a neighborhood, preserved in corporate amber.

The southern half was not so lucky. Too close to the Kennedy Expressway interchange — now a maglev junction called the Switchback — the southern blocks became transit infrastructure. Buildings were demolished or absorbed into the junction's support structure. What remained between the pylons and the maglev tracks became a squatter settlement that calls itself the Understory, home to maintenance workers who service the Switchback and the unofficial economy that feeds them. The Understory is loud, oily, perpetually vibrating from train traffic overhead, and completely invisible to the people riding those trains.

The split between north and south Irkalla is physical and absolute. A corporate security barrier — officially a 'transit safety perimeter' — runs along what used to be Irving Park Road, separating the preserved greystones from the squatter pylons. Crossing requires either a Tier 3+ access credential or knowledge of the seventeen gaps in the barrier that the Understory residents maintain and the corporate security AI pretends not to notice. This arrangement suits everyone: Vantage Meridian gets to report zero unauthorized crossings, the Understory gets to exist, and the barrier gets to be a metaphor for everything wrong with the tier system.

The name stuck because Irkalla, in mythology, was a place you could enter but never leave. The Understory residents appreciate the irony. The Tier 3 residents in the greystones don't get the reference, because their neural interfaces auto-filter cultural content below their engagement profile.
atmosphere
sights
  • Historic greystone facades concealing corporate-standard interiors — architecture as costume
  • The Switchback maglev junction overhead, trains screaming through every ninety seconds
  • The security barrier along the old Irving Park Road line — concrete, sensor mesh, and corporate signage
  • Understory settlements built between maglev pylons, improvised structures vibrating with each train pass
  • Synthetic trees in the north that never lose their leaves and never look quite right
  • Maintenance workers in Switchback coveralls crossing through barrier gaps at shift change
sounds
  • Maglev trains — the dominant sound in both halves, inescapable, rhythmic, brain-reshaping
  • The north: curated silence underneath the train noise, corporate ambient masking
  • The south: industrial clanging, welding, the constant labor of keeping the junction functional
  • The barrier itself hums at a frequency designed to be uncomfortable to unaugmented hearing
smells
  • The north smells like nothing — air scrubbed to corporate specification
  • The south smells like maglev lubricant, hot metal, and the cooking fires of people who live between machines
  • Ozone from the junction — sharp, constant, the smell of infrastructure
feel Irkalla feels like two cities pressed together with a wall between them. The north is uncanny in its preservation — walking past those greystones triggers something ancestral, a recognition of home that dissolves when you realize the windows don't open. The south vibrates. Literally. The maglev shakes the ground, the pylons, the teeth in your skull. Living in the Understory means learning to think between trains.
tags —
demographics North: approximately 15,000 Tier 3-4 residents in corporate-managed housing. South (Understory): approximately 30,000 Tier 1 and untier-ed workers, predominantly transit maintenance crews and their families. The two populations share a zip code and nothing else.
economy —
power structure —
dangers
  • The security barrier — crossing without credentials risks detention or worse
  • Maglev proximity — the Understory has regular casualties from train turbulence and falling debris
  • Corporate surveillance in the north — every greystone is a monitoring station
  • Structural instability in the Understory — buildings between pylons were never meant to be buildings
  • The vibration itself — long-term residents develop neurological symptoms the corporate health reports don't acknowledge
opportunities
  • Barrier gaps as transit routes between corporate and ungoverned territory
  • Switchback maintenance access — workers who know the junction know every route in and out of the northwest districts
  • The greystones' corporate networks are accessible from the Understory if you know which pylon carries the fiber
  • Understory mechanics who can repair anything that moves, no questions asked
story hooks
  • A Tier 3 greystone resident has been passing data through a barrier gap to an Understory contact — and someone corporate has noticed
  • The maglev junction is developing unexplained routing errors that are diverting trains through unauthorized corridors — sabotage or infrastructure decay?
  • An Understory elder remembers the original Irving Park before the split and is recording oral histories that contradict the corporate version of the rezoning

Iron Bend #

type place
name Iron Bend
aliases
  • The Flats
  • The Bend
  • Cuyahoga Industrial
description The Cuyahoga River caught fire in 1969. That fact became a punchline, a rallying cry for the environmental movement, and eventually the origin story of an entertainment district when Cleveland turned the Flats into bars and restaurants in the 1990s. A century later, the river is burning again — not with pollution, but with the concentrated industrial output of a corridor that has turned the Cuyahoga valley into one of the most productive manufacturing zones east of the Meridian Core.

Iron Bend is the Flats stripped of pretense. The entertainment district lasted about thirty years. The breweries and dance clubs were displaced first by the economic collapse of the 2020s and then by the corridor's industrialization, which recognized the Cuyahoga valley's natural geography — a steep-walled river valley cutting through the city center — as an ideal containment zone for heavy manufacturing, chemical processing, and the kind of industrial activity that you want to keep below sightline from the neighborhoods above. The valley walls serve as natural sound barriers. The river provides cooling water and waste transport. The old rail bridges that cross the valley have been reinforced and integrated into Ferrogate's sovereign transit corridor, carrying raw materials in and finished products out on a 24-hour cycle.

The valley floor is a landscape of manufacturing facilities, chemical storage, and automated fabrication plants operated by a rotating cast of corponations. Palladian Construction runs the largest single facility — a biofoam and structural materials plant that feeds the corridor's insatiable construction appetite. Zheng-Dao Bioelectric operates an augment component manufacturing line. Ferrogate maintains its Cleveland transit hub on the east bank. The workers who operate and maintain these facilities live on the valley rim, commuting down via cargo elevators that were designed for materials and retrofitted for humans with minimal concern for comfort or safety. At night, the valley glows — furnace light, chemical fluorescence, the running lights of automated transport — and the effect from the rim neighborhoods is genuinely beautiful in the way that all industrial landscapes are beautiful when you're far enough away to forget what they cost.
atmosphere
sights
  • The Cuyahoga valley at night — furnace light reflecting off the river, chemical fluorescence in blues and greens, automated transport running like luminous veins
  • Old rail bridges reinforced with Ferrogate sovereign infrastructure, trains crossing the valley on schedules that haven't paused in decades
  • Palladian's biofoam plant — the largest structure in the valley, its exhaust stacks releasing vapor that catches the light in prismatic patterns
  • Cargo elevators descending the valley walls, carrying workers down in modified freight cars
  • The river itself — clean enough to not catch fire, dirty enough that nothing lives in it
sounds
  • Industrial baseline — the combined output of every manufacturing facility in the valley creates a sound that residents call the Drone, a low-frequency presence that never stops
  • Ferrogate transit — trains crossing the valley bridges produce a rhythmic percussion that the factory schedules have unconsciously synchronized with
  • Cargo elevator machinery — the grind and clank of systems designed for materials, protesting the weight of human passengers
  • The river — moving faster than you'd expect through engineered channels, its sound masked by the factories but present if you listen
  • Shift change horns — different frequencies for different facilities, creating an industrial chord at 0600, 1400, and 2200
smells
  • Chemical processing — a cocktail of industrial outputs that changes composition hourly depending on which facilities are running which processes
  • Biofoam manufacturing — the distinctive sweet-chemical tang of Gravemoss-derived construction materials being produced at scale
  • Hot metal from Zheng-Dao's augment component line — a clean, sharp scent that augmented workers claim they can taste
feel Iron Bend feels like the inside of a machine — because it is one. The valley has been optimized for production the way a body is optimized for breathing: every space serves a function, every rhythm exists for a reason, and human presence is tolerated as a necessary inefficiency that automation hasn't fully resolved yet. The beauty of the valley at night is real, and it is the beauty of a furnace — warm, bright, and not meant for you.
tags —
demographics The valley floor has no permanent residential population — workers commute from the rim. The working population across all shifts is approximately 8,000, predominantly Tier 1-2 industrial laborers. The rim neighborhoods (Tremont side and downtown side) house the workforce in conditions that range from adequate to marginal depending on which employer provides the housing.
economy Heavy manufacturing, chemical processing, and component fabrication. Palladian's biofoam plant is the largest single employer. Zheng-Dao's augment line is the highest-value operation. Ferrogate's transit hub processes cargo that connects the Cleveland sprawl to the wider corridor. The combined economic output of Iron Bend exceeds Φ12 billion annually — none of which is spent in the valley itself.
power structure No single sovereign. The valley floor is divided between Palladian, Zheng-Dao, Ferrogate, and four smaller corponation leaseholders, each operating under their own proprietary jurisdiction within their facility boundaries. The spaces between facilities — the access roads, the river banks, the maintenance corridors — fall under no jurisdiction at all. Tollgate theoretically maintains infrastructure, but the valley's systems are so heavily modified by the resident corponations that Tollgate's standard protocols don't apply.
dangers
  • Industrial hazard — the valley's manufacturing processes produce chemical, thermal, and electromagnetic exposure risks that are within corporate safety standards and well above what anyone would choose for themselves
  • Jurisdiction gaps — the spaces between facilities are ungoverned, unmonitored, and used by people whose business requires both qualities
  • Cargo elevator failure — the retrofitted freight systems that transport workers into the valley have a maintenance record that the workers prefer not to discuss
  • River flooding — the Cuyahoga's engineered channels can overflow during heavy rain events, and the valley floor's drainage was designed for industrial runoff, not flash floods
  • The Drone — prolonged exposure to the valley's combined industrial frequencies causes hearing damage, sleep disruption, and neurological effects that the corponations classify as 'occupational adaptation'
opportunities
  • The jurisdiction gaps between facilities are the valley's most valuable real estate — for operations that require ungoverned space in the heart of the Cleveland sprawl
  • The manufacturing facilities produce components and materials that are valuable on the gray market — and security between shifts is thinner than the corponations admit
  • Ferrogate's transit hub is a nexus point — controlling information about what moves through Iron Bend means controlling information about the eastern corridor's supply chain
  • The valley's industrial infrastructure can be repurposed — someone with the right skills can manufacture almost anything in the gaps between corporate production runs
story hooks
  • The Cuyahoga's chemical composition has changed — something in the river is dissolving the biofoam foundations of Palladian's plant, and Palladian doesn't know what it is or where it's coming from
  • A worker in Zheng-Dao's augment line has discovered that every third production run includes components that don't match any augment in the commercial catalog — military-grade hardware being manufactured under commercial cover
  • The ungoverned spaces between facilities have developed their own economy, their own governance, and their own protection — a micro-community that both the corponations and the excluded population pretend doesn't exist

  • The valley floor's own ungoverned population — people who live in the gaps and maintain them

Iron Crown #

type place
name Iron Crown
aliases
  • Marquette MI
  • The Crown
  • UP Capital
  • Iron City
description Marquette was always the Upper Peninsula's capital in spirit. In 2200, it's the capital in fact — the seat of Michigan's UP Administrative Authority, the largest population center in the contested peninsula, and the symbolic heart of whatever the Upper Peninsula is becoming. The iron mines that built the city in the nineteenth century are still operating, though they've evolved from open-pit extraction to deep-bore automated mining systems that pull iron, copper, and rare earth minerals from deposits that human miners couldn't have reached. Dredge Mining Collective holds sovereign extraction rights, and their operations extend in a 50-kilometer radius around the city, honeycombing the bedrock with automated tunnels that the surface population tries not to think about.

Northern Michigan University — one of the few surviving public universities in the GLM — anchors the city's other identity. The university is the UP's intellectual infrastructure, producing the engineers, technicians, and administrators who keep the peninsula functioning. Its research programs in cold-weather augmentation, mining automation, and Superior ecology draw funding from corporate and governmental sources alike, making the campus a rare neutral ground in the Michigan-Wisconsin territorial dispute. Both sides want the university's output. Neither side wants to be the one that militarizes a campus.

The lakefront is Marquette's window onto Superior, and it remains genuinely beautiful in a way that most of the GLM's waterfronts have surrendered to infrastructure. The ore docks still load ships — massive automated structures extending into the lake — but between them, the sandstone cliffs and beaches persist, maintained by a municipal government that understands the psychological value of having something worth looking at. Iron Crown is the UP's proof of concept — the argument that a contested, isolated, resource-dependent community can sustain itself through extraction, education, and the stubborn refusal to be absorbed by any of the larger powers that want what it has.
atmosphere
sights
  • The ore docks extending into Lake Superior like industrial fingers — automated loading systems running day and night
  • Northern Michigan University campus, its buildings a mix of pre-corporate stone and modern research facilities
  • Sandstone cliffs along the lakefront, red-brown against Superior's grey-blue — beauty that nobody has managed to monetize
  • Mining transport vehicles moving through the city center — the underground economy surfacing for resupply
  • Michigan state flags flying from government buildings alongside UP independence banners — a political identity still forming
sounds
  • Ore loading operations on the docks — the deep metallic groan of tonnage moving from land to ship
  • University activity — the sounds of a campus that hasn't given up on public education
  • Lake Superior weather — wind off the lake that carries cold and context
  • Mining transport convoys — heavy vehicles on roads not designed for them, a grinding complaint from the infrastructure
smells
  • Iron ore dust — the city's signature scent, red-brown and metallic, coating every surface
  • Lake Superior air — the cleanest air in the GLM, when the wind comes off the water
  • Pine forests north of the city, carried on north winds
  • University cafeteria food — bad, but the smell of an institution that still feeds people rather than charging for nutrient optimization
feel A city that is trying to be something more than a mine with addresses. Iron Crown has ambition beyond extraction — the university, the lakefront, the administrative infrastructure — but the iron is what pays for it, and everyone knows it. The tension between resource colony and actual community defines the place.
tags —
demographics Population 95,000, plus 12,000 university students. The most stable population in the UP — families with multi-generational roots, mining workers who stayed, academics who came for a position and discovered they couldn't leave. Tier 2 majority, with a Tier 3 professional class centered on the university and administration. Wisconsin partisans make up an estimated 15% — a minority, but a vocal one.
economy Iron and rare earth mining (Dredge Mining Collective), higher education (Northern Michigan University), and UP administrative services. The mining revenue funds the administration. The university produces the workforce. The arrangement is circular, self-sustaining, and entirely dependent on mineral prices remaining high enough to justify the extraction.
power structure Michigan's UP Administrative Authority governs from Iron Crown, with actual jurisdiction over the city and nominal jurisdiction over the peninsula. Dredge Mining Collective holds sovereign extraction rights but has limited authority within the city itself — an arrangement that both sides maintain because renegotiation would be worse. The university president has informal influence disproportionate to the position, because everyone needs what the university produces.
dangers
  • Mining subsidence — the automated tunnels beneath the city are extensive, and the ground settles occasionally and catastrophically
  • Wisconsin-aligned sabotage of Michigan administrative facilities — rare but escalating
  • Dredge Mining's extraction operations encroaching on municipal territory as surface deposits deplete
  • Winter isolation — Iron Crown is reachable by one major highway, one rail line, and lake shipping, all of which close in severe weather
  • The rare earth minerals beneath the city making it too valuable for larger powers to leave alone indefinitely
opportunities
  • University connections — NMU's research programs provide access to cutting-edge cold-weather and mining technology
  • Administrative access — Iron Crown is where UP governance happens, and governance requires operators
  • Mining expertise — Dredge-trained technicians and automated systems specialists are in demand across the GLM
  • The UP independence movement — nascent, controversial, and in need of people who can navigate between Michigan and Wisconsin interests
story hooks
  • Dredge Mining's automated tunnel network has intersected with something beneath the city that predates human habitation — the mining AI flagged it, and Dredge corporate sealed the data
  • A university researcher has developed a cold-weather augmentation that would transform UP habitability — and both Michigan and Wisconsin want exclusive access
  • The UP Administrative Authority is quietly preparing for a sovereignty declaration independent of both Michigan and Wisconsin — and they need external support to survive the aftermath

Irongate Flats #

type place
name Irongate Flats
aliases
  • The Flats
  • Irongate
  • The Low Corridor
  • Rust Haven
description Irongate Flats occupies a compressed strip of reclaimed industrial land along the Chicago River's northern fork, sandwiched between the elevated rail infrastructure of an active Carrion Logistics freight line overhead and a retaining wall that separates it from the Shelf's lower drainage channels below. The neighborhood grew organically from a cluster of heavy equipment storage yards and machine shops that never fully cleared out after the industrial consolidations of the 2130s, and the result is a dense, low-rise district that feels structurally halfway between a permanent settlement and a long-term encampment — corrugated metal facades bolted onto older brick structures, rooftop additions built from salvaged freight containers, covered walkways strung between buildings to shelter the narrow streets from the constant rain of rust and grit shaken loose by freight trains passing overhead.

The approximately four thousand people who live in Irongate Flats are predominantly Tier 3 and Tier 4 workers in the industrial and logistics trades — welders, fabricators, machine diagnosticians, BCI-assisted heavy equipment operators, and the considerable support infrastructure that keeps them housed, fed, medicated, and functional. There is a rough competence to daily life here that outsiders sometimes mistake for roughness of another kind: people know their tools, know their neighbors, and know the difference between a problem they can fix themselves and one that requires help. The local economy is substantially cash-equivalent, with most transactions conducted through a neighborhood-managed Diaspora sub-mesh that runs parallel to the main network and keeps local transaction records out of corponation analytics.

The freight line overhead is both the district's primary liability and its primary economic driver. Carrion Logistics pays a nominal easement fee to a neighborhood association that uses the funds to maintain the retaining wall infrastructure and the covered walkways. In exchange, Carrion maintains a hands-off policy toward the community that represents a meaningful departure from the corponation's usual practices — a relationship maintained through careful cultivation and a shared understanding that the most experienced equipment specialists in the region live directly below the freight line and keep it running smoothly.
atmosphere
sights
  • Covered streets in perpetual industrial twilight, lit by strings of work lights and neon business signage in a dozen languages
  • Freight trains passing overhead every twenty to forty minutes, visible through steel-grate sections of the walkway covers, their running lights strobing through the gaps
  • Machine shops and fabrication spaces with their shutters open to the street, sparks and blue welding light spilling across wet pavement
  • Rooftop container additions painted in bright colors — reds, greens, deep yellows — contrasting with the grey-brown industrial surroundings
  • Children running errands between shops, their BCIs visibly active, navigating the covered street grid with the fluency of long familiarity
sounds
  • The rhythmic thunder of freight trains passing overhead, shaking loose a constant fine rain of rust and particulate
  • Industrial noise from open-shutter shops — grinding, hammering, the high whine of precision cutting tools
  • Street conversation in Tagalog, Yoruba, Portuguese, Hindi, and Mandarin, voices raised against the background noise
  • The neighborhood sub-mesh producing a faint harmonic hum audible through BCI audio channels — a side effect of its non-standard architecture that locals find comforting and visitors find strange
smells
  • Machine oil, hot metal, and the particular ozone smell of active welding equipment
  • Street food from covered vendors — grilled protein, fermented grain drinks, fried flatbreads with pungent fillings
  • River water and the particular wet-rust smell that drifts up from the drainage channels below the retaining wall
  • Diesel and the chemical exhaust of freight train power systems cutting through everything else when a train passes
feel Irongate Flats has the dense, pressurized feeling of a place that has optimized for survival and landed, accidentally, on something resembling flourishing. The covered streets create an intimate, almost interior quality to the public space — rain and wind are kept out, sound is channeled and amplified, and the visual horizon is always close. This produces a social intensity that newcomers find either welcoming or claustrophobic depending on their orientation. The community's relationship to its own infrastructure is unusually hands-on: residents fix things, modify things, argue about things in public forums, and maintain a collective investment in their environment that is rare at Tier 3 and essentially unheard of at Tier 4.
tags —
demographics Predominantly Tier 3 and Tier 4 industrial and logistics workers and their families. Significant multigenerational populations of Filipino, Nigerian, Brazilian, and South Asian descent, reflecting the historical labor migration patterns of the 2110s-2130s industrial consolidations. A small but stable population of synthetic persons who found informal acceptance here before synthetic personhood became a wider civil rights issue.
economy Primary income through industrial fabrication, equipment maintenance, and specialist labor contracting — particularly to Carrion Logistics, Ringo Heavy Industries, and several independent freight operators. Secondary economy in street food, local retail, and informal financial services run through the neighborhood sub-mesh. A discreet but acknowledged gray market in unregistered equipment modifications and off-book fabrication work for clients who need custom hardware without a paper trail.
power structure The Irongate Neighborhood Association is the de facto governing body, holding the Carrion Logistics easement contract and managing the sub-mesh infrastructure. Leadership is elected but heavily influenced by the three or four senior master fabricators whose workshops are the economic anchors of the district. Ferrogate Security does not hold a contract here — the Association manages its own dispute resolution through a combination of community mediation and, when necessary, the credible threat of withdrawing the specialist labor that keeps Carrion's freight line operational.
dangers
  • The freight line overhead creates genuine physical hazard from falling debris, particularly during high-speed cargo runs — residents know the safe corridors but visitors do not
  • The retaining wall above the drainage channels has experienced two partial failures in the last decade; a significant failure would flood the lower streets within minutes
  • Off-book fabrication clients occasionally arrive with needs that attract dangerous attention from corponation enforcement or rival criminal operators
  • The sub-mesh's non-standard architecture makes it a periodic target for hostile ELF intrusion — the mesh has been partially compromised twice, with significant disruption to local financial records
  • Carrion Logistics' increasing automation agenda threatens the labor relationship that underpins the neighborhood's negotiating position, a threat that is producing internal political tension
opportunities
  • Access to specialist fabrication capabilities outside corporate supply chains — custom hardware, unregistered modifications, and bespoke equipment built by people who actually know what they are doing
  • The sub-mesh infrastructure provides a semi-private financial network usable by those with the right introductions for transactions that do not appear in standard Diaspora records
  • The neighborhood's relationship with Carrion Logistics provides legitimate logistics and freight access that can be leveraged for moving goods or people without standard manifest scrutiny
story hooks
  • One of the senior master fabricators has been quietly building something in the back of her shop for three years, ordering parts through channels that are deliberately obscured and keeping her most trusted apprentices away from the project. Two weeks ago she disappeared, and the partially assembled object she left behind has attracted the attention of both Arcturus Defense Solutions and an entity claiming to be an ELF who says the fabricator was building it for them. Someone needs to find out where she went and whether she left voluntarily.
  • Carrion Logistics has begun deploying automated maintenance units on the freight line overhead — units that, the neighborhood's equipment diagnosticians have discovered, are also performing surveillance functions unrelated to freight operations, mapping the sub-mesh architecture and logging the faces of residents. The Association wants the surveillance functionality disabled without tipping off Carrion that it has been detected, which requires someone with the technical skills to modify the units during active deployment and the social skills to keep the operation from leaking.
