Neshkoro Verdant #

type place
name Neshkoro Verdant
aliases
  • Neshkoro
  • The Verdant
  • Green Nesh
  • The Overgrowth
description Neshkoro was five hundred people and a gas station. That's not dismissive — it's the kind of honest smallness that defined thousands of Wisconsin villages, places that existed because someone built a church and a tavern at a crossroads and enough people agreed to stay. When the Corporate Consolidation came, Neshkoro didn't resist or negotiate or even particularly notice. The young people had already left for the Nexus or Meridian. The old people died. The buildings emptied. By 2155, the village was officially depopulated — a status that meant, in practice, that it was deleted from every corporate database and left to whatever came next.

What came next was the forest. Central Wisconsin's rewilding, accelerated by climate shift and the absence of human management, was already pushing hardwood and pine back into abandoned agricultural land. But Neshkoro got something else. In 2162, a Helix BioSystems atmospheric seeding experiment — part of a carbon capture initiative designed more for tax credits than environmental benefit — deposited a modified mycorrhizal network across a two-hundred-square-kilometer zone that included Neshkoro. The modified fungi were designed to accelerate root growth and soil carbon fixation. They worked. They worked far too well. Within a decade, the forest around Neshkoro had grown with a density and speed that alarmed the few people still monitoring satellite imagery. Trees that should have taken fifty years to mature reached full canopy in eight. Undergrowth became impenetrable. The mycorrhizal network itself became visible — bioluminescent threads running through the soil and up tree trunks, pulsing faintly at night, creating a forest that glowed from within. Helix classified the experiment as 'completed' and stopped monitoring. The forest kept growing.

Neshkoro Verdant is what grew back. The village structures are still there — engulfed, incorporated, dissolved into a forest that treats human architecture as scaffolding. The old church steeple rises from a canopy of engineered oaks. The gas station is a root-wrapped cavern. And people live here — not many, maybe three hundred — drawn by the forest's strange beauty, its pharmaceutical potential, and its absolute impermeability to surveillance technology. The mycorrhizal network interferes with signal propagation in ways that Saltmarsh engineers can't explain and Helix scientists won't discuss. Drones that fly over the canopy lose navigation. Satellites can't penetrate the leaf cover. The Verdant is a black hole on every map, and the people who live in it prefer it that way. They are herbalists, mystics, biotech scavengers, and a handful of rogue Helix researchers who came to study what went wrong and stayed because they realized it might have gone right.
atmosphere
sights
  • Engineered forest canopy so dense it creates permanent twilight at ground level, with shafts of light piercing through like spotlights on a stage
  • Bioluminescent mycorrhizal threads running up tree trunks and across the forest floor, pulsing with a slow blue-green rhythm that suggests respiration
  • Old village structures consumed by growth — a church steeple wrapped in vines, a gas station converted into a root cavern, road signs absorbed into tree bark
  • Medicinal gardens cultivated in canopy clearings, tended by residents who've learned to work with the accelerated growth rather than against it
  • The occasional Helix BioSystems monitoring drone, crashed and overgrown, its signal light still blinking beneath a blanket of moss
sounds
  • The forest breathing — a rhythmic creak and sigh as the engineered canopy responds to atmospheric pressure changes with an almost biological regularity
  • Mycorrhizal network activity — a subsonic vibration that residents claim they can feel through their feet, below the threshold of hearing
  • Wildlife that shouldn't be here — species displaced by climate change, species modified by biotech runoff, and species that don't match any known taxonomy
  • Water movement through the root network, audible in quiet moments as a distributed murmur like a crowd whispering
  • The absolute absence of electronic noise — no hum, no ping, no transmission. The silence of a world before signals.
smells
  • Mycorrhizal output — a rich, complex, almost narcotic organic smell that first-time visitors describe as 'what soil is supposed to smell like'
  • Bioluminescent spore release — periodic, sweet, faintly chemical, accompanied by visible clouds of luminous particulate
  • Medicinal plant cultivation — sharp herbal notes from the gardens, some recognizable, some entirely novel
  • Decay accelerated by the fungal network — organic matter breaks down visibly fast here, and the smell is constant and fertile
feel Alien. Not hostile, not welcoming — alien, in the sense of encountering an intelligence that operates on different principles. The forest feels aware, though residents insist that's anthropomorphism. The bioluminescence pulses in patterns that seem responsive to movement. The growth accommodates human presence without encouraging it. Walking through Neshkoro Verdant feels like being tolerated by something vast and patient. It is the most beautiful and most unsettling place within a hundred kilometers of the Fox Cities Nexus, and the people who live here have the particular calm of those who've made peace with being small.
tags —
demographics Approximately 300 permanent residents. No tier classification — the Verdant exists outside corporate cartography entirely. A mix of herbalists and traditional medicine practitioners, rogue Helix BioSystems researchers who went native, biotech scavengers harvesting pharmaceutical compounds from the engineered ecosystem, and a small spiritual community that has developed practices around the mycorrhizal network. Youngest average age of any settlement in the region — something about the Verdant attracts people in their twenties who are looking for an alternative to corridor life.
economy Pharmaceutical harvesting — compounds produced by the engineered mycorrhizal network and its associated flora have significant medical and recreational value, traded through runners to Freebank, Wautoma Null, and occasionally the Nexus gray market. The Verdant also trades in knowledge — the rogue Helix researchers have accumulated data on the modified ecosystem that the parent company would pay dearly to suppress or recover.
power structure Informal and distributed, mirroring the mycorrhizal network the community lives within. Decisions emerge from consensus among long-term residents, with the rogue Helix researchers holding outsized influence due to their technical knowledge. A figure known only as the Gardener — who may have been among the original Helix team that deployed the mycorrhizal modification — is consulted on major decisions but holds no formal authority.
dangers
  • The forest itself — accelerated growth means structures must be constantly maintained against encroachment, and the ecosystem produces organisms that don't follow known biological rules
  • Pharmaceutical toxicity — not everything the engineered ecosystem produces is beneficial, and the line between medicine and poison is experimentally determined
  • Helix BioSystems recovery operations — the company periodically sends teams to retrieve data, samples, or personnel, and these teams are not gentle about the distinction between research subjects and residents
  • Navigation — the canopy blocks GPS, the mycorrhizal network disrupts signal, and the forest changes faster than maps can be drawn. Getting lost in the Verdant can be fatal.
  • Unknown biology — the engineered mycorrhizal network is evolving in ways its creators didn't predict, and some of those evolutionary directions involve organisms that treat human tissue as a growth substrate
opportunities
  • Pharmaceutical goldmine — compounds unique to the Verdant's engineered ecosystem have medical applications that could be worth billions on the corridor market
  • Signal darkness — the mycorrhizal network's interference with electronic signals makes the Verdant the most secure meeting location in central Wisconsin
  • Ecological intelligence — understanding what happened here could inform bioengineering projects across the corridor, or serve as a warning about what happens when they go wrong
  • The Gardener's knowledge — whoever this person is, they know things about Helix BioSystems' atmospheric seeding program that the company has classified at the highest level
story hooks
  • The mycorrhizal network is expanding beyond its original two-hundred-square-kilometer zone, and the rate of expansion is accelerating — within a decade it could reach the Fox Cities Nexus, and nobody knows what happens when an engineered fungal intelligence encounters a data center hub
  • Helix BioSystems sends a recovery team for the Gardener specifically, suggesting this person knows something critical about the seeding program — something more significant than a failed carbon capture experiment
  • A pharmaceutical compound harvested from the Verdant cures a neural interface rejection syndrome that affects thousands of corridor residents — but it can only be produced by the living ecosystem, not synthesized, making Neshkoro Verdant suddenly and dangerously valuable to every corponation with augmented employees
connections

  • Wautoma Null (north)
  • Wild territories (south and west)

  • Runners using the Verdant's signal darkness for secure transit between corridor and wild territories
  • Rogue researchers studying the mycorrhizal network's ongoing evolution
  • People seeking healing — both medical and spiritual — that corridor infrastructure can't or won't provide

New Stockton #

type place
name New Stockton
aliases
  • New City
  • Back of the Yards
  • The Pens
  • Jungle Floor
description New Stockton remembers what it was built on, even if Meridian 88 would prefer it didn't. The Union Stock Yards closed in 1971, but the ground never forgot. When Upton Sinclair wrote The Jungle about the meatpacking district that occupied this land, he described a place where human beings were fed into an industrial machine and rendered down alongside the cattle. A century and a half later, New Stockton has replaced the cattle with synthetic protein bioreactors and the meatpacking workers with bioprocessing technicians, and the fundamental equation hasn't changed: bodies go in, product comes out, and the people doing the work are the last to benefit from what they produce.

The bioreactor complex dominates the district -- a sprawling industrial campus that produces 30% of Meridian 88's protein supply. The vats are cathedral-sized, filled with engineered cell cultures that grow muscle tissue without the inconvenience of an animal. The process is efficient, scalable, and deeply, viscerally disturbing to witness. Workers monitor the cultures through neural interface links, their consciousness partially merged with the biological systems they manage, spending eight-hour shifts perceiving the world as a growth medium. The long-term psychological effects of this are documented in studies that NutriVat Corporation, the facility's operator, has classified as proprietary research data. The workers call it 'vat head' -- a persistent derealization that makes the real world feel less solid than the culture medium. It's not listed as an occupational hazard.

Outside the complex, New Stockton is the neighborhood the workers come home to, and it carries the exhaustion in its architecture. Housing blocks are functional and grim, built by NutriVat as employee accommodation in the same efficient, joyless style as the bioreactor facility itself. The commercial strip exists to serve shift schedules -- bars that open at 0600 for night shift workers, cafeterias that serve the synthetic protein the district produces at prices that amount to paying the workers in their own product. But Back of the Yards was always more than its industry, and New Stockton is too. The community organizing tradition that fought the meatpackers in Sinclair's day survived, adapted, and is now fighting NutriVat over the same issues with different vocabulary: worker safety, environmental contamination, and the right to not be destroyed by the thing that employs you.
atmosphere
sights
  • The bioreactor complex -- vat towers rising like industrial organs, condensation streaming down their surfaces
  • Workers in NutriVat coveralls moving between shifts with the particular gait of people returning from somewhere else mentally
  • Housing blocks in corporate beige, identical and dispiriting, arranged in efficiency-optimized grids
  • Community organizing posters on every available surface, echoing the labor movement imagery of a century ago
  • The old stockyard gate arch, preserved as a historical monument, now dwarfed by the bioreactor towers behind it
  • Protein culture runoff channels, iridescent and faintly biological, running along district gutters
sounds
  • The bioreactor hum -- a deep, organic vibration that's felt more than heard, like being inside something alive
  • Shift change announcements echoing from the complex PA system, audible across the entire district
  • Worker support group meetings in community halls -- people trying to describe vat head to people who haven't experienced it
  • The absence of animal sounds, which shouldn't be notable but somehow is in a place that used to hold millions of cattle
smells
  • Synthetic protein in process -- warm, yeasty, faintly meaty, and inescapable within a kilometer of the complex
  • Culture medium chemical compounds -- amino acids and growth factors that coat the neighborhood in a biological sweetness
  • Antiseptic from the decontamination showers workers pass through leaving the complex
  • The old stockyard soil, which still smells of blood when it rains, according to long-time residents who might be remembering or might not
feel Haunted by repetition. New Stockton feels like history stuttering -- the same exploitation wearing different clothes, the same resistance using different tools, the same workers asking the same questions about what they're owed. There's a grim humor here, born from the awareness that Sinclair wrote the book, and nobody learned the lesson, and the jungle just got a new species.
tags —
demographics Approximately 45,000 residents, predominantly Tier 1 bioprocessing workers and their families. The community is ethnically diverse -- the meatpacking immigrant tradition continues, with newer arrivals from climate displacement zones joining legacy Latino, Black, and Eastern European populations.
economy NutriVat Corporation's bioreactor complex is the economy. Supplementary businesses serve the workforce -- bars, cafeterias, medical clinics specializing in neural interface complications, and a growing informal market in vat head remediation therapies that NutriVat refuses to provide.
power structure NutriVat Corporation holds sovereign industrial authority over the bioreactor complex and effective control over the district through employer leverage. The Back of the Yards Workers Alliance, directly descended from the original meatpacking unions, provides organized opposition. The balance of power favors NutriVat. The balance of moral authority does not.
dangers
  • Vat head -- long-term neural interface exposure to biological systems causing persistent derealization
  • NutriVat security enforcement of proprietary information policies -- workers who talk about conditions face termination and blacklisting
  • Culture medium contamination events -- bioreactor leaks are rare but catastrophic
  • The psychological weight of a neighborhood built on a century and a half of industrial exploitation
  • Protein culture runoff in the district's water system -- officially within safety parameters, functionally untested for chronic exposure
opportunities
  • Bioreactor technology expertise -- New Stockton workers understand synthetic protein production at a level NutriVat's executives don't
  • The Workers Alliance has organizational infrastructure that could support broader labor actions across the Southwest
  • NutriVat's proprietary research on vat head is a corporate vulnerability -- the data exists and someone will eventually extract it
  • The old stockyard historical archives contain pre-Meridian land use records that could challenge NutriVat's territorial claims
story hooks
  • A senior bioreactor technician has discovered that the culture medium is developing unexpected cellular patterns -- not contamination, something more organized, something that might be emergent -- and NutriVat's response to her report was to revoke her research access
  • The Workers Alliance is preparing a coordinated walkout that would shut down 30% of Meridian's protein supply, and every corponation in the city has a stake in whether it succeeds or fails
  • Kyle is hired to extract the classified vat head research data from NutriVat's internal servers -- a job that requires spending a shift inside the bioreactor neural link to access the isolated network

New Windsor / Novaya Windsorka #

type place
name New Windsor / Novaya Windsorka
aliases
  • Windsor ON
  • The Other Side
  • Tunnel Town
  • Dual-Sov
description New Windsor sits across the Detroit River from the GLM's industrial heartland, and that proximity defines everything about it. The Ambassador Bridge — reinforced, widened, and draped in sensor arrays — and the Detroit-Windsor Tunnel form the two arteries connecting Canadian sovereign territory to the American corporate zones, and every drop of commerce that flows between them gets taxed, scanned, and surveilled twice. Once by each side. The result is a city that exists primarily as a jurisdictional membrane — a place where goods, people, and data change legal status simply by crossing a river.

The old automotive plants that once built cars for the North American market have been retooled into fabrication centers for neural interface components, autonomous vehicle subsystems, and military-grade augmentation hardware. Tessera Corponation and Zheng-Dao Bioelectric both maintain sovereign manufacturing enclaves here, exploiting the dual-sovereignty arrangement to dodge regulations on both sides of the border. Workers commute between jurisdictions daily, their legal rights flickering on and off like a bad connection as they cross the river. Canadian labor protections apply on the north bank. Corporate sovereign law applies on the south. The tunnel between is a legal no-man's-land where neither applies and everyone knows it.

The residential districts sprawl south and east from the riverfront, a patchwork of climate-refugee housing blocks, mid-tier corporate dormitories, and the decaying bones of twentieth-century suburbia that nobody has bothered to demolish. The population skews young, transient, and bilingual in ways that have nothing to do with French and English — Shelf Cant, Mandarin trade pidgin, and machine-interface shorthand are the languages that actually matter here. The city smells like ozone and river water, and on bad days the chemical plumes from Sarnia drift east and add a third note that makes your eyes water.
atmosphere
sights
  • The Ambassador Bridge lit with customs scanning arrays, a neon-traced spine over black water
  • Fabrication centers running 24-hour shifts, robotic arms visible through translucent walls
  • Dual-sovereignty markers on every street corner — Canadian maple leaf on one side, corporate logo on the other
  • The Detroit skyline across the river, arcology towers dwarfing everything on the Windsor side
  • Climate-refugee housing blocks with laundry strung between balconies, a defiant splash of color against grey concrete
sounds
  • The low thrum of tunnel traffic — a vibration you feel in your teeth more than hear
  • Customs drones overhead, their scanning pings a constant irritant
  • Fabrication equipment running triple shifts — the sound of money being made for someone else
  • River barges sounding horns in the pre-dawn fog
  • Arguments in three languages at once at the bridge checkpoints
smells
  • Ozone from the bridge scanning arrays
  • Detroit River water — industrial, metallic, and alive despite everything
  • Chemical drift from Sarnia on east winds, sharp enough to taste
  • Fabrication coolant from the manufacturing enclaves
feel A city that exists in the hyphen between two systems. Everyone here is performing a jurisdictional magic trick — they are Canadian citizens and corporate subjects simultaneously, and the trick only works as long as nobody examines it too closely. The tension is mundane, quotidian, built into the commute.
tags —
demographics Population 1.2 million registered, an estimated 300,000 undocumented transients cycling through. Heavy representation of climate refugees from the American Gulf Coast who crossed through Detroit and kept going. Dual-citizenship holders make up 40% of the workforce — people who carry two legal identities and trust neither.
economy Manufacturing and border commerce. The fabrication enclaves produce augmentation components for export to M88. The tunnel and bridge generate customs revenue that funds what passes for municipal government. Smuggling — of goods, data, and people — accounts for an estimated 25% of actual economic activity, and everyone from the customs agents to the corponations takes a cut.
power structure Nominally Canadian municipal government, practically a joint administration between the Canadian Border Authority and the corporate sovereigns who maintain manufacturing enclaves. Tessera and Zheng-Dao have more employees in Windsor than the city has civil servants. The mayor is elected; the mayor is irrelevant.
dangers
  • Dual-sovereignty jurisdiction traps — commit an act legal in Canada but illegal in corporate territory, and you can be arrested on the bridge
  • Chemical exposure from Sarnia drift events — the air quality warnings come after the damage is done
  • Corporate labor disputes that escalate into physical lockdowns of entire districts
  • Smuggling operations that treat human cargo the same as any other inventory
  • The tunnel's legal no-man's-land, where disappearances happen and no jurisdiction investigates
opportunities
  • Border arbitrage — legal in one jurisdiction, profitable in the other
  • Fabrication work for the skilled — augment technicians are always in demand
  • Intelligence brokerage — information about corporate activity in Windsor is valuable in Detroit and vice versa
  • Refugee networks that connect Windsor to every displaced community in the GLM
story hooks
  • A fabrication worker discovers the augmentation components she's building contain an undocumented surveillance substrate — and the specs came from both sides of the border
  • The tunnel's ventilation system is being retrofitted with neural-frequency emitters — crowd control infrastructure disguised as air quality management
  • A dual-sovereignty legal case threatens to collapse the entire jurisdictional framework that Windsor's economy depends on

Nordpark Sanctuary #

type place
name Nordpark Sanctuary
aliases
  • North Park
  • The Sanctuary
  • Seminary Row
  • The Quiet College
description Nordpark Sanctuary is the district that traded its future for its library. When the Corporate Reconstruction swept through Meridian 88's northern districts, North Park University — the small Christian college that had anchored this quiet neighborhood for over a century — made a deal that its founders would have found either pragmatic or damning, depending on their theology. The university surrendered its accreditation, its degree-granting authority, and its right to operate as an independent educational institution. In exchange, Axiom agreed to leave the campus and its surrounding residential blocks alone, designated as a Cultural Preservation Zone — a status that grants no political power but provides legal protection from development, demolition, and corporate acquisition. The university kept its buildings, its library, and its community. It lost everything else.

What remains is not a university in any functional sense but something harder to define: a sanctuary. The campus buildings — modest brick structures along the North Branch of the river — house a library collection that has become one of the most valuable information resources in northern Meridian. Not because the books are rare (though some are) but because they're physical. In a city where digital information is controlled, curated, and deletable by corporate systems, a building full of paper books that no one can remotely edit or erase is a strategic asset. The library's collection includes pre-corporate history texts, unredacted news archives, theological and philosophical works that challenge corporate ideology, and — most valuably — a complete set of Chicago municipal records from the decades before the Reconstruction, donated by a city clerk who saw what was coming and wanted someone to remember what was lost.

The residential blocks around the campus have taken on the character of the institution they surround. Quiet, scholarly, maintained with modest care. The population is small — mostly former faculty, students who never left, and families who value the Sanctuary's peace above the amenities that other districts offer. The North Branch river flows through the district, less channelized here than in the Commons, almost natural in places. A small seminary operates informally on campus — not granting degrees, just teaching theology, philosophy, and ethics to anyone who shows up. The students are a mix of genuine seekers and people who've discovered that a campus setting is a safe place to think dangerous thoughts.

The Sanctuary's value to Meridian's underground information economy cannot be overstated. The Collective maintains an unofficial relationship with the library, sending researchers to access the municipal archives and physical texts that can't be found on any network. Data brokers from the Circuit make pilgrimages to verify information against print sources. Corporate historians — the ones who work off the record — use the library to cross-reference official narratives against pre-Reconstruction documentation. The library staff are aware of all this and permit it with the understanding that the library serves everyone and belongs to no faction. It's the last neutral ground in a city of territories, and its neutrality is protected by the one thing that even Axiom respects: the fact that destroying a library looks bad, even for a corporation that doesn't care about looking bad.
atmosphere
sights
  • The university campus — modest brick buildings, a bell tower, paths worn smooth by generations of students who no longer attend
  • The library's reading rooms — natural light through old windows, physical books on wooden shelves, readers working in analog silence
  • The North Branch river flowing through the district, less channelized here, almost remembering what it used to be
  • Seminary students debating on campus benches — young people discussing ethics in a city that considers ethics an inefficiency
  • The residential blocks' maintained modesty — clean, cared-for homes that don't draw attention or envy
  • Handwritten signs on campus: READING ROOM OPEN, THEOLOGY SEMINAR TUESDAY, ALL WELCOME
sounds
  • Pages turning — the library's reading rooms are the quietest inhabited spaces in Meridian, and the sound of paper is the soundtrack
  • The river — audible here in a way it isn't in the Commons, flowing over rocks that haven't been removed
  • Seminary discussions — earnest, sometimes heated, occasionally brilliant arguments about what it means to be human in a city that's stopped asking
  • The bell tower — rung manually, marking the hours with a sound that predates everything Meridian has become
  • Wind through campus trees — smaller than the Hollow's forest but real, living, and cherished
smells
  • Old books — paper, binding glue, aged ink. The specific, irreplaceable smell of physical knowledge.
  • River water — cleaner here than downstream, with a mineral freshness that smells like the old geography
  • Campus grounds — cut grass, garden plots, the faint mustiness of old brick buildings breathing
  • Candle wax from the chapel — still lit, still used, still serving a purpose that can't be quantified
feel Sacred. Not in a religious sense — or not only in a religious sense — but in the older meaning: set apart, protected, important beyond its material value. The Sanctuary feels like a place that has been deliberately preserved against the current of history, maintained by people who understand that some things matter more than efficiency. It's calm in a way that the Quiet mimics but the Sanctuary genuinely achieves, because the Sanctuary's calm comes from purpose, not avoidance.
tags —
demographics Approximately 4,000 residents, predominantly former academic community — retired faculty, long-term students, families with university connections. Tier 1 and Tier 2. Older than average but not as elderly as Norwood Quiet — the seminary attracts younger residents who choose scholarship over employment. The most educated population per capita in Meridian's northern districts.
economy The library — information services, research access, and archival preservation. The seminary's informal education program. Small-scale residential economy. The Sanctuary doesn't produce goods; it preserves knowledge, and in Meridian 88, that's an economy unto itself.
power structure The Library Council — former faculty and senior staff who manage the campus and make community decisions. The head librarian holds outsized influence as the custodian of the collection. No corporate governance, no militia. The Sanctuary's protection is cultural — it survives because destroying it would mean destroying a library, and nobody wants to be the person who orders that.
dangers
  • Corporate reclassification — the Cultural Preservation Zone designation could be revoked if Axiom finds sufficient reason
  • Information theft — the library's physical archives are irreplaceable, making them targets for anyone who wants to control the narrative
  • Dependency on neutrality — the Sanctuary's survival strategy requires all factions to respect its non-aligned status, and that respect could erode
  • Resource scarcity — the campus needs maintenance, and the community has limited means
  • Infiltration — the open-door policy makes the Sanctuary vulnerable to agents seeking to identify who accesses which records
opportunities
  • The library — physical documentation of pre-corporate history, unredacted and uneditable
  • The seminary — ethics and philosophy education in a city that has abandoned both
  • Neutral ground — the Sanctuary is one of the few places where representatives of different factions can meet without territorial implications
  • Research access — the municipal archives contain information that could challenge corporate legitimacy
  • Community — a small, educated, thoughtful population that values discourse and preserves knowledge as a moral obligation
story hooks
  • A researcher from the Collective discovers that the library's municipal archives contain documentation of the original corporate charter that established Axiom's sovereignty — and the documentation reveals a legal flaw that, if publicized, could unravel the corporation's authority. The Library Council must decide whether to allow the information to leave the Sanctuary.
  • Someone is systematically removing pages from the library's pre-Reconstruction news archives — physical pages, cut from physical books, the only copies in existence. The head librarian hires Kyle to find the thief before the historical record is permanently damaged.
  • The seminary's newest student is a former Axiom executive who claims to have experienced a crisis of conscience. She wants to teach ethics. The community is divided between those who see redemption and those who see infiltration.

North Branch Commons #

type place
name North Branch Commons
aliases
  • North Center
  • The Commons
  • Riverbank
  • The Nursery
description North Branch Commons is the district that tried to stay normal. When every neighborhood in Meridian was busy reinventing itself as a corporate asset, a fortified enclave, or a drowned ruin, the residential blocks along the North Branch of the Chicago River simply kept being a place where people raised children. The river itself — diverted, channelized, and partially covered during the Corporate Reconstruction — still flows through the district, though it's been reduced from a waterway to a utility channel, its banks lined with water reclamation systems that process the flow for reuse in the upper tiers. The river doesn't belong to the Commons anymore. It passes through on its way to being useful to someone else.

The family-friendly character of old North Center persists here in a form that is both admirable and heartbreaking. Parents still walk their children to schools — small, unlicensed cooperative schools run by retired teachers and community volunteers, because the corporate education system requires Tier 3 credentials to access. Playgrounds exist, though the equipment is salvaged and the surfaces are whatever the community could scrounge. The residential streets are cleaner than anything in the Shelf, maintained by residents who take shifts sweeping and repairing because the alternative is watching their neighborhood deteriorate into somewhere they wouldn't want their kids to play. It's the most normal-looking district in this part of Meridian, which makes it the most surreal — a pocket of domestic mundanity in a city that has forgotten what mundane looks like.

The Commons functions as northern Meridian's childcare and education hub, a role that emerged organically and has become its economic identity. Families from Rogers Reef, Upturn, and even the edges of Lakeview Neon send their children to the Commons' cooperative schools, paying in barter, labor, or whatever they can manage. The schools aren't good by pre-collapse standards — overcrowded, under-resourced, teaching from salvaged textbooks and donated tablets. They're miraculous by Meridian standards. The teachers are fierce. The parents are fiercer. The unspoken rule of the Commons is that whatever else happens in this city, whatever contracts are broken and whatever districts flood, the children will be educated and the children will be safe.

The North Branch itself serves as the Commons' most valuable and most contested resource. The water reclamation infrastructure that Axiom installed along the river generates clean water as a byproduct — water that the corporation considers corporate property and that the Commons has been quietly siphoning for decades. It's an open secret. Axiom knows. The Commons knows Axiom knows. Neither side forces the issue because the political optics of a corporation cutting off water to a children's district would be worse than the cost of the stolen water. This detente defines the Commons: a place that survives by being too sympathetic to crush and too small to matter.
atmosphere
sights
  • Children walking to school in groups, monitored by rotating parent patrols on the residential streets
  • The North Branch river channel, visible through grated covers, its water processing infrastructure humming below
  • Cooperative school buildings — repurposed residential homes with hand-painted signs and window gardens
  • Salvaged playground equipment in small parks, maintained with visible care and creative repair
  • Parent volunteers sweeping streets and repairing walkways in organized morning shifts
  • Laundry drying on lines between buildings — the most domestic skyline in Meridian
sounds
  • Children — laughing, arguing, reciting lessons from open classroom windows
  • The river's reclamation systems humming beneath the street grates — a mechanical lullaby
  • Parent-patrol radio chatter — calm, organized, tracking every child's location during school hours
  • The quiet of the residential blocks after school hours — one of the few genuinely quiet places in Meridian
  • Teachers' voices carrying from open windows, explaining concepts from textbooks that are three decades out of date
smells
  • School lunch being prepared in community kitchens — simple food, made in bulk, nutritious if not exciting
  • Clean water — the siphoned reclamation water has a mineral quality that smells different from the recycled supply
  • River channel moisture seeping through the street grates — damp concrete and treated water
  • Garden plots behind the schools — herbs and vegetables grown by students as practical botany lessons
feel Determined. The Commons feels like a place that has decided what it is and refuses to be anything else. The domesticity isn't naive — these are people who know exactly how bad Meridian is and have chosen to build a space where children don't have to know that yet. There's a ferocity beneath the normal surface, the quiet rage of parents who will do whatever it takes to give their kids one more year of childhood.
tags —
demographics Approximately 12,000 residents, predominantly young families with children. Tier 1 and Tier 2, with a significant population of parents who moved specifically for access to the cooperative schools. The youngest median age of any district in northern Meridian.
economy Cooperative education services, childcare, water trade from siphoned reclamation supplies, and a domestic barter economy centered on child-rearing needs — clothing, food, medical care, tutoring.
power structure The School Council — representatives from each cooperative school — makes most community decisions. Parents' associations wield significant influence. No formal militia, but the parent patrols are organized, networked, and protective enough to function as one.
dangers
  • Axiom enforcing water rights — the siphoning detente could collapse at any time
  • Resource scarcity — the schools run on donations and barter, with no surplus for bad months
  • Predatory recruitment — corporate and criminal organizations both target the Commons' children as they age out
  • Infrastructure decay — residential buildings need maintenance the community can barely afford
  • The river itself — reclamation chemical leaks have happened before and the runoff reaches the streets
opportunities
  • Education — the cooperative schools produce literate, numerate young people in a city that doesn't
  • Clean water access — the siphoned supply is a tradeable resource and a community lifeline
  • Community trust networks — the parent associations know everyone and share information freely within the community
  • Safe harbor — the Commons is one of the few places in Meridian where children can be children
  • Recruitment pipeline — the schools' graduates are sought after by every faction that values competence over credentials
story hooks
  • A cooperative school teacher discovers that one of her students has an unlicensed neural implant of military specification — the kind that doesn't end up in a child by accident. Someone placed this child in the Commons deliberately.
  • Axiom announces a 'partnership' with the Commons schools that would provide corporate-grade resources in exchange for curriculum control and student data access. The School Council is split — the resources are desperately needed, but the price is everything they've built.
  • Kyle is hired to protect a Commons family whose child witnessed something in a neighboring district. The family can't leave without abandoning their school community, and the threat is patient enough to wait.

Norwood Quiet #

type place
name Norwood Quiet
aliases
  • Norwood Park
  • The Quiet
  • Bungalow Belt
  • The Sleep
description Norwood Quiet is the neighborhood that decided the best response to the end of the world was to pretend it hadn't happened. The old Norwood Park — Chicago's historic bungalow district, with its arts-and-crafts homes and tree-lined streets — has achieved something that shouldn't be possible in Meridian 88: it looks almost exactly the same as it did before the Corporate Reconstruction. The bungalows are still standing. The trees are still growing, maintained by a community arborist program that's been running for forty years. The streets are still quiet. And the residents — predominantly elderly, predominantly long-tenured, predominantly determined — maintain their neighborhood with the kind of stubborn attention to detail that makes reality bend around willpower.

The trick is simple and brilliant: Norwood Quiet is boring. Strategically, intentionally, aggressively boring. There's nothing here for the corporations to want. No commercial potential, no strategic infrastructure, no exploitable population. The residential stock is pre-collapse bungalows that are historically protected under a designation the old city government issued before it ceased to exist — a designation that Axiom has never formally recognized but has also never formally challenged, because challenging it would require acknowledging that pre-corporate law has standing, which opens legal doors that Axiom's attorneys would rather keep sealed. So the bungalows persist, legally ambiguous and physically immaculate, a quiet act of civil disobedience expressed through maintained gutters and painted trim.

Beneath the suburban surface, Norwood Quiet serves a function that its residents would never publicly acknowledge: it's a safe house district. The combination of minimal surveillance, boring optics, and a community that minds its own business while maintaining total awareness of who enters and leaves makes the Quiet an ideal location for people who need to disappear temporarily. Not criminals — or not exclusively criminals. Whistleblowers, corporate defectors, witnesses under threat, families fleeing Iron Lotus debts. They arrive quietly, stay in guest rooms that several bungalow owners maintain for exactly this purpose, and leave when it's safe. No records. No questions. The neighborhood watch knows who belongs and who's visiting. They don't share that information with anyone outside the community.

The Quiet's greatest vulnerability is time. The population is old and getting older. The bungalows are maintained but cannot be maintained forever. The historic protection designation exists in a legal limbo that could be resolved at any moment by a corporate attorney with a motive. The trees, real trees in real soil, are irreplaceable if they die. Norwood Quiet is a time capsule with a slowly expiring seal, and its residents know it. They maintain the houses, tend the trees, and shelter the people who need sheltering, because that's what they've always done. When the last bungalow finally falls, they want it to fall clean.
atmosphere
sights
  • Pre-collapse bungalows in maintained condition — painted, repaired, landscaped, impossible
  • Real trees lining real streets, their canopy creating shade that feels like a memory of the old city
  • Elderly residents on porches, watching the street with the calm attention of people who notice everything
  • No corporate signage — none. Not a single Axiom logo, holographic ad, or branded surface
  • Garden plots in every yard — flowers in front, vegetables in back, a pattern that hasn't changed in decades
  • The neighborhood watch — not visible as a patrol, but visible in the way every window has a line of sight to the street
sounds
  • Birdsong — real birds in real trees, a sound that most of Meridian has forgotten
  • Wind through leaves — actual rustling, not atmospheric simulation
  • The near-total absence of electronic noise — no drone hum, no holographic buzz, no ambient corporate audio
  • Lawnmowers — hand-powered, maintained like heirlooms, used on Saturday mornings as a communal ritual
  • Screen doors closing — the most domestic sound in Meridian, preserved here like an artifact
smells
  • Cut grass and garden soil — the authentic versions, not the engineered scents of the Palisade
  • Baked goods from kitchens — the Quiet's residents bake, and the smells carry on the quiet air
  • Old wood and paint — the bungalows have their own scent profile, preserved materials breathing in the sun
  • Seasonal change — Norwood Quiet is one of the few places in Meridian where you can smell autumn arriving
feel Ghostly. Norwood Quiet feels like visiting a place that time forgot, or more accurately, a place that time remembers and the present has abandoned. The peace is genuine — this is a calm, safe, beautiful neighborhood. But there's an unreality to it, the sense that you've stepped out of Meridian and into a memory. The residents' determination to maintain normalcy is admirable and heartbreaking in equal measure, because normalcy is exactly what the world they live in is no longer capable of providing.
tags —
demographics Approximately 6,000 residents, the majority over sixty. Long-tenured families, many in the same bungalows for three generations. Predominantly Tier 1 and Tier 2. The youngest demographic in the district is the rotating population of temporary residents in the safe-house rooms, who skew younger and more desperate.
economy Minimal — residential maintenance, small-scale gardening, and the invisible safe-house economy. The Quiet's residents are mostly retired or working in neighboring districts. The community is self-sustaining but not productive in any way that registers on economic metrics, which is part of the strategy.
power structure The Norwood Homeowners Association — the oldest continuously operating civic organization in Meridian's northwest. Authority is exercised through consensus, social norms, and the quiet understanding that the community's survival depends on collective discipline. No one person is in charge. Everyone is in charge of their own house.
dangers
  • Legal challenge to the historic protection designation — if Axiom decides the bungalows are worth more as rubble, the legal defense is thin
  • Aging infrastructure — the bungalows and community systems need maintenance that gets harder every year
  • Safe-house discovery — if corporate intelligence identifies the Quiet's shelter function, the consequences would be severe
  • Demographic collapse — the community is aging out with insufficient replacement, and the bungalows may outlast their owners
  • Complacency — the Quiet's strategy of being boring only works as long as no one decides boring is interesting
opportunities
  • Disappearance — the Quiet's safe-house network is one of the most discreet in Meridian
  • Real nature — trees, soil, birdsong, seasonal change. Therapeutic for people who've forgotten what the outdoors used to feel like
  • Historical knowledge — the Quiet's elderly residents remember the old city and maintain oral histories that have been lost elsewhere
  • Social camouflage — no one looks for anything in Norwood Quiet, which makes it ideal for hiding things in plain sight
  • Community model — the Homeowners Association's governance structure is studied by people interested in alternatives to corporate control
story hooks
  • A corporate defector with critical information about Axiom's plans for the northern districts is sheltered in the Quiet — but the corporation's search is getting closer, and the community must decide whether to protect one stranger at the risk of exposing the entire safe-house network
  • One of the Quiet's oldest residents dies, and the contents of her bungalow reveal a hidden archive of pre-corporate city records — including documents that prove Axiom's original incorporation was built on forged municipal approvals
  • Kyle needs a place to recover after a job goes wrong. The Quiet takes him in — but the community's rules require him to contribute, which means helping with the mundane maintenance that keeps the bungalows standing. It's the most human work he's done in years.

  • Community arborists tending the last real urban tree canopy in northwest Meridian

  • Nobody else — and the Quiet prefers it that way

O'Hare Sovereign #

type place
name O'Hare Sovereign
aliases
  • O'Hare
  • The Port
  • O'Hare Free Zone
  • The Runway
description O'Hare Sovereign is the hole in the map. When corporate sovereignty claims carved Meridian 88 into jurisdictional territories, the airport was the first piece claimed and the most completely transformed. It is no longer an airport in any traditional sense — it is a sovereign logistics zone, a corporate free port, and the single most important physical node in Meridian 88's connection to the outside world. Three corponations share sovereignty over O'Hare's territory in a rare joint-governance arrangement: Helion controls passenger processing and data, Vantage Meridian controls cargo and logistics, and Axiom Industrial controls the aerospace infrastructure itself. The three-way governance creates jurisdictional complexity that would be bureaucratic nightmare if it were not, in fact, the point — the complexity is the product, because complexity creates gaps, and gaps create opportunities for the kind of commerce that thrives in the spaces between rules.

The physical footprint is immense — O'Hare Sovereign occupies more land area than any other single jurisdiction in Meridian 88. The original airport's footprint has expanded outward, consuming the surrounding neighborhoods and replacing residential blocks with logistics infrastructure: automated cargo handling systems, drone launch platforms, VTOL pads, fuel processing facilities, and the Runway — an eight-kilometer strip that can accommodate the suborbital freight carriers that connect Meridian 88 to the global supply chain. The scale is inhuman, designed for machines and cargo rather than people, and the human population that exists within the zone reflects this: workers are temporary, badged, tracked, and discarded when their contracts expire.

The Terminal is where humans interface with the machine. A vast, multi-level processing facility that handles the passengers, refugees, diplomats, corporate transfers, and undocumented travelers who move through O'Hare's gates daily. The upper levels are corporate transit — clean, efficient, surveilled, and expensive. The lower levels are general processing — crowded, slow, invasive, and designed to extract maximum data from every person who passes through. Below general processing, there are levels that do not appear on any public directory — the transit detention facilities where people whose documentation does not satisfy the three-way jurisdictional requirements are held in a legal limbo that can last days, weeks, or indefinitely.

The free-port economy is O'Hare Sovereign's true purpose. Cargo that enters the zone is subject to the governance of whichever corponation processes it, which means that by routing goods through the right jurisdictional channel, importers can subject their cargo to whichever regulatory framework is most permissive. Weapons that are prohibited in Helion territory can be processed through Axiom's jurisdiction. Data that Vantage restricts can be routed through Helion's processing. Biological materials that all three nominally prohibit somehow find their way through the gaps between their overlapping authorities. The free port is not lawless — it is over-lawed, with three competing legal systems creating a regulatory labyrinth that only specialists can navigate, and navigating it is one of the most lucrative professions in Meridian 88.
atmosphere
sights
  • The Runway — eight kilometers of landing strip lit by approach lighting that is visible from orbit
  • Automated cargo systems moving containers with inhuman precision, twenty-four hours without pause
  • The Terminal's layered architecture — corporate transit gleaming above, general processing grinding below
  • Suborbital freight carriers descending on approach — massive, loud, trailing heat signatures visible for kilometers
  • Badge-tracked workers moving in shift patterns, color-coded by corponation jurisdiction
  • VTOL pads launching in sequence, the staccato rhythm of logistics in motion
sounds
  • Engine noise — constant, layered, ranging from the deep rumble of freight carriers to the high whine of VTOL systems
  • The Terminal's public address system announcing in twelve languages, the same information in different jurisdictional contexts
  • Automated cargo handling — the mechanical percussion of containers being sorted, scanned, and routed
  • The particular silence of the transit detention levels, insulated by design
  • Security checkpoint tones — badge verification, access granted, access denied, repeated thousands of times per hour
smells
  • Aviation fuel — the chemical baseline of every breath in the zone
  • Recycled air in the Terminal, processed to different quality standards by level
  • Cargo holds opened in processing — the mixed scents of goods from every origin point on the planet
  • Ozone and overheated electronics from the automated systems
  • The detention levels smell like disinfectant and fear — a combination that is universal across holding facilities
feel Overwhelming and dehumanizing. O'Hare Sovereign operates at a scale that reduces people to cargo — processed, sorted, routed, and valued by throughput rather than identity. The three-way jurisdiction creates a permanent sense of uncertainty about which rules apply, which makes the zone simultaneously the freest and most controlled space in Meridian 88. Power here is not about authority — it is about knowing which authority to invoke.
tags —
demographics Transient worker population of approximately 40,000-60,000, badge-tracked and jurisdiction-assigned. Permanent residents effectively zero — the zone is not designed for habitation. Transit population varies between 100,000-200,000 on any given day. The detention levels hold an undisclosed number of people in jurisdictional limbo.
economy The free-port economy is Meridian 88's primary interface with the global supply chain. Revenue is split between the three sovereign corponations according to processing jurisdiction. The regulatory arbitrage industry — specialists who route cargo and people through optimal jurisdictional channels — generates billions annually. The underground economy within the zone focuses on transit services, document fabrication, and the movement of goods and people through jurisdictional gaps.
power structure Three-way corporate sovereignty: Helion (passenger and data), Vantage Meridian (cargo and logistics), Axiom Industrial (aerospace infrastructure). A joint coordination body called the Triad Commission manages inter-jurisdictional disputes, but in practice each corponation governs its domain independently. Security is provided by each corponation within its jurisdiction, creating overlapping patrols with different rules of engagement. The gaps between jurisdictions are where the real power operates — the fixers, brokers, and regulatory arbitrage specialists who know how to move through the seams.
dangers
  • Three overlapping security jurisdictions with different rules of engagement — crossing the wrong line can trigger an incident with no clear resolution authority
  • Transit detention — being flagged by any of the three jurisdictions can result in indefinite holding without recourse
  • The free-port economy attracts the full spectrum of organized criminal enterprise, operating behind regulatory arbitrage cover
  • Badge tracking means total surveillance within the zone — every movement logged by at least one jurisdiction
  • Suborbital freight operations create physical danger zones where ground-level humans are not expected to survive
  • Document seizure — the three jurisdictions do not share data, which means travel documents valid in one zone may be flagged in another
opportunities
  • O'Hare Sovereign is the only way in or out of Meridian 88 for most people — controlling access to transit is enormously valuable
  • Regulatory arbitrage skills are among the most lucrative in the corridor — knowing the three jurisdictions is a career
  • The jurisdictional gaps create space for moving goods and people that cannot be moved through any single corporate system
  • The transit population includes people from everywhere — O'Hare is the best place in Meridian 88 for global intelligence
  • The Triad Commission's inter-jurisdictional disputes create leverage opportunities for anyone with information about corporate wrongdoing in the zone
story hooks
  • A person is being held in transit detention who should not exist — their biometric data matches someone who died in corporate records three years ago, and all three jurisdictions are claiming authority over the case while secretly trying to acquire the detainee for different reasons. Someone needs to extract them before any of the three corponations succeeds.
  • A cargo container routed through Axiom's jurisdiction has been flagged by Helion's data systems as containing biological material that violates all three sovereignty codes. The container is sitting on a processing pad, and the clock is ticking before Axiom's automated systems route it to its destination. The contents could be evidence of corporate bioweapons research — or it could be a Helion false-flag operation designed to trigger a Triad Commission investigation that weakens Axiom's position.
  • A regulatory arbitrage specialist has disappeared inside the zone — last badged entering Vantage's cargo jurisdiction and never badged out. Their client list includes some of the most sensitive operations in the free port. Whoever finds them first controls a significant amount of leverage over multiple powerful interests.

Old Harbor #

type place
name Old Harbor
aliases
  • The Drowned District
  • The Deep
  • Below
  • The Forgotten
description Old Harbor is what Meridian was built to replace and couldn't quite bury. When the sea wall failed in Year 8 — a catastrophic breach that Axiom's own engineering reports had predicted and Axiom's own budget committee had declined to prevent — the lowest sections of the original city flooded permanently. The water came in and never left. What remains is a partially submerged urban landscape: buildings standing in two meters of water, their ground floors drowned and their upper stories colonized by the people nobody else would take. Streets have become canals. Rooftops have become docks. The city gave up on Old Harbor twenty years ago, and Old Harbor returned the favor.

It's beautiful, in the way ruins are always beautiful when nature starts winning. Bioluminescent algae — an engineered strain that escaped from a corporate lab years ago — coats the waterline, turning the flooded streets into rivers of soft blue-green light after dark. Flooded temples and churches rise from the water like stone ghosts, their interiors visible through broken windows, pews floating in lazy circles. Makeshift bridges connect the upper stories of buildings, creating an elevated network of walkways that constitutes Old Harbor's actual street grid. Below, in the water, there are things — salvage, secrets, and according to some residents, the preserved remains of the original city's data infrastructure, still humming away on waterproofed servers nobody has found yet.

Kael grew up here. He arrived as a refugee child in one of the waves of climate displaced people who washed up in Meridian with nothing and were pointed downward. Old Harbor taught him two things: how to survive when no one is coming to help you, and that beauty doesn't require permission. He left when he was old enough to climb to the Shelf, but Old Harbor is still in him — in the way he moves through water, in his comfort with darkness, in his refusal to trust any structure that someone with money built.
atmosphere
sights
  • Partially submerged buildings, their lower floors underwater, upper floors alive with squatter communities
  • Bioluminescent algae painting the waterline in shifting blue-green light
  • Makeshift bridges connecting rooftops and upper stories — wood, metal, cable, whatever works
  • Flooded temples and churches, eerily beautiful, candles still burning on upper altars
  • Small boats and rafts navigating the canal-streets — the only transit that works here
  • Murals painted on exposed walls above the waterline — art that nobody commissioned and everybody sees
  • The sky, fully visible — Old Harbor has no roof, no upper tiers, just open air and weather
  • Salvage divers disappearing beneath the surface, headlamps visible underwater like deep-sea creatures
sounds
  • Water — lapping, dripping, flowing. The constant soundtrack of a drowned place.
  • Boat motors — small, electric, humming across the canals
  • Birdsong — real birds, not the synthetic kind. Old Harbor has the best bird population in Meridian.
  • The creak of makeshift bridges under foot traffic
  • Silence — more of it here than anywhere else in the city. Old Harbor is quiet in a way that can be peaceful or menacing.
  • Distant thunder — real weather, not AtmoSync. Old Harbor gets the storms the system can't be bothered to redirect.
  • Children singing — there are kids here too, and they sing while they paddle.
smells
  • Salt water and algae — the base note of everything
  • Wet concrete and rusted metal — the smell of infrastructure returning to the sea
  • Cooking fires on rooftop platforms — fish, mostly, caught from the harbor itself
  • Rain — real rain, not corporate rain, and it smells different, wilder
  • Rot, sometimes — the water brings things up and the sun breaks them down
  • Bioluminescent algae has its own smell — faintly sweet, faintly chemical, like a memory of a lab
feel Haunted. Not with ghosts, but with the awareness that a city used to stand here and was allowed to drown. Old Harbor feels like grief that's grown moss — it's still sad, but it's also alive in ways the rest of Meridian isn't. There's a freedom here that comes from total abandonment: no surveillance, no corporate branding, no one telling you what the weather should be. It's dangerous and beautiful and completely honest, which makes it the opposite of everything above.
tags —
demographics ~200,000 (nobody counts — there is no census, no registry, no records). The invisible. Refugees, outcasts, the undocumented, the deliberately disappeared.
economy Salvage operations — the drowned city contains pre-collapse technology, data archives, and infrastructure that's worth a fortune to the right buyer. Smuggling routes run through Old Harbor's waterways into and out of the city entirely.
power structure No formal governance. Community elders and territorial groups enforce unwritten rules. Axiom Security doesn't come here — there's nothing to optimize.
dangers
  • Drowning — the water is everywhere and not all of it is shallow
  • Structural collapse — waterlogged buildings fail without warning
  • No emergency services — if you get hurt here, you'd better know someone
  • Territorial disputes — some zones are claimed by groups who don't welcome visitors
  • The water itself — contaminated with industrial runoff, old chemicals, and things nobody's tested for
  • Predators — not the human kind. The harbor ecosystem has adapted, and some of what swims here has teeth.
  • Getting lost — the canal-streets don't match any surviving map
  • Storms — real weather hits hard when there's no AtmoSync to soften it
opportunities
  • Disappearance — Old Harbor is the best place in Meridian to stop existing
  • Salvage — pre-collapse tech pulled from submerged ruins can be worth a fortune
  • Freedom — no surveillance, no corporate rules, no access credentials required
  • Community — Old Harbor's residents are tight-knit and help those who earn trust
  • History — the drowned city remembers things the new one wants forgotten
  • Beauty — if you need to remember what the sky looks like, come here
story hooks
  • Kael's childhood — the refugee camp where he grew up, now a permanent community
  • The submerged data centers — pre-collapse records that could shake the foundations of Axiom's legitimacy
  • A salvage diver who found something down there that someone upstairs wants recovered — or destroyed
  • The community elder who remembers the original city and tells stories the corps would rather forget
  • Old Harbor as sanctuary — when Kael needs to disappear, this is where he comes home to
  • The bioluminescent algae — engineered, escaped, and now evolving. It might be developing rudimentary intelligence. The corps don't know. The divers suspect.

Omro Relay #

type place
name Omro Relay
aliases
  • Omro
  • The Relay
  • Pipe Town
  • Nexus Runoff
description Omro died the way most Fox River towns died — not with a bang but with a purchase order. When the Fox Cities Nexus began its second expansion phase in 2161, Cinderblock AI and Saltmarsh Telecom needed coolant infrastructure that the Nexus proper couldn't support. The Fox River, already chemically lobotomized by a century of paper mill runoff, turned out to be the perfect thermal sink for secondary data processing nodes. Omro's 3,500 residents were offered relocation packages by Cinderblock's legal team — packages that were technically voluntary in the same way that breathing is technically optional. By 2165, the town had been converted into a coolant relay station: massive heat exchangers lining both banks of the Fox, connected by buried fiber to the Nexus twenty kilometers east. The original town grid still exists beneath the infrastructure, like bones under chrome.

The town came back, in a way. Not as a town — as a parasite on the infrastructure it had been replaced by. Relay technicians needed housing. Housing attracted food vendors. Food vendors attracted people who couldn't afford the Nexus. Within a decade, Omro Relay had a population of twelve thousand, most of them Tier 1 and Tier 2 coolant workers, data janitors, and the families they'd dragged west from Meridian hoping the air would be better. The air is not better. The heat exchangers pump thermal waste into the atmosphere twenty-four hours a day, creating a permanent microclimate — Omro Relay is eight degrees warmer than surrounding terrain year-round, and the humidity makes your skin feel like it's wearing a second skin. In winter, the town steams. Locals call it living inside a mouth.

But the data pipes are here, and where data pipes go, gray market follows. Omro Relay has become the Fox Cities Nexus's unofficial back door — a place where Collective-affiliated data miners tap the fiber lines, where unlicensed technicians sell Nexus processing time to anyone with Quanta, and where Saltmarsh Signal Guard patrols end at the town boundary because the jurisdictional agreements were written by lawyers who assumed nobody would ever want to live here. The town's economy runs on two things: legitimate coolant maintenance for Cinderblock, and illegitimate everything else for everyone who needs Nexus access without Nexus surveillance. It's a company town that learned to pick the company's pockets.
atmosphere
sights
  • Massive heat exchanger arrays lining the Fox River, venting steam clouds that never fully dissipate
  • Fiber optic conduits thick as tree trunks running along every street, pulsing with data traffic visible through diagnostic panels
  • Makeshift housing built between and on top of coolant infrastructure — shanties welded to relay housings
  • The Fox River glowing faintly at night from thermal waste, a sickly amber ribbon cutting through the steam
  • Cinderblock AI maintenance drones moving in silent formation overhead, ignoring the human settlement beneath them
sounds
  • The constant bass thrum of heat exchangers cycling — felt in the chest more than heard
  • Coolant pumps surging on irregular schedules, the town's mechanical heartbeat
  • Data traffic hum from the fiber conduits — technicians claim they can hear bandwidth fluctuations
  • Steam venting from pressure relief valves, sudden hisses that punctuate every conversation
  • The Fox River, flowing warmer than it should, making sounds water shouldn't make
smells
  • Hot metal and coolant fluid — the permanent baseline smell of Omro Relay
  • The Fox River's chemical-organic stew, heated to emphasize its worst notes
  • Ozone from data processing equipment bleeding through imperfect seals
  • Cooking smells from food stalls — aggressive spices fighting the industrial baseline
feel Oppressively warm and humid year-round, like the inside of a machine that's running too hot. The air feels thick, heavy, used. There's an energy to the place despite the discomfort — the energy of people who've figured out how to survive in a space that wasn't designed for survival, extracting value from infrastructure that was never meant to benefit them.
tags —
demographics Approximately 12,000 residents, predominantly Tier 1 and Tier 2. A mix of coolant relay technicians, data janitors, gray-market operators, and climate refugees who migrated west from the denser Nexus zones. Small but growing Collective presence among the technically literate population.
economy Legitimate: coolant system maintenance contracts from Cinderblock AI, with some Saltmarsh signal relay work. Illegitimate: gray-market Nexus processing time resale, data tapping, unlicensed tech repair, and a thriving trade in salvaged Cinderblock components that 'fell off the relay.'
power structure Cinderblock AI owns the infrastructure and employs about 30% of the workforce directly. A relay station supervisor named the Town Manager handles day-to-day logistics, but actual power belongs to whoever controls access to the fiber taps. Currently that's a loose consortium of Collective-affiliated technicians who call themselves the Siphon.
dangers
  • Heat exposure — the microclimate causes chronic health issues, and coolant system failures can create lethal thermal events
  • Cinderblock AI crackdowns — periodic sweeps to find and seal unauthorized fiber taps, with collateral damage to the surrounding settlement
  • Toxic river contact — the Fox River's chemical load is concentrated by thermal processing, and the riverbank is not a safe place to be
  • Jurisdictional void — Omro Relay exists in a gap between Cinderblock sovereign territory and whatever remains of county governance, meaning nobody is coming to help
  • Signal Guard overreach — Saltmarsh occasionally extends DEADBAND protocols into Omro to flush unauthorized transmissions, blacking out the entire town
opportunities
  • Nexus back door — access to Fox Cities Nexus processing power without Nexus-level surveillance, if you know the right people
  • Salvage economy — decommissioned Cinderblock components have significant resale value in the Circuit and other gray markets
  • Recruitment ground — skilled technicians who maintain the relay are in demand by every faction that needs infrastructure expertise
  • Information laundering — data routed through Omro Relay's tapped lines can be anonymized before reaching its destination
story hooks
  • The Siphon discovers anomalous traffic in the fiber lines — something is being routed through Omro Relay that Cinderblock's own systems don't seem to know about, and it's coming from the direction of the Nexus
  • A coolant system failure threatens to cook the entire settlement, and the Cinderblock maintenance AI won't authorize repairs because the affected infrastructure is 'non-essential' — meaning the human habitation built around it
  • Someone is buying up gray-market Nexus processing time in bulk through Omro Relay, and the volume suggests they're building something that requires more computational power than most corponations possess

  • Collective data miners exploiting the fiber taps for intelligence gathering
  • Gray-market tech brokers buying and selling Nexus processing time
  • Fox Cities Nexus workers who can't afford Nexus housing and commute from the margins

Pale Harbor Anchorage #

type place
name Pale Harbor Anchorage
aliases
  • The Float
  • Pale Harbor
  • The Anchorage
  • Whitecap
description Three kilometers off the Chicago shoreline, sixty-odd vessels of wildly mismatched origin have been lashed, welded, and bridged into a floating settlement that the city does not officially recognize and Ferrogate Security has chosen not to pursue — the jurisdictional ambiguity of open Lake Michigan water being a bureaucratic problem nobody has budgeted to resolve. The Anchorage began in the 2160s as a handful of decommissioned Carrion Logistics barges used as overflow housing during a Shelf overcrowding crisis. It is now home to nearly four thousand people.

The vessels range from rusted bulk freighters converted into vertical housing stacks, to sleek stolen pleasure craft that serve as the settlement's administrative core, to a half-submerged Ringo Heavy Industries ore carrier whose flooded lower decks have been colonized by hydroponic operators growing protein algae and modified freshwater kelp. Bridges between ships are improvised: cargo net walkways, salvaged gangplanks, welded steel catwalks that flex visibly in high wind.

The Anchorage sits in a legal gray zone that attracts people who need distance from the shore: debt-fugitives, ELF sympathizers, unlicensed biotech researchers, and a growing population of synthetic persons who have found that Meridian 88's civil rights ordinances technically extend to international waters, though enforcement of those rights is another matter entirely.
atmosphere
sights
  • The settlement's silhouette at dusk is a jagged skyline of mismatched hulls, antenna clusters, and the soft glow of solar-charged LED strings running between masts.
  • Children navigate the cargo net bridges between ships with practiced ease, ignoring the thirty-meter drop to the lake below.
  • The ore carrier's flooded mid-decks are visible through porthole grilles — green-lit tanks of algae casting bioluminescent light upward through the water.
  • Weather-worn flags of no recognizable nation fly from every high point, a tradition whose origin nobody aboard can fully explain.
sounds
  • The settlement groans and shifts as a collective entity when lake swells pass beneath it, metal speaking to metal in low complaint.
  • Wind off the lake is constant and directional, carrying cooking smells and arguments from the residential barges to the quieter admin vessels.
  • A community radio station broadcasting from the pleasure craft hub plays continuous music, audible across most of the settlement at low volume.
smells
  • Lake water and algae are the baseline — clean and cold and faintly vegetable.
  • Cooking smoke from improvised exhaust stacks on the residential barges carries fish, synthetic meat, and spiced grain.
  • Diesel and machine oil linger near the generator barges on the settlement's windward edge.
feel The Anchorage moves. Not dramatically, but constantly — a slow flex and sway that residents call 'the breath' and newcomers find quietly destabilizing. There is a frontier self-sufficiency to life here that coexists with genuine community warmth, but the lake's moods are not negotiable and the settlement's infrastructure is never more than one bad storm from a crisis.
tags —
demographics Approximately four thousand permanent residents, majority Tier 3 and Tier 4, with a notable synthetic population of several hundred who represent a higher proportion of community leadership than in most shore-side settlements. Crew lineages from Carrion Logistics, Ringo Heavy Industries, and independent Great Lakes shipping form the settlement's founding families.
economy The Anchorage earns Φ through algae and kelp sales to shore-side distributors, unlicensed data hosting on servers kept deliberately off the Diaspora's indexed nodes, and discrete ferry services for people who need to travel without logging a transit record.
power structure A Ship Council of twelve vessel captains — each representing a major hull — makes collective decisions by consensus, with the captain of the central pleasure craft hub holding a traditional casting vote in deadlocks; the synthetic community has two non-voting advisory seats, a compromise that remains a source of ongoing tension.
dangers
  • Lake Michigan storm seasons regularly damage bridge connections between vessels, isolating sections of the settlement for days at a time.
  • Axiom Industries has filed three separate jurisdictional claims on the anchorage site, each quietly stalled but never fully dismissed.
  • Pirates operating reconditioned speedboats have targeted the settlement's supply barges twice in the past year, and the council's defensive capabilities are improvised at best.
  • The ore carrier's structural integrity is a known issue — the engineering team's estimates on hull lifespan vary between five and twenty years, and the council has not yet decided what to do about either estimate.
opportunities
  • The Anchorage's off-index data servers offer genuinely private hosting for Φ rates significantly below any shore-side competitor.
  • The algae operation on the ore carrier is quietly developing modified strains with pharmaceutical applications — the lead researcher is looking for outside funding and discretion in equal measure.
  • The settlement's ferry network provides unlogged transit between the Anchorage and three separate shore points, a service with obvious value to anyone who needs to move without Ferrogate documentation.
story hooks
  • A Zheng-Dao Bioelectric research vessel has been circling the Anchorage at a consistent two-kilometer distance for six days, running no lights after dark and responding to no hails. The Ship Council is divided between those who want to send a boarding party and those who believe that doing so will give Zheng-Dao exactly the provocation they need.
  • One of the synthetic council advisors, a former Tessera Corporation logistics AI named Fenwick, has begun transmitting on a frequency that other synthetic residents describe as distress-adjacent — but when asked, Fenwick insists everything is fine, with a consistency that is itself alarming.
  • The community radio station played eighteen minutes of dead air last night at 0300, followed by a single sentence repeated four times in a voice nobody aboard recognizes, describing coordinates in the middle of the lake. Three separate residents recorded it. None of them have told the others.
