Riverbottom #

type place
name Riverbottom
aliases
  • Riverdale
  • The Pit
  • Altgeld
  • Ground Floor
description Riverbottom is the lowest point in Meridian 88 that isn't underwater. That distinction matters here more than anywhere else, because the water is always coming. The district sits at the absolute southern terminus of the megacity, where the engineered drainage systems that protect the Meridian Core and the Shelf thin out to nothing. When the lake surges or the spring melt overwhelms the pumping stations, Riverbottom floods first and drains last. The old Altgeld Gardens public housing blocks -- themselves a monument to decades of environmental racism in pre-Meridian Chicago -- were rebuilt as Meridian Residential Block South-9, a name so deliberately forgettable it amounts to erasure. The new blocks are identical modular stacks, six stories of poured composite with neural-compatible wiring and nothing else. No common spaces. No green areas. No pretense.

The environmental justice concerns that defined old Riverdale didn't go away when the neighborhood got a new name. They got a corporate rebrand. Three waste processing facilities ring the district, handling chemical reclamation for the southern industrial zone. The air quality index in Riverbottom regularly exceeds Meridian safety thresholds by 200%, but the thresholds are advisory, not mandatory, and advisories don't apply below Tier 3. Residents have filed 14,000 environmental complaints through the Meridian civic interface in the past decade. The system logs them, categorizes them, and routes them to a processing queue that has never, in its operational history, produced a response.

But Riverbottom endures, the way things endure at the bottom of gravity wells -- not by climbing out but by becoming so dense that nothing can compress them further. The community organizing tradition that existed in Altgeld Gardens survived the transition to Meridian, adapted, and hardened. Block councils operate with military discipline, coordinating flood response, air filtration maintenance, and the distribution of smuggled medical supplies for the respiratory conditions the waste plants cause and the corporate health system doesn't cover. There is a saying in Riverbottom: the water rises, and so do we. It's painted on the side of Block South-9 in letters three stories tall. Nobody has tried to remove it.
atmosphere
sights
  • Identical modular housing stacks stretching in grid formation, brutalist and unadorned
  • Waste processing facility smokestacks rimming the horizon, exhaust plumes lit amber at night
  • High-water marks stained on building walls at varying heights -- a flood history written in grime
  • Community murals on Block South-9 -- defiant, colorful, repainted after every flood
  • Makeshift levee barriers stored on every block, ready for deployment
sounds
  • The constant industrial drone of waste processing -- a low frequency hum felt in the chest
  • Pumping station machinery cycling on and off, the sound of borrowed time
  • Block council alert sirens -- three tones: flood warning, air quality alert, all clear
  • Children coughing -- the sound Riverbottom can't escape
smells
  • Chemical processing byproduct -- metallic, acrid, and inescapable on bad air days
  • Standing water from the last flood event that hasn't fully drained
  • Bleach and industrial cleaner from the constant post-flood remediation
  • Community kitchens cooking with whatever the supply chain delivered this week
feel Compressed. Riverbottom feels like a place that has been pushed down so many times it has become structurally incapable of surprise. The anger here isn't hot -- it's geological. Layers of grievance compressed into something harder than the composite walls. People don't hope for rescue. They organize for survival.
tags —
demographics Overwhelmingly Tier 1 and untier-ed residents. The legacy Black community from Altgeld Gardens persists alongside environmental refugees and workers displaced from shuttered southern industrial operations. Population approximately 35,000, though flooding events cause periodic displacement.
economy Waste processing plant employment, block council mutual aid systems, and a surprisingly sophisticated gray market in air filtration components. Some residents earn supplemental income as flood remediation specialists -- skills learned from necessity, marketed to wealthier districts that flood less often.
power structure The waste processing facilities are operated by Axiom Environmental Services under sovereign industrial charter, making them functionally immune to local complaint. Block councils hold real authority within the residential stacks, operating as the only functional governance Riverbottom has ever known.
dangers
  • Flooding -- chronic, recurring, and worsening as climate infrastructure degrades
  • Toxic air quality from the waste processing ring -- respiratory illness rates are four times the Meridian average
  • Infrastructure collapse during flood events -- the modular blocks weren't built for water exposure
  • Axiom Environmental Security patrols protecting plant perimeters with escalation-of-force protocols
  • Despair -- the most dangerous thing in Riverbottom is the rational conclusion that nothing will change
opportunities
  • Block council networks are the tightest community infrastructure in southern Meridian -- trust is real here
  • Environmental data from Riverbottom could be devastating if it reached the right journalist or activist
  • Flood remediation expertise is genuinely valuable and in demand across the city
  • The waste plants process materials that occasionally include salvageable tech and rare elements
story hooks
  • A block council leader has been compiling environmental health data for twenty years and is ready to release it -- but the last three people who tried to whistleblow on Axiom Environmental are dead or missing
  • The flood patterns are changing in ways the pumping station data doesn't explain -- someone is diverting drainage capacity away from Riverbottom deliberately
  • Underneath Block South-9, the original Altgeld Gardens foundation contains a sealed community archive from the pre-Meridian environmental justice movement

Rogers Reef #

type place
name Rogers Reef
aliases
  • Rogers Park
  • The Reef
  • Roj-Par
  • The Drowning Mosaic
description Rogers Reef is what happens when the lake decides to take back what the city borrowed. The northernmost edge of Meridian 88's lakefront, once a haven of affordable diversity where Jamaican patties shared a block with Ethiopian injera and Polish pierogi, now exists in a state of permanent negotiation with Lake Michigan. The old sea walls here were never corporate-grade — they were municipal leftovers, patched and re-patched by a city government that stopped existing before it could finish the job. The result is a district that floods on a schedule, a twice-monthly tidal incursion the residents call the Rinse. The water comes in knee-deep, fills the ground floors, and recedes twelve hours later, leaving behind silt, debris, and the particular resignation of people who've learned to keep their valuables above waist height.

The multicultural character of old Rogers Park didn't die — it adapted. The Devon corridor food stalls became amphibious, their owners building elevated serving platforms and waterproof storage beneath. The old loyola campus, half-submerged, was claimed by a loose collective of unlicensed educators who run classes in the upper floors during dry periods and distribute lesson packets on waterproof tablets when the Rinse is in. The lakefront itself has become a reef in the literal sense: decades of flooded infrastructure have created an artificial ecosystem where engineered coral clings to rusted CTA rail supports and fish schools navigate the submerged remains of Sheridan Road. Divers harvest the reef for biotech compounds that the pharmaceutical corps will pay handsomely for, no questions asked.

What makes Rogers Reef unique in Meridian is its stubborn cosmopolitanism. In a city that sorts people by tier and function, the Reef sorts by nothing. Tier 1 climate refugees from the Gulf share walkways with Tier 2 biotech harvesters and untier-ed families who've been here since before the floods. Six languages are spoken on any given block. Three different religious communities maintain temples on the upper floors of the same building, sharing a single generator and arguing about the electricity schedule with the kind of intensity that only neighbors who actually depend on each other can muster. The Reef doesn't have diversity as an aspiration. It has diversity as a survival strategy.

Axiom has designated Rogers Reef as a Managed Decline Zone, which means they've stopped maintaining infrastructure but haven't bothered to formally abandon it. This limbo status gives the Reef a peculiar freedom: corporate security doesn't patrol here because there's nothing to protect, but the district isn't lawless enough to attract the kind of attention that triggers a crackdown. It exists in the gap — too flooded to gentrify, too alive to demolish, too complicated to categorize. Kyle passes through occasionally, buying reef-harvested biotech for his medical kit and eating jerk chicken from a woman named Mrs. Adebayo who remembers when Sheridan Road had cars on it.
atmosphere
sights
  • Ground floors filled with murky lake water during the Rinse, residents wading through on elevated walkway planks
  • Engineered coral formations growing on rusted CTA rail supports, visible through translucent shallows
  • Food stalls on elevated platforms — hand-painted signs in Amharic, Spanish, Urdu, Polish, and Shelf Cant
  • The half-submerged Loyola campus, upper windows glowing with makeshift classroom light
  • Fishing nets strung between buildings, drying in the lake wind
  • Bioluminescent algae creeping north from Old Harbor, painting the waterline in pale green during floods
sounds
  • Water — always water. Lapping against foundations, dripping from eaves, sloshing under foot traffic
  • Multilingual haggling at the elevated market stalls, three conversations overlapping in different languages
  • The groan of waterlogged building foundations settling after the Rinse recedes
  • Call to prayer from the third-floor mosque mixing with hymns from the fourth-floor church next door
  • Dive boats putting out at dawn, small electric motors humming across the flooded streets
  • Children splashing — they treat the Rinse as a swimming pool, which terrifies their parents
smells
  • Lake brine and wet concrete — the permanent base note
  • Spices from six continents drifting from the elevated food stalls
  • The chemical-sweet smell of engineered coral when the tide is low
  • Mildew in the lower floors, a smell the Reef's residents have stopped noticing
  • Fresh fish being gutted and cleaned on rooftop platforms
feel Exhausting and beautiful. Rogers Reef demands constant adaptation — you have to time your movements to the flood schedule, keep your gear elevated, maintain relationships with neighbors who speak different languages and worship different gods. But there's a warmth to it that comes from mutual dependence. The Reef is a community that floods together and dries out together, and that shared rhythm creates something that the perfectly climate-controlled tiers above can never replicate.
tags —
demographics Approximately 25,000 residents in a rotating population that swells during dry periods. Predominantly Tier 1 and untier-ed, with a significant population of climate refugees and first-generation immigrants. The most ethnically diverse district in northern Meridian — over forty languages documented in the last informal census.
economy Reef biotech harvesting, informal food economy, unlicensed education services, and salvage diving. Mrs. Adebayo's jerk chicken alone probably constitutes a measurable percentage of the local GDP.
power structure No single authority. A loose council of community elders from the major ethnic groups meets irregularly to resolve disputes and coordinate flood response. The Reef Divers Guild controls access to the most profitable harvesting sites and functions as the closest thing to an organized power bloc.
dangers
  • The Rinse — twice-monthly flooding that can trap the unprepared in lower floors
  • Structural collapse from water damage — buildings here have been soaking for decades
  • Reef predators — the artificial ecosystem includes things with teeth that weren't in the original design
  • Contaminated water during heavy floods — industrial runoff from upshore mixing with lake water
  • Isolation during storms — the Reef can become unreachable when weather overwhelms the makeshift infrastructure
  • Biotech poachers from corporate labs who don't ask permission and don't leave witnesses
opportunities
  • Reef-harvested biotech compounds — pharmaceutical corps pay premium prices, no questions asked
  • Cultural exchange — the Reef's diversity means access to knowledge, skills, and networks from across the globe
  • Anonymity — Axiom's Managed Decline designation means minimal surveillance
  • The Loyola collective's education services — free, unlicensed, and genuinely excellent
  • A community that actually functions as a community — trust networks that money can't buy
story hooks
  • A reef diver discovers something growing in the submerged infrastructure that isn't coral and isn't natural — it responds to neural interface signals
  • The Loyola collective intercepts a corporate communication suggesting the Managed Decline designation is about to be upgraded to Active Reclamation — which means eviction for 25,000 people
  • Mrs. Adebayo's food stall is a dead drop for information moving between Old Harbor and the northern districts — she's been doing it for twenty years and nobody knows

Roseland Drift #

type place
name Roseland Drift
aliases
  • Roseland
  • The Drift
  • Dutchtown
  • The Long Block
description Roseland Drift stretches across the far South Side like a scar that won't close. The original Roseland was vast — one of Chicago's largest community areas, first settled by Dutch immigrants who built a planned residential community and named it for the roses they planted along the main boulevard. Over the decades it became a predominantly African American neighborhood, carrying forward the community infrastructure the Dutch had established while making it something entirely new. The roses are gone now. The boulevard is cracked. What remains is the scale — Roseland Drift is still enormous, and its size is both its defining characteristic and its central problem.

Axiom's governance model works best in concentrated districts where surveillance infrastructure can be amortized across dense populations. Roseland Drift is the opposite: sprawling, low-density, with long residential blocks that stretch between service points like distances between oases. Axiom looked at the cost-per-resident of maintaining tier services across this much geography and decided, in the quiet language of budget allocation, that the math didn't work. The result is a district that is technically governed and practically abandoned — tier services exist on paper, infrastructure maintenance follows a schedule that is always running behind, and emergency response times are measured in hours rather than minutes. The residents of Roseland Drift call this the drift: the slow, steady movement away from any system that was supposed to support them.

The community has adapted to the drift by building lateral. Block-level mutual aid networks function as micro-communities, each responsible for its own stretch of street. These networks share resources, coordinate security, and maintain communication through a mix of salvaged tech and human runners who carry messages between blocks. The runners — mostly teenagers, mostly fast, always aware — are the nervous system of a district too large for any single communication infrastructure. They know every shortcut, every safe house, every block captain by name. The runner network is Roseland Drift's most valuable asset, and the runners know it.

The district's far-south position puts it at the edge of Meridian 88's effective boundary. Beyond Roseland Drift, the urban fabric thins into the ungoverned transition zone between Meridian and the remains of the southern suburbs. This borderland position makes the Drift a natural gateway — goods, people, and information moving into and out of Meridian pass through here, and the block networks that manage this traffic have developed a sophistication that rivals any corporate logistics operation. Roseland Drift may be neglected, but it is not irrelevant. It is the back door to the city, and the people who hold the door know exactly what that's worth.
atmosphere
sights
  • Long residential blocks stretching toward a horizon that feels further than it should inside a megacity
  • Runners on foot and bike, moving between blocks with the purposeful speed of people carrying messages that matter
  • Block captain posts — marked houses or storefronts where the local mutual aid network centers operations
  • Axiom service infrastructure in visible states of disrepair — cracked road surfaces, flickering streetlights, deactivated monitoring stations
  • The southern edge where the urban grid begins to dissolve into the ungoverned transition zone
  • Community gardens on vacant lots, large-scale and productive, feeding blocks that the supply chain forgot
sounds
  • Distance — the sound of a neighborhood where the next block is far enough away that you hear the gap between them
  • Runners calling out approach signals — coded, rhythmic, changing daily
  • Block-level activity: generator hum, community radio, children, the sounds of life organized at the smallest functional scale
  • The absence of corporate audio branding — no franchise chimes, no Axiom announcements, just the neighborhood talking to itself
  • Wind across open lots, carrying sounds from blocks away, making the Drift feel even larger than it is
smells
  • Open air with a quality that the denser districts don't have — space has its own smell
  • Community garden soil, composted and maintained, the smell of food security built from scratch
  • Diesel from salvaged generators that keep block networks powered when the grid fails
  • Cooking smoke from block gatherings, visible and aromatic, a social signal as much as a meal
feel Roseland Drift feels like a place that was left behind and decided to keep going anyway. The distances are real — between blocks, between services, between the life this neighborhood was promised and the life it has. But the connections are real too, maintained by runners and block captains and the simple refusal to let distance win. The Drift is lonely and communal at the same time, which shouldn't be possible but is.
tags —
demographics Approximately 50,000 residents across a vast geographic area, making it one of the most sparsely populated districts in the southern corridor. Predominantly Black, predominantly Tier 1-2. The Dutch heritage survives only in street names and building foundations. Young population skews toward the runner networks; aging population anchors the block captain system.
economy Block-level mutual aid and barter. Gateway logistics — managing the flow of goods and people between Meridian and the ungoverned southern transition zone. Runner services are both an internal communication system and a for-hire courier network. Community agriculture on vacant lots produces food that enters the informal economy.
power structure No effective corporate governance despite nominal Axiom jurisdiction. Block captains form a decentralized network that coordinates through runners. No single leader — authority is distributed, local, and earned through service. The runner network operates with its own internal hierarchy and code.
dangers
  • Emergency response is effectively nonexistent — medical emergencies, fires, and security threats are handled by block networks or not at all
  • The gateway position attracts transit traffic that includes people and goods the block networks can't always control
  • Axiom occasionally sweeps through the Drift for tier compliance, rounding up untier-ed residents for processing
  • The ungoverned transition zone to the south bleeds instability northward — armed groups, scavengers, and unknowns
  • Distance between blocks means help is never immediate, and isolation is a constant tactical vulnerability
  • Runners face physical dangers — exhaustion, territorial disputes, and the simple hazard of moving fast through unmaintained infrastructure
opportunities
  • The runner network is the most reliable communication and courier system in the far South Side — hiring runners is hiring competence
  • Gateway logistics offer significant revenue for block networks willing to manage the risk
  • The Drift's vast geography includes abandoned structures suitable for operations that need space and privacy
  • Block captain networks provide ground-truth intelligence that corporate surveillance cannot match
  • The ungoverned transition zone is accessible through the Drift — for those who need to leave Meridian or bring something in
story hooks
  • A runner has gone missing on the route between the Drift's southern edge and the ungoverned zone. The block captains suspect she found something she wasn't supposed to, but the route she was running was supposed to be empty — a routine message to a contact that, it turns out, doesn't exist.
  • Axiom has announced a sweep of the Drift's southern blocks — not the usual tier compliance check, but a full security operation with military-grade support. No explanation has been given. The block captains have seventy-two hours to decide whether to evacuate, resist, or negotiate.
  • Someone has been establishing supply caches across the Drift — food, medical supplies, weapons — in a pattern that the block captains recognize as preparation for sustained operations. Nobody knows who's building the infrastructure or what it's for.

Saginaw Barrens #

type place
name Saginaw Barrens
aliases
  • Bay City / Saginaw MI
  • The Barrens
  • Lumber Ghost
  • Sag-Bay
description The Saginaw River valley was once the lumber capital of the world. Then it was a manufacturing center. Then it was a rust belt cautionary tale. Now it is the Barrens — a sprawling, depopulated urban landscape along the Lake Huron shore where the Saginaw River meets Saginaw Bay. The lumber is gone. The manufacturing is gone. The people are mostly gone. What remains is infrastructure built for 400,000 people occupied by 90,000, and the particular atmosphere of a place that was abandoned not by catastrophe but by the slow withdrawal of economic purpose.

The Saginaw Barrens is what happens when the GLM's economic engine moves on and nobody turns off the lights. The old manufacturing districts along the river have been partially reclaimed by automated recycling operations — Ashgrave Materials runs a sovereignty facility that processes salvage from the abandoned industrial buildings, extracting metals, composites, and construction materials for resale. The operation employs 3,000 people in a city that once employed 150,000 in manufacturing. The math is the message. The residential areas that remain occupied cluster around the recycling facility and the waterfront, where a stubborn community maintains services, schools, and something resembling civic life through a combination of mutual aid and refusal to leave.

Saginaw Bay itself has become an automated aquaculture zone — Ironclad Agrisystems operates protein farming platforms across the shallow bay, producing synthetic fish and kelp-based nutrients for the GLM's lower-tier food supply. The platforms are visible from shore, geometric grids of floating infrastructure that produce food without requiring the presence of the people who eat it. The bay's natural fishery is gone — the water chemistry won't support it — but the aquaculture platforms thrive in conditions that killed the original ecosystem. The irony writes itself. The Barrens is a place where the future arrived, found the present lacking, and automated the replacement.
atmosphere
sights
  • Abandoned manufacturing buildings stretching along the Saginaw River — roofless, windowless, being slowly dismantled by Ashgrave recycling drones
  • Aquaculture platforms on Saginaw Bay, geometric and precise, producing food in water that can't support natural life
  • Occupied residential blocks surrounded by empty ones — islands of habitation in a sea of vacancy
  • The Saginaw River carrying recycling runoff to the bay — water the color of rust and progress
  • Deer and coyotes in the abandoned districts — nature reclaiming what the economy released
sounds
  • Ashgrave recycling drones dismantling buildings — the sound of a city being converted into raw materials
  • Wind through empty structures — the Barrens generates its own weather sounds, and they sound like loneliness
  • Aquaculture platform machinery on the bay — mechanical, rhythmic, and audible from the shore on quiet nights
  • The occupied districts' community sounds — children, conversation, music — concentrated and defiant
smells
  • Industrial rust and recycling chemical residue — the scent of buildings being reduced to components
  • Saginaw Bay aquaculture — a synthetic marine smell, close to fish but chemically wrong
  • Vegetation growing through concrete in the abandoned districts — earth reclaiming human ambition
feel A place that is both ending and persisting simultaneously. The Barrens is not dead — 90,000 people live here, work here, raise children here — but it is dying around them, and they know it. The atmosphere is not despair. It is something more complex: the knowledge that your home is being recycled, and the decision to stay anyway.
tags —
demographics Population 90,000, down from 300,000 a generation ago and 400,000 at the manufacturing peak. The remaining population is overwhelmingly Tier 1 — the people who couldn't afford to leave, or who chose not to. Median age is rising. Community cohesion is high — shared adversity does that. The excluded don't come to the Barrens; there's nothing to be excluded from.
economy Recycling and salvage (Ashgrave Materials) and automated aquaculture (Ironclad Agrisystems). The two operations account for 80% of formal employment. The remaining 20% is community economy — services, small-scale agriculture, and the barter networks that develop when formal currency becomes scarce. The Barrens produces raw materials and food for the GLM and receives almost nothing in return.
power structure Ashgrave Materials and Ironclad Agrisystems hold sovereignty over their respective operations. Michigan municipal government maintains jurisdiction over the residential areas, but with a tax base of 90,000 in infrastructure built for 400,000, governance is triage. A community council — elected informally, recognized reluctantly by the municipal government — handles the day-to-day decisions that keep the occupied districts functioning.
dangers
  • Structural collapse in the abandoned districts — the buildings are being recycled, but not fast enough to prevent random failure
  • Ashgrave recycling operations encroaching on occupied residential areas — the drones don't always distinguish between abandoned and inhabited
  • Aquaculture chemical runoff in Saginaw Bay — the platforms produce food and contamination in equal measure
  • Isolation — the Barrens is low-priority for emergency services, supply deliveries, and anyone else's attention
  • Economic death spiral — the population is too small to sustain services, and the lack of services drives the population smaller
opportunities
  • Cheap real estate — the abandoned districts contain buildings, infrastructure, and space that can be acquired for almost nothing
  • Salvage — Ashgrave doesn't process everything, and what they leave behind has value to someone with the right contacts
  • Aquaculture expertise — Bay-trained operators are employable across the GLM's food production network
  • Privacy — the Barrens' low surveillance footprint makes it useful for operations that prefer not to be observed
story hooks
  • Ashgrave's recycling drones have excavated something beneath one of the old manufacturing buildings — not construction material, something older, something that shouldn't be there
  • The aquaculture platforms on Saginaw Bay have started producing organisms that aren't in the growth program — the synthetic ecosystem is evolving
  • A community in the Barrens has declared independence from Michigan municipal governance, establishing the first self-governing territory in the GLM based on nothing more than occupation and refusal to leave

Saltgrave Sublevel #

type place
name Saltgrave Sublevel
aliases
  • The Salt
  • Brine Deck
  • Old Sublevel Four
  • The Pickled Quarter
description Saltgrave Sublevel occupies the drowned basement infrastructure of what was once Chicago's South Loop transit interchange — a labyrinth of flooded pedestrian tunnels and former parking structures sealed off after the 2147 Lake Surge and never properly reclaimed. Brine from Lake Michigan seeps through cracked concrete walls, leaving thick white salt deposits that encrust every surface like mineral frost. Salvagers broke through from below in the 2170s and have since carved out a thriving gray-market settlement across four interconnected levels, using repurposed buoyancy platforms to keep living quarters above the standing water.

The settlement is famous — or infamous — for its salt trade. Saltgrave's residents harvest the mineral deposits and process them for industrial use, food preservation, and certain chemical synthesis operations that corponations prefer not to conduct in their own facilities. Zheng-Dao Bioelectric maintains a quiet purchasing agreement with Saltgrave's council, though neither party acknowledges it publicly. The deeper levels, perpetually flooded and lit only by bioluminescent algae cultivated along the walls, serve as neutral meeting ground for parties who cannot afford to be seen in any official venue.
atmosphere
sights
  • Salt crystal formations bloom across every concrete pillar like white coral, some reaching half a meter long and catching the blue-green glow of cultivated algae.
  • Salvaged buoyancy platforms drift in loose clusters, connected by rope bridges and rusted gangplanks above black standing water.
  • Handmade lamps fashioned from repurposed BCI housing units cast warm amber pools across market stalls selling mineral blocks, preserved foods, and unregistered chem supplies.
  • Waterlines stain the walls in brown and gray bands, a geological record of every flood surge dating back decades.
sounds
  • A constant low drip echoes from every direction, merging into white noise that muffles conversation and makes surveillance difficult.
  • The creak and slap of platform pontoons shifting underfoot follows every step through the upper market levels.
  • Voices carry strangely in the tunnels — a whisper fifty meters away can arrive clearer than someone standing beside you.
smells
  • Sharp mineral brine dominates everything, a clean chemical smell undercut by the damp rot of old concrete.
  • Cooking fires on the upper platforms push woodsmoke and rendered fat down into the lower corridors where it pools and lingers.
  • Certain deep passages carry a faint sweet-chemical odor from unlicensed synthesis operations that the council officially denies.
feel Saltgrave feels like the city forgot it existed and the people inside decided that was fine. The dampness gets into your joints, and the acoustics keep you permanently uncertain of where sounds are coming from. There's a claustrophobic intimacy to the place — everyone knows everyone's business, but they've collectively agreed not to say so.
tags —
demographics Roughly 1,200 permanent residents, heavily weighted toward Shelf-tier salvagers, displaced transit workers, and a small population of unregistered synthetics who have found safety in the council's deliberate blindness toward legal identity. Turnover is low — people who find Saltgrave tend to stay.
economy Salt harvesting and processing form the economic backbone, supplemented by gray-market chemical synthesis, data brokering conducted in the acoustically scrambled deep levels, and a modest trade in recovered pre-Surge artifacts pulled from the flooded lower chambers.
power structure The Saltgrave Council — seven elected platform-holders who control the buoyancy infrastructure — govern by consensus and collect a ten-percent tithe on all commerce. Ferrogate Security has no presence here; the council enforces its own order through platform access denial, the ultimate threat being eviction into the flooded tunnels below.
dangers
  • Sudden flood surges from Lake Michigan pressure events can raise water levels in the lower passages by two meters in under an hour, with minimal warning.
  • The salt-saturated air aggressively corrodes unprotected electronics, including BCI hardware, causing glitches and data loss with extended exposure.
  • Unregulated synthesis operations in the deep levels occasionally produce toxic byproduct clouds that migrate through the tunnel system unpredictably.
  • The council's neutrality policy means rival factions meet here — and sometimes resolve their disputes violently in the dark water of the lower levels.
opportunities
  • The flooded deep chambers contain intact pre-Surge transit infrastructure and data vaults that no one has fully mapped or salvaged.
  • Saltgrave's acoustic properties and council-enforced neutrality make it the premier location in the southern corridor for sensitive meetings that cannot be recorded.
  • Salt and mineral extraction contracts with industrial buyers like Zheng-Dao represent legitimate income streams for operators willing to work outside corponation oversight.
story hooks
  • A council member has gone missing in the deep levels — officially a flood accident, but her platform partner insists she had just discovered something in the pre-Surge vaults and is convinced the death was arranged. The council wants the matter handled quietly before it attracts outside attention.
  • An unregistered synthetic has been operating as Saltgrave's de facto doctor for three years, beloved by the community. A Helix Biosystems bounty hunter has tracked it here and is pressuring the council to hand it over. The synthetic claims to have information about illegal Helix experiments that would be worth far more than the bounty.
  • A new synthesis crew has moved into the deep levels and is producing something that isn't chem — the byproduct odors are wrong, the workers don't socialize, and two Saltgrave residents who got too curious have quietly disappeared.

Shallowgrave #

type place
name Shallowgrave
aliases
  • The Flat Reef
  • Erie Free City
  • Pancake Town
  • The Sprawl on the Water
description Lake Erie is the shallowest of the Great Lakes — average depth nineteen meters, which is roughly the depth of a bad decision. This posed a fundamental engineering problem for the seacrete pioneers who arrived in 2173 to build the fifth free city: you can't grow a deep-keeled reef structure in water that barely covers a four-story building. Shallowgrave's founders solved this by going wide instead of deep, spreading their accretion frameworks across the lakebed in flat, interlocking platforms that grew upward from the bottom rather than downward from the surface. The result is a city that sits on the lake like a lily pad — vast, thin, and disturbingly close to the water. In rough weather, waves wash over the outer platforms entirely. Residents call these events 'baptisms' and have developed a culture of waterproofing everything they own.

The shallow construction created an unexpected advantage: Shallowgrave's platforms are anchored directly to the lakebed, making the city effectively immovable. Where Freestone and Deepwell float, tethered but mobile, Shallowgrave is fused to the earth beneath the water. This permanence gave the city a legal argument that the other lake cities lacked — Shallowgrave claimed not just water rights but lakebed territory, filing a sovereign land claim under obscure pre-collapse mining law. The claim has never been recognized by M88 or any remnant government, but it has never been successfully challenged either, because challenging it would require acknowledging that the pre-collapse legal framework still applies, which would open a catastrophic can of jurisdictional worms that no corponation wants to touch.

Shallowgrave's proximity to Cormorant Naval Systems' Lake Erie operations and Crestfall Aquaculture's protein platforms makes it the most politically complex of the lake cities. It exists in contested water, surrounded by corporate sovereign interests, and survives through a combination of strategic usefulness and deliberate unpalatability. The city is ugly — flat, sprawling, perpetually wet, its seacrete stained green with algae growth that the shallow, sunlit water encourages. But it produces something nobody else can: freshwater algae-derived pharmaceuticals. Shallowgrave's biotech labs, built into the sunlit shallow-water platforms where algae cultivation thrives, produce raw compounds that Lazarus Pharmaceuticals and Novafold would prefer to manufacture in-house but cannot replicate at Shallowgrave's quality or scale. This biochemical leverage keeps the corponations negotiating instead of invading.

Governance is a technocratic council — the Algae Board, as residents call it without irony. Six elected biotech specialists and six elected general representatives manage the city's affairs with a bias toward technical competence that occasionally shades into arrogance. Population: 95,000, most of them damp.
atmosphere
sights
  • A vast, flat expanse of seacrete platforms barely rising above the waterline — the city has almost no vertical profile
  • Green — algae cultivation gives Shallowgrave a verdant, living-carpet appearance from above
  • Biotech labs with transparent roofing, their algae tanks glowing green-gold in sunlight
  • Waves washing across outer platforms during moderate weather — residents walk through ankle-deep water like it's normal, because it is
  • Crestfall Aquaculture platforms visible on the horizon — a reminder that corporate neighbors are always watching
sounds
  • Water — not the distant lap of deeper lakes, but the immediate, constant slosh of a city that barely clears the surface
  • Biotech processing hums from the algae labs — centrifuges, bioreactors, extraction equipment
  • The squelch of wet footsteps on algae-filmed seacrete — the city's ambient soundtrack
  • Wind across flat water with no structures to break it — Shallowgrave is exposed
smells
  • Algae — rich, green, organic, pervasive. You smell Shallowgrave before you see it.
  • Pharmaceutical processing compounds — chemical sharpness from the biotech labs
  • Lake Erie's particular chemistry — warmer, more biologically active than the upper lakes
  • Wet seacrete — a musty, mineral smell that never fully dries
feel Damp, practical, and quietly powerful. Shallowgrave doesn't inspire the way Freestone does or intimidate the way Deepwell does. It impresses you the way a fungus impresses a biologist — by being far more important than it looks. The city is uncomfortable, wet, architecturally uninspiring, and absolutely essential to the Great Lakes pharmaceutical economy. Residents have the resigned humor of people who live in a place nobody visits for pleasure but everyone needs. They track mud everywhere and they hold patents that keep corponations at bay.
tags —
demographics 95,000 permanent residents. Heavily skewed toward technical and scientific backgrounds — Shallowgrave actively recruits biotech talent from shore universities and offers citizenship in exchange for five-year service commitments. The population is younger and more educated on average than any shore-based community in M88.
economy Primary export: algae-derived pharmaceutical precursors and specialty biochemicals. Shallowgrave supplies raw compounds to Lazarus Pharmaceuticals, Novafold, and several smaller pharma corponations at prices that undercut synthetic alternatives. Secondary exports: algae-based food supplements, biofuel feedstock, and water filtration organisms. Annual external trade: approximately Φ11.4 billion, almost entirely from biotech. The economy is a monoculture, and the city knows it — diversification is a permanent agenda item that never quite gets funded.
power structure Technocratic council — the Board of Twelve. Six seats elected from the biotech sector, six from general population. The biotech seats carry effective veto power on trade policy, which is where the real power lies. No corporate sovereignty permitted, but Shallowgrave licenses pharmaceutical extraction rights to shore-based corponations under carefully negotiated terms that both sides consider exploitative.
dangers
  • Flooding — Shallowgrave's low profile means that major storms can submerge entire districts temporarily
  • Cormorant Naval Systems — Lake Erie is their claimed water, and Shallowgrave's presence irritates them enormously
  • Crestfall Aquaculture — protein platforms and algae farms compete for the same shallow, sunlit water
  • Economic monoculture — if the pharma market shifts, Shallowgrave has no fallback
  • Biological hazard — algae cultivation at this scale creates risks of toxic bloom events if containment fails
opportunities
  • Pharmaceutical leverage — Shallowgrave's biotech output makes it indispensable to multiple corponations
  • Scientific research — the city's algae labs are doing work that shore-based institutions can't replicate
  • Strategic position — located between Cormorant and Crestfall, Shallowgrave is a useful intermediary
  • Biofuel production — a growing secondary market that could reduce the monoculture risk
story hooks
  • Novafold Pharmaceuticals attempts to acquire exclusive rights to Shallowgrave's algae-derived TX-4 precursor compounds. The deal would make the city rich and dependent. The Board of Twelve is split.
  • A toxic algae bloom escapes containment on Shallowgrave's eastern platform, threatening Crestfall Aquaculture's nearby protein farms. Both cities blame the other. Someone needs to find out what actually happened before Cormorant uses the crisis as an excuse to intervene.
  • A Shallowgrave biochemist has synthesized something that shouldn't be possible from algae — and three corponations have independently dispatched acquisition teams.

  • Crestfall Aquaculture platforms (visible from Shallowgrave's eastern edge)
  • Threshold (Lake Huron — northern trade route)
  • Tidebreak (Lake Ontario — eastern trade corridor via Welland Canal)

Sheboygan Reef #

type place
name Sheboygan Reef
aliases
  • Sheboygan
  • The Reef
  • Kohler Zone
  • Plumbworks
description Sheboygan was a lakefront city whose identity was inseparable from the Kohler Company — a plumbing fixture manufacturer that grew into a hospitality and lifestyle conglomerate, then contracted back to a manufacturing core, then was acquired by Axiom Industries in 2169 as part of Axiom's Great Lakes infrastructure consolidation. Sheboygan's residents joke that they've been a company town since 1873 and the only thing that changed was the logo on the water tower. The joke is accurate. The water tower still says Kohler. Axiom hasn't gotten around to repainting it, or more likely, someone in Axiom's cultural integration division ran the numbers and determined that the legacy branding generates more goodwill than the corporate rebrand would be worth.

Sheboygan Reef — the district name adopted during the Milwaukee Administrative Zone's northern expansion in 2181 — occupies an awkward position in the Corridor's geography: too far north to benefit from Milwaukee's economic density, too far south to escape its jurisdictional reach, and too small to sustain an independent economy. The solution has been specialization. Axiom converted the Kohler manufacturing campus into a fabrication center for water infrastructure components — filtration systems, atmospheric moisture extractors, and the desalination units that the Corridor's upper tiers use to process Lake Michigan water into something drinkable. In a world where clean water is the most valuable commodity after neural bandwidth, Sheboygan Reef produces the machinery that makes water usable. The irony of a former plumbing company's factory now producing survival-grade water technology is appreciated by the workforce and lost on Axiom's management.

The residential city wraps around the fabrication campus in the standard company-town pattern: worker housing within commuting distance, commercial strip serving the workforce, and a lakefront that the factory's intake pipes have made unsuitable for anything except industrial access. The old Kohler resort — a luxury destination that once attracted visitors from across the Midwest — operates as an Axiom executive retreat, its golf courses maintained by automated groundskeepers that outnumber the human staff. Workers who pass the resort's entrance on their way to the fabrication facility observe the grounds with the particular expression of people who build water filtration systems and can't afford the water that comes out of them.
atmosphere
sights
  • The Kohler water tower — legacy branding visible from the entire district, a monument to corporate continuity
  • Axiom fabrication campus — industrial architecture wrapped around the original Kohler manufacturing buildings, old brick and new composite layered like geological strata
  • The lakefront intake array — massive pipes extending into Lake Michigan, drawing water that the factory processes into components for other people's survival
  • The resort grounds — visible over the perimeter wall, impossibly green against the surrounding industrial landscape
  • Worker housing in the standard Axiom modular style, differentiated from Racine's only by the Kohler-branded street signs that Axiom kept
sounds
  • Fabrication — the sound of water infrastructure being manufactured, a constant industrial hum with the specific tonal quality of pressure-testing equipment
  • Lake Michigan — audible along the shoreline, its waves hitting the intake pipes with a hollow, metallic resonance
  • The resort — on quiet evenings, the sound of the automated groundskeepers maintaining the golf course carries to the worker housing, a mechanical whir that sounds like money being spent on grass
  • Shift change — smaller than Racine's but with the same rhythm: 6,000 workers flowing between the campus and the surrounding blocks
  • Wind off the lake — Sheboygan's lakefront position means the wind is constant, carrying the lake's smell and the factory's sound in equal measure
smells
  • Industrial water processing — a clean, chemical smell that is technically the smell of water being purified, which doesn't make it pleasant
  • Lake Michigan — stronger here than in Milwaukee, the open-water smell of a lake that is simultaneously dying and being treated for its death
  • The resort grounds — cut grass and horticultural perfume, detectable from the perimeter on calm days, a smell the workers describe as 'money'
  • Fabrication materials — composite compounds and testing chemicals, the industrial smell of survival technology being manufactured
feel A company town that knows it's a company town and has made peace with the arrangement because the alternative is no town at all. Sheboygan Reef's workers have a craftsman's pride in the water infrastructure they produce — it saves lives, and they know it — combined with the simmering resentment of people who build essential technology and are compensated as though they're replaceable. The resort visible from the factory floor is a daily reminder that the same company that employs them also employs a golf course. The workers' feelings about this are not complex.
tags —
demographics Approximately 52,000 residents. Tier 2, predominantly. The workforce is drawn from multi-generational Sheboygan families supplemented by Milwaukee Administrative Zone labor pipeline placements. Historically white and German-American, now mixed through the standard Corridor demographic blending that happens when economic necessity overrides ethnic enclave patterns. The Axiom executive population at the resort is small, transient, and invisible.
economy Axiom water infrastructure fabrication — the dominant economic activity. The fabrication campus employs 6,000 people. Commercial strip economy serves the workforce. The resort generates revenue that is accounted to Axiom's hospitality division, not to Sheboygan Reef's economic statistics. Estimated district economic output: Φ4 billion, primarily infrastructure components.
power structure Axiom Plant Director holds practical authority. The Milwaukee Administrative Zone's northern district office processes administrative functions. A workers' advisory council operates within Axiom's guidelines. The resort has its own management and security, operating as an enclave within the enclave.
dangers
  • Axiom employment dependency — same company-town vulnerability as Racine: job loss cascades into housing, medical, and status loss
  • Water infrastructure as strategic target — the components manufactured here are essential to the Corridor's upper-tier water supply, making the facility a target for anyone who wants leverage over the Corridor's elite
  • Lake contamination — the intake array processes water whose quality is declining, and exposure events affect workers who maintain the intake infrastructure
  • Resort security overlap — the executive retreat's security perimeter extends into worker-adjacent areas, creating friction points
  • Northern isolation — Sheboygan Reef is far enough from Milwaukee that emergency response from the Administrative Zone is measured in hours, not minutes
opportunities
  • Water infrastructure access — the components manufactured here are essential and valuable, both on the legitimate market and off it
  • Resort intelligence — Axiom executives use the retreat for meetings they don't want recorded in corporate spaces, and the service staff observes
  • Lake access — Sheboygan Reef's position on the lake provides water routes north toward Manitowoc and the Fox Cities
  • Worker expertise — the fabrication workforce understands water purification systems at a granular level, knowledge with survival applications throughout the Corridor
story hooks
  • The fabrication facility has received a rush order for water infrastructure components specified for an environment that doesn't match any known Corridor installation — the specifications suggest a facility that operates underground, at depth, and in conditions that no publicly documented location requires
  • A resort guest — a Tier 5 executive from a non-Axiom corponation — was found dead in their suite, and the resort's security footage for the relevant hours has been corrupted in a way that Axiom's IT division says is 'unprecedented'
  • A group of intake array maintenance workers has been documenting chemical compounds in the lake water that don't match any known industrial discharge. The compounds are organic. They're increasing. And they're not coming from the shore.

  • Administrative Zone officials making the long trip from Milwaukee to process paperwork that could be done remotely but isn't, because the resort has good restaurants

Sherman Heights #

type place
name Sherman Heights
aliases
  • Sherman Park
  • The Heights
  • Sherman
  • The Heritage
description Sherman Park was Milwaukee's premier Black neighborhood before 'premier' and 'Black' and 'neighborhood' all got redefined by people who didn't live there. The area's history is a compressed timeline of American racial geography: white flight in the 1960s, Black community building in the 1970s-2000s, disinvestment, partial recovery, more disinvestment, and finally the sovereignty transition, which replaced municipal neglect with corporate indifference — a lateral move that felt like a demotion. Sherman Heights, as the district is now known, survived all of it. The community's institutional memory runs deeper than the corporations that claim jurisdiction over it, and the institutions — churches, community organizations, family networks — that carried the neighborhood through a century of deliberate underinvestment are still operating, still funded by their members, and still more trusted than anything with a corporate logo on it.

The sovereignty transition left Sherman Heights in Sentinel North's security franchise, which means private security patrols the streets with the authority of police and the accountability of a contractor. Sentinel North's approach to Sherman Heights is the approach of every security force to every community it doesn't understand: high presence, low engagement, and a statistical model that treats the neighborhood's demographics as a risk profile rather than a population. The community's response has been the response of every Black community to every hostile authority: parallel institutions, internal governance, and the quiet maintenance of resources that the official system doesn't know about and wouldn't understand if it did.

The housing stock is solid — 1920s-era bungalows and duplexes built with a quality that post-war construction never matched, maintained by residents who understand that the house they're maintaining is not just shelter but inheritance. Home ownership in Sherman Heights is the highest in Milwaukee's lower tiers, not because the residents are wealthier but because the families have been here for three and four generations and the houses have been passed down, each generation adding modifications — solar, atmospheric processing, water recycling — that transform the original structures into self-sufficient systems. A Sherman Heights bungalow in 2200 produces its own power, filters its own air, recycles its own water, and contains enough stored food for three months. The residents learned to be self-sufficient because nobody was going to do it for them.

The commercial corridor along Villard Avenue is community-owned in a literal sense: a cooperative purchasing agreement in 2168 allowed fifty families to collectively acquire the commercial strip from an absentee landlord, and the co-op has operated it since. The businesses are community-serving: a food cooperative, a community medical clinic (one of three in Milwaukee staffed by doctors who treat patients without verifying tier status), a credit union that predates the sovereignty era, and Mama June's, a restaurant that has been serving the community for forty years and whose proprietor knows everything that happens in Sherman Heights and will tell you exactly none of it unless she decides you need to know.
atmosphere
sights
  • Bungalow streets — solid, well-maintained homes with century-old architecture wearing 22nd-century technology, solar skins on slate roofs, atmospheric processors beside original chimneys
  • Villard Avenue co-op — community-owned commercial strip, signage that hasn't changed in thirty years because the businesses haven't changed either
  • Church buildings — three major congregations, their buildings maintained with the care of institutions that measure their history in generations
  • Sentinel North patrols — armored vehicles moving through streets designed for pedestrians, conspicuously out of scale with the neighborhood
  • Community gardens on every third lot — organized, productive, and defended by grandmothers who are more effective than any security system
sounds
  • Church music on Sundays — audible for blocks, choral traditions that predate the sovereignty era by a century
  • Villard Avenue — the sound of a commercial strip that serves its community: conversation, commerce, children sent to the store
  • Sentinel North patrols — the low rumble of armored vehicles and the scanner tones of surveillance equipment, sounds the community has learned to ignore without ceasing to notice
  • Block party music in summer — Sherman Heights holds monthly gatherings that are part celebration, part community governance, and entirely non-negotiable
  • Conversation across porches — the neighborhood communication network that Sentinel North's surveillance can't intercept because it's analog, encrypted by familiarity
smells
  • Mama June's — whatever she's cooking today, drifting down Villard Avenue like a community summons
  • Community gardens — soil, growing food, and the mulch that the gardening collective produces from household organic waste
  • Home cooking from bungalow kitchens — the smell of a neighborhood where people still eat together, still cook for each other, still consider a meal an act of community
  • Clean air — Sherman Heights' atmospheric processors, maintained by the community's own technicians, produce air quality that rivals districts two tiers above
feel Rooted. Sherman Heights has the particular energy of a community that has survived everything the system has thrown at it and emerged with its identity intact. The institutions are real, the relationships are generational, and the mutual aid is not a program but a culture. There is a quiet anger here — the anger of people who have been failed by every government, every corporation, and every institution that claimed authority over them, and who built everything they have themselves. The anger doesn't make them hostile. It makes them careful. Sherman Heights takes care of its own, and the definition of 'its own' is determined by the community, not by any tier system.
tags —
demographics Approximately 22,000 residents. Predominantly Black, multi-generational, with the deepest continuous community roots of any district in Milwaukee. Tier 2 by official classification, effectively Tier 3 in quality of life due to community self-sufficiency infrastructure. Median household tenure: thirty-eight years. Home ownership rate: 72% — the highest in Milwaukee's Tier 1-2 districts.
economy Community cooperative economy. The Villard Avenue co-op generates Φ8 million annually. The community credit union manages Φ120 million in assets. Residents work throughout Milwaukee's economy — corporate positions, fabrication, service sector — and contribute to community fund assessments that maintain shared infrastructure. The informal economy is modest and community-serving: home repair, childcare, food production, and the particular form of economic activity that consists of neighbors helping neighbors without involving currency.
power structure The Sherman Heights Community Council — an elected body with roots in the neighborhood associations of the pre-sovereignty era. Three church congregations hold significant influence. Mama June (June Washington, age 74) holds no official title and is the most influential person in the district. Sentinel North patrols the streets but does not govern them — the community cooperates with Sentinel exactly enough to prevent escalation and not one interaction more.
dangers
  • Sentinel North profiling — the security franchise's algorithmic risk assessment treats Sherman Heights' demographics as inherently suspicious, producing disproportionate stop-and-scan rates
  • Institutional memory as target — the community's archives, credit union records, and property deeds represent a wealth of data that corporate actors would find valuable
  • Gentrification pressure — the neighborhood's self-sufficiency and community quality of life make it attractive to the same forces that have displaced Black communities for two centuries
  • Youth pipeline — corporate recruitment targets Sherman Heights' young people with tier-advancement promises that require leaving the community
  • Infrastructure aging — the community maintains its own systems, and some of those systems are running on expertise that is generational and not easily replaced
opportunities
  • Community trust — earning Sherman Heights' trust opens access to the deepest social network in Milwaukee's working-class districts
  • Self-sufficiency model — the community's infrastructure knowledge has value throughout the Corridor for anyone building autonomous systems
  • Institutional connections — Sherman Heights' churches, credit union, and cooperative are connected to similar institutions across the GLM
  • Mama June's network — June Washington knows everyone worth knowing in Milwaukee and most of them owe her a favor
story hooks
  • A Sentinel North patrol unit has been reassigned from Sherman Heights to a corporate priority zone, and the replacement unit's commander has a history of escalation. The community is preparing, quietly and thoroughly.
  • The community credit union has received an acquisition offer from Axiom Financial Services — a generous offer that would give Axiom access to forty years of community financial data. The board is meeting at Mama June's.
  • A young Sherman Heights resident, recruited into a Tessera tier-advancement program, has returned home with a neural implant and information about what the program actually does with the data from the communities it recruits from.

  • Young people navigating between community identity and corporate opportunity
  • People from surrounding districts who come to Sherman Heights for the medical clinic, the credit union, and Mama June's cooking

Shorewood Terrace #

type place
name Shorewood Terrace
aliases
  • Shorewood
  • The Terrace
  • North Shore Annexed
description Shorewood was a wealthy lakefront suburb that Milwaukee's sprawl absorbed the way a rising tide absorbs a sandcastle — gradually, then completely. The village's independent municipal charter was dissolved in the 2172 Milwaukee Consolidation Act, which folded fourteen surrounding municipalities into the Milwaukee Administrative Zone's jurisdiction. Shorewood's residents, who had spent a century maintaining the fiction that a municipal boundary could separate them from the city that surrounded them on three sides, discovered that legal autonomy is a function of political leverage, and their political leverage had been declining since the sovereignty transition made municipal charters less valuable than corporate ones.

Shorewood Terrace — the name the consolidated district adopted, because 'Shorewood' alone sounded too much like the suburban enclave it still wanted to be — is now Milwaukee's wealthiest residential corridor north of the Milwaukee Core. The lakefront properties along Lake Drive command Tier 4 prices, their owners a mix of senior corporate management, Sentinel North executive staff, and legacy families who bought in before the consolidation and are now sitting on property values that have quintupled because lakefront residential in a surveilled, security-franchised district turns out to be exactly what Tier 4 families want. The architecture is a timeline of wealth expression: Tudor revival from the 1920s, mid-century modern from the 1960s, glass-and-steel minimalism from the 2020s, and the current style, which can best be described as 'security aesthetic' — beautiful homes with beautiful perimeters that are beautifully designed to prevent unauthorized entry.

The commercial district along Oakland Avenue serves the residential population with the curated precision of a neighborhood that knows its market: organic food retailers (using actual organic food, not the nutrient-paste-branded-as-organic that the lower tiers receive), boutique augment maintenance (appointment only, Tier 3 minimum), and restaurants that charge more for a meal than a Bay View family spends on food in a week. The commercial strip is also where Shorewood Terrace's internal contradiction is most visible: the service workers who staff these establishments commute from the East Bank and Bay View, spend their shifts serving clients who earn thirty times their income, and return home on the same transit line. The Terrace does not discuss this. The Terrace does not discuss many things.
atmosphere
sights
  • Lake Drive properties — stately homes behind security perimeters, lakefront views worth more than the houses themselves
  • Oakland Avenue commercial strip — boutique retail with tasteful signage, the visual language of wealth that doesn't need to advertise
  • The lakefront — Lake Michigan visible between estates, its shoreline maintained by the Terrace's homeowners' association to standards that the surrounding districts cannot afford
  • Service workers arriving at dawn, departing at dusk — the transit of labor that sustains the Terrace's lifestyle
  • Security — less visible than The Canopy's but equally present, integrated into architecture and landscaping with the subtlety that old money prefers
sounds
  • Quiet — the Terrace maintains noise ordinances that the East Bank's students find incomprehensible
  • Lake waves against maintained shoreline — a sound the properties are priced to include
  • Transit — the commuter line that delivers service workers, its schedule synchronized to the Terrace's commercial hours
  • Birdsong — the lakefront corridor supports actual wildlife, maintained by the homeowners' association's environmental committee
  • The absence of commercial noise — no street vendors, no public advertising, no audible commerce. Money moves silently here.
smells
  • Clean lake air — the Terrace's shoreline treatment produces the best air quality in Milwaukee's residential districts
  • Estate gardens — maintained landscapes with seasonal plantings, the smell of professional horticulture
  • Oakland Avenue restaurants — high-quality cooking, detectable from the street, a reminder that food at this price point has a different smell entirely
feel Comfortable and claustrophobic. Shorewood Terrace has achieved the particular kind of perfection that requires the systematic exclusion of everything imperfect, including spontaneity, diversity, and the physical evidence that the city surrounding it exists. The residents are not unkind. They are insulated, and the insulation is so complete that the world beyond the Terrace's boundaries has become theoretical — a place that exists on news feeds and in the stories told by service workers, but not in any way that requires action. The Terrace is beautiful. The beauty is a wall.
tags —
demographics Approximately 14,000 residents. Tier 3-4, with a concentration of Tier 4 along the lakefront. Historically white and affluent, now affluent and less white — the Terrace's demographic shift reflects the corponation executive class's diversity, which is genuine in ethnicity and uniform in wealth. Service worker population commutes from lower-tier districts. Median property value: Φ12 million.
economy Residential wealth management and lakefront property market. Oakland Avenue commercial strip serves the local population. No significant production or industrial activity. The Terrace's economic contribution to Milwaukee is primarily through property assessments and the tax revenue that the Administrative Zone collects and spends elsewhere.
power structure The Shorewood Terrace Homeowners' Association operates with the quiet authority of an organization whose members sit on corporate boards and Sentinel North advisory committees. The Milwaukee Administrative Zone's district representative attends HOA meetings and implements their requests. Sentinel North's patrol presence is calibrated to the Terrace's preferences: visible enough to deter, invisible enough to not disrupt.
dangers
  • Social surveillance — the Terrace's community is small and observant, and being noticed as out of place generates attention faster than any electronic system
  • Property security — the lakefront estates' integrated defense systems are designed by people who can afford the best, and 'the best' includes lethal autonomous countermeasures
  • Economic exposure — challenging Terrace interests means challenging people with access to corporate legal divisions and Sentinel North's executive services
  • Service worker vulnerability — the commuting workforce is dependent on Terrace employment and has no representation within the community
  • The HOA — the homeowners' association has more practical authority than the Administrative Zone's district government, and it exercises that authority with the decisiveness of people accustomed to making decisions without consultation
opportunities
  • Proximity to wealth — the Terrace's residents are decision-makers in eleven corponations and Sentinel North
  • Service worker access — the commuting workforce moves between the Terrace and lower-tier districts daily, carrying information in both directions
  • Lakefront access — the Terrace's maintained shoreline provides water access to Lake Michigan's northern cargo routes
  • The HOA records — a comprehensive database of the district's residents, properties, and governance decisions, maintained with corporate-grade security and worth a fortune to anyone who could access it
story hooks
  • A Shorewood Terrace resident has been receiving deliveries at unusual hours — deliveries that are not logged in the HOA's package management system, which logs everything. The HOA security committee has noticed. They have not yet acted.
  • A service worker who commuted to the Terrace for twelve years has been fired without cause. She has a neural recording of a conversation she overheard during a dinner party. The conversation involves people whose names she recognized from the news.
  • The Terrace's environmental committee has discovered that the lakefront water treatment system has been processing compounds that shouldn't be in the water — compounds that match no industrial discharge profile and suggest someone is using the lake for disposal.

Slavic Breaks #

type place
name Slavic Breaks
aliases
  • Slavic Village
  • The Breaks
  • Foreclosure Mile
description Slavic Village broke first. Before the corridor, before the corponations, before Meridian 88 existed as a concept, this neighborhood was already a case study in what happens when capital abandons a place and doesn't come back. The 2108 foreclosure crisis hit Slavic Village harder than almost anywhere else in America — block after block of boarded-up houses, stripped copper, and families who discovered that the American Dream had an expiration date printed in the fine print of their subprime mortgages. A century later, the scars haven't healed. They've been built over, but scars built over are not the same as scars healed.

The Eastern European immigrant legacy that gave the neighborhood its name survives in fragments. The Polish and Czech social clubs are still standing — their reinforced basements serve as community shelters and black-market trading posts. Saint Stanislaus Church, built in 1886, has been converted into a combined medical clinic and augmentation facility operated by a collective of unlicensed practitioners who serve the excluded and Tier 1 populations that corporate healthcare won't touch. The old commercial strips along Fleet Avenue and Broadway have been colonized by salvage operations, repair shops, and the kind of small-scale manufacturing that exists because it's too low-margin for any corponation to bother claiming jurisdiction over.

Slavic Breaks is what the corridor looks like when no one is looking. No corponation has claimed sovereignty here because the economics don't justify the cost of enforcement. Tollgate maintains the water and power infrastructure because it's connected to systems that serve more profitable neighborhoods, but the maintenance is minimal and the outages are frequent. The population is predominantly Tier 1 and excluded — climate refugees, displaced workers, families who have been here for generations and have nowhere else to go. What they have built in the absence of corporate governance is not pretty, but it functions. Mutual aid networks distribute food and medical supplies. The social clubs serve as dispute resolution centers. The old foreclosure houses have been rebuilt by hand, using salvaged materials and Gravemoss biofoam that falls off the supply trucks with suspicious regularity. Slavic Breaks doesn't need the corponations. It has needed them before, and it remembers what happened.
atmosphere
sights
  • Rows of rebuilt foreclosure houses — original frames wrapped in salvaged materials, Gravemoss biofoam patching the gaps like organic scar tissue
  • Saint Stanislaus Church, its 1886 stonework intact, a red cross painted on the door marking it as an unlicensed medical facility
  • Polish and Czech social club signs, faded but maintained, their basements lit by generator power when the grid fails
  • Salvage yards stretching for blocks, organized with a precision that suggests this economy is not as informal as it appears
  • Children playing in streets that have no surveillance drones, no corporate signage, no jurisdiction markers — just pavement and people
sounds
  • Generator hum during the frequent power outages — a sound the neighborhood has learned to sleep through
  • The clang and grind of salvage operations — metal being sorted, components being tested, value being extracted from waste
  • Polish and Czech spoken alongside Shelf Cant and Standard — the old languages persist here
  • Church bells from Saint Stanislaus — rung manually, on a schedule that has nothing to do with the liturgical calendar and everything to do with neighborhood alerts
  • Quiet — Slavic Breaks is quieter than any corporate zone because there are no drones, no advertisements, no algorithmic soundscapes
smells
  • Biofoam curing — the sharp chemical tang of Gravemoss material setting into structural form
  • Wood smoke from heating systems that predate the corridor's power grid
  • Pierogi and kielbasa from the social club kitchens — recipes that survived the Atlantic crossing and the collapse of the country they crossed to
feel Slavic Breaks feels like a place that has been punched in the face so many times it has stopped flinching. There is no optimism here, but there is no despair either — just a pragmatic determination to keep functioning that transcends any economic system imposed from outside. The neighborhood doesn't resist the corponations. It has simply outlasted every institution that has ever claimed authority over it.
tags —
demographics Approximately 18,000 residents, predominantly Tier 1 and excluded. Significant populations of Eastern European descent families (fourth and fifth generation), Gulf Coast climate refugees, and displaced industrial workers. One of the highest concentrations of unaugmented adults in the Cleveland sprawl — not by choice, but by economics.
economy Salvage, repair, and small-scale manufacturing. The social clubs operate as informal banks, lending in scrip and barter credits. Medical services through Saint Stanislaus generate a small revenue stream from patients across the city's lower tiers. Gravemoss biofoam, officially 'lost in transit,' is the neighborhood's primary construction material and an informal currency.
power structure No corporate sovereignty. Tollgate maintains minimum infrastructure. Governance operates through the social clubs — the Polish American Club, the Czech Heritage Society, and the Fleet Avenue Mutual Aid Collective — which function as a distributed council. Disputes are resolved internally. External threats are met collectively. The system is imperfect and sometimes brutal, but it has kept the neighborhood alive for a century without corporate assistance.
dangers
  • Infrastructure failure — power outages, water contamination, and structural collapse are regular occurrences
  • Medical risk — Saint Stanislaus provides essential healthcare but the practitioners are unlicensed and equipment is salvaged
  • Isolation — Slavic Breaks' lack of corporate jurisdiction means no emergency services, no legal protections, no safety net beyond the community itself
  • Exploitation — the absence of surveillance makes the neighborhood attractive to criminal operations that the residents did not invite and cannot easily expel
  • Biofoam instability — the 'lost in transit' Gravemoss material is sometimes defective batches, and structural failures have killed people
opportunities
  • Anonymity — Slavic Breaks is one of the few places in the Cleveland sprawl with no surveillance infrastructure, making it valuable to anyone who needs to disappear
  • Community trust — earning the social clubs' trust opens access to a mutual aid network that spans the city's excluded population
  • Salvage expertise — the neighborhood's repair and manufacturing capabilities are sought by operators who need equipment maintained off the books
  • The foreclosure houses contain pre-collapse infrastructure — fiber optic lines, copper wiring, sometimes things more interesting — that nobody has fully mapped
story hooks
  • A sealed basement in one of the foreclosure houses has been opened, revealing a pre-collapse data cache that contains financial records someone in the current corponation hierarchy would kill to suppress
  • Saint Stanislaus' unlicensed augmentation practice has attracted the attention of Tessera's enforcement division — and the neighborhood is preparing to resist
  • The Gravemoss biofoam supply chain has been disrupted, and without it, a third of the neighborhood's housing stock will begin to fail within months
