South Calumet #

type place
name South Calumet
aliases
  • South Chicago
  • The Forge
  • Steelgrave
  • Callie
description South Calumet is where the old world died loudest. When U.S. Steel, Republic Steel, and Wisconsin Steel were running three shifts a day, the far Southeast Side was the muscle of a city that built things — actual, physical things made of iron and carbon and labor. The Calumet River carried ore and slag. The air tasted like metal. The work was brutal and the pay was enough. Then the mills closed, one by one, and the neighborhood learned what every industrial community learns: the company needed you, until it didn't. South Calumet was already a ruin before the collapse. The collapse just made it official.

What Axiom Industries found when it surveyed the far Southeast Side was a ready-made industrial zone — brownfield sites, deepwater river access, existing heavy infrastructure, and a population too small and too low-tier to resist rezoning. Axiom reactivated the Calumet River corridor as a Tier 1 industrial processing zone, running automated recycling and material reclamation operations in the shells of the old steel mills. The mills that once employed thousands now employ dozens — human oversight for robotic systems that strip, sort, and reprocess the material output of Meridian's consumption. The work is toxic, monotonous, and pays just enough to keep a Tier 1 credential active. The workers call themselves steelgrave diggers, because they're mining the corpse of the industry that made this place.

The residential community clings to the edges of the industrial zone like moss on a factory wall. Housing is dense, low-rise, and located downwind of operations that Axiom's environmental reports describe as within acceptable parameters. The acceptable parameters are set by Axiom. Lake Michigan is visible from the eastern blocks, but the shoreline is restricted — Axiom controls waterfront access for cargo operations. The Calumet River, once the neighborhood's economic artery, is now a corporate logistics channel: automated barges moving reclaimed materials to processing facilities further north. Residents can see the river. They cannot reach it without crossing corporate sovereign territory.

But South Calumet has a resource that Axiom's surveys didn't account for: institutional memory. The union halls are still standing. The organizing traditions that built the labor movement in this part of the city didn't disappear when the mills closed — they went dormant. The steelgrave diggers have started talking in the old vocabulary: collective bargaining, work actions, solidarity. It's small, it's quiet, and it's the first labor organizing in Axiom's industrial zones in over a decade. If it succeeds, the implications extend far beyond one district. If it's discovered, the implications for the organizers will be personal and severe.
atmosphere
sights
  • Automated recycling operations in the skeletal frames of old steel mills — robots working where thousands once stood
  • The Calumet River choked with automated barges, moving in formation, navigation lights reflecting off dark water
  • Residential blocks huddled against the industrial zone perimeter, laundry lines strung between buildings like flags of occupation
  • Lake Michigan visible between industrial structures — a glimpse of open water you can't reach
  • The old union hall, its facade weathered but intact, lights on inside after shift change
  • Smokestacks that haven't produced smoke in decades standing like headstones over the industrial zone
sounds
  • The grinding rhythm of automated material reclamation — metal on metal, continuous, the district's heartbeat
  • Barge navigation signals on the Calumet River, mechanical and regular
  • Wind off the lake hitting the industrial structures, producing a low moan that residents stop hearing after the first year
  • Shift-change announcements from Axiom's facility speakers, audible in the residential blocks whether they want to hear them or not
  • Quiet conversations in the union hall after hours, voices kept low out of habit and necessity
smells
  • Metal and chemical processing — a taste more than a smell, coating the back of the throat
  • River water carrying industrial runoff, a particular stink that South Calumet natives identify as home
  • Lake air when the wind shifts east, briefly clean, a reminder of what air could be
  • Machine oil and recycled lubricant from the automated facilities, drifting into the residential blocks
feel South Calumet feels like a place that has been used up and is being used again. The exhaustion is in the buildings, the soil, the water, the people. But there's something under the exhaustion — a stubbornness inherited from the union era, a refusal to accept that labor has no leverage. The feeling is pre-storm: everything is quiet and everything is charged.
tags —
demographics Approximately 15,000 residents, down from 40,000 in the steel era. Mixed-heritage community — historically Eastern European and Mexican-American, now joined by climate refugees and displaced workers from other collapsed industrial zones. Predominantly Tier 1. The population is aging and the young leave when they can.
economy Axiom automated recycling and material reclamation. Subsistence wages for human oversight positions. Small-scale fishing on restricted lake access. An informal economy of repair and salvage that operates in the margins of the industrial zone.
power structure Axiom Industries holds sovereign authority over the industrial zone and waterfront. Residential blocks fall under general Axiom governance with minimal services. The nascent labor organizing in the union hall represents the only challenge to Axiom's authority, and it hasn't revealed itself yet.
dangers
  • Toxic exposure from industrial operations — respiratory and neurological effects are documented by community clinicians and ignored by Axiom
  • Axiom security monitors the industrial zone perimeter and treats unauthorized access as trespassing in sovereign territory
  • Labor organizing, if discovered, will be met with termination, tier demotion, and possible relocation to lower-tier zones
  • The Calumet River's automated barge traffic is hazardous to anyone in the water — the systems don't detect human-sized objects
  • Structural decay in the residential blocks, where Axiom has no maintenance obligation and the residents have no maintenance budget
opportunities
  • The union hall's organizing effort, if supported, could become the first successful collective action against Axiom's industrial operations
  • Axiom's automated systems have documented vulnerabilities — the recycling facilities run on legacy software that hasn't been updated
  • The Calumet River provides water access to the broader southern waterway network, if you can navigate the barge traffic
  • Institutional memory of labor organizing tactics is a strategic resource that other districts lack
  • Environmental data from South Calumet could support legal challenges to Axiom's industrial operations across Meridian
story hooks
  • The steelgrave diggers' organizing effort has been infiltrated — someone in the union hall meetings is reporting to Axiom. The organizers need to identify the informant before their next action, planned for the month's end.
  • An automated recycling facility has uncovered something in the material stream that wasn't supposed to be there — pre-collapse military hardware, still functional, mixed into a shipment of reclaimed construction materials. Axiom doesn't know yet. The shift supervisor who found it has forty-eight hours before the next inventory audit.
  • A retired steelworker from the original mills has been mapping the underground infrastructure beneath the industrial zone — tunnels, pipes, access points that predate Axiom's occupation. He's offering the maps to anyone who'll promise to use them.

South Deering Sump #

type place
name South Deering Sump
aliases
  • South Deering
  • The Sump
  • Slag Beach
  • Wisconsin Grave
description South Deering Sump is where Meridian 88 keeps its worst secrets, sealed under contaminated water and abandoned industrial infrastructure. The original South Deering was already haunted before the collapse — the Wisconsin Steel plant closure in 1980 was one of the most brutal in American industrial history, three thousand workers losing their jobs in a single day with no warning and no severance, their pension fund looted by management. The land the plant stood on was so contaminated that remediation estimates exceeded the property value by a factor of ten. Nobody cleaned it up. Nobody ever does.

When the Calumet River's water levels rose, the contaminated industrial sites along its banks didn't just flood — they dissolved. Decades of industrial waste that had been sitting in soil and slag heaps entered the water column, creating a toxic soup that now fills the low-lying areas of the former industrial zone. The Sump, as locals call it, is a landscape of half-submerged factory ruins standing in water that changes color depending on what the current is stirring up. Orange means iron compounds. Green means copper salts. Black means don't ask. The water is warm in places where underground chemical reactions are still running, steam rising from the surface on cold mornings like breath from a sleeping industrial corpse.

Axiom classified South Deering Sump as an exclusion zone — corporate territory in name, abandoned in practice, maintained at the minimum level required to prevent contamination from spreading to adjacent districts. This means a perimeter fence, monitoring stations that are checked quarterly, and a total absence of residential services. But people live here anyway, because people live everywhere that institutions abandon. The Sump's population consists of the truly excluded — those whose tier status is so far below the floor that even the Shelf won't have them. They live in the upper floors of factory ruins, above the waterline, in conditions that no one with options would accept. They fish the contaminated water for mutated species that they eat because the alternative is not eating.

The Sump's value, such as it is, lies in its toxicity. Nobody comes here willingly, which makes it an effective hiding place for things that need hiding. Smugglers use the flooded factory complexes as warehouses — the contamination keeps casual intruders out and the Axiom exclusion zone classification keeps corporate security from patrolling beyond the perimeter. The Calumet River provides water access to South Calumet, Old Harbor, and eventually Lake Michigan. And beneath the water, in the sealed vaults of the old Wisconsin Steel administrative complex, there are records — personnel files, financial documents, corporate communications — that were never digitized because the company died before the digital transition and nobody thought paper records at the bottom of a toxic lake were worth recovering. Someone might think differently now.
atmosphere
sights
  • Half-submerged factory ruins rising from discolored water — industrial cathedrals slowly being consumed
  • Water that shifts color by the hour: orange, green, iridescent black, depending on subsurface chemistry
  • Steam rising from warm spots where underground chemical reactions continue decades after operations ceased
  • The perimeter fence, more symbolic than functional, its warning signs faded to illegibility
  • Improvised shelters in factory upper floors, lights visible through broken industrial windows after dark
  • Mutated aquatic life visible in the shallows — oversized, discolored, moving in ways that suggest adaptation to something
sounds
  • Water moving through industrial ruins — a gurgling, echoing sound unique to flooded structures
  • Chemical reactions bubbling to the surface in the warm zones, a low persistent fizz
  • The creak of metal structures under water stress, factory skeletons shifting on their foundations
  • Quiet — the Sump is one of the quietest places in Meridian because almost no one is here
  • Occasionally, the sound of a hull moving through water — smugglers navigating the flooded channels
smells
  • Chemical contamination — sharp, metallic, with an organic undertone that suggests biological processes nobody wants to study
  • Rust and decay — the smell of industrial infrastructure returning to its constituent elements
  • Steam from the warm zones carrying a sulfurous edge
  • Nothing clean — the Sump has no clean smell. Every breath carries a reminder of what was done here.
feel South Deering Sump feels like guilt made physical. This is what happens when industry takes everything from a place and then leaves the corpse for someone else to deal with. The contamination is not an accident or a tragedy — it's a ledger entry, a cost that was calculated, accepted, and externalized onto people who couldn't refuse it. Living here means breathing that calculation every day.
tags —
demographics Population estimates range from 2,000 to 5,000, though no census has been attempted. Entirely untier-ed or functionally Tier 0. The most marginalized population in Meridian 88 — those with nowhere else to go. Mixed origins, united by exclusion.
economy Subsistence fishing in contaminated water. Smuggling infrastructure — warehouse space in the flooded factories, water route access via the Calumet River. Salvage operations in the industrial ruins, extracting metals and materials that retain value despite contamination. No formal economy exists.
power structure No governance. Axiom's exclusion zone classification means the district exists on paper as corporate territory with no corporate presence. Informal authority belongs to whoever controls the most functional factory shelter and the best water access points. Smuggling operations bring external power dynamics into the Sump on a transactional basis.
dangers
  • Toxic exposure — the water, the air, the soil are all contaminated, and the health effects are cumulative and severe
  • Structural collapse — flooded factory ruins are structurally unpredictable and fail without warning
  • Isolation — the Sump is far from medical care, mutual aid networks, and emergency response of any kind
  • The things in the water — mutated aquatic life that has adapted to the contamination and doesn't always avoid humans
  • Smuggling operations attract attention that the Sump's vulnerable population cannot defend against
  • The contamination itself is not stable — chemical reactions continue underground, and sudden toxic releases have occurred
opportunities
  • The flooded factory complexes provide unmonitored warehouse space accessible by water
  • Calumet River access connects to the broader southern waterway network
  • The Wisconsin Steel administrative vault contains undigitized records that may have significant intelligence value
  • The Sump's exclusion zone status means Axiom security does not patrol inside the perimeter — an increasingly rare condition in Meridian
  • Environmental contamination data, properly documented, could support legal action against Axiom or its predecessor entities
story hooks
  • A salvage diver working the Wisconsin Steel ruins has found the sealed administrative vault and realized the paper records inside are intact. She can't read them — they're in 20th-century corporate accounting notation — but she knows someone who can, if she can get the documents out without them dissolving in the contaminated water.
  • The warm zones in the Sump are getting warmer. Underground chemical reactions are accelerating, and the excluded population is reporting new symptoms — neurological, not just respiratory. Something has changed in the chemistry, and no one with the expertise to diagnose it is willing to enter the exclusion zone.
  • A smuggling operation has established a major waypoint in the Sump, and the traffic has attracted attention from a competing faction. The excluded population is caught in the middle, and the only person who's offered to help them is asking for something in return that they don't understand.

South Shore Strand #

type place
name South Shore Strand
aliases
  • South Shore
  • The Strand
  • The Ballroom District
description South Shore Strand takes its name from the thing it lost: the shoreline. When Lake Michigan's levels rose and the southern sea wall proved inadequate — a Meridian Infrastructure Corp project that came in under budget and under specification — the lakefront blocks of the old South Shore neighborhood went the way of Old Harbor, slowly and then all at once. What remains is a half-drowned waterfront district where the water has been incorporated into daily life rather than fought. Elevated walkways connect the surviving inland blocks. The flooded eastern edge has become a littoral zone — not quite land, not quite lake — where houseboats, floating platforms, and anchored barges form a waterborne community that the Meridian census doesn't count and Axiom Security doesn't patrol.

The crown jewel is still the South Shore Cultural Center, though nobody calls it that anymore. The building — originally a private country club, then a public cultural center, then abandoned, then reclaimed — sits on elevated ground just above the flood line, its Spanish Revival architecture weathered but standing. The community seized it during the infrastructure collapse and has held it since, converting it into the closest thing the southern corridor has to a free cultural institution. The ballroom hosts community gatherings, concerts, mutual aid distributions, and, on certain nights, gatherings that Axiom would classify as seditious assembly. The building's legal status is contested — three different entities claim ownership, and the court case has been in continuance for eleven years. In the meantime, the people who use it keep the lights on and the doors open.

The Strand's inland blocks retain the character of the original South Shore — residential, community-oriented, historically Black, with a middle-class pride that survived the collapse even as the economic basis for it didn't. The bungalows and apartment buildings are maintained with a ferocity that borders on devotion, painted and patched and reinforced against flooding, each one a statement that the people who live here are not leaving. Small businesses operate from ground floors: barbers, neural interface repair, a fish market supplied by the waterborne community's daily catch. The economy is local, circular, and largely invisible to Meridian's official metrics.

The waterborne community on the flooded eastern edge is its own ecosystem. Houseboats range from engineered flotation platforms with solar arrays to barely-floating scrap rafts held together by cable and determination. The residents are a mix of untier-ed flood refugees, fishermen who work the lake's increasingly strange ecology, and people who simply prefer a life that no corporation has jurisdiction over. The water here connects to Old Harbor's canal network to the south, making the Strand a waypoint on the aquatic smuggling routes that move goods and people through Meridian's ungoverned waterways.
atmosphere
sights
  • The South Shore Cultural Center rising above the flood line, its Spanish Revival arches reflected in standing water
  • Elevated walkways connecting inland blocks, strung with solar lanterns that glow amber at dusk
  • Houseboats and floating platforms on the flooded eastern edge, a waterborne neighborhood with its own geography
  • Well-maintained bungalows with sandbag foundations and hand-painted trim, defiant against the water
  • Fishing boats heading out at dawn toward the lake, their running lights visible from shore
  • The flood line itself — a visible mark on every building, measuring what was lost
sounds
  • Water lapping against elevated walkway supports — the Strand's metronome
  • Music from the Cultural Center ballroom, carrying across the district on quiet nights
  • Fishing boats returning, engines cutting as they approach the floating docks
  • Community radio broadcasting from somewhere in the waterborne district, signal crackling but persistent
  • The creak and groan of houseboats settling in their moorings
smells
  • Lake water — cleaner here than in Old Harbor, but carrying its own chemical signature
  • Fresh fish from the morning catch, sold dockside before the sun gets high
  • Paint and sealant from buildings under perpetual maintenance against the water
  • Cooking from the Cultural Center kitchen on distribution days — enough food for the block, barely
feel The Strand feels like a place that refused to drown. The water came and the people stayed, and now the water is just another neighbor. There's a dignity here that has nothing to do with tier status and everything to do with the decision, made daily, to keep the lights on and the doors open.
tags —
demographics Approximately 35,000 residents across inland and waterborne communities. Historically Black residential core with a growing waterborne population of mixed origins. Tier 1-2 inland, untier-ed on the water. The community's middle-class identity predates the collapse and persists despite economic reality.
economy Fishing, local services, and waterway logistics. The Cultural Center operates as a community economic hub — barter exchange, skills training, mutual aid distribution. The waterborne community trades fish and salvage for supplies from the inland blocks. Gray market water transport connects to broader smuggling networks.
power structure No single entity holds clear authority. The Cultural Center's community board is the closest thing to governance, managing the building and mediating disputes. Axiom claims jurisdiction over the inland blocks but doesn't invest in enforcement. The waterborne community is self-governing by necessity. The three-way ownership dispute over the Cultural Center keeps any one entity from asserting control.
dangers
  • Flooding — water levels are unpredictable and storm surges can swamp the elevated walkways
  • Structural failure in waterlogged buildings — the maintenance is heroic but not always enough
  • The waterborne community includes people hiding from serious trouble, and some of that trouble follows them
  • Axiom occasionally runs enforcement sweeps through the inland blocks, checking tier credentials and making arrests to meet quarterly metrics
  • The lake ecology has changed — what comes out of the water isn't always fish, and some of it is aggressive
opportunities
  • The Cultural Center is a neutral ground where factions that wouldn't meet elsewhere can negotiate
  • Waterway access connects to Old Harbor and the broader aquatic smuggling network
  • The waterborne community's knowledge of lake conditions and aquatic infrastructure is unmatched in Meridian
  • Community loyalty here is real and reciprocal — earn it and you have allies who don't fold under pressure
  • The contested ownership of the Cultural Center creates a legal gray zone that creative operators can exploit
story hooks
  • Someone is poisoning the lake catch in the Strand's fishing waters — the fish are dying and the waterborne community is losing its economic base. The contamination traces back to a source upstream, in Axiom-controlled territory.
  • The Cultural Center's eleven-year ownership case is about to be resolved, and the ruling will establish precedent for community-held property across Meridian. All three claimants are making moves, and at least one is willing to burn the building rather than lose it.
  • A waterborne resident found something on the lake bottom — a sealed container with pre-collapse military markings. She brought it home. Now people are asking about it, and the people asking aren't from the neighborhood.

Steelmouth #

type place
name Steelmouth
aliases
  • Hamilton ON
  • The Hammer
  • Slagtown
  • Steel City
description Hamilton was built on steel, and steel is still what Hamilton tastes like. The foundries that lined Burlington Bay in the twentieth century have been replaced by advanced metallurgical facilities producing augmentation-grade alloys, structural composites for arcology construction, and military-specification armor plating. Palladian Construction and Ashgrave Materials maintain sovereign manufacturing zones along the waterfront, their territory extending from the bay shore to the escarpment face — a vertical boundary that divides the city as cleanly as any corporate jurisdiction line. Below the escarpment: industry, smoke, and the people who make things. Above: residential towers for the managers, the engineers, and the people who profit from what gets made below.

The escarpment itself — a 100-meter limestone cliff running east-west through the city — is Steelmouth's defining geographic feature and its most literal class boundary. Elevators and cargo lifts connect the upper and lower cities, and access is controlled by Palladian security at every transition point. Workers descend in the morning and ascend in the evening, their movements tracked, their productivity monitored, their bodies gradually absorbing the particulate matter that the filtration systems don't quite catch. The lower city's air quality is rated 'acceptable' by corporate standards, which means it will kill you slowly rather than quickly.

Burlington Bay has been converted into a shipping hub for metallurgical products, connected to the broader Lake Ontario cargo network by automated barge lines. The waterfront is industrial infrastructure — cranes, smelters, cargo handling systems — with no concession to aesthetics or public access. The old Bayfront Park is now a materials staging area. The residential neighborhoods south and east of the escarpment maintain a grim vitality — these are communities that have survived a century of industrial exploitation by developing an immunity to corporate promises and a talent for mutual aid. Steelmouth's people are hard, practical, and deeply skeptical of anyone who arrives with a plan for their improvement.
atmosphere
sights
  • The escarpment face lit by cargo elevator lights at shift change — a vertical river of workers ascending
  • Foundry glow reflecting off Burlington Bay at night, turning the water copper and orange
  • Smoke stacks and processing towers rising above the lower city like a forest of industrial trees
  • Palladian security checkpoints at every escarpment elevator — scanners, ID verification, the daily ritual of proving you belong
  • The upper city's residential towers, clean and modern, looking down on the source of their wealth
sounds
  • The foundries — a deep, rhythmic pounding that the lower city's residents feel in their bones
  • Cargo cranes on the bay, hydraulic and relentless, loading barges around the clock
  • Shift-change sirens — the city's actual clock, more reliable than anything digital
  • Wind off the escarpment carrying industrial particulate — you hear it hit the filtration masks before you feel it
smells
  • Hot metal — the dominant note, always, everywhere in the lower city
  • Ozone from the electric arc furnaces, sharp and persistent
  • Burlington Bay water, mineral-heavy and warm from industrial discharge
  • The upper city smells like nothing, which is the most expensive smell there is
feel A city divided vertically by geology and horizontally by class. Steelmouth doesn't pretend. The escarpment makes the hierarchy visible, literal, carved into the landscape. Everyone knows their elevation, and everyone knows what it means.
tags —
demographics Population 1.8 million. The lower city is 70% Tier 1 and Tier 2 manufacturing workers. The upper city is Tier 3 and 4 corporate employees. The excluded live in the escarpment tunnels — old mine shafts and drainage channels converted into informal housing. Nobody counts them.
economy Advanced metallurgy and construction materials. Steelmouth produces 30% of the augmentation-grade alloys used in the eastern GLM and 60% of the structural composites for arcology construction. The economy is monoculture — when the foundries slow, everything slows. Palladian and Ashgrave set the pace, and the city walks to it.
power structure Palladian Construction holds the largest sovereign enclave. Ashgrave Materials holds the second. Between them they employ 65% of the working population. The municipal government administers the upper city residential zones and maintains the polite fiction that it governs the whole. The lower city's informal labor council has more practical authority than the mayor.
dangers
  • Industrial accidents — the foundries are dangerous, the safety standards are 'adequate,' and the distinction kills people
  • Escarpment access control — get your credentials revoked and you're trapped in the lower city
  • Particulate exposure — the long-term health effects are documented, ignored, and fatal
  • Labor disputes that turn physical — Steelmouth's workers have a history of direct action
  • Escarpment tunnel collapses in the informal housing zones
opportunities
  • Metallurgical expertise is rare and valuable — skilled workers can name their price outside Steelmouth
  • The labor council needs operatives for contract disputes that can't be resolved through negotiation
  • Ashgrave and Palladian sabotage each other constantly — there's always work for someone willing to get their hands dirty
  • The escarpment tunnels connect to pre-corporate infrastructure that nobody has fully mapped
story hooks
  • A new alloy being produced in the Palladian foundries has properties that don't match any known metallurgical process — and the engineers who developed it have stopped showing up to work
  • The escarpment tunnel network connects to something beneath the bay that predates the foundries by centuries — and Ashgrave is quietly excavating it
  • Steelmouth's labor council is organizing a cross-corporate strike that would shut down augmentation-grade alloy production across the eastern GLM

Substation Null #

type place
name Substation Null
aliases
  • The Null
  • Under-Zero
  • The Quiet Place
  • Station Nothing
description Substation Null is a decommissioned power relay hub occupying several interconnected levels beneath the northern stretch of The Shelf, accessible through maintenance tunnels, a handful of unofficial entry points, and one known surface entrance that most people who use it pretend doesn't exist. Originally constructed to manage power distribution for a now-demolished industrial sector, the station was officially abandoned during the infrastructure consolidation of the 2040s and subsequently removed from city maintenance records — an omission that was either bureaucratic error or deliberate, depending on who you ask.
atmosphere
sights
  • Enormous decommissioned transformer housings repurposed as walls, rooms, and structural supports
  • Bioluminescent fungal growth cultivated along certain corridors as low-maintenance lighting
  • Jury-rigged power taps drawing from nearby active conduits — the wiring is a palimpsest of decades of ad hoc additions
  • Chalk and spray-paint wayfinding marks in evolving community shorthand
  • Condensation dripping from ceiling infrastructure, collected in improvised cisterns
sounds
  • The deep subsonic hum of power conduits running overhead — felt more than heard
  • Dripping water echoing in high-ceilinged chambers
  • Muffled conversations from behind closed-off sections
  • Distant transit rumble from city infrastructure above
  • The occasional burst of sound from the deeper levels where noise discipline relaxes
smells
  • Damp concrete and mineral water
  • Old machine oil soaked into every surface
  • Cooking smells from the inhabited sections — usually something with a lot of spice
  • Ozone from the live power infrastructure
  • The particular staleness of recycled air that has been breathed too many times
feel The Null feels like the city's held breath — removed from the noise and surveillance above, heavy with the knowledge that the people here have chosen or been forced into invisibility. There is community in the dark, but also paranoia, and the infrastructure that shelters residents could kill them if it failed.
tags —
demographics A rotating population of 300-800 individuals depending on conditions above ground. Off-grid residents, fugitives, political dissidents, individuals escaping debt or corporate indenture, and a core of long-term inhabitants who have built permanent lives here. Also hosts a significant transient population using it as a waypoint.
economy Barter-dominant with some scrip circulating from the surface. Residents trade skills, scavenged materials, information, and labor. A small number of above-ground operators provide essential supplies in exchange for services the Null's population can uniquely offer: discretion, access to the tunnel network, and off-record technical work.
power structure The Council of Conductors — an ironic title adopted by seven long-term residents who manage resource allocation, dispute resolution, and security policy. Membership is earned through tenure and community trust rather than election. Their authority is real but consensus-based; they can be overruled by collective action and they know it.
dangers
  • Infrastructure failure — aging power conduits, unstable ceilings, and flooding from above are constant threats
  • City utility crews occasionally enter for maintenance and must be redirected or avoided
  • Bounty runners and corporate retrieval teams probe the tunnel network for specific targets
  • Interpersonal violence in a closed environment with no external authority
  • Air quality in the deeper sections requires monitoring and can degrade without warning
  • The power taps are illegal and any significant draw could trigger automated fault detection above ground
opportunities
  • Unmonitored meeting space with no surveillance infrastructure
  • Access to the tunnel network connecting to multiple districts across the city
  • A community of people with strong motivation to stay off official records — ideal for sensitive recruitment
  • Technical expertise concentrated among residents who have learned to maintain infrastructure with nothing
  • A repository of information about city infrastructure that predates current digital records
story hooks
  • The Council of Conductors has sent word through careful channels that something is moving through the deeper tunnels — something they cannot identify and are not willing to investigate alone
  • A child born in the Null has been identified by a corporate genetic database as carrying a proprietary gene sequence, triggering a legal claim of ownership that the above-ground courts are taking seriously
  • A section of the Null that has been sealed for fifteen years has begun broadcasting a repeating signal on a frequency that interferes with local neural implants
  • A long-term resident who served as an unofficial historian has died, and their records — which reportedly document the real reasons the station was decommissioned — have gone missing
  • The Council needs help negotiating with a new group that has moved into the deep tunnels — armed, organized, and not interested in the existing arrangement

name The Main Hall
description The largest interior space in the Null, occupying the footprint of the original primary relay chamber. The decommissioned transformer housings have been converted into residences, workshops, and communal spaces. A central fire pit — vented through a carefully maintained chimney improvised from old conduit — serves as the community's social center. The Council meets here in open session on the first of each month.

Maintained by a rotating archivist, it represents an unofficial history of both Substation Null and the city above from the perspective of those the city forgot.
tags —

description A tunnel extending beyond the known inhabited sections of the Null, running beneath city blocks that have changed ownership multiple times. The walls here predate the station itself, incorporating older infrastructure of uncertain purpose. The Council discourages exploration without escort, citing structural instability — though longtime residents suspect the reasons are more complicated.

The Alban Souk #

type place
name The Alban Souk
aliases
  • Albany Park
  • The Souk
  • Little Corridor
  • The Bazaar Quarter
description The Alban Souk is the last place in Meridian 88 where you can hear six languages in a single city block and none of them are corporate Standard. What was once Albany Park — Chicago's most ethnically diverse community area — became, after the incorporation, a jurisdiction gap that nobody wanted badly enough to claim. The big corponations carved up the profitable districts and left this one to itself, which turned out to be the best thing that ever happened to it. The Souk organized. Korean tech-repair dynasties merged their supply chains with Syrian fabrication workshops. Ethiopian coffee houses became dead-drop locations for data couriers. The old Lawrence Avenue commercial strip transformed into a covered market that stretches twenty-three blocks, roofed in salvaged solar panels and advertising screens running firmware so old the ads still show prices in dollars.

The covered market is the Souk's beating heart — a dense, noisy, sweltering corridor where you can buy unlicensed neural interface calibration from a Korean grandmother whose hands are steadier than any surgical robot, eat kibbeh made from vat-grown lamb that tastes better than the real thing ever did, and fence stolen corporate hardware in the same afternoon. The vendors operate on reputation networks that predate the corponation tier system by decades. Trust here is ethnic, familial, personal — encoded in relationships, not algorithms. Corporate scouts have tried to map these networks and failed every time, because the mapping requires understanding that commerce is a social act, and that is not something that fits in a quarterly report.

The demographics have shifted but not flattened. The Middle Eastern community anchors the western end, where the old mosque — now a community server farm cooling its racks with repurposed HVAC from a demolished Axiom subsidiary — still calls the faithful to prayer five times a day. The broadcast cuts through every frequency in the district, overriding even corporate emergency channels, and nobody has managed to stop it because nobody in the Souk will say where the transmitter is. The Korean corridor runs east, dominated by tech repair, augment customization, and a thriving market in refurbished military-grade optics that fell off the back of a Vantage Meridian logistics drone. Between these anchors, every other community in the Corridor has staked a claim: Guatemalan, Filipinx, Congolese, Romani. The Souk doesn't integrate. It adjacents. Everyone keeps their thing and shares the street.

Kyle comes here when he needs work done on his augments by someone who won't ask questions and won't cut corners. The Souk's technicians are unlicensed but excellent — trained in traditions that combine formal engineering with improvisational brilliance, passed down through families that have been fixing things since before the corps decided fixing things required a subscription.
atmosphere
sights
  • The covered market stretching twenty-three blocks under salvaged solar panels and dead advertising screens
  • Neon in Arabic, Korean, Amharic, and Spanish layered over each other like competing prayers
  • Augment technicians working in open shopfronts, chrome limbs hanging from hooks like butcher's wares
  • The old mosque's minaret retrofitted with signal arrays, blinking red against the haze
  • Street food stalls with steam rising through gaps in the market roof into filtered corporate air above
  • Children running courier routes between shops, faster than any drone in the narrow corridors
sounds
  • The adhan cutting through all frequencies five times daily — the Souk's unofficial clock
  • Haggling in languages the corporate translation AIs cannot parse because the dialects evolved post-incorporation
  • K-pop remixed with dabke beats bleeding from competing speakers in adjacent stalls
  • The hiss of soldering irons and the whine of augment calibration in the Korean tech corridor
  • The market's own white noise — thousands of transactions happening simultaneously in a space designed for hundreds
smells
  • Cardamom coffee and sesame from the Middle Eastern anchor, strong enough to taste
  • Hot solder and ozone from the tech repair shops
  • Fermented kimchi and gochugaru from the Korean corridor
  • The particular smell of too many people in a covered space — sweat, spice, and survival
feel Overwhelming and alive. The Souk assaults every sense simultaneously and makes no apology for it. There is a fundamental honesty here that the corporate districts cannot replicate — the honesty of people who have been trading face-to-face for generations and know that reputation is the only currency that doesn't inflate. It feels like the opposite of the Core: messy, loud, human, and functional.
tags —
demographics Approximately 95,000 residents representing over forty ethnic communities. Predominantly Tier 1 and Tier 2, with a merchant class that would qualify for Tier 3 if they acknowledged the tier system's legitimacy, which most do not. The Souk is the Corridor's most genuinely diverse district — not curated diversity, but the kind that happens when nobody with power cares enough to sort people.
economy —
power structure —
dangers
  • Getting lost — the covered market has no consistent addressing system and locals prefer it that way
  • Cultural misunderstandings that escalate fast in a place where honor still means something
  • Counterfeit augment components mixed in with quality goods — buyer expertise required
  • Protection rackets operating in the gaps between ethnic community territories
  • Corporate intelligence operatives trying to map the Souk's networks, and the people hunting them
  • The market roof is structurally questionable in the older sections and nobody wants to talk about it
opportunities
  • Augment work of exceptional quality at non-corporate prices
  • Intelligence networks that operate entirely outside corporate surveillance
  • Cultural knowledge and contacts spanning every community in the Corridor
  • Dead drop networks for data courier operations
  • The best food in Meridian 88, and this is a defensible claim
story hooks
  • The mosque transmitter that overrides corporate frequencies — someone wants it found, someone else wants it protected, and Kyle is caught between
  • A Korean augment dynasty is being pressured to sell their patents to Vantage Meridian, and their matriarch has decided she would rather fight than comply
  • Data hidden in the Souk's analog reputation networks — information that exists only in human memory, which makes it both invaluable and fragile

  • Fixers recruiting from the Souk's deep talent pool
  • Anyone who wants to eat well and doesn't care about ambiance

The Amber Stacks #

type place
name The Amber Stacks
aliases
  • The Stacks
  • Amber Row
  • The Resin District
  • Goldblock
description A vertical farming and pharmaceutical synthesis district rising from the flooded eastern fringe of what was once Waukegan's residential core, the Amber Stacks earned its name from the honeyed glow that pours from its tiered hydroponic bays at all hours — amber UV lamps burning through translucent polycarbonate panels stacked fourteen stories high across six interconnected tower blocks. The complex was originally built by Helix Biosystems as a controlled agricultural pilot in the 2160s, but corporate interest waned after the second Great Lakes salinity event, and the towers were sold piecemeal to a consortium of Tier 3 agricultural cooperatives, black-market chemists, and a surprisingly organized community land trust run by a collective of displaced Hmong and Somali-Bantu families who had been farming the lower levels without authorization since 2171.

Today the Amber Stacks is a contradictory place: part legitimate food production hub supplying leafy greens and fungal protein to a significant slice of the Lakeshore Corridor, part labyrinthine gray-market biosynthesis operation tucked into the upper floors where the elevator shafts stop and rope ladders begin. The air inside the towers is thick and tropical even in January, the humidity pressed into every surface by the constant transpiration of thousands of plant rows. Walkways between grow beds double as informal markets during the day, vendors selling clipped herb bundles, homegrown supplements, and unlicensed pharma compounds in plain brown sachets.

The towers are connected at the third and eighth floors by enclosed sky-bridges that have been colonized into something resembling a permanent bazaar — corrugated shelving, hanging privacy screens, the smell of cooking oil mixing with chlorophyll and damp earth. BCI signal here is intentionally throttled by a community-managed mesh that keeps corporate surveillance nodes from indexing the upper floors. Ferrogate Security holds a nominal contract for the ground level, but their operatives rarely venture above floor five, and everyone in the Stacks knows it.
atmosphere
sights
  • Amber and violet UV light bleeding through frosted panels, casting warm halos across wet grating
  • Cascading rows of lettuce, herbs, engineered grain-stalks, and bioluminescent mushroom clusters climbing every available surface
  • Sky-bridge markets strung with hand-painted inventory signs and tangled extension cords powering portable cold-storage units
  • Residents moving through grow lanes in rubber clogs and moisture-resistant coveralls, their BCI headsets fogged with condensation
  • Helix Biosystems corporate branding half-scraped from the tower facades, replaced with community murals in Somali and Hmong patterns
sounds
  • The constant low hum of irrigation pumps and circulation fans creating a droning white noise throughout every floor
  • Calls in Somali, Hmong, Tagalog, and Mandarin echoing across the sky-bridges during market hours
  • The wet drip of nutrient solution cycling through overhead pipes and the occasional clatter of a dropped harvest crate
  • Distant bass from a sound system someone has rigged into the eighth-floor bridge, playing low-tempo electronic folk
smells
  • Rich, green, slightly sweet smell of photosynthesizing plants layered over humid earth and nutrient solution
  • Cooking oil and fermented grain from the informal kitchen stalls in the sky-bridges
  • A sharp pharmaceutical undertone on the upper floors — solvents, acetone, something floral and slightly wrong
  • Mold and rot in the darker maintenance corridors where the irrigation drainage pools
feel The Amber Stacks feels like stepping into a living organism — warm, breathing, slightly resistant to movement, the air itself a presence that clings to clothing and skin. There is a low-level industriousness here that never quite stops, people trimming and harvesting and hauling at all hours, and a social density that reads as neighborly rather than threatening during daylight. After dark the upper floors acquire a different quality: quieter, more purposeful in a way that discourages questions. The mesh network's suppression of external BCI signals creates a subtle disorientation for newcomers, a slight cognitive flatness that the long-term residents have adapted to and newcomers find unsettling.
tags —
demographics Majority Tier 3 with pockets of Tier 2 cooperative stakeholders. Predominantly multigenerational families from the Hmong and Somali-Bantu communities who established the land trust, with a significant secondary population of independent chemists, unlicensed pharmacists, and agricultural workers of mixed global origin. Small but influential population of Tier 4 residents who moved up from the Shelf after finding stable work in the cooperative.
economy Dual economy: the legitimate face is a cooperative food production network supplying vegetables, fungi, and plant-based proteins to the Lakeshore Corridor and parts of the Northwest Sprawl, generating modest but stable Φ income distributed through the land trust. The gray-market economy in the upper floors is substantially more lucrative — unlicensed biosynthetics, agricultural compounds repurposed as pharma precursors, and a significant trade in unregistered BCI-compatible nootropics. The cooperative officially denies knowledge of the upper-floor operations.
power structure The Amber Stacks Community Land Trust holds formal authority over the lower floors and is governed by a rotating council of twelve elected representatives from the founding families. Above floor nine, authority is informal and syndicate-adjacent — a loose coalition of synthesis operators who pay a tithe to the land trust in exchange for non-interference. Ferrogate Security's ground-level contract gives them nominal access but no real leverage. Helix Biosystems retains a dormant legal claim to the tower infrastructure that everyone pretends does not exist.
dangers
  • Upper-floor biosynthesis operations attract periodic raids from Ferrogate corporate enforcement units acting on behalf of pharmaceutical clients — raids that are rarely announced and sometimes violent
  • The throttled BCI mesh means emergency services cannot be easily summoned and medical assistance is slow to arrive
  • Structural instability in towers four and five, where the original Helix construction was never fully completed — certain floors are weight-restricted and the restrictions are not always observed
  • Rival synthesis operators from outside the Stacks occasionally attempt to muscle into the upper floors, bringing armed pressure
  • Contamination events from improperly contained synthesis processes have twice required evacuation of grow floors below
opportunities
  • The land trust's leadership is actively seeking a negotiator or fixer capable of neutralizing the dormant Helix Biosystems legal claim before it is weaponized
  • The gray-market pharma network provides access to unlicensed compounds unavailable elsewhere in the Lakeshore Corridor at below-market rates for those with the right introductions
  • The community mesh network's architecture offers a rare zone of genuine BCI-surveillance dead space useful for sensitive meetings or data transfers
story hooks
  • A Helix Biosystems subsidiary has quietly retained a Palladian Group legal team to reactivate the tower infrastructure claim — not to reclaim the facility, but to use the legal threat as leverage to force the land trust's synthesis operators to supply precursor compounds exclusively to a Helix distribution network. The land trust council has one month before the filing goes public and is desperately looking for someone with the skills to find and destroy the evidence trail that Helix is using to establish the claim's validity.
  • A child from one of the founding families has developed a severe neurological reaction to something synthesized in the upper floors — something that was never supposed to leave that floor, and whose presence in the lower levels suggests either an accident or deliberate contamination. The family wants answers without involving Ferrogate or any outside authority, which means someone needs to go into the upper floors alone and find out what went wrong and why.

  • Buyers from Lakeshore Corridor food distribution networks picking up weekly produce contracts
  • Fixers and couriers using the mesh dead zone for sensitive handoffs
  • Ferrogate Security patrols conducting perfunctory ground-level checks

description The larger of the two sky-bridges, running between towers two and three at the eighth floor. The primary informal market space, active from mid-morning to late night, with a density of vendors and social activity that makes it feel like a compressed neighborhood street.

The Ashen Quorum #

type place
name The Ashen Quorum
aliases
  • The Quorum
  • Ashpit
  • The Convocation
description A sprawling subterranean civic ruin occupying the collapsed lower levels of what was once a Chicago municipal complex near the old Loop perimeter. Centuries of sediment, flood damage, and hasty structural reinforcement have transformed it into a labyrinthine underworld of half-flooded chambers and improvised galleries where displaced Tier 3 and 4 residents broker informal governance. The ceilings drip with mineral deposits that glow faintly under UV lighting rigs salvaged from Axiom Industries waste runs.

Despite its decrepit foundation, the Ashen Quorum functions as one of the corridor's most active gray-market legislative spaces, where neighborhood bloc leaders, syndicate liaisons, and rogue synthetic advocates hash out territorial agreements beyond the reach of Ferrogate Security patrols. The walls are plastered with decades of faction graffiti, printed manifestos, and Diaspora-linked AR overlays that shift depending on whose BCI credentials you're broadcasting.
atmosphere
sights
  • Bioluminescent mineral stalactites casting blue-white halos over crowded negotiation tables
  • Holographic faction banners flickering where water has damaged the projection nodes
  • Long corridors of cracked municipal tile stenciled with obsolete ward designations
sounds

The Austin Threshold #

type place
name The Austin Threshold
aliases
  • Austin
  • The Threshold
  • The West Wall
  • A-Town
description Austin was once the most populous community area in Chicago — a historically significant Black neighborhood that bore the accumulated weight of a century of racist disinvestment, white flight, redlining, and every other tool the American machine used to break communities it didn't value. When the incorporation came, Austin didn't fall. It was already down. The corps simply stepped over it.

The Austin Threshold is the western edge of Meridian 88's governed territory — the place where corporate jurisdiction doesn't end so much as evaporate, thinning from token presence to complete absence over the space of about two miles. The eastern blocks still have functioning MeriRail stations, intermittent Axiom Security patrols, and the basic infrastructure that comes with being technically inside the city. The western blocks have none of this. The western blocks have themselves. And that, it turns out, is substantial.

What corporate cartography calls the Threshold, residents call A-Town, and A-Town has been surviving on its own terms for longer than the corponations have existed. The community organizations that anchored Austin through the worst of the 20th and early 21st centuries — churches, mutual aid networks, neighborhood associations — evolved into something harder and more durable when the incorporation stripped away the last pretense of institutional support. The Austin Community Trust operates as a de facto government: managing water distribution, maintaining a community power grid running on solar arrays installed on every available rooftop, operating schools that teach practical skills alongside the academic curriculum, and running a community health system that is primitive by corporate standards and miraculous by Shelf standards. The Trust's leadership is elected, accountable, and ruthlessly practical. They do not waste time on ideology. They waste time on nothing.

The Threshold's population is predominantly Black, and the community's historical consciousness is razor-sharp. The Trust maintains an oral history project that traces Austin's trajectory from prosperous neighborhood to disinvested wasteland to abandoned zone to self-governing community — a narrative arc that the corporate version of history would prefer to forget. The elders who carry this history are treated with a reverence that has practical dimensions: they remember how the community survived before, and that knowledge is the Trust's most valuable asset.

Kyle respects A-Town in a way he respects few other places. Not because it's safe — it isn't — but because it is honest about what it costs to survive without permission. The Threshold doesn't pretend. It doesn't brand itself. It just continues, stubbornly, to exist, and to make that existence mean something.
atmosphere
sights
  • Rooftop solar arrays stretching block after block — the community's self-built power grid visible from above
  • The gradient from governed to ungoverned: streetlights thinning, corporate signage disappearing, community infrastructure replacing it
  • Austin Community Trust banners on public buildings — hand-painted, functional, unbranded
  • Community gardens occupying vacant lots — food production at a scale that suggests long-term planning
  • Churches that still function as churches, their steeples the tallest structures for blocks
  • Children walking to Trust-run schools in organized groups, watched by community monitors
sounds
  • Gospel music from Sunday services that haven't stopped for any apocalypse
  • Community Trust radio — low-power FM broadcasting weather, security updates, and cultural programming
  • The relative silence of the western blocks — no corporate ambient, no surveillance hum, just the city's actual voice
  • Construction — the Trust is always building, always repairing, always maintaining what it has
smells
  • Garden soil and growing food — the Trust's agricultural program is the most productive in the Corridor
  • Church cooking — community meals prepared in institutional kitchens that feed hundreds
  • The absence of corporate air treatment — A-Town breathes unfiltered, for better and worse
feel Dignified. That's the word that fits, even though it shouldn't have to be remarkable that a community maintains its dignity. A-Town feels like a place that has been told it doesn't matter by every institution with the power to say so, and has responded by mattering harder. There is grief here — for what was taken, for what was never given, for the people who didn't make it — but the grief is load-bearing. It holds things up.
tags —
demographics Approximately 100,000 residents, predominantly Black with growing populations of climate refugees and tier-displaced families from across the Corridor. Self-governing through the Austin Community Trust. Tier status: technically Tier 1, functionally autonomous. The Trust keeps its own records and does not share population data with corporate census systems.
economy —
power structure —
dangers
  • The western blocks' complete absence of emergency services — everything is community-managed or nothing
  • Territorial boundaries enforced by community security patrols that don't answer to anyone you can complain to
  • Resource scarcity — the Trust manages carefully, but there isn't enough of anything
  • Corporate neglect weaponized — infrastructure failures that the city won't repair and the Trust can barely patch
  • Being mistaken for a corporate scout — the community's patience for outside interference is exhausted
  • The emotional weight of a place where survival requires constant effort and has for generations
opportunities
  • Alliance with the most resilient self-governing community in the Corridor
  • The Trust's agricultural surplus as a trade commodity
  • Community intelligence networks refined over decades of institutional abandonment
  • Historical knowledge that corporate archives have suppressed — the elders remember
  • The Threshold's position at the Corridor's western edge — the gateway to everything beyond
story hooks

  • The Trust's solar grid is failing, and the only replacement components are in a Vantage Meridian warehouse — the Trust's leadership debates whether to buy, beg, or take
  • An elder carrying irreplaceable oral history is critically ill, and the only treatment exists in the Core — getting her there and back requires navigating every tier boundary in the Corridor

The Brine Scaffold #

type place
name The Brine Scaffold
aliases
  • The Salt Tier
  • Scaffold Row
  • The Hanging Flats
description A decommissioned water-treatment megastructure extending roughly two kilometers into Lake Michigan, its original Ringo Heavy Industries filtration towers now colonized by squatters, black-market fabricators, and those who prefer their addresses off the Diaspora's geotag grid. The scaffold's multiple decks were designed for industrial machinery, leaving open-grate walkways and massive vertical shafts that residents have converted into elevator markets, vertical farms, and tenement warrens threaded with improvised power taps from a single aging Zheng-Dao Bioelectric tidal siphon.

Wind off the lake hits the Brine Scaffold from every angle, carrying salt mist that corrodes exposed metal and ruins unprotected BCI hardware within months. Residents have adapted, coating gear in lacquer resins and wearing layered weather-wraps year-round. Despite its brutal conditions, the Scaffold maintains a fierce internal community identity, its floating isolation granting it a strange autonomy that Tier 1 and 2 residents elsewhere envy in quiet, ashamed ways.
atmosphere
sights
  • Laundry and signal-dampening mesh strung between rusted filtration towers, snapping in lake wind
  • Bioluminescent algae cultivated along handrail cables, casting cold blue-green light on wet grating
  • Cargo drones from Carrion Logistics making illegal low-altitude drops into the mid-deck markets
sounds
  • The low structural groan of the scaffold flexing against wave pressure
  • Hawkers shouting prices in Tagalog, Yoruba, and Mandarin through handheld voice amplifiers
  • The rhythmic clang of fabrication hammers two decks below, never fully stopping
smells
  • Heavy brine and algae rot carried on every gust
  • Cooking fat and chili oil from open-flame stalls on the mid-market deck
  • Burnt polymer insulation from overtaxed power taps
feel The scaffold feels perpetually precarious, as though the next storm system might finally finish what decades of neglect began. Yet residents move through it with practiced ease, ducking structural members and stepping gaps without looking down. There is an intimacy to the exposure—everyone out here is equally subject to the lake's indifference.
tags —

economy Informal fabrication, untaxed resale of salvaged Diaspora hardware, small-batch aquaculture, and a brisk trade in BCI-masking lacquers that Ferrogate Security would very much like to classify as contraband.
power structure No formal governance; a loose council of deck bosses—each controlling one scaffold level—negotiates resource access and settles disputes through a combination of reputation, muscle, and the implicit threat of cutting a rival's power tap.
dangers
  • Structural collapses during storm seasons, with failing grate sections dropping into the lake without warning
  • Ferrogate Security interdiction raids targeting unlicensed fabricators, occasionally turning violent in the confined scaffold corridors
  • E.L.F. entities that have nested inside the scaffold's original industrial control network, occasionally rerouting power or sealing bulkhead doors for unknown reasons
opportunities
  • Access to off-grid fabrication services capable of producing items that would flag corporate surveillance anywhere on the mainland
  • The E.L.F. network inside the old control systems may hold archived Ringo Heavy Industries data predating the Diaspora—valuable to the right buyer
  • Deck bosses quietly seek outside mediators for inter-level disputes, offering scaffold residency rights and deep-cover addresses as payment
story hooks
  • A Helix Biosystems whistleblower has been living under a false BCI signature on the Scaffold's upper deck for eleven months. Someone from the mainland has just arrived asking questions that are too specific to be coincidental, and the deck boss wants the situation resolved before Ferrogate shows up with a warrant.
  • The E.L.F. in the scaffold's control network has begun broadcasting a narrow-band signal detectable only to BCI users within fifty meters of the central filtration tower. The signal appears to be a request—but for what, and to whom it is addressed, no one on the Scaffold can determine.

The Brine Warrens #

type place
name The Brine Warrens
aliases

description Carved into the sediment beneath the old lakefront infrastructure, the Brine Warrens are a sprawling subterranean neighborhood formed by the slow collapse and flooding of pre-Meridian municipal tunnels, drainage systems, and the basements of buildings long since swallowed by the city's expansion westward. Seawater — or rather the chemical cocktail that passes for lake water this far into the industrial corridor — has seeped through every crack, leaving white salt crystals and rust blooms on every surface. The residents who call this place home have learned to live with perpetual damp, building upward on platforms and catwalks to stay above the tidal fluctuations that shift the water table twice daily.

The Brinewell #

type place
name The Brinewell
aliases
  • The Sump
  • Saltdown
  • The Drowned Deck
  • Brineworks
description The Brinewell occupies what was once the lower utility infrastructure of the Chicago lakefront's flood-mitigation system — a network of enormous cisterns, pump chambers, and drainage corridors that were supposed to keep the rising Lake Michigan at bay. They failed. By 2140, the entire sublevel complex had been partially inundated, and by 2160, a permanent community had taken root in the upper chambers where the water-line stabilized at roughly chest height on a standing adult. Residents built on elevated platforms, rope bridges, and salvaged pontoon structures, threading their lives through the half-flooded architecture like organisms adapted to an intertidal zone.

The Brinewell is neither fully aquatic nor fully terrestrial — it exists in a perpetual state of damp compromise. The old pump machinery still groans and cycles, maintained by a loose collective of engineers who trade their labor for living space and a kind of informal citizenship. The water itself has a brackish quality, a mix of lake ingress and old runoff that has taken on a faint greenish luminescence from the bioluminescent algae cultivated by Zheng-Dao Bioelectric's abandoned research substrate. Nobody planned the glow. It simply happened, and now it is the only light in the deeper sections.

Above the waterline, the inhabited platforms are dense with improvised structures — sleeping pods, food stalls, repair shops, and the occasional medical kiosk staffed by off-the-books practitioners. The BCI signal is weak and fragmented here; the metal walls and water scatter the Diaspora feed into unreliable static, which suits many residents just fine. The Brinewell has become a place where people go when they want to be functionally unfindable, at least by anything that relies on standard network infrastructure. Carrion Logistics operates two discrete courier relay points here, and nobody asks why their shipments don't appear in official manifests.
atmosphere
sights
  • Bioluminescent green-blue water casting rippling light patterns across corroded concrete ceilings twenty meters overhead
  • Rope-and-plank bridges swaying between rusted pump housings, strung with salvaged LED strips and paper lanterns
  • Silhouettes of residents poling flat-bottomed skiffs through flooded corridors below the inhabited platforms
  • Ancient flood-warning signage half-submerged, the red emergency text still legible above the waterline
  • Vertical gardens of water-tolerant greens hanging in wire frames from the platform undersides, roots trailing into the brine
sounds
  • The deep rhythmic clanking of pump machinery still cycling on automated schedules, felt as much as heard
  • Water lapping against pontoons and platform supports in syncopated overlapping rhythms
  • Voices echoing strangely off curved cistern walls, conversations arriving from unexpected directions
  • The occasional hiss and pop of a short-circuiting conduit somewhere in the deeper dark
smells
  • Salt and algae, a clean oceanic smell undercut by the faint mineral sharpness of old concrete
  • Cooking smells — fried lake protein, fermented soy paste — drifting across standing water in ways that concentrate rather than dissipate
  • Machine oil and rust from the pump housings, a metallic tang that settles on the back of the throat
  • The faint sweetness of the bioluminescent algae itself, something between petrichor and green tea
feel The Brinewell operates at a different tempo than the city above. Sound behaves wrongly here — dampened in some directions, amplified in others — and the constant ambient moisture means that every surface is slightly slick, every material slightly softened. The bioluminescent glow is beautiful in a way that feels almost manipulative, as though the place is performing serenity to compensate for its genuine precariousness.

The community here has a self-possessed insularity that isn't quite hostile but isn't warm either. Newcomers are watched. Long-termers are known by name, platform number, and skill set. The absence of reliable BCI connectivity creates a strange social texture — conversations happen face-to-face in ways that feel almost archaic, and the resulting community bonds are tighter and more fractious than anything in the networked city above.
tags —
demographics Approximately 800-1,200 permanent residents on any given cycle, with a transient population of several hundred more moving through. Heavily mixed ethnicity and origin — a significant population of second-generation migrants from Gulf Coast climate-displacement, alongside long-term Chicago Shelf overflow residents. A notable subgroup of voluntary disconnects, people who have had their BCI hardware removed or suppressed. Median tier: 1-2.
economy Informal barter supplemented by small Φ flows from surface-side patrons. Primary economic activities include water management labor, algae cultivation and processing (sold to surface markets through intermediaries), repair and salvage work, and discreet storage and courier relay services for parties who prefer undocumented logistics. Carrion Logistics maintains informal arrangements worth an estimated Φ40,000-60,000 annually through the community.
power structure A loose Pump Council of seven engineers who control access to the mechanical systems theoretically holds authority, but actual governance is distributed and contentious. Platform captains hold informal sway over their immediate neighborhoods. No corponation has formal claim — Ferrogate Security has twice attempted to establish a presence and twice been encouraged to leave through means that were never officially reported.
dangers
  • Unexpected flood surges from Lake Michigan storm events, which can raise water levels two to three meters within hours
  • Structural failure of aging pontoon and platform infrastructure, particularly in the deeper older sections
  • Fragmented BCI and Diaspora access making emergency communication and medical response nearly impossible
  • Criminal elements using the undocumented logistics infrastructure for cargo that ranges from contraband tech to worse
  • Zheng-Dao Bioelectric occasionally sends retrieval teams for proprietary research substrate — the algae — and these visits are not friendly
opportunities
  • Undocumented storage and transit services for parties who need things to move without appearing on any manifest
  • Access to bioluminescent algae derivatives with pharmaceutical and industrial applications that surface-side suppliers cannot legally source
  • Off-grid medical, identity, and communications services for those who need to exist outside normal network visibility
  • Salvage access to partially submerged pre-flood infrastructure containing recoverable technology and materials
story hooks
  • A Zheng-Dao Bioelectric research team arrives claiming rights to the algae bloom that has sustained the Brinewell community for decades — their proprietary substrate, their IP, their property. The Pump Council has three days to respond before Ferrogate Security contractors arrive to enforce the claim. Someone inside the community has been feeding Zheng-Dao location data for months, and the betrayal is about to surface along with everything else.
  • A sealed maintenance corridor in the deepest flooded section has started emitting a regular low-frequency signal that residents can feel in their chests but can't locate on any spectrum analyzer. Three people who investigated independently have returned altered — not harmed, not visibly changed, but different in ways their neighbors can't quite articulate. Someone needs to go deeper and find out what's broadcasting, and whether it started recently or has been transmitting for years unnoticed.
  • A child born in the Brinewell has never had a BCI implant and has never been registered in any corponation or municipal system — legally, she doesn't exist. She's seventeen now and has developed an uncanny ability to navigate the Diaspora through salvaged external hardware, doing things with fragmented signal that licensed operators can't explain. Three separate parties have arrived in the same week to find her: a Sterling-Nakamura recruiter, someone claiming to be a civil rights advocate for synthetic and unregistered persons, and a person who won't say who they represent at all.
