The Burnished Market #

type place
name The Burnished Market
aliases
  • Ohio City
  • West Side Market District
  • The Burnish
description The West Side Market survived. That is the first thing anyone tells you about Ohio City, and it is both true and insufficient. The 1912 market building still stands at West 25th and Lorain, its clock tower rebuilt three times and its interior converted from open-air stalls to a sealed, climate-controlled food processing and distribution hub. But survival here means transformation. The market that once sold produce from local farms now distributes synthetic protein, vat-grown vegetables, and nutrient pastes manufactured by Gravemoss Biofoundry subsidiaries. The old vendor stalls have been replaced by automated dispensing units and small-batch artisan operations that cater to Tier 3 and above — real food, made from biological ingredients, at prices that would feed a Tier 1 family for a month.

The neighborhood surrounding the market has followed the same trajectory. Ohio City's craft breweries and farm-to-table restaurants evolved into a curated food-technology district where synthetic biology startups test consumer products on a population that can afford to be adventurous. The streets are cleaner than The Gate but messier than the corporate zones — a lived-in quality that the marketing materials call 'authentic' and residents call 'underfunded.' The old Victorian houses that made Ohio City architecturally distinctive in the 22nd century are mostly intact, their facades preserved by heritage ordinances that Tollgate enforces because the aesthetic drives property values. Behind the preserved facades, the interiors have been gutted and rebuilt with modern infrastructure — neural-integrated climate systems, biometric security, the standard kit of a Tier 2-3 residential zone.

The Burnished Market is Ohio City's street name, derived from the copper-toned patina that Gravemoss biofilm coatings have given to most of the neighborhood's exterior surfaces. The coating is functional — it regulates humidity and provides passive air filtration — but the visual effect is a warm, metallic sheen that makes the entire district look like it's been dipped in old pennies. Residents either love it or hate it. Gravemoss doesn't care. The coating contract pays Φ4.2 million annually and gives them a consumer-facing showcase for their biofilm technology.
atmosphere
sights
  • The West Side Market clock tower, rebuilt in carbon fiber but shaped to match the 1912 original
  • Gravemoss biofilm coating on every surface — a warm copper-bronze sheen that shifts color with humidity
  • Preserved Victorian row houses with gutted-and-rebuilt interiors visible through smart-glass windows
  • Artisan food stalls competing with automated dispensing units — old economy and new economy, side by side
  • Small-batch fermentation labs with transparent walls, cultures glowing in calibrated bioluminescence
sounds
  • Market vendors — both human and AI-assisted — calling out products in a cadence that hasn't changed in two centuries
  • The low gurgle of biofilm maintenance systems circulating through building facades
  • Kitchen noise from the food-tech startups — industrial mixers, centrifuges, the occasional small explosion
  • Street musicians playing analog instruments, which is a political statement here
  • The 6 AM market bell — a tradition maintained by the neighborhood council since 1912
smells
  • Fermentation — the sweet-sour tang of biocultures and the sharper note of traditional brewing coexisting block by block
  • Synthetic protein being seasoned and cooked — close to real meat, never quite right
  • The copper-mineral scent of Gravemoss biofilm after rain
  • Real coffee, real bread, real garlic — from the artisan stalls that serve Tier 3 and above
feel The Burnished Market feels like a compromise between what Cleveland was and what the corridor has become. It is gentrified in the deepest sense — the original character preserved as a selling point while the substance is replaced — but enough of the original stubbornness remains that the neighborhood resists full corporate absorption. People here cook. People here argue about food. That means something, even if the food is grown in a vat.
tags —
demographics Residential population of approximately 22,000, predominantly Tier 2-3. A mix of food-technology professionals, Tollgate mid-level employees, and a stubborn enclave of original Ohio City families who have held their properties through three generations of corporate rezoning. The market itself draws 40,000 visitors daily from across the Cleveland sprawl.
economy Food technology is the primary industry — synthetic protein development, biofilm applications, fermentation science, and artisan food production for the upper tiers. The market serves as both retail hub and product testing ground. Gravemoss Biofoundry holds three subsidiary operations in the district. Tollgate collects infrastructure fees on every transaction.
power structure Tollgate holds infrastructure sovereignty. Gravemoss holds significant economic influence through its biofilm contracts and subsidiary operations. The West Side Market Council — a neighborhood governance body with roots in the original market vendor association — negotiates between them with surprising effectiveness, leveraging the district's cultural cachet as a bargaining chip.
dangers
  • Biofilm exposure — prolonged contact with improperly maintained Gravemoss coatings can cause respiratory sensitization
  • Food fraud — the line between 'artisan' and 'synthetic marketed as artisan' is policed inconsistently
  • Gentrification enforcement — Tollgate's heritage ordinances are selectively applied to push out residents who lower property algorithms
  • Corporate testing — some food-tech startups test products on lower-tier consumers without full disclosure
  • Price volatility — real food prices fluctuate wildly based on supply chain disruptions from the lake shipping routes
opportunities
  • The food-tech sector is growing and hires across tiers — genuine upward mobility exists here
  • The market's reputation as neutral ground makes it a preferred meeting spot for fixers and their clients
  • Gravemoss is always recruiting taste testers and biofilm maintenance workers — low-barrier employment
  • The old Ohio City tunnel network connects to the Red Line system beneath The Gate
story hooks
  • A batch of Gravemoss biofilm has started behaving unpredictably — changing color, emitting sounds, possibly growing in patterns that suggest rudimentary intelligence
  • The West Side Market Council is being pressured to sell the market building to Tollgate for full corporate conversion, and the holdout families are looking for leverage
  • Someone is selling real meat at the market — actual animal protein — and nobody can figure out where it's coming from

The Burnline #

type place
name The Burnline
aliases
  • Fuller Park
  • The Burn
  • Dead Zone
  • The Gap
description Fuller Park was the least populated community area in Chicago, a small South Side pocket bisected by the Dan Ryan Expressway, which cut through it like a blade through already-thin fabric. It was a neighborhood defined by what had been taken from it — residents, investment, attention, hope. When the corporate sovereignty treaties redrew Meridian 88's map, Fuller Park was not annexed. It was not developed. It was not even officially abandoned. It was simply not included. The Burnline exists in the gap between corporate jurisdictions, a district that belongs to no one because no one wanted it.

The Dan Ryan's footprint was converted into a Ferrogate Transit maglev corridor in the 2040s, its massive concrete infrastructure repurposed as the support structure for an elevated transit line connecting the South Side to the Core. The construction process incinerated what remained of Fuller Park's built environment on either side of the corridor — demolition, clearing, scorch-and-build. When the maglev was complete, the cleared land on either side was designated as a transit buffer zone. No construction permitted. No habitation authorized. The Burnline gets its name from this process: the neighborhood was burned to make room for a transit system that does not stop here.

But people live in the Burnline. They always have. The buffer zone's prohibition on construction is enforced by Ferrogate Transit's security drones, which patrol the corridor and destroy unauthorized structures. The residents have adapted. They build nothing permanent. Shelters are assembled from materials that can be disassembled in the time it takes a drone to complete its patrol circuit — approximately seven minutes. Entire camps appear and vanish on this rhythm, a community that exists in the gaps between surveillance sweeps, constructing and deconstructing its own neighborhood multiple times per day. It is exhausting. It is also a form of engineering that no corporate architect could replicate.

The Burnline's population is the most vulnerable in M88 — untier-ed individuals, the displaced, the excluded, people for whom even the Shelf's minimal protections are unavailable. There is no economy here in any formal sense. There is sharing. There is mutual aid. There is the particular solidarity of people who have nothing left to lose and therefore nothing left to protect except each other. The maglev passes overhead every four minutes, carrying Tier 3 passengers between the South Side and the Core. They do not look down. The Burnline is invisible from above, which is exactly how its residents survive.
atmosphere
sights
  • The Ferrogate maglev corridor overhead: massive concrete supports, the train passing every four minutes, casting rhythmic shadows
  • Temporary shelters assembling and disassembling on a seven-minute cycle — architecture as performance
  • Drone patrol lights sweeping the buffer zone, the residents timing their movements to the gaps
  • Scorched earth on either side of the corridor — the original neighborhood's ghost visible in foundation outlines
  • Small fires in concrete depressions, invisible from above, providing warmth and cooking heat
sounds
  • The maglev every four minutes: a building roar, a doppler whine, silence, repeat
  • Drone patrol hum: predictable, mechanical, the clock by which the Burnline sets its life
  • The rapid assembly of shelter materials — clicks, snaps, the sound of practice
  • Quiet human conversation in the gaps between train passes
  • Wind through the open buffer zone — no buildings to block it, no walls to muffle it
smells
  • Scorched concrete — the original demolition's residue, still present after decades
  • Small cooking fires: whatever is available, prepared quickly
  • Maglev ozone and lubricant drifting down from the elevated track
  • Open air — the Burnline has no enclosed spaces and therefore no enclosed smells
feel Survival stripped to its essential rhythm. The Burnline feels like living inside a clock — everything timed to the drone patrols, the train passes, the seven-minute construction windows. It is the most precarious place in M88 and paradoxically the most free, because nobody is trying to control the people here. They have simply been forgotten, and in that forgetting, they have found a space that belongs to them.
tags —
demographics Population uncounted and fluctuating — estimates range from 500 to 2,000 depending on season and displacement patterns. Entirely untier-ed. The most demographically diverse district in M88 by default, as the excluded come from every community the corporate system has ejected.
economy No formal economy. Mutual aid, barter, and sharing constitute the entirety of economic activity. Scavenging from the maglev corridor's maintenance waste provides raw materials. The Burnline produces nothing and consumes almost nothing — it exists outside the economic system entirely.
power structure Ferrogate Transit holds jurisdiction over the maglev corridor and buffer zone. No entity governs the residents. Informal leadership emerges from experience and generosity — those who have survived longest and share most freely. There is no hierarchy because there is nothing to be hierarchical about.
dangers
  • Ferrogate drone patrols destroy unauthorized structures — being inside one when it is detected is lethal
  • No emergency services, no medical care, no infrastructure of any kind
  • Exposure to weather in an open buffer zone with no permanent shelter
  • The maglev corridor's electromagnetic field may cause long-term health effects — no studies have been conducted
  • Periodic Ferrogate 'clearance operations' that force total population displacement
opportunities
  • The Burnline is genuinely invisible to corporate surveillance — the buffer zone is monitored for structures, not people
  • Transit corridor maintenance access points connect to infrastructure networks throughout the South Side
  • The seven-minute construction cycle has produced engineering expertise unavailable anywhere else in M88
  • Information passes through the Burnline without being intercepted because no one is listening
  • The excluded population includes former corporate employees, researchers, and specialists who fell through the tier system
story hooks
  • A former Ferrogate engineer living in the Burnline knows how to access the maglev's control systems from the maintenance access points beneath the corridor — she has not used this knowledge, but someone has found out she has it
  • The Burnline's seven-minute construction technique has caught the attention of Arcturus Defense Solutions, who see military applications in rapid-deployment shelter systems — they want to recruit, and recruitment in the Burnline looks a lot like conscription
  • A child in the Burnline has been building something during the seven-minute windows — not a shelter, something else, something complex, assembled and disassembled hundreds of times until it works, and nobody knows what it does yet
connections

tags —

  • Displaced people from adjacent districts using the Burnline as temporary refuge
  • Couriers and freelancers using the invisible corridor for unmonitored transit
  • Ferrogate maintenance workers who have learned to unsee the residents
  • Former professionals who fell through the tier system and landed here

The Calcine Terrace #

type place
name The Calcine Terrace
aliases
  • Calcine
  • The Burn Shelf
  • Whitewall
  • The Ledge
description A sprawling industrial plateau perched at the southern lip of the Waukegan transitional zone, The Calcine Terrace is the remnant of a mid-21st-century lime-processing complex that was never properly decommissioned. Decades of calcium dust and chemical runoff have bleached every surface a ghostly, chalky white — walls, railings, even the scrub vegetation that clings to cracked expansion joints glows pale under UV lighting at night. Squatters and Tier 2 laborers converted the upper processing levels into a dense residential warren in the 2150s, threading hab-pods and tension-cable walkways between the old kilns.

The lower kiln chambers still radiate ambient heat year-round, making The Calcine Terrace a coveted refuge during brutal Great Lakes winters but a slow suffocation risk in summer. Ferrogate Security holds a nominal contract here but rarely sends patrols deeper than the outer access ramp. The real authority belongs to a loose confederation of kiln-block bosses who tax passage, utilities, and water ration drops with ruthless consistency.
atmosphere
sights
  • Every horizontal surface is coated in pale mineral dust that catches the sodium glow of jury-rigged lamp strips, making the whole terrace look lit from within.
  • Hab-pods are stacked four and five high against the old kiln towers, connected by swaying rope-and-rebar bridges draped in laundry and signal-mesh tarps.
  • Chalky handprints and territorial tags streak the white walls in every color, accumulating in dense palimpsests near communal water spigots.
  • Steam vents from the still-warm kiln interiors rise through grate floors, giving residents a permanently hazy, fog-wrapped lower level.
sounds
  • A deep, low thrumming resonates through the kiln walls at all hours — the residual heat cycling through old ceramic chambers.
  • Children's voices bounce strangely off the bleached concrete, arriving slightly too late and from the wrong direction.
  • The clank and groan of the tension-cable bridges under foot traffic creates a rhythmic percussion that long-timers learn to read like weather.
smells
  • A sharp alkaline bite underlies everything, like the air after lightning — the permanent ghost of lime-processing chemistry.
  • Communal cookfires burn repurposed biofuel pellets, layering a fatty, slightly sweet smoke over the mineral baseline.
  • Near the lower kilns, a dry mineral heat rises that smells faintly of baked earth and old ceramic, oddly comforting.
feel The Calcine Terrace has the dense, pressurized intimacy of a place where too many people have learned to survive in too little space. Residents are wary of strangers but fiercely communal among themselves. The white dust settles on your clothes within minutes and marks you as someone who has been here, long after you leave.
tags —
demographics Primarily Tier 2 and borderline Tier 1 laborers, many employed in Waukegan's adjacent industrial operations, alongside a growing population of unregistered workers and a small enclave of Synthetic persons denied housing elsewhere.
economy Cash-and-barter economy centered on water ration resale, secondhand BCI hardware, heat-access fees charged by kiln-block bosses, and a brisk trade in counterfeit Ferrogate security clearance chits.
power structure Authority is divided among roughly seven kiln-block bosses, who maintain an uneasy council called the Whiteboard — disputes are settled by negotiation or, when that fails, by controlled access to water and heat.
dangers
  • Calcium dust accumulation in respiratory systems causes a progressive condition locals call 'chalk lung,' for which treatment is expensive and rarely sought in time.
  • Kiln-chamber collapses are a documented hazard — three partial failures in the last decade have each killed between two and nine residents.
  • The Whiteboard bosses enforce their tax collections through hired muscle that operates with no external oversight or accountability.
  • Ferrogate Security uses The Calcine Terrace as an informal detention staging area, periodically sweeping residents for outstanding warrants or Synthetic registration violations.
opportunities
  • The kiln-block boss network provides a ready-made distribution infrastructure for anyone needing to move goods discreetly through the Waukegan transitional zone.
  • Several former lime-processing sub-levels remain unmapped and unsecured, potentially containing salvageable industrial equipment or sealed chemical stores.
  • The Synthetic enclave maintains quiet connections to underground civil rights networks and can provide forged identity credentials for the right price.
story hooks
  • A Whiteboard boss has gone missing two days before a scheduled water ration delivery negotiation, and the other bosses are quietly panicking — someone needs to find her before a power vacuum turns violent, and the trail leads into the unmapped sub-levels.
  • A Zheng-Dao Bioelectric field agent is offering Φ8,000 for a soil and air sample kit retrieved from the deepest kiln chamber — the company claims it's an environmental liability survey, but the payment is absurdly high for routine compliance work.
  • A child from the Synthetic enclave has developed anomalous BCI feedback symptoms that no local medic can explain, and her caretakers believe she may have stumbled onto a buried data cache beneath the kiln floors that is actively broadcasting.

The Calumet Sink #

type place
name The Calumet Sink
aliases
  • The Sink
  • Calumet Hollow
  • The Drain
description A submerged industrial basin stretching along the old Calumet River corridor, partially flooded by Lake Michigan's creeping shoreline over the past century. What remains above water is a labyrinthine tangle of corroded processing infrastructure, collapsed rail bridges, and semi-permanent floating settlements lashed together from salvaged materials. Zheng-Dao Bioelectric once ran experimental filtration operations here, and the legacy of those years lingers in luminescent algae blooms that cast eerie blue-green light across the water at night.

The Sink attracts those who need to disappear — debt runners, unlicensed surgeons, ELF sympathizers moving synthetic persons through informal networks. Carrion Logistics maintains a semi-official waystation on the eastern berm, processing off-manifest cargo no legitimate port would accept. Tier 4 and 5 residents eke out subsistence lives on the floating platforms, while below the waterline, pressurized access tunnels rumored to pre-date Meridian 88 itself snake through the silt.
atmosphere
sights
  • Bioluminescent algae painting the floodwater in shifting cyan and jade gradients beneath cracked catwalks
  • Rusted ore-processing towers half-collapsed into the basin, draped in salvage netting and hand-painted territorial markings
  • Floating platform clusters lit by mismatched lanterns and jury-rigged solar strips, connected by swaying rope bridges
sounds
  • The low, rhythmic groan of metal contracting in the cold lake wind
  • Muffled Diaspora signal bursts from hidden relay nodes competing with water lapping against corroded hull plating
  • Distant pneumatic hissing from the Carrion Logistics waystation's unloading arms
smells
  • Sulfurous residue from decades of chemical processing baked into the concrete banks
  • Damp rust and algae bloom, faintly metallic and organic at once
  • Cooking oil and recycled protein stock drifting from platform kitchens
feel The Sink carries a persistent sense of being watched without ever identifying the source. The air is heavy and close even in open spaces, as if the basin itself is exhaling. Most visitors develop a low-grade paranoia within hours that longtime residents mistake for good survival instinct.
tags —
demographics Overwhelmingly Tier 4 and 5, with a significant population of undocumented synthetic persons and individuals who have legally ceased to exist on Meridian 88's civil registry. Ethnically diverse with heavy representation from South and Southeast Asian diasporic communities.
economy Black-market logistics, salvage operations, unlicensed biotech services, and informal labor brokering dominate. Carrion Logistics provides the closest thing to stable employment, paying in scrip redeemable only at company-controlled supply depots.
power structure No formal governance. Practical authority is divided between Carrion Logistics' site foreman and a loose council of platform elders who adjudicate disputes. Ferrogate Security holds a nominal contract but rarely responds to calls.
dangers
  • Structural collapse of aging elevated walkways and partially submerged tunnel sections with little to no warning
  • Zheng-Dao Bioelectric retrieval teams conducting unauthorized sweeps for proprietary biotech allegedly still active in the water table
  • ELF entities that have colonized decommissioned processing control systems, exhibiting territorial and unpredictable behavior
opportunities
  • Pre-Meridian 88 infrastructure maps rumored to exist in waterlogged Zheng-Dao data caches beneath the basin floor
  • Carrion Logistics off-manifest contracts paying triple standard rate for no-questions cargo movement
  • Unlicensed BCI surgeons operating at a fraction of licensed costs, some with legitimate Helix Biosystems training
story hooks
  • A Tier 2 journalist contacts the players after her source — a synthetic person who claimed to have witnessed an Axiom Industries black-site operation — went silent somewhere in the Sink's tunnel network three days ago. The Diaspora signal from his last known BCI ping is still active, but it's moving in patterns inconsistent with human locomotion.
  • Carrion Logistics' waystation foreman offers a lucrative off-manifest job that turns out to involve transporting a sealed cryogenic container with a Helix Biosystems hazard classification that legally requires military escort. The buyer is waiting somewhere below the waterline, and they're not answering follow-up pings.

The Canopy #

type place
name The Canopy
aliases
  • Lake Forest
  • The Estate District
  • Canopy Row
  • The Green
description Lake Forest was wealthy when wealth meant owning lakefront property. Now wealth means owning the jurisdiction the lakefront property exists in, and Lake Forest has adapted accordingly. The Canopy is a sovereign residential enclave — technically chartered under Axiom Industries' environmental governance subsidiary, practically governed by a homeowners' association with its own security force, its own courts, and its own definition of trespassing that includes 'existing within sensor range without authorization.' The name comes from the engineered tree canopy that covers the district: a bioengineered forest of modified oaks and elms that filter air, generate power through photovoltaic leaf coatings, and — not incidentally — block satellite and drone surveillance. Privacy, it turns out, is a natural resource if you can afford to engineer it.

The estates here belong to Tier 5 families — the executive class of the Big 20, legacy wealth dynasties that predate the sovereignty era, and the particular category of person who has enough money to live anywhere and chooses to live behind walls. The properties range from renovated historical mansions — some dating to the 1890s, maintained with the obsessive care of people who believe architecture is heritage — to new construction that looks like someone asked an AI to design a house for a person who has never experienced a consequence. The average lot size is four acres. The average property value is Φ180 million. The average occupancy is 2.3 people. The math of that is the point.

Corporate operations don't happen here — that's what downtown offices are for. But corporate decisions do. The Canopy's private dining rooms, estate libraries, and climate-controlled gardens are where the deals that shape M88's power structure are negotiated away from surveillance, documentation, and the inconvenience of witnesses. When the CEOs of competing corponations need to agree on something that would be illegal if it were recorded, they meet in Lake Forest. When a board member needs to disappear for a weekend while a scandal is managed, they come here. The Canopy is not where power lives. It's where power sleeps, which is more honest.

The service population — approximately 4,000 people who maintain the estates, operate the security systems, cook the meals, and raise the children of people who are too important to do it themselves — live in a carefully designed staff quarter on the western edge of the district. The staff quarter is clean, well-maintained, and completely separated from the residential zones by a sensor barrier that the residents call 'the garden wall' and the staff call 'the leash.'
atmosphere
sights
  • The engineered canopy — a continuous forest ceiling that filters sunlight into something golden and permanent, like a memory of weather that no longer exists
  • Estate gates set back from tree-lined roads, each entrance a statement of architectural philosophy and personal mythology
  • Security drones disguised as birds — convincing at a distance, unsettling up close
  • The lakefront bluffs, where the water below is somehow cleaner than anywhere else on the shore — because The Canopy's water treatment extends offshore
  • Staff vehicles moving along designated routes, never on the main residential roads
sounds
  • Silence — engineered, maintained, and enforced. The Canopy is the quietest place in the Corridor
  • Birdsong — real birds, attracted by the engineered canopy, supplemented by audio emitters when migration patterns disappoint
  • The faint hum of the perimeter security grid, audible only if you know what you're listening for
  • Wind through bioengineered leaves — a sound designed by acoustic botanists to be 'psychologically restorative'
  • Occasionally: children laughing. There are children here. They are well-fed and profoundly lonely.
smells
  • Clean air — genuinely clean, filtered through the photovoltaic canopy and supplemented by atmospheric processors
  • Old wood and estate gardens — the smell of maintained wealth, of things that are cared for because caring for them is someone's job
  • Lake breeze from the treated shoreline — what Lake Michigan would smell like if Lake Michigan had a budget
feel A place that has solved every problem except the one that matters. The air is clean, the grounds are beautiful, the security is absolute, and the loneliness is architectural. The Canopy is designed to separate its residents from every form of discomfort, including the discomfort of encountering other human beings. It succeeds completely. The people here are the most powerful individuals in the Corridor. They are also the most insulated, which is not the same thing as the most protected, no matter how much they've paid to make it feel that way.
tags —
demographics Approximately 8,000 residents, plus 4,000 service staff. Residents are exclusively Tier 5 — corporate executives, legacy wealth holders, and the small number of people whose net worth qualifies them for sovereign residential status. Staff are Tier 2-3, vetted through extensive background checks and neural loyalty screening. Average resident age: 58. Average staff tenure: 7 years, after which most are 'rotated' for 'security freshness,' which means fired before they learn too much.
economy Wealth management, estate maintenance, and the informal economy of ultra-high-net-worth social networking. No commercial activity is permitted within The Canopy's boundaries. Everything is delivered. The economic output of The Canopy is measured not in production but in decisions — the agreements made in private rooms that redirect billions of Q in corporate spending.
power structure The Canopy Residents' Council — an elected body that functions like a corporate board for a municipality. Current chair rotates annually among the six founding families. Axiom's environmental governance charter provides the legal framework, but the Residents' Council holds effective authority. Security is provided by Sentinel Residential Services, a boutique firm that employs former Tier 3 Ringo and Axiom operators at salaries that ensure absolute loyalty.
dangers
  • Perimeter security — the automated defense grid treats unauthorized entry as a lethal threat, and it has the hardware to back that up
  • Social exposure — being seen in The Canopy without a reason to be there draws attention from people who can make problems disappear
  • Information asymmetry — The Canopy's residents know things about M88's power structure that outsiders don't, and they protect that knowledge aggressively
  • The staff quarter — entering through the service entrance is possible but requires credentials that are neurally verified and time-limited
  • Disappearance — people who cause problems in The Canopy don't get arrested. They stop existing in records.
opportunities
  • Intelligence — The Canopy is where M88's real decisions are made, and staff members occasionally talk
  • Blackmail material — the residents' personal lives are hidden behind the best security money can buy, which means the material behind that security is proportionally valuable
  • Service contracts — The Canopy's residents need things done that they can't ask their regular staff to do
  • The lakefront — The Canopy's treated shoreline is the only accessible clean water on the North Shore, and clean water has value
story hooks
  • A Canopy resident — a Tessera board member — has requested a discreet meeting with someone from the Shelf, through intermediaries. The agenda is sealed. The urgency is real.
  • A former staff member, 'rotated' after nine years of service, has surfaced in the Circuit with a neural recording device that was never supposed to leave the estate grounds
  • The Canopy's perimeter security logged an intrusion that the system immediately reclassified as a false positive. The reclassification was manual. Someone inside authorized it.

The Catalytic Mile #

type place
name The Catalytic Mile
aliases
  • Midtown
  • CatMile
  • The Culture Trap
description The Catalytic Mile is Detroit's cultural preservation district — a roughly one-mile stretch of Woodward Avenue anchored by the Detroit Institute of Arts on one end and the Wayne State University Cognitive Sciences Campus on the other. The name is corporate marketing, coined by the Palladian Construction subsidiary that rebuilt the district in the 2060s, referencing both the catalytic converter (automotive heritage) and the idea of cultural catalysis. Locals just call it Midtown, because they called it that before the corps arrived and they'll call it that after the corps leave, assuming the corps ever leave.

The DIA survived the collapse years because someone — the historical record is deliberately vague about who — negotiated a cultural preservation easement with Cinderblock AI in exchange for data rights to every visitor's neural interface. The museum still stands, its Diego Rivera murals intact behind climate-controlled glass, and every person who looks at them has their aesthetic response recorded, analyzed, and sold on the Tessera Behavioral Exchange. Rivera would have appreciated the irony. Wayne State University was absorbed into the Tessera Academic Partnership Network in 2158, its cognitive sciences department becoming one of Tessera's primary research feeders. The campus is technically independent. The funding is not.

The district between these two anchors is a curated bohemia — galleries, performance spaces, restaurants, and residential blocks designed to feel organic while being entirely corporate-planned. Artists live here on subsidized leases, producing work that makes the district attractive to the Tier 3 residents whose rents actually pay for things. It's a terrarium. The art is real, the community is real, the subsidies create a dependency structure that means the entire cultural ecosystem exists at the pleasure of the corporate landlords. Pull the subsidies and the Mile dies in six months. Everyone knows this. Nobody says it at gallery openings.
atmosphere
sights
  • The DIA's Beaux-Arts facade preserved in amber — literally encased in transparent protective shielding
  • Street murals refreshed by AR overlay, the original paint preserved beneath digital augmentation layers
  • Wayne State's cognitive sciences tower, its upper floors glowing with Tessera branding after dark
  • Gallery windows displaying art that your neural interface automatically prices and attributes
  • Students and artists mixing on Woodward, distinguishable by the age of their augments
sounds
  • Live music from subsidized venues — jazz, electronic, neo-Motown, all of it genuine, all of it funded
  • The murmur of gallery crowds, punctuated by the soft chime of neural interface art-purchase confirmations
  • University lecture broadcasts leaking from open windows — cognitive science terminology in excited voices
  • Street performers who are actually good, because the bad ones get algorithmically de-prioritized by the district management AI
  • The 5 PM autonomous transit chime, when the subsidized artist shuttles run to cheaper districts
smells
  • Coffee and paint thinner — the two fuels of the creative class
  • Restaurant row along Cass Avenue, where the food is excellent and the prices exclude anyone below Tier 2
  • Old building materials — the district preserved some original structures, and they smell like history slowly losing to chemistry
feel Beautiful and compromised. The Catalytic Mile feels like a place where genuine creativity happens inside a corporate terrarium. The art is real. The music is real. The community is real. The fact that all of it exists because a construction corponation decided cultural districts increase adjacent property values by 23% does not make the art less real. It makes everything else less honest.
tags —
demographics Approximately 45,000 residents. A mix of subsidized artists (Tier 1-2), university students and faculty (Tier 2-3), and the Tier 3-4 professionals whose market-rate rents cross-subsidize the entire district. The demographic balance is carefully managed by Palladian's district algorithms.
economy Cultural tourism, university research funding, gallery sales, and the invisible economy of neural data harvested from every aesthetic experience in the district. The DIA alone generates Φ2.1 billion annually in behavioral data licensing.
power structure Palladian Construction owns the land and manages the district through an AI-driven property management system called the Curator. Wayne State's administration answers to the Tessera Academic Partnership Board. The artists' cooperative has a seat at district planning meetings but no vote.
dangers
  • Subsidy dependency — cross the wrong corporate sponsor and lose your housing in 30 days
  • Neural data harvesting — every aesthetic experience in the district is recorded and monetized
  • Academic surveillance — Wayne State research is monitored for commercially exploitable discoveries
  • Gentrification pressure — the district's success constantly pushes outward, consuming adjacent neighborhoods
  • The Curator algorithm — Palladian's district AI makes residency decisions that no human reviews
opportunities
  • Access to Wayne State's cognitive sciences research — cutting-edge BCI work with less security than a corporate lab
  • The artist community is a network of people who see things differently — valuable for intelligence and perspective
  • Gallery openings are where corporate executives drop their guard and talk to people they consider harmless
story hooks
  • A Wayne State researcher discovers that the DIA's neural harvesting system has been modified to do more than record — it's been inserting cognitive suggestions into visitors for years
  • The Curator algorithm is about to terminate subsidies for an entire block of artist housing. The residents have 30 days to find Φ4 million or become homeless.
  • A student collective has been using Wayne State's cognitive lab after hours to develop open-source BCI firmware — Tessera has noticed

The Cinder Nave #

type place
name The Cinder Nave
aliases
  • The Nave
  • Ashfield
  • The Old Cathedral
  • Cinder Row
description The Cinder Nave is what happens when a structure meant for transcendence becomes infrastructure for survival. The building at its core is a massive neo-Gothic Catholic cathedral dating to the early twentieth century — Our Lady of the Perpetual Flame — which survived the 2097 Chicago firestorm, the subsequent flooding of its lower nave, and a century of urban decay with its primary stone structure essentially intact, its stained-glass long gone and its interior a gutted shell. It sits in what is technically the boundary zone between the Shelf's upper tier and the lower reaches of the South Side, in a neighborhood that the official city zoning maps classify as a transitional remediation corridor — civic planning language for 'we have given up on this.'

Sometime in the 2140s the cathedral was colonized by a community of Shelf-tier residents who recognized that its stone walls, its height, and its structural integrity made it one of the most defensible and durable buildings within a two-kilometer radius. The lower nave, flooded to about knee-depth and home to a remarkable algal ecosystem that provides a modest but consistent food supplement, was sealed off and designated communal resource space. The upper nave, choir loft, and crossing were built out over decades into a multi-story vertical living and working community of approximately eight hundred people, with additional overflow population sheltering in the cathedral's attached rectory, school building, and a cluster of parasitic structures that have grown onto the cathedral's exterior like architectural barnacles.

The Cinder Nave takes its name from the blackened stone of the cathedral's exterior, scorched in the 2097 fire and never cleaned, and from the nave's current aesthetic — the interior walls are still scorched above the renovation line, and the community has incorporated the charred texture into its visual identity, lining interior walkways with cinder-block planters, using ash-grey in its painted murals, and maintaining a central fire in the crossing that burns continuously in a salvaged iron basin. There is a spiritual community here, loosely organized and interfaith, that tends the fire and runs the Nave's primary mediation and conflict resolution services. They are not a formal religious body and resist any such characterization, but they are the closest thing the Cinder Nave has to a moral center, and their influence on community governance is substantial.
atmosphere
sights
  • The cathedral's massive scorched exterior rising incongruously from the surrounding low-rise ruins and improvised structures, still visibly Gothic in its proportions despite decades of modification
  • The central fire burning in its iron basin in the crossing, visible through the open clerestory windows from outside at night as an orange glow in the cathedral's upper reaches
  • The flooded lower nave visible through sealed glass panels in the floor — dark water, algal mats, and the occasional movement of something living beneath the surface
  • Vertical living structures built into the side aisles and up into the triforium gallery, their façades a patchwork of salvaged materials in warm earth tones
  • The community murals covering every surface above the flood line — densely detailed, continuously added to, a visual record of the Nave's history and its residents' origins
sounds
  • The central fire crackling and the sound of the crossing's natural acoustics amplifying and transforming every sound in the cathedral — voices, footsteps, and the distant sounds of the city take on a resonant, cathedral quality
  • Children and daily life sounds echoing through the nave's stone spaces with a warmth and reverberation that feels architectural
  • The water in the lower nave shifting with pressure changes, audible as a low, intermittent slosh through the floor panels
  • Interfaith prayer and chanting from the fire-tenders during their morning and evening observances — brief, unobtrusive, and audible throughout the nave
smells
  • Wood smoke from the central fire, deeply embedded in every surface and coating everything with a faint, permanent warmth
  • The green, slightly sulfurous smell of the algal ecosystem rising through the floor panels from the lower nave
  • Cooking, human habitation, and the particular compressed smell of a dense vertical community — food, bodies, laundry, and the ongoing business of living
  • Old stone and the faint mineral smell of water-damaged masonry — the smell of the building itself, unchanged since the fire
feel The Cinder Nave produces an immediate and powerful emotional response in nearly every visitor — the combination of the building's scale, its acoustic properties, its central fire, and its dense human habitation creates something that resists straightforward categorization. It is simultaneously a ruin, a home, a community, and something that feels almost intentionally sacred despite the entirely pragmatic origins of its current use. Residents move through the space with an ease that comes from deep familiarity, and the community's norms — the fire-tenders' quiet authority, the mediation culture, the shared stewardship of the algal floor — create a social texture that is notably different from other Shelf-tier communities. Outsiders are watched with curiosity rather than hostility, but the watching is thorough.
tags —
demographics Approximately eight hundred permanent residents, overwhelmingly Tier 4 with some Tier 3 skilled workers, drawn from a wide range of ethnic and national backgrounds reflecting the Shelf's demographic diversity. The fire-tending community is interfaith and multiethnic. A small number of synthetic persons live here under informal community protection and are integrated into the community's daily life.
economy The algal ecosystem in the lower nave provides a supplemental food source and a small trade good — the community cultivates and sells specific algal strains with pharmaceutical and nutritional applications to buyers in the South Side and the Lakeshore Corridor. Primary income is through labor export — Nave residents working in the industrial and service economies of adjacent districts — and through a modest trade in artisan goods produced in the community workshops built into the side aisles. The fire-tenders provide mediation services for a requested contribution, not a fixed fee.
power structure Community governance is conducted through a general assembly that meets weekly in the crossing, with the fire-tenders holding a formal advisory role and significant informal moral authority. There is no relationship with Ferrogate Security — the community manages its own security through a rotating watch system. No corponation holds any contractual relationship with the Nave, a status that is actively maintained as a matter of community principle.
dangers
  • The lower nave's flood infrastructure requires continuous maintenance — a significant failure would flood the ground-level community spaces within hours
  • The cathedral's Gothic stone structure, while durable, has load-bearing concerns in the northeast tower where the parasitic external structures have added significant weight
  • The Nave's known policy of providing informal sanctuary to synthetic persons has attracted periodic attention from Ferrogate operatives acting on behalf of corponation clients seeking specific individuals
  • The community's lack of formal security contracts leaves it vulnerable to organized pressure from outside actors who are not deterred by community resistance alone
  • The algal trade has attracted the interest of Helix Biosystems, which has made two acquisition attempts on the algal strains and been refused both times — a refusal the corponation has not accepted gracefully
opportunities
  • The fire-tenders' mediation services are genuinely skilled and conducted in a space with strong community enforcement of neutrality — a rare option for disputes that cannot be taken to any formal authority
  • The community's informal sanctuary tradition and lack of corponation relationships make it a viable safe harbor for people who need to disappear from the corporate surveillance grid temporarily
  • The algal cultivation in the lower nave represents a bioprospecting opportunity that Helix Biosystems has not yet succeeded in accessing — the specific strains being cultivated have applications the community does not fully understand
story hooks
  • A synthetic person who has been living under the Nave's informal sanctuary for two years has been identified by a Ferrogate contractor operating on behalf of Arcturus Defense Solutions — identified not as a civil matter but as a recovered asset, implying the synthetic was the product of Arcturus military research rather than civilian development. The community has refused to surrender them and is now facing escalating pressure. The fire-tenders are looking for someone who can find out what the synthetic actually is and whether there is a legal or extra-legal strategy that can make Arcturus back down before the situation turns violent.
  • The lower nave's algal ecosystem has begun producing something new — a bioluminescent compound that the community's amateur scientists cannot identify and that produces unusual effects on the BCI interfaces of people who spend extended time near the floor panels. The fire-tenders believe it is a natural mutation; a Helix Biosystems researcher who has been making unauthorized visits to the Nave believes it is something considerably more significant. Both parties want to know the truth, and both are asking different people to find it, which means two separate investigations are converging on the same flooded basement.

The Cinder Notch #

type place
name The Cinder Notch
aliases
  • Notch Town
  • The Char
  • Ember Row
description A compressed industrial wedge squeezed between decommissioned Ringo Heavy Industries rail spurs and the eroded embankment of a long-buried canal, The Cinder Notch occupies a geographic crease in the southern corridor that most city planners forgot to demolish. Blackened retaining walls still bear the scorched logos of pre-Meridian foundries, and the structures built against them—lean-tos, stacked shipping modules, jury-rigged hab cubes—have calcified into something almost intentional over the decades.

Residents have carved a stubborn community from the wreckage, running bootleg power taps off Ringo's dormant rail grid and selling thermal credits skimmed from industrial runoff. Ferrogate Security patrols the perimeter only when a corporate contract demands it, leaving internal order to a rotating council of block captains who settle disputes through a mixture of old-neighborhood loyalty and quiet intimidation. The Notch is not lawless so much as self-governed on terms outsiders rarely understand.
atmosphere
sights
  • Soot-darkened corrugated walls stenciled with faded union markings and fresh gang tags layered atop one another like geological strata
  • Amber emergency lighting strung on repurposed rail cable casting long, uneven shadows across narrow alleys
  • Children playing on decommissioned ore hoppers converted into communal platforms, their BCI halos glowing faint blue in the dim
sounds
  • The low rhythmic groan of thermal expansion in the old rail spurs as temperatures shift overnight
  • Muffled Diaspora feeds bleeding through thin module walls—multiple languages, overlapping beats, argument and laughter indistinguishable
  • A distant Ringo freight drone buzzing along the elevated track above, never stopping, never looking down
smells
  • Persistent char and iron oxide baked into every surface, stirred loose by wind off the buried canal
  • Cooking oil and fermented soy protein from communal stalls wedged into old loading bays
  • Chemical sweetness from the thermal runoff stream that locals call the Warm Ditch
feel The Notch presses in from all sides—walls too close, ceilings too low, alleys that dog-leg without warning. There is warmth here that is partly literal, the residual heat of industrial infrastructure, and partly the dense proximity of people who have decided to stay. Outsiders feel watched without ever seeing who watches.
tags —
demographics Predominantly Tier 4 and Shelf-adjacent residents, heavily multigenerational with deep roots in pre-Meridian labor families—Congolese, Polish, Filipino, and Haitian surnames dominating block rosters. A small enclave of unregistered synthetics lives quietly in the canal-side structures, tolerated but not acknowledged.
economy Thermal credit skimming, gray-market BCI hardware repair, and informal labor brokering for Ringo and Carrion Logistics day contracts form the economic backbone. A modest underground market in reclaimed foundry materials feeds into Oxidian-adjacent resale networks.
power structure A seven-seat block captain council holds nominal authority, with a former Ringo shift supervisor named Dagna Przybylski wielding outsized influence through control of the power tap infrastructure. Ferrogate maintains a hands-off stance unless corporate property is directly threatened.
dangers
  • Unstable rail spur segments overhead—decades of deferred maintenance mean sections can shed debris or collapse without warning
  • Rival labor brokers from Carrion Logistics occasionally send enforcers to discipline workers who broke contract terms
  • The Warm Ditch chemical runoff causes long-term neurological symptoms in residents who have lived near it for years, a fact quietly suppressed by Ringo's legal division
opportunities
  • Unregistered synthetic residents may possess skills or information they'll trade for documentation assistance or legal cover
  • The buried canal beneath the Notch reportedly connects to a pre-Meridian tunnel network with access points no current map acknowledges
  • Block captain Przybylski is quietly assembling leverage against a Ringo mid-level executive and needs outside operators with no local ties
story hooks
  • A Notch child has begun broadcasting fragmented, non-human data patterns through her BCI during sleep—patterns that match known E.L.F. communication signatures. Her family wants answers before Axiom's autonomous detection sweeps reach the neighborhood, which locals estimate is less than seventy-two hours away.
  • Someone has been systematically destroying the thermal tap infrastructure, plunging modules into cold darkness one by one. The block council suspects a Ringo contractor softening the Notch for forced clearance, but the sabotage pattern is too precise and too patient for a simple corporate play—and the only witness is an elderly man who claims the saboteur had no face.

The Cinderblock #

type place
name The Cinderblock
aliases
  • The Block
  • Cinder
  • The Gray Quarter
  • Burn Row
description The Cinderblock occupies what was once a dense residential neighborhood on Chicago's near west side, a zone that experienced three separate corponation industrial fires in the 2140s and 2150s — two attributed to Axiom Industries chemical storage failures and one to what the official Palladian Group report called 'an uncontrolled energetic event' at a Palladian-contracted demolition site. None of the fires were fully suppressed. They burned into each other. The result was twenty-two blocks of structural scorching so severe that the buildings didn't collapse — they carbonized. The Cinderblock is a neighborhood of standing burned buildings, their walls intact but black, their interiors gutted, their windows hollow. It looks like a city that died upright.

In the three decades since the last fire, the Cinderblock has been recolonized. Not rebuilt — recolonized. People moved back into the carbonized structures because the Shelf was worse and the Cinderblock was free. They hung tarps where windows were. They ran extension cables from illegal taps on the Axiom substations that caused the original fires. They built markets in ground floors where the charring was shallow enough to be scraped away and the concrete still held. By 2200, roughly eight thousand people live in the Cinderblock, in structures that every structural survey says should not be occupied and that nobody is paying for structural surveys to actually condemn.

The ash is everywhere. It doesn't go away. It settles in hair and lungs and the food you cook and the water you drink, because the water filtration in the Cinderblock is inadequate and the ash is still leaching into groundwater from the deeper burn zones. Respiratory illness rates are the highest in Meridian 88. Life expectancy in the Cinderblock is eleven years below the city median. The community health workers who operate the three informal clinics in the zone have submitted fourteen formal petitions to the Meridian 88 Municipal Authority requesting remediation funding. They have received three form-letter responses.
atmosphere
sights
  • Rows of carbonized buildings standing intact, their facades black and textured like charcoal, windows gaping
  • Colored tarps and salvaged panels providing color against the overwhelming gray-black — the only brightness in the zone
  • Ash drifting in the air on still days, visible as a fine gray haze
  • Ground-floor market stalls with scraped-clean concrete floors and careful, deliberate color — residents fighting the visual weight of the environment
  • Community murals painted on the least-damaged walls, bright and detailed and constantly being added to
sounds
  • Coughing — frequent, from multiple directions, the background sound of a sick community
  • Market noise from the ground floors: vendors, bargaining, children, the specific acoustic quality of sound in a roofless or half-roofed space
  • Wind moving through the hollow upper floors of carbonized buildings, producing low tonal notes
  • Ferrogate Security drones on perimeter passes, their rotors distinctive
smells
  • Ash and old carbon — decades old but still present, especially after rain
  • Cooking food, which smells slightly wrong because the ash gets into everything
  • The sharp chemical undertone of industrial fire residue in groundwater — detectable in anything boiled with local water
  • Antiseptic from the three community health clinics
feel The Cinderblock produces a specific kind of exhaustion in visitors that is not physical. It is the exhaustion of sustained injustice made visible and permanent. The burned buildings do not let you forget what happened here. They are the evidence, still standing, still black, still leaching into the water table. Residents have developed a complex relationship with this — some find the burned walls galvanizing, proof of what was done that cannot be demolished or redeveloped away. Others find it suffocating.

There is, underneath the exhaustion, something fierce. The community clinics are extraordinary. The murals are extraordinary. The mutual aid networks that keep eight thousand people fed and medicated in a zone that no corponation or municipal authority will meaningfully support are extraordinary. The Cinderblock is a place where people are surviving something that was done to them, and doing it together.
tags —
demographics Predominantly Tier 1 and Shelf-level residents, many of whom were displaced from other zones and settled here because it was the only place available. High proportion of elderly residents who were present during the original fires and chose not to leave. Significant population of community health workers, mutual aid organizers, and activist-journalists operating on minimal resources. A growing population of younger residents who were born here and have no other home to reference.
economy Informal and mutual. Ground-floor markets trade in food, medication, and salvaged materials. The community health clinics operate on a combination of donation, barter, and sporadic grey-market pharmaceutical supply. Some residents earn Φ doing contract labor in adjacent zones — the Cinderblock is close enough to Axiom industrial sites that there is a grim irony in residents commuting to work for the company whose storage failures burned their homes. A small underground economy in ash-processed industrial byproducts, some of which have legitimate chemical value, provides additional income.
power structure The Block Council — informal, non-elected, composed of the longest-tenured residents and the heads of the three community clinics — coordinates mutual aid and external negotiations. There is no enforcement mechanism; the Block Council operates on moral authority alone. Ferrogate Security maintains a perimeter contract but does not operate inside the Cinderblock, a fact that is simultaneously a protection (no corponation security inside) and a vulnerability (no enforcement if something bad happens). Axiom Industries and Palladian Group both maintain legal teams whose primary function is ensuring the fire liability cases from the 2140s and 2150s remain unresolved.
dangers
  • Structural failure of carbonized buildings — the charring has compromised load-bearing elements throughout, and collapses occur without warning
  • Chronic ash and chemical exposure — the health effects are documented, ongoing, and cumulative
  • Axiom Industries periodically sending representatives to assess 'redevelopment potential,' which residents interpret correctly as precursor to displacement
  • Complete absence of emergency services — fire suppression, medical emergency response, and structural rescue do not reliably reach the Cinderblock
  • The deep burn zones in the zone's center, where the fires overlapped — structurally unstable, chemically active groundwater, and reportedly strange acoustic effects from the carbonized material
opportunities
  • The unresolved Axiom and Palladian fire liability cases contain evidence that has been suppressed — a lawyer or investigator who can access the sealed discovery files has leverage worth significant Φ
  • The Block Council will pay, in favors and information, for anyone who can document Axiom's current redevelopment assessment activities
  • The ash-processed industrial byproducts trade needs people who can move product discreetly into legitimate chemical markets
story hooks
  • A structural survey team hired by Axiom Industries has been quietly working in the deep burn zones — not assessing buildings, but drilling core samples from the ground. A Cinderblock resident who works as a salvager caught them at it and followed one of the surveyors back to an Axiom subsidiary office. Whatever Axiom found in the ground during the fires, they want it back badly enough to be moving carefully instead of through the courts. The Block Council needs to know what it is before Axiom decides careful isn't working.
  • One of the community health clinic workers has been compiling a comprehensive health database for the Cinderblock — fifteen years of respiratory illness, cancer incidence, developmental effects in children — and is preparing to submit it as evidence in a renewed liability case. She has received two credible death threats in the past month. The Block Council has asked quietly for someone to keep her alive long enough to file, and to find out whether the threats are coming from Axiom, Palladian, or somewhere else entirely.

The Cinnabar Exchange #

type place
name The Cinnabar Exchange
aliases
  • The Red Floor
  • Cinnabar Station
  • The Exchange Pit
description Buried three levels below the mid-tier transit interchange at Old Harbor's northern edge, The Cinnabar Exchange occupies the gutted chassis of a pre-Meridian commodities trading floor—a vast octagonal room with a tiered gallery and a central pit where brokers once shouted futures contracts into existence. The Palladian Group used it as a data clearinghouse until 2183, then sealed it following a catastrophic BCI network breach that killed eleven analysts and left the building's local mesh permanently scarred with ghost-signal artifacts. Now it operates as the megacity corridor's most significant underground information market, its blood-orange emergency lighting never replaced, its walls still crawling with corrupted Diaspora echoes that experienced BCI users find deeply disorienting.

Dealers at the Exchange trade in data exclusively—corporate intelligence, personal records, blackmail material, and, most lucratively, identity packages that allow Tier 5 residents or undocumented synthetics to pass as higher-tier citizens. Palladian Group security makes periodic attempts to reclaim or destroy the space; so far, the Exchange's operators have anticipated every raid, a fact that suggests significant intelligence penetration of Palladian itself.
atmosphere
sights
  • Tiered gallery seating filled with hooded figures interfacing via BCI, their eyes uniformly rolled back and flickering
  • The central pit's floor inlaid with a corroded brass commodity-price display that still cycles random numbers in the dark
  • Corrupted Diaspora ghost-signals manifesting as faint geometric light artifacts that drift across walls like slow, silent fireworks
sounds
  • A subsonic hum from the damaged mesh infrastructure that sits just below conscious hearing and accumulates into headache over hours
  • Clipped, low-voiced negotiations in a dozen languages, never rising above a murmur in the acoustically dead room
  • The occasional sharp crack of a BCI user hitting a ghost-signal artifact and disconnecting hard, followed by controlled breathing
smells
  • Ozone from overworked signal boosters and jury-rigged mesh amplifiers
  • Stale recycled air underlaid with the faint chemical sweetness of BCI interface fluid
  • Old metal and concrete dust, dry and mineral, unchanged since the Palladian era
feel The Cinnabar Exchange demands a specific kind of calm. The ghost-signals in the mesh press against active BCI users like a crowd at the edge of vision, and the orange light makes everyone look either feverish or dead. Trust here is purely transactional, enforced not by loyalty but by mutual knowledge of what everyone else has on everyone else.
tags —
demographics A deliberately anonymous clientele spanning all tiers, with identity obfuscation strongly enforced by house rules. Operators and permanent staff are almost exclusively Tier 3-4 former corporate data analysts, several of whom survived the 2183 Palladian breach.
economy Pure information brokerage denominated in Φ and occasionally in data-for-data exchange. Identity package sales represent the highest-margin business; corporate intelligence on Axiom, Sterling-Nakamura, and Palladian itself moves in the highest volume.
power structure Run by a collective of seven brokers who survived the 2183 breach and refer to themselves only as the Remainder. Decisions are made by consensus with disputes resolved by a rotating arbitration role; the current arbitrator is believed to be a synthetic who has been running a human identity package for eleven years.
dangers
  • The residual ghost-signals in the local mesh can trigger BCI feedback cascades in users with older or poorly maintained implants—medical emergencies are handled in-house and quietly
  • Palladian Group infiltration is an ongoing reality; at least one active Palladian asset is believed to be operating among the regular clientele
  • Identity package buyers who attract too much scrutiny outside the Exchange are sometimes traced back to their source, creating violent blowback against brokers and sellers
opportunities
  • The Remainder is offering a significant finder's fee for anyone who can identify the Palladian asset currently operating in the Exchange without tipping the target
  • A complete Axiom Industries executive BCI-log archive from 2197-2199 is available for auction—the contents are unknown but the provenance is verified, and three parties are already competing
  • A Tier 5 synthetic needs a Tier 2 identity package and is offering something unusual in exchange: direct access to an E.L.F. communications channel it has been quietly monitoring for eight months
story hooks
  • A Sterling-Nakamura mid-level manager approaches the party outside the Exchange, terrified—she purchased an identity package here for a family member and has since learned the package belonged to someone who did not sell it willingly. The original identity's owners are looking for it, and they are not interested in negotiation.
  • The ghost-signal artifacts drifting through the Exchange's corrupted mesh have begun forming patterns that BCI-sensitive users recognize as structured language—not random corruption but something that survived the 2183 breach and has been slowly reconstituting itself in the dark for seventeen years. The Remainder wants it contained; someone else wants to talk to it.

The Circuit #

type place
name The Circuit
aliases
  • The Circus
  • Hacktown
  • The Bazaar
  • Robin Hood's Mall
description The Circuit started as a server farm. Specifically, it started as twelve city
blocks of data centers that Axiom Industries decommissioned when they moved to
quantum infrastructure and couldn't be bothered to demolish. Within six months,
the hollowed-out server racks had been converted into market stalls, the cooling
systems had been repurposed for climate control, and the backup generators were
running what might be the most productive illegal economy in the western
hemisphere. The Circuit is Meridian's black market, tech bazaar, and unofficial
innovation hub. It's where you go to buy augments that aren't in the corporate
catalog, sell data you shouldn't have, or hire someone whose skillset doesn't
appear on any licensed professional registry.

The aesthetic is cyberpunk flea market — tangled cables overhead like vines in a
digital jungle, holographic price tags floating above stalls selling everything
from military-grade neural interfaces to homemade ramen. Rogue AIs run some of
the shops, their consciousness distributed across salvaged hardware, negotiating
prices through speakers bolted to the walls. Data brokers sit in neon-lit alcoves,
trading corporate secrets like baseball cards. Augment shops range from genuinely
skilled technicians doing unlicensed but excellent work to butchers who'll install
anything in anyone for the right price. The Circuit has its own internal economy,
its own reputation systems, and its own justice — which mostly amounts to "cheat
someone and see what happens."

This is Robin Hood territory. The Collective operates openly here, redistributing
stolen corporate data, running free net access points, and maintaining the
Circuit's infrastructure as a public service. The philosophy is simple: the corps
stole everything first, so stealing it back is just accounting. Not everyone in
the Circuit is an idealist — plenty of people here are straightforward criminals
who'd sell their grandmother's augments for the right price — but the idealism
provides a framework, a story the Circuit tells about itself. And stories matter,
especially in a city that runs on corporate ones.
atmosphere
sights
  • Cables and fiber optics strung overhead in dense canopies, pulsing with data traffic
  • Holographic signage in every color, advertising in Shelf Cant, Standard, and machine code
  • Stalls built into decommissioned server racks — some still have the original Axiom branding
  • Rogue AIs manifesting as floating geometric shapes, holographic animals, or just text on a wall
  • Augment technicians working in open-air shops, chrome and flesh under bright surgical lights
  • Data brokers in neon-lit alcoves, faces hidden behind privacy screens
  • The occasional spark shower from someone doing something ambitious with a soldering iron
  • Screens everywhere — showing net traffic visualizations, security feeds, pirated entertainment, and art
sounds
  • The hum of repurposed cooling systems — a low, constant thrum that the Circuit is built on
  • Haggling in five languages plus machine code
  • Electronic music from competing stalls, creating an accidental remix that changes block to block
  • The whine of augment calibration tools
  • AI voices — some human-passing, some deliberately synthetic, some that sound like singing math
  • The occasional shout of 'SWEEP' when someone spots an Axiom Security drone, followed by coordinated scrambling
smells
  • Ozone and hot solder — the smell of tech being born
  • Street food — the Circuit has the best dumplings in Meridian, and this is not debatable
  • Coolant fluid leaking from overtaxed server repurposements
  • The sharp, clean smell of brand-new augment components, fresh from the smuggling crate
  • Energy drinks. So many energy drinks. The Circuit runs on caffeine and bad decisions.
feel Electric. The Circuit buzzes with possibility and danger in equal measure. It
feels like the internet made physical — chaotic, creative, democratic in theory,
predatory in practice, and absolutely vital. There's an energy here that the Core
can't replicate with all its optimization: the energy of people building things
because they want to, not because a quarterly target demands it. It's exciting.
It's also the kind of place where you check your wallet, your augments, and your
exits, in that order.
tags —
demographics A dense, hyper-diverse population of roughly 200,000, skewing young, technically literate, and economically informal. Heavy representation of first-generation immigrants, former corpo contract workers who aged out of usefulness, and self-taught engineers. Tier 1 and Tier 2 predominate, with a small but influential class of unlicensed entrepreneurs who would be Tier 3 if anyone were issuing paperwork. The Circuit does not ask where you came from.
economy —
power structure —
dangers
  • Scams — the Circuit's reputation system is imperfect and exploitable
  • Bad augment work — unlicensed doesn't always mean skilled
  • Data theft — your personal information is a commodity here
  • Axiom Security sweeps — rare but devastating when they happen
  • Rogue AI instability — most are fine, some are very much not fine
  • Getting in over your head — the Circuit will sell you anything, including trouble
  • Addiction — the Circuit has stimulants, neural narcotics, and experience chips that are hard to put down
  • Owing the wrong people — debts in the Circuit are collected creatively
opportunities
  • Cutting-edge augment technology, available nowhere else
  • Data — corporate secrets, personal information, historical records the corps tried to delete
  • Contracts — the Circuit is where fixers find operators for every kind of job
  • Community — the Circuit's maker culture is genuine and generative
  • Free net access — Collective-maintained nodes, uncensored and unmonitored
  • AI collaboration — working with rogue AIs who think differently than any human
  • The dumplings. Seriously. The dumplings.
story hooks
  • The rogue AI who runs the Circuit's most reliable augment shop — and who might know something about Kyle's past
  • The Collective's open-source weapon designs — making arms impossible to monopolize
  • A data cache from the Corporate Wars surfaces in the Circuit, containing something someone will kill to suppress
  • The Circuit's annual 'Swap Meet' — a massive bazaar where anything goes, and frequently does
  • Kyle's fixer — the person who finds him work — operates out of a Circuit noodle shop
  • The tension between the Circuit's idealism and its reality — Robin Hood mythology vs. actual crime
connections

  • The Meridian Core (hard border — security checkpoint, heavily monitored)

exits —

  • Augment technicians and body modifiers
  • Rogue AIs operating businesses or just existing freely
  • Collective members and sympathizers
  • Fixers who broker contracts between clients and operators like Kyle
  • Corporate employees shopping for things their employer won't provide
  • Artists, musicians, and creators who can't afford Core gallery fees
  • People who need to disappear and the people who help them do it
