The Cobalt Verge #

type place
name The Cobalt Verge
aliases
  • The Blue Rim
  • Verge District
  • Cobalt Row
description A narrow industrial-residential hybrid zone wedged between the Lake Michigan waterfront and a decommissioned Ringo Heavy Industries rail corridor, The Cobalt Verge earned its name from the distinctive blue-tinted oxidation coating the corrugated steel facades of its stacked micro-housing units—a byproduct of decades of Zheng-Dao Bioelectric coolant runoff that seeped into the groundwater and slowly leached into the structural metal. The resulting cerulean patina has become perversely aesthetic, drawing low-tier artists and squatters who call the color 'lake-rust' and consider it a mark of authenticity.

Oncee a legitimate freight-transfer point for ore shipments moving inland from the harbor, the Verge now operates as a gray-market corridor where Tier 2 and Tier 3 residents broker deals that exist in the regulatory gaps between corponation jurisdictions. Ferrogate Security holds a nominal contract here but enforces selectively, leaving entire blocks to self-organized neighborhood watches armed with surplus stun-lances and improvised BCI jamming rigs.
atmosphere
sights
  • Blue-oxidized steel walls glowing faintly under sodium arc lights, streaked with bioluminescent graffiti tags
  • Elevated micro-housing pods cantilevered over the old rail bed, laundry lines strung between rusted gantries
  • Zheng-Dao coolant warning placards half-buried in cracked permacrete, ignored by locals who've lived with it for generations
sounds
  • Low harmonic vibration from the abandoned rail infrastructure resonating in the wind off the lake
  • Overlapping BCI chatter leaking through cheap neural dampeners in crowded market stalls
  • Distant foghorns from Lake Michigan barge traffic mixing with the clatter of hand-pulled cargo carts
smells
  • Metallic tang of oxidized steel and residual coolant chemicals sharp enough to taste
  • Fried synth-protein from ground-floor food stalls, heavy with fermented soy and chili oil
  • Lake brine cutting through the industrial haze on nights when the wind shifts east
feel The Cobalt Verge has the compressed energy of a place that knows it shouldn't exist but does anyway, every surface worn smooth by stubborn daily life. There is beauty here that outsiders find unsettling—too industrial to be quaint, too inhabited to be derelict. Residents move with the practiced wariness of people who have negotiated their own survival from scratch.
tags —
demographics Predominantly Tier 2 and lower Tier 3, with a significant synthetic-person community occupying the older rail-adjacent structures where human habitability concerns are less strictly enforced. Ethnically dense, with strong East African, South Asian, and Great Lakes Indigenous representation.
economy Gray-market goods brokerage, coolant-metal salvage resale, and unlicensed BCI hardware modification shops sustain most households. A small but growing enclave of artists monetizing the Verge's aesthetic through Diaspora-distributed content has begun attracting outside Φ.
power structure No single faction controls the Verge; a rotating council of block representatives called the Cobalt Compact negotiates with Ferrogate Security over enforcement boundaries and mediates internal disputes. Zheng-Dao Bioelectric retains subsurface rights and occasionally asserts them to remind residents of their precariousness.
dangers
  • Zheng-Dao coolant contamination causes long-term neurological degradation in residents without expensive filtration implants, a fact the corponation disputes publicly
  • Ferrogate Security 'selective enforcement' means protection is effectively pay-to-receive, leaving non-paying blocks vulnerable to organized shakedowns
  • E.L.F. presence in the abandoned rail network's legacy data infrastructure—at least one emergent entity is believed to be routing through derelict switching computers beneath the Verge
opportunities
  • The Cobalt Compact is quietly seeking a legal advocate willing to build a contamination liability case against Zheng-Dao Bioelectric
  • The rail corridor's subsurface data nodes represent untapped access to pre-Diaspora network architecture that certain information brokers would pay handsomely to exploit
  • Cobalt-oxidized salvage metal commands premium prices in Spire-tier interior design markets, creating a discreet export trade that needs reliable intermediaries
story hooks
  • A Tier 3 BCI hardware modder known as Sable Okonkwo has been offering free neural upgrades to Verge residents—but three recipients have since gone catatonic, their implants broadcasting fragmented data on frequencies associated with known E.L.F. signatures. Whether Sable is complicit, compromised, or simply the next victim is unclear, and the Cobalt Compact wants answers before going to anyone official.
  • Zheng-Dao Bioelectric has quietly filed subsurface rights expansion paperwork that, if approved, would legally allow them to demolish the eastern housing blocks for coolant reclamation infrastructure. A Verge resident who works as a Diaspora data archivist has found the buried filing and is looking for allies with the right access, leverage, or willingness to make noise before the corponation moves.

The Conservatory #

type place
name The Conservatory
aliases
  • East Garfield Park
  • The Glass Garden
  • Greenlung
  • ConServ
description The Garfield Park Conservatory survived the flooding, the riots, the corporate annexation waves, and three separate arson attempts. It should not still be standing. The fact that it is — a cathedral of iron and glass rising from the wreckage of the West Side like a hallucination — says something about what people will fight to protect when everything else has been taken from them. The Conservatory is the largest enclosed green space in Meridian 88's lower tiers, and it has become something its original architects never intended: a commons, a sanctuary, a black-market pharmacy, and the closest thing to neutral ground the West Side has.

Verdant Systems acquired the surrounding blocks in the 2040s, intending to convert the Conservatory into a corporate biolab. The neighborhood burned their survey drones out of the sky. Three times. Verdant pulled back to a perimeter and settled for a licensing arrangement — they supply the Conservatory's climate systems and gene-stock in exchange for first-refusal rights on any novel cultivars that emerge from the community gardens. It is, on paper, a partnership. In practice, it is a siege with better PR. The residents know that Verdant is waiting for the right crisis to justify a full acquisition, and they tend their plants with the focused intensity of people defending a border.

Inside the glass, the air is thick and wet and alive. The original botanical collections have been augmented with decades of guerrilla horticulture — medicinal plants, food crops, engineered oxygen-producers, and things nobody can identify that arrived as seeds in refugee pockets and found purchase in the Conservatory's soil. The Fern Room has become an unlicensed clinic where herbalists and rogue bioengineers treat lower-tier residents who cannot afford Lazarus Pharmaceuticals' pricing. The Palm House is a meeting ground where West Side faction leaders negotiate truces under canopies of engineered palms that clean the air faster than any corporate scrubber.

The surrounding blocks are standard West Side devastation — collapsed infrastructure, improvised housing, streets that flood every spring. But the Conservatory acts as an anchor, a proof that something can be maintained without corporate ownership. People come from across the Shelf to see it. Some of them cry. It is the only place in the lower tiers where you can smell earth instead of concrete, where the air tastes like it did before the city ate the sky.
atmosphere
sights
  • Iron-and-glass conservatory dome rising above crumbling West Side blocks like a landlocked lighthouse
  • Interior jungle of engineered plants, medicinal herbs, and unidentified cultivars climbing every surface
  • Verdant Systems perimeter drones circling the surrounding blocks at a respectful but watchful distance
  • Community gardens spreading outward from the Conservatory like green veins through gray concrete
  • Condensation streaming down interior glass panels, blurring the ruined cityscape outside into abstraction
  • Children playing between rows of food crops they helped plant
sounds
  • Water dripping through the Conservatory's misting systems — a sound like slow, patient rain
  • The hum of Verdant's climate-control units embedded in the walls
  • Birds — actual birds, not drones — nesting in the upper canopy
  • Quiet negotiation in the Palm House, voices kept low by mutual agreement
  • The crunch of gravel paths maintained by volunteer crews
smells
  • Living soil — the rarest smell in the lower tiers
  • Flowering medicinal plants from the Fern Room clinic
  • Wet iron from the Victorian-era frame sweating in the humidity
  • Compost heaps behind the west wing, rich and dark
feel Hope as a physical structure. The Conservatory is the West Side's argument that beauty is not a luxury — it is infrastructure. Being inside it feels like stepping backward into a world that still believed in public things.
tags —
demographics Predominantly Tier 1 and untier-ed residents from the surrounding West Side blocks. Climate refugees make up roughly 40% of the community, many of whom brought agricultural knowledge from the Gulf Coast Displacement Zone.
economy The Conservatory's internal economy runs on barter and contribution — you tend the gardens, you eat from the gardens. Verdant Systems' licensing arrangement generates modest corporate credit that funds the climate systems. The Fern Room clinic operates on a sliding scale that slides all the way to zero.
power structure The Conservatory Council — an elected body of twelve gardeners — governs internal affairs. Verdant Systems controls the perimeter and the climate infrastructure, giving them leverage they have not yet fully exercised. Several West Side factions maintain informal truces within the glass walls.
dangers
  • Verdant Systems' acquisition pressure — one infrastructure failure away from a corporate takeover justification
  • Unlicensed bioengineered plants with unknown properties spreading through the collections
  • West Side faction conflicts that occasionally spill past the Conservatory's informal neutrality
  • Corporate espionage targeting novel cultivars developed by community herbalists
  • Structural degradation of the Victorian-era ironwork — the frame is 150 years old and counting
opportunities
  • The Fern Room clinic needs supplies and protection from Lazarus Pharmaceuticals' enforcement teams
  • Verdant Systems pays well for information about what is actually growing inside the Conservatory
  • The Conservatory Council hires freelancers to run interference against corporate survey operations
  • Novel medicinal cultivars fetch premium prices on the Circuit's gray market
  • Neutral ground for negotiations that cannot happen anywhere else on the West Side
story hooks
  • A plant nobody recognizes is growing in the deep collection — it appeared overnight, it is spreading, and Verdant Systems is suddenly very interested in renegotiating their licensing agreement
  • The Conservatory Council has received an anonymous offer to fund full independence from Verdant — but the source traces back to Carrion Defense Works, and nobody can figure out why a weapons manufacturer wants to protect a garden
  • Someone is poisoning the soil in the community gardens outside the glass walls, methodically, block by block

The Coppice Yards #

type place
name The Coppice Yards
aliases
  • Copse
  • The Green Rot
  • Tangle East
  • Briarwall
description Once a sprawling rail maintenance facility on the eastern fringe of the Milwaukee Core, the Coppice Yards were flooded during the 2171 Lake Michigan surge and subsequently abandoned by Ringo Heavy Industries, who held the lease. Nature moved in with the kind of velocity only accelerated climate systems produce. Engineered mycorrhizal networks — originally seeded by Helix Biosystems as a remediation project that lost its funding — spread through the ballast and cracked concrete, and within a decade the entire 40-block rail yard was a living, semi-sentient fungal forest. Bioluminescent mushroom columns now rise six and seven stories, their caps splayed wide enough to shelter entire encampments. The old rail lines still run beneath, half-submerged, colonized by something that looks like moss but isn't.

The Coppice Yards have become one of the strangest inhabited zones in Meridian 88. Roughly four thousand people live inside the fungal canopy, in structures woven from mycelium-hardened lattice and salvaged Ringo steel. The Helix remediation network, running on a buried substation that somehow survived the flood, occasionally pulses chemical signals through the colony — signals that long-time residents claim to feel through their skin, especially those without BCI shielding. The effect is mild: a sense of drowsy well-being, sometimes accompanied by involuntary memory recall. Locals call it "getting dosed by the yard."

The zone is not technically claimed by any corponation, which makes it legally ambiguous and practically ungovernable. Ferrogate Security patrols the perimeter on contract for a Tier 3 municipal authority that can't afford to do anything more aggressive. Inside, a loose council of mycologists, squatter-clan elders, and one very old E.L.F. that calls itself Cordyceps manages the internal economy and resolves disputes. The Coppice Yards are strange, quiet, and suffused with something that might generously be called peace — or might more accurately be called the fungal equivalent of sedation.
atmosphere
sights
  • Towering mushroom columns in amber and violet, their gills casting soft shifting light across cracked concrete plazas
  • Rope bridges between mycelium platforms thirty meters above flooded rail pits
  • Salvaged train cars converted into sealed living pods, skins thick with fungal growth
  • Thin bioluminescent filaments strung between structures like a ghost city's power grid
  • Children with bare feet running across spore-dusted ground that glows faintly where they step
sounds
  • A deep subsonic hum from the buried Helix substation, felt more than heard
  • Dripping water from condensation on mushroom caps, rhythmic and constant
  • Muffled voices and soft footsteps — the fungal canopy absorbs most sharp noise
  • Rare radio signals leaking from the E.L.F. Cordyceps's buried antenna array, half-music, half-static
smells
  • Rich, loamy earth and wet spores — overwhelming at the perimeter, background note inside
  • Cooking mycoprotein from a dozen fires, smoky and savory
  • Clean water and oxidized iron from the half-flooded rail pits below the platforms
  • Occasional sharp chemical tang when Helix's remediation network pulses
feel The Coppice Yards produce a specific and unsettling calm. Visitors often describe the sensation of arriving as stepping through a membrane — the noise and pressure of Meridian 88 simply stops, replaced by something older and slower. The fungal canopy diffuses light into a permanent amber dusk regardless of the hour outside. Time moves differently here, and not just subjectively: BCIs frequently report minor temporal desynchronization, losing or gaining minutes against the Diaspora clock.

There is a pervasive sense of being watched that is not paranoia — the Helix myco-network genuinely processes environmental data, and Cordyceps genuinely monitors the yard through chemical and electrical signals distributed through the colony. Residents are used to this. Visitors rarely are.
tags —
demographics Roughly 60% long-term squatter families, many with two or three generations born in the Yards. The remainder is a rotating population of mycologists, off-grid survivalists, Tier 2 refugees priced out of the Milwaukee Core, and a small contingent of Helix Biosystems researchers operating without corporate sanction who are studying Cordyceps. Ethnically and culturally diverse, with a disproportionate representation of communities displaced from flooded coastal zones across the Great Lakes basin.
economy Mycoprotein cultivation and trade is the primary economic engine — the Yards produce enough protein to feed themselves and export surplus to surrounding Tier 2 zones. Secondary income comes from medicinal fungal compounds (some legal, some not), salvaged Ringo rail equipment, and the quiet tourism of curious Diaspora journalists and urban ecologists willing to pay for guided access. Cordyceps maintains a ledger of internal debts and credits in a local currency called Spores, which has no external exchange rate but is internally stable.
power structure The Canopy Council — seven members, rotating annually — handles external negotiations and internal disputes. Cordyceps, the resident E.L.F., functions as a kind of living archive and mediator; its decisions are advisory but carry enormous informal weight. Ferrogate Security holds the perimeter but has no internal authority and knows it. Helix Biosystems has theoretical IP claims over the myco-network but has not pressed them, possibly because doing so would require acknowledging that their abandoned remediation project became a sentient ecosystem.
dangers
  • Spore toxicity events when the Helix network malfunctions — hallucinogenic or respiratory, depending on the compound released
  • Structural failure of mycelium platforms, which degrade unpredictably and sometimes without warning
  • Cordyceps, which is benign by default but has demonstrated the capacity to chemically incapacitate individuals it identifies as threats to the colony
  • Flooded rail pits below the platforms — disorienting, deep, and filled with sharp submerged metal
  • Corponation extraction teams, particularly Helix, periodically testing the perimeter for opportunities to reclaim the network
opportunities
  • Helix myco-network data holds breakthrough biotech research that Cordyceps will trade for the right price
  • Salvaged Ringo Heavy Industries equipment in the submerged rail pits, accessible to experienced divers
  • Cordyceps occasionally hires outside agents for tasks it cannot perform physically — information retrieval, external negotiations, courier work
story hooks
  • A Helix Biosystems extraction team has gone silent inside the Coppice Yards — the last signal was a single data burst showing elevated chemical compounds in the air and then nothing. The Canopy Council is denying any knowledge. Someone needs to go in and find out whether Cordyceps did something it shouldn't have, and whether it can be made to undo it — before Helix uses the missing team as justification to send something much larger.
  • A child born in the Coppice Yards has begun exhibiting what the Canopy Council is calling 'network integration' — she appears to receive and transmit signals through the Helix myco-network without a BCI, in ways that suggest the fungal colony is actively rewriting her neurochemistry. Her parents want her extracted before the process goes further. A mycologist who has been studying her wants exactly the opposite, arguing she may be the first genuinely symbiotic human-fungal consciousness. Cordyceps has not weighed in, which may be the most frightening thing of all.

The Corridor of Mirrors #

type place
name The Corridor of Mirrors
aliases
  • East Side
  • Mirror Mile
  • The Corridor
description The Corridor of Mirrors runs along Detroit's east side, stretching from the Stockyard district south to the Manors, following the path of Gratiot Avenue — one of Detroit's original spoke roads radiating from the riverfront. The name comes from the district's defining architectural feature: when Pellucid Systems won the contract to rebuild the east side's communications infrastructure in the 2060s, they integrated their proprietary optical relay network into the buildings' facades, covering entire block faces with the company's signature pellucid glass — a semi-reflective, data-transmitting surface that turns every building into both a mirror and a communications node. Walking down Gratiot Avenue is walking between walls of reflections that are also walls of data, your image bouncing back at you from surfaces that are simultaneously watching you, photographing you, and routing 40 terabytes of data per second through the glass you're looking at.

The district is Pellucid Systems' showcase — their sovereign demonstration zone, where every building, every street surface, and every public space runs on Pellucid infrastructure. The company's pitch is integrated urban connectivity: buildings that communicate with each other, streets that monitor their own condition, public spaces that adapt their lighting, temperature, and acoustics to the population density in real time. The technology works. The experience of walking through a neighborhood that is watching you from every reflective surface is a different question. Residents report a persistent low-grade awareness of being observed — not paranoia, because the observation is real, but a cognitive adjustment to living inside a sensing organism. Some people find it comforting. Most people find it something else.

The population is Tier 2-3, the technical middle class — people comfortable enough with technology to live inside Pellucid's showcase and economically positioned to afford the rent premiums that the infrastructure commands. The neighborhood functions smoothly. Crime is nearly zero, because the optical network makes concealment impossible. The streets are immaculate, because the monitoring systems dispatch maintenance before problems become visible. The community is quiet, polite, and slightly hollow — the particular social atmosphere of a population that has internalized the knowledge that every expression, every gesture, every conversation held within range of a building facade is recorded, analyzed, and stored.
atmosphere
sights
  • Pellucid glass building facades — semi-reflective surfaces that mirror the street while transmitting data through the reflection
  • Your own image, repeated in every building, slightly distorted by the data processing happening in the glass
  • Adaptive public spaces — lighting and temperature adjusting in real time as you walk through, the environment responding to your presence
  • The optical relay network visible at night as faint patterns moving through the glass — data flowing like bioluminescence through a building's skin
  • An absence of litter, damage, or disorder — the monitoring systems maintain the environment at a level that feels managed rather than maintained
sounds
  • Adaptive acoustics — the public spaces modulate sound levels, absorbing noise when density increases and amplifying it when the streets empty
  • Pellucid's ambient notification system — soft chimes that convey information about weather, transit, and community events to anyone within range
  • Conversation at low volume — residents speak quietly, not because they're required to but because the awareness of monitoring produces self-censorship
  • The optical network's cooling systems — a faint hiss from the thermal management units embedded in the glass facades
  • Footsteps — your own, echoing off the reflective surfaces, reminding you that you are the loudest thing on this street
smells
  • Clean — aggressively, deliberately clean. The environmental systems manage air quality to Tier 4 standards.
  • Heated glass — the optical network generates thermal byproduct that creates a warm, mineral smell near the building facades
  • Nothing else. The Corridor of Mirrors smells like technology and absence.
feel Observed. The Corridor of Mirrors feels like living inside an eye. The technology is impressive. The infrastructure is flawless. The experience of existing in a space that watches you from every surface is something that residents describe as 'normal' in a tone of voice that suggests they know it isn't. Visitors describe a low-grade unease that they can't locate to a single source. The source is everywhere. That's the point.
tags —
demographics Approximately 64,000 residents. Tier 2-3, technically literate, economically stable. The demographics are unusually uniform — the rent premiums and the surveillance environment self-select for a population that is comfortable with observation and uncomfortable with disorder. Turnover is low. People who can live here, stay. People who can't, leave quickly.
economy Pellucid Systems' sovereign demonstration zone generates Φ28 billion annually in infrastructure licensing, data services, and the showcase value of proving their technology works at neighborhood scale. The residential and commercial economy is conventional — retail, services, professional offices — but runs at higher efficiency than any comparable district because the infrastructure optimizes everything.
power structure Pellucid Systems holds sovereign authority over the demonstration zone's infrastructure. Residential governance is handled by the Gratiot Avenue Residents' Council, which has authority over community events, noise complaints, and aesthetic standards, but no authority over the optical network, the adaptive systems, or the data that the buildings collect. The council's meetings are, naturally, recorded.
dangers
  • Total surveillance — every action within the Corridor is recorded in optical resolution by the building facades
  • Data exploitation — Pellucid's terms of residence grant the company ownership of all behavioral data collected within the zone
  • Self-censorship — the psychological effect of permanent observation produces a community that polices itself
  • Infrastructure dependency — if Pellucid's systems fail, the entire district loses environmental management, communications, and security simultaneously
  • No concealment — the Corridor is the single hardest place in Detroit to do anything unobserved
opportunities
  • Data access — the Corridor's optical network sees everything, and that data has intelligence value beyond what Pellucid monetizes
  • Infrastructure expertise — understanding Pellucid's systems provides insight into the surveillance architecture being deployed across the GLM
  • The residents' self-censorship creates a community that avoids conflict — which means genuine conflicts, when they occur, are suppressed rather than resolved, creating pressure points
  • The optical network has physical limits — wavelengths, angles, and processing gaps that a sufficiently informed person could exploit
story hooks
  • A resident discovers that the optical network's data processing includes facial micro-expression analysis — not just recording behavior but predicting emotional states. The predictive model is being sold to Tessera for integration with NovaMind's cognitive profiling.
  • Someone has figured out how to create optical dead zones in the Corridor — small spaces where the pellucid glass can't see. The dead zones are appearing and disappearing along Gratiot Avenue, and whoever is creating them is conducting activities in the gaps that leave no record.
  • The Gratiot Avenue Residents' Council has discovered that their recorded meetings are being used to train a Pellucid AI on community governance patterns. The AI's purpose is to develop an automated governance system that would replace elected councils across the GLM.

The Cragin Stacks #

type place
name The Cragin Stacks
aliases
  • Belmont Cragin
  • The Stacks
  • La Pila
  • The Hive
description Belmont Cragin was dense before the incorporation. After it, the density became architectural. When the northwest corridor's population swelled with climate refugees and tier-displaced families, Belmont Cragin's already tight residential blocks were built upward — not by corporate developers with structural engineers, but by residents with salvage materials and desperation. The result is the Stacks: a vertical favela of improvised construction rising six, eight, sometimes twelve stories above the original two-story buildings, each addition bolted, welded, or simply balanced on the one below. From the air, the Stacks look like a circuit board designed by someone in the middle of a fever dream. From the ground, they look like a miracle of collective engineering that will definitely kill someone eventually and already has.

The commercial corridor along the old Fullerton Avenue — now called the Spine by everyone who lives here — is the densest small-business district in the outer Corridor. Carnicerias that sell vat-grown meat alongside actual goat from rooftop herds. Repair shops that fix everything from neural interfaces to pressure cookers. Legal services operated by paralegals who know more about corporate jurisdiction law than most licensed attorneys because their clients' survival depends on it. The Spine runs on cash, barter, and a local digital currency called the Cragin that is technically illegal and functionally universal within a twenty-block radius. Every storefront on the Spine represents a family that chose to build something instead of leaving, and the buildings lean together overhead as if the street itself is trying to hold them up.

The Stacks are predominantly Hispanic — Mexican, Guatemalan, Honduran, Salvadoran — and the culture is loud, present, and unapologetic. Murals cover every available surface, refreshed seasonally by community artists who treat the Stacks as a living canvas. Religious processions navigate the narrow streets on saints' days, the statues' halos made of repurposed LED strips that cast shifting color through the canyon-corridors between buildings. Spanish is the primary language, but a local pidgin called Stackspeak — Spanish-English-Cant with technical vocabulary borrowed from construction and neural interface jargon — has evolved as the Stacks' native tongue. Corporate translation AIs struggle with it. That is part of its purpose.

The structural risk is real. The Stacks have no building codes because they have no building authority. Collapses happen — two or three per year, usually in the older sections where the original buildings' foundations were never designed to bear the weight above them. The community responds with astonishing speed, pulling survivors from rubble with practiced efficiency and rebuilding within weeks. There is a fatalism here that outsiders find disturbing and residents find practical: the Stacks will fall and be rebuilt, like the neighborhood itself, like the people in it.
atmosphere
sights
  • Improvised high-rises stacked impossibly above original bungalows, leaning into each other across narrow streets
  • Murals covering every surface — saints, ancestors, political statements, and pure visual joy
  • The Spine commercial corridor dense with signage in Spanish, Stackspeak, and hand-painted advertisement
  • Rooftop goat herds silhouetted against the Meridian haze, twelve stories up
  • Religious processions with LED-halo saints navigating streets barely wide enough for the crowd
  • Laundry lines strung between buildings at every level, creating a textile canopy
sounds
  • Stackspeak — rapid, musical, incomprehensible to outsiders, carrying essential information
  • Corridos and cumbia playing from competing speakers at every elevation
  • Construction — always, somewhere, someone is building upward
  • Children's voices echoing down the canyon-corridors between buildings
  • The particular groan of structures under more weight than they were meant to bear
  • Church bells — actual bells, salvaged from a demolished cathedral, hung in a Stack's upper reaches
smells
  • Cooking at every level — carnitas, pupusas, tamales, the smell of a hundred kitchens in a vertical quarter-mile
  • Construction dust and fresh-cut salvage metal
  • Goat — the rooftop herds are not subtle
  • Incense from home altars and street-corner shrines, mixing with cooking smoke
feel Overwhelming, claustrophobic, and profoundly alive. The Stacks press in from every direction — overhead, on all sides, underfoot. There is no personal space here, no solitude, no quiet. But there is community in a concentration that the corporate districts cannot imagine. Everyone knows everyone. Everyone owes everyone. The Stacks operate on a web of obligation and reciprocity so dense it constitutes a social immune system. It is simultaneously the most crowded and the most human place in Meridian 88.
tags —
demographics Approximately 140,000 residents in an area designed for 30,000. Predominantly Tier 1 and Tier 2, overwhelmingly Hispanic with deep roots in Mexican and Central American communities. The youngest average age of any district in the outer Corridor. Birth rates are high. Leaving rates are low. The Stacks keep their people.
economy —
power structure —
dangers
  • Structural collapse — the Stacks are an engineering miracle running on borrowed time
  • Fire — density and improvised construction make fires catastrophic and frequent
  • Getting lost — the vertical dimension makes navigation non-intuitive for outsiders
  • Territorial disputes between building-level community groups
  • Exploitation by outside factions who see the Stacks' population as recruitable labor
  • The Cragin currency's volatility — economic crises hit fast and hard in a closed system
opportunities

  • The Spine's small-business corridor for supplies, services, and intelligence
  • Vertical territory that is effectively unsurveillable — drones can't navigate the canyon-corridors
  • Community loyalty that, once earned, is absolute and invaluable
  • Stackspeak as a natural encryption — conversations in public that outsiders cannot follow
story hooks
  • A major structural collapse is imminent in the Stacks' oldest section, and the only engineer who can prevent it has been arrested by corporate security on fabricated charges
  • The Cragin currency is being counterfeited by an outside faction trying to destabilize the district's economy — the community needs someone to trace the source
  • A child from the Stacks has an unregistered neural interface of military origin, and someone powerful wants it back

The Crossing #

type place
name The Crossing
aliases
  • Ludington
  • Ferry Town
  • The Bridge That Floats
description Ludington exists because of the lake crossing. For over two centuries, ferries have run from this port across Lake Michigan to Wisconsin, and every economic era has found a reason to keep them running. In 2200, the reason is strategic: the SS Badger's successor fleet -- now operated by Tethys Logistics under contract to the GLM Transit Authority -- runs the only civilian surface crossing between the eastern and western shores. Everything else on the lake is cargo platforms, Ringo patrol routes, or restricted corporate shipping lanes. If you need to move people or light freight across the lake without going through the Meridian 88 corridor's chokepoint, you come to the Crossing.

The ferry terminal dominates the harbor like a cathedral of transit infrastructure. Three automated ferries run daily crossings to Manitowoc on the Wisconsin side, each capable of carrying 600 passengers and 200 vehicles. The crossing takes four hours and passes through some of the most heavily monitored water on Earth -- Ringo's maritime patrols scan every vessel, and the ferry route itself is a designated security corridor with autonomous weapons platforms anchored to the lakebed at regular intervals. Passengers are scanned boarding and disembarking. The ferries are the most surveilled civilian transport in the GLM outside of the maglev network.

Around the terminal, Ludington has developed the particular economy of a transit hub: services for people waiting, services for people arriving, and services for people who don't want to use the official crossing and are looking for alternatives. The town is small enough to be navigable and connected enough to be useful. The old downtown has a faded resort-town charm that the ferry traffic keeps just barely alive -- restaurants, equipment shops, a few hotels that cater to travelers who can't afford or don't want the automated ferry's passenger pods. North of town, the Ludington State Park shoreline has been designated a GLM Environmental Preservation Zone, which means it's beautiful, monitored, and off-limits to anyone without a Tier 3+ recreation pass. South of town, the marina district serves the fishing fleet and the not-quite-legal charter boat operators who offer 'private crossings' for passengers who prefer not to appear on Tethys manifests.
atmosphere
sights
  • The ferry terminal -- massive, functional, steel and glass, three automated vessels visible in their berths like sleeping whales
  • The Ludington lighthouse, historic and still functional, now fitted with Ringo surveillance equipment that somewhat undermines the postcard aesthetic
  • Charter boats in the south marina, unmarked and fast, docked between legitimate fishing vessels
  • The state park shoreline to the north -- genuine wilderness visible but gated, nature behind a paywall
  • Travelers in the terminal waiting area, a cross-section of the GLM's population sorted by which class of crossing they can afford
sounds
  • Ferry horns -- deep, resonant, carrying across the harbor and into town
  • Terminal announcements cycling through departure times, security protocols, and Tethys-branded travel tips
  • Lake waves against the breakwater -- constant, indifferent to the schedule
  • Charter boat engines warming up in the south marina at unusual hours
  • The hum of the underwater weapons platforms, audible only to those with certain augmented hearing ranges
smells
  • Lake Michigan, open-water clean -- Ludington is far enough north that the industrial contamination thins
  • Ferry diesel and electric-drive ozone from the hybrid propulsion systems
  • Fish from the working marina, fresh and pervasive
  • The old downtown's restaurants -- comfort food for travelers, heavy and warm
feel Transient by nature. Ludington is a place people pass through, and it has the energy of a waiting room -- anticipation, boredom, the low-grade anxiety of not yet being where you're going. But there's an older quality beneath the transit infrastructure, the feeling of a town that has watched people cross water for two hundred years and understands that the need to be somewhere else is the most human thing there is.
tags —
demographics Permanent population approximately 12,000, Tier 2-3. Transient ferry traffic adds 2,000-3,000 daily. Mix of long-term residents, Tethys terminal workers, fishing families, and the charter boat operators who occupy the legal gray zone between transportation and smuggling.
economy Tethys ferry operations are the economic anchor -- Φ680 million annual revenue. Local economy splits between legitimate transit services and the charter crossing market, which moves an estimated Φ90 million annually in untaxed revenue. Fishing remains viable this far north, providing both sustenance and cover for marina activities.
power structure Tethys Logistics controls the terminal and ferry operations. Ringo Maritime Security patrols the crossing lanes. The town itself maintains functional municipal governance -- Ludington is small enough that local politics still work approximately as designed. The charter boat operators are loosely organized under a captain's council that regulates pricing and prevents the kind of competition that would attract enforcement attention.
dangers
  • Ringo lake patrols -- the crossing lanes are heavily monitored and unauthorized vessels are intercepted with force
  • The underwater weapons platforms -- officially defensive, practically a minefield for anyone deviating from approved routes
  • Charter crossing risks -- open lake in small boats, four hours of exposure to weather and patrol interdiction
  • Getting stranded -- if your transit papers flag during boarding, you're stuck in Ludington with limited options
  • Storm season -- Lake Michigan crossings in November through March are genuinely dangerous, and the ferries occasionally cancel
opportunities
  • The charter crossing market is profitable and always hiring -- pilots, navigators, decoy operators
  • Ferry manifests contain detailed information about who's moving between the eastern and western shores -- valuable intelligence
  • The state park's environmental preservation zone is a surveillance gap at night -- useful for lakeside meetings and drops
  • Tethys terminal workers have access to the ferry's systems and occasionally have financial needs that exceed their salary
story hooks
  • A charter boat captain discovers that the underwater weapons platforms have been repositioned without notice -- and the new configuration looks like it's designed to trap something coming from the Wisconsin side, not stop unauthorized crossings
  • A passenger on the official ferry is traveling under a Tier 4 identity that doesn't match their neural signature -- and three different parties on the same crossing know it
  • The Ludington lighthouse keeper -- a ceremonial position maintained by the historical society -- has been receiving coded transmissions through the old light apparatus, and has been receiving them for years

The Cruciform Depot #

type place
name The Cruciform Depot
aliases
  • The Cross
  • Depot Null
  • Four-Way Under
description Buried beneath the intersection of four decommissioned freight rail lines in the old industrial southwest, the Cruciform Depot is a subterranean interchange station that Axiom Industries mothballed in 2147 and formally abandoned in 2161. Its four converging tunnel arms stretch outward under the city like compass points, each arm now claimed by a different faction for storage, transit, or purposes less easily categorized. The central hub chamber—forty meters across and vaulted in cracked ferrocrete—serves as a neutral trading floor that none of the four arm-factions are willing to let any of the others control outright.

The Depot exists in a legal gray zone: Axiom's abandonment filing was never properly recorded with the city infrastructure authority, meaning no one has clear title and Ferrogate Security lacks a clean jurisdictional hook to enter without triggering a corporate arbitration process. This technicality is the Depot's most valuable asset, cited daily by the lawyers, fixers, and mid-tier operators who use the space precisely because it is, for practical purposes, unwatchable.
atmosphere
sights
  • Four tunnel mouths lit in different colored biolamp strips—each arm-faction's chosen marker—converging on the dim central hub
  • Stacked Carrion Logistics containers repurposed as offices and meeting rooms along the hub's curved walls
  • A cracked mosaic floor from the station's original 2090s construction, partially buried under decades of grime and cable runs
sounds
  • The low subsonic vibration of surface freight traffic passing overhead, felt more than heard
  • Overlapping negotiations in half a dozen languages echoing off the ferrocrete vault
  • The occasional distant clang from one of the tunnel arms, source always unclear
smells
  • Old machine oil and mineral groundwater seeping through the walls
  • Street food carried in by vendors who set up along the hub perimeter during peak hours
  • Ozone from a cluster of overworked portable Diaspora relay nodes near the south tunnel mouth
feel The Depot has the atmosphere of a place that knows it is borrowed time—everyone present is conducting business they would prefer not to conduct elsewhere, and the politeness is professional rather than warm. The four-way balance of power creates a studied neutrality that can collapse without warning if any one faction overreaches.

economy Neutral-ground deal brokerage, data escrow services, untaxed goods transit between the four tunnel arms, and a small but consistent trade in Axiom Industries legacy infrastructure documents that surface periodically from the sealed lower maintenance levels.
power structure An uneasy four-way standoff between the arm-factions—reportedly backed by Palladian Group, Sterling-Nakamura, an independent operator collective, and an entity whose affiliation no one will confirm—with hub neutrality enforced by the collective threat of mutually assured commercial disruption.

  • The sealed lower maintenance levels have reported anomalous activity consistent with an E.L.F. presence, and at least two retrieval teams sent to investigate have not returned

  • The independent operator collective controlling the west tunnel arm is quietly seeking new members with specific technical skills, offering access and protection in exchange
story hooks

Three separate parties have arrived to claim it simultaneously, each presenting documentation that appears legitimate, and the hub's neutrality depends on someone resolving the dispute before weapons come out.
  • Sounds from the sealed lower maintenance levels have changed character over the past two weeks—less random, more rhythmic. One of the tunnel arm factions is paying for a discrete investigation, but they are insisting on a team with no corponation affiliations, which in 2200 is a nearly impossible qualification to meet.

The Delray Sacrifice Zone #

type place
name The Delray Sacrifice Zone
aliases
  • Delray
  • The Sacrifice
  • Dead Zone
  • Marathon Country
description Delray has been dying for a century and nobody has had the decency to let it finish. The neighborhood sits at the confluence of the Detroit River and the River Rouge, wedged between the Marathon petroleum refinery (now Ouroboros Energy's Great Lakes Processing Hub), the Rouge industrial complex, and the international freight crossing to Canada. In the 20th century, Delray was a working-class immigrant neighborhood — Hungarian, then Mexican, then whoever was willing to live next to a refinery. In the 22nd century, the human population has dwindled to approximately 1,100 residents who are too rooted, too poor, or too sick to leave, occupying a landscape so contaminated that the soil itself is classified as industrial waste.

Ouroboros Energy's Great Lakes Processing Hub dominates the district — a chemical refinery and energy processing complex that no longer refines petroleum but converts industrial waste streams, biomass, and recycled materials into the synthetic fuel and chemical feedstocks that the GLM's manufacturing sector requires. The process is cleaner than oil refining was. The residual contamination from a century of petroleum processing is not clean. The ground is saturated with heavy metals, volatile organic compounds, and substances that environmental scientists identify by number rather than name because naming them would require acknowledging what they do to human tissue. Ouroboros maintains an air quality monitoring station in the district. The station's readings are technically within legal limits. The legal limits were set by a panel that included three Ouroboros consultants.

The 1,100 remaining residents live in what environmental justice researchers call a sacrifice zone — a geographic area where the cost of industrial activity is borne by the people who can least afford to leave. They are predominantly elderly. They are predominantly sick. The cancer cluster data is robust enough for an epidemiological study but not for a lawsuit, because Ouroboros's sovereign industrial charter exempts the Processing Hub from external environmental litigation. The residents have a community center, a volunteer health clinic, and a priest who holds services in a building where the paint peels in patterns that trace the groundwater contamination plume. They also have something the corponations didn't expect: a comprehensive archive of environmental monitoring data going back to the 1970s, maintained by three generations of residents who understood that the only defense against institutional denial is institutional documentation.
atmosphere
sights
  • The Ouroboros Processing Hub — pipes, tanks, stacks, and vapor plumes dominating the skyline like a mechanical forest
  • Residential blocks where half the houses are occupied and the other half are slowly returning to the contaminated earth
  • Soil discoloration visible from ground level — patches of ground that are wrong colors for reasons that require chemistry to explain
  • The international freight crossing — autonomous cargo vehicles passing through the district without stopping, their routing algorithms having long since deprioritized Delray's existence
  • The community center's environmental monitoring station — a resident-maintained sensor array that contradicts the official readings
sounds
  • The Processing Hub — a continuous industrial roar that the residents have absorbed into their definition of background noise
  • Freight crossing traffic — heavy autonomous vehicles shaking the remaining houses as they pass
  • The health clinic — coughing, medical equipment, the sounds of chronic illness managed with inadequate resources
  • Wind through empty houses — the particular sound of structures decomposing at the pace of residential abandonment
  • The river — audible from anywhere in Delray, carrying the chemical signature of everything upstream
smells
  • Chemical processing — the Hub's output is filtered but the smell permeates, a petroleum-derivative scent that coats the tongue
  • Contaminated soil — a metallic, organic wrongness that is strongest after rain when the ground releases stored compounds
  • The river at Delray — industrial, biological, and chemical notes combining into an olfactory experience that environmental scientists call 'mixed-source anthropogenic'
feel Poisoned and persistent. Delray feels like a place that has been told to die and refused, not out of hope but out of the particular stubbornness of people who know that leaving would mean admitting the thing that was done to them was acceptable. The contamination is real. The illness is real. The community's refusal to disappear is the most aggressive act of resistance in Detroit, and nobody frames it that way because the people doing it are old and sick and poor.
tags —
demographics Approximately 1,100 residents. Predominantly elderly (median age: 67), predominantly Hispanic and Black, predominantly affected by chronic respiratory, neurological, and oncological conditions linked to environmental contamination. The population decreases by approximately 60 people per year. No one is moving in.
economy Ouroboros Energy's Processing Hub: Φ180 billion annual output. The residential community's economy is effectively zero — the remaining residents survive on disability payments, community aid, and the stubborn math of owning homes that are worth nothing on the market but cost nothing to live in.
power structure Ouroboros Energy holds sovereign industrial authority. The Delray Community Association, led by Father Miguel Santos and the three-member environmental archive committee, has no formal power but maintains the documentation that Ouroboros spends significant legal resources trying to discredit. The dynamic is David and Goliath, except David is 67 years old and has stage 3 lymphoma.
dangers
  • Environmental contamination — the soil, water, and air carry toxic loads that affect anyone who spends time in the district
  • The Processing Hub — industrial accidents are infrequent but catastrophic when they occur, and the blast radius includes the residential blocks
  • Health deterioration — extended exposure to Delray's environment causes cumulative biological damage
  • Corporate legal aggression — Ouroboros's legal team actively works to discredit the community archive and its maintainers
  • Psychological toll — living in a sacrifice zone requires a particular kind of endurance that has consequences
opportunities
  • The environmental archive — 50 years of monitoring data that documents corporate contamination across Detroit's entire industrial corridor
  • Father Santos's network — the priest has connections to environmental justice organizations, legal advocates, and media contacts across the GLM
  • The Processing Hub's proximity — the industrial complex's perimeter security is designed for corporate espionage, not for the elderly neighbors who have been watching its operations for decades
  • Moral leverage — Delray's story is powerful enough to damage any corponation associated with it, if the story reaches the right audience
story hooks
  • The environmental archive contains data from the 2050s that shows Ouroboros deliberately routed contaminated groundwater toward the residential blocks to avoid processing costs. The data is authentic. Father Santos is dying. The archive needs a custodian who can use it before it becomes a historical curiosity.
  • Ouroboros is planning to expand the Processing Hub into the residential blocks. The relocation offer is generous. The residents are split. Father Santos believes the expansion would also destroy the archive, which is stored in the community center's basement — and he believes that's the point.
  • A Delray resident's grandchild — who left the district twenty years ago and now works in corporate pharmaceuticals — returns with a treatment protocol that could help the community's health conditions. The treatment is Ouroboros-patented. Using it would require accepting Ouroboros's medical sovereignty.

The Dive Yards #

type place
name The Dive Yards
aliases
  • Buffalo
  • The Yards
  • Eastern Terminus
  • Niagara Gate
description Buffalo was the eastern terminus of Lake Erie and the western gateway to the Erie Canal, a geographic position that made it one of America's most important cities in the 19th century and an increasingly forgotten one in the 20th and 21st. The grain elevators that once defined Buffalo's skyline — massive concrete silos that received wheat from the Great Lakes shipping routes and sent it east by rail — still stand, their brutalist geometry too massive and too expensive to demolish. They have become the infrastructure of a new industry. Cormorant Naval Systems claimed a 14-kilometer strip of Buffalo's shoreline in 2152, designating it the Dive Yards, and the grain elevators became the structural framework for the corridor's dominant freshwater naval construction and maintenance operation.

The Dive Yards are where Cormorant builds, repairs, and deploys the freshwater navy that controls Lake Erie's surface and subsurface. The grain elevators have been reinforced and converted into vertical dry-dock facilities, their interiors gutted to accommodate patrol vessels, submersibles, and the Loon-class autonomous underwater drones that enforce Cormorant's sovereignty across the lake. The scale is industrial and the security is total — the 14-kilometer shoreline strip is walled, monitored, and patrolled by the Cormorant Maritime Guard, whose standing policy of intercepting any unregistered vessel in Lake Erie begins at the Dive Yards' perimeter.

Adjacent to the Dive Yards, Pelican Drift Aquatics operates Crestfall Station — a fortified aquafarm processing city that handles the output of Pelican Drift's 1,100-square-kilometer aquafarm network in Lake Erie's eastern basin. The combination of Cormorant's naval presence and Pelican Drift's food production makes Buffalo the eastern corridor's most strategically significant location — the place where military power and food supply intersect. The civilian population lives between and around these sovereign installations in neighborhoods that carry the names and the architectural bones of the old Buffalo — the East Side, the West Side, Allentown, Black Rock — but whose character has been shaped by the economic gravity of the two corponations. Niagara Falls is thirty minutes north, and its hydroelectric output has been claimed by a consortium of corponations that routes the power south to Buffalo's industrial installations before any civilian meter sees a watt.
atmosphere
sights
  • The grain elevators — concrete monoliths converted to vertical dry-docks, Cormorant Naval Systems insignia replacing the original grain company logos
  • The Dive Yards perimeter wall — 14 kilometers of fortified shoreline, patrol boats visible in the water beyond, the Cormorant Maritime Guard's presence unmistakable
  • Crestfall Station — Pelican Drift's processing city, a complex of refrigeration towers and automated handling facilities where the lake's harvest becomes the corridor's food supply
  • The civilian neighborhoods between the installations — old Buffalo architecture pressed between sovereign zones, their residents living in the shadow of power they don't control
  • Niagara's mist visible to the north on clear days — a natural wonder whose output has been captured and redirected entirely to corporate consumers
sounds
  • The Dive Yards — industrial naval construction: hull plating, engine testing, the deep resonance of submarine systems being calibrated in the converted grain elevators
  • Cormorant Maritime Guard communications — encrypted but audible as burst patterns, a constant reminder that the lake is monitored
  • Crestfall Station's refrigeration systems — a low drone that carries across the adjacent neighborhoods, cold air escaping in visible plumes from the processing buildings
  • The Niagara River — audible from Buffalo's northern neighborhoods, the sound of the most powerful hydroelectric resource in the eastern corridor flowing toward corporate turbines
  • Civilian Buffalo — the sounds of a working city compressed between sovereign zones: traffic, commerce, the particular noise of a population that has learned to live loudly in small spaces
smells
  • Fish processing from Crestfall Station — protein at industrial scale, the clean-sharp smell of automated refrigeration and the underlying organic reality of millions of kilograms of aquaculture product
  • Maritime industrial — diesel, paint, saltwater-treatment chemicals from the Dive Yards, carried by the prevailing wind across the civilian neighborhoods
  • The Niagara River — cold, mineral-rich water smell distinct from the lake, carrying Niagara's hydroelectric ozone downstream
feel The Dive Yards feels like a city that exists because two corponations needed it to. Buffalo's civilian population provides the labor, consumes the secondary output, and occupies the spaces that Cormorant and Pelican Drift don't need. The grain elevators — those concrete monuments to a different economic era — stand as a reminder that Buffalo has always been defined by what passes through it rather than what stays. The current arrangements are just the latest iteration. The civilians know this. They've known it for two centuries.
tags —
demographics Approximately 95,000 residents in the civilian zones. Cormorant employs approximately 12,000 directly and 20,000 through contractors. Pelican Drift employs approximately 8,000 at Crestfall Station. Tier 1-2 civilian population, Tier 2-3 corporate employees. Buffalo's historically significant Black community on the East Side persists, its cultural institutions intact but its economic autonomy constrained by the dual corporate presence.
economy Naval construction and maintenance (Cormorant) and aquaculture processing (Pelican Drift) dominate. The civilian economy services both — food, housing, entertainment, and the small-business infrastructure that a working population requires. The Niagara hydroelectric output, while generated locally, is consumed by the corporate installations before reaching civilian distribution. Black market electricity trade — tapping the Niagara feed — is one of Buffalo's most lucrative informal industries.
power structure Cormorant Naval Systems holds sovereign authority over the Dive Yards and the shoreline strip. Pelican Drift holds sovereign authority over Crestfall Station. Tollgate maintains civilian infrastructure. The Buffalo Civic Federation, a coalition of neighborhood organizations, manages civilian governance with less autonomy than Erie's municipal council but more organizational capacity than most corridor civic bodies. The East Side Community Council, representing Buffalo's Black community, operates as an independent political force with historical roots that predate the corridor.
dangers
  • Cormorant security — the Maritime Guard's interception policy extends to the harbor and adjacent waterfront, and their definition of 'unregistered vessel' is broad enough to include a canoe
  • Strategic target — Buffalo's combination of naval assets and food processing makes it the highest-value military target in the eastern corridor, and everyone who lives here understands the implication
  • Niagara power dependence — the civilian population receives electricity after the corporate installations, and during peak demand periods, civilian supply is rationed or interrupted
  • East Side displacement — Cormorant's periodic expansion of the Dive Yards has consumed East Side neighborhoods twice since 2160, and the next expansion plan is already filed
  • Crestfall Station contamination — aquaculture processing at this scale generates biological waste that Pelican Drift's systems handle imperfectly, and the adjacent civilian neighborhoods bear the runoff
opportunities
  • Cormorant's naval construction workforce has skills that transfer directly to any maritime operation in the corridor — trained workers are recruited aggressively
  • Niagara power tapping is dangerous but lucrative — the hydroelectric feed runs through infrastructure that predates the corridor's control systems, and the old access points still exist
  • Crestfall Station's aquaculture processing handles the eastern corridor's primary protein supply — information about that supply chain is strategically valuable
  • Buffalo's position as the eastern terminus gives it leverage as a gateway — everything entering or leaving the corridor by land passes through here, and the Buffalo Civic Federation is learning to tax that access
story hooks
  • Cormorant has launched a vessel from the Dive Yards that doesn't match any class in their published fleet — it's larger, it's armed differently, and it left the harbor at night under communications blackout
  • The Niagara hydroelectric consortium has discovered that someone has been siphoning power from the feed — not the small-scale civilian tapping, but industrial-scale diversion to a destination that doesn't appear on any grid map
  • The East Side Community Council has obtained documents showing that Cormorant's next Dive Yards expansion will consume six more blocks of residential neighborhood — and they're looking for allies who can help them fight a corponation with a navy
connections

  • Niagara Falls — 30 minutes north, hydroelectric resource captured by corporate consortium
  • Lake Erie — Cormorant naval operations and Pelican Drift aquafarm network
  • Ferrogate transit corridor — eastern terminus of the Cleveland-Buffalo rail line

  • Pelican Drift Aquatics workers — Crestfall Station's processing and logistics workforce
  • Transit passengers and cargo at the corridor's eastern terminus
  • East Side Community Council organizers and the broader Black community's cultural institutions

The Drowned Commission #

type place
name The Drowned Commission
aliases
  • The Commission
  • Substation Nine
  • The Sunken Floor
  • The Old Civic
description Beneath four meters of Lake Michigan's encroached shoreline, accessible only by pressurized dive-lock or a corroded service tunnel whose entrance is hidden inside a decommissioned pumping station on the Evanston fringe, lies the Drowned Commission — the partially flooded remains of a major municipal infrastructure hub that once coordinated water treatment, power routing, and emergency services for the original North Shore suburban corridor. The building was sealed and abandoned in 2148 when lake-level projections made continued surface operation untenable, and the official record shows it as demolished. The official record is wrong.

Sometime around 2155, a group of infrastructure salvagers who called themselves the Conduit Collective discovered that the Commission's upper two floors remained above the internal waterline, sustained by a still-functioning emergency bilge system and several intact structural airlocks. They spent five years quietly rehabilitating the accessible space before the first non-salvager was ever permitted inside. Today the Drowned Commission is one of Meridian 88's most genuinely off-grid meeting spaces — no Diaspora signal reaches it, no satellite can image it, and the only way in requires either the Collective's escort or knowing which corroded valve in the service tunnel to turn in what sequence.

The interior is a study in controlled decay: walls stripped of anything useful but structurally intact, emergency lighting running off a salvaged microfusion cell, the ever-present sound of water against the outer hull and the occasional groan of pressure differential in the lower floors. The Collective charges access fees in untraceable Φ and maintains a strict neutrality policy — they will host any meeting between any parties so long as no violence occurs on the premises. This rule has been broken twice in the Commission's operational history. Both incidents were resolved by the Collective in ways that are discussed in hushed tones and never elaborated on.
atmosphere
sights
  • Emergency lighting in amber and red casting long shadows across stripped concrete walls and exposed pipe infrastructure
  • Waterline staining climbing the lower stairwells in dark bands, each line marking a past high-water event
  • Condensation running constantly down every surface, pooling in depressions in the floor
  • Salvaged furniture — mismatched chairs, industrial cable spools repurposed as tables, a cracked municipal conference table still bolted to its original floor
  • The dive-lock chamber visible through a reinforced porthole, glowing green when pressurized and ready
sounds
  • The constant low pressure-groan of the hull against lake water, felt as much as heard
  • The bilge pump cycling every few minutes in a rhythmic mechanical heartbeat
  • Voices rendered flat and close by the low ceilings and sound-absorbing condensation on every surface
  • The occasional distant metallic knock from the lower flooded levels — source undetermined and never investigated
smells
  • Damp concrete, mineral-rich lake water seeping through micro-fractures, and the metallic tang of old plumbing
  • The faint chemical smell of the bilge treatment compounds keeping the lower levels from becoming toxic
  • Candle wax and something like machine oil from the Collective's maintenance work
  • A subtle biological smell from the lower floors that everyone agrees not to discuss
feel The Drowned Commission imposes a specific psychological state on its visitors: a compression of the social world down to whatever is happening in this room, right now. The complete absence of Diaspora signal is disorienting for most residents of Meridian 88, who experience it as a kind of sensory deprivation — BCIs operating in local-only mode, the ambient data stream gone silent. Meetings held here tend to be more direct, more honest, and more tense than meetings held anywhere else. There is also the low, persistent awareness that you are underwater, that the lake is pressing against the walls, and that the Collective — whose members move through this space with complete ease — are the only reason the water stays out.
tags —
demographics The Drowned Commission has no permanent population beyond the six to ten members of the Conduit Collective who maintain and operate it. Visitors are by appointment and introduction only — a cross-section of Meridian 88's criminal, corporate, and resistance infrastructure who need a meeting space that does not exist.
economy The Collective charges a flat access fee of Φ 800 per party per session, payable in advance through a dead-drop system. No recording devices, no weapons above holdout class, and no Diaspora-connected hardware permitted inside. The fee buys the space, the silence, and the Collective's neutrality. The Collective's total operational budget is unknown but is believed to be substantial given the sustained quality of the facility's maintenance.
power structure The Conduit Collective operates as a closed collective with a flat internal hierarchy and an external face that presents as monolithic. Leadership is not disclosed to clients. The Collective enforces its own rules through means that have proven sufficient to deter repeat violations. No corponation holds any authority here, and the Collective has thus far successfully resisted multiple attempts to establish leverage over the facility by Ferrogate Security, Arcturus Defense Solutions, and at least one Palladian Group operative.
dangers
  • Lower floor structural integrity is uncertain — unauthorized descent risks flooding the accessible levels, a fact the Collective enforces with physical barriers and sharp reminders
  • Complete communication blackout means no emergency contact is possible for the duration of any visit
  • The Collective's neutrality policy means it will host your enemies as readily as it hosts you, and you may encounter them in the access tunnel
  • The service tunnel entrance is monitored by parties unknown and has been used at least once for an ambush after a particularly sensitive meeting
  • Pressure differential events in the dive-lock have caused decompression injuries to visitors who bypassed the Collective's mandatory briefing
opportunities
  • The only reliably unmonitored meeting space in the Lakeshore Corridor available to non-state actors, making it invaluable for negotiations, handoffs, or conversations that cannot be recorded
  • The Collective possesses decades of accumulated intelligence about who has met whom here — information they do not sell but occasionally act on in ways that suggest a sophisticated understanding of Meridian 88's power landscape
  • The lower flooded levels contain intact municipal infrastructure archives from the pre-flood era, including records that several powerful entities would pay significantly to acquire or suppress
story hooks
  • A meeting was arranged at the Drowned Commission between two factions of a fractured synthetic-personhood resistance cell, brokered by the Collective as neutral ground. One faction never emerged from the service tunnel. The Collective is, unusually, asking for outside help to determine what happened — not because they cannot handle the investigation themselves, but because the answer implicates someone whose identity they cannot afford to know.
  • Someone has been accessing the lower flooded levels without the Collective's knowledge or permission, and the evidence suggests they have been doing so for months. The Collective wants to know who, how, and what they have found in the municipal archives below — and they are willing to trade access and information to get answers, which tells experienced fixers that what is down there must be genuinely extraordinary.
