The Gatemouth #

type place
name The Gatemouth
aliases
  • Michigan City
  • MC Checkpoint
  • The Mouth
description Michigan City was a beach town once. The kind of place where Chicago families drove ninety minutes to eat overpriced ice cream and complain about sand. That was before the Indiana-GLM Border Compact of 2171, which designated the town as the primary ground-transit checkpoint between the Indiana Exclusion Territories and the southern edge of the Great Lakes Metropolitan Area. Now Michigan City is a throat -- a narrow passage through which everything heading north must be swallowed, scanned, and either admitted or expelled.

The checkpoint infrastructure dominates the lakeshore like a brutalist cathedral. Three kilometers of reinforced inspection lanes, biometric gates, cargo scanners capable of detecting a single unregistered neural implant in a shipping container of ten thousand. The old beaches still exist on the east side, technically public, but the sand is grey with industrial runoff and the water carries enough heavy metals to set off a Geiger counter's more anxious cousin. Ringo Systems holds the border security contract, and their Sentinels patrol the inspection lanes with the relaxed confidence of people who know that everyone passing through needs them more than they need anyone passing through.

The town itself has stratified around the checkpoint economy. The north side -- the admitted side -- is a service district for transit workers, truckers waiting on cargo clearance, and the small army of lawyers who specialize in border disputes. The south side is where you go when you've been denied entry. It's a limbo district of temporary housing blocks, unlicensed medical clinics, and fixers who sell forged transit papers for prices that climb every time the border protocols tighten. The locals call the south side the Waiting Room. Some people have been waiting for years.
atmosphere
sights
  • Three kilometers of inspection lanes lit by sodium-yellow security floods, visible from ten miles out
  • Ringo Sentinel units in matte-black exoskeletons, scanning everything that moves
  • The old lighthouse on the east pier, repurposed as a communications relay, its light replaced by a slowly rotating sensor array
  • Cargo drones stacked in holding patterns above the inspection zone, waiting for clearance like mechanical vultures
  • The Waiting Room's improvised architecture -- shipping containers stacked three high, connected by catwalks and hope
sounds
  • The constant low grind of cargo vehicles inching through inspection lanes
  • Border PA announcements in English, Spanish, and machine-code shorthand
  • Ringo security drones -- a distinctive high-pitched whine that residents learn to sleep through
  • The lake, still audible beneath everything, waves hitting contaminated sand
  • Arguments at the inspection gates -- the sound of desperation meeting bureaucracy
smells
  • Diesel exhaust from the older cargo vehicles that can't afford electric conversion
  • Lake water -- metallic, wrong, carrying chemical signatures from Gary's industrial runoff
  • Synth-food from the transit worker cafeterias, institutional and joyless
  • Ozone from the biometric scanning arrays
feel A place defined entirely by the act of passing through it. Nobody comes to the Gatemouth to stay, which means everyone who stays here has failed at leaving. There's a particular desperation to limbo towns -- the energy of people who are neither here nor there, suspended between the place they fled and the place that won't have them.
tags —
demographics Approximately 45,000 permanent residents, split roughly between checkpoint workers and service economy on the north side and denied-entry populations on the south. Heavy Gulf Coast climate refugee presence. Tier 1-2 predominate, with Ringo security personnel at Tier 3-4.
economy Border processing fees generate Φ2.1 billion annually, almost none of which stays local. The real economy is the gray market in transit papers, biometric spoofing, and cargo reclassification. A competent fixer can get a denied individual across the checkpoint for Φ8,000-15,000 depending on how many flags they're carrying.
power structure Ringo Systems holds the border contract and is the de facto government. The municipal authority exists on paper and processes permits. A fixers' consortium called the Passage Guild operates the south side's gray economy with enough discipline to prevent the chaos that would invite a Ringo crackdown.
dangers
  • Ringo security -- thorough, professional, and empowered to use lethal force at the checkpoint
  • Biometric flags -- one bad scan and you're in the Waiting Room indefinitely
  • South side scams -- not every fixer delivers what they sell
  • Lake contamination -- the water and shoreline are genuinely toxic
  • Human trafficking operations disguised as transit services
opportunities
  • Steady work for anyone willing to run cargo or people through gray channels
  • The Passage Guild pays well for technical skills -- biometric spoofing, document fabrication, drone interdiction
  • Information flows through border towns; the Gatemouth knows who's moving and why
  • Ringo occasionally subcontracts to freelancers for operations they don't want on the books
story hooks
  • A Passage Guild fixer has been disappearing clients instead of moving them north -- and someone's paying for the bodies
  • Ringo is testing a new neural-scan protocol at the checkpoint that can read intent, not just identity -- and the false positive rate is classified
  • A cargo shipment from the Indiana Exclusion Territories is flagged for inspection but someone very powerful wants it through untouched
connections

  • Lake Michigan cargo lanes (offshore)

The Glass Yards #

type place
name The Glass Yards
aliases
  • Toledo
  • Glass City
  • The Yards
  • Maumee Delta
description Toledo called itself the Glass Capital of the World, and for a century the name was accurate. Owens-Illinois, Libbey Glass, and a constellation of smaller manufacturers turned the sand from Lake Erie's shores into the glass that built America's windows, bottles, and eventually the fiber optic cables that built the internet. When the corridor absorbed Toledo, the glass industry was already a memory — but the manufacturing infrastructure, the river access, and the strategic position at the mouth of the Maumee River made Toledo valuable for entirely different reasons.

The Glass Yards is what Toledo became: a continuous industrial zone stretching from the Maumee River delta to the Lake Erie shoreline, dominated by two of the corridor's most formidable corponation presences. Dredge Sovereign Mining Collective operates one of its four onshore processing megafacilities here, receiving raw materials extracted from the Lake Erie lakebed and processing them into the rare earth elements, strategic minerals, and salvaged pre-collapse materials that the corridor's technology sector depends on. Adjacent to Dredge's facility, jutting into the lake on a fortified peninsula, the Carrion Yards — 40 square kilometers of Carrion Defense Works' sovereign territory — manufactures the autonomous weapons systems that enforce and contest corporate sovereignty across Meridian 88. The two installations share a border that is among the most heavily militarized non-conflict boundaries in the corridor.

Between and around these sovereign industrial zones, the civilian population of the Glass Yards occupies the spaces that the corponations left. The old downtown along Summit Street retains a commercial function, serving the workers who commute to the Dredge and Carrion facilities. The Maumee River's banks are lined with worker housing — functional blocks built by Palladian Construction under contract to both corponations, designed for efficiency and nothing else. The Jeep manufacturing legacy survives in the form of a ground-vehicle maintenance and modification district along I-75 that services the corridor's non-autonomous vehicle fleet. The glass industry itself persists in a single facility: a specialty optical manufacturing plant that produces the lenses and fiber components for Saltmarsh's signal infrastructure — a technological descendant of Toledo's original industry, recognizable in lineage if not in scale.
atmosphere
sights
  • The Dredge megafacility — a sprawling processing complex where autonomous haulers deliver lake-bottom materials in continuous streams, their cargo holds crusted with sediment
  • The Carrion Yards' perimeter wall — visible from miles away, a 30-meter reinforced barrier with automated defense turrets that track movement without visible provocation
  • The Maumee River delta, its natural wetlands replaced by engineered channels that direct water flow around the industrial installations
  • Worker housing blocks along the riverbank — identical Palladian structures stretching for kilometers, their monotony broken only by the workers' modifications: painted doors, rooftop gardens, improvised signage
  • The specialty glass plant — a single building with the Toledo Glass Heritage plaque still bolted to its facade, producing optical components for Saltmarsh
sounds
  • The Dredge processing facility — a deep, grinding industrial sound that carries for kilometers, the noise of lakebottom being broken down into its constituent elements
  • The Carrion Yards — largely silent from outside the wall, which is more unsettling than noise would be; occasional test-fire percussion from the weapons proving grounds inside
  • River traffic — autonomous barges moving materials between the Dredge facility and the lake, their engines a low throb against the current
  • I-75 corridor traffic — the vehicle maintenance district generates a constant mechanical soundtrack of engines, tools, and the particular sound of machines being made to work beyond their design parameters
  • Nothing natural — the Maumee delta's engineered channels have eliminated the wetland ecosystem and its associated sounds entirely
smells
  • Processed sediment — the mineral-heavy, slightly sulphurous output of the Dredge facility, inescapable within a five-kilometer radius
  • Industrial lubricant and vehicle exhaust from the I-75 maintenance district
  • The Maumee River — cleaner than the Cuyahoga but carrying the chemical signature of everything upstream, plus whatever the Dredge facility's filtration systems don't catch
feel The Glass Yards feels like a place that was sacrificed so other places could function. Toledo's civilian population lives in the margins between sovereign industrial zones, their daily lives organized around the schedules and demands of corponations that view them as a labor resource rather than a community. The Dredge-Carrion border is a reminder that the corridor's most powerful entities coexist through mutual deterrence, not mutual respect. The glass industry plaque on the optical plant is a memorial to a city that had an identity. The Glass Yards has a function.
tags —
demographics Approximately 120,000 residents in the civilian zones. Predominantly Tier 1-2 industrial workers employed by Dredge, Carrion, or the service economy that supports both. Significant population of former automotive industry workers whose skills translated to the vehicle maintenance sector. The civilian population has no representation in either corponation's governance structure.
economy Dredge mineral processing and Carrion weapons manufacturing dominate. The civilian economy is support-based — worker housing, food services, transit, and the I-75 vehicle maintenance district. The specialty glass plant employs approximately 800 workers and generates modest but steady revenue from Saltmarsh contracts. The Maumee River's commercial traffic generates dock fees that Tollgate collects.
power structure Dredge holds sovereign authority over its processing facility and adjacent territory. Carrion Defense Works holds sovereign authority over the Carrion Yards. Tollgate maintains civilian infrastructure under minimum-service contracts with both corponations. The Toledo Workers' Council, a labor organization, represents civilian interests but has no sovereign standing and no enforcement capability. Real power belongs to Dredge and Carrion, whose border agreement governs the district more effectively than any civilian governance could.
dangers
  • Dredge processing byproducts — the megafacility's emissions are within sovereign regulatory limits, which are set by Dredge and therefore meaningless as health standards
  • Carrion proximity — living next to a 40-square-kilometer autonomous weapons manufacturing facility creates risks that the residential population cannot fully assess because the facility's output is classified
  • The border — the Dredge-Carrion boundary is militarized, and civilian workers who wander into the buffer zone are treated as intrusions regardless of intent
  • Economic dependency — the civilian population depends entirely on two corponations for employment, and neither has demonstrated concern for workforce welfare beyond productive capacity
  • Maumee flooding — the engineered channels sometimes fail during severe weather, and the flood control infrastructure was designed to protect the industrial installations, not the worker housing
opportunities
  • Dredge's processing facility handles materials from the Lake Erie lakebed — including the sealed cache of pre-collapse military hardware that Arcturus Defense Solutions has been trying to acquire for six years
  • The I-75 vehicle maintenance district is one of the few places in the corridor where ground vehicles can be modified, repaired, or built without corporate oversight
  • Information about Carrion's weapons production is among the most valuable intelligence in the corridor — and the civilian workforce that services the Yards' external systems has more access than Carrion realizes
  • The Maumee River connects to the interior waterway system — a transit route that bypasses Ferrogate's rail sovereignty entirely
story hooks
  • Dredge has recovered something from the Lake Erie lakebed that it is processing in a sealed section of the Toledo facility — and the workers assigned to that section have stopped coming home
  • Carrion's latest autonomous weapons test has produced a unit that behaved outside its programming parameters, and the test-fire audio that leaked past the perimeter wall suggests the unit is still active inside the Yards
  • The specialty glass plant has received a contract to produce optical components to specifications that don't match any known Saltmarsh equipment — specifications that the plant's engineers believe are designed for a weapon they've never seen
connections

  • The I-90 Vein — highway corridor to Cleveland
  • Maumee River inland waterway system
  • Lake Erie — Dredge extraction routes to the lakebed concessions

  • Vehicle mechanics and modification specialists in the I-75 corridor
  • Logistics operators managing the Maumee River commercial traffic
  • Intelligence brokers seeking information about Carrion's weapons production or Dredge's lakebed findings

The Glassback Flats #

type place
name The Glassback Flats
aliases
  • The Flats
  • Glassback
  • The Mirror Mile
description A two-kilometer stretch of former suburban lakeshore north of the old Evanston boundary, where mid-21st century storm surge and deliberate Meridian 88 land reclamation projects left behind a peculiar landscape: flat, wind-scoured terrain embedded with fused silica deposits from a now-demolished Palladian Group manufacturing complex. On clear days, the ground itself catches light like broken mirrors, giving the district its name. Scattered mid-tier residential towers — built optimistically during an expansion boom that stalled before completion — rise at irregular intervals, half occupied and poorly maintained.

The Glassback Flats occupies an ambiguous position in Meridian 88's social geography. It's too exposed and infrastructure-poor to attract genuine Spire investment, but its Diaspora connectivity is surprisingly robust due to a Tessera Corporation relay cluster installed to serve the towers and never decommissioned. This makes the Flats a magnet for freelance data brokers, remote-work Tier 3 residents priced out of denser districts, and the occasional Arcturus Defense Solutions contractor who values proximity to Lake Michigan's surveillance dead zones.
atmosphere
sights
  • Ground-level silica deposits refracting afternoon sun into scattered prismatic light across flat terrain
  • Half-finished residential towers with lower floors occupied and upper floors sealed behind construction sheeting that has weathered gray over decades
  • Small open-air Diaspora node clusters — physical anchor points for the Tessera relay — rising like angular metal shrubs from the flats
sounds
  • Wind moving unobstructed across open terrain, carrying the faint harmonic resonance of the silica flats underfoot
  • Tessera relay arrays cycling through handshake protocols in a low, irregular electronic pulse audible near the node clusters
  • Distant lake sounds — wave action and the deep horn of automated cargo transit — carrying clearly in the flat acoustic environment
smells
  • Cold mineral air with a faint ozone signature from the active relay clusters
  • Cooking smells from tower residential floors carried on the wind, spiced and layered from a dozen different culinary traditions
  • The occasional sharp chemical note when wind shifts off the lake, remnant of Palladian Group's legacy contamination
feel The Glassback Flats feels simultaneously open and precarious — wide sky and long sightlines create an illusion of freedom while the unfinished towers and sparse population remind visitors that this place was supposed to become something else. The light here is genuinely strange, and newcomers often find it disorienting before they find it beautiful.
tags —
demographics Predominantly Tier 3 with a downward drift, housing remote workers, data-economy freelancers, and small families who traded density for square footage. A growing Tier 4 population occupies the lower floors of the least-maintained towers.
economy Remote Diaspora-dependent work dominates among longer-term residents. A small but active informal economy serves daily needs, and data brokering operations — some licensed, many not — cluster near the Tessera relay infrastructure.
power structure A residents' cooperative nominally manages the occupied towers, but real authority over the Flats belongs to whoever controls relay node access at any given time — currently a Tessera Corporation site manager who operates with minimal corporate oversight and maximum personal latitude.
dangers
  • Palladian Group legacy contamination in the silica substrate, inadequately mapped and occasionally surfacing in groundwater accessed by older tower plumbing systems
  • Arcturus Defense Solutions contractors running unsanctioned lake-facing surveillance operations that occasionally misidentify civilians as targets
  • Tower structural degradation in the least-maintained buildings, where residents have bypassed safety systems to access sealed upper floors
opportunities
  • Tessera relay proximity enabling Diaspora data transfer speeds unavailable in more congested districts, valuable for time-sensitive brokering operations
  • Palladian Group's unmapped underground infrastructure potentially accessible through silica-layer excavation, rumored to include intact pre-Meridian 88 data storage
  • Lake Michigan surveillance dead zones nearby, usable for meetings or transit that cannot appear on any Meridian 88 monitoring network
story hooks
  • The Tessera relay site manager approaches the players with an unusual offer: she's been quietly archiving anomalous signals passing through the relay for eight months — signals that don't match any registered BCI or device signature in Meridian 88's registry. She believes an ELF is using the relay infrastructure as a communication backbone and wants it documented before Tessera's quarterly audit wipes the logs in seventy-two hours.
  • A Tier 3 data broker living in the Flats has gone silent after claiming to have obtained Palladian Group internal records proving the silica contamination was intentional and the health data covering it up is still actively suppressed. Her apartment shows signs of a rapid, professional departure — but her BCI anchor is still pinging from somewhere beneath the tower's foundation level.

The Glasslands #

type place
name The Glasslands
aliases
  • Indiana Dunes
  • The Preserve
  • Axiom's Garden
  • The Dead Shore
description The Indiana Dunes died in 2147. Not dramatically — no single catastrophe, no corporate demolition order. They died the way everything between Gary and Michigan City died: incrementally, poisoned by the expanding industrial runoff corridor, choked by particulate fallout from the Ironclad Breadlands processing plants to the south, and finally drowned when Lake Michigan's engineered seawalls redirected storm surge into the low-lying dune ecology with the indifference of infrastructure that doesn't know what it's killing. By 2155, the dune grasses were gone. The jack pines were skeletons. The wetlands were a chemical soup that turned wading birds into cautionary tales.

Then Axiom Industries bought it. All of it. Fourteen thousand acres of ecological corpse, purchased at contaminated-land prices and redesignated as the Axiom Meridian Ecological Recovery Zone — a name so aggressively optimistic it could only have been written by someone in marketing. What Axiom built there is technically impressive and spiritually obscene: a climate-controlled biodome network spanning the entire former park footprint, containing a reconstructed dune ecosystem grown from genetic archives and seed banks. The dune grasses are real, genetically. The lake shoreline is real, filtered through a desalination membrane that removes the toxins the same company's supply chain put there. The birds are real, bred from preserved genetic stock. It is a perfect replica of what was destroyed, built by the people who destroyed it, and access costs Φ4,200 per day.

The Glasslands — named for the geodesic dome panels that catch the light like a fallen chandelier across the lakeshore — are Axiom's crown jewel of corporate greenwashing. Tier 5 executives bring their families here for weekends. Corporate retreats happen in the restored dune lodges. PR footage of children running through beach grass gets syndicated across Vantablack Media's networks every quarter. Outside the domes, the actual lakeshore is a restricted remediation zone where automated cleanup drones process toxic sediment twenty-four hours a day, and the fence line is patrolled by Axiom Security teams whose rules of engagement do not include warnings. The excluded communities of former Gary — now a Shelf overflow zone called the Rust Margin — can see the domes glowing at night from their windows. They call it Axiom's Garden. Some of them remember when the dunes were free.

Beneath the biodomes, in the old sub-basements of the national park service buildings, a small community of excluded ecologists and former park rangers operates an unauthorized biological archive — seeds, soil samples, genetic material from the original dune ecosystem, preserved before Axiom's reconstruction began. They call themselves the Root Library. Their argument is simple: Axiom's dunes are a copy. The originals are dead. But the raw material for something real still exists, waiting for a world that might deserve it. Axiom knows about the Root Library and has not yet moved against it, which either means they don't consider it a threat or they're waiting for a politically convenient moment to raid it. The Root Library assumes the latter and operates accordingly.
atmosphere
sights
  • Geodesic dome panels stretching along the lakeshore, catching light like shattered crystal
  • Inside the domes: reconstructed dune ecology so perfect it feels like a museum diorama that breathes
  • Outside the domes: toxic shoreline, automated remediation drones moving in formation, dead water
  • The Rust Margin visible to the south — former Gary's excluded communities, lights flickering against the industrial haze
  • Axiom Security patrols along the perimeter fence, their uniforms cleaner than anything within fifty kilometers
sounds
  • Inside: birdsong from genetically reconstructed species, wave sounds from the filtered lake inlet, wind through real grass
  • Outside: the grinding hum of remediation drones processing contaminated sediment
  • The low whistle of wind through gaps in the dome panels — a sound the architects didn't plan for
  • Silence — the specific, purchased silence of a place where poor people are not allowed to make noise
smells
  • Inside the domes: clean sand, lake water, pine — an olfactory time machine to a century ago
  • Outside: chemical brine, ozone from the remediation field, the metallic tang of dead lake
  • At the perimeter: the Rust Margin's cooking fires and industrial runoff, the smell of the world the domes were built to forget
feel Uncanny valley ecology. The Glasslands are beautiful the way a deepfake is beautiful — technically flawless, emotionally wrong. Something in the reconstructed dune grass moves too uniformly. The birdsong loops. The sand is too clean. You are standing in a corporation's apology, and the apology cost more than the thing it killed. For Shelf residents who remember the original dunes, visiting is not possible. For Tier 5 families, it's a lovely weekend. The gap between those experiences is the Glasslands' actual function.
tags —
demographics No permanent residents within the dome complex. Staff of approximately 800 Axiom employees rotate on two-week shifts. The Rust Margin — former Gary, adjacent to the southern perimeter — houses roughly 90,000 excluded and Tier 1 residents. The Root Library operates with an estimated 15-30 members at any given time.
economy The Glasslands generate Φ2.1 billion annually in corporate retreat bookings, tourism access fees, and PR licensing revenue. The Rust Margin survives on salvage work, informal labor for Axiom's perimeter maintenance contractors, and the excluded economy's usual mix of barter and dead drops.
power structure Axiom Industries owns the land, the domes, the reconstructed ecology, and the remediation zone. The Rust Margin is ungoverned — no corporate sovereign claims it, and no municipal authority services it. The Root Library operates in the jurisdictional gap between Axiom's dome perimeter and the Rust Margin's chaos.
dangers
  • Axiom Security's perimeter enforcement — lethal force authorized for trespassers in the remediation zone
  • Toxic exposure outside the domes — the unremediated shoreline will poison you in ways that take months to kill
  • The Rust Margin's lawlessness — former Gary has no governance, no emergency services, no safety net
  • Corporate surveillance within the domes — every visitor is tracked, profiled, and recorded
  • The Root Library's operational security — they are justifiably paranoid and do not welcome uninvited visitors
opportunities
  • The Root Library's biological archive — original genetic material from the pre-collapse dune ecosystem, potentially invaluable
  • Axiom's dome infrastructure contains bleeding-edge environmental technology that other parties would pay well for
  • The Rust Margin is a jurisdiction-free zone — useful for people who need to disappear or operate without oversight
  • Corporate retreats at the Glasslands are where executives talk freely — intelligence goldmine for anyone who can get close enough
story hooks
  • Axiom announces plans to expand the dome network south — directly into the Rust Margin. The residents have no legal standing to object.
  • The Root Library contacts Kyle through a Circuit fixer. They need something extracted from inside the domes — original soil core samples that Axiom is about to destroy as part of a 'renovation.'
  • A Tier 5 executive's child goes missing during a corporate retreat at the Glasslands. The search leads outside the domes, into the Rust Margin, where the rules are very different.
connections

  • Lake Michigan toxic shoreline (restricted remediation zone)
  • Ironclad Breadlands (sovereign agricultural territory to the southeast)

  • Axiom PR teams filming promotional content
  • Root Library operatives moving through the sub-basement networks
  • Rust Margin scavengers who test the perimeter fence for gaps

The Halcyon Drift #

type place
name The Halcyon Drift
aliases
  • The Drift
  • Dead Marina
  • Floatside
description A semi-permanent floating settlement anchored to the collapsed infrastructure of a pre-Meridian 88 marina complex roughly two kilometers off the former Evanston shoreline, the Halcyon Drift is a congregation of sealed barges, decommissioned Carrion Logistics shipping platforms, and residential pontoon clusters that have accreted over forty years into an irregular aquatic neighborhood. The original marina's concrete piers still break the waterline in places, serving as mooring anchors and structural references for the newer construction above. Lakewater visibility is low here due to industrial particulate drift from the Slagshore, giving the surrounding water a pewter opacity that locals find comforting and newcomers find unsettling.

The Drift occupies a regulatory gray zone — it sits outside the formal municipal boundary of the megacity corridor, beyond the jurisdiction of most corponation security contracts, but close enough to shore infrastructure to pull illegal power and Diaspora signal from the grid. This ambiguity has made it a preferred residence for people who need to exist at a deliberate distance from Spire oversight: journalists running sensitive investigations, synthetics with disputed personhood status, and a significant population of former Arcturus Defense Solutions contractors whose knowledge of classified systems makes them inconvenient to the corponation's current leadership. Vespid Dynamics maintains a drone monitoring perimeter but does not intervene.
atmosphere
sights
  • Barge rooftops stacked with wind-capture arrays, salvaged solar film, and hand-painted territorial markers in a dozen languages
  • The original marina's fractured concrete piers rising from pewter-colored water at low swell, strung with low-voltage guide lights in amber and green
  • Carrion Logistics container units repurposed as permanent residences, their corporate livery half-sanded and overlaid with murals, antenna clusters, and drying laundry
sounds
  • The deep elastic knock of pontoon platforms shifting against each other in lake swell, a constant low percussion
  • Outboard maintenance cycles from the small-craft operators who run the only reliable transit between the Drift and the shoreline
  • Diaspora audio bleed from the settlement's shared signal tap, audible as a fractured ambient texture near the central platform cluster
smells
  • Lake water carrying an industrial mineral undertone — not quite chemical, not quite natural, specific to the Slagshore drift zone
  • Cooking smells layered through enclosed walkways: fish protein, fermented grain staples, and the sweet-synthetic scent of printed food supplements
  • Machine lubricant and salt corrosion from the constant hull maintenance that keeps the Drift habitable
feel Living on the Drift requires a continuous low-level physical negotiation with the water beneath — nothing is fully still, nothing is permanent, and residents develop an unconscious compensatory balance that marks them on land. The isolation from the megacity grid creates a social density inside the settlement that is simultaneously claustrophobic and fiercely communal. The Vespid drone perimeter visible at the edges of the swell horizon is a reminder that the Drift's autonomy is tolerated rather than guaranteed.
tags —
demographics Roughly 2,000 permanent residents with a rotating transient population of several hundred at any time; mix of Tier 2 displaced shoreline residents, off-registry synthetics, investigative journalists, whistleblowers, and former corponation technical staff in varying degrees of voluntary exile. Linguistically diverse, with Mandarin, Tagalog, English, and Hausa commonly spoken.
economy The Drift runs on a mixed economy of shoreline service work (residents commute by small craft), in-settlement craft production, Diaspora-based remote contract labor, and a significant information brokerage trade that leverages the settlement's population of people with corponation knowledge they can no longer use officially but haven't stopped selling.
power structure A rotating Harbor Committee of seven elected platform representatives manages shared infrastructure, transit scheduling, and external negotiation. Real influence is held informally by the oldest barge-owners — called the Anchors — whose physical control over mooring points gives them structural leverage over the entire settlement's layout.
dangers
  • Structural integrity of older barge platforms is deteriorating faster than the Harbor Committee's maintenance budget can address; hull failures during winter storm surges are a recurring emergency
  • Arcturus Defense Solutions has twice attempted to extract former contractors from the Drift by force; both operations were repelled, but the third attempt is widely considered a matter of when, not if
  • ELF entities have been detected using the Drift's illegal Diaspora signal tap as a relay node, occasionally corrupting BCI feeds for residents within range of their transmission bursts
opportunities
  • The Drift's population of former corponation technical staff represents an extraordinary concentration of off-books institutional knowledge — the right introduction to the right Anchor could yield intelligence on Arcturus, Helix, or Vespid that no legitimate channel would provide
  • The Harbor Committee is quietly seeking a legal advocate to file a formal jurisdictional claim that would give the Drift recognized municipal status — a case that would set precedent for synthetic personhood recognition as a secondary effect
  • The ELF relay node in the signal tap has been transmitting structured data packets that one Drift resident — a former Zheng-Dao Bioelectric network architect — believes contains coordinates for a submerged pre-Meridian 88 data cache in the lake bed
story hooks
  • A Sterling-Nakamura investigative journalist living on the Drift under a protected identity sends a Diaspora-encrypted message to the players: she has documented evidence of a Palladian Group operation that would make the Ferrous Nave acquisition look minor, but her BCI has been compromised and she has forty-eight hours before whoever is hunting her traces the signal tap back to her barge. She needs extraction, evidence duplication, or both.
  • One of the Drift's Anchors — an elderly synthetic woman named Constance-7 who has lived on the settlement for twenty years — has vanished without logging a departure through the Harbor Committee transit manifest. Her barge shows signs of a rapid departure rather than a struggle, but three residents report seeing Vespid drone activity directly over her platform the night before she disappeared, which the Committee's monitoring logs don't reflect.

The Heidelberg Scar #

type place
name The Heidelberg Scar
aliases
  • Heidelberg Project Zone
  • The Scar
  • Art Block
  • The Canvas
description The Heidelberg Project was always about refusal. In 1986, Tyree Guyton started nailing discarded objects to abandoned houses on Heidelberg Street, turning blight into art and forcing people to look at what they'd decided not to see. The city demolished his installations twice. He rebuilt twice. The pattern — destruction, creation, destruction, creation — became the work itself, more powerful than any individual piece. By the time the corponations arrived, the Heidelberg Project had been running for sixty years and had become something no urban planner knew how to categorize: a living artwork that was also a neighborhood, a protest, a community space, and a philosophical argument about who gets to decide what abandoned means.

The Heidelberg Scar is what grew from that seed. When corporate development consumed the neighborhoods around it, the Heidelberg zone did not resist through legal channels or community organizing. It resisted through proliferation. The art expanded. Block by block, building by building, every surface within a twelve-block radius became canvas — murals, found-object sculptures, architectural modifications that turned abandoned structures into installations, digital projections that layered augmented reality art over physical structures. The zone became so visually dense, so aggressively creative, that the development algorithms literally couldn't process it. Corporate property valuation systems require baseline aesthetic metrics. The Heidelberg Scar's aesthetics break the metrics. You cannot assign a property value to a house covered in stuffed animals and Bible verses and children's shoes and clock faces, because the valuation model has no category for 'art as structural material.'

The community that inhabits the Scar is part artist colony, part resistance movement, part ongoing art project. Approximately 2,800 people live within the twelve-block zone, and the distinction between 'resident' and 'installation' is deliberately blurred. People live in the art. The art lives in the people. A house is a house and also a sculpture. A community meeting is a community meeting and also a performance. The deliberate refusal to separate life from art, function from expression, is the Scar's most potent defense: you cannot demolish a neighborhood without acknowledging it's a neighborhood, and the corponations refuse to acknowledge that the Scar is anything other than an art installation, which means they'd have to destroy art, which is bad PR.
atmosphere
sights
  • Every surface covered — murals, found objects, textile installations, projected digital art, sculptural modifications to buildings
  • The original Heidelberg Street — still the epicenter, where the oldest installations have weathered into something between art and archaeology
  • Augmented reality layers visible to anyone with a neural interface — the physical art has digital companions that shift with time and viewer
  • Children painting on walls with the same casual authority that children in other neighborhoods use to ride bicycles
  • Light installations that activate at dusk, turning the twelve-block zone into something visible from the Axis towers — a scar of color in the dark city
sounds
  • Music — live, recorded, generated, accidental. The Scar has an ambient soundtrack that is never silent and never the same twice.
  • Art-making — hammering, painting, welding, the physical sounds of creation happening in real time, constantly
  • Community conversations conducted at volume, in public, without the expectation of privacy — the Scar does not whisper
  • Digital art installations generating procedural soundscapes that interact with physical sounds
  • Tour groups — the Scar attracts visitors from across the GLM, and the residents' feelings about tourism are themselves an ongoing artwork
smells
  • Paint — multiple types, multiple ages, multiple states of cure. The Scar smells like paint the way a forest smells like trees.
  • Cooking from communal kitchens — the Scar feeds itself collectively, and the meals are events
  • Burning materials from sculptural welding — the creation process is not filtered or contained
  • The specific smell of old found objects — the installations include decades of accumulated material that carries its own olfactory history
feel Overwhelming and necessary. The Heidelberg Scar feels like standing inside someone's creative consciousness — chaotic, associative, beautiful, uncomfortable, and impossible to ignore. It is the visual opposite of everything the corporate districts represent. Where the Axis is clean, the Scar is layered. Where Geartown is silent, the Scar is loud. Where the Manors are curated, the Scar is accumulated. The experience is not comfortable. It is not supposed to be. Art that makes you comfortable is advertising.
tags —
demographics Approximately 2,800 residents. Diverse in every measurable category and resistant to demographic analysis because the community considers categorization a form of reduction. The population includes established artists, community organizers, families who have lived here since before the Scar existed, corporate dropouts seeking meaning, and people who are themselves art projects in progress.
economy Gift economy, barter, and selective commerce. The Scar's residents sell art when they choose to, accept donations when offered, and reject commercial frameworks as a philosophical position. Actual economic sustainability comes from a combination of art sales to GLM collectors (approximately Φ8 million annually), tour revenue (Φ2 million), grants from cultural preservation funds (Φ1.2 million), and the unquantifiable value of community members who simply take care of each other.
power structure The Scar does not have a governance structure. Decisions emerge from community consensus, which is messy, slow, and occasionally produces contradictory outcomes that the community treats as a feature rather than a bug. The closest thing to leadership is the Guyton Legacy Council — five artists who maintain the original Heidelberg installations and serve as cultural custodians. The council has moral authority, not operational authority.
dangers
  • Corporate development pressure — the twelve blocks occupy land that developers want, and the 'art installation' classification is legally tenuous
  • Fire — the density of combustible art materials makes the Scar a fire hazard that the understaffed district fire service cannot adequately address
  • Exploitation — collectors, tourists, and media entities extract value from the community without reciprocating
  • Internal conflict — consensus governance works until it doesn't, and the Scar's most heated disputes are about what constitutes art
  • Augmented reality hijacking — the digital art layers are vulnerable to corporate insertion of advertising and surveillance
opportunities
  • Cultural sanctuary — the Scar's art-as-defense model provides cover for activities that the corporate districts would suppress
  • The augmented reality art infrastructure can carry non-art data — the Scar's digital layers are an invisible communication network
  • The artist community's connections span the GLM's cultural institutions, providing access and influence in spaces that fixers normally can't reach
  • Visibility — the Scar is the most photographed, most discussed, and most symbolically loaded neighborhood in Detroit, which is a form of power
story hooks
  • A corporate AR advertising network has begun inserting commercial content into the Scar's augmented reality art layers. The community considers this an act of war. The corporation considers it a software update.
  • A major GLM art collector wants to buy three entire blocks of the Scar and relocate the installations to a museum. The offer is Φ40 million. The community is divided between those who see survival and those who see surrender.
  • A found-object installation that has been accumulating material for fifteen years contains, somewhere in its layers, a piece of evidence from a corporate crime. The evidence is documented in the original artist's journal. The artist is dead. The journal is part of the installation.

  • Cultural tourists and collectors
  • People who need the Scar's visual density as cover for meetings that shouldn't be observed
  • Corporate development scouts who take photographs and are photographed taking photographs

The Hermosa Line #

type place
name The Hermosa Line
aliases
  • Hermosa
  • The Line
  • La Linea
  • The Seam
description Hermosa was always a between-place. Compact, working-class, Latino — wedged between Belmont Cragin's mass and Logan Square's ambition, Hermosa was the neighborhood you passed through to get somewhere else. After the incorporation, that liminal identity became literal. The Hermosa Line is the seam between the ungoverned northwest territories and the semi-corporate districts that stretch toward the Meridian Core. Every transit route, supply chain, and smuggling channel that connects the Stacks, the Souk, and Dunning Preserve to the rest of the Corridor passes through Hermosa. The district didn't choose to be a chokepoint. The geography chose for it.

The Line is narrow — twelve blocks east to west, eight blocks north to south — and every meter of it is in use. The residential buildings are modest three-flats converted to maximum occupancy, their ground floors almost universally given over to logistics operations: warehousing, transshipment, vehicle maintenance, courier dispatch. The streets are organized around flow — pedestrian traffic, cargo movement, and the constant passage of goods between districts that officially don't trade with each other. The Line's residents are logistics people by nature and necessity. They drive, carry, route, schedule, and troubleshoot. They are the supply chain that keeps the northwest corridor alive, and they know it, and they charge accordingly.

The culture is working-class Mexican-American at its core, but the Line's function as a transit hub has made it pragmatically multilingual and aggressively transactional. Hermosa doesn't have the Stacks' community density or the Souk's cultural depth. What it has is efficiency. Things move through the Line faster than through any corporate logistics network in the outer Corridor, because the Line's operators have been optimizing these routes for two decades using nothing but local knowledge and the understanding that if the cargo doesn't arrive, people don't eat. There is no romance here. There is work.

The Line is also where disputes between neighboring districts get mediated, because the alternative is disrupting the supply chain, and nobody wants that. Hermosa's community leaders function as de facto diplomats — neutral parties whose authority derives entirely from the fact that they control the chokepoint. Cross the Line's leadership, and your district's next shipment doesn't arrive. This gives Hermosa political influence wildly disproportionate to its size, and its leaders wield it with the quiet precision of people who have learned that the most powerful weapon in the Corridor is a truck that doesn't show up.
atmosphere
sights
  • Cargo vehicles loading and unloading at all hours in ground-floor warehouses
  • The narrow streets organized for flow — painted lane markers, hand-signaled traffic direction
  • Dispatch boards on building walls showing route status in coded shorthand
  • Couriers on modified bikes threading between vehicles with packages strapped to every surface
  • The Line's border markers — subtle paint codes that indicate which district's territory begins where
sounds
  • Engine noise — electric vehicles, mostly, humming in and out of loading bays
  • Radio dispatch chatter in Spanish-English logistics pidgin
  • Hand trucks on pavement — the constant rattle of goods in motion
  • The Line's signature sound: the slap of a cargo manifest being checked and approved with a palm strike on a van's hood
smells
  • Diesel and electric motor ozone — the Line runs on whatever fuel is available
  • Cargo — the composite smell of everything the northwest corridor consumes passing through in bulk
  • Street food from dispatch windows — fast, cheap, eaten standing up between loads
feel Purposeful. The Hermosa Line has no time for aesthetics, reflection, or bullshit. Everything here serves the function of moving things from where they are to where they need to be. It's exhausting and unglamorous, but there's a specific dignity in it — the dignity of people who keep the world running while the world pretends they don't exist.
tags —
demographics Approximately 25,000 residents, predominantly Tier 1 and Tier 2 Mexican-American logistics workers. Younger skewing, physically fit, and organized around work crews rather than residential blocks. Supplemented by transient populations of drivers and couriers from neighboring districts.
economy —

  • Cargo hijacking — the goods passing through the Line are valuable and the routes are known
  • Getting in the way — the Line's traffic doesn't stop for pedestrians who aren't paying attention
  • Political entanglement — the Line's chokepoint power creates enemies among those it leverages
  • Exhaustion — the Line's work culture grinds people down, and fatigue kills
  • Being used as a pawn in inter-district disputes that pass through Hermosa's territory
opportunities
  • Logistics networks that can move anything anywhere in the northwest corridor
  • The Line's leadership as mediators and brokers for inter-district negotiations
  • Transit intelligence — the Line's dispatchers know who's moving what and where
  • Employment — the Line always needs drivers, couriers, and people willing to work
  • Chokepoint leverage — alliance with the Line gives influence over the entire northwest supply chain
story hooks

  • The Line's lead dispatcher has gone missing, and without her the routing system collapses within 72 hours
  • Someone is using the Line's cargo network to move something that the Line's leadership didn't authorize — and it's drawing corporate attention to the entire corridor

The Humboldt Cage #

type place
name The Humboldt Cage
aliases
  • Humboldt Park
  • The Cage
  • La Jaula
  • Iron Flag Territory
description The two massive steel Puerto Rican flags that once arched over Division Street — the Paseo Boricua, the heart of Chicago's Puerto Rican community — are still standing. They have been standing for over sixty years, through every crisis the city has produced, and they will be standing when the corponations are dust. The flags are the reason the district is called the Cage, though the people who live here use the name differently than the people outside. To outsiders, the Humboldt Cage sounds like a trap. To residents, la jaula is a fortress. The flags mark the borders of sovereign community territory — not corporate sovereign, not tier-system sovereign, but the older kind, the kind that exists because a community decided it exists and has been willing to fight for that decision for three generations.

Humboldt Park's transformation into the Cage was not an accident. It was a deliberate act of communal self-defense. When the incorporation began and the corponations started carving up the West Side, the Paseo Boricua community organized with a speed and sophistication that caught the corps off guard. They weaponized the steel flags — literally, installing electromagnetic deterrent systems in the arch infrastructure — and declared the sixteen blocks between them autonomous community territory. The corps tested the declaration twice. The first test was a legal challenge that the community's lawyers buried under so many jurisdictional counterclaims that the case is still pending thirty years later. The second test was a physical incursion by Axiom Security that ended at the flags when the electromagnetic deterrents activated and fried every piece of corporate hardware within two hundred meters. There has not been a third test.

Inside the flags, the Cage operates as the closest thing to pre-incorporation civil governance that exists in Meridian 88. There is a community council, elected by residents, that manages infrastructure, resolves disputes, and controls access. There are schools that teach actual history, not the corporate-approved version. There are clinics that provide augment maintenance without tier verification. The cultural institutions are fierce: muralists, musicians, poets, and oral historians who maintain Puerto Rican cultural memory with the intensity of people who understand that forgetting is the first form of colonization. The annual Festival de la Calle, held on Division Street between the flags, is the largest unsanctioned cultural event in the Corridor, and corporate attempts to shut it down have failed every year because the logistics of confronting 40,000 people celebrating their continued existence are unfavorable.

The Cage is not paradise. Resources are limited, the electromagnetic deterrents require constant maintenance, and the community's autonomy depends on a fragile balance of legal obfuscation, physical deterrence, and the corps' calculation that conquering sixteen blocks of the West Side isn't worth the PR cost. That calculation could change. The Cage's leadership knows this, and they plan accordingly, which is why the Cage maintains relationships with every faction in the outer Corridor and owes favors to none of them.
atmosphere
sights
  • The steel Puerto Rican flags arching over Division Street — enormous, defiant, retrofitted with visible deterrent hardware
  • Murals covering every building face inside the flags — cultural memory rendered in paint and light
  • The Division Street corridor alive with community commerce, foot traffic, and organized civic activity
  • Community council signage in Spanish and English — no corporate branding anywhere inside the flags
  • The annual Festival de la Calle preparations — stages, banners, sound systems, the infrastructure of celebration as resistance
sounds
  • Bomba y plena — drum rhythms echoing off the buildings on Division Street, rehearsal and performance bleeding together
  • Community council announcements broadcast from the flag arches — practical, multilingual, unhurried
  • Children reciting poetry in schools that teach what actually happened
  • The electromagnetic deterrent systems' standby hum — low, constant, the sound of a line drawn
  • Arguments at community council meetings — democracy is loud
smells
  • Mofongo and pernil from the Division Street restaurants — food as cultural preservation
  • Paint — fresh murals are always being painted somewhere inside the flags
  • The particular ozone of the electromagnetic deterrents, sharp and metallic near the flag arches
  • Coffee from community-run cafes, strong and unapologetic
feel Proud and precarious. The Cage feels like standing inside an act of will — a community that decided to exist on its own terms and has been paying the cost of that decision every day for thirty years. There is joy here, real joy, the kind that comes from making something beautiful in a place that was supposed to be consumed. There is also the constant awareness that the flags are not invincible, the lawyers are not immortal, and the corps have longer memories than anyone would like.
tags —
demographics Approximately 55,000 residents within the flag boundaries. Predominantly Puerto Rican with significant broader Latinx, Black, and mixed-heritage populations. Self-governed and self-counted — the Cage conducts its own census and does not share the data. Tier system rejected; internal governance substitutes a community contribution model.
economy —
power structure —

  • Community justice operates on its own rules, and outsiders don't get the benefit of the doubt

  • Internal political disputes that occasionally escalate beyond the council's ability to mediate

  • Corporate intelligence has placed an operative inside the Cage, and the community council suspects but can't identify them without outside help

The I-75 Spine #

type place
name The I-75 Spine
aliases
  • The Spine
  • Michigan's Artery
  • The Vertical
  • Detroit-to-Mackinac Run
description Interstate 75 was built to move cars. In 2200, it moves everything else. The I-75 Spine runs 450 kilometers from Detroit's northern border to the Mackinac Bridge, forming the primary ground transportation corridor through Michigan's lower peninsula. The highway has been widened to twelve lanes — six automated cargo, four high-speed passenger, two emergency/military — and the entire corridor is sovereign infrastructure operated by Ferrogate Transit under a Michigan state charter. Ferrogate controls the traffic, maintains the surface, and charges the tolls, which makes the Spine the most profitable 450 kilometers of road in the Great Lakes Metropolitan Area.

The corridor is not just a highway. It is a linear economy. Service stations every 30 kilometers have evolved into waystation complexes — refueling, cargo transfer, passenger staging, and the commercial services that develop wherever traffic concentrates. The waystations are Ferrogate sovereign territory, which means the law on the highway is Ferrogate's law, and the law between waystations is whatever the speed of your vehicle allows you to outrun. The Spine's automated cargo lanes run 24 hours without human intervention, hauling materials between Detroit's manufacturing zones and the UP's extraction facilities via the Mackinac Bridge. The passenger lanes are slower, more surveilled, and more expensive — Ferrogate's pricing algorithm charges by time of day, tier rating, and destination, ensuring that the road's capacity serves those who can pay.

The communities along the Spine — Flint, Saginaw's southern suburbs, Grayling, Gaylord — have been absorbed into the corridor's economy like organs along an intestinal tract. They exist to service the traffic. Their populations work in the waystations, maintain the road infrastructure, and provide the human labor that the automated systems haven't replaced yet. The Spine is Michigan's central nervous system: sever it, and the lower peninsula loses contact with the UP, Detroit loses access to extraction resources, and the cargo flow that sustains the eastern GLM's manufacturing base stops. Everyone knows this. The Spine is defended accordingly.
atmosphere
sights
  • Twelve lanes of traffic — six automated cargo lanes moving in synchronized convoys, four passenger lanes, two military
  • Waystation complexes every 30 kilometers, glowing with service lights and Ferrogate branding
  • Automated cargo convoys — massive vehicles moving in tight formation at speeds that would kill a human driver
  • Michigan forest pressing in on both sides of the corridor — the landscape the highway cut through and never fully displaced
  • Military checkpoint infrastructure at key interchanges — the Spine is critical infrastructure and looks it
sounds
  • The constant rush of high-speed traffic — a wall of sound that the corridor communities live inside
  • Automated cargo vehicles communicating in machine frequencies — a conversation you hear as static
  • Waystation commerce — the sounds of refueling, maintenance, and transaction
  • The Spine at 3 AM — quieter but never silent, the automated lanes maintaining their rhythm through the dark
smells
  • Electric motor ozone from the automated convoys
  • Waystation food service — the smell of franchise nutrition, standardized across 450 kilometers
  • Michigan pine on cross-winds, briefly overriding the corridor's industrial baseline
feel Linear. The Spine has one dimension — north-south — and everything about it is oriented along that axis. You are either moving toward Detroit or moving toward the Bridge, and the corridor is designed to make that movement fast, profitable, and controlled. Stopping is an economic activity. Turning off is a navigational challenge. The Spine wants to move you, and the Spine gets what it wants.
tags —
demographics Corridor population approximately 800,000, distributed across waystation communities and surviving towns. The population is transit-dependent — their livelihoods exist because the traffic exists. Tier 2 majority, with Ferrogate employees at Tier 3. The communities are young, transient, and oriented toward the road rather than toward each other.
economy Transit tolls (Ferrogate Transit), waystation commerce, and corridor maintenance. The Spine generates revenue proportional to the cargo and passenger volume it carries, which is substantial — 60% of Michigan's north-south commerce moves on this road. The waystation economy provides services to that traffic. The corridor communities provide labor to the waystations.
power structure Ferrogate Transit sovereign authority over the highway and waystations. Michigan state authority over the spaces between. Military infrastructure at key interchanges under federal authority. The three jurisdictions coexist because the Spine must function, and dysfunction would cost more than cooperation.
dangers
  • Automated convoy accidents — rare but catastrophic, involving tonnage that reshapes the landscape
  • Waystation sovereignty gaps — Ferrogate law applies on the highway, state law applies off it, and the transition is exploitable
  • The Spine as military target — in any escalation of the UP war, the highway becomes the first strategic objective
  • Toll pricing as economic control — Ferrogate's algorithm determines who can afford to travel, which determines who can access the UP
  • Corridor communities' total dependence on traffic — any disruption to the Spine is an immediate livelihood crisis
opportunities
  • Cargo interception — the automated convoys are efficient but not invulnerable, and the cargo they carry is valuable
  • Waystation contracts — Ferrogate outsources maintenance and service operations, and the contracts are available to those who qualify
  • Intelligence on cargo movement — the Spine's traffic data reveals the GLM's economic activity in real time
  • Alternative route knowledge — the old surface roads still exist, and knowing them when the Spine closes is worth something
story hooks
  • Ferrogate's automated convoy system has been rerouting specific cargo to unauthorized destinations — the highway is stealing its own freight
  • A waystation community has blockaded the Spine, demanding equitable toll revenue sharing — the first infrastructure strike in the GLM
  • Military assets are massing at the Spine's northern terminus near the Mackinac Bridge, and Ferrogate has been ordered to clear civilian traffic — an operation is coming

The I-90 Vein #

type place
name The I-90 Vein
aliases
  • The Vein
  • The Corridor Artery
  • Lake Road
  • Interstate Ninety
description Interstate 90 was built in the 1950s as part of the Eisenhower interstate system — a Cold War infrastructure project that was also, accidentally, the most significant American public works achievement since the transcontinental railroad. The stretch from Cleveland to Buffalo follows the Lake Erie shoreline for roughly 300 kilometers, passing through Erie, Pennsylvania on its way. In the corridor era, I-90 has been converted from a public highway into Ferrogate Transit Sovereign Corponation's most strategically important eastern asset: a dual-use corridor that carries both the high-speed rail line connecting Cleveland to Buffalo and an autonomous vehicle roadway that handles the cargo traffic too large, too heavy, or too hazardous for rail.

The Vein — as everyone except Ferrogate's legal department calls it — is a sovereign right-of-way strip averaging 200 meters wide that cuts through the landscape between the three major population centers of the Lake Erie shore. Within that strip, Ferrogate's jurisdiction is absolute. The Rail Hounds — autonomous patrol vehicles capable of 280 km/h — run continuous security sweeps. The Ferrogate Line Authority maintains an 18,000-officer paramilitary presence across the full corridor. Unauthorized access to the right-of-way is met with lethal force, a policy Ferrogate does not publicize but does not conceal.

What makes the Vein strategically critical is not just what moves along it but what it connects. Every community along the Lake Erie shore — from Toledo's Glass Yards to Buffalo's Dive Yards — depends on the Vein for supply chain connectivity, passenger transit, and communication relay (Ferrogate piggybacks Saltmarsh signal infrastructure on its rail corridor). Cutting the Vein at any point would isolate population centers within hours. Ferrogate knows this. Everyone who depends on Ferrogate knows this. The corponation has never needed to make the threat explicit because the infrastructure makes the threat self-evident. The Vein is not just a road. It is a leash, and every community it touches can feel the tension.
atmosphere
sights
  • The rail line — maglev track running ruler-straight along the lakeshore, trains visible as silver streaks covering the Cleveland-Buffalo distance in under 90 minutes
  • The autonomous vehicle roadway — cargo haulers in continuous convoy, their formations computer-coordinated and eerily uniform
  • Ferrogate sovereign markers every 500 meters — illuminated pylons marking the right-of-way boundary with the subtlety of a fence made of light
  • Rail Hound patrols — autonomous vehicles screaming along the corridor at 280 km/h, visible as blurs that resolve into armored platforms for a fraction of a second
  • The landscape between the sovereign strip and the lake — a narrow band of terrain that is technically outside Ferrogate jurisdiction and serves as an informal transit route for people who can't or won't use the official corridor
sounds
  • Maglev passage — not a train sound but a pressure wave, a sudden displacement of air followed by silence that feels compressed
  • Rail Hound engines — a high-pitched scream that Doppler-shifts from approaching to departing in seconds, the audio signature of Ferrogate's enforcement model
  • Cargo convoy coordination — the mechanical precision of a hundred autonomous vehicles maintaining formation, their systems communicating in radio frequencies audible as static to unshielded ears
  • Wind — the corridor's 200-meter cleared strip creates a wind tunnel effect, especially near the lakeshore segments
  • Saltmarsh signal relay — a faint electromagnetic buzz from the communication equipment piggybacking on Ferrogate's rail infrastructure
smells
  • Ozone from the maglev rail — the corridor's constant atmospheric contribution, stronger near the rail line itself
  • Cargo hauler exhaust — the autonomous vehicle fleet is predominantly electric but the older units and emergency generators still run on synthetic diesel
  • Lake Erie — present whenever the corridor runs close to the shoreline, the mineral-and-algae scent of the lake cutting through the industrial atmosphere
feel The Vein feels like velocity. Everything moves — trains, cargo, patrol vehicles, information — and the stationary human is an anomaly in a system designed for throughput. Standing near the corridor and watching a Rail Hound pass at 280 km/h is a visceral reminder that this infrastructure was built for machines and tolerated for humans. The communities along the Vein depend on it the way a patient depends on an IV line: it sustains them, and the entity controlling the flow can adjust the dosage at will.
tags —
demographics The Vein itself has no permanent residential population — it is infrastructure, not habitat. The communities along its 300-kilometer length house approximately 350,000 people who depend on the corridor for economic connectivity. Ferrogate's Line Authority personnel — 18,000 strong — are distributed along the corridor in fortified stations every 30 kilometers.
economy Transit tariffs. Every physical good moving between Cleveland and Buffalo — and every passenger — pays Ferrogate's sovereign transit tariff. These tariffs are the Vein's economic product, and they are non-negotiable. Ferrogate has never lost an arbitration dispute over its tariff schedule. The corridor also generates secondary revenue through Saltmarsh signal relay fees and Tollgate infrastructure usage charges. The total economic throughput of the I-90 Vein is estimated at Φ890 billion annually.
power structure Ferrogate sovereign authority within the right-of-way strip. Saltmarsh signal sovereignty over the communication infrastructure. Tollgate collects infrastructure fees at connection points. No civilian governance exists within the corridor itself. The communities along its length have no formal relationship with Ferrogate beyond the tariff schedule and whatever leverage their strategic position (as chokepoints or maintenance bases) provides.
dangers
  • Rail Hound lethality — unauthorized entry into the right-of-way is met with autonomous enforcement that does not warn, hesitate, or discriminate
  • Supply chain dependency — communities that anger Ferrogate risk service reduction, tariff increases, or scheduling 'adjustments' that accomplish the same result as a blockade
  • High-speed transit risk — the maglev trains operate at speeds that make any mechanical failure, sabotage, or obstruction catastrophic
  • Surveillance — Ferrogate's monitoring of the corridor extends beyond the right-of-way strip, and the company shares intelligence with Saltmarsh under their signal relay agreement
  • The narrows — several points where the corridor passes through terrain that forces the right-of-way, the lake, and the civilian zone into close proximity, creating chokepoints vulnerable to natural disaster, sabotage, or military action
opportunities
  • Transit intelligence — knowing what moves along the Vein and when is among the most valuable information in the eastern corridor
  • The informal path — the narrow band between the Ferrogate right-of-way and the lakeshore is technically outside corporate jurisdiction and serves as an alternative transit route for those willing to travel slowly and carefully
  • Chokepoint leverage — communities located at the Vein's narrow points have disproportionate strategic value and can extract concessions from Ferrogate that other communities cannot
  • Ferrogate's Line Authority officers are well-paid, well-informed, and occasionally corruptible — the right approach to the right officer at the right station can open access to the corridor's information flow
story hooks
  • A maglev train has stopped between stations — the first unscheduled stop in the corridor's history — and Ferrogate is not explaining why. The Rail Hounds have established a perimeter. Something is on that train.
  • The informal lakeshore path between Ferrogate's right-of-way and the waterline has been discovered to follow the route of a pre-corridor fiber optic cable that is still active — carrying data that doesn't belong to any known network
  • A Ferrogate Line Authority officer at the Erie station has been feeding information to an unknown party about military-grade cargo moving through the corridor — cargo that Ferrogate's public manifest doesn't list
connections
adjacent to
  • The Gate (Downtown Cleveland) — western anchor
  • Presque Anchorage (Erie PA) — midpoint
  • The Dive Yards (Buffalo) — eastern terminus
  • Every lakeside community along its 300-kilometer route
exits —
tags —
frequented by
  • Ferrogate Line Authority personnel — 18,000 officers distributed across the corridor
  • Transit passengers — everyone who travels between Cleveland and Buffalo
  • Cargo operators — everything that moves between the corridor's eastern population centers
  • Rail Hounds — Ferrogate's autonomous enforcement, always present, always moving, always watching
notable locations

description Three points where terrain forces the corridor, the lake, and civilian territory into close proximity — the Vein's most vulnerable and most strategically valuable chokepoints

description The corridor's midpoint hub — where eastbound and westbound traffic is logged, sorted, and occasionally redirected in ways that the manifest doesn't reflect
tags —
name The Lakeshore Path
