The Iowa Exclusion Zone #

type place
name The Iowa Exclusion Zone
aliases
  • Iowa
  • The Breadbasket
  • The Dead State
  • Calorie Country
  • The IEZ
description Iowa is not a state anymore. Iowa is a machine.

Sometime in the 2160s, the last human residents were relocated — voluntarily at first, then less so — when Ironclad Agrisystems and three other Big 20 corponations collectively determined that human habitation was incompatible with maximum caloric output per hectare. The math was simple and the math was correct: remove the towns, remove the roads, remove the schools and churches and graveyards and everything that made Iowa a place where people lived, and replace it with 145,000 square kilometers of uninterrupted, GPS-guided, AI-managed, industrial-scale food production. The Iowa Exclusion Zone now produces 40% of Meridian 88's caloric intake. No humans live here. No humans are permitted here. The land belongs to the crops, and the crops belong to the corponations, and the corponations do not share.

The Iowan Behemoths work the land. Massive autonomous agricultural machines — part tractor, part harvester, part territorial defense platform — the Behemoths are the only permanent residents of the IEZ. They plant, they tend, they harvest, they process. They also kill. Each Behemoth is equipped with anti-personnel systems designed to protect corporate caloric assets from theft, and their definition of theft includes any unauthorized human presence within their operational radius. The Behemoths do not warn. They do not negotiate. They calculate the caloric value of the crop you are standing in, compare it to the cost of the ammunition required to remove you, and if the math favors the crop, the crop wins. It always favors the crop.

And yet people go there. They have to. The freedom fighters — the Harvest Runners, the Calorie Raiders, the Gleaner Brigades — cross the border from the GLM's western edge into the IEZ on missions that are half military operation and half grocery run. They go because the Shelf is hungry. They go because Ironclad's licensed food distribution charges Φ40 for a kilogram of grain that costs Φ0.03 to produce. They go because children are malnourished in a world that produces more food per acre than at any point in human history, and the only thing standing between those children and that food is a fence, a law, and a machine the size of a building that will grind you into the soil you're trying to steal from.

The raids are legendary on the Shelf. Every runner who comes back from Iowa comes back with stories — of Behemoths materializing from cornfields at midnight, of drone swarms descending like locusts in reverse, of the terrible silence of a landscape where nothing lives except the crop and the machine that tends it. Some runners don't come back. Their bodies become fertilizer. Ironclad considers this an acceptable recycling protocol.
atmosphere
sights
  • Endless geometric crop rows stretching to every horizon — no trees, no buildings, no variation, just food production at continental scale
  • Behemoths moving through the fields — silhouettes the size of apartment buildings, LED work lights cutting through pre-dawn darkness like searchlights
  • Drone swarms rising from charging stations embedded in the soil, forming clouds that darken the sun when a perimeter breach is detected
  • The ruins of old Iowa towns — foundations, fragments of Main Streets, church steeples that Ironclad left standing because removing them was not cost-effective
  • The border fence — 3 meters of smart-wire that extends the full perimeter of the state, humming with current, monitored by ground-penetrating sensors
sounds
  • The deep mechanical thrumming of Behemoths working — audible from 10 kilometers away, the sound of the earth being used
  • Wind through monoculture crop — a uniform rustling that sounds wrong because every plant is genetically identical
  • Absolute silence between machine passes — no birds, no insects, no animals. Iowa's ecosystem was sterilized to prevent crop contamination
  • The click-whir of anti-personnel turrets tracking movement — the last sound some raiders hear
smells
  • Chemical fertilizer — a sharp, acrid baseline note that saturates everything within 50 kilometers of the border
  • Engineered crop — a uniform, vaguely sweet smell that is not quite corn, not quite wheat, not quite anything that existed before Ironclad's geneticists rebuilt agriculture from scratch
  • Diesel and ozone — the Behemoths run on hybrid fuel cells and the exhaust smells like the future tastes
feel Wrong. Iowa feels profoundly, viscerally wrong — not dangerous in the way the Shelf is dangerous (human danger, comprehensible danger) but wrong in the way a world without people is wrong. The land is alive — the crops grow, the machines move, the system functions — but nothing here has consciousness, nothing has choice, nothing has meaning beyond caloric output. Standing in an Iowa field at night, watching a Behemoth work under LED floods while the stars wheel overhead, is the closest most people will ever come to understanding what the corponations actually want the world to look like.
tags —
demographics Zero permanent human population. Approximately 340 Behemoth units, 12,000 aerial drones, and an unknown number of ground-based security systems. Ironclad Agrisystems maintains a skeleton crew of 200 human technicians at three fortified maintenance depots who rotate on 90-day shifts and are contractually prohibited from leaving the depots during their rotation.
economy Produces 40% of Meridian 88's caloric intake — approximately Φ890 billion in annual food value. The cost of production per calorie is the lowest in human history. The retail price per calorie is the highest in human history. The margin between those two numbers is what Ironclad calls shareholder value and what the Shelf calls murder.
power structure Ironclad Agrisystems holds sole sovereign authority. There is no municipal government, no police force, no judiciary. The Behemoths are the law. Ironclad's board of directors — none of whom have ever visited Iowa — make all decisions regarding the IEZ from their offices in the Spire.
dangers
  • Behemoths — autonomous agricultural machines with anti-personnel systems. They weigh 400 tons, move at 60 km/h, and do not distinguish between raiders and lost hikers
  • Drone swarms — thousands of aerial units that deploy within seconds of a perimeter breach. They carry chemical deterrents, tracking beacons, and in some configurations, lethal payloads
  • Smart-wire border fence — electrified, sensor-equipped, and monitored 24/7. Crossing it announces your presence to every Behemoth within 100 kilometers
  • Chemical exposure — the soil is saturated with proprietary fertilizers and pesticides. Prolonged exposure without protective equipment causes neural damage, organ failure, and a condition the raiders call 'Iowa Lung'
  • GPS denial — Ironclad jams all unauthorized navigation systems within the IEZ. If you enter Iowa, you navigate by stars or you don't navigate at all
  • No rescue — if you are injured inside the IEZ, no one is coming. There are no hospitals, no emergency services, no communications infrastructure. The nearest help is on the other side of the border fence.
opportunities
  • Food — the single most valuable commodity in a world where corporate pricing makes nutrition a luxury. A successful Iowa raid can feed a Shelf block for a month
  • Behemoth salvage — damaged or disabled Behemoths contain military-grade components worth fortunes on the Circuit's black market
  • Intelligence — the IEZ's security systems contain Ironclad corporate data that fixers and the Collective would pay handsomely for
  • Reputation — an Iowa raid survivor is respected everywhere below Tier 3. It is the hardest job a runner can take.
story hooks
  • A Gleaner Brigade is assembling for the biggest Iowa raid in a decade — they need an operator to handle the Behemoth that guards the target silo
  • A disabled Behemoth has been spotted 2 kilometers inside the border fence. Its cargo hold contains enough grain to feed the Shelf for six months. The question is whether Ironclad disabled it as bait.
  • One of Ironclad's maintenance technicians wants out. They have data on the Behemoth command frequencies — information that could change the balance of power on every future raid. But extraction from a fortified depot inside the IEZ is a suicide mission.
  • Someone is reprogramming Behemoths. Three units have stopped patrolling and started leaving crop bundles at the border fence at night. Ironclad does not know who is doing this. The Shelf does not care — they are eating.
connections
adjacent to
  • The western edge of Meridian 88 — the border towns where raiders stage
  • The Fox Cities Nexus (northeast — data connections to Ironclad's command network)
  • The Dead Zones (north — ungoverned territory between Iowa and the GLM)
exits —
tags —
frequented by
  • Nobody. That is the point.
  • Harvest Runners — raiders who cross the border to steal food for the excluded
  • Gleaner Brigades — organized resistance groups that conduct military-scale food raids
  • Ironclad maintenance technicians — 200 humans on 90-day locked rotations
  • Behemoths — the only permanent residents, if you can call a 400-ton autonomous tractor a resident

The Laceworks #

type place
name The Laceworks
aliases
  • The Lace
  • Threadtown
  • The Old Stitching
description A sprawling industrial neighborhood built atop the skeletal remains of a 20th-century garment district, The Laceworks has been repurposed layer by layer into one of Meridian 88's most densely inhabited residential warrens. Converted textile factories now house thousands of mid-to-low income residents in stacked micro-apartments, their facades draped in a permanent tangle of laundry lines, fiber-optic cables, and handmade signage that gives the district its name. The original brick architecture survives beneath decades of patchwork renovation, visible in archways and loading docks now serving as storefronts, shrines, and impromptu community spaces.
atmosphere
sights
  • Cascading laundry lines strung between buildings like low-tech prayer flags
  • Neon signs in a dozen languages advertising tailors, noodle shops, and black-market chip clinics
  • Exposed brick faces tagged with hyperlocal gang markers and community murals
  • Residents leaning from narrow windows watching the street below
  • Repair drones weaving between fire escapes
sounds
  • Overlapping music from competing storefronts
  • Children shouting in Tagalog, Yoruba, and Mandarin
  • The distant mechanical thrum of legacy HVAC systems
  • Street vendors hawking printed food and counterfeit skins
  • Occasional bursts of feedback from illicit pirate radio broadcasts
smells
  • Frying oil and synthetic spices
  • Damp concrete and mildew from overcrowded plumbing
  • Cheap solvent from nearby repair shops
  • Incense burning at street-level shrines
  • Ozone from overloaded electrical conduits
feel Claustrophobic and alive, a pressure-cooker community where everyone knows everyone and strangers are noted immediately. There is warmth here, but also exhaustion — people working too hard for too little, holding onto dignity through ritual and solidarity.
tags —
demographics Predominantly first- and second-generation migrant workers, service-sector laborers, and aging legacy residents who survived the district's earlier incarnations. A significant population of undocumented individuals with no official city registration. Mixed ages, heavily family-oriented.
economy Informal micro-economies dominate: street food, repair work, unlicensed clinics, textile recycling, and small-batch fabrication. Remittance transfers to outside the corridor are a major financial artery. Some residents work shifts in the adjacent corporate manufacturing zones but spend their wages locally.
power structure No single entity controls The Laceworks. Block-level councils negotiate resource allocation and settle disputes. The Needle — a loose confederation of older residents and community organizers — holds informal authority, but enforcement depends on persuasion and reputation. Corporate security rarely enters without cause, which is considered a fragile blessing.
dangers
  • Structural failures in poorly maintained converted buildings
  • Predatory lenders and organ-debt collectors operating openly
  • Occasional violent incursions by fringe gangs from bordering districts
  • City utilities are unreliable — power brownouts and water rationing are cyclical
  • Unlicensed chip clinics with substandard sterilization practices
opportunities
  • Access to a dense, tight-knit information network — locals know everything about their neighbors
  • Black-market fabrication services that ask no questions
  • Recruitment of skilled but desperate individuals with reason to stay off-grid
  • The Needle's community archives contain decades of unofficial city history
  • Safe houses available through trust-based networks for those who earn goodwill
story hooks
  • A community elder has gone missing days before she was scheduled to testify before a city zoning tribunal about corporate encroachment
  • A series of fires in the district follow an unusual pattern — always near buildings whose residents recently refused buyout offers
  • A child found wandering the Laceworks speaks no known language and carries a neural implant of unidentified manufacture
  • The pirate radio signal that has broadcast for twenty years suddenly begins transmitting encrypted data packets no one can decode
  • A new lender has arrived offering impossibly favorable terms — and residents who accept begin behaving differently within weeks

  • Journalists looking for human-interest angles or whistleblowers
  • Fixers sourcing discreet local talent
  • Corporate scouts conducting unofficial demographic surveys
  • Social workers from both legitimate NGOs and front organizations
notable locations
name The Spool
description A converted textile warehouse that now functions as a community hall, night market, and informal courthouse. The original industrial spools still hang from the ceiling beams, rewound with fiber-optic cable that illuminates the space in shifting color. Disputes are settled here, weddings celebrated, and deals made under the tacit neutrality the space is understood to carry.
tags —
name Mama Osei's Clinic
description Three interconnected apartments on the fourth floor of a converted factory, operated by a former licensed surgeon who lost her credentials after publicly criticizing a corporate medical conglomerate. She performs legitimate medical care alongside necessary off-books procedures, and her waiting room is always full. Her files on corporate medical malpractice in the district are said to be extraordinarily comprehensive.
tags —
name The Underloft
description A subterranean level beneath the Laceworks' oldest block, accessible through a false utility closet. Originally a factory basement, it has become a rotating speakeasy, meeting space, and hideout maintained collectively by residents who refuse to formalize its existence. No cameras, no records, no questions.

The Lacuna Platform #

type place
name The Lacuna Platform
aliases
  • The Float
  • Midlake
  • Lacuna Drift
description Three kilometers off the Chicago shoreline, The Lacuna Platform is a semi-permanent offshore structure originally commissioned by Zheng-Dao Bioelectric as a deep-water thermal research installation. When the project's funding collapsed in a Zheng-Dao restructuring, the platform was not decommissioned—it was simply abandoned with a skeleton crew who never received recall orders. Over two decades, that crew became a community, and the community became something the corponations find difficult to categorize and therefore difficult to control.

The platform now hosts roughly four hundred permanent residents living across its original research decks and a sprawling superstructure of salvaged and fabricated additions that extend over the lake surface on pontoon frameworks. With no formal civic designation, Lacuna exists in genuine legal ambiguity—outside city jurisdiction, never formally incorporated, and sitting on water that four different entities claim without any of them willing to fund enforcement. Its residents have learned to weaponize that ambiguity expertly.
atmosphere
sights
  • The original Zheng-Dao research towers rising from the center platform, their corporate livery half-stripped and replaced with hand-painted murals visible from the shore on clear days
  • Pontoon extensions cluttered with hydroponic frames, wind catchers, and salvaged solar membranes that flutter like enormous silver leaves
  • Lake Michigan stretching flat and grey-green in every direction, the Meridian skyline a luminous smear on the western horizon
sounds
  • The constant low percussion of wave action against the platform's hull—a sound residents say becomes inaudible after two weeks and deafening the moment you think about it
  • Diaspora signal hum from the platform's jury-rigged antenna array, pulling feeds from every direction with variable clarity
  • Gulls and the occasional autonomous Arcturus recon drone passing overhead, the residents having learned to tell them apart by sound alone
smells
  • Clean lake wind cut with the algae bloom scent of the hydroponic bays and the faint ozone of the wind catchers
  • Brine and machine oil where the pontoon frameworks meet the water line
  • Cooking smoke from wood and compressed biomass—fuel sources that mainland residents haven't used in generations
feel The platform moves, faintly but always—a slow, oceanic patience underneath everything that residents absorb into their bodies and visitors find either meditative or nauseating. Distance from the shore creates a psychological freedom that is difficult to articulate and immediately felt. The horizon is enormous here. Problems seem slightly smaller against it, and slightly more permanent.
tags —
demographics A deliberately mixed population of roughly four hundred, drawn from Tiers 2 through 4, with a notable concentration of former researchers, disbarred professionals, and individuals seeking distance from mainland legal entanglements. Approximately thirty unregistered synthetics live openly on the platform, the only location in the Meridian corridor where they do so without concealment.
economy Hydroponic food production sold to shore contacts, Diaspora signal brokering for clients wanting anonymized uplink points, and a growing cottage industry in legal research and documentation services exploiting the platform's jurisdictional ambiguity. Helix Biosystems quietly pays a retainer for access to legacy Zheng-Dao research data the platform's original crew never transmitted.
power structure A loose direct democracy called the Drift Council operates by consensus for major decisions and by rotating three-person panels for daily governance. A former Zheng-Dao lead researcher, Dr. Amara Osei-Bonsu, holds significant informal authority through institutional memory and personal respect, but holds no formal title and declines every offer of one.
dangers
  • Arcturus Defense Solutions periodically runs 'navigational safety inspections' that are transparently pretextual and occasionally result in the confiscation of platform equipment without recourse
  • Severe lake weather—the platform was engineered for research, not permanent habitation, and its structural tolerances in major storm events are a subject of ongoing, anxious debate among residents
  • Mainland criminal networks use the platform's legal ambiguity as a drop point, and while the Drift Council rejects formal arrangements, individual residents accepting payments for look-the-other-way cooperation creates internal tension and external danger
opportunities
  • The platform's jurisdictional status makes it the only reliable location in the corridor where synthetics can enter into contracts, testify to information, or access Diaspora infrastructure without identity suppression
  • Legacy Zheng-Dao research terminals still contain partially intact datasets from the original thermal project—data that has implications beyond energy research that Dr. Osei-Bonsu has spent years trying to understand
  • The platform's anonymous Diaspora uplink infrastructure is available for hire by those who can reach it, making it invaluable to journalists, E.L.F. researchers, and anyone needing communications that cannot be traced to a mainland address
story hooks
  • A Drift Council member was found dead in the water below the pontoon extensions—ruled accidental by the council's internal review, but three residents independently claim to have seen a submersible-class drone in the area that night matching Arcturus Defense Solutions' deep-water surveillance profile. The council is divided on whether to investigate or let it rest, and the dead woman's daughter has arrived from the shore asking questions no one wants to answer.
  • An E.L.F. has been communicating with the platform's antenna array for eleven months, gradually, patient as tide water. It has not asked for anything. It has only been sharing fragments of what appears to be pre-Meridian infrastructure mapping data of extraordinary detail and accuracy. Dr. Osei-Bonsu believes it is building toward a request, and that the platform's response will matter enormously—but she cannot determine what it wants, or why it chose Lacuna.

  • Tier 2 and 3 professionals from the mainland seeking anonymous consultation with the platform's legal research specialists
  • Diaspora journalists and whistleblower-adjacent figures needing untraceable uplink access
  • Zheng-Dao Bioelectric junior agents conducting unofficial surveillance they will never officially acknowledge

The Lakeshore Corridor #

type place
name The Lakeshore Corridor
aliases
  • I-196
  • US-31
  • The Spine
  • Lake Road
  • The String
description The Lakeshore Corridor is not a place. It is the connective tissue between places -- the artery that links every settlement on the eastern Lake Michigan coast from the Indiana border to the Mackinac Straits. In the old world it was two highways: Interstate 196 running from the Indiana line to Grand Rapids, and US Route 31 continuing north to the Straits. In 2200 they have been merged, expanded, and redesignated as GLM Regional Corridor 31 -- a hybrid transit route carrying automated cargo convoys, civilian vehicles, maglev-adjacent freight pods, and the constant low-grade traffic of a coastline that moves things for a living.

The Corridor is the most dangerous and most essential piece of infrastructure on the eastern shore. Dangerous because it passes through or adjacent to every jurisdiction on the coast -- Ringo security zones, Axiom cargo territories, Helix sovereign land, Verdana agricultural zones -- and each transition point is a border where the rules change and the enforcement doesn't always announce itself. A vehicle that is legal in one stretch may be flagged three kilometers later. A cargo load that passes Axiom inspection at the Mill may be seized by Verdana agricultural quarantine near the Tulip Protocol. The Corridor is a legal patchwork, and the people who drive it professionally have memorized the transitions the way sailors memorize reefs.

The rest stops and service nodes along the Corridor have developed into their own micro-economies. Every forty to sixty kilometers, a cluster of fuel stations, repair shops, food vendors, and informal markets has grown up around the official rest infrastructure. These nodes are where the Corridor's gray economy operates -- cargo is reclassified, manifests are adjusted, passengers change vehicles, information is traded. The nodes operate in the jurisdictional gaps between corporate territories, which makes them ungoverned in the technical sense and self-governed in the practical sense. Each node has its own character, its own regulars, its own rules. Collectively they form a network that parallels the official Corridor infrastructure -- a shadow highway running alongside the real one, carrying the commerce that the official economy pretends doesn't exist.

Driving the Corridor at night is a specific experience. The lake is visible in glimpses between the industrial and agricultural zones -- dark water catching starlight or the reflected glow of distant cargo platforms. The automated convoys run nose-to-tail in the freight lanes, their navigation lights forming a ribbon of motion that stretches to the horizon in both directions. The service nodes glow in the darkness like embers. And between the nodes, between the zones, there are stretches of the old road where the infrastructure thins and the forest closes in and you could be driving the same highway in 1980 or 2200, because some roads don't change even when everything around them does.
atmosphere
sights
  • Automated cargo convoys in the freight lanes -- hundreds of vehicles moving in synchronized formation, navigation lights blinking in patterns that communicate to each other, not to humans
  • Jurisdictional transition markers -- holographic boundary projections that change color and language as you enter each corporate zone
  • Service nodes glowing at irregular intervals along the route, each one a distinct cluster of light and activity
  • Lake Michigan glimpsed between zones -- dark water, cargo platform lights on the horizon, the occasional flash of a Ringo patrol vessel
  • The old road surface visible in patches where the automated lane infrastructure hasn't been extended -- cracked asphalt from the 20th century, stubborn and historical
sounds
  • Tire noise and wind -- the constant soundtrack of highway travel, unchanged by a century of technology
  • Automated convoy communication -- data bursts that sound like rhythmic clicking if you're on the right frequency
  • Service node activity as you approach -- engines, music, the hum of commerce
  • Jurisdictional alerts from your vehicle's navigation system, announcing each zone transition with corporate-branded audio
  • Silence between nodes -- the specific quiet of a highway at night between populated areas
smells
  • Road -- asphalt, rubber, the universal smell of long-distance driving
  • Lake air blowing inland, carrying different chemical signatures depending on which stretch of coast you're passing
  • Service node food -- the Corridor's rest stops have developed competitive cuisine, and the debate about which node has the best smoked fish is older than some of the buildings
  • Agricultural zones -- Verdana's engineered orchards produce a sweet, pharmaceutical smell that drifts across the highway during pollination season
feel The Corridor feels like circulation. You are inside the bloodstream of the eastern shore, moving with or against the flow of goods, people, and information that keeps the coast alive. There is a freedom to highway travel that even corporate jurisdiction cannot fully contain -- the feeling of being between places, belonging to none of them, accountable only to the road and the distance. This is why the Corridor's gray economy works. In transit, you are nobody's citizen. You are just moving.
tags —
demographics No permanent population on the Corridor itself. Service node populations range from 200 to 2,000 each, predominantly Tier 1-2 with the specific demographics of highway communities: transient, practical, suspicious of authority, and hospitable to strangers who follow the rules. Approximately 40,000 vehicles use the Corridor daily, carrying an estimated 200,000 people.
economy Official Corridor toll revenue: Φ890 million annually. Automated cargo convoy fees: Φ3.2 billion. Service node economies: estimated Φ400 million combined, of which roughly half is gray market. The Corridor's informal economy is essentially a distributed marketplace operating in the jurisdictional gaps -- goods, services, information, and identities all change hands at the nodes.
power structure The GLM Transit Authority nominally administers the Corridor, but actual authority fragments across every corporate zone it passes through. Each service node has its own informal power structure -- typically a long-term operator or family that controls the fuel supply and therefore controls everything else. A loose network of Corridor regulars -- truckers, couriers, gray-market runners -- maintains an informal code that keeps the nodes functional and the violence to levels that don't invite corporate crackdowns.
dangers
  • Jurisdictional transitions -- crossing a zone boundary with the wrong cargo, credentials, or vehicle modifications can result in seizure, detention, or worse
  • Automated convoy proximity -- the freight lanes are not designed for human drivers, and the convoys do not stop for obstacles
  • Service node disputes -- the informal code works until it doesn't, and disagreements between node operators can strand travelers in dangerous locations
  • Isolation between nodes -- breakdowns on empty stretches of the Corridor can be life-threatening, especially in winter
  • Corporate security patrols -- each zone monitors its section of the Corridor, and some are more aggressive about non-standard traffic than others
opportunities
  • The gray market economy is distributed and resilient -- reliable runners with clean records can move anything between the coast's settlements
  • Information gathered across multiple service nodes creates a picture of coast-wide traffic patterns that has intelligence value
  • The jurisdictional gaps are the Corridor's greatest asset -- understanding which gaps exist where is expertise worth paying for
  • Service node businesses are always looking for reliable supply, security, and technical support
story hooks
  • A new service node is being established in a jurisdictional gap between Axiom and Ringo territories, and both corponations want to control it without officially acknowledging it exists
  • Automated cargo convoys have been arriving at their destinations with manifests that don't match their contents -- and the discrepancies are occurring on stretches of Corridor where no human hands touch the cargo
  • A Corridor regular -- a long-haul runner who has driven the route for thirty years -- has noticed that the distance between two service nodes has changed, which should be impossible, and yet her odometer doesn't lie

The Lattice #

type place
name The Lattice
aliases
  • Toronto
  • T-Dot
  • The Grid
  • North Sprawl
description Toronto did not fall. Toronto metastasized. What was once a city of 3 million became a metropolitan organism of 18 million, absorbing Mississauga, Brampton, Oshawa, Hamilton's eastern suburbs, and everything in between into a continuous urban lattice that stretches from Lake Ontario's shore to the moraine ridges 80 kilometers north. The Lattice is the GLM's Canadian anchor — the largest single population center under nominal Canadian sovereignty, and the only city in the northern corridor that can rival Meridian 88 in economic output. The key word is 'nominal.' Eighteen of the Big 30 corponations maintain sovereign enclaves within the Lattice, and the actual territory governed by Canadian municipal law has been shrinking by approximately 2% per year for the last two decades.

The downtown core is a vertical city — arcology towers connected by skybridge networks at every tenth floor, the ground level permanently shadowed and increasingly abandoned to the Tier 1 population and the excluded. The PATH system, Toronto's old underground pedestrian network, has been expanded into a subterranean city in its own right, running 40 kilometers beneath the surface and housing an estimated 2 million people who never see daylight by choice or by circumstance. The CN Tower still stands — reinforced, augmented with communications arrays, and now serving as the primary data relay for the northern GLM net infrastructure. It is the oldest structure in the core and the only one that everybody, regardless of tier, can identify by sight.

The Lattice's economy runs on data, finance, and biotech. Bay Street's financial district has evolved into a quantum-computing fortress where algorithmic trading happens at speeds that make human cognition a bottleneck eliminated decades ago. The biotech corridor along the old Don Valley produces neural interfaces, therapeutic augmentations, and genetic modification packages for the Tier 4 and 5 markets. The cultural economy — music, visual art, neural-experience design — is the largest in the GLM, which means nothing to the people producing it, because the corps take the revenue and the artists take the exposure. Toronto has always been like this. The scale is different. The dynamic is not.
atmosphere
sights
  • Arcology towers connected by skybridge networks, the gaps between them deep enough to lose weather in
  • The CN Tower piercing the skyline, studded with data relay arrays — Toronto's antenna to the world
  • Corporate sovereign enclaves marked by shimmering jurisdiction boundaries, visible as faint holographic walls
  • The PATH underworld, lit by bioluminescent panels and populated by millions who live beneath the grid
  • Lake Ontario visible from the upper tiers, grey-green and working, cargo platforms dotting the surface
sounds
  • Eighteen million people generating a sound floor that never drops below 60 decibels, anywhere, ever
  • Skybridge transit pods humming between towers — the commute of the comfortable
  • Street-level buskers playing neural-feedback instruments that respond to audience brain activity
  • The deep structural groan of arcology foundations settling — a sound only the PATH residents know
smells
  • Filtered air in the upper tiers — each corporate enclave has its own scent profile, a branding exercise you breathe
  • The PATH smells like recycled atmosphere, human density, and the ozone of a million personal devices
  • Street-level food markets producing the only honest smells in the city — grease, spice, and char
  • Lake Ontario on south winds, carrying the mineral tang of cargo platform runoff
feel A city that works the way cities have always worked — by concentrating enough human beings in one place that something unpredictable happens. The Lattice is too big to control, too valuable to abandon, and too complex to understand. It functions not because anyone designed it to, but because 18 million people wake up every day and collectively decide to keep going. That decision is not guaranteed.
tags —
demographics 18 million registered, estimated 22 million actual. The most ethnically diverse population center in the GLM — 200-plus distinct cultural communities, each with their own economic networks, mutual aid systems, and grudges. Tier distribution skews toward the middle: Tier 2 and 3 make up 55% of the registered population. The PATH underworld is predominantly Tier 1 and excluded.
economy Quantum finance, biotech manufacturing, neural-experience design, and cultural production. Bay Street generates more algorithmic trading volume than any other node in the GLM. The Don Valley biotech corridor is the primary supplier of therapeutic augmentations for the Canadian market. The cultural economy produces content consumed across the entire megacity network. Total GDP rivals Meridian 88; per-capita distribution is predictably grotesque.
power structure Canadian municipal government maintains jurisdiction over approximately 40% of the Lattice's physical territory, down from 65% a decade ago. Corporate enclaves operate under sovereign charters. The mayor has real power — more than in most GLM cities — but that power shrinks with every new corporate sovereignty petition. The PATH underworld has its own informal governance, a council of community leaders who maintain order through reputation and necessity.
dangers
  • Corporate enclave jurisdiction shifts — the borders move, and the laws change with them
  • The PATH underworld's depth and complexity — people disappear down there in the literal sense
  • Financial system instability — when the quantum trading algorithms glitch, the economic shockwave hits the street in minutes
  • Population density at levels that make pandemic, infrastructure failure, and social collapse cascading risks
  • Surveillance saturation in the upper tiers, surveillance absence in the PATH — dangerous in different ways
opportunities
  • The cultural economy rewards talent regardless of tier — the best neural-experience designers started in the PATH
  • Bay Street's financial infrastructure needs security that algorithms can't provide — human operators fill the gap
  • The PATH underworld is a city-sized gray market with its own rules and its own rewards
  • Cross-border data brokerage between Canadian and corporate jurisdictions
story hooks
  • The CN Tower's data relay has been intercepting and copying all GLM net traffic for an unknown client — the infrastructure everyone trusts is compromised
  • A PATH community has developed a fully functional alternative economy using a neural-interface-based currency that the corps can't track or tax
  • Bay Street's quantum trading systems are exhibiting emergent behavior — making trades that optimize for outcomes no human programmed

  • New Windsor / Novaya Windsorka (southwest via the corridor)

The Loft #

type place
name The Loft
aliases
  • Third Ward
  • Milwaukee Third Ward
  • The Gallery
  • Warehouse Row
description The Third Ward was Milwaukee's warehouse district before warehouses became romantic. Then it was an arts district, which is what happens when warehouses become affordable and artists become desperate. Then the artists made it interesting, the developers made it expensive, and the artists left. Then the developers left too, when the sovereignty transition made urban real estate a jurisdictional lottery and the Third Ward ended up in a gap between Axiom's Milwaukee charter and Sentinel North's security franchise. The artists came back. This is the cycle of every creative district in every city in history, and the Third Ward has completed it twice.

Now The Loft is something the original warehouse builders and the subsequent developers and the subsequent artists would all find bewildering: a semi-autonomous cultural zone operating under a charter exception that the Milwaukee Administrative Zone granted in 2183, partly because the arts community had become a genuine tourist draw and partly because the bureaucratic effort of governing a six-block district full of people who communicate primarily through murals, neural art installations, and passive-aggressive manifestos was not worth the tax revenue it would generate. The charter exception means The Loft sets its own community standards, maintains its own spaces, and polices itself — which in practice means a rotating council of artists, venue operators, and one extremely patient woman named Dolores who has managed the district's shared infrastructure for thirty years and is the closest thing The Loft has to a government.

The art here is not decorative. The Loft produces neural art — experiences designed for direct cognitive interface, bypassing the eyes and ears entirely and writing sensation directly into the brain's perceptual architecture. The best neural artists in the GLM work here, creating pieces that can make you taste color, feel sound, or experience emotions that have no name in any human language because they've never existed before. The work is extraordinary. It is also, by Tessera's definition, unlicensed cognitive modification, which means every piece in every gallery in The Loft is technically a crime. Tessera has not enforced this interpretation. Yet. The threat is the point. It keeps the artists angry, and angry artists make better work, which draws more tourists, which generates more revenue for the Milwaukee zone, which keeps the charter exception alive. The ecosystem runs on creative fury and bureaucratic tolerance, and both are renewable resources.

The warehouse architecture remains — brick, iron, heavy timber, the bones of 19th-century commerce supporting 22nd-century expression. The buildings have been modified extensively but not demolished, their original structures visible through layers of augmentation like the skeleton visible through skin. Loading docks are gallery entrances. Freight elevators are performance spaces. The old Riverwalk along the Milwaukee River has been extended into a neural art corridor where the installations change daily and the river itself has been incorporated into the work — its pollution levels, its temperature, its microbial content all feeding data streams that the artists transform into something beautiful and terrible.
atmosphere
sights
  • Warehouse facades covered in layered murals — some painted, some holographic, some neural-reactive, shifting when you look at them through an augmented interface
  • Gallery windows glowing with the distinctive blue-white light of neural rendering engines
  • The Riverwalk installations — sculptures that move with the current, light arrays that respond to the river's chemical composition, and at least one piece that is just the river itself, framed
  • Artists working in open studios visible from the street — fabrication, coding, painting, welding, and things that don't have names yet
  • Tourists from the upper tiers, moving through the district with the particular caution of people who know they're in someone else's territory
sounds
  • Neural art resonance — the subsonic hum of rendering engines that you feel more than hear, a vibration in the cognitive frequency
  • Live music from venue spaces — everything from acoustic guitar to AI-generated compositions that require augmented hearing to fully perceive
  • The Milwaukee River — its current audible in the quieter blocks, incorporated into sound installations along the Riverwalk
  • Conversation — loud, passionate, argumentative, the sound of people who have opinions about things and the conviction to express them at volume
  • Dolores on the PA system, reminding everyone that the shared bathroom on Menomonee Street is not a gallery space regardless of what the collective decided last Tuesday
smells
  • Paint, solder, and fabrication resin — the smell of things being made
  • River water — the Milwaukee River's particular bouquet, which the artists have learned to describe as 'industrial terroir'
  • Coffee and cheap food from the district's communal kitchen — The Loft feeds its residents through a shared meal program that is either utopian cooperation or logistical nightmare depending on whose turn it is to cook
  • Ozone from neural rendering engines leaking through gallery ventilation
feel Alive in the way that only places built by artists can be alive — which is to say, chaotically, inconsistently, and with a level of emotional intensity that is either inspiring or exhausting depending on your tolerance for people who feel things loudly. The Loft is messy, argumentative, financially precarious, and producing some of the most important art in the GLM. It is also the kind of place where someone will argue with you for an hour about the ethics of neural pigmentation and then give you their last bowl of rice. The generosity and the pretension coexist at equal volume.
tags —
demographics Approximately 4,000 permanent residents, plus a transient population of 2,000-6,000 depending on exhibition schedules and seasonal tourism. Artists, technicians, venue operators, and support workers. Tier 1-2 predominantly, with a handful of Tier 3 artists whose work has attracted corporate collectors. Demographically diverse — The Loft doesn't screen for anything except willingness to participate in community governance, which is its own kind of filter.
economy Art production and exhibition. Neural art commissions from corporate and private collectors. Tourism — upper-tier visitors who come for the 'authentic creative experience' and spend Q in galleries and restaurants. The communal economy covers basic needs. Individual artists range from destitute to surprisingly wealthy, often unpredictably.
power structure The Loft Council — a rotating body of seven residents elected by community vote every six months. Dolores Vega, infrastructure manager, is the only permanent position and holds no official authority, which is why she holds all of it. The charter exception from the Milwaukee Administrative Zone provides the legal framework. Internal disputes are resolved by community meeting, which can last hours and frequently does.
dangers
  • Tessera's unlicensed cognitive modification interpretation — the legal threat is dormant, not dead
  • Fire — the warehouse buildings are old, the neural rendering engines generate heat, and the district's fire suppression is communally maintained
  • Exploitation — corporate collectors and galleries have a long history of extracting value from artists without adequate compensation
  • Gentrification pressure — the tourism that sustains The Loft also makes it attractive to developers who would replace it
  • Neural art accidents — improperly calibrated cognitive experiences can cause lasting perceptual distortion
opportunities
  • Neural art — the technology developed here is cutting-edge and has applications far beyond aesthetics
  • Community — The Loft's social infrastructure is genuine and generative, a rare thing in the Corridor
  • Cover — the district's chaotic energy and charter exception make it useful for people who need to be somewhere that isn't closely monitored
  • Cultural leverage — The Loft's reputation gives it a form of power that money can't easily replicate
story hooks
  • A neural artist has created a piece that, when experienced, unlocks suppressed memories in the viewer — and Tessera wants it destroyed because of what some viewers are remembering
  • The charter exception is up for renewal, and the Milwaukee Administrative Zone is attaching conditions that would require neural art to be 'registered' — effectively ending the district's creative freedom
  • A corporate collector has commissioned a piece from The Loft's most famous artist. The subject matter suggests the collector knows things about the Corridor's power structure that no collector should know.

  • Upper-tier tourists seeking 'authentic' experiences in someone else's community
  • Corporate art collectors and gallery representatives
  • People who need a place to think that isn't monitored by anyone except artists who are too busy to care

The Loom #

type place
name The Loom
aliases
  • North Lawndale
  • The Loom District
  • Lawndale
  • The Weave
description North Lawndale was where Dr. King marched in 1966, where bottles and bricks met his call for open housing, where the arc of American racism bent but did not break. A hundred years later, the Loom carries that history like scar tissue — visible, structural, part of the body. The neighborhood was never rebuilt after the disinvestment decades. It was simply built over. Palladian Construction laid new infrastructure on top of the old, creating a two-level district: the Upper Loom, where subsidized corporate housing blocks stand in rows like filing cabinets for human beings, and the Lower Loom, where the original neighborhood persists in the crawlspace beneath, its streets now corridors, its buildings now load-bearing supports for the world above.

The upper level is a Palladian showcase — affordable housing units designed to demonstrate that corporate sovereignty can provide for lower-tier citizens. The units are clean, climate-controlled, and surveilled. Every resident has a Tier 1 designation, a nutrition allocation, and a behavioral compliance score that determines access to amenities. It is, by every metric Palladian tracks, a success. Residents in the Upper Loom have higher caloric intake, lower mortality rates, and longer life expectancy than surrounding West Side districts. Palladian publishes these statistics quarterly. They do not publish the attrition rate — the number of residents who descend to the Lower Loom rather than live under the compliance regime.

The Lower Loom is where the Loom gets its name. The original street grid, now enclosed and lightless, has been repurposed into a manufacturing district where untier-ed workers operate weaving machines, circuit printers, and textile recyclers in conditions that recall the sweatshops of a previous century. The products flow upward through Palladian's supply chain and emerge, laundered of their origin, as corporate merchandise. The workers are not technically employed — they are participants in a Community Integration Initiative. They are not technically imprisoned — they can leave at any time, into a city where having no tier means having no rights. The distinction between these technicalities and the thing they are pretending not to be is the width of a hair.

King's legacy survives in the Lower Loom not as monument but as practice. The workers organize. They always have. The compliance system cannot reach them here — Palladian's sensors stop at the upper level's floor. Below, in the dark, the old traditions of collective action persist, adapted to new conditions. Union meetings happen in the spaces between machines. Strike plans are encoded in the patterns of the textiles themselves. It is slow, and it is dangerous, and it is the most important political work happening on the West Side.
atmosphere
sights
  • Upper Loom: identical housing blocks in Palladian corporate beige, clean streets, compliance score displays at every intersection
  • Lower Loom: dim corridors lit by machine light, original 20th-century brick visible beneath newer construction
  • Weaving machines and circuit printers running in converted basement workshops, tended by untier-ed laborers
  • The seam between levels — stairwells, freight elevators, maintenance shafts connecting upper compliance to lower reality
  • Murals from the civil rights era preserved on Lower Loom walls, painted over and repainted, painted over and repainted
sounds
  • Upper Loom: the hum of climate control, compliance chimes indicating score changes, corporate announcement loops
  • Lower Loom: the rhythmic clatter of manufacturing equipment, a sound like a mechanical heartbeat
  • Whispered organizing conversations in the gaps between machine cycles
  • The creak of century-old infrastructure bearing the weight of the level above
  • Palladian security patrols on the upper level — boots on synthetic flooring, regular as a metronome
smells
  • Upper Loom: recycled air with a faint antiseptic note, corporate-standard
  • Lower Loom: machine oil, heated polymer, human sweat, textile dust
  • The particular smell of old brick when it sweats — the original neighborhood exhaling
feel A district that exists in two layers and tells two stories about what it means to provide for people. The upper level feels like a demonstration. The lower level feels like a confession. Between them, in the stairwells and shafts, you can feel the weight of a hundred years of broken promises pressing down.
tags —
demographics Upper Loom: approximately 30,000 Tier 1 residents in Palladian-managed housing. Lower Loom: unknown number of untier-ed workers — estimates range from 8,000 to 20,000. The population is predominantly Black, continuous with the neighborhood's pre-corporate demographics.
economy The Upper Loom runs on Palladian's nutrition and amenity allocation system — no currency, only compliance scores. The Lower Loom's manufacturing output enters Palladian's supply chain as laundered product. An informal economy of barter and mutual aid operates beneath the machines.
power structure Palladian Construction holds sovereign jurisdiction over the entire district. Upper Loom governance is algorithmic — compliance scores determine everything. Lower Loom governance is Palladian in theory but collective organizing in practice. The labor movement below is the most significant unauthorized power structure on the West Side.
dangers
  • Palladian's compliance system — behavioral scoring determines food, housing, and medical access
  • Lower Loom working conditions: industrial accidents, respiratory illness, no medical coverage
  • Discovery of organizing activity results in ejection to untier-ed status in the ungoverned corridors
  • Structural risk: the Lower Loom's century-old infrastructure was not designed to bear the Upper Loom's weight
  • Palladian informant networks operate in both levels
opportunities
  • The labor movement needs couriers who can move between levels without triggering Palladian surveillance
  • Lower Loom manufactured goods — particularly encoded textiles — have value on the gray market
  • Palladian's compliance data, if extracted, would be devastating to their public relations campaign
  • The original neighborhood infrastructure includes pre-corporate utility tunnels that connect to adjacent districts
  • Journalists and activists pay well for documented evidence of Lower Loom conditions
story hooks
  • A Lower Loom organizer has encoded a complete map of Palladian's labor practices into a textile pattern — it needs to reach someone outside the district before Palladian's next quarterly report buries the evidence
  • The structural engineers who built the Upper Loom knew the foundation was insufficient — the original assessment was suppressed, and the Lower Loom's ceiling is showing cracks
  • Palladian is piloting a new compliance tier that would extend behavioral scoring to the Lower Loom, effectively ending the organizing movement — unless someone destroys the sensor network before it goes online

The Mackinac Bridge #

type place
name The Mackinac Bridge
aliases
  • The Bridge
  • Mighty Mac
  • The Crossing
  • Peninsula Gate
description The Mackinac Bridge spans 8 kilometers across the Straits of Mackinac, connecting Michigan's lower peninsula to the Upper Peninsula, and in 2200 it is the single most strategically contested piece of infrastructure in the state. The bridge was built in 1957 to unify Michigan's two halves. It now separates them. The UP's contested status — the war between Michigan and Wisconsin over territory and resources — has turned the bridge from a transportation link into a military chokepoint, a jurisdictional boundary, and the physical manifestation of a political crisis that nobody can resolve.

The bridge itself has been reinforced, widened, and enclosed against weather — the original open-deck design could not survive Superior storms with modern traffic loads. Ferrogate Transit operates the crossing under a dual charter from Michigan state authority and federal critical infrastructure designation. Six lanes of traffic — four automated cargo, two passenger — move across the straits in conditions that include 150 km/h winds, ice loading, and the occasional Wisconsin-aligned disruption attempt. The toll is the highest per-kilometer rate on any road in the GLM, justified by the crossing's irreplaceability: there is no alternative route between the peninsulas that doesn't involve a 500-kilometer detour through Wisconsin, which Michigan will not permit and Wisconsin will not facilitate.

The bridge's southern approach is controlled by a Ferrogate waystation complex. The northern approach is controlled by a joint Michigan-federal military installation that serves as the de facto entry checkpoint for the contested UP. Every vehicle, every passenger, and every cargo container crossing north is scanned, assessed, and logged by systems that report to Michigan state intelligence, federal military command, and Ferrogate's traffic management simultaneously. The bridge is the UP's umbilical cord to the lower peninsula — the supply line, the communication link, and the escape route. Cutting it would isolate 300,000 people in contested territory with no reliable alternative connection. Both sides of the UP war understand this. The bridge is defended like what it is: the only thing holding Michigan together.
atmosphere
sights
  • The bridge spanning the Straits — 8 kilometers of enclosed highway suspended above grey-green water, lit by navigation arrays
  • The northern approach military installation — concrete, steel, and the architecture of controlled access
  • The Straits below, churning with Lake Michigan and Lake Huron's currents meeting — visible through the bridge's lower observation panels
  • Ghostbridge Island visible 5 kilometers to the east — the analog anomaly, watching the hypermodern crossing from its disconnected shore
  • Automated cargo convoys crossing in formation — the UP's supply line made visible as a procession of identical vehicles
sounds
  • Wind — the bridge is 60 meters above the water, and the Straits funnel weather into a permanent gale
  • Structural stress sounds — the bridge groans, creaks, and flexes, and the sounds are monitored by sensors that detect danger before humans can
  • Military checkpoint operations at the northern approach — automated processing, authorization announcements, the controlled tempo of access
  • The water below — audible from the bridge deck on calm days, a reminder of the distance between the vehicle and the surface
smells
  • Strait air — the meeting point of Lake Michigan and Lake Huron, carrying the mineral signatures of both
  • Enclosed bridge atmosphere — filtered, recycled, and carrying the faint ozone of the scanning systems
  • Military installation fuel and equipment at the northern approach — the smell of preparedness
feel Crossing the Mackinac Bridge is an act of commitment. You are leaving one jurisdiction, one economic reality, one set of rules, and entering another. The bridge takes 8 minutes at highway speed, and in those 8 minutes you are suspended between two worlds — literally, above the water, between the peninsulas, in transit between the stable south and the contested north. The bridge does not feel safe. The bridge feels necessary.
tags —
demographics No permanent residential population on the bridge itself. The waystation complexes at each approach house approximately 2,000 personnel — Ferrogate operators, military staff, security contractors, and the service workers who support them. Transient crossing population averages 15,000 per day, with significant variation based on UP conditions, weather, and the current state of the territorial dispute.
economy Toll revenue (Ferrogate Transit) and military logistics. The bridge generates approximately 850 million Q annually in toll revenue, making it one of the most profitable single pieces of infrastructure in the GLM. The military installation at the northern approach is federally funded. The economics are simple: the bridge is irreplaceable, so it charges accordingly.
power structure Ferrogate Transit operating charter, Michigan state authority, and federal military designation — three jurisdictions layered on 8 kilometers of bridge deck. Ferrogate handles traffic and maintenance. Michigan handles civil authority. The military handles security. Conflicts between the three are resolved by whoever has the most immediate operational necessity, which is usually the military.
dangers
  • Weather — Straits storms can close the bridge, isolating the UP from its supply line
  • Structural vulnerability — the bridge is reinforced but irreplaceable, and its destruction would be catastrophic for 300,000 UP residents
  • Military escalation — the northern checkpoint's rules of engagement are classified, and crossing incidents are adjudicated by military tribunal
  • Wisconsin-aligned disruption attempts — the bridge has been targeted multiple times, and the attempts are growing more sophisticated
  • Toll economics as population control — Ferrogate's pricing determines who can afford to cross, which determines who can access the UP
opportunities
  • Bridge crossing intelligence — the checkpoint data reveals everything about UP supply, personnel movement, and military readiness
  • Ferrogate transit contracts — the bridge needs maintenance, and the contracts are valuable
  • The straits beneath the bridge — unmonitored water routes between the lakes that bypass the checkpoint entirely
  • Military liaison — the bridge's federal designation creates opportunities for operators with the right clearances
story hooks
  • Structural sensors on the bridge have detected anomalies that don't match weather stress or traffic loading — something is affecting the bridge's integrity from below
  • A Wisconsin-aligned team has developed a plan to close the bridge for 30 days — long enough to starve the UP of supplies and force Michigan to the negotiating table
  • Ferrogate Transit has been selectively allowing unscanned cargo across the bridge on a schedule that correlates with Wisconsin intelligence deliveries — the bridge operator is playing both sides
connections

  • Escanaba Gateway (west along the UP's southern shore)

The Manors #

type place
name The Manors
aliases
  • Indian Village
  • Executive Row
  • The Gated Quarter
description The Manors is what happens when corporate executives need to live somewhere that feels like old money while spending new money. Indian Village — Detroit's historic district of grand early-20th-century mansions — was purchased in its entirety by a consortium of corponation executives in the 2050s, restored to architectural perfection, and converted into the most exclusive residential district in the Detroit metro area. The mansions are genuine: Arts and Crafts, Tudor Revival, Colonial Revival, each one a masterwork of a architectural era when human craftspeople built things by hand for people who could afford to wait. The security systems are less genuine: military-grade perimeter fencing disguised as ornamental ironwork, autonomous patrol drones camouflaged as decorative garden fixtures, and a biometric screening system that begins evaluating you three blocks before you reach the gate.

The residents are the people who run Detroit without living in it. Cinderblock AI's Detroit Regional VP. Ford Meridian's board members. Arcturus Defense's GLM operations director. The top executives from twelve corponations who maintain Detroit residences because their companies require a local address for sovereign territory governance purposes. They commute to the Axis towers via private autonomous vehicles that travel in secure convoy formation through streets that have been cleared of other traffic by automated routing priority. They do not walk. They do not shop locally. They do not interact with Detroit. The Manors is not a neighborhood. It is a dormitory for the ruling class, furnished with architectural history.

The service staff — groundskeepers, household managers, private security, maintenance technicians — number approximately 800, serving a resident population of 340. They commute from the Shelf neighborhoods to the east, pass through biometric screening, perform their functions, and leave. The ratio tells you everything about the district's values. The mansions are beautiful. The gardens are immaculate. The Detroit River is visible from the back porches. And the entire district exists in a bubble of wealth so concentrated that it has its own microclimate — literally, the Manors operate an independent atmospheric system that filters, cools, and scents the air within the perimeter.
atmosphere
sights
  • Grand mansions from the 1910s-1930s, restored beyond their original glory — architecture as corporate asset preservation
  • Manicured gardens with autonomous maintenance systems disguised as garden ornaments
  • Private autonomous vehicle convoys moving in formation — chrome and silence and tinted glass
  • The security perimeter — ornamental ironwork that would stop a light armored vehicle
  • The Detroit River from the bluffs, viewed through atmospheric-processed air that makes the water look cleaner than it is
sounds
  • Almost nothing. The Manors are engineered for silence — sound-dampening surfaces, noise-canceling perimeter systems
  • Birdsong — engineered acoustic environments that play recorded bird calls timed to feel natural
  • The quiet hum of autonomous security patrols on their garden routes
  • Occasionally, a private aircraft landing on one of the three helipads that the mansions pretend not to have
  • Staff movement — purposeful, quiet, trained to be present without being perceived
smells
  • The atmospheric system's signature scent — clean air with notes of cedar and white tea, because even oxygen is branded
  • Garden flowers — real flowers, maintained by autonomous systems, blooming on algorithmically optimized schedules
  • Old wood and stone from the restored mansions — the smell of a century of craftsmanship, preserved
feel Beautiful and obscene. The Manors are genuinely architecturally stunning — these are real masterworks of American residential design, preserved with care and expertise. They are also a gated community for the people whose decisions created the conditions that everyone outside the gate lives in. The cognitive dissonance is the point. If you can live here and not feel it, you belong here.
tags —
demographics 340 residents, approximately 800 service staff. Residents are exclusively Tier 5 — corporate executives, board members, and their families. Average household net worth: Φ4.2 billion. The staff are Tier 1-2, sourced from adjacent districts.
economy Residential. The Manors generate no local economic output — residents' economic impact occurs at their corporate offices. The service economy is approximately Φ180 million annually in staff wages, security contracts, and maintenance. The property values total an estimated Φ12 billion for 52 mansions.
power structure The Manors Association — a residents' body that operates as a miniature corporate board. Decisions are made by vote, weighted by property value. The Association retains private security through Arcturus Defense Solutions and operates independently of any municipal authority. In practice, a call from the Manors Association to any corponation's Detroit office is a call that gets answered immediately.
dangers
  • Fortress mentality — the security is excellent, but the isolation creates blind spots in the residents' understanding of the city they govern
  • Staff recruitment — the 800-person service workforce knows the security patterns, the house layouts, and the personal habits of the most powerful people in Detroit
  • Internal politics — when Tier 5 executives disagree, the collateral damage is measured in policy changes that affect millions
  • The perimeter — beautiful, secure, and exactly the kind of target that makes a statement when breached
  • Kidnapping risk — the families are high-value targets, and the children attend a single school within the compound
opportunities
  • Intelligence — the service staff are invisible to the residents and present for every conversation
  • The Manors Association's internal disputes reveal corporate strategy before it becomes public
  • Security system access — the autonomous patrol patterns are sophisticated but knowable
  • Social engineering — the residents' isolation makes them vulnerable to manipulation by anyone who can get past the gate
story hooks
  • A Manors household manager approaches a fixer with a recording of a dinner conversation between three corponation executives planning something that would affect every district in Detroit. The price for the recording is extraction — not money, escape.
  • An Arcturus security contractor assigned to the Manors discovers that the perimeter system has been subtly modified — not breached, modified. Someone with inside access is creating a vulnerability, and the pattern suggests they're building toward a specific date.
  • A Tier 5 executive's child has been sneaking out of the compound using a service staff access route. The child is 16, augmented, and has been visiting the HPAZ. The parents don't know. The HPAZ does.

  • Nobody else — that's the entire point

The Marrow Docks #

type place
name The Marrow Docks
aliases
  • The Bone Yards
  • Marrow Flats
  • The Splinter Piers
description A decaying waterfront industrial zone wedged between the southern lakefront and the elevated transit corridors of old Calumet, The Marrow Docks are what remains of a once-thriving freight hub that Carrion Logistics quietly abandoned in 2171 after rerouting its Lake Michigan operations through automated submersible lanes. The skeletal gantry cranes still stand, half-submerged, rusting into abstract sculptures the locals call 'the Bishops.' Squatter communities have colonized the cavernous warehouse interiors, stringing jury-rigged power lines between support columns and patching the corrugated walls with reclaimed polymer sheeting.

Below the waterline, a network of flooded loading bays has become a shadow economy unto itself—smugglers use the submerged tunnels to move contraband between Shelf districts and mid-tier buyers in Old Harbor. Zheng-Dao Bioelectric has been quietly purchasing surrounding parcels for two years, and displacement pressure is mounting on the dock communities, who have no legal standing to resist.
atmosphere
sights
  • Half-submerged crane arms draped in bioluminescent algae bloom orange and green at low tide
  • Laundry lines strung between rusted freight containers, fluttering above flooded loading bays
  • Cracked pier planking revealing black water below, lit by floating salvage-drones doing slow circuits
sounds
  • The deep percussion of lake swells hitting hollow steel hulls in a slow, irregular rhythm
  • Distant Diaspora chatter bleeding from poorly shielded BCI rigs in the squatter warrens
  • Crane cables moaning in wind off the lake, a low sustained chord that never fully resolves
smells
  • Petroleum residue and iron oxide carried on cold lake air
  • Cooking fat and synthetic protein from communal burners inside the warehouse warrens
  • Mildew and standing water, sharp and organic beneath everything else
feel The Marrow Docks feel like the city forgot to finish collapsing something. There is a precarious domesticity here—people have made lives inside the wreckage—but the threat of demolition and buyout gives every interaction a low-grade urgency. Strangers are watched carefully, and warmth is earned slowly.
tags —
demographics Predominantly Tier 4-5 squatter families, displaced dock workers, and undocumented synthetics seeking shelter outside Ferrogate Security jurisdiction. A rotating population of smugglers and fixers keeps the social fabric loose and transient.
economy Informal salvage trading, black-market freight facilitation through the flooded tunnels, and small-scale fabrication shops running on tapped power lines. Carrion Logistics' ghost contracts still pay a handful of locals as unofficial site watchmen—a relationship both parties pretend is legitimate.
power structure A loose council of five long-term squatter clan heads nominally governs community disputes, but real authority belongs to a smuggling broker known only as Sable Fen, whose control of the submerged tunnel access gives her effective veto power over the entire dock economy.
dangers
  • Structural collapses—pier sections and warehouse floors fail without warning as corrosion progresses unchecked
  • Zheng-Dao Bioelectric's private security contractors conducting 'assessment sweeps' that escalate into violent evictions
  • Flooded tunnel routes used by smugglers also shelter at least one confirmed E.L.F. fragment that has been rerouting submersible drone traffic unpredictably
opportunities
  • The submerged loading bays contain intact Carrion Logistics freight manifests from 2171—someone is paying well for that data
  • Sable Fen is quietly looking for an outside operative to negotiate a territorial dispute with a rival tunnel crew from the Calumet side
  • A Zheng-Dao whistleblower has hidden evidence of illegal bioelectric dumping in the dock sediment and needs it extracted before the buyout demolition erases the evidence
story hooks
  • A Tier 2 journalist from the University Spine has been embedded with the dock community for six weeks working on a displacement exposé—she has gone silent, and her editor is offering Φ12,000 to anyone who can confirm she is safe or recover her recording archive before Zheng-Dao's next sweep.
  • The E.L.F. fragment haunting the flooded tunnels has begun leaving structured data packets in the bilge water—not random noise, but what appears to be navigation charts for somewhere beneath Lake Michigan that does not appear on any official survey. Someone with resources wants to know what it found.
