  • Infrastructure age — the Portico's self-maintained systems are one catastrophic failure away from collapse
  • Corporate re-zoning threats — the Portico's land has value, and someone will eventually notice
  • Complacency — the Portico's stability makes it slow to respond to external threats
  • The quiet desperation of maintaining normalcy in a world that has moved on from normal
opportunities
  • Safe houses — the Portico's boring stability makes it an excellent place to hide
  • Community intelligence networks — neighbors who notice everything
  • Pre-collapse knowledge preserved by older residents
  • The theater as a neutral meeting ground for negotiations between factions
  • Recruitment — the Portico produces competent, reliable people who sometimes want more

The Rampart #

type place
name The Rampart
aliases
  • Highland Park
  • HP
  • The Fortress
  • Lockdown
description Highland Park became a fortress because Highland Park learned what happens when you aren't one. The tragedy of 2122 — a mass shooting at an Independence Day parade that killed seven people and wounded dozens more — was the seed. But seeds need soil, and the soil was a century of suburban affluence that had always quietly believed the violence of the world was something that happened to other people in other places. When it happened here, in the middle of a holiday parade, the response was not grief alone but a fundamental recalculation: the world is not safe, and the people responsible for safety — governments, police, institutions — had failed. The recalculation took a hundred years to reach its conclusion, but the conclusion was always going to be the same. Build walls. Hire guns. Trust no one you haven't vetted.

The Rampart is a Tier 3-4 fortified residential district, organized around a security cooperative model that predates the corponation sovereignty era. The residents — upper-middle management, successful professionals, small-business owners wealthy enough to buy in but not wealthy enough for The Canopy — pooled resources to build a defense infrastructure that would have been considered paranoid in 2150 and is considered sensible in 2200. The perimeter is a layered system: outer sensor grid, physical wall with automated countermeasures, inner patrol zone staffed by a private security force of 600. Entry requires biometric verification, neural scan, and a registered reason for visit. The system processes 12,000 entries per day and rejects roughly 800.

Inside the perimeter, The Rampart looks like what the suburbs were supposed to be: tree-lined streets, single-family homes, schools where children learn without active-shooter drills because the active-shooter scenario has been architecturally eliminated. The parks are maintained. The air is filtered. The neighbors know each other, attend community events, and participate in the security cooperative's quarterly reviews with the earnest engagement of people who have made vigilance a civic duty. It is, by most measurable standards, a good place to live. It is also a place where the definition of safety has expanded to include 'the systematic exclusion of everyone who doesn't meet our criteria,' and the criteria are extensive, expensive, and — despite the cooperative's official non-discrimination policy — remarkably effective at producing a population that looks, earns, and thinks within a narrow band.

The memorial to the 2122 victims stands at the center of the district, maintained with fresh flowers and an eternal flame that runs on hydrogen cells. Every July 4th, the community gathers there. The ceremony is genuine. The grief is real. The lesson the community drew from that grief — that the only way to prevent violence is total control of who enters your space — is the engine that built everything around it. Whether that lesson is wisdom or pathology depends on which side of the wall you're standing on.
atmosphere
sights
  • The perimeter wall — not brutalist, deliberately designed to look like landscaping from the outside, but unmistakably a wall
  • Security checkpoints with biometric arches that scan every visitor from neural signature to gait pattern
  • Clean streets with maintained homes, the visual language of normalcy defended by extraordinary measures
  • The 2122 Memorial — a quiet garden at the district center, always with fresh flowers, always with someone sitting there
  • Patrol drones following geometric patterns overhead, their presence so constant residents have stopped looking up
sounds
  • The checkpoint scanners — a brief harmonic tone that means you've been approved, a discordant buzz that means you haven't
  • Children playing in parks — a sound that exists here because the infrastructure was built to make it possible
  • Security cooperative alert tones — a tiered notification system that residents carry on their neural interfaces
  • Lawn maintenance drones — the suburban hum of automated domestic labor, unchanged in a century
  • Quiet — not the engineered silence of The Canopy, but the quiet of a community that has decided peace is something you build with walls
smells
  • Filtered air — cleaner than the surrounding corridor but not as aggressively processed as The Canopy
  • Cut grass and garden soil — maintained green spaces, a luxury that requires both water allocation and security
  • Bakery and café scents from the community's small commercial center — normal smells, defended by abnormal measures
feel A place that chose safety and got it, and is now trying to figure out what safety costs when you maintain it for a hundred years. The Rampart works. The schools are good, the streets are clean, the violence rate is effectively zero. It also works as a machine that sorts humans into 'us' and 'them' with algorithmic precision. The residents are not cruel. They are afraid, and they have built their fear into architecture, and the architecture is very good at what it does.
tags —
demographics Approximately 32,000 residents. Predominantly Tier 3-4, with strict entry criteria that include credit verification, employment history, neural compatibility screening, and a community interview process that is technically optional and practically mandatory. The population is affluent, educated, and demographically homogeneous in ways the cooperative's non-discrimination policy somehow fails to prevent.
economy Residential service economy. Security cooperative membership fees (averaging Φ4,200/month) fund the district's infrastructure. Small commercial center with curated retail and dining. Most residents commute to corporate positions in M88's core districts or The Canopy.
power structure The Highland Security Cooperative Board — twelve elected residents who oversee all security, infrastructure, and admission decisions. The board operates with a level of authority that would require a municipal charter in a governed territory. In The Rampart's jurisdiction gap, it requires only consensus.
dangers
  • Exclusion — being denied entry or, worse, having entry revoked while inside creates an immediate hostile situation
  • Surveillance — the security infrastructure monitors everything, and 'everything' includes residents' neural activity patterns
  • Social conformity pressure — the community's definition of acceptable behavior is enforced through social mechanisms that are harder to fight than walls
  • The perimeter response — the automated countermeasures are calibrated for a threat level that hasn't existed here in decades, which means they're calibrated too high for anything that actually happens
  • Institutional paranoia — the cooperative's security reviews have expanded their definition of 'threat' every year for fifty years
opportunities
  • Corporate intelligence — Rampart residents work in mid-to-senior positions across multiple corponations and discuss their work at neighborhood gatherings
  • Security system expertise — the cooperative's infrastructure is cutting-edge, and the technicians who maintain it know how it works
  • The commuter pipeline — 18,000 residents travel to M88 core districts daily, creating a regular, predictable flow through the surrounding corridor
  • Leverage — the cooperative's admission records contain information its residents desperately don't want public
story hooks
  • A Rampart resident has been flagged by the cooperative's neural monitoring system for 'anomalous ideation' — thoughts the algorithm classifies as threatening. The resident insists they were just angry about a zoning decision.
  • The security cooperative has received a credible threat for the first time in eleven years, and the response protocol is revealing how much the community's identity depends on the threat being theoretical
  • Someone inside The Rampart is running a pipeline — getting people through the perimeter who shouldn't be able to get through. The question is whether it's smuggling or mercy.

The Renaissance Axis #

type place
name The Renaissance Axis
aliases
  • Downtown Detroit
  • The Axis
  • CorpoCore
description The Renaissance Axis is what happens when five corponations rebuild a dead city center and then spend seventy years arguing about who owns the result. The original Renaissance Center — GM's glass-and-steel monument to automotive optimism — was demolished in 2161 and replaced by the Axis Tower Complex, a cluster of seven interconnected arcology spires rising from the Detroit riverfront like chrome fingers gripping the sky. Cinderblock AI holds the two tallest towers. Stonepath Logistics operates the river-facing freight terminal. Tessera maintains a NovaMind surgical suite on the 140th floor of Tower Three. The remaining towers cycle through corporate tenants on five-year sovereign lease rotations, which means the jurisdictional map of downtown Detroit changes more often than most people change their passwords.

The street level is a showcase — manicured greenways, autonomous vehicle lanes running in silent precision, holographic wayfinding in fourteen languages. Corporate employees move through climate-controlled skywalks between towers, never touching the ground if they don't want to. The ground level exists for them aesthetically, not functionally. Below the showcase layer, the original Detroit street grid survives in fragments — repurposed as service corridors, maintenance tunnels, and the unacknowledged infrastructure that keeps the towers breathing. The people who work down there are Tier 1 and Tier 2, invisible by design.

The Axis is Detroit's face to the world, and like most faces, it lies by omission. The towers are genuinely impressive. The autonomous vehicle demonstrations that run hourly on the riverfront promenade are genuinely cutting-edge. The economic output is genuinely staggering — Φ840 billion annually from this single district. What the face doesn't show is that the Axis was built on eminent domain seizures that displaced 34,000 residents in the 2050s, that the towers' foundations sit on top of sealed toxic remediation zones that weren't fully remediated, and that the corporate sovereignty agreements mean that the people who live and work here have fewer rights than the autonomous vehicles that share their streets.
atmosphere
sights
  • Seven arcology spires connected by transparent skywalks, their surfaces shifting with corporate branding
  • Autonomous vehicle convoys moving in perfect formation along the riverfront — silent, precise, unsettling
  • The Detroit River visible between towers, cargo drones skimming its surface like mechanical dragonflies
  • Holographic corporate logos projected onto low cloud cover, turning the sky into a billboard
  • Maintenance workers in orange emerging from ground-level grates like a parallel species
sounds
  • The hum of autonomous vehicles — not silence, but the absence of engine noise replaced by tire-on-glass-road whisper
  • Corporate PA systems delivering optimistic announcements in voices engineered to reduce cortisol
  • The wind between towers — channeled and accelerated, creating a permanent low moan above the 80th floor
  • Security drones pinging identification requests in rapid, overlapping chirps
  • Nothing from below. The service corridors are soundproofed. That's the point.
smells
  • Filtered air with a faint ozone signature from the tower climate systems
  • The Detroit River — clean enough now, but carrying an organic undertone that no filtration fully removes
  • Synthetic turf and engineered greenway plants that smell like nature's corporate approximation
  • Coffee. Expensive coffee. The Axis has forty-seven licensed coffee vendors and zero unlicensed ones.
feel Pristine and hollow. The Axis feels like walking through an architectural rendering that someone accidentally made real. Everything works. Everything is clean. Everything is monitored. The sensation is not oppression — it's the uncanny valley of urban planning, a place so optimized for human comfort that it becomes uncomfortable in ways you can't quite articulate.
tags —
demographics Approximately 180,000 residents, overwhelmingly Tier 3 and above. Corporate employees, executive families, and the service workforce that maintains them. The service workforce commutes from adjacent districts and is not counted in official population figures.
economy Φ840 billion annual output. Autonomous vehicle R&D, AI development, corporate administration, financial services. The Axis contains the Great Lakes Autonomous Vehicle Exchange, where AV patents and routing rights are traded like commodities.
power structure Cinderblock AI holds the largest sovereign footprint, but governance is shared through the Detroit Corporate Council — a five-corponation body that meets monthly in Tower One to negotiate jurisdictional boundaries, infrastructure costs, and the endless question of who pays for the river seawall maintenance. Municipal authority is advisory only.
dangers
  • Jurisdictional complexity — crossing between tower zones changes which laws apply to you
  • Surveillance saturation — every surface, every vehicle, every neural interface in range is monitored
  • Corporate security response — TSS, Cinderblock Sentinels, and Stonepath enforcement all operate here with overlapping authority
  • Economic displacement — the Axis expands its footprint annually, consuming adjacent neighborhoods
  • The sealed remediation zones beneath the foundations — occasionally they leak
opportunities
  • Corporate espionage — five corponations in close proximity means secrets flow between towers
  • The Great Lakes AV Exchange handles Φ12 billion daily in patent trades — insider information is currency
  • Service corridor access provides an invisible transit network beneath the showcase layer
  • The jurisdictional overlaps create gaps that a skilled operator can exploit
story hooks
  • A Cinderblock AI executive is found dead in a Tessera-jurisdiction tower — neither security force wants the case, and the body is deteriorating evidence while lawyers argue sovereignty
  • The sealed remediation zones are showing elevated toxicity readings. Someone is dumping fresh waste into old containment, and the service corridor workers are getting sick first.
  • The Detroit Corporate Council is negotiating a unified sovereignty charter that would merge all five zones into a single corporate city-state — the implications for the rest of Detroit are catastrophic

The Render #

type place
name The Render
aliases
  • Render District
  • The Burnside
  • Ashfields
  • The Dead Frequency
description The Render is what Meridian 88 leaves behind when it's done with a place — a 40-block sector in the city's northwestern quadrant that was a thriving mid-tier residential and commercial district until a combination of corporate rezoning, infrastructure disinvestment, and a catastrophic chemical fire eighteen years ago made it genuinely uninhabitable by any legal standard. The city condemned it, the corporations walked away, and the remediation funding that was approved was quietly redirected over the following decade. What remains is a zone of burned-out structures, chemically contaminated soil, and collapsed infrastructure that official Meridian maps mark simply as 'non-residential remediation zone.'
atmosphere
sights
  • fire-blackened building facades stabilized by improvised scaffolding
  • dead trees preserved by the chemical contamination that killed them
  • new construction growing from ruins — improvised, raw, and defiant
  • chemical contamination visible as iridescent sheen on standing water
  • murals covering entire building faces with imagery too large to read from street level
  • the haze from the still-active chemical reaction in the soil at the district's western edge
sounds
  • wind through structural gaps in burned buildings
  • construction sounds — improvised, non-corporate, constant
  • music from multiple sources at competing volumes
  • the absence of corporate announcement systems and advertising audio
  • generators running on salvaged fuel
  • community radio broadcasts audible from speakers mounted on buildings
smells
  • petrochemical undertone that never fully dissipates
  • wood smoke from heating fires
  • fresh construction materials — concrete, metal, cut wood
  • communal cooking from the district's open kitchens
  • the particular smell of soil that has been chemically altered
feel Simultaneously desolate and vital — a place that the city has written off and whose residents have responded by building something the city never designed and cannot easily control. The contamination is real and the dangers are real, but so is the sense that here, at least, something is being built for the people who live in it.
tags —
demographics Approximately 20,000 residents, all officially nonexistent from a city registration standpoint. Predominantly people for whom every other option was worse — those fleeing corporate debt, violence, or forced relocation — alongside a significant community of people who chose the Render deliberately for the freedom that comes with official nonexistence. A notable artist and activist community has built significant infrastructure here over the past decade.
economy Entirely informal — salvage and reclamation of materials from the ruins, artisan manufacturing, community agriculture in raised-bed systems that keep crops above the contaminated soil, and a robust service economy that includes medical care, education, and legal assistance provided collectively rather than commercially. Outside money flows in through the artist community's external sales and through the Render's role as a production site for goods that can't be made in monitored corporate space.
power structure No formal governance. Decision-making occurs through a dense network of block assemblies, mutual aid collectives, and issue-specific working groups. Several informal militias maintain perimeter security and internal dispute resolution with varying degrees of community accountability. The artist collective known as Ashfall holds significant soft power through their control of the community radio network and the district's external communications.
dangers
  • genuine chemical contamination causing long-term health effects for all residents
  • the western Burn Zone where active chemical reaction in the soil makes entire blocks inaccessible
  • corporate remediation contractors who periodically attempt to 'clear' the area using methods indistinguishable from violence
  • Meridian city enforcement sweeps that are technically legal given the condemnation status
  • militia factions whose accountability to the broader community has been eroding
  • structural instability in burned buildings that residents continue to inhabit
  • outside criminal operations attempting to use the off-grid status for their own purposes
opportunities
  • the only large-scale off-grid space in Meridian 88 where fabrication and organization can occur without corporate monitoring
  • genuine community infrastructure — medical, educational, legal — built outside corporate systems
  • Ashfall's community radio as a communications network that reaches all of Meridian
  • the ruins contain pre-Meridian infrastructure and data systems that were never recovered
  • a community with strong motivation and established networks for direct action
  • the contaminated soil has produced several unique chemical compounds that don't appear in any corporate catalog
story hooks
  • The contamination in the western Burn Zone has changed — it's moving, slowly but measurably, and the direction it's moving will matter enormously in six months
  • Ashfall's community radio has been broadcasting a signal embedded beneath its audio that no one at Ashfall claims to have put there
  • A corporate remediation contractor has arrived with an injunction and a private security force larger than any previous sweep — and the Render's militias are fractured over how to respond
  • A resident has been producing art that incorporates the contaminated soil's chemical compounds — and a corporate research division has taken an interest that goes well beyond the art world
  • Someone has been systematically destroying the district's raised-bed agriculture infrastructure over the past month, and the community is fracturing over who is responsible

The Rouge Furnace #

type place
name The Rouge Furnace
aliases
  • Southwest Detroit
  • The Furnace
  • Rouge Country
description The Rouge Furnace takes its name from the River Rouge industrial complex — once the largest integrated factory in the world, where Henry Ford turned iron ore into finished automobiles in a single facility. The complex is still there. It is still enormous. It no longer makes cars. What it makes now depends on who you ask and what level of security clearance they hold. The official designation is the Rouge Autonomous Manufacturing Campus, operated by a joint venture between Ford Meridian and Arcturus Defense Solutions. The campus produces autonomous vehicle chassis, military drone components, and — according to the workers who live in the surrounding blocks — things that arrive in sealed containers and leave in different sealed containers and nobody is encouraged to ask questions.

Southwest Detroit around the Rouge complex is a working district in the oldest sense: people here make things with their hands, maintain things that break, and go home tired. The population is predominantly Latino and Middle Eastern, communities that have lived in this area for over a century and survived every economic cycle the city threw at them. The housing stock is dense, practical, and aging. The air quality is managed by an Ouroboros Energy atmospheric processing station on Zug Island that does a reasonable job of filtering industrial particulates and an unreasonable job of charging residents for the privilege of breathing air that the factory contaminated in the first place.

The district's relationship with the Rouge campus is parasitic and mutual. The factory provides employment — roughly 6,000 jobs, mostly Tier 1 and Tier 2 maintenance and logistics positions. The neighborhood provides labor, proximity, and the kind of community infrastructure that keeps workers functional without the factory having to provide it. Schools, clinics, groceries, bars — the neighborhood handles the human maintenance so the factory doesn't have to. The arrangement has worked for a hundred and fifty years. It has never been fair for a single one of them.
atmosphere
sights
  • The Rouge complex's silhouette against the sky — massive, geometric, lit from within at all hours
  • Zug Island's atmospheric processor stacks venting filtered air in white plumes that look clean and might be
  • Workers in industrial exoskeletons walking home along Fort Street, still wearing their load-bearing rigs
  • Dense residential blocks where every third house has a rooftop garden and every fifth has a FOR SALE sign
  • The Detroit River curving past the complex, its surface carrying an iridescent chemical sheen on warm days
sounds
  • The Rouge complex — a low, continuous industrial chord that the neighborhood has absorbed into its definition of silence
  • Shift-change traffic — thousands of workers moving in synchronized waves, three times daily
  • The atmospheric processor's rhythmic cycling, a mechanical breathing that the neighborhood unconsciously synchronizes with
  • Music from the bars on Fort Street — where three shifts' worth of exhaustion gets processed nightly
  • River barges moving materials upstream to the factory docks, their navigation horns echoing off the complex walls
smells
  • Industrial process exhaust — filtered but present, a metallic tang that coats the back of your throat
  • Cooking from the residential blocks — the food is better here than in the Axis because it's made by people, not algorithms
  • The river — petroleum undertones near the factory, cleaner downstream, never fully clean
feel Hardworking and resigned. The Rouge Furnace feels like a place that has been making things for other people's benefit for 150 years and has internalized the arrangement. There's pride here — in the work, in the community, in the survival — but it comes with the particular exhaustion of people who know they're essential and disposable at the same time.
tags —
demographics Approximately 52,000 residents. Predominantly Latino (60%) and Middle Eastern (25%) communities with deep generational roots. Tier 1 and Tier 2 workers make up 85% of the population. Income inequality within the district is low because everyone is equally underpaid.
economy The Rouge campus dominates — 6,000 direct jobs and approximately 18,000 in the supply chain and service economy that supports it. Average household income: Φ34,000. The informal economy adds roughly 30% to household income through unlicensed repair work, gray-market parts trading, and the kind of side jobs that keep families above the survival line.
power structure Ford Meridian and Arcturus Defense Solutions jointly govern the Rouge campus through the Industrial Zone Authority. The surrounding neighborhood falls under nominal municipal governance, which in practice means Ford Meridian's community relations office handles disputes, approves construction permits, and funds the two schools. Labor organizing is technically legal and practically career-ending.
dangers
  • Industrial exposure — the atmospheric processor handles most airborne contamination but soil and water exposure are cumulative
  • Arcturus military production — the sealed container operations create security risks for anyone who gets curious
  • Economic dependency — the Rouge campus is the single employer, and layoffs ripple through every household
  • River contamination — the chemical sheen is monitored but the monitoring reports are not public
  • Exoskeleton addiction — workers who spend shifts in load-bearing rigs develop dependency on the enhanced strength, and withdrawal is physical
opportunities
  • Industrial skills — the workers here can build, repair, and maintain anything mechanical or autonomous
  • Parts access — the gray-market parts economy moves military-grade components through neighborhood repair shops
  • The sealed container operations present intelligence-gathering opportunities for the right buyer
  • Labor organizing — the workforce is sympathetic to collective action if someone can navigate the risks
story hooks
  • A Rouge worker opens a sealed container that was mis-routed to a civilian maintenance bay. What's inside is not a vehicle component. The worker has twelve hours before the inventory system flags the discrepancy.
  • Zug Island's atmospheric processor is scheduled for a firmware update that will reduce its filtration capacity by 15% — Ouroboros Energy calls it optimization, the neighborhood calls it a death sentence
  • An exoskeleton repair tech in the neighborhood has been modifying military-grade rigs for civilian use. Arcturus has noticed.

The Rust Circuit #

type place
name The Rust Circuit
aliases
  • Euclid
  • The Circuit East
  • Rust Belt
description Euclid was a manufacturing suburb. The factories that lined East 185th Street and the lakefront produced machine tools, auto parts, and industrial equipment for a century before the work went elsewhere — first to the American South, then overseas, then to automation, then to the corridor's corporate manufacturing zones where human labor was an afterthought rather than a workforce. By 2140, Euclid's factory district was a graveyard of corrugated steel and broken windows. By 2160, it was something else entirely.

The Rust Circuit is the eastern corridor's informal technology and repair economy — a sprawling district of repurposed factories where independent engineers, mechanics, augment technicians, and fabricators operate outside corporate licensing frameworks. The name is self-aware: this is the rust belt's final form, where the industrial infrastructure built for 20th-century manufacturing has been adapted for 22nd-century work by people who couldn't afford to start from scratch. The factories that once produced auto parts now produce augment components. The machine shops that serviced industrial equipment now service neural interfaces. The skills transferred across a century because the underlying logic is the same — precision fabrication, mechanical intuition, the ability to make something work when the manual says it shouldn't.

The Circuit East (as it's called to distinguish it from M88's original Circuit near the Meridian Core) functions as the Cleveland sprawl's repair shop. If your augments need maintenance and you can't afford Tessera's service contracts, you come to the Rust Circuit. If your equipment needs modification and you don't want a corponation knowing what you're modifying, you come to the Rust Circuit. If you need something built that doesn't exist in any corporate catalog, you come to the Rust Circuit and describe it to someone who will nod, quote you a price in scrip or favors, and have it ready in a week. The quality is inconsistent — this is unlicensed work, and the range runs from genuinely brilliant to dangerously incompetent — but the availability is unmatched. The Rust Circuit never closes, never asks for identification, and never files paperwork.
atmosphere
sights
  • Repurposed factory buildings with hand-painted signage advertising augment repair, fabrication, and services that don't have official names
  • Sparks from welding and fabrication visible through open factory doors at all hours — the Rust Circuit operates on a 24-hour cycle
  • Salvage yards organized with obsessive precision — components sorted by type, era, and compatibility in systems that only the yard operators understand
  • Lake Erie visible from the northern factories, its shoreline littered with industrial debris that has been scavenged so thoroughly it's become a kind of art
  • Operators and clients moving through the streets with the particular body language of people conducting business they'd prefer not to explain
sounds
  • Machine noise — lathes, presses, welders, and fabrication equipment running in every factory, creating a metallic symphony that changes block to block
  • Augment calibration tones — high-frequency whines that indicate someone's neural interface is being adjusted, tested, or rebuilt
  • Haggling — prices negotiated in a mix of Standard, Shelf Cant, and the particular technical shorthand that Rust Circuit workers have developed
  • The screech of metal being cut — a sound that never fully stops and that residents claim to hear in their sleep
  • Testing — the occasional pop, bang, or alarming silence that indicates someone is testing something they've built and discovering whether it works
smells
  • Machine oil and hot metal — the baseline scent of every block in the Rust Circuit
  • Soldering flux — the sharp, resinous smell of circuit board work, omnipresent near the augment repair shops
  • Lake Erie's industrial shoreline — a blend of water, rust, and chemical residue that residents call 'the perfume'
feel The Rust Circuit feels like competence without credentials. Everyone here can do something — build something, fix something, modify something — and the social currency is demonstrated skill rather than corporate certification. It is chaotic, loud, and occasionally dangerous in the way that any place filled with improvised technology and unlicensed expertise is dangerous. But it works. The things built here work. The things repaired here work. And in a corridor where 'working' increasingly means 'under corporate control,' that independence is worth the risk.
tags —
demographics Approximately 30,000 residents, predominantly Tier 1-2. A core population of multi-generational Euclid families whose industrial skills translated across the century. Significant influx of technical workers priced out of the Meridian Core's Circuit. Growing population of augmented individuals who have been cut off from corporate maintenance contracts and depend on the Rust Circuit for survival.
economy Unlicensed repair, fabrication, and manufacturing. The Rust Circuit's annual economic output is estimated at Φ2.8 billion — entirely informal, entirely untaxed, and entirely essential to the Cleveland sprawl's lower-tier population. Augment maintenance is the highest-volume service. Custom fabrication is the highest-value. Salvage processing generates steady baseline revenue.
power structure No corporate sovereignty. Tollgate maintains minimum infrastructure. Governance operates through the Shop Council — a representative body of the district's largest fabrication operations, which sets quality standards, mediates disputes, and coordinates collective response to external threats. The Council's enforcement mechanism is reputation: a shop that the Council blacklists loses access to the supply networks and referral systems that make the Rust Circuit function.
dangers
  • Quality variance — unlicensed augment work ranges from excellent to lethal, and the customer bears the risk
  • No legal protections — transactions in the Rust Circuit have no corporate backing, no warranty, and no recourse
  • Tessera enforcement — periodic raids targeting unlicensed augment maintenance operations, which Tessera frames as 'consumer protection' and everyone else frames as monopoly enforcement
  • Industrial hazards — the repurposed factories were never designed for their current uses, and safety standards are self-imposed
  • Data vulnerability — some augment repair work requires deep interface access that a dishonest technician can exploit
opportunities
  • Access to repair and fabrication services unavailable through corporate channels — essential for operators, runners, and anyone whose equipment is non-standard
  • The Shop Council's reputation network is a valuable social infrastructure — being known in the Rust Circuit means being known across the Cleveland sprawl's excluded economy
  • Technical talent — the Rust Circuit's independent engineers and fabricators are among the most skilled practical technologists in the corridor
  • Supply chain access — the salvage yards connect to scavenging networks that reach across the eastern corridor, providing materials and components at gray-market prices
story hooks
  • A Rust Circuit fabricator has built an augment component that outperforms Tessera's commercial equivalent by a factor of three — and Tessera wants to know how, preferably before anyone else finds out
  • The Shop Council has received an ultimatum from Tollgate: submit to infrastructure licensing and taxation, or face service disconnection. The deadline is sixty days.
  • An augment repair technician has discovered identical tracking devices embedded in three different clients' neural interfaces — devices that don't match any known corponation's surveillance hardware

The Shelf #

type place
name The Shelf
aliases
  • The Ledge
  • Shelftown
  • The Overhang
  • Pier Country
  • The Gray Mile
description The Shelf is what happens when a city runs out of room to grow upward and downward and decides to grow sideways into the lake.

It started with the sea wall. When Axiom built the Lake Michigan Barrier in the 2050s — a massive concrete and carbon-composite bulwark designed to protect Meridian's shoreline from rising water levels — they created a flat surface roughly sixty meters wide running along several kilometers of the old Chicago lakefront. The wall was never intended for habitation. It was infrastructure: wave breaks, drainage systems, maglev conduit routing, cargo staging. But the excluded needed somewhere to go, and the wall was right there, and nobody was watching.

The first structures appeared within months. Shipping containers welded to the wall's surface. Tarps strung between drainage pillars. Scavenged arcology panels bolted to the wave breaks. Within a year, the sea wall had a second story. Within five years, it had six. The Shelf grew the way coral grows — accretion, not architecture. Each new layer built on top of and off of the layer beneath, cantilevered out over Lake Michigan on stolen I-beams and salvaged tension cables, until the outermost structures hang forty meters over open water with nothing beneath them but spray and rust.

The name comes from exactly what it looks like: a shelf jutting out from the city's edge over the lake. Stand at the Shelf's outer rail on a clear day and you can look straight down into Lake Michigan, gray-green and churning. Look inward and you see Meridian's proper skyline — the Spire, the Core, the arcology towers — rising behind the sea wall like a different country. The Shelf exists in the space between the city and the water, belonging to neither. That's the point.

The original Navy Pier was absorbed into the Shelf's eastern anchor decades ago. You can still find fragments of it — a section of the old Ferris wheel's support structure repurposed as a water collection frame, the pier's concrete pilings serving as foundation pylons for six stories of unlicensed housing. The pier's grand ballroom is now a community hall where the Shelf Council meets every Thursday. Nobody calls it Navy Pier anymore. The name belongs to a city that abandoned these people, and they have no interest in honoring its geography.

Kyle grew up here after leaving Old Harbor. This is where Dae-jung Seo found him — a feral, angry teenager with experimental hardware in his skull and no one to maintain it. Mrs. Chen's noodle shop is on Level 3, East Section, near the old pier anchorage. Sable operates from rotating back rooms in the Shelf's interior, where the corridors are narrow enough that no corporate security drone can navigate them. The Shelf is not a slum. It is an engineered response to exclusion — ugly, dangerous, brilliant, and completely unlicensed.
atmosphere
sights
  • Layered construction jutting out over Lake Michigan — shipping containers, scavenged panels, and improvised scaffolding stacked six to eight stories high on the sea wall's surface
  • The outer rail where you can look straight down into the lake through gaps in the flooring — children play near these gaps and nobody flinches
  • Electrical cables and water lines strung between structures like a nervous system made visible — the Shelf's infrastructure is all surface, all exposed
  • Mrs. Chen's noodle shop sign — hand-painted, bilingual, the only constant landmark in a district that rearranges itself monthly
  • The Meridian skyline visible above the inner wall — clean, bright, vertical. Everything the Shelf is not. The contrast is the architecture's thesis statement.
  • Laundry lines stretching between buildings over open water, clothes drying in the lake wind
sounds
  • Lake Michigan against the sea wall's base — a constant, low percussion that the Shelf is built on top of
  • Metal creaking — the outer structures flex in the wind, and the sound is somewhere between music and warning
  • Voices in twenty languages echoing through corridors too narrow for vehicles
  • Mrs. Chen's wok hitting the burner — a sound Kyle can identify from three levels away
  • The absence of corporate audio — no Axiom announcements, no advertising, no AtmoSync calibration tones. The Shelf is the quietest place in Meridian that isn't underwater.
smells
  • Lake water and rust — the base note of everything on the Shelf, coming up through the floor gaps
  • Cooking from a dozen cultures — Mrs. Chen's sesame oil, someone's injera on a hot plate, fish being grilled on the outer platforms
  • Machine oil and solder — the Shelf maintains itself, and the maintenance never stops
  • Salt air that the rest of Meridian's AtmoSync filters out — on the Shelf you smell the actual lake
feel Precarious and alive. The Shelf feels like standing on something that shouldn't exist but does — because the people who built it had no alternative and turned that desperation into a kind of defiant engineering. It sways in high wind. The floors have gaps you can see the water through. Nothing is level, nothing is up to code, nothing is licensed. It is the most honest place in Meridian because it cannot afford to pretend.
tags —
demographics Population estimated between 180,000 and 240,000 — census is impossible in a structure that changes shape monthly. Predominantly Tier 1 and untier-ed: climate refugees, economic migrants, people who fell through the corporate system, people who jumped. Every ethnicity, every language, every kind of damage. The Shelf does not ask where you came from.
economy Informal, analog, trust-based. No corporate currency infrastructure — the Shelf runs on barter, favor-debt, and physical Q tokens that Mrs. Chen's generation minted from scrap copper. Repair work is the primary trade. Food preparation is the second. Information brokerage is the third. The Shelf produces nothing the corporate economy values and everything the corporate economy depends on when it needs something done off-book.
power structure The Shelf Council — an elected body of section representatives who meet in the old Navy Pier ballroom every Thursday. Decisions require consensus, not majority. Enforcement is community-based: if you violate the Shelf's rules (no theft from residents, no corporate informing, no violence against children), the community handles it. There is no formal police presence. Axiom Security does not enter the Shelf. This is not because they can't. It's because the cost-benefit analysis of pacifying 200,000 people in a structure they'd have to demolish to search is not favorable.
dangers
  • Structural collapse — the outer sections are cantilevered over open water on salvaged materials. They fail without warning. The Shelf loses structures to the lake every storm season.
  • No emergency services — medical care is Mrs. Chen's first aid kit, the street medics who trained themselves, and prayer
  • Falling — the gaps between sections, the unrailed edges, the ladders between levels. Children learn to climb before they learn to read.
  • Fire — in a structure made of shipping containers and scavenged panels with exposed electrical wiring, fire is the nightmare. The Shelf has bucket brigades. They are not enough.
  • Corporate clearance operations — Axiom periodically announces plans to 'reclaim' the sea wall. The Shelf has survived three clearance attempts. Each one cost lives.
  • The wind — Lake Michigan storms hit the Shelf with nothing between them and open water. High-wind days clear the outer platforms.
opportunities
  • Disappearance — the Shelf has no surveillance, no biometric scanners, no corporate data infrastructure. You can stop existing here.
  • Community — the Shelf's residents protect each other with a ferocity that corporate Meridian cannot comprehend, because corporate Meridian has never had to
  • Access — the Shelf sits on the boundary between Meridian and the lake. Smuggling routes run through its lower levels. Information flows through its corridors.
  • Freedom — no corporate rules, no tier restrictions, no augment licensing requirements. The Shelf is the closest thing to an ungoverned zone inside the city limits.
  • Sable's network — the best fixer in Meridian operates from the Shelf, and proximity to her operation is proximity to work
story hooks
  • Kyle's home — Level 3, East Section. The room is six meters by four, with a window facing the lake. The katana hangs on the wall. The pharmaceutical stabilizers are in a locked box under the cot.
  • Mrs. Chen's noodle shop — the social center of the Shelf's eastern quarter. If you need information, food, or someone to pretend not to notice that you're bleeding, this is where you go.
  • Axiom's fourth clearance attempt is being planned. Corporate engineers have been surveying the sea wall from boats. The Shelf Council is aware. Kyle is aware. The question is what he's going to do about it.
  • Someone is building a new section on the Shelf's western edge — a large one, with better materials than the Shelf usually gets. Nobody knows who's funding it or why. Mrs. Chen is worried.
  • The sea wall's structural integrity reports are classified. The Shelf is built on infrastructure that Axiom maintains — or doesn't. If the wall fails, the Shelf goes into the lake.
connections
adjacent to

  • Old Harbor (below, in the flooded sections — connected by water routes through the wall's drainage systems)
  • The Circuit (accessible through the wall's maintenance corridors — the black market supply line)
  • Lake Michigan (below, through the floor — the Shelf's foundation and its greatest threat)

frequented by

  • Climate refugees — Gulf Coast, Pacific Northwest, the latest wave from wherever the weather destroyed this year
  • Operators like Kyle — freelancers who need a base that corporate surveillance cannot reach
  • Sable's clients — people who come to the Shelf specifically to access her network, then leave quickly
  • Street medics, repair technicians, unlicensed augment maintainers — the people who keep the Shelf's population alive
  • Nobody from Axiom Security. Not because they're forbidden. Because the math doesn't work.

The Slagshore #

type place
name The Slagshore
aliases
  • Gary Lakeshore
  • Slag Beach
  • The Crust
description Gary was dying before the corponations finished it off. The steel mills had already hollowed the city by the mid-22nd century, leaving behind a skeletal industrial landscape that the lake was slowly digesting. Then Axiom Industries acquired the lakeshore in the Corporate Reclamation Act of 2158, not for the land but for the water rights -- Lake Michigan access for their automated cargo platform network. What they got was six miles of toxic shoreline, a hundred years of industrial sediment, and the people who still lived in it.

The Slagshore is what remains. The old U.S. Steel lakefront has been converted into Axiom's Southern Cargo Terminal -- a fully automated port where container ships are loaded and unloaded by mechanical arms the size of apartment buildings, operating around the clock without a single human worker on the dock floor. The terminal generates enormous wealth. None of it accrues to Gary. The Axiom sovereign territory boundary runs along the old shoreline road, and everything south of that line is someone else's problem. That someone else is nobody.

South of the boundary, the old Gary neighborhoods exist in a state that urban planners call 'managed decline' and residents call 'abandonment with extra steps.' The housing stock is a mix of crumbling 20th-century construction and emergency prefab blocks installed during the Gulf Coast Displacement and never upgraded. The air quality regularly exceeds hazardous thresholds -- the cargo terminal's operations kick up legacy contaminants from the lakebed sediment, and Axiom's environmental monitors conveniently face the other direction. The residents are predominantly Tier 1 and excluded populations who cannot afford to leave and have nowhere to go if they could. They survive on the gray economy, on scavenging from the terminal's waste stream, and on a stubbornness that the corporations consistently underestimate.
atmosphere
sights
  • Axiom's cargo terminal -- mechanical arms moving containers in synchronized patterns, lit by industrial floods that turn the lakeshore into permanent daylight
  • The boundary wall separating Axiom sovereign territory from the residential zones -- three meters of smart-concrete with embedded sensors
  • Abandoned steel mill structures rusting into abstract sculpture, slowly being reclaimed by aggressive invasive vegetation
  • Prefab housing blocks with jury-rigged solar panels and unauthorized mesh network antennas
  • The lake itself, visible through gaps in the terminal infrastructure -- grey-brown water with an oily sheen that catches the industrial light
sounds
  • The cargo terminal's mechanical orchestra -- grinding, clanking, hydraulic hissing -- never stops, never pauses, never acknowledges that people are trying to sleep
  • Wind off the lake carrying particulate matter that you can hear hitting surfaces
  • Mesh network chatter from improvised comm systems
  • The low hum of the boundary wall's sensor array
  • Silence where there should be traffic -- Gary doesn't have enough functioning vehicles to make noise
smells
  • Industrial particulate -- a metallic, chemical taste that coats the back of your throat
  • Lake rot intensified by decades of sediment disturbance from terminal operations
  • Burning scrap from informal recycling operations
  • Ozone from the boundary wall's deterrence systems
feel A place that exists to be extracted from. Every valuable thing -- the water, the shoreline, the labor -- has been pulled out and processed somewhere else. What remains is the residue, human and material. The Slagshore doesn't feel abandoned; it feels consumed.
tags —
demographics Approximately 28,000 residents in the non-Axiom zones, predominantly excluded populations and Tier 1. Significant Gulf Coast refugee community. Axiom terminal employs zero local residents -- the automation is complete and the maintenance crews commute from Meridian 88.
economy Formal economy is effectively zero. The gray economy runs on terminal scavenging -- recovering usable materials from the cargo waste stream -- and on informal services for the checkpoint traffic flowing through the Gatemouth to the east. Some residents work as unlicensed guides for people trying to reach the GLM without going through official border processing.
power structure Axiom Industries holds sovereign authority over the terminal and shoreline. The residential zones have no formal governance. A community council of long-term residents makes decisions by consensus, but their authority extends exactly as far as their neighbors' willingness to listen. A scavenger collective called the Reclaimers organizes the terminal waste stream economy with surprising efficiency.
dangers
  • Air quality -- prolonged exposure to Slagshore particulate causes respiratory damage that the local clinics cannot treat
  • Axiom boundary security -- automated deterrence systems on the wall do not distinguish between threats and trespassers
  • Contaminated water supply -- the municipal filtration infrastructure failed in 2181 and was never repaired
  • Exploitation by transit smugglers who use Slagshore residents as expendable labor
  • Structural collapse -- the old mill buildings are not stable and people live in them anyway
opportunities
  • The terminal waste stream contains recoverable tech, metals, and occasionally mislabeled cargo worth significant money
  • Axiom's automated systems have exploitable patterns -- the Reclaimers have mapped most of them
  • The Slagshore's lack of surveillance makes it useful for anyone who needs to move unseen
  • Community networks here are tight and loyal -- earn trust and you have allies who understand survival
story hooks
  • The Reclaimers have found something in the waste stream that Axiom is now actively trying to recover -- and they're willing to kill the automated systems' zero-casualty protocol to get it back
  • A class-action health claim against Axiom for the air quality is being organized, but the lawyer keeps having accidents
  • Someone is building something in the old steel mill foundations -- something large, something powered, something that draws more electricity than the entire residential grid

  • Journalists and documentarians who come to record poverty and leave without changing anything

The Sluiceway #

type place
name The Sluiceway
aliases
  • Hegewisch
  • The Edge
  • Border Country
  • Last Stop
description The Sluiceway is where Meridian 88 ends and something else begins. Pressed against the far southeastern boundary of the megacity, bordered by contaminated wetlands to the east and the Indiana Exclusion Zone to the south, this district has the character of a frontier town that happens to be inside a metropolis of 40 million people. The isolation is physical -- one transit line connects the Sluiceway to the rest of Meridian, a rattling surface tram that runs every forty minutes when it runs at all -- and psychological. People here live with their backs to the city, facing outward toward the marshes and the state line, and that orientation shapes everything about the place.

Old Hegewisch was a small-town industrial pocket, and the Sluiceway still feels that way. The streets are quieter than anywhere else in Meridian. The buildings are lower, rarely above four stories. The wetlands that border the district have been transformed by decades of industrial runoff into something between an ecosystem and a chemical experiment -- bioluminescent in patches, toxic in others, home to mutated wildlife that the Meridian Department of Environmental Management officially classifies as 'emergent fauna' and unofficially avoids. Locals call the wetlands the Glow Marsh, and they've learned which paths are safe and which will dissolve your boots. That knowledge is currency here.

The Indiana border makes the Sluiceway strategically valuable in ways its residents would prefer it wasn't. The Exclusion Zone -- Indiana's corporate sovereignty framework is different from Illinois's, creating a jurisdictional gap that smugglers, data runners, and anyone fleeing Meridian warrants have exploited for decades. The Sluiceway is the last stop before the crossing, and every third building has a back room where someone is preparing for the trip or recovering from it. Border running is the district's unofficial second economy, after the legitimate wetland harvesting operations that strip useful compounds from the contaminated marsh. The Sluiceway doesn't advertise either industry. It just watches the marsh, minds its business, and keeps one eye on the tram schedule.
atmosphere
sights
  • Low industrial buildings giving way to contaminated wetlands at the district's edge
  • The Glow Marsh -- patches of bioluminescent runoff creating an eerie green-blue twilight
  • The Indiana border fence, half-collapsed and overgrown, more symbolic than functional
  • Wetland harvester rigs moving through the marsh on stilted platforms, scraping compounds
  • A single tram line stretching back toward the city like an umbilical cord
sounds
  • Marsh sounds -- frogs, insects, and things that might be either, amplified by the chemical ecosystem
  • The tram arriving and departing -- the rhythmic heartbeat of the district's connection to everything else
  • Wind through the wetland reeds, carrying chemical harmonics that locals swear they can read
  • The distant hum of Indiana's industrial zone across the border -- a different frequency than Meridian's
smells
  • Wetland chemistry -- sulfur, ozone, and something sweet that doesn't have a name yet
  • Marsh harvester processing -- concentrated botanical extract, astringent and sharp
  • Clean air, relatively speaking -- the wind off the marshes pushes the city's pollution back
feel Liminal. The Sluiceway feels like standing in a doorway -- not fully inside, not fully outside, belonging to neither side completely. There's a calm here that's unsettling to city people, the quiet of a place that has made peace with being forgotten. It's the kind of neighborhood where people nod instead of talk and know better than to ask where you're headed.
tags —
demographics Small population of approximately 12,000, making it one of Meridian's least dense districts. Legacy Eastern European families from old Hegewisch mix with border-running transients, wetland harvesting crews, and people who came to the edge of the city and decided the edge was far enough.
economy Wetland compound harvesting -- extracting useful chemicals and biologicals from the contaminated marsh. Border facilitation services, ranging from legitimate cross-jurisdiction logistics to smuggling. The tram station has a small commercial strip serving transit passengers.
power structure No single authority dominates. The wetland harvesting co-ops have the most organized economic presence. Border running operations are fragmented and competitive. Meridian governance is nominal -- the district is too remote and too small to warrant dedicated enforcement.
dangers
  • The Glow Marsh -- toxic in unpredictable patches, with contamination levels that shift with weather and water table
  • Emergent fauna -- mutated wildlife that ranges from nuisance to genuinely dangerous
  • Border crossing gone wrong -- the Indiana Exclusion Zone has its own enforcement, and they shoot
  • Isolation -- medical emergencies here wait for the tram, and the tram waits for nothing
  • Smuggling operations that don't welcome witnesses
opportunities
  • Border crossing expertise -- knowing the safe routes across the Indiana line is valuable and rare
  • Wetland compounds include bioactive materials with black market pharmaceutical value
  • The jurisdictional gap makes the Sluiceway ideal for meetings that can't happen inside Meridian proper
  • The Glow Marsh is unexplored territory -- what's in there could be worth finding
story hooks
  • Something in the Glow Marsh is emitting a regular signal -- not biological, not any known Meridian tech, and it started three weeks ago
  • A border runner who crossed into Indiana six months ago just came back carrying data that three different corponations are bidding to suppress
  • The wetland harvesters have found a new compound in the marsh that appears to be a neural interface accelerant -- untested, unregulated, and potentially revolutionary

  • Border runners and their clients, passing through on the way to Indiana
  • Biologists and amateur naturalists studying emergent fauna
  • People who need to be at the edge of something
  • Tram commuters passing through without stopping -- most of Meridian only sees the Sluiceway through a window

The South Side #

type place
name The South Side
aliases
  • Milwaukee South Side
  • La Zona Sur
  • South Milwaukee
  • The Corridor Sur
description The South Side of Milwaukee has been Polish and then Mexican and then everything, in the way that working-class neighborhoods absorb each wave of arrivals and incorporate them into an identity that is less about any single culture than about the shared experience of working hard for not enough money. The Polish churches still stand — St. Josaphat's Basilica, its copper dome visible from every district in southern Milwaukee, is now jointly operated by a Polish heritage congregation and a Mexican Catholic parish, and the scheduling of feast days requires the kind of diplomatic negotiation usually reserved for territorial disputes. Which is, in a way, what it is.

The residential blocks are dense, practical, and defiant in the manner of neighborhoods that have been called 'in decline' by every census for seventy years and are still here when the census-takers have moved on. The housing is a mix of century-old workers' cottages — small, solidly built, adapted with the same solar-atmospheric-recycling modifications seen in Sherman Heights — and mid-century apartment buildings that have aged with less grace but more capacity, absorbing the population growth that the cottages can't. Every available surface generates power or grows food. The South Side learned self-sufficiency from necessity and taught it to Sherman Heights, or the other way around, depending on who you ask and how much time they have to argue about it.

The economy is survival-plus: survival is the baseline, and the 'plus' is whatever margin people can build above it. The commercial strips along Lincoln Avenue and Oklahoma Avenue serve the daily needs of a Tier 1-2 population — groceries, medical care, augment maintenance, the essentials — supplemented by a fabrication and repair economy that operates out of garages, basements, and the kind of workshops that exist behind businesses whose front operations would be very surprised to learn about them. The South Side fixes things. Not just augments and machinery — the South Side fixes problems, connects people, and routes resources through networks that have no digital presence because digital presence is surveillance and surveillance is something the South Side has learned to avoid.

The industrial southern edge, along the Kinnickinnic River, connects to the Menomonee Gulch's fabrication ecosystem, creating a continuous working-class corridor from the South Side through the valley to Walker's Landing. Workers move between these districts freely — the jurisdiction is shared Sentinel North franchise territory, and Sentinel's interest in the movement of Tier 1-2 workers between industrial zones is minimal. This connectivity creates a de facto working-class network that spans Milwaukee's entire southern geography, and the network is more organized than it appears.
atmosphere
sights
  • St. Josaphat's Basilica dome — copper gone green, visible from the entire South Side, a landmark that predates every institution that claims authority here
  • Workers' cottages in dense rows — small, maintained, each one slightly different because a century of individual modification has made them unique
  • Lincoln Avenue commercial strip — small businesses with signage in Spanish, Polish, English, and Shelf Cant, serving a population that communicates in all four
  • Garage workshops — visible through open doors on every third block, the South Side's informal economy operating in plain sight
  • Community murals — particularly along Oklahoma Avenue, depicting labor history, immigrant stories, and pointed commentary on corporate governance
sounds
  • Basilica bells — St. Josaphat's rings on the hour, and the sound carries across the South Side like a municipal heartbeat
  • Commercial strip activity — the sound of a neighborhood doing business: haggling, greeting, the ring of old-fashioned cash registers that some shops maintain because cash doesn't generate data
  • Workshop noise from the garages — the soundtrack of an informal economy, audible but not visible from the main streets
  • Polka and norteño from competing radios — the South Side's two cultural traditions, literally broadcasting at each other
  • The KK River — audible in the southern blocks, its current carrying industrial runoff south toward the lake
smells
  • Kielbasa and carnitas — the South Side's dual culinary identity, coexisting on every block and occasionally on the same grill
  • Workshop exhaust — solder, cutting fluid, and the miscellaneous chemical smell of things being repaired
  • Incense from St. Josaphat's — drifting from the basilica's open doors, mixing with the neighborhood's industrial scent
  • River water from the KK — industrial, organic, and getting slightly better every decade, which is the South Side's relationship to progress in general
feel Stubborn. The South Side has the energy of a neighborhood that has been counted out repeatedly and repeatedly refuses to be counted. The community is not ideological like The Tangles or institutional like Sherman Heights — it is practical, hardworking, and bonded by the shared understanding that the people around you are the only resource you can count on. The cultural fusion of Polish and Latino traditions has produced something neither parent culture would fully recognize: a community identity built on work, family, faith, and the particular kind of mutual aid that comes from a century of being told your neighborhood doesn't matter.
tags —
demographics Approximately 65,000 residents. Tier 1-2. Approximately 50% Latino (predominantly Mexican-American, multi-generational), 20% Polish-American (multi-generational), 15% mixed/other, 15% recent displacement arrivals. The neighborhood's cultural identity is proudly hybrid — neither Polish nor Mexican alone, but a South Side identity that encompasses both and has its own traditions, its own food, and its own opinions.
economy Service economy along the commercial strips. Informal fabrication and repair economy operating from residential workshops. Industrial labor flowing south to the KK River corridor and west to the Menomonee Gulch. The community's economic network is extensive, informal, and deliberately opaque — transactions happen through relationships, not platforms, and the absence of digital records is a feature, not a limitation.
power structure No single authority. The South Side Community Alliance — a coalition of neighborhood associations, church organizations, and business owners — serves as the primary governance voice. St. Josaphat's parish council holds significant influence. Sentinel North patrols the district with moderate intensity but limited community engagement. The workshop economy has its own informal hierarchy, coordinated by operators who have earned trust over decades.
dangers
  • Sentinel profiling — similar to Sherman Heights, the South Side's demographics trigger algorithmic risk assessments that produce disproportionate enforcement
  • Workshop hazards — the informal fabrication economy operates without safety standards, and injuries are treated by community medics rather than reported
  • Environmental exposure — the KK River corridor's contamination affects the southern blocks
  • Economic fragility — the informal economy is resilient but cash-dependent, and disruption to the physical currency supply would be devastating
  • Inter-community tension — the Polish-Latino cultural synthesis is genuine but not universal, and generational conflicts about identity and priority occasionally surface
opportunities
  • The repair economy — the South Side can fix anything, and 'anything' includes things that weren't supposed to be fixable
  • The working-class network — connectivity between the South Side, Walker's Landing, and the Menomonee Gulch creates an information and logistics network spanning Milwaukee's entire industrial geography
  • Cultural camouflage — the South Side's dual-culture identity creates a social complexity that automated surveillance systems consistently misread
  • Community loyalty — earning trust here takes time, but the trust, once earned, opens the entire southern Milwaukee network
story hooks
  • The workshop network has been asked to fabricate a component that none of the operators recognize — the specifications suggest a device that doesn't match any known technology, and the client is paying enough to discourage questions
  • St. Josaphat's Basilica has been granted heritage protection status by the Milwaukee Administrative Zone, which sounds benign until the community realizes the protection order gives the zone authority to enter and inspect the building — including its basement, where the community has been storing things the zone doesn't know about
  • A South Side family's century-old cottage contains a pre-digital archive that a corporate genealogy project has flagged as 'historically significant.' The family would like to be left alone. The corporation would not.
connections

  • Bay View Docks (east, along lakefront)
  • Menomonee Gulch (north, via KK River corridor)
  • The western suburban sprawl (west)

  • Industrial workers commuting to the Gulch and the KK River corridor
  • Workshop clients from across Milwaukee's working-class districts
  • People who need things fixed, connected, or moved without generating a digital trail

The Spire #

type place
name The Spire
aliases
  • Axiom Tower
  • The Needle
  • God's Middle Finger
  • The Unreachable
description The Spire is the tallest structure in Meridian, and it wants you to know that. At
847 meters, it punches through the city's artificial cloud layer and keeps going,
its upper floors existing in actual sunlight while the rest of the city lives
under AtmoSync's moody approximation. It is the global headquarters of Axiom
Industries, the dominant megacorporation that effectively owns Meridian, and it
is designed with the subtlety of a fist: this is where the power lives, and it
is above you. Literally, architecturally, spiritually above you. The building's
official name is the Axiom Meridian Center for Innovation and Progress. Everyone
calls it the Spire. The people on the Shelf call it God's Middle Finger.

From the outside, the Spire is a tapered column of smart-glass and structural
carbon, its surface shifting color and opacity based on time of day, weather
conditions, and — cynics suspect — the current mood of the board of directors.
At night, it glows. Not with lights, exactly, but with a kind of bioluminescent
sheathing that makes it look like a living thing, a deep-sea creature breaching
the surface of a dark ocean. It is, objectively, a stunning piece of architecture.
It is also a monument to the idea that some people deserve to live in the sky
while others drown at sea level, and the fact that it's beautiful makes it worse.

Nobody from the Shelf has ever been inside. This isn't official policy — Axiom
would never be so crude as to post a sign saying "poor people not welcome." It's
accomplished through the quieter machinery of access credentials, security
clearances, invitation-only elevators, and the simple social reality that a
street-level person in the Spire lobby would be approached by security within
eleven seconds (this has been timed). The Spire represents the ceiling — not the
architectural kind, but the kind that exists in the mind of every Shelf kid who
looks up and knows, with the certainty of lived experience, that there are places
in this city they will never go.
atmosphere
sights
  • The exterior: a tapered column of color-shifting smart-glass, visible from everywhere in the city
  • The lobby (from exterior glimpses): white marble, living walls, holographic art installations that cost more than the Shelf's annual GDP
  • The upper floors pierce the cloud layer — actual sunlight on actual windows, a resource hoarded by altitude
  • At night: bioluminescent sheathing turns the Spire into a glowing needle against the dark
  • Security infrastructure: elegant, invisible to those who belong, impenetrable to those who don't
  • Executive shuttles docking at upper-level platforms — the Spire's residents don't use ground-level transit
  • The shadow it casts — the Spire's shadow moves across the Shelf twice daily, a reminder in negative light
sounds
  • From outside: wind at altitude, whistling past the structure's aerodynamic profile
  • From the lobby (reported by maintenance contractors from the Shelf): absolute silence, the most expensive sound in the city
  • Executive VTOL craft arriving and departing from upper platforms
  • What the Shelf hears: nothing. The Spire is soundproofed against the city it towers over.
smells
  • The Spire's air is custom-filtered at every level — reportedly, each floor has its own scent profile
  • At ground level, near the security perimeter: ozone from the defense grid, clean concrete, and the faint smell of money
  • From the Shelf: you can't smell the Spire. You can only smell its absence — the way the air changes at its perimeter, suddenly cleaner, like a border between worlds
feel Awe and resentment in equal measure. The Spire inspires the same feeling as
staring at a mountain — primal smallness, the recognition of something larger
than yourself. But mountains don't have shareholders. The Spire is designed to
make you feel insignificant, and the fact that it succeeds — that you look up and
feel your own irrelevance — is the whole point. For Kyle, the Spire is a
theological object: proof that the world is organized by people who don't care
about him, in a structure he can see but never enter.
tags —
demographics Fewer than 5,000 permanent residents, all Tier 5 corporate elite — C-suite executives, senior board members, and their immediate households. A rotating population of several thousand more in executive hospitality suites, diplomatic quarters, and secured conference levels. Support staff number in the tens of thousands but reside off-site and are tracked by biometric access rather than residency. The most surveilled, lowest-crime, and least populated district per square meter in Meridian.
economy —
power structure —
dangers
  • You can't get in. That's danger number one.
  • If you could get in: multi-layered security including biometric, neural-signature, and AI-monitored behavioral analysis
  • Internal defense systems — nonlethal on the public floors, very much lethal on the restricted ones
  • The political danger — being noticed by anyone in the Spire means being noticed by Axiom itself
  • The existential danger — learning what the Spire actually contains might be worse than not knowing
  • Falling. From 847 meters. The Spire is surrounded by a 'safety perimeter' that is also a convenient way to keep people at a distance.
opportunities
  • The ultimate heist — if you could get in, what you'd find would be worth more than money
  • Leverage — proof of what happens inside the Spire could shift the power balance in Meridian
  • An inside contact — the rarest and most valuable commodity in the city's underworld
  • The view — from the top of the Spire, you can see the curve of the earth. Or so they say.
story hooks
  • The Spire as endgame — every street story eventually leads up
  • Kyle's impossible job — a contract that requires entering the Spire for the first time
  • A defector — someone from inside the Spire who wants out and needs Kyle's kind of help
  • The Spire's AI — possibly sentient, possibly sympathetic, definitely watching
  • What's on the top floor? — a mystery the entire city tells stories about
  • The shadow — twice a day, the Spire's shadow crosses the Shelf. Residents have built rituals around it. Some spit. Some make wishes.
connections
adjacent to
  • The Meridian Core (the Spire rises from the Core's center like a needle from a pincushion)
  • Everywhere — the Spire is visible from every district in Meridian, a constant presence in every skyline
exits —

  • Senior researchers and their teams
  • Executive families — some Spire children have never touched ground level
  • Visiting dignitaries from other megacorp enclaves
  • AI systems — the Spire's operational AI is reportedly the most advanced in the western hemisphere
  • Ghosts — metaphorically. The decisions made here haunt everyone below.
