The Steel Shore #

type place
name The Steel Shore
aliases
  • Lorain
  • Steel Town
  • The Shore
description Lorain built ships and made steel. The U.S. Steel plant and the American Shipbuilding Company defined the city for a century, employing tens of thousands and creating a working-class community whose identity was inseparable from the industries that fed it. When the steel left, Lorain experienced the same slow death as every Rust Belt city — population decline, economic collapse, and the particular despair of a place that knows exactly what it used to be and has no blueprint for what to become. The corridor provided a blueprint. Whether Lorain is grateful depends on who you ask.

The Steel Shore is Lorain's current identity: a continuous industrial-residential zone along the Lake Erie shoreline where the old shipbuilding infrastructure has been repurposed for vessel maintenance and modification. The Black River, which cuts through the center of the city, divides two distinct zones. West of the river, Palladian Construction operates a maritime construction facility that builds the cargo platforms, dock infrastructure, and floating industrial installations that the corridor's lake economy depends on. East of the river, the old steel mill site has been converted into a Ferrogate sovereign maintenance depot — the facility where the rail corponation's eastern fleet is serviced, repaired, and occasionally modified in ways that the maintenance logs don't reflect.

The civilian population occupies the streets between these industrial anchors with the resigned practicality of a community that has been through worse. The old Broadway commercial district still functions, though the businesses have changed — augment maintenance shops, synthetic food distributors, and the kind of general stores that serve a population whose needs are basic and whose budgets are tight. The Puerto Rican community that became a significant part of Lorain's population in the mid-20th century persists, its cultural presence visible in the remaining businesses along Pearl Avenue and in the annual festival that the Steel Shore's corporate landlords tolerate because it costs them nothing and the workers enjoy it. Lorain was always a city that worked. The Steel Shore works too. The difference is who benefits.
atmosphere
sights
  • The Black River dividing the city — west bank Palladian maritime construction, east bank Ferrogate maintenance depot, civilian streets in between
  • Palladian's maritime construction yard — cargo platforms in various stages of assembly, cranes that work the waterline like mechanical herons
  • Ferrogate maintenance depot — rail cars in long rows being serviced by mixed human-autonomous crews, the sovereign right-of-way corridor entering the facility like a metal river
  • Broadway's commercial strip — functional, unadorned, serving a population that needs things to work more than it needs them to look good
  • Lake Erie from the shore — open water dotted with the Palladian-built cargo platforms that the Steel Shore helped construct
sounds
  • Shipyard percussion — the rhythmic bang of hull plates being formed, the whine of cutting tools on steel, the deep thud of maritime construction at scale
  • Ferrogate depot operations — rail car wheels being ground, couplings tested, the intermittent shriek of metal-on-metal that maintenance workers have learned to ignore
  • The Black River — flowing through engineered channels, its sound a lower-frequency counterpoint to the industrial noise on both banks
  • Pearl Avenue — music from the Puerto Rican businesses, Spanish mixed with Shelf Cant and Standard
  • Lake wind carrying the sound of cargo platforms being loaded offshore — a distant industrial rhythm that serves as the Steel Shore's ambient clock
smells
  • Hot steel and welding flux — the shipyard's contribution to the local atmosphere, unchanged in a century
  • Ferrogate lubricant — the maintenance depot's signature scent, a petroleum-synthetic blend that permeates the east side
  • The Black River — carrying whatever the upstream industrial operations contribute, which varies daily
  • Cooking from Pearl Avenue — sofrito, roasted pork, and coffee from the Puerto Rican restaurants that anchor the civilian commercial district
feel The Steel Shore feels like a place that has been rebuilt without being renewed. The infrastructure is modern. The work is steady. The industrial output is significant. But the community that exists between the corponation facilities carries the weight of a century of displacement — first by economics, then by corporate sovereignty — and the resulting mood is one of competent endurance rather than vitality. People here are good at their work. They are also tired of working for someone else's benefit.
tags —
demographics Approximately 40,000 residents. Mixed working-class population with significant Puerto Rican community (approximately 25%, multi-generational). Tier 1-2 universally. High employment rate due to Palladian and Ferrogate labor demand, but wages are fixed at levels that maintain the population without enabling mobility.
economy Maritime construction (Palladian) and rail maintenance (Ferrogate) are the primary employers. The civilian economy serves the workforce — food, housing, basic goods. Pearl Avenue's Puerto Rican businesses represent the district's only independent commercial sector, sustained by community loyalty and cultural identity. The Black River's commercial traffic generates dock fees that Tollgate collects.
power structure Palladian holds sovereign authority on the west bank. Ferrogate holds sovereign authority on the east bank. The civilian streets between them fall under Tollgate minimum infrastructure jurisdiction. The Steel Shore Workers' Alliance negotiates with both corponations and manages civilian governance. The Puerto Rican Cultural Association on Pearl Avenue operates as an independent community organization with significant social influence.
dangers
  • Industrial hazards — both the Palladian shipyard and Ferrogate depot generate exposure risks that the workforce accepts as a condition of employment
  • The Black River — flooding during severe weather events, combined with whatever chemical load the river carries, creates periodic contamination events in the civilian zones
  • Dual sovereignty tension — Palladian and Ferrogate occasionally contest the boundary between their jurisdictions, and civilians caught in the overlap have no clear legal standing
  • Economic dependency — the entire civilian economy depends on two employers, and either could automate or relocate without obligation to the workforce
opportunities
  • Maritime construction skills are in high demand across the lake economy — Palladian-trained workers are recruited by every lakefront operation in the corridor
  • Ferrogate's maintenance depot handles the eastern fleet's most sensitive equipment — information about modifications and non-standard configurations is valuable
  • The Black River provides water access between the lake and the interior that bypasses both Palladian and Ferrogate sovereignty — if you know the channels
  • The Puerto Rican community's independence and cultural cohesion provide a social infrastructure that outsiders can access through demonstrated respect
story hooks
  • Ferrogate has begun modifying a subset of rail cars with equipment that doesn't match any known transit or cargo configuration — and the maintenance workers assigned to the project have been sworn to secrecy
  • Palladian's maritime construction yard has received a contract to build something that doesn't appear in any public shipbuilding catalog — the specifications suggest a military vessel, but Palladian isn't a defense contractor
  • The Black River's chemical composition has changed abruptly, and the contamination pattern traces upstream to a source that doesn't appear on any industrial registry

  • The I-90 Vein — highway corridor connecting to the Cleveland sprawl

  • Pearl Avenue community — the district's cultural anchor and social hub

The Steelyard #

type place
name The Steelyard
aliases
  • Armour Square
  • The Yard
  • Chinatown Gate
  • Sox Ground
description Armour Square was always small — a compressed district defined by the things pressed against it: the expressway, the railyards, the stadium, Chinatown. When the compression intensified under corporate sovereignty, the Steelyard did not expand. It densified. Every cubic meter of the district is in use. Buildings grow inward and downward, subdivided and sub-subdivided until the original architecture is just a shell containing a honeycomb of activity. The White Sox stadium became a Rictus Entertainment franchise venue — the Rictus Yard — and its footprint dominates the district like a cathedral dominates a medieval village, except the religion here is spectacle and the congregation pays by the minute.

Chinatown survived by becoming essential. When the corporate sovereignty treaties disrupted conventional supply chains, the Chinatown merchant networks — which had been operating parallel import systems for decades — became the most reliable logistics infrastructure in the lower South Side. Kelpline Logistics tried to formalize a partnership; the Chinatown Merchant Association accepted the contract and then proceeded to fulfill it on their own terms, using Kelpline's corporate charter as legal cover for a logistics operation that Kelpline's actual managers barely understand. The result is a district within a district: Chinatown Gate, three blocks of dense commercial activity where the signage is in Cantonese and Mandarin, the food is real, the supply chains reach across the Pacific, and the Merchant Association's authority is absolute.

The Rictus Yard hosts combat sports, drone races, and neural-experience competitions — entertainment engineered for maximum audience engagement, which in practice means maximum violence calibrated to the threshold of what corporate liability insurance will cover. On game days, the Steelyard's population triples as spectators flood in from across M88. The streets become a carnival of food vendors, ticket scalpers, and pickpockets. The Merchant Association tolerates this because the influx of credit funds Chinatown's actual operations. Rictus Entertainment tolerates the Merchant Association because the food and logistics support make the Yard functional. It is a symbiosis built on mutual exploitation, and it works.

Between the Yard and the Gate, in the compressed residential blocks where the district's permanent population lives, the Steelyard is simply dense — human density, architectural density, density of sound and smell and transaction. Every hallway is a market. Every stairwell is a meeting place. The expressway that once bisected the neighborhood was enclosed and converted into a covered thoroughfare lined with vendor stalls, creating an indoor street that never closes and never sleeps. The Steelyard is not comfortable. It is not quiet. It is not beautiful. But it is alive in a way that the corporate districts above it will never be, because everything here exists because someone needed it to.
atmosphere
sights
  • The Rictus Yard: a stadium wrapped in holographic entertainment signage, pulsing with light on game days
  • Chinatown Gate: three blocks of dense commercial architecture, signage in Cantonese and Mandarin, red lanterns and neon competing
  • The enclosed expressway thoroughfare: a covered street of vendor stalls stretching the length of the district
  • Buildings subdivided into visible honeycombs — windows, balconies, and access points packed into every surface
  • Kelpline logistics drones threading between buildings, carrying packages along routes the Merchant Association controls
sounds
  • The Rictus Yard crowd: a wall of sound on game days that vibrates through every structure in the district
  • Merchant Association radio traffic in Cantonese, coordinating logistics movements across the district
  • Vendor calls in the expressway thoroughfare — overlapping languages, overlapping transactions
  • Mahjong tiles clacking in the back rooms of Chinatown Gate tea houses
  • The constant hum of density: voices, machinery, cooking, commerce, layered into white noise
smells
  • Chinatown Gate kitchens: ginger, garlic, chili oil, roast duck — real food prepared at volume
  • The expressway thoroughfare's accumulated smell of a thousand vendor stalls
  • Rictus Yard on game day: sweat, synthetic beer, ozone from the arena's containment fields
  • Incense from a dozen temples compressed into three blocks
feel Compression as a way of life. The Steelyard feels like being inside a fist — everything pressed together, everything touching, no wasted space, no wasted moment. It is overwhelming and it is honest, a district that has accepted its constraints and filled them completely.
tags —
demographics Approximately 15,000 permanent residents in one of M88's smallest districts. Chinese-American community centered in Chinatown Gate (roughly 40%), mixed lower-tier residents in the surrounding blocks. Game-day population surges to 50,000+.
economy Dual economy: Rictus Entertainment's spectacle industry generates massive event-day revenue; the Chinatown Merchant Association's logistics network generates steady trade income that reaches across the Pacific. The expressway thoroughfare's vendor economy fills the gaps. Kelpline Logistics holds the corporate charter but the Merchant Association holds the actual supply chains.
power structure The Chinatown Merchant Association and Rictus Entertainment share de facto control through mutual dependence. Kelpline Logistics holds nominal jurisdiction but exercises it only through the Merchant Association's cooperation. The permanent residents navigate between these powers through established relationships and long memory.
dangers
  • Game-day crowd surges in a district not designed for triple population
  • Rictus Entertainment's liability thresholds are tested regularly — arena containment failures are not hypothetical
  • The Merchant Association's logistics network moves things other than food and merchandise
  • Compression-related infrastructure stress — the buildings were not designed for this density
  • Territorial disputes between Merchant Association factions occasionally escalate in Chinatown Gate's back alleys
opportunities
  • The Merchant Association's Pacific logistics network can move anything anywhere, for the right price
  • Rictus Yard events create cover for operations that would be visible in quieter districts
  • The expressway thoroughfare is a marketplace for goods unavailable through corporate channels
  • Chinatown Gate's tea houses are preferred meeting spaces for South Side negotiations
  • The district's density provides natural surveillance countermeasures — too many people for effective tracking
story hooks
  • A Kelpline Logistics manager has realized that the Merchant Association has been using their corporate charter to import something that is definitely not merchandise — the shipping containers are shielded and the manifests are fabricated, and the manager needs to decide between reporting it and surviving
  • A Rictus Yard fighter has died during a match that was supposed to be non-lethal — the neural-interface logs show the kill command came from outside the arena, and someone in the audience was the weapon
  • The Merchant Association is preparing for a succession — the current chair is dying, two factions are positioning, and the logistics network that feeds half the South Side hangs in the balance

The Stockyard #

type place
name The Stockyard
aliases
  • Eastern Market
  • The Yard
  • Feedlot
description The Stockyard is the food distribution hub for the entire eastern GLM corridor, and it is exactly as romantic as that sounds. The original Eastern Market — a public farmers' market operating since 1891 — has been swallowed by a logistics operation so vast that the charming brick sheds where Detroiters once bought tomatoes on Saturday mornings now serve as administrative offices for IronClad Agrisystems' Great Lakes Distribution Center. The center processes 40 million metric tons of food annually, most of it synthetic protein, hydroponic produce, and nutrient-dense crops engineered by Verdant Systems to grow in the contaminated soils that climate change left behind. Real food — actual meat, actual grain-fed produce, actual anything — passes through a separate facility that serves the Tier 3+ market. The two supply chains share a loading dock and nothing else.

The district surrounding the distribution center is a 24-hour logistics machine. Autonomous freight vehicles run continuous loops between the Stockyard, the Rouge river port, and distribution hubs across the GLM. Human labor persists in the sorting facilities, where the combination of irregular package sizes, contamination screening, and the occasional live organism shipment defeats current automation. The sorters work twelve-hour shifts in climate-controlled warehouses that are climate-controlled for the food, not the workers. The wage is Φ22 per hour. The turnover rate is 200% annually. IronClad considers this acceptable.

But the market's ghost persists. On Saturday mornings, in the shadow of the distribution center, an unauthorized farmers' market still operates in the old shed district. Local growers, urban farmers from Mexicantown Libre and Brightmoor, and gray-market food traders set up stalls and sell actual food to actual people. IronClad tolerates it because shutting it down would create PR problems and because the volume is negligible — a few hundred people buying tomatoes doesn't threaten a 40-million-ton operation. The Saturday market is a museum of how food used to work, operating in the loading shadow of how food works now.
atmosphere
sights
  • Autonomous freight vehicles stacked three high on loading platforms, moving in choreographed silence
  • The original Eastern Market brick sheds, dwarfed by the IronClad distribution megastructure behind them
  • Sorting facility workers in hazmat-adjacent protective gear, visible through warehouse observation windows
  • The Saturday market — color, chaos, handwritten signs, actual vegetables — a temporal anomaly
  • Refrigeration units the size of city blocks, their condensation creating localized fog banks in winter
sounds
  • The continuous low roar of refrigeration — the Stockyard's baseline frequency, present even in dreams
  • Autonomous freight loading sequences — mechanical precision sounds like a percussion ensemble
  • Sorting facility alerts — contamination warnings, temperature deviations, routing errors — in rapid mechanical cadence
  • Saturday market: human voices haggling, laughing, arguing about the ripeness of a peach
  • The 3 AM shift change — 4,000 workers moving through turnstiles, badge scanners clicking like insect mandibles
smells
  • Cold. The dominant smell of the Stockyard is refrigeration — a chemical cold that numbs the sinuses.
  • Synthetic protein in bulk — a yeasty, vaguely biological odor that clings to workers' clothing
  • Saturday market: actual soil, actual herbs, actual food smells that make the rest of the week feel like a lie
  • Spoilage from the waste processing facility on the district's southern edge — the smell of what doesn't make the grade
feel Industrial and relentless. The Stockyard never stops. It doesn't have hours or seasons — it has throughput targets. The district feels like the inside of a machine that happens to have neighborhoods attached. Saturday mornings are the exception: for six hours, the ghost of a real market haunts the machine, and for six hours, food feels like food again instead of logistics.
tags —
demographics Approximately 28,000 residents, predominantly Tier 1 sorting and logistics workers. High turnover population — many workers stay less than a year before burning out or being replaced. A stable core community of approximately 8,000 has lived here for decades, predating the IronClad acquisition.
economy IronClad Agrisystems' Great Lakes Distribution Center: Φ280 billion annual throughput. Local economy is entirely dependent on distribution center employment. The Saturday market circulates approximately Φ200,000 weekly — a rounding error in IronClad's books, a lifeline for the people who participate.
power structure IronClad Agrisystems holds operational authority over the distribution center and effectively governs the surrounding blocks through employment leverage. A neighborhood association exists on paper. IronClad's community liaison attends meetings and takes notes that no one reads.
dangers
  • Food contamination — the sorting facilities catch most problems, but 'most' is not 'all' at 40 million tons
  • Worker exploitation — twelve-hour shifts, inadequate protection, and a turnover model that treats humans as consumable
  • The waste processing facility — what doesn't make the grade gets processed, and the processing is not gentle on adjacent air quality
  • Food chain manipulation — controlling the food supply means controlling everything downstream
  • Autonomous freight traffic — the vehicles are programmed to prioritize schedule over pedestrian proximity
opportunities
  • Food supply intelligence — knowing what's moving through the Stockyard means knowing what every district in the GLM is eating
  • The Saturday market is an information exchange disguised as a farmers' market — people talk over tomatoes
  • Contamination data — the sorting facility rejection logs reveal what's wrong with the food supply before anyone else knows
  • The IronClad workforce is large, underpaid, and disgruntled — a recruitment pool for anyone offering something better
story hooks
  • The sorting facility's contamination logs show a pattern — someone is systematically introducing a compound into the Tier 1 food supply that doesn't trigger standard screening but accumulates over time
  • IronClad is negotiating to acquire the Saturday market sheds for warehouse expansion. The market vendors have nowhere else to go.
  • A sorting worker finds a shipment labeled as synthetic protein that contains something biological and non-food. The manifest says it came from Lacuna Genomics.

The Sullen Reach #

type place
name The Sullen Reach
aliases
  • The Reach
  • Deadwater
  • The Mud Shelf
  • South Surge
description The Sullen Reach is a flooded zone at Meridian 88's southern margin, where the 2171 Lake Michigan surge met the pre-existing floodplain of a channelized river system and simply didn't leave. The water is between one and four meters deep across approximately sixty square kilometers of what was once dense urban and industrial fabric. The Reach is not open water — it is a drowned city, its streets still navigable by flat-bottomed boat, its taller buildings still projecting above the waterline, its traffic signals still visible beneath the surface on clear days, still cycling through green and yellow and red on a timer that nobody has turned off and nobody can reach to turn off.

The Sullen Reach is inhabited in the way that very difficult places are inhabited — out of necessity, ingenuity, and the particular human stubbornness that refuses to acknowledge that a place has become uninhabitable. Roughly two thousand people live in structures that project above the waterline: the upper floors of apartment buildings, the rooftops of single-story commercial buildings converted into platforms, purpose-built stilt structures erected on the roofs of submerged buildings. The community is called the Reachfolk by outsiders and just the Reach by themselves. They move by boat, by bridge, by rope line. They fish in their own streets. They dive the submerged lower floors of their own buildings for salvage.

The water is not clean. The Reach is downstream of both the Axiom industrial corridor and the pre-surge Chicago sewage infrastructure, significant portions of which ruptured during the flooding. The specific cocktail of industrial effluent, sewage, and lake water that makes up the Reach has been tested four times by different organizations and produced four different reports, all of which agree on two things: it is not safe for consumption without extensive filtration, and the long-term health effects of regular skin contact are unknown but probably bad. The Reachfolk know this. They have developed filtration systems, skin barrier practices, and a certain fatalism that outsiders mistake for ignorance.
atmosphere
sights
  • A drowned cityscape — rooftops, upper floors, and stilt platforms rising from brown-gray water, connected by bridges and rope lines
  • Flat-bottomed boats moving through what were once streets, passing submerged traffic lights and half-visible signage
  • The underwater city on clear days or with diving lights — intact interiors, furniture still in place, cars on flooded streets
  • Laundry drying on rooftop lines, colorful against the gray water and gray sky
  • The surface of the water itself — textured, never fully still, reflecting the structures around it in fragmented pieces
sounds
  • The sound of water against structures — not waves but the constant small noise of a flooded city
  • Boat motors and oar strokes, the primary transportation audio of the Reach
  • Voices carrying across open water with disorienting clarity
  • Below the surface, when diving: near silence broken by the structural groans of flooded buildings settling, and sometimes, from deeper down, what may be Diaspora signal bleed from submerged infrastructure
smells
  • The Reach's water — difficult to describe precisely, somewhere between organic decay, industrial solvent, and the specific smell of things that have been wet too long
  • Woodsmoke from above-water cook fires
  • Fish — the Reach is heavily fished and the community smokes and dries its catch
  • The clean counterpoint of rain, which falls often and which the Reachfolk collect aggressively
feel The Sullen Reach produces a sensory experience unlike anywhere else in Meridian 88. The city is present but inaccessible — the streets are there, the buildings are there, the pre-surge infrastructure is there, and none of it is reachable by foot. You move through a different layer of the same place. Visitors consistently describe the Reach as dreamlike, and the word is accurate in the specific sense that the familiar is present but wrong, the normal rules of urban navigation don't apply, and the depth below you is uncertain.

Reachfolk are pragmatic, insular, and possessed of a specific dry humor about their circumstances that newcomers sometimes mistake for bitterness. It isn't. It is what you develop when you live in a place that requires constant ingenuity to survive and you have found that ingenuity is, actually, enough. The Reach is hard. It is also home to people who have made something real out of impossible circumstances, and they know it.
tags —
demographics Predominantly Tier 1 and Shelf — people who had nowhere else to go when the surge didn't recede. A significant portion are multigenerational, families who rode out the initial surge and adapted. There is a small but notable population of divers and salvagers who moved to the Reach specifically for access to the submerged urban fabric, and a tiny community of researchers — hydrologists, urban archaeologists, bioremediators — who live and work in the Reach on long-term projects. Synthetic persons are present but few; the physical demands of Reach life are significant and some synthetic body types are poorly suited to constant water exposure.
economy Fishing and fish processing is the primary economy — the Reach's waters, despite their contamination, support substantial fish populations, and the community smokes and packages product for trade with shore zones. Salvage diving is the second economy: the submerged buildings contain decades of intact goods, and a skilled diver with the right equipment can retrieve everything from salvageable electronics to pre-surge cultural artifacts. There is also a growing trade in guided diving experiences for shore-dwellers who want to see the drowned city, which the Reachfolk manage carefully to avoid contaminating their water further.
power structure The Reach has no formal governance. The community functions through a combination of clan-family structures (the major boat families have disproportionate influence), practical expertise hierarchies (the head diver's word on water conditions is law; the chief filtration engineer's word on water quality is law), and regular open meetings that anyone can attend and speak at. External authorities have effectively no presence — the Reach is inaccessible to wheeled enforcement, and the drone patrols that nominally cover the zone are cursory. Vespid Dynamics has a standing interest in the Reach's submerged infrastructure, which includes buried Vespid-era fiber optic cable, but has not found a way to access it without Reachfolk cooperation.
dangers
  • Water contamination — skin contact, inhalation of aerosolized water, and consumption of anything not through the community's filtration system all carry health risks
  • Structural collapse of submerged buildings during diving — the buildings are degrading at different rates and without predictable warning
  • Navigation — the Reach's submerged street grid is disorienting to anyone without local knowledge, and the water's turbidity drops visibility sharply
  • The deep water between structures, where currents from the original river channel still run beneath the surge water — strong enough to disorient a diver
  • Vespid Dynamics extraction operations: the company has twice attempted to access the buried fiber cable by force and been driven off both times; a third attempt is considered likely
opportunities
  • The submerged buildings contain intact pre-surge goods, records, and in several known cases, sealed vaults from financial and corporate offices — diving access is negotiable with the right boat family
  • Vespid Dynamics will pay significantly for a negotiated access arrangement for the buried fiber cable — or for intelligence that could let them extract it without negotiation
  • The Reach's bioremediator community is working on a filtration system that, if successful, could be commercialized across every flooded zone in Meridian 88 — the project needs funding and protection from the corporations whose contamination it would implicitly document
story hooks
  • A salvage diver has surfaced with something from a submerged building in the Reach's deep center: a sealed data drive in a waterproof corporate case bearing the Palladian Group logo and an access classification that, according to the diver's contact, corresponds to executive-level disaster planning documents from 2169 — two years before the surge. If Palladian had classified surge planning documents that early, they had warning of the flood's severity that they did not share with the communities that are now living in its aftermath. The diver is scared and wants the drive gone. A Reachfolk elder wants it opened. Multiple parties want both.
  • The Reach's chief filtration engineer has died suddenly, and she was the only person with full knowledge of how the community's filtration system actually works. Her apprentice has partial knowledge. The system will begin failing in approximately three weeks without someone who can maintain it, and three weeks of contaminated water consumption will be a public health crisis. The Reachfolk need someone to either recover the engineer's full technical documentation from the submerged building where she worked, or find an outside expert who can be brought in quietly before the crisis becomes visible to the corponations that are always looking for leverage.

The Tangles #

type place
name The Tangles
aliases
  • Riverwest
  • The Tangle
  • Free Riverwest
  • The Autonomous Zone
description Riverwest declared autonomy in 2179 and nobody stopped them, which tells you everything you need to know about both Riverwest's determination and its strategic importance — which is to say, none. The neighborhood, wedged between the Milwaukee River and the old Beerline rail corridor, has been Milwaukee's countercultural enclave since the 1970s, cycling through folk musicians, punk houses, co-op groceries, anarchist bookstores, and every other iteration of organized nonconformity that American cities produce. When the sovereignty transition gave corporate charters authority over Milwaukee's districts, Riverwest's residents held a community meeting at the Linneman's Riverwest Inn, voted unanimously to reject all corporate jurisdiction, and issued a Declaration of Autonomous Community that was printed on the back of a beer coaster and is now framed behind the bar.

The Milwaukee Administrative Zone's response was to draw the jurisdictional map around Riverwest, leaving it as an unincorporated gap. The cost of enforcing governance over six square blocks of ideologically committed people with extensive experience in property modification, community organizing, and creative resistance to authority was not justified by the tax revenue those six square blocks would generate. Axiom and Sentinel North agreed. Riverwest was officially designated an 'unincorporated community zone,' which is bureaucratic language for 'your problem, not ours.'

The result, forty years later, is a functioning anarchist neighborhood in the middle of a corporate megacity. The Tangles — named for the dense, improvised infrastructure that has grown organically over decades — operates on consensus governance, communal resource sharing, and a barter economy supplemented by a local currency called Tangle Scrip that is backed by nothing except the community's agreement that it has value, which is also what backs every other currency in history but at least Riverwest is honest about it. Housing is communal or cooperative. Food is grown in community gardens and vertical farms. Energy is generated by a patchwork of solar, wind, and a biogas system that runs on organic waste and produces both electricity and a smell that permeates the eastern blocks on warm days.

The Tangles works. Not perfectly — the community meetings are legendary for their length, the infrastructure breaks regularly, and the ideological disputes about whether to allow neural interfaces within community boundaries have split households and ended relationships. But it works in the way that matters: people are fed, housed, and free, and the freedom is not theoretical. In The Tangles, no corporation owns your data, no algorithm determines your tier, and no surveillance system tracks your movements. You are responsible for yourself and accountable to your neighbors, and your neighbors will tell you what they think of your behavior directly, at length, and with a sincerity that corporate HR departments would find terrifying.
atmosphere
sights
  • Improvised infrastructure everywhere — cables, pipes, and walkways connecting buildings in a dense organic network that gives the district its name
  • Community gardens occupying every available horizontal surface — rooftops, vacant lots, the median of the old Center Street
  • Hand-painted signage replacing corporate branding — directions, community announcements, poetry, and arguments continued in public
  • The Linneman's — a bar that has been the community's living room for over a century, its walls covered in layers of flyers, art, and history
  • People visibly unaugmented — or with augments that have been community-modified to remove corporate firmware — a rarity in the Corridor
sounds
  • Community meeting debates — audible from the street, passionate, interminable, and occasionally productive
  • Live music from multiple venues — The Tangles has more musicians per capita than any district in the GLM
  • The biogas system — a low gurgle from the eastern blocks that residents have learned to describe as 'the neighborhood's digestion'
  • Children, chickens, and dogs — The Tangles has all three in quantities that would violate any corporate district's noise ordinances
  • Silence from surveillance — the absence of drone hum, scanner tones, and automated announcements. The quietest district in Milwaukee for the loudest reason.
smells
  • Community gardens — soil, compost, growing things, the smell of food production at the neighborhood scale
  • The biogas system — honest and unavoidable, strongest on the eastern blocks, the smell of sustainability
  • Brewing and baking — communal kitchens and home breweries, the smell of a community that feeds itself
  • River water from the Milwaukee River, which forms the district's western boundary and smells better than the lake but that's not saying much
feel Free. Genuinely, functionally, exhaustingly free. The Tangles asks more of its residents than any corporate district — participation, contribution, engagement, accountability — but it asks on terms the residents chose. There is no surveillance, no tiered citizenship, no corporate firmware updating your thoughts while you sleep. There is also no reliable hot water on Tuesdays, the community meetings last four hours, and someone will have an opinion about your composting technique. Freedom, it turns out, is labor-intensive. The Tangles does it anyway.
tags —
demographics Approximately 6,000 residents. No tier system — The Tangles does not recognize corporate citizenship categories. Demographically diverse, with a historical core of white countercultural families supplemented by anyone willing to participate in community governance. Significant population of people who left the tier system deliberately: former corporate employees, disillusioned academics, and people who simply couldn't tolerate being owned anymore. Age range is wide — multi-generational households are common.
economy Barter, communal labor, and Tangle Scrip. Some residents earn Q through work outside the district and contribute to the community fund. The communal economy covers basic needs. Surplus food production is traded with surrounding districts. The Tangles' real economic product is expertise — community members consult on autonomous governance, sustainable infrastructure, and de-augmentation for clients throughout the Corridor.
power structure Consensus governance through weekly community meetings. No executive authority. Decisions require 70% agreement from attending residents. The system is slow, contentious, and democratic in a way that nothing else in the Corridor is. Key community functions — food production, energy, infrastructure maintenance, conflict resolution — are managed by volunteer committees. Linneman's Riverwest Inn serves as the de facto community center.
dangers
  • Isolation — The Tangles' autonomy means no external emergency services. Medical emergencies are handled by community medics with limited equipment.
  • Infrastructure failure — the improvised systems work until they don't, and when they don't, the fix takes time and community meetings
  • Ideological conflict — the community's commitment to consensus means deep disagreements can paralyze governance for weeks
  • External pressure — the jurisdictional gap protects The Tangles only as long as the surrounding powers find it more convenient to ignore than to absorb
  • De-augmentation risks — residents who remove corporate neural firmware without professional support face cognitive side effects that the community's medics can manage but not always cure
opportunities
  • True privacy — The Tangles is one of the only places in the Corridor where your thoughts are your own
  • Community expertise — the governance, infrastructure, and de-augmentation knowledge here is valuable to anyone seeking alternatives to the corporate system
  • Safe harbor — The Tangles doesn't ask where you came from or why you left, which makes it useful for people who need to not be found
  • Ideological network — The Tangles is connected to autonomous communities throughout the GLM, forming an informal alliance of ungoverned zones
story hooks
  • A corporate defector has arrived in The Tangles carrying a neural implant full of data they want extracted — but the implant is booby-trapped, and removing it requires expertise the community doesn't have
  • The Milwaukee Administrative Zone is reconsidering the 'unincorporated community zone' designation, and the political maneuvering around it is revealing who in the corporate structure benefits from The Tangles' existence
  • A Tangles resident has developed a de-augmentation protocol that cleanly removes Tessera firmware without cognitive damage. Tessera has noticed.

  • People seeking de-augmentation or neural firmware removal

The Threshold #

type place
name The Threshold
aliases
  • Evanston
  • The Gate
  • Academic Row
description The Threshold is what happens when a world-class university survives the collapse of the nation-state that chartered it. Northwestern University — now NovaTern University after the 2171 Tessera educational partnership agreement — anchors the northern edge of Meridian 88's formal jurisdiction. The campus stretches along the lakefront in a fortress of glass and biofiltered air, its research towers visible from the Shelf on clear days, which is to say never. The Threshold is the name for the surrounding district: the border zone where M88's tiered jurisdiction system meets the ungoverned sprawl of the North Shore corridor. Cross the wrong street and your insurance changes. Cross the next one and you don't have insurance.

NovaTern is a Tier 4 institution — one of eleven universities in the GLM authorized to conduct neural interface research on human subjects. The distinction between 'authorized research' and what NeoCortex Industries does is, depending on who you ask, a matter of informed consent, institutional review boards, and careful documentation — or a matter of better paperwork. The campus generates Φ8.2 billion annually in research licensing alone, mostly in neural architecture, bioelectric engineering, and the field politely called 'cognitive enhancement ethics,' which is the study of how to make what the corponations are already doing sound like it was someone's choice.

The residential blocks surrounding the campus are a pressure gradient. East of Sheridan Road: faculty housing, Tier 3-4 families, curated green spaces maintained by Axiom Environmental. West of the Purple Line tracks: a compressed sprawl of student housing, unlicensed augment clinics catering to grad students who can't afford campus medical, and the kind of bars where people who study cognitive freedom drink until they can't think at all. The Threshold earned its name because it is one: a literal boundary between the ordered interior of M88 and the increasingly ungoverned territories to the north. Every day, 40,000 commuters cross it in both directions. The ones heading south have credentials. The ones heading north have reasons.
atmosphere
sights
  • NovaTern's neural research towers glowing pale blue against the permanent haze
  • The Sheridan Line — a physical boundary wall disguised as landscaping, sensor arrays hidden in decorative stonework
  • Students with visible augment scarring walking between classes, neural interfaces glinting at the temple
  • Protest murals on the west side of the Purple Line overpass, painted over weekly, repainted within hours
  • Lake Michigan visible from the campus bluffs — grey, flat, and dotted with cargo platform lights
sounds
  • The hum of NovaTern's research servers — a subsonic vibration you feel in your teeth more than hear
  • Argument fragments in six languages drifting from seminar windows left open because the climate system is being 'optimized'
  • The clatter of the Purple Line maglev — M88's oldest still-operating transit link, and it sounds like it
  • Campus security drones emitting soft chimes when they detect unauthorized neural activity in the research zone
  • Street musicians on the west side playing instruments made from salvaged university equipment
smells
  • Filtered campus air with a faint antiseptic quality — the smell of funded research
  • Coffee from the student district — real coffee, one of the few luxuries NovaTern's stipend covers
  • Lake wind carrying the chemical signature of the cargo platform array
  • Ozone from the research towers' neural calibration labs, drifting into the surrounding blocks on humid days
feel A place that believes in knowledge and has watched knowledge become a product. The campus is beautiful and the beauty is a sales pitch. The students are brilliant and the brilliance is being harvested. Everyone here knows this. Half of them think they can change it from inside. The other half are right.
tags —
demographics Approximately 180,000 residents. NovaTern's student body of 34,000 skews Tier 3-4, drawn from corponation scholarship pipelines that select for cognitive aptitude and neural compatibility. The surrounding district is Tier 2-3, with a significant population of former academics who aged out of institutional relevance and can't afford to leave. West of the tracks: Tier 1-2, high turnover, many undocumented.
economy NovaTern's research licensing and tuition revenue dominate. The university is technically independent but functionally a Tessera-Axiom joint venture. Surrounding economy is service-based: housing, food, augment maintenance, and the particular form of commerce that exists wherever young people with stipends and bad judgment congregate.
power structure NovaTern's Board of Regents holds de facto authority, with Tessera and Axiom each holding two board seats. Campus security is NovaTern's own force, but they coordinate with Axiom Enforcement at the jurisdictional boundary. West of the tracks, authority is informal — a rotating coalition of student organizations, local business owners, and at least one fixer who has operated out of the same noodle shop for twenty years.
dangers
  • Jurisdictional boundary — the transition from campus security to Axiom Enforcement to ungoverned territory happens within six blocks
  • Neural research accidents — NovaTern's safety record is good, not perfect, and 'not perfect' means occasional cognitive contamination events
  • Student radicalization — the gap between what students study and what they experience produces predictable results
  • Data harvesting — every neural interface on campus feeds research databases, and consent forms are 400 pages long for a reason
  • The west side after dark — not dangerous in the way the Shelf is dangerous, but dangerous enough
opportunities
  • Academic connections — NovaTern graduates populate every corponation's R&D division
  • Research data — the university generates information that corps pay enormous sums for and students sometimes leak for free
  • The student underground — idealistic, technically skilled, and willing to take risks that older operators won't
  • Recruitment ground — every faction in M88 scouts talent at The Threshold
story hooks

  • The university's neural research archive contains pre-corporate data from the original Northwestern — including records of early BCI trials that contradict Tessera's official founding narrative
  • Someone is recruiting NovaTern students for augment work that pays too well and asks too few questions

The Trans-Canada Corridor #

type place
name The Trans-Canada Corridor
aliases
  • The TCC
  • The Ribbon
  • Highway 17/401
  • The Canadian Spine
description The Trans-Canada Highway was built to connect a nation. In 2200, it connects a series of corporate sovereign enclaves that happen to share a national flag. The Trans-Canada Corridor runs 1,900 kilometers from New Windsor to Grainfort, following the Lake Huron and Lake Superior shorelines through some of the most sparsely populated territory in the GLM. The highway has been upgraded — widened, automated, and partially enclosed against the climate — but the distance remains. The distance is the point. The TCC is not a highway so much as a logistical argument against Canadian geography, a continuous assertion that these cities are connected despite every natural feature suggesting they shouldn't be.

Ferrogate Transit and Stonepath Logistics share the corridor's operating charter, dividing the route at Lockhaven North — Ferrogate handles Windsor to the Soo, Stonepath handles the Soo to Thunder Bay. The arrangement is competitive rather than cooperative, and the service quality varies accordingly. The Ferrogate section — running through the populated southern corridor past London, Kitchener, and The Lattice — is twelve lanes, fully automated, and maintained to GLM infrastructure standards. The Stonepath section — running along the Superior shore through towns that are barely towns — is six lanes, partially automated, and maintained to whatever standard Stonepath's quarterly budget allows. The gap between the two sections is visible from a vehicle window and legible as a statement about economic priorities.

The corridor's most critical function is not passenger transport but data. Fiber-optic trunk lines run beneath the highway surface, carrying 40% of the GLM's Canadian data traffic. Bathysphere Networks maintains the fiber infrastructure under a separate sovereignty charter, and their relay stations — positioned every 50 kilometers along the corridor — are the physical backbone of the Canadian net. Severing the TCC doesn't just stop traffic. It partitions the Canadian internet. This fact makes the corridor critical infrastructure in the military sense, and the security presence reflects it — Canadian military checkpoints at key positions, automated surveillance along the entire route, and the understood reality that attacking the TCC is an act of war against the data it carries, not just the vehicles.
atmosphere
sights
  • The southern section — twelve automated lanes cutting through the Ontario corridor, waystation complexes glowing at intervals
  • The northern section — six lanes narrowing through boreal forest along the Superior shore, service gaps measured in hours
  • Fiber-optic relay stations every 50 kilometers — Bathysphere Networks installations, small and heavily secured
  • The landscape transition from southern Ontario agriculture to northern Shield bedrock — visible geology telling the story of the corridor
  • Canadian military checkpoints at strategic positions — the nation's data infrastructure defended in physical space
sounds
  • Automated traffic on the southern section — continuous, efficient, and unremarkable
  • Wind and silence on the northern section — long stretches where the only sound is weather and vehicle
  • Relay station equipment hum — the sound of 40% of Canada's data passing through a box by the roadside
  • Superior weather on the northern shore sections — storms that close the highway and make the distance feel infinite
smells
  • Southern section: waystation services, vehicle discharge, Ontario agriculture on cross-winds
  • Northern section: boreal forest, Superior air, and the mineral scent of Shield bedrock cuts
  • Relay station ozone — the smell of data having a physical presence
feel A corridor that performs connection. The TCC insists that Windsor and Thunder Bay are part of the same country, the same economy, the same network. The insistence is heroic, expensive, and not entirely convincing. The distance between the two ends is not just geographic — it is economic, cultural, and temporal. The southern section lives in 2200. The northern section lives in whatever year the maintenance budget allows.
tags —
demographics Corridor population approximately 2.5 million, concentrated heavily in the southern section between Windsor and Toronto. The northern section's population is sparse — small communities at waystation intervals, military checkpoint personnel, and Bathysphere relay technicians. The corridor connects 18 million people in The Lattice to 150,000 in Grainfort, and the infrastructure gradient reflects the population gradient.
economy Transit tolls (Ferrogate/Stonepath), data transmission (Bathysphere Networks), and waystation commerce. The corridor's economic value is primarily as a conduit — it generates revenue by moving things between the cities it connects, not from the territory it occupies. The fiber-optic infrastructure's revenue exceeds the highway's, which tells you what the corridor actually carries.
power structure Ferrogate Transit (southern section), Stonepath Logistics (northern section), and Bathysphere Networks (fiber infrastructure) hold overlapping sovereignty charters. Canadian military authority applies at checkpoints and to the fiber-optic trunk lines. The arrangement works because each party needs the others — Ferrogate needs the highway, Stonepath needs the highway, Bathysphere needs the conduit, and the military needs the data to flow.
dangers
  • Northern section weather closures — Superior storms can seal the corridor for days, isolating everything north of the Soo
  • Fiber-optic sabotage — cutting the trunk line partitions the Canadian internet, making it the highest-consequence infrastructure target in the corridor
  • Service gaps on the northern section — mechanical failure between waystations means hours of waiting in conditions that can kill
  • Military checkpoint escalation — the corridor's critical infrastructure status means security incidents are treated as national security events
  • The quality differential between the Ferrogate and Stonepath sections — a vehicle maintained for southern conditions may not survive northern ones
opportunities
  • Data infrastructure access — the relay stations carry 40% of Canadian data traffic, and proximity to that traffic has intelligence value
  • Northern section isolation — the long gaps between waystations provide unmonitored space
  • Cross-corridor commerce — the waystation economy provides cover for operations that prefer to remain mobile
  • The Ferrogate-Stonepath rivalry — competing operators on the same corridor create jurisdictional gaps at the handover point
story hooks
  • A Bathysphere relay station on the northern section has been modified to duplicate specific data streams — someone is copying 40% of Canada's internet traffic and nobody knows where it's going
  • The Ferrogate-Stonepath handover point at Lockhaven North has become a jurisdictional dead zone — the two operators blame each other for a series of disappearances along the corridor
  • A northern section weather closure has sealed 200 kilometers of highway with 3,000 travelers trapped inside — and the military checkpoint that should be coordinating rescue has gone silent
connections

  • Grainfort (Thunder Bay, northern terminus)

  • Bathysphere Networks relay technicians on the maintenance circuit
  • Canadian military personnel at checkpoint installations

The Undertow #

type place
name The Undertow
aliases
  • South Haven
  • Undertow Beach
  • The Drowning
description South Haven was a resort town built on sunsets. The kind of place where the entire economy ran on people driving three hours to watch the sun go down over Lake Michigan and then buying fudge. It was charming. It was seasonal. It was exactly the kind of economy that does not survive climate destabilization, lake-level rise, and the collapse of the middle class that used to fund weekend getaways.

What South Haven became is harder to categorize. The old downtown -- what's left above water -- has been repurposed as an offshore recreation zone for mid-tier corporate workers from the Meridian 88 corridor. Tessera Leisure Holdings operates the beachfront, offering 'authentic lakeside experiences' to employees who earn enough to afford a weekend pass but not enough to access the elite resorts further north. The experience is manufactured nostalgia: reconstructed beach cottages, artisanal ice cream that costs more per scoop than the original shops charged per gallon, and sunset viewing decks with augmented reality overlays that filter out the cargo platform traffic on the horizon. It is a theme park version of a place that used to be real.

Below the tourist layer, the Undertow earns its name. The lake has risen nearly two meters since South Haven's resort heyday, and the lower sections of the old town are permanently flooded. This submerged district -- locally called the Undertow -- is where the people who actually live here year-round have settled. Houseboats, converted marina structures, and floating platform homes connected by walkways and rope bridges. The Undertow community is small, insular, and deeply suspicious of outsiders. They fish the lake, maintain their own power grid from wave-energy converters, and operate one of the most effective smuggling networks on the eastern shore. Cargo that enters the lake from offshore and needs to reach the inland corridor without passing through any checkpoint goes through the Undertow. The residents don't advertise this. They don't need to. Everyone who needs to know already does.
atmosphere
sights
  • The Tessera beachfront above -- neon-lit boardwalk, holographic sunset enhancement, tourists in branded leisure wear
  • Below, the Undertow -- houseboats and floating platforms connected by rope bridges, lit by salvaged LEDs and bioluminescent panels
  • Flooded storefronts visible through clear water on calm days, the old town preserved like a museum nobody curates
  • Wave-energy converters bobbing offshore, their rhythmic motion the Undertow's heartbeat
  • The lighthouse at the harbor mouth, still functional, now serving as both navigation aid and Undertow community meeting point
sounds
  • Water everywhere -- lapping, dripping, the constant conversation between the lake and the structures built on it
  • Tourist noise from the upper boardwalk -- filtered, distant, another world
  • Boat engines at odd hours -- the smuggling runs happen between 2 and 5 AM
  • Wave-energy converters churning -- a rhythmic mechanical pulse
  • The creak of floating structures adjusting to swell -- the Undertow is never still
smells
  • Clean lake water -- South Haven is far enough from the industrial zones that the lake actually smells like a lake here
  • Fish, fresh and smoked -- the Undertow eats what it catches
  • Salt-treated wood and marine sealant from constant structural maintenance
  • Manufactured nostalgia scents pumped onto the Tessera boardwalk -- cotton candy and sunscreen, algorithmically optimized
feel Two places occupying the same coordinates. The surface is a corporate vacation simulation, pleasant and hollow. Below the waterline is something older and more honest -- a community that lives with the lake rather than on top of it. The Undertow has the specific energy of a place that has decided the official world is irrelevant and built its own. It's peaceful in a way that the upper boardwalk can only simulate.
tags —
demographics Surface tourist district serves approximately 15,000 visitors per week during high season. Year-round Undertow population is roughly 1,200 -- tight-knit, multi-generational fishing and maritime families, predominantly Tier 1-2 with a handful of former Tier 3 residents who chose this life deliberately.
economy Surface economy is Tessera Leisure Holdings tourism revenue -- significant but entirely extracted. Undertow economy is fishing, wave-energy generation, boat repair, and smuggling. The smuggling income alone is estimated at Φ40 million annually, distributed across the community through a share system that ensures nobody starves and nobody gets rich enough to attract attention.
power structure Tessera Leisure Holdings controls the surface tourist infrastructure. The Undertow is governed by a harbor council of senior residents who operate by consensus and enforce decisions through social pressure and the ultimate sanction: exile from the community, which in a place this isolated is effectively a death sentence for your livelihood.
dangers
  • Lake storms -- the Undertow's floating structures are resilient but not invincible, and rescue services don't extend below the boardwalk
  • Tessera security occasionally sweeps the waterline district, looking for smuggling infrastructure they know exists but can't map
  • Drowning -- the flooded lower town has currents, submerged structures, and no lifeguards
  • Getting caught in a smuggling run -- the penalties are corporate jurisdiction, which means Tessera decides your sentence
  • Trust -- the Undertow doesn't forgive outsiders who betray their confidence
opportunities
  • The smuggling network moves anything that fits on a boat -- cargo, people, data stored on physical media
  • The Undertow's wave-energy tech is innovative and could be scaled if someone provided capital without strings
  • Clean lake water is increasingly rare and increasingly valuable -- South Haven has it
  • Information passes through the Undertow from offshore sources that the inland surveillance networks can't monitor
story hooks
  • A Tessera Leisure executive discovers the Undertow and sees not a community to displace but a 'lifestyle brand' to monetize -- and the harbor council is divided on whether to negotiate or fight
  • Something is surfacing from the flooded lower town -- artifacts from before the rise, including sealed data storage that predates the corporate era and might contain records someone deleted
  • A smuggling run goes wrong and the cargo turns out to be a person who multiple corponations are looking for
connections

  • Smugglers moving cargo along the eastern lake shore
  • The occasional outsider who earned enough trust to be allowed below the boardwalk

The Vagrant #

type place
name The Vagrant
aliases
  • The Wanderer
  • The Moving City
  • Nomad Platform
  • That Damn Barge
description The Vagrant is a city that refuses to stay put. A mobile seacrete-and-steel platform approximately 800 meters long and 400 meters wide, the Vagrant moves between the Great Lakes via the canal and lock systems that connect them — the Welland Canal between Erie and Ontario, the Soo Locks between Huron and Superior, the Straits of Mackinac between Huron and Michigan, and the Chicago Sanitary Canal connecting Michigan to the Mississippi watershed (though the Vagrant has only used this route twice, both times under circumstances its captain describes as 'interesting'). It is, depending on your perspective, a nomadic free city, a floating trade bazaar, a diplomatic headache, or the most creative interpretation of maritime law since someone first nailed a flag to a boat.

The Vagrant started as a conventional barge platform — a decommissioned Great Lakes ore carrier called the SS Edmund Reborn (the name was deliberate and nobody aboard apologizes for it) — purchased in 2176 by a collective of traders, smugglers, and maritime engineers who wanted access to every lake city without belonging to any of them. Over two decades, the original hull has been expanded, reinforced, and encrusted with seacrete growth that the collective encourages along the waterline and hull, creating an organic armor layer that makes the Vagrant look like a ship that a reef is slowly eating. Which is accurate. The seacrete accretion is continuous — every lake the Vagrant visits adds minerals to its hull in different chemical signatures, and marine geologists can read the Vagrant's travel history in cross-sections of its encrustation the way dendrochronologists read tree rings.

The Vagrant's legal status is its masterpiece. Because it moves between lakes, it is simultaneously in and out of every jurisdiction. When it's on Lake Michigan, it's outside M88's territorial waters. When it's on Erie, Cormorant Naval Systems classifies it as a 'transient vessel.' When it's on Ontario, the remnant Canadian government lists it as an 'unincorporated maritime entity.' The Vagrant's captain — elected by the resident population every three years, currently a former Cormorant Naval Systems deserter named Idris Achebe — maintains that the Vagrant is a sovereign vessel under maritime common law and that its residents are citizens of the Vagrant and nowhere else. Every legal authority on the Great Lakes has a different opinion about this claim's validity. None of them can agree on whose jurisdiction it falls under, which is exactly the point.

The Vagrant serves as a mobile marketplace, connecting the lake cities' economies in ways that fixed trade routes cannot. It carries goods, passengers, mail, and information between all seven settlements, plus shore communities that the corponations would prefer remained unconnected. It is the circulatory system of the free lake city network — the moving platform that turns isolated settlements into a connected civilization. Population: 12,000 permanent residents, plus a transient population of traders, passengers, and stowaways that varies between 3,000 and 8,000 depending on the season and which lake the Vagrant is currently on.
atmosphere
sights
  • A massive barge-platform encrusted in multi-colored seacrete layers — each lake's mineral signature visible in the hull like geological strata
  • Market stalls lining the main deck, their goods changing completely depending on which lake the Vagrant is currently transiting
  • The navigation tower — the original Edmund Reborn's bridge, now elevated on seacrete-grown pylons, flying the Vagrant's flag (a compass rose on black)
  • Docking clamps and gangway systems designed to interface with every lake city's unique harbor architecture
  • The wake — the Vagrant displaces enough water that its passage is visible from shore, a moving V-shape that announces its arrival hours before docking
sounds
  • Engines — the Vagrant runs on a hybrid system of converted diesel, wave energy, and a single Charnel Propulsion plasma-electric drive (acquired through channels the captain declines to discuss)
  • Trade — the constant negotiation of a floating bazaar, in every language spoken on the Great Lakes
  • The hull groaning as seacrete layers shift with temperature changes between lakes — the Vagrant complains audibly about weather
  • Lock mechanisms when transiting canals — the grinding, rushing, mechanical symphony of water levels changing
smells
  • Every lake simultaneously — the Vagrant carries the mineral signatures of all five Great Lakes in its seacrete layers, and they off-gas differently in different temperatures
  • Market goods — whatever's being traded this week, from Shallowgrave algae compounds to Deepwell ore samples to Tidebreak artwork
  • Engine exhaust from the hybrid drive system — cleaner than diesel, dirtier than plasma, distinctively Vagrant
  • The particular smell of a ship that has been lived on continuously for twenty-five years and has developed its own microbiome
feel Freedom as a vehicle. The Vagrant feels like what it is — a city that decided the best way to avoid being controlled was to never stop moving. There's an energy aboard that's different from any fixed settlement: the transience, the constant change of scenery and trading partners, the knowledge that tomorrow you'll be on a different lake surrounded by different water. It's exciting and unstable in equal measure. The permanent residents have a particular looseness — people who've chosen motion over roots, who define home as a heading rather than a location. The Vagrant doesn't belong anywhere. That's the whole idea.
tags —
demographics 12,000 permanent residents, plus 3,000-8,000 transient population. Permanent residents are a self-selected community of traders, mechanics, sailors, and people who cannot or will not stay in one place. Demographically diverse — the Vagrant draws from every lake city and every shore community. Children born aboard are 'wave-born' — citizens of the Vagrant from birth, which means citizens of nowhere that any shore-based authority recognizes.
economy Trade arbitrage — buying where goods are cheap and selling where they're expensive, which is the oldest economic model and still the most effective. The Vagrant's mobility gives it access to every market on the Great Lakes, and its cargo holds are a rotating inventory of whatever the lake cities need from each other. Annual trade volume: approximately Φ5.7 billion, most of it in physical goods that can't be transmitted digitally. The Vagrant charges transit fees, docking fees, and a percentage on all transactions conducted aboard. Captain Achebe calls this 'the motion tax.' The residents call it rent.
power structure The Captain — elected every three years by permanent residents — holds executive authority over navigation, defense, and external relations. A Ship's Council of eight elected members manages internal affairs, trade regulation, and dispute resolution. The Vagrant's security force, the Hull Watch, is a volunteer militia of 600 armed residents trained in shipboard combat and canal defense. Governance is pragmatic: the Captain decides where the ship goes, the Council decides what happens aboard, and the residents decide both by vote when they disagree strongly enough.
dangers
  • Canal transit — the Vagrant is large enough that lock passage is a complex, vulnerable operation. Ambush during canal transit is the city's nightmare scenario.
  • Jurisdictional hostility — every authority on the Great Lakes has a reason to impound the Vagrant. None can agree on who has the right to, which is protection, but it's not permanent.
  • Mechanical failure — the Vagrant is a twenty-five-year-old converted ore carrier. Things break.
  • Smuggling — the Vagrant's cargo holds contain legitimate trade and things that are very much not. The line between the two is the Captain's judgment call.
  • Weather — a mobile platform cannot anchor and hunker like a fixed city. The Vagrant must navigate storms, not endure them.
opportunities
  • Access to every lake city market — the Vagrant is the only entity that trades with all seven settlements
  • Information flow — the Vagrant carries news, intelligence, and rumors between isolated communities
  • Jurisdictional immunity — the Vagrant's legal ambiguity protects people and goods that need protecting
  • The Captain's network — Idris Achebe knows everyone on the Great Lakes, and everyone knows him. His introductions open doors.
story hooks
  • The Vagrant is transiting the Welland Canal when Cormorant Naval Systems attempts to board, citing a new sovereignty enforcement order. Captain Achebe needs someone on shore to challenge the order's legality before the Hull Watch has to fight.
  • A sealed cargo container loaded at Tidebreak turns out to contain something alive. The Vagrant is mid-lake with no port for 200 kilometers, and the container is making sounds.
  • Kyle needs to get from Meridian 88 to a lake city without any corponation knowing. The Vagrant is his only option — but passage requires a favor that the Captain will collect at the worst possible time.
connections
adjacent to

  • All five Great Lakes (accessible via canal systems)
  • All seven lake city settlements (regular trade partner)
  • Shore communities along the canal routes (informal trade relationships)
  • Meridian 88 (via Lake Michigan approach — the Vagrant docks at independent piers outside Cormorant's patrols)
exits —
tags —
frequented by

  • Passengers transiting between settlements without fixed schedules
  • Information couriers who use the Vagrant's mobility to move data physically
  • People who need to disappear — the Vagrant's constant motion makes tracking difficult

The Vestige #

type place
name The Vestige
aliases
  • Old Evanston Remnant
  • The Museum Quarter
  • Ghostrow
  • The Kept
description A narrow corridor of pre-Meridian architecture preserved — some say imprisoned — within the megacity's northward expansion, the Vestige is a six-block stretch of late 20th and early 22nd century residential and commercial buildings that a coalition of preservation interests, academic institutions, and wealthy nostalgia investors have maintained in a state of deliberate historical stasis. The buildings have been reinforced, weatherproofed, and in some cases entirely reconstructed from archival photographs, but they are kept deliberately free of visible modern infrastructure. Power and data lines run beneath the streets. Climate control is hidden inside original-looking facade elements. The effect is unsettling — a pocket of another era surrounded on all sides by Meridian's towers.
atmosphere
sights
  • intact pre-Meridian storefronts with period-accurate signage
  • brick and mortar facades maintained to appear weathered but not deteriorated
  • period street lighting casting warm incandescent-style glow
  • tourists with recording implants on guided historical experiences
  • the jarring vertical wall of modern Meridian architecture at every street's end
  • uniformed preservation staff maintaining the illusion of authenticity
sounds
  • deliberately curated ambient audio pumped from hidden speakers
  • tour guide narration in multiple languages
  • the absence of industrial noise — conspicuously quiet
  • wind channeled oddly by the surrounding megastructures
  • muffled modern city sounds from just beyond the perimeter
smells
  • engineered 'old city' scent pumped through climate systems
  • real brick and aged wood from genuinely old structures
  • coffee from the preservation-compliant cafes
  • the faint antiseptic of hidden climate control systems
feel Profoundly artificial in its authenticity — a place where the past has been taxidermied rather than preserved, and the people who live and work here exist in a performance of history that benefits interests they may not fully understand.
tags —
demographics A small permanent resident population of academics, preservation staff, and the extremely wealthy who pay extraordinary sums for 'authentic' addresses. A much larger daily population of tourism workers, students from the attached university annex, and researchers. The buildings' actual heritage community — descendants of the neighborhoods that existed here — are largely absent, priced and curated out.
economy Heritage tourism, academic research grants, luxury residential leasing at rates that exclude essentially everyone, corporate event hosting in 'authentic historical settings,' and a significant underground economy among preservation staff who supplement their incomes by facilitating after-hours access for clients who want the Vestige without the curated experience.
power structure The Meridian Heritage Conservancy, a nominally nonprofit organization controlled in practice by a board of five investment entities, holds total administrative control. Meridian city government defers entirely to Conservancy decisions within the perimeter. Informal power rests with long-tenured preservation staff who know where every camera blind spot and access tunnel is located.
dangers
  • Conservancy security that treats unauthorized documentation as intellectual property theft
  • the social and legal exposure of whatever is being hidden beneath the authentic-looking streets
  • wealthy residents with significant corporate connections and fragile egos
  • the Conservancy's aggressive use of historical designation laws to suppress adjacent development — and anyone who threatens that control
  • AI-assisted surveillance disguised as period street fixtures
opportunities
  • off-grid meeting spaces in buildings with hidden modern infrastructure but no corporate network presence
  • access to genuine pre-Meridian physical archives maintained by the university annex
  • preservation staff as sources on what the Conservancy is actually protecting
  • the tunnels beneath the Vestige predate Meridian's surveillance infrastructure entirely
  • wealthy residents with historical obsessions who can be leveraged or cultivated as patrons
story hooks
  • A preservation staff member has found something in a sealed sub-basement that doesn't belong to any historical period — and it appears to be recent
  • The Conservancy is attempting to have a neighboring district designated as 'historically incompatible' — which would trigger forced demolition — and the residents there need evidence of the process's corruption
  • A wealthy Vestige resident has commissioned a private investigator to find out why their 'authentic' home is broadcasting a signal they can't account for
  • An academic at the university annex has found that the Conservancy's archive contains deliberate falsifications of pre-Meridian history, and she's missing
