The Vitreous Banks #

type place
name The Vitreous Banks
aliases
  • The Glass Flats
  • Vitreaux
  • The Banks
description A three-kilometer stretch of reclaimed Lake Michigan shoreline north of the old Evanston boundary where centuries of industrial glass waste, slag dumping, and subsequent geological pressure have fused the lakebed shallows into vast planes of cloudy, greenish sea-glass. At low water cycles — when the lake's managed sluice gates drop the shoreline level — the exposed flats catch Meridian 88's tower-glow and scatter it in thousands of fractured directions, creating an eerie, beautiful light field visible from Spire observation decks on clear nights.

The Vitreous Banks are officially designated an environmental remediation zone under a dormant Palladian Group land-use agreement, which has kept heavy development at bay while simultaneously preventing any legitimate community from establishing permanent roots. In practice, the Banks host a transient population of salvagers, off-grid artists, and Tier 1 refugees who've built precarious stilt settlements in the shallows, trading in sea-glass artifacts, filtered lake water, and whatever bioelectric components wash ashore from Zheng-Dao's offshore processing platforms.
atmosphere
sights
  • Vast shallow flats of fused greenish glass glowing with refracted megacity light at dusk
  • Rickety stilt platforms connected by rope bridges and salvaged composite walkways
  • Zheng-Dao offshore rigs blinking red on the horizon through lake-haze
sounds
  • Glass fragments grinding and clicking softly as wave action shifts the shallows
  • Wind carrying distorted Diaspora signal fragments from poorly shielded stilt-community uplinks
  • The low foghorn cycling of lake traffic management buoys marking the shipping exclusion zone
smells
  • Cold lake water with a faint chemical sweetness from dissolved industrial mineral residue
  • Woodsmoke and recycled cooking oil from the stilt settlement cook-fires
  • Ozone and hot metal when Zheng-Dao's offshore platforms vent processing exhaust
feel The Vitreous Banks feel like the end of something — a place where the city's momentum finally runs out against the water. There's genuine beauty here that sits uneasily alongside desperation, and the silence between wave cycles is the kind that makes people confess things.
tags —
demographics Almost entirely Tier 1 and Shelf-adjacent residents, with a small rotating population of off-grid artists, environmental surveyors working covert contracts, and salvagers of indeterminate affiliation.
economy Subsistence-level barter economy centered on sea-glass artifact sales to Spire collectors, filtered water trading, and salvage recovery of Zheng-Dao bioelectric components that wash ashore from platform discharge.
power structure No formal authority; the largest stilt settlement cluster, called the Raft Council, mediates disputes informally, but Palladian Group's dormant land claim means any serious conflict invites corporate legal enforcement.
dangers
  • Glass flats fracturing without warning under foot traffic, especially after storm-driven wave cycles shift subsurface pressure
  • Zheng-Dao security drones sweeping the shore for unauthorized recovery of platform discharge components
  • Palladian Group periodically activating its land-use claim to displace settlements when development interest resurfaces
opportunities

  • Accessing the Banks' unique position outside Ferrogate Security jurisdiction for meetings that cannot happen inside the corridor
  • Finding Palladian Group's original remediation survey data, which locals claim is buried in a waterproofed archive beneath the oldest stilt platform
story hooks

Someone on the Raft Council suspects the collector isn't buying art — they're buying something that's embedded in specific pieces, and salvagers are starting to disappear when they ask too many questions.
  • Zheng-Dao Bioelectric has filed an emergency activation of the dormant Palladian land-use agreement, giving the stilt settlements forty-eight hours to vacate. The Raft Council is convinced it's connected to something their salvagers recovered from a platform discharge three weeks ago — a canister that nobody will describe in detail but that everyone on the council has seen.

The Waukegan Industrial Shelf #

type place
name The Waukegan Industrial Shelf
aliases
  • Waukegan
  • The Rust Shelf
  • WaukeGone
  • North Shore Docks
description Waukegan was an industrial city before the word 'industrial' became a euphemism for 'expendable.' The lakefront that once hosted a naval training station and a pharmaceutical campus now hosts the northern terminus of M88's automated cargo logistics network — a sprawl of container yards, drone maintenance hangars, and processing facilities where Lake Michigan's cargo platforms offload goods that will be distributed throughout the Corridor. The work that remains for human hands is the work machines can't do cheaply enough yet, which is a category that shrinks every fiscal quarter.

The old naval station — Great Lakes Naval Training Center, decommissioned by the remnant federal government in 2158 — was acquired by Ringo Defense Solutions in the sovereignty charter fire sale of 2161. Ringo converted it into a regional security operations base, which means the northern edge of Waukegan is a walled compound where private military contractors train, refit, and stage for operations throughout the upper GLM. The base employs 12,000 people and contributes exactly nothing to the surrounding community except a perimeter wall, a no-fly zone, and the occasional sound of live-fire exercises at 3 AM.

Between the cargo yards and the Ringo wall, the residential district survives the way organisms survive in extreme environments: by adapting to conditions that would kill anything designed for comfort. The housing stock is a mix of 20th-century bungalows — some of them literally a hundred and fifty years old, patched with whatever was available — and modular refugee housing units dropped by the GLM Metropolitan Authority during the Gulf Coast Displacement crisis of the 2070s. The modulars were supposed to be temporary. Temporary, in municipal planning, means 'until someone allocates a budget that will never be allocated.' They're still here. The people inside them have made them home, which is what people do.

The lakefront itself is poisoned. A century of industrial runoff, compounded by the cargo platform chemical discharge that nobody regulates because the platforms operate in federal — now corporate — waters, has made the shoreline a dead zone. The water is technically Lake Michigan. The color is not.
atmosphere
sights
  • Cargo platform drones descending in formation over the container yards, navigation lights blinking in synchronized patterns
  • The Ringo compound wall — three meters of reinforced concrete topped with sensor arrays, visible from most of the district
  • Modular housing units stacked two and three high, connected by improvised walkways and exterior staircases
  • The dead lakefront — grey-brown water, no vegetation, automated warning buoys marking chemical discharge zones
  • Old bungalow neighborhoods where century-old architecture meets salvaged solar panels and jury-rigged power taps
sounds
  • Container yard automation — the grinding of cargo cranes, the hiss of pneumatic seals, running 24 hours
  • Ringo live-fire exercises — distant but unmistakable, a sound the residents have learned to sleep through
  • Wind off the lake carrying a faint chemical whistle through gaps in the modular housing stacks
  • Children playing in the spaces between housing units, their games adapted to the narrow corridors available
  • The low thrum of the cargo maglev running containers south toward M88's distribution centers
smells
  • Chemical lake — an acrid, metallic smell that residents stop noticing after a few months and visitors never forget
  • Diesel exhaust from the backup generators that keep the modular units running when the grid fails, which is often
  • Cooking smells from the housing corridors — a dense mix of Gulf Coast, Central American, and Southeast Asian cuisines, the smell of every displacement crisis blended together
  • Ozone and machine lubricant from the cargo yards
feel A place that works hard and gets nothing for it. The cargo moves through Waukegan at enormous volume and none of it stops here. The wealth generated by the logistics network is measured in billions of Q and accrues to companies headquartered in buildings the residents of Waukegan will never enter. The community is real, the mutual aid is genuine, and the anger is justified. This is what a company town looks like when the company doesn't even bother to pretend it's a town.
tags —
demographics Approximately 140,000 residents. Heavily working class, Tier 1-2. Significant Gulf Coast displacement population (roughly 30%). Large Latino community predating the displacement era. Ringo base personnel technically reside in Waukegan but exist in a separate jurisdiction and economy. Median age skews young — people leave when they can afford to, which means the ones who stay can't.
economy Logistics labor — the cargo yards employ approximately 15,000 people in roles that automation hasn't eliminated yet. Ringo base support services. Informal economy is substantial: repair work, food service, unlicensed medical care. The nearest licensed medical facility is in The Threshold, twenty minutes south by Purple Line.
power structure No single authority. Ringo controls the northern perimeter. Axiom Logistics controls the cargo yards. The residential district falls into a jurisdiction gap — nominally under GLM Metropolitan Authority, which maintains a single administrative office staffed by two people who process complaints they cannot act on. Real authority is community-based: block captains, mutual aid networks, and the occasional intervention by whoever is currently running the local gray market.
dangers
  • Ringo perimeter enforcement — the compound's automated defense systems have a documented shoot-first protocol for the buffer zone
  • Cargo yard accidents — automation failures kill roughly twenty workers per year, classified as 'operational incidents'
  • Environmental exposure — the lakefront contamination causes elevated cancer rates that nobody is studying because nobody is funding the study
  • Jurisdiction void — no reliable law enforcement means disputes are settled by whatever means are available
  • Displacement violence — resource competition between established residents and newer refugee populations
opportunities
  • Cargo theft — the logistics network moves Q billions in goods through a district with no effective security
  • Ringo intelligence — the base leaks information through its support staff, who live in the community and talk
  • Mutual aid networks — the community infrastructure here is among the strongest in the upper Corridor
  • Labor organizing — the cargo yard workforce is large, angry, and increasingly coordinated
story hooks
  • A cargo container from the Ringo base was accidentally routed to the civilian yard — and its contents don't match any known Ringo inventory
  • The lakefront contamination is getting worse, and a community health worker has data suggesting it's not just industrial runoff — someone is actively dumping
  • A Ringo contractor has gone AWOL into the residential district, carrying information worth enough to change jurisdictions

The Wickfield Remnant #

type place
name The Wickfield Remnant
aliases
  • The Remnant
  • Wickfield
  • Old Wickfield
  • The Preservation Zone
description The Wickfield Remnant is a seventeen-block section of a pre-collapse suburban district preserved — partially, imperfectly — within the northwestern expansion zone of Meridian 88. The preservation is not official, exactly: a series of contested heritage designations, property ownership disputes, and the organic resistance of a long-term resident community have combined to slow the redevelopment pressure that has consumed everything around it. The Remnant sits in a zone that should, by every corponation logistics map, be a Vespid Dynamics light industrial corridor or a Palladian Group mid-tier residential development. It isn't. It remains, with the stubborn persistence of something that simply refused to stop existing.

The built environment is extraordinary in the context of 2200 Meridian 88: intact two-story residential structures from the 2020s-2040s, their original architectural character preserved by residents who have maintained them with whatever materials were available, which means that the preservation is improvisational and vernacular rather than museum-precise. Original facades have been patched with materials from four different eras. Original windows have been replaced with whatever glass was available when they broke. Original gardens have been converted to food production while retaining their structural relationship to the houses. The result is a neighborhood that is genuinely historical while looking nothing like a historical recreation.

The Remnant's population skews older — a significant number of residents have lived here for thirty, forty, fifty years, and a few can claim lineage back to the original neighborhood before it was subsumed by Meridian 88's expansion. This has created a particular social texture: deep institutional memory, strong informal governance, and a collective identity built around the act of remaining. Younger residents who move here tend to do so because they specifically seek this quality, which means the community selects for a certain temperament. The Remnant is not unwelcoming, but it is clear about what it values, and what it values is continuity.

Palladian Group's development interest is the current primary pressure point. Their proposal for the site involves heritage-compliant reconstruction — which means demolishing the actual buildings and replacing them with architectural reproductions while displacing the current residents — and the community's legal and political resistance to this proposal has been ongoing for seven years. The Remnant has become, in some circles, a cause.
atmosphere
sights
  • Original residential streetscapes from a century past, maintained and modified in ways that show every decade of occupation clearly
  • Front gardens converted to dense productive planting — vegetables, herbs, dwarf fruit trees — in what were once ornamental spaces
  • Palladian Group survey equipment and heritage assessment markers on street corners, some spray-painted over and replaced multiple times
  • Children playing in streets that have no vehicle traffic, a sight genuinely unusual in any part of Meridian 88
  • The visual contrast at the Remnant's edges: 2200 Meridian 88 architecture beginning abruptly where the protected zone ends, the difference between eras compressed into a single block
sounds
  • A quietness unusual in the city — reduced mechanical noise, reduced BCI broadcast infrastructure, the sounds of a neighborhood at a human scale
  • Communal activity sounds from the shared garden spaces: voices, tools, the specific acoustic character of people working together on productive tasks
  • The distant persistent sound of the surrounding city, present as a reminder of what the Remnant is preserved within
  • Community meetings from the central gathering house, voices rising and falling through open windows in the warm season
smells
  • Green growing things in density — vegetable gardens, fruit trees, flowering plants — in a concentration unusual for urban space
  • Wood smoke and cooking from traditional fuel-based hearths that some households maintain alongside modern systems
  • The smell of old buildings: plaster, timber, the specific mineral quality of architecture that has been inhabited for a hundred years
  • Rain on old concrete and organic soil, a smell that residents describe as the smell of the place itself
feel The Wickfield Remnant operates at a different phenomenological scale than the city around it. The streets are quiet enough to hear individual voices. The architecture is low enough to see the sky continuously. The BCI signal is weaker here — the community has successfully resisted full-density infrastructure installation — and the resulting reduction in ambient data-traffic creates a mental quietness that visitors often describe as disorienting before they describe it as desirable.

The community's relationship to its own precariousness is complex. The threat of displacement is not abstract — it is present in the survey markers on the corners, in the legal correspondence that occupies the community's governance council, in the Palladian Group vehicles that park at the edges and don't enter. The community has been living with imminent loss for seven years. Some residents have developed a kind of fierce present-tense engagement with the place as a result; others carry a grief that hasn't fully arrived yet.
tags —
demographics Approximately 400-500 permanent residents. Significantly older median age than surrounding Meridian 88 zones, with a notable multi-generational core of families who have been present for decades. Mixed ethnicity but with strong roots in the specific community that was here before Meridian 88's expansion — primarily working-class Central and Eastern European and East African heritage, reflecting the original neighborhood's composition. Tiers 2-3.
economy Local economy is largely self-sustaining in food production, repair, and services. External income comes from skilled labor exported to the surrounding city, a growing heritage-tourism micro-economy that the community has ambivalent feelings about, and the indirect economic activity of the legal advocacy network that has grown up around the displacement case. Palladian Group's development proposal would, if executed, generate significant Φ flows for the company but nothing for current residents.
power structure The Remnant Community Council, an informal but functional governance body with deep resident legitimacy and no formal legal standing. The council coordinates the heritage designation legal challenge, manages community resources, and makes decisions about external engagement by consensus with occasional contentious exception. Palladian Group is the primary external power, exerting pressure through legal and financial mechanisms rather than direct presence.
dangers
  • Palladian Group's heritage-compliant redevelopment proposal, which has come within a single legal ruling of approval twice in the past seven years
  • The community's aging infrastructure — the buildings are maintained, but maintenance with improvised materials has limits, and some structural conditions are genuinely concerning
  • The Remnant's visibility as a cause has attracted outside interests that don't always align with community needs, including political actors who want to use the case without engaging the actual community
  • Younger residents' economic precarity — the Remnant doesn't offer the employment infrastructure of the surrounding city, and some leave, which changes the community's demographic character
  • Opportunistic property speculation in the legal grey zones around the heritage designations
opportunities
  • The community's deep institutional memory and historical documentation represent genuine archival value for parties interested in pre-Meridian 88 history
  • The Remnant's self-governing community infrastructure could serve as a model or staging ground for organizing efforts in other contested zones
  • The heritage-tourism micro-economy is underdeveloped relative to genuine interest, representing commercial opportunity if the community can control its terms
  • The legal case has established precedents that have value beyond this specific situation for displacement and heritage rights advocacy throughout Meridian 88
story hooks
  • A Palladian Group heritage assessment team has delivered a report claiming that one of the Remnant's central structures — the oldest intact building in the zone, occupied by a family for four generations — is not in fact the historical structure it appears to be, but a replica constructed in the 2140s on the original foundation. If true, this would invalidate the heritage designation for the entire block. The community insists it's false. The assessment methodology is questionable. Someone needs to find the actual historical documentation, which may or may not exist, and may or may not be where anyone expects it.
  • One of the Remnant's oldest residents — a woman in her nineties named Bozena Wrzesień who has lived in the same house for sixty-three years — has died, and her death has revealed that she was, for the last twenty years of her life, maintaining a detailed encrypted record of every interaction between the community and Palladian Group, every survey visit, every legal communication, every informal conversation. The record contains information that would be professionally and legally devastating to several named Palladian Group executives. Her family has the files and doesn't know what to do with them. Palladian Group has become aware the files exist.
  • A small group of Remnant residents — younger, economically stressed, facing the real prospect of being priced out even of this community — have been approached by an intermediary offering a deal: individual buyouts at significantly above-market rates, contingent on a critical mass of residents accepting, which would effectively dissolve the community's legal standing to resist Palladian Group's development application. The deal is structured so that the first accepters receive the best terms, and the offer expires in thirty days. The community council doesn't know yet. The intermediary has asked the approached residents to keep it quiet. Some of them are going to tell the council anyway. Some of them are going to accept. The question is which happens first.

The Woodline #

type place
name The Woodline
aliases
  • Woodlawn
  • The Promise District
  • Obama's Ghost
description The Woodline is the neighborhood that was saved and then wasn't. In the old city, Woodlawn was supposed to be transformed by the Obama Presidential Center — a beacon of investment and community renewal anchored to the South Side like a promise kept. The Center was built. It was beautiful. And then the collapse happened, and the beautiful building became the most expensive ruin on the South Side. The Center still stands, its modernist angles and landscaped grounds now enclosed within an Axiom Security perimeter, repurposed as a Tier 3 administrative processing hub. The exhibits about democracy and civic engagement are still inside, behind locked doors, in rooms now used for tier reclassification hearings. The irony is not lost on the residents. The irony is the only thing they have left from the original promise.

The Woodline earned its name from the treeline that marks the boundary between the old residential blocks and the University of Chicago's expanding security perimeter to the north. Hydewood's campus wall casts a literal shadow over the Woodline's northern blocks, and the relationship between the two districts is the relationship between a castle and the village that feeds it. Woodline residents work service jobs on campus — cleaning, maintenance, food preparation — crossing through checkpoints each morning and returning each evening to a neighborhood that receives none of the campus infrastructure investment. The streets here are pre-collapse pavement, cracked and unrepaired. The housing is dense and aging. Community organizations do the work that municipal government abandoned, running everything from childcare to neural interface clinics out of converted storefronts.

But the Woodline has something that makes it unusual in the southern corridor: construction. Axiom Industries has been running a redevelopment initiative here for three years — new residential towers, upgraded grid connections, a promised transit link to the Meridian Core. The official narrative is urban renewal. The actual pattern is displacement. Each new tower that goes up has tier requirements for residency that the current population cannot meet. Each grid upgrade connects to Axiom infrastructure that requires Axiom service contracts. The Woodline is being rebuilt, block by block, into a neighborhood its own residents can't afford to live in. The community calls it the Second Displacement, after the first one — the one that happened when the old city died.

The resistance is quiet and structural. Community land trusts, originally established in the pre-collapse era, still hold title to a handful of residential blocks that Axiom's redevelopment hasn't been able to legally absorb. These blocks are the Woodline's immune system — pockets of Tier 1-2 housing surrounded by rising Tier 3 construction, stubbornly refusing to sell. The people who live there know that holding land is the only leverage that outlasts a corporate news cycle. Kyle has allies here. The land trust organizers are the kind of people who plan in decades, not days, and they understand something that most street-level operators don't: the fight isn't always in the moment. Sometimes the fight is just still being here.
atmosphere
sights
  • The Obama Presidential Center — modernist architecture behind Axiom security fencing, repurposed and repurposed again
  • New residential towers rising beside crumbling pre-collapse housing, the contrast deliberate and cruel
  • Construction drones moving materials overhead, building a neighborhood designed for other people
  • Community land trust signs on residential blocks — small, hand-painted, defiant
  • The Hydewood campus wall visible to the north, casting its shadow into the Woodline's morning streets
  • Service workers queuing at the campus checkpoint at dawn, badge readers glowing amber
sounds
  • Construction noise — constant, mechanical, the sound of a neighborhood being overwritten
  • The campus checkpoint scanner — a tone that means you're cleared to serve, another tone that means you're not
  • Community meetings in land trust buildings, where the agenda hasn't changed in three years: hold the line
  • Children in after-school programs run by volunteers, their laughter carrying further than it should because the old blocks are emptying
  • The hum of new Axiom grid infrastructure, powering buildings the current residents can't access
smells
  • Fresh construction materials — synthetic concrete, polymer insulation — the smell of new buildings for new people
  • Cooking from the remaining community kitchens, heavy with spices that have been in these blocks for generations
  • Exhaust from construction drones that haven't been fitted with emission filters because the Woodline's air quality isn't monitored
feel The Woodline feels like watching your home being packed up by strangers who smile and tell you this is progress. There's grief here, but it's the kind of grief that sharpens into something useful. The people who are still holding on know exactly what they're holding on to and exactly what it costs.
tags —
demographics Approximately 25,000 current residents, declining as displacement accelerates. Historically Black community with strong institutional roots. New construction is attracting Tier 3 residents with no connection to the neighborhood's history. The demographic shift is the point, though Axiom's press releases describe it as organic growth.
economy Service employment at Hydewood's campus. Community-run mutual aid networks. Axiom redevelopment construction provides temporary jobs that evaporate when each phase completes. Land trust properties maintain a small internal economy of shared resources and cooperative labor.
power structure Axiom Industries holds redevelopment authority. Community land trusts hold legal title to approximately fifteen residential blocks and resist absorption through a combination of pre-collapse property law and organized collective action. The Obama Center site is Axiom sovereign territory. Hydewood's campus exerts gravitational pull on the local labor market.
dangers
  • Axiom redevelopment displaces residents through pricing, not force — harder to fight because there's no visible violence
  • Construction sites are hazardous and underregulated — injuries among temp workers are common and unreported
  • The campus checkpoint creates a daily vulnerability for service workers whose tier status is reviewed on each crossing
  • Community organizers face legal harassment through Axiom's property litigation division
  • New residents in Tier 3 towers and existing Tier 1-2 residents occupy the same streets with different rights — friction is structural
opportunities
  • Community land trusts need outside support — legal, financial, informational — and will work with operators who prove trustworthy
  • Axiom redevelopment data reveals patterns useful to anyone fighting corporate displacement across Meridian
  • The Obama Center's original archives may still be intact inside the repurposed facility — pre-collapse civic records with legal and historical value
  • Construction logistics create temporary security gaps in Axiom's perimeter — useful for those who need access to the redevelopment zone
story hooks
  • A community land trust is about to lose its last legal challenge against Axiom's eminent domain filing. The case hinges on a pre-collapse municipal record that should be in the Obama Center's archives — now locked inside an Axiom facility.
  • Axiom's redevelopment plan includes a classified Phase 4 that hasn't been publicly announced. A construction foreman found the plans and doesn't understand what he's looking at, but he knows it's wrong.
  • Service workers crossing the campus checkpoint are being quietly screened for neural interface compatibility. The ones who qualify are offered transfers. None of them have been seen since.

Thornfield Data Necropolis #

type place
name Thornfield Data Necropolis
aliases
  • The Necropolis
  • The Dead Stack

  • The Tomb
description A decommissioned hyperscale data center complex occupying twelve city blocks in the city's eastern industrial fringe, Thornfield was once the primary data infrastructure backbone for four merged corporate entities before a combination of technological obsolescence and a catastrophic cooling failure rendered it economically unviable in 2167. The buildings were sealed rather than demolished — the cost of safely removing the legacy hardware and the toxic materials used in its cooling systems exceeded the land's redevelopment value. What remained was 1.4 million square meters of sealed server halls, cooling infrastructure, subterranean cable runs, and administrative facilities, slowly being reclaimed by entropy.
atmosphere
sights
  • Brutalist concrete exteriors with sealed windows and rusted blast doors
  • Warning signage in corporate livery that no longer exists
  • Vegetation forcing through cracked exterior pavement
  • Thermal shimmer from still-active legacy systems in the deeper levels
  • Emergency lighting still cycling on decade-old backup power in some sections
  • Cable bundles as thick as tree trunks running along corridors and through walls
  • Server racks stretching to five-meter ceilings in rows that disappear into darkness
sounds
  • The distant hum of hardware that was never fully shut down
  • Cooling infrastructure groaning under thermal stress
  • Dripping water where the sealed roof has failed
  • Echoing footsteps across vast empty floors
  • Occasional electronic tones from systems completing unknown processes
  • Wind through cracked ventilation shafts
  • The absence of human sound — a specific, weighted silence
smells
  • Hot electronics and burning dust on old heating elements
  • Coolant chemical tang — mildly toxic with prolonged exposure
  • Concrete dust and mold in the flooded lower sections
  • Old plastic slowly outgassing in warm server halls
  • Clean, filtered air in sections where environmental systems still function
  • Something organic and unidentifiable in the deepest sublevels
feel Cathedral-scale and deeply uncanny. The Necropolis was built for machines, and its proportions reflect that — spaces too large, corridors too long, silence where there should be the noise of human activity. Those who spend extended time inside report a persistent sense of being observed that rational analysis cannot dispel.
tags —
demographics Officially uninhabited and legally restricted. Actual population estimated at 300-500 individuals occupying the most stable and habitable sections — a mix of squatters, urban explorers who never left, a community of hardware salvagers, and at least two organized groups using the facility for purposes they have not disclosed. A small number of highly skilled netrunners have established semi-permanent installations to access whatever legacy data remains on still-active systems.
economy Hardware salvage is the primary legitimate activity — the Necropolis contains decades of obsolete but valuable components, rare materials, and infrastructure that can be repurposed. The data salvage economy is more lucrative and more dangerous: the still-active systems contain information that various parties are willing to pay significantly to retrieve or permanently destroy. The facility's isolation and lack of official oversight also makes it attractive for activities that require neither.
power structure No formal authority. The salvager community has informal territorial agreements — certain sections belong to certain crews, and disputes are handled through negotiation or, occasionally, violence. A figure called the Archivist has claimed sole jurisdiction over the deepest server levels and enforces this claim with lethal competence and unknown resources. The original owning corporation's successor entity holds the legal title and periodically sends security teams that the facility's inhabitants have become expert at evading.
dangers
  • Structural instability — floors, ceilings, and internal walls collapse without warning in degraded sections
  • Toxic coolant exposure from ruptured legacy systems
  • Getting lost — the facility's internal navigation systems are offline and the floor plans are not publicly available
  • The Archivist's response to unauthorized access to the deep levels
  • Corporate security teams on irregular sweep schedules
  • Legacy ICE — automated intrusion countermeasure systems that were never decommissioned and do not distinguish between cyberspace and physical threats
  • Other salvagers with territorial claims and few scruples
  • Psychological effects of extended isolation in the facility's deeper sections
opportunities
  • Hardware salvage with significant resale value
  • Data retrieval from legacy systems — corporate secrets decades old but potentially still actionable
  • A location where activities can be conducted without any official oversight
  • The facility's still-functional network infrastructure offers unusual cyberspace access points
  • Architectural and infrastructural features that cannot be built legally in the current city
  • The Archivist is rumored to trade access to deep-level data for specific services
story hooks
  • A routine salvage run has found an active server cluster in a section of the facility that no map shows — and the data it's processing is current, not legacy, suggesting someone has been running operations through Thornfield's dead infrastructure without anyone knowing
  • The Archivist has sent an intermediary with a job offer: retrieve a specific hardware unit from a section of the facility they cannot safely enter themselves. The pay is extraordinary. The section in question is one the salvager community considers cursed, having lost four people there in the last year
  • The successor corporation to Thornfield's original owners has quietly sold the facility to a development company, and demolition is scheduled to begin in six weeks — the current inhabitants have that long to extract what they can, including data that several powerful parties would pay to have destroyed before a construction crew finds it
  • Something in the lowest sublevel of the Necropolis has begun broadcasting on a frequency that shouldn't exist — the signal contains what appears to be fragments of communications from inside Thornfield dated fifteen years in the future

  • Netrunners seeking legacy data or unusual access points
  • Urban explorers and documentarians
  • Corporate security on sweep operations
  • People who need to conduct business with no witnesses
  • Researchers studying legacy infrastructure and data archaeology
  • Those seeking the Archivist
notable locations
name Hall Seven
description The largest single server hall in the complex, 400 meters long and still partially operational — roughly 15% of the original hardware continues to run on degraded backup power, cycling through processes nobody has been able to fully interpret. The heat differential between the active and inactive sections creates persistent fog at floor level. Hall Seven is considered the most navigable large space in the facility and serves as the informal gathering point for the salvager community.
tags —
name The Sublevel Threshold
description A heavy blast door at the bottom of a service stairwell that marks the boundary of the Archivist's claimed territory. The door is functional and locked, but more significantly it is surrounded by warning signs in the Archivist's own hand, several non-functional pieces of hardware that have been clearly shot multiple times, and a single dried flower that is replaced with a fresh one every few weeks. Nobody knows who replaces it.
tags —
name The Garden
description A former administrative courtyard where the roof has partially collapsed, allowing natural light and rain in. Over the years, vegetation has colonized the space aggressively — full-grown trees have forced through the floor, vines have covered the surrounding walls, and a small but surprisingly clear pool has formed in one corner. The facility's squatter community treats the Garden as neutral ground and a place of rest. It is inexplicably beautiful.

Threshold #

type place
name Threshold
aliases
  • The Disputed Reef
  • Huron Free City
  • The Border
  • Half-and-Half
description Threshold exists in the space between two countries that no longer meaningfully exist, and it has turned that ambiguity into a national identity. Built on Lake Huron's central ridge — roughly equidistant from the former Michigan and Ontario shorelines — Threshold occupies water that both the remnant Canadian federal government and M88's Corridor Council claim jurisdiction over and neither can effectively enforce. The city was founded in 2171 by a mixed Canadian-American group who recognized that the sovereignty confusion created a permanent legal vacuum. They dropped their first accretion framework into water that was simultaneously Canadian, American, and neither, and started growing.

Threshold's seacrete is pale grey, built from Huron's lighter mineral profile — cleaner water, less iron than Superior, more calcium carbonate. The resulting structures have an almost marble-like quality, smooth-surfaced and bright compared to Deepwell's volcanic darkness or Freestone's rough organic textures. The city sprawls horizontally rather than vertically, its platforms connected by arched walkways and canal channels that give it the appearance of a floating Venice built from living stone. This horizontal spread is strategic: Threshold covers more surface area than any other lake city, making it harder to blockade and giving its defense forces — the Borderwatch — multiple angles of engagement.

The sovereignty dispute is Threshold's defining feature and its greatest asset. Both Canada and M88 claim the city is in their waters. Neither can act on the claim without provoking the other. Threshold exploits this deadlock ruthlessly, maintaining diplomatic relations with both sides while acknowledging neither's authority. The city has become the de facto neutral ground of the Great Lakes — a place where shore-based factions can meet, negotiate, and trade without either side having jurisdictional advantage. Diplomats, fixers, intelligence operatives, and criminals all use Threshold as a meeting point. The city charges handsomely for this neutrality, and the revenue funds an infrastructure that's more refined than any other lake city's.

Governance is bicameral — a nod to the city's dual-heritage founding. The Shore Council handles external relations and trade, while the Reef Council manages internal infrastructure and civil affairs. Elections are annual, contested, and occasionally theatrical. Threshold's culture is cosmopolitan in a way that Deepwell's mining solidarity and Freestone's anarchist idealism are not — this is a trading city, a diplomat's city, a city that understands that its survival depends on being useful to everyone and loyal to no one. Population: 185,000, most of them bilingual in English and French, and all of them fluent in the language of strategic ambiguity.
atmosphere
sights
  • Pale grey seacrete architecture with an almost marble-like luminosity — Threshold glows on the water
  • Canal channels threading between platforms, crossed by arched walkways — a freshwater Venice grown from mineral
  • Diplomatic quarter flags — dozens of faction and city-state banners flying from the neutral meeting halls
  • Trade vessels from both shores docked side by side in the harbor platforms — Canadian and M88 flags within arm's reach
  • The Borderwatch patrol boats — sleek, fast, painted in Threshold's grey-and-white livery
sounds
  • Multilingual conversation — English, French, Shelf Cant, and the lakeside trade pidgin overlapping in markets and meeting halls
  • Water traffic — more boats dock at Threshold than any other lake city. The harbor never sleeps.
  • The accretion hum here is higher-pitched, almost musical — Huron's calcium-carbonate chemistry sings differently
  • Diplomatic protocol announcements echoing across the neutral quarter — formal, multilingual, perpetually ongoing
smells
  • Clean lake air — Huron's central waters are cleaner than Michigan or Erie
  • Imported goods from both shores — coffee from M88, timber resin from Canadian north
  • The mineral-chalk scent of fresh seacrete growth, lighter and less metallic than Deepwell's iron
  • Cooking from the multicultural market district — a fusion cuisine that exists nowhere else
feel Sophisticated and watchful. Threshold has the energy of a place where everyone is negotiating something. The architecture is beautiful, the infrastructure works, the food is excellent, and everyone you meet is probably not telling you the whole truth. It's the most comfortable lake city to visit and the most dangerous to underestimate. The neutrality is real — Threshold will shelter anyone — but it's neutrality as a business model, not a moral position. The city smiles at you because it's calculating what you're worth.
tags —
demographics 185,000 permanent residents, roughly 55% American-heritage, 40% Canadian-heritage, 5% international. Strong bilingual culture. The diplomatic and trade sectors employ approximately 30% of the population directly. Threshold attracts a transient population of diplomats, traders, and intelligence operatives that can swell the effective population by 20,000 on any given day.
economy Threshold's economy is built on neutrality. Diplomatic hosting, trade facilitation, and information brokering generate the majority of revenue. The city charges docking fees, meeting-hall rental, and 'neutrality premiums' to factions using its space for negotiations. External trade volume: approximately Φ14.3 billion annually — the highest of any lake city, reflecting its role as the Great Lakes' commercial crossroads. Imports heavily; produces relatively little itself.
power structure Bicameral democracy. The Shore Council (external affairs, seven members, elected annually) and the Reef Council (internal governance, seven members, elected annually) share power with built-in checks. The Borderwatch — 3,200 personnel with patrol craft and surveillance systems — reports to both councils jointly. Corporate entities are prohibited from holding sovereignty but are permitted to operate trade offices under strict licensing. This compromise is Threshold's pragmatic concession to commercial reality.
dangers
  • Espionage density — every intelligence service on the Great Lakes has assets in Threshold
  • The sovereignty dispute escalating — if Canada or M88 ever resolves their standoff, Threshold loses its legal shield
  • Being played — Threshold's neutrality makes it a venue for manipulation by shore-based factions
  • The Borderwatch's limits — 3,200 personnel can't patrol the city's entire horizontal spread simultaneously
  • Trade dependency — Threshold produces little and imports much. A coordinated embargo could be devastating.
opportunities
  • Intelligence — Threshold is the best place on the Great Lakes to learn what every faction is doing
  • Neutral ground — deals that can't happen anywhere else can happen here
  • Trade access — goods from both shores flow through Threshold's markets
  • Diplomatic immunity by proximity — the neutral quarter's conventions protect visitors from shore-based warrants
story hooks
  • A secret negotiation between Axiom Industries and the remnant Canadian government is happening in Threshold's neutral quarter. The outcome would reshape Great Lakes sovereignty. Both sides have hired operatives to ensure the talks go their way.
  • Threshold's Shore Council discovers that one of its members has been a Cormorant Naval Systems intelligence asset for six years. The political fallout threatens the city's neutrality.
  • Kyle is offered a contract that requires him to operate in Threshold — a city where his street-level instincts are worth less than his ability to read a room full of diplomats.
connections

  • Freestone (Lake Michigan — trade route via Straits of Mackinac)
  • Shallowgrave (Lake Erie — southern trade corridor)
  • Canadian shore communities (direct trade relationships)
exits —
tags —

  • Independent traders exploiting Threshold's dual-shore access
  • Intelligence operatives from every major corponation and government remnant
  • Fixers who use Threshold's neutrality to broker cross-jurisdictional contracts

Tidebreak #

type place
name Tidebreak
aliases
  • The Refugee Reef
  • Ontario Free City
  • New Hope
  • The Raft of the Displaced
description Tidebreak was not planned. It was panicked. In 2169, when the New York Coastal Inundation Events — a sanitized term for the systematic drowning of a city that had been told for fifty years it was going to drown — displaced 4.2 million people in eighteen months, the refugee wave crashed westward along the old I-90 corridor toward the Great Lakes like water finding its own level. Most ended up in M88's lower tiers, absorbed into the Shelf's excluded population. But a contingent of roughly 40,000 — organized by a coalition of displaced NYC community leaders, union organizers, and one profoundly stubborn marine engineer named Rosa Espinoza — refused to become someone else's underclass. They had seen what happened when you trusted institutions to house you. They had seen the refugee camps. They chose the water instead.

Espinoza had studied the seacrete cities. She'd corresponded with Freestone's Reef Council. She understood the electrodeposition process — low-voltage current through submerged wire mesh, mineral accretion from dissolved lake carbonates, structures that grow from the water itself. She also understood that Lake Ontario, the easternmost Great Lake, was the closest to the displaced New York population and the least claimed by existing corponation interests. The first frameworks went into the water in the winter of 2169, powered by generators salvaged from flooded Con Edison substations. The accretion was slow in Ontario's cold water. People lived on rafts and barges lashed together while the reef grew beneath them. They called the settlement Tidebreak — a name that referenced both the lake's currents and what they were trying to do to the tide of displacement that had swept them here.

Tidebreak grew unevenly, desperately, and beautifully. Unlike Freestone's organic expansion or Deepwell's engineered precision, Tidebreak's architecture reflects the chaos of its founding: platforms at different heights, structures that lean, walkways that zigzag around obstacles that were living spaces before they were obstacles. The city looks improvised because it was improvised, and the improvisation became an aesthetic — layered, dense, human-scaled, full of the kind of detail that emerges when forty thousand people are all building at once without a master plan. New Yorkers brought New York with them: the density, the vertical ambition, the stubborn belief that a city is defined by its people rather than its infrastructure. Tidebreak is the most culturally vibrant of the lake cities — music, art, food, theater, argument. It is also the poorest, the most crowded, and the most in need of everything from medical supplies to structural engineers.

Governance is a borough system adapted from New York's old structure — five boroughs, each with an elected borough council, overseen by a General Council that manages inter-borough affairs and external relations. The system is chaotic, loud, and functional in the way that democracy is functional when the alternative is drowning. Population: 210,000 — the second-largest lake city, and growing, because refugees keep coming and Tidebreak keeps saying yes.
atmosphere
sights
  • Layered, uneven seacrete architecture — platforms at different heights, structures leaning into each other, a vertical density that echoes old Manhattan
  • Murals everywhere — Tidebreak's artists have covered every available surface with color, memory, and defiance
  • Refugee arrival platforms on the eastern edge, where boats from shore still bring new residents regularly
  • Laundry lines strung between structures, flags and banners from a hundred communities of origin
  • The Espinoza Monument — a seacrete statue of the founder, grown organically from the city's first accretion framework, perpetually being added to by residents
sounds
  • Music — constantly, from everywhere. Tidebreak's musicians play on platforms, in corridors, on boats. The city has more live music per capita than any settlement on the Great Lakes.
  • Argument — Tidebreak is loud, opinionated, and never not having a political discussion
  • Construction — the city is always building, always expanding, always accreting
  • Languages — English, Spanish, Mandarin, Haitian Creole, and a dozen others. Tidebreak's linguistic diversity exceeds M88's.
smells
  • Cooking from a hundred culinary traditions — Tidebreak's food scene is legendary among the lake cities
  • Fresh seacrete — the mineral-chalk smell of new growth, a constant presence in a city that never stops building
  • Lake Ontario — cleaner than Erie, warmer than Superior, carrying the faint organic scent of the St. Lawrence outflow
  • Paint and adhesive from the mural artists — Tidebreak smells like art being made
feel Alive and desperate and beautiful. Tidebreak has the energy of a place that was built by people who had no other option and decided to make it extraordinary anyway. It's crowded, chaotic, structurally questionable, and more culturally alive than anything on shore. Walking through Tidebreak feels like walking through a city that is simultaneously falling apart and being born. The people here have already lost one home. They will fight for this one with everything they have.
tags —
demographics 210,000 permanent residents, predominantly descended from the New York Coastal Displacement wave of 2169-2172. Ethnically and culturally diverse — Tidebreak reflects New York's demographics compressed onto a seacrete reef. Significant communities of Caribbean, East Asian, Latin American, and Eastern European heritage. The city continues to accept refugees from shore-based displacement events and has never turned anyone away.
economy The poorest lake city in per-capita terms. Economy is service-based, cultural, and aid-dependent. Primary exports: artisanal goods, cultural products (music recordings, art, handcrafted items), and labor — Tidebreak residents hire out as construction workers, seacrete engineers, and translators to the other lake cities. Imports: almost everything. Annual external trade: approximately Φ3.1 billion, supplemented by Φ1.8 billion in mutual aid from Freestone and Threshold. The economy is precarious and everyone knows it.
power structure Borough council system. Five boroughs — Midtown, Battery, Heights, the Yards, and Newtown — each elect a borough council of five. The General Council of twenty-five manages external affairs and resource allocation. Decision-making is slow, contentious, and broadly legitimate. No corporate entities permitted under the founding charter. The Harbor Guard — 1,400 volunteers with converted civilian vessels — provides defense.
dangers
  • Structural instability — Tidebreak's improvised construction means that some sections are genuinely unsafe
  • Resource scarcity — the city doesn't produce enough food, medicine, or building materials internally
  • Proximity to old New York ruins — salvage expeditions into the flooded city are lucrative and frequently fatal
  • Population pressure — Tidebreak keeps accepting refugees without the infrastructure to support them
  • Political exploitation — shore-based factions see Tidebreak's poverty as leverage
opportunities
  • Cultural capital — Tidebreak's art, music, and cuisine are valued across the Great Lakes
  • New York salvage — the flooded ruins of the old city contain technology, data, and materials worth fortunes
  • Labor force — Tidebreak's people are resourceful, multilingual, and willing to work
  • Moral authority — Tidebreak's refugee-founded identity gives it a rhetorical power that richer cities lack
story hooks
  • A salvage team returns from the flooded New York ruins with a sealed data archive from a pre-collapse financial institution. The contents could shift the balance of power among the corponations. Multiple factions converge on Tidebreak to acquire it.
  • Tidebreak's General Council votes to accept 30,000 new refugees from a Gulf Coast displacement event. The city's infrastructure can't handle the influx. Freestone offers help — with conditions.
  • Kyle is hired to escort a cargo shipment to Tidebreak. The cargo is medical supplies. The client who hired him is Lazarus Pharmaceuticals. Something doesn't add up.

Tulip Protocol #

type place
name Tulip Protocol
aliases
  • Holland
  • The Greenhouse
  • Protocol City
  • Blooming Corporate
description Holland, Michigan, was famous for two things: Dutch heritage and tulips. The annual Tulip Time Festival drew half a million visitors to see millions of flowers and watch people in wooden shoes scrub the streets. It was wholesome. It was midwestern. It was exactly the kind of cultural asset that Verdana BioSystems identified as a 'brand alignment opportunity' when they acquired the city's commercial district in 2166.

Verdana turned Holland into the Tulip Protocol -- a showcase city for corporate botanical engineering and agricultural biotech. The tulips are still here. They are also unrecognizable. Verdana's genetic modification labs have produced flowers that change color based on air quality readings, tulips that generate bioluminescence sufficient to light walkways at night, tulips that function as distributed air purification systems, and -- in the restricted R&D greenhouses on the south side -- tulips that produce pharmaceutical compounds in their pollen. The old downtown has been enclosed under a transparent bioshell, maintaining Dutch Golden Age architectural aesthetics while the streets are lined with engineered botanical displays that cycle through seasonal presentations on a six-week schedule. It is beautiful. It is controlled down to the molecular level. It is a garden that has been optimized until it forgot how to be wild.

Outside the bioshell, the workers who maintain the Protocol live in housing blocks along the US-31 corridor. These are the greenhouse technicians, the genetic engineers who weren't talented enough for the R&D labs, the maintenance crews who keep the bioshell climate systems running. They earn decent wages by lakefront standards -- Verdana pays better than most corponations for skilled labor -- but they live in the permanent shadow of a paradise they can enter only during work hours. The Dutch heritage culture survives in the worker districts as a form of quiet resistance: klompen on porches, stroopwafels in the break rooms, language classes taught in church basements. Verdana encourages this. Heritage culture in the worker districts gives the Protocol 'authenticity' that they can reference in marketing materials. The workers know this. They maintain the culture anyway, because it was theirs before Verdana made it a product.
atmosphere
sights
  • The bioshell dome catching sunlight and refracting it into prismatic patterns across engineered flower beds
  • Bioluminescent tulip rows lining the main streets at night -- blue, green, gold, shifting with air quality data
  • Dutch Golden Age architecture preserved to museum standards beneath the transparent dome
  • Verdana BioSystems logos integrated into every botanical display -- the flowers are branded
  • The restricted R&D greenhouses on the south side, opaque and climate-sealed, growing things that don't appear in any catalog
sounds
  • The bioshell's climate regulation -- a soft, constant hiss of temperature and humidity management
  • Tourist commentary and guided tour narration in multiple languages
  • Pollinators -- engineered drone-bees maintaining the flower beds with mechanical precision
  • Church bells from the worker districts, still rung on the hour, the one sound Verdana hasn't replicated
  • The quiet hum of genetic sequencing equipment from the R&D greenhouses, audible if you press your ear to the wall
smells
  • Flowers -- overwhelming, engineered, every scent calibrated for optimal psychological response
  • The bioshell's filtered air, clean to a degree that feels artificial because it is
  • Outside the dome: Lake Michigan wind, vehicle exhaust from the corridor, and the honest smell of soil from the worker district gardens
feel Inside the Protocol, nature has been perfected to the point of uncanniness. Every flower is flawless. Every sight line is composed. The beauty is genuine and the control is total and the combination produces a feeling that takes most visitors a few hours to identify: the discomfort of being in a garden that will never surprise you. The worker districts outside have a different energy -- quieter, less polished, but alive in the way that things growing without permission are alive.
tags —
demographics Bioshell district: 3,000 Verdana employees and visiting researchers, Tier 3-5. Worker districts: approximately 22,000 residents, Tier 2-3, with a core Dutch-heritage community that predates the corporate acquisition and an immigrant workforce drawn by Verdana's relatively fair labor terms.
economy Verdana BioSystems generates Φ3.4 billion annually from the Protocol's biotech output, pharmaceutical botanical research, and licensing fees for proprietary plant genetics. The worker district economy includes Verdana wages, small-scale traditional agriculture (tolerated by Verdana as 'heritage practice'), and a modest tourist service economy.
power structure Verdana BioSystems holds sovereign authority over the bioshell district. The worker districts are nominally under GLM municipal jurisdiction but practically governed by Verdana's labor relations office. The Dutch Heritage Preservation Society serves as an informal community government and cultural anchor, operating with Verdana's approval as long as they don't organize around labor issues.
dangers
  • Pollen exposure -- the R&D greenhouses produce compounds that are not tested on humans, and containment is not perfect
  • Verdana security treats unauthorized access to the R&D sector as corporate espionage, with all the jurisdictional consequences that implies
  • Monoculture dependency -- if Verdana leaves, nothing replaces them
  • The engineered pollinators have occasionally malfunctioned in ways that suggest their programming includes capabilities beyond flower maintenance
  • Allergic reactions to engineered botanical compounds -- the local clinic sees patterns they're not allowed to publish
opportunities
  • Verdana's proprietary plant genetics are worth fortunes to agricultural competitors
  • The R&D greenhouses contain pharmaceutical breakthroughs that haven't reached market -- and some that were never intended to
  • The worker district's Dutch heritage community maintains networks that predate and operate independently of corporate infrastructure
  • Clean agricultural knowledge -- the greenhouse techs know how to grow things, which is an increasingly rare and valuable skill
story hooks
  • The R&D greenhouses are growing something that isn't a plant -- or isn't only a plant -- and a greenhouse technician has seen enough to be scared but not enough to understand
  • Verdana's pharmaceutical tulips are producing a compound that enhances neural interface receptivity, and someone wants to put it in the public flower beds
  • The Heritage Preservation Society has been secretly seed-banking unmodified plant genetics for decades -- an act of botanical resistance that multiple parties would kill to control

University Spine #

type place
name University Spine
aliases
  • University Circle
  • The Spine
  • Case District
  • Clinic Row
description University Circle was Cleveland's cultural and intellectual center — home to Case Western Reserve University, the Cleveland Clinic, the Cleveland Museum of Art, and a concentration of educational and medical institutions that made the neighborhood one of the most institutionally dense square miles in America. All of those institutions still exist, technically. What they have become is something their founders would not recognize.

Case Western Reserve University was acquired by Tessera CorpoNation in 2158 as part of a broader strategy to secure academic research pipelines for neural interface development. The university's name was preserved — Tessera understands the value of institutional branding — but its research agenda is now entirely aligned with Tessera's product roadmap. The Cleveland Clinic underwent a parallel transformation, absorbed into Helix Biosystems' medical services division in 2163. The Clinic's famous research campus is now a Helix sovereign medical zone where experimental procedures are conducted under proprietary jurisdiction, exempt from whatever remains of medical ethics oversight. The Cleveland Museum of Art, unable to compete with neural-direct experience galleries, was converted into a Vantablack Media production facility in 2171, its permanent collection digitized, archived, and reportedly sold to private collectors whose identities Vantablack declines to disclose.

What connects these institutions is the Spine — a climate-controlled elevated walkway system that links every major building in the district, creating a continuous interior environment that Tessera, Helix, and Vantablack employees can traverse without ever touching the ground-level streets. The Spine is the district's real architecture. Below it, the original streets serve as loading docks, maintenance access, and housing for the service workers who keep the elevated institutions running. The vertical segregation is literal: the people who work in the Spine look down at the people who work beneath it, and the sightline goes only one way because the Spine's windows are one-way smart glass.
atmosphere
sights
  • The Spine — an elevated climate-controlled walkway connecting every major institution, its smart-glass walls opaque from below
  • Case Western's original Gothic architecture visible beneath Tessera's carbon-fiber expansion modules, like a church consumed by a laboratory
  • The Cleveland Clinic's Helix sovereign medical zone — pristine white buildings behind biometric barriers, no windows on the research floors
  • The former Cleveland Museum of Art, its neoclassical facade now displaying Vantablack Media's shifting holographic projections
  • Ground-level service housing beneath the Spine — functional, overlooked, deliberately invisible from above
sounds
  • Climate control in the Spine — the whispered hum of a perfectly regulated environment
  • Medical transport drones moving between Helix facilities, their navigation pings a constant background rhythm
  • Tessera research audio — the faint whine of neural interface testing equipment, audible through the walls during calibration cycles
  • Below the Spine: the noise of a working neighborhood — delivery vehicles, maintenance crews, residents living lives the institutions above have engineered out of view
  • The silence of the former museum — Vantablack's production facility operates on neural-direct workflows that produce no audible sound
smells
  • The Spine: filtered, temperature-controlled air with Helix's proprietary 'Clarity' scent profile — clean linen and something meant to enhance cognitive focus
  • Below the Spine: diesel from delivery vehicles, cooking from service worker housing, and the faint chemical bite of Helix medical waste processing
  • Tessera's research buildings: ozone and biocompatible polymer, the smell of neural interfaces being manufactured
feel University Spine feels like walking through a body — the elevated walkway is the nervous system, the institutions are the organs, and the ground-level neighborhoods are the parts the body doesn't think about. Everything above the Spine is designed for productivity, efficiency, and the particular comfort of people whose minds are corporate assets. Everything below is designed to support what's above while remaining invisible. The segregation is architectural, economic, and absolute.
tags —
demographics Above the Spine: approximately 8,000 Tessera, Helix, and Vantablack employees, predominantly Tier 3-4, universally augmented. Below the Spine: approximately 20,000 service workers, maintenance staff, and their families, predominantly Tier 1-2. The two populations share physical space and inhabit different worlds.
economy Neural interface R&D (Tessera), experimental medicine and biotech (Helix Biosystems), media production (Vantablack). The above-Spine economy is entirely corporate. The below-Spine economy is service-based — food preparation, cleaning, maintenance, delivery — compensated at rates that keep workers functional but never mobile. The three corponations maintain a joint economic zone agreement that standardizes wages below the Spine at levels that are, by pure coincidence, identical across all three employers.
power structure Tripartite corporate sovereignty. Tessera controls the university campus. Helix controls the medical campus. Vantablack controls the cultural campus. The Spine itself is jointly administered under a shared governance protocol called the Circle Compact. Ground-level territory is technically under Tollgate infrastructure sovereignty, but Tollgate's presence is minimal — they collect fees and maintain systems, but the three resident corponations effectively control everything.
dangers
  • Corporate jurisdiction complexity — three overlapping sovereignties create legal ambiguities that are dangerous for anyone without a corporate attorney
  • Helix medical testing — the sovereign medical zone operates without external oversight, and the below-Spine population is a convenient source of test subjects who have limited legal recourse
  • Tessera neural research proximity — experimental BCI signals occasionally leak from the research campus, causing interface glitches in anyone within range
  • Surveillance density — above the Spine is one of the most monitored environments in the corridor, with three corporate security systems operating simultaneously
  • Below-Spine exploitation — the wage-fixing arrangement keeps service workers in permanent economic stasis with no pathway to above-Spine employment
opportunities
  • Tessera's research campus is a source of cutting-edge neural interface intelligence — data that's valuable to every fixer and operator in the corridor
  • Helix's medical capabilities are accessible to those who can pay or trade — including experimental treatments unavailable elsewhere
  • The below-Spine workforce knows the physical infrastructure of every institution in the district — knowledge that is operationally invaluable
  • The Circle Compact's joint administration creates bureaucratic gaps between the three sovereignties that can be exploited
story hooks
  • A below-Spine maintenance worker has discovered that Helix's medical waste processing facility is not processing waste — it's processing something else entirely, and the chemical signatures match NeoCortex Industries' known protocols
  • Tessera's research campus has produced a neural interface prototype that its own engineers are afraid of — and the prototype has gone missing somewhere in the Spine
  • The Cleveland Museum of Art's permanent collection was supposed to be digitized and archived. A below-Spine delivery worker has found evidence that it was never digitized — it was moved, physically, to a location that doesn't appear on any corporate map

Upturn #

type place
name Upturn
aliases
  • Uptown
  • The Stage
  • Neon Graveyard
  • The Comeback District
description Upturn is a district that refuses to stop performing. The old Uptown entertainment district — home to the Aragon Ballroom, the Riviera Theatre, and a century of Chicago music history — was supposed to die when the floods came and the corporations redrew the map. The lakefront venues took water damage. The entertainment economy collapsed when people stopped going out and started jacking into neural entertainment feeds. The residential hotels that once housed the neighborhood's eclectic mix of immigrants, artists, and the marginally housed were condemned, cleared, or converted to data storage. Uptown should have become another Managed Decline Zone, another name on the list of places the city used to have.

But the stages wouldn't close. The Aragon — that impossible Moorish fantasy of a building, its terra cotta facade cracked and patched with industrial sealant — reopened as an unlicensed neural entertainment venue within two years of the last official show. The Riviera became a black-market performance space where musicians, storytellers, and experience-chip artists perform for audiences who are tired of corporate-curated content. The entertainment economy didn't die. It went underground, went gray, went weird. Upturn's venues now host something that doesn't have a clean name: live performance enhanced by neural interface technology, where the audience doesn't just watch the show but feels it, transmitted directly through their implants by performers who've turned their own nervous systems into broadcast equipment. It's art as infection. The corps call it unlicensed neural transmission. The performers call it communion.

The residential character survived too, though transformed. Upturn is still where the city's misfits wash up — people too strange for the Shelf's tight-knit conformity, too broke for the Core, too analog for the Circuit. The old single-room-occupancy hotels now function as vertical communes, their residents sharing generators, food prep, and a collective commitment to being left alone. The lakefront blocks that flood during storms have been surrendered to the water, their lower floors converted to aquaculture tanks that feed the district. Mental health services — never adequate in old Uptown, criminally absent in Meridian — are provided by a network of unlicensed counselors and AI therapy programs running on donated server space. The need is enormous. The resources are not.

Upturn sits on the knife edge between revival and collapse. Every season, another venue reopens. Every season, another building fails a structural assessment that nobody conducts because nobody official cares. The district has an energy that's part creative renaissance, part hospice — the desperate brightness of people making art because the alternative is despair. Kyle comes here when he needs to remember that there's more to Meridian than contracts and chrome. The shows at the Aragon can make you weep, if you're open to it. Most of Kyle's work doesn't leave room for that kind of openness, which is exactly why he needs it.
atmosphere
sights
  • The Aragon's cracked Moorish facade lit from within by shifting neural-reactive light installations
  • Street performers broadcasting emotional states through jury-rigged neural transmitters, passersby stopping as feelings wash over them
  • Aquaculture tanks glowing green in flooded ground floors, fish shadows moving behind dirty glass
  • Hand-painted venue posters layered decades deep on every available wall surface
  • The Riviera's marquee, half its letters missing, still spelling out tonight's unlicensed show
  • Commune residents on fire escapes, sharing meals and cigarettes and watching the lakefront darken
sounds
  • Music — always music. Live drums from a basement rehearsal, synth drones from a rooftop installation, someone singing in a language that might not exist yet
  • The hum of neural broadcast equipment warming up before a show — a subsonic vibration you feel in your teeth
  • Lake waves hitting the flooded lower blocks, a rhythm the musicians have learned to play against
  • Applause — real applause, from real hands, which sounds different from anything a neural feed can simulate
  • The creak of old theater seats in the Aragon, designed for a city that doesn't exist anymore
smells
  • Greasepaint and ozone — the smell of performance in the neural age
  • Aquaculture tanks — wet vegetation and fish, not unpleasant, just biological
  • Old building interiors — dust, aged wood, the ghost scent of a century of cigarette smoke baked into plaster
  • Street food from the vendors who set up outside venues before shows, capitalizing on the crowd
  • Lake air from the flooded eastern blocks, cleaner here than in Rogers Reef
feel Manic. Upturn vibrates between euphoria and exhaustion with nothing in between. The shows are transcendent. The mornings after are brutal. Everyone here is creating something or recovering from creating something, and the line between art and breakdown is drawn in pencil and erased frequently. It feels like the last party in a building that's being condemned — joyful, desperate, and absolutely essential.
tags —
demographics Roughly 20,000 residents, heavily skewed toward Tier 1 and untier-ed. High population of artists, performers, unlicensed neural technicians, and the marginally housed. Significant mental health needs across the population. The most transient district in northern Meridian — people flow through Upturn constantly, staying for a season or a decade.
economy Neural entertainment performances, experience-chip production, aquaculture, unlicensed therapy services, and the gray-market creative economy. The Aragon alone generates enough foot traffic to support a surrounding ecosystem of food vendors, augment-cosmetics artists, and stimulant dealers.
power structure The Venue Collective — operators of the Aragon, the Riviera, and six smaller performance spaces — functions as Upturn's de facto government. Decisions are made by consensus, which means slowly, loudly, and with dramatic walkouts. No corporate presence. No formal law enforcement.
dangers
  • Neural broadcast exposure — unlicensed transmissions can overwhelm unprepared implants, causing seizures or emotional flooding
  • Structural failure in the older venue buildings — the Aragon's balcony has been condemned and reopened four times
  • Exploitation of vulnerable populations — Upturn's mentally ill and marginally housed are targets for predatory augment dealers
  • Stimulant addiction fueled by the performance economy's demand for constant creative output
  • Flooding in the eastern blocks during storms — worse than the Rinse and less predictable
  • Experience-chip addiction — some of the content produced here is designed to be psychologically habit-forming
opportunities
  • Neural entertainment experiences unavailable anywhere else in Meridian — art that rewrites your emotional state
  • The creative community's network — performers, writers, and experience-chip artists who know people everywhere
  • Aquaculture products — fresh fish in a city that mostly eats synth-protein is a valuable commodity
  • Information exchange at venues — shows are also social gatherings where deals are made and secrets traded
  • Unlicensed therapy — the AI counseling programs here are better than nothing, and for many residents, they're the only option
story hooks
  • A neural performer at the Aragon discovers she can transmit specific memories — not emotions, memories — through her broadcast equipment. Someone else's memories. She doesn't know whose, and they're getting darker
  • The Venue Collective receives an anonymous offer to buy the Aragon and convert it to a licensed corporate entertainment space. The offer is generous. The alternative is implied arson.
  • An experience-chip circulating in Upturn contains a hidden data payload — someone is using the entertainment distribution network to smuggle information, and the content of that information could destabilize Axiom's grip on the northern districts
