West Garfield Hollow #

type place
name West Garfield Hollow
aliases
  • West Garfield Park
  • The Hollow
  • The Gap West
  • WGP
description West Garfield Park lost half its population before the incorporation even happened. Decades of disinvestment, the war on drugs, the foreclosure crisis, the school closings — every institutional failure Chicago could produce landed here, and the people absorbed it until they couldn't, and then they left. The incorporation finished what neglect started. When the corps mapped the city for value extraction, West Garfield Park registered as a gap — not a district, not a zone, not even a problem. Just an absence. The corporate designation is Sector 26-W, Low Priority. The people who remain call it the Hollow, and the name is accurate and insufficient.

The Hollow is small — a few dozen blocks of mixed residential and commercial structures in various states of occupation and collapse. The population has stabilized at roughly 8,000, down from a pre-incorporation peak of over 17,000 and a historical peak of over 48,000. Those 8,000 people are the ones who wouldn't leave, or couldn't, or chose to stay because someone has to hold the ground or it stops being ground and starts being nothing. They are organized, furious, and effective in ways that their numbers shouldn't allow.

The Garfield Community Collective — the Hollow's governing body — operates with the intensity of a wartime cabinet. Every resource is tracked. Every decision is collective. The Collective runs a tool library, a seed bank, a community kitchen, a school, and a conflict mediation service, all from a single converted commercial building on Madison Street that used to be a currency exchange. The building still has the old bulletproof glass in the windows, and the Collective has never removed it because it's still useful. The Collective's philosophy is simple: they have been abandoned by every institution that was supposed to help, and they have responded by becoming the institution. Their leaders are exhausted, underfunded, and the most competent local governors in the Corridor.

The Hollow's physical landscape is defined by vacancy — empty lots, empty buildings, empty blocks where structures have been stripped for materials and the foundations have been reclaimed by prairie grass. But the Hollow's vacancy is not the same as the corporate districts' emptiness. Corporate emptiness is designed. The Hollow's vacancy is a wound that the community is actively composting. Empty lots become gardens. Empty buildings become workshops. The Collective treats every abandoned space as an asset waiting for a use, and their land bank — an informal registry of available spaces — is one of the most valuable resources in the western Corridor. In a city where space is fought over, the Hollow has space. The irony is not lost on anyone.

Kyle has done work for the Collective. They pay what they can, which isn't much, but they pay in other currencies too: safe passage, information, and the kind of loyalty that comes from being helped by someone who didn't have to help. The Hollow remembers its debts. Both kinds.
atmosphere
sights
  • Vacant lots being converted to community gardens — prairie grass and tomato plants side by side
  • The Madison Street Collective building — bulletproof glass, community signage, lights always on
  • Empty blocks where buildings used to be — foundations visible through ground cover like architectural graves
  • Solar panels on every occupied structure, angled and maintained with obvious care
  • Community murals on remaining walls — memorials, maps, declarations of continued existence
  • The contrast between maintained and abandoned: one block alive, the next reclaimed by nature
sounds
  • Wind — the Hollow has enough open space for wind to be a presence, which is unusual in the Corridor
  • Community radio from the Collective's low-power station — news, music, practical information
  • Children in the Collective's school, audible through open windows — the most hopeful sound in the district
  • Construction when the Collective has materials — the sound of reclamation, not development
smells
  • Garden soil and compost — the Hollow smells like things growing from things that ended
  • The Madison Street kitchen's community meals — simple, sufficient, shared
  • Prairie grass and wildflowers in the vacant lots — the smell of a city returning to earth
  • Old building interiors — dust, plaster, the scent of structures settling into their final rest
feel Defiant. The Hollow feels like a place that should be dead and isn't — a community that has transformed abandonment into a kind of terrible freedom. There's grief everywhere, built into the landscape of empty lots and missing buildings, but the grief doesn't dominate. What dominates is the stubborn, exhausted, ferocious determination to keep going. The Hollow makes you angry — at the systems that created it, at the people who allowed it, at the comfortable assumption that places like this are inevitable. The Collective's response to that anger is not despair. It's a seed bank, a school, and a kitchen that never closes.
tags —
demographics Approximately 8,000 residents, predominantly Black, governed by the Garfield Community Collective. Tier 1 and untier-ed. The population is stable for the first time in decades — those who remain have chosen to remain. Supplemented by a small but growing number of idealistic arrivals from other districts who come to help and, if they last, become part of the community.
economy —
power structure —
dangers
  • Resource scarcity — the Collective operates on margins so thin they're theoretical
  • Structural collapse — the remaining buildings are old and maintenance is triage
  • Isolation — the Hollow's western position means help is far away if something goes wrong
  • Scavengers from outside the community who treat the Hollow's vacancy as a free supply depot
  • Emotional burnout — the Collective's leaders are running on willpower and not much else
  • Corporate rezoning — the Hollow's land has value precisely because it's empty, and someone will eventually want it
opportunities
  • Space — the Hollow's most valuable resource is the empty land the market forgot
  • The Collective's governance model as a template for other abandoned districts
  • Community loyalty that is genuine, deep, and extended to those who earn it
  • Agricultural knowledge and seed stock developed for urban growing conditions
  • The Hollow's land bank — available space for operations, storage, or development that no one else is watching
story hooks

  • The Collective's seed bank contains a strain of engineered crop developed by a pre-incorporation researcher — and a corporation has just realized it still holds the patent
  • A Collective elder has died, and her handwritten records of pre-incorporation property ownership are the only evidence that the community's land claims are legitimate — and they've gone missing

West Lawn Line #

type place
name West Lawn Line
aliases
  • West Lawn
  • The Line
  • Marquette Shadow
  • Lawnside
description West Lawn Line takes its name from the border it straddles: the invisible but intensely felt boundary between the Southwest's residential districts and the Marquette Park exclusion perimeter. Old West Lawn was working-class and unexceptional, defined more by what it was near than what it contained. Meridian 88 preserved that identity with ruthless accuracy. West Lawn Line is the neighborhood you pass through to get somewhere else, and the people who live here have made a science of being the place between places.

Marquette Park, the green space that once anchored the area, was enclosed during the early Meridian years as part of a Vantage Meridian environmental rehabilitation project that has never produced a public status report. The park's perimeter is fenced with corporate-grade security mesh, monitored by AI-controlled surveillance that tracks everything within 200 meters of the boundary, and officially designated as 'restoration in progress.' What's being restored, and why it requires military-grade security to restore it, is the subject of speculation that ranges from plausible (contaminated soil remediation) to paranoid (underground research facility) to darkly humorous (they're growing Tier 6 people in there). The residents of West Lawn Line live in the shadow of that fence, both literally and psychologically, and the not-knowing has become its own kind of weather.

The neighborhood's growing Hispanic majority has transformed the commercial strips into a network of family businesses, community centers, and informal gathering spaces that serve as the social infrastructure the city doesn't provide. The proximity to the Marquette perimeter gives these spaces an edge -- there's always a window facing the fence, always someone watching, always the unspoken question of what happens when the restoration is complete and whoever is inside the park decides they need the land on the outside too. West Lawn Line is a neighborhood waiting for the other shoe to drop, and it's been waiting long enough that the waiting has become the defining characteristic of daily life. People here are patient, observant, and prepared for something they can't name.
atmosphere
sights
  • The Marquette Park perimeter fence -- corporate security mesh stretching the length of the district, featureless and humming
  • AI surveillance nodes mounted on the fence at regular intervals, tracking movement within their radius
  • Family-run commercial strips with every third storefront offering a view of the perimeter
  • Residential blocks painted in bright colors -- a deliberate contrast to the gray security fence
  • Community watch posts, unofficial but unmistakable, positioned at key sightlines to the park boundary
sounds
  • The security mesh hum -- a low-frequency vibration that residents feel in their teeth on quiet nights
  • Normal neighborhood sounds layered over the perimeter's ambient drone -- children, commerce, conversation
  • Occasionally, sounds from inside the park -- machinery, maybe, or something else, muffled by the fence's acoustic properties
  • Community radio broadcasting from a converted garage, covering local news and perimeter observation reports
smells
  • Cooking from the commercial strips -- West Lawn Line eats well despite everything
  • Ozone from the security mesh, strongest after rain
  • Park vegetation -- even through the fence, the smell of growing things escapes occasionally, which is either reassuring or concerning
feel Watchful. West Lawn Line has the emotional texture of a neighborhood that lives next to a locked door and has learned to listen for sounds behind it. The community is warm, functional, and fundamentally shaped by proximity to something unexplained. It's not fear exactly. It's the particular alertness of people who know they're adjacent to a secret and have decided to be ready for whatever it turns out to be.
tags —
demographics Approximately 35,000 residents, Tier 1 and Tier 2, with a growing Hispanic majority alongside legacy Eastern European and Black families. The population skews younger than the Southwest average, with new families attracted by relatively affordable housing that the Marquette perimeter's presence keeps undervalued.
economy Family commercial businesses serving the local community, supplemented by an informal economy in perimeter observation -- detailed logs of fence activity, sound recordings, electromagnetic readings sold to interested parties including journalists, academics, and unidentified buyers who pay in untraceable scrip.
power structure Community council governance handles neighborhood affairs. The Marquette perimeter is controlled by Vantage Meridian Environmental Division, which maintains a liaison office in the district that is staffed, polite, and provides no information. The community radio station has become an unofficial authority through its perimeter coverage.
dangers
  • The Marquette perimeter's AI surveillance extends 200 meters beyond the fence -- residents in that radius are permanently monitored
  • Whatever is inside the park -- the not-knowing is a danger in itself, preventing accurate threat assessment
  • Vantage Meridian's tolerance for perimeter observation has limits that haven't been tested yet
  • The fence's electromagnetic output is untested for long-term residential exposure
  • Being the neighborhood next to the secret when the secret stops being secret
opportunities
  • Perimeter observation data is valuable to multiple parties and the community has years of it
  • The depressed property values create entry points for operators who need a Southwest base
  • Community radio infrastructure could be expanded into a broader independent media network
  • Whatever is inside Marquette Park is the biggest unanswered question in the Southwest, and answers have value
story hooks
  • The community radio station received an anonymous data packet containing what appears to be a partial schematic of the Marquette Park interior -- it shows something underground, something large, and something that doesn't match any known Vantage Meridian project classification
  • The perimeter's AI surveillance recently expanded its tracking radius from 200 to 300 meters without announcement -- three additional residential blocks are now inside the monitoring zone, and the residents are organizing
  • A family that's lived next to the fence since it was erected claims their neural interfaces have been receiving fragmented transmissions from inside the park -- the transmissions appear to be automated status reports from a system that isn't supposed to exist

West Pulldown #

type place
name West Pulldown
aliases
  • West Pullman
  • The Dropout
  • Pulldown
  • The Fade
description West Pulldown earned its name the honest way. When the southern residential blocks of old Chicago were absorbed into Meridian 88's tier restructuring, West Pullman was designated Tier 2 transitional housing -- a bureaucratic phrase that meant the neighborhood would receive just enough infrastructure funding to survive and not one credit more. The historic homes, many dating back to the 1880s Pullman worker housing experiment, were retrofitted with cheap neural-compatible wiring and subdivided into efficiency units. Three families where one used to live. The craftsmanship of those original homes -- the stone lintels, the ornamental brickwork -- still shows through in places, like good bones visible through bad skin. Residents call the contrast between what the neighborhood was built to be and what it became 'the dropout,' and the name stuck to the district itself.

The southern edge still carries industrial DNA. Automated fabrication plants replaced the old steel works, churning out modular housing components for corporate construction projects in districts that will never include West Pulldown on their shipping manifests. The plants run three shifts, staffed by Tier 1 and Tier 2 workers whose neural interfaces are locked to factory firmware -- no personal customization, no unauthorized apps, no agency. The commute from residential blocks to the plant floor is eleven minutes on foot. The commute from the plant floor to anything resembling economic mobility is infinite.

What keeps West Pulldown from collapsing entirely is stubbornness. The neighborhood associations that formed around the original Pullman housing model never fully dissolved -- they just went underground, operating as mutual aid networks that share resources, maintain the aging infrastructure the city ignores, and keep a census that the corporate authorities don't know exists. There's a quiet pride here, rooted in the historical awareness that this neighborhood was literally built as an experiment in worker housing, and that the experiment is still running, and that the workers are still losing.
atmosphere
sights
  • Historic stone row houses with neural-relay antennas bolted to Victorian cornices
  • Automated fabrication plants glowing dull orange along the southern horizon line
  • Subdivided interiors visible through uncurtained windows -- three households sharing what was one living room
  • Mutual aid markers chalked on doorframes in a code the corps haven't cracked
  • Factory shift workers walking in silent streams, neural interfaces dimmed to standby
sounds
  • The rhythmic thudding of fabrication presses, audible from six blocks away
  • Children playing in alleyways between shift changes, filling the silence the workers leave
  • Neural interface firmware update tones -- mandatory, synchronized, district-wide at 0300
  • The creak of 140-year-old floor joists under modern weight
smells
  • Hot polymer from the fabrication plants -- sweet and chemical, coating the throat
  • Cooking from communal kitchens -- pooled resources stretch further
  • Old wood and stone dust from buildings that refuse to be modern
feel Tired but unbroken. West Pulldown has the emotional texture of a long shift -- exhausting, repetitive, but underwritten by the knowledge that stopping isn't an option. The history here isn't decorative. It's load-bearing.
tags —
demographics Predominantly Tier 1 and Tier 2, multi-generational families packed into subdivided historic housing. A mix of legacy Black residents who've held on since pre-Meridian Chicago and newer arrivals displaced downward from restructured zones. Factory employment is near-universal.
economy Fabrication plant wages, mutual aid barter networks, and under-the-table repair work on the historic housing stock that the city refuses to maintain. The plants export; the neighborhood imports nothing it doesn't absolutely need.
power structure The fabrication plants are owned by Vantage Meridian subsidiary CastForm Industries, which controls employment and therefore controls everything. Underground mutual aid networks provide the only counterweight, operating through neighborhood associations that predate the megacity by a century.
dangers
  • Factory firmware lockdowns that can brick a worker's neural interface for contract violations
  • Structural decay in subdivided historic buildings -- load-bearing walls removed for more units
  • CastForm security patrols that double as labor compliance enforcement
  • Polymer particulate exposure from the plants -- respiratory damage is endemic
  • Isolation from the rest of Meridian -- no maglev stop, limited transit options
opportunities
  • The mutual aid networks are genuine and protective -- earning trust here means real community
  • The fabrication plants produce components that occasionally go missing, feeding a quiet salvage market
  • The hidden census contains population data the corps don't have -- valuable to the right buyer
  • Historic architecture knowledge makes Pulldown residents sought-after for restoration work in wealthier districts
story hooks
  • CastForm is planning to automate the last human-staffed fabrication line, which would eliminate West Pulldown's entire economic reason for existence
  • The mutual aid networks have discovered that their hidden census data matches anomalies in Axiom's population management algorithms -- someone is already counting the people they thought were uncounted
  • A sealed sub-basement in one of the original Pullman houses contains records from the 1894 Pullman Strike -- and someone in the Spire wants them destroyed before a historian finds them

West Town Upside #

type place
name West Town Upside
aliases
  • West Town
  • The Upside
  • Wicker-Buck
  • The Flip
description West Town was three neighborhoods pretending to be one: Wicker Park, Bucktown, and Ukrainian Village. Each had its own identity, its own pride, its own argument about where the boundaries were. The incorporation resolved the argument by dissolving all three into a single corporate development zone and renaming it West Town Upside — 'upside' being corporate real estate jargon for unrealized property value. The name stuck because the residents found it grimly appropriate. Everything here has been flipped: community into commodity, culture into content, neighborhood into investment vehicle.

Wicker Park's six-way intersection — the old heart of the neighborhood's indie music, art, and nightlife scene — is now the Hexagon, a corporate entertainment complex operated by an Axiom lifestyle subsidiary. The Hexagon's six streets radiate outward like spokes, each themed to a different 'authentic urban experience': live music (approved), street art (commissioned), vintage shopping (curated), craft dining (algorithmic), nightlife (monitored), and 'community' (a word that has been emptied of meaning and refilled with brand strategy). The Hexagon draws Tier 3-5 visitors from across the Corridor for a night out that feels dangerous without being dangerous, creative without being challenging, and urban without being urban. It is the most profitable entertainment district in the outer Corridor, and the most soulless.

Bucktown's residential streets have been converted to what the developer calls 'Heritage Housing' — pre-collapse homes maintained in original condition on the outside and gutted to corporate specification on the inside. The Ukrainian Village section retains its churches — the golden domes are too photogenic to demolish — but the congregations are gone, replaced by event spaces, corporate retreats, and a neural-interface meditation center called 'Cathedral' that charges by the minute for spirituality optimized to your neurochemical profile.

The soul of old West Town didn't die. It moved to the attics. Literally. The Upside's underground scene operates in the literal upper stories of the Heritage Housing blocks — attic spaces, rooftop additions, the vertical margins that corporate renovation didn't reach. Musicians, artists, designers, and the kinds of creative people who can't afford to live in the neighborhoods they made interesting have colonized the spaces between the corporate floors. They call themselves the Garret, and their work — music, art, fashion, code — is the real thing that the Hexagon's corporate subsidiaries spend millions trying to simulate. The irony sustains them. The rent does not.
atmosphere
sights
  • The Hexagon intersection blazing with themed entertainment lighting in six directions
  • Heritage Housing with pre-collapse facades and corporate interiors — the architectural uncanny valley
  • Ukrainian Village's golden church domes repurposed as corporate event venue branding
  • Garret artists visible in upper-story windows, creating the culture the ground floors monetize
  • The contrast between the Hexagon's curated street art and the Garret's actual street art, often on the same wall
  • Nightlife crowds moving through monitored entertainment corridors — fun under surveillance
sounds
  • The Hexagon's live music — professional, polished, algorithmically setlisted
  • Garret music bleeding through Heritage Housing attic windows — raw, unpermitted, alive
  • The Cathedral's neural-interface meditation tones — synthetic tranquility at premium rates
  • Nightlife crowd noise — laughter, shouting, the collective sound of people spending money
  • The specific silence of the Ukrainian churches between corporate events — stone remembering prayer
smells
  • The Hexagon's curated food scene — each street themed to a different cuisine, all excellent, all corporate
  • Paint and turpentine from Garret studios — the smell of art made without permission
  • Old incense in the Ukrainian churches, lingering beneath the corporate event catering
  • Alcohol — the Upside has the highest density of bars in the outer Corridor, and it smells like it
feel The Upside feels like watching someone wear your clothes. Everything here was taken from somewhere real, polished, branded, and resold. For people who remember what these neighborhoods were — or for people who create the kind of culture the Hexagon commodifies — the Upside is infuriating. For everyone else, it's a good night out. Both reactions are valid, and the tension between them is the Upside's actual energy source.
tags —
demographics Approximately 85,000 residents. Tier 3-4 in Heritage Housing and the Hexagon's residential towers. Tier 1-2 in the Garret attic spaces and service-worker housing at the margins. The Ukrainian community that gave Ukrainian Village its name is functionally extinct here — a handful of elderly residents remain, and the churches outlived their congregations.
economy —
power structure —
dangers
  • The Hexagon's surveillance — entertainment districts are monitored with nightclub-level density
  • Getting identified as Garret-affiliated in a corporate space — the Upside's owners don't appreciate the competition
  • The nightlife economy attracts predatory behavior — augment theft, credit fraud, neural-interface exploitation
  • Heritage Housing's corporate security mistaking residents for intruders in their own attic spaces
  • The emotional damage of watching your culture sold back to you at markup
opportunities
  • The Garret's creative network — artists, musicians, and designers with skills and connections across the Corridor
  • The Hexagon as a hunting ground for corporate intelligence, high-value targets, and social engineering
  • The Ukrainian churches as neutral meeting spaces — corporate event scheduling leaves gaps
  • Cultural credibility — association with the Garret carries weight in the Counterfeit and the Circuit
  • Nightlife as cover — the crowds, the noise, the neural-interface distortion make the Upside excellent operational territory
story hooks
  • A Garret musician has composed a piece that, when played through neural interfaces, unlocks suppressed memories of pre-incorporation West Town — and the corporate licensee wants it destroyed
  • The last Ukrainian church congregation is fighting eviction from their own building, and the elder who holds the original property deed needs someone to retrieve it from a corporate archive
  • Kyle is hired to protect a Garret artist during a covert exhibition in the Hexagon itself — guerrilla culture in the belly of the beast
